editorialDecl.p: EEBO-TCP is a partnership between the Universities of Michigan and Oxford and the publisher ProQuest to create accurately transcribed and encoded texts based on the image sets published by ProQuest via their Early English Books Online (EEBO) database (http://eebo.chadwyck.com). The general aim of EEBO-TCP is to encode one copy (usually the first edition) of every monographic English-language title published between 1473 and 1700 available in EEBO.

EEBO-TCP aimed to produce large quantities of textual data within the usual project restraints of time and funding, and therefore chose to create diplomatic transcriptions (as opposed to critical editions) with light-touch, mainly structural encoding based on the Text Encoding Initiative (http://www.tei-c.org).

The EEBO-TCP project was divided into two phases. The 25,363 texts created during Phase 1 of the project have been released into the public domain as of 1 January 2015. Anyone can now take and use these texts for their own purposes, but we respectfully request that due credit and attribution is given to their original source.
Users should be aware of the process of creating the TCP texts, and therefore of any assumptions that can be made about the data.

Text selection was based on the New Cambridge Bibliography of English Literature (NCBEL). If an author (or for an anonymous work, the title) appears in NCBEL, then their works are eligible for inclusion. Selection was intended to range over a wide variety of subject areas, to reflect the true nature of the print record of the period. In general, first editions of a works in English were prioritized, although there are a number of works in other languages, notably Latin and Welsh, included and sometimes a second or later edition of a work was chosen if there was a compelling reason to do so.

Image sets were sent to external keying companies for transcription and basic encoding. Quality assurance was then carried out by editorial teams in Oxford and Michigan. 5% (or 5 pages, whichever is the greater) of each text was proofread for accuracy and those which did not meet QA standards were returned to the keyers to be redone. After proofreading, the encoding was enhanced and/or corrected and characters marked as illegible were corrected where possible up to a limit of 100 instances per text. Any remaining illegibles were encoded as <gap>s. Understanding these processes should make clear that, while the overall quality of TCP data is very good, some errors will remain and some readable characters will be marked as illegible. Users should bear in mind that in all likelihood such instances will never have been looked at by a TCP editor.
The texts were encoded and linked to page images in accordance with level 4 of the TEI in Libraries guidelines.

Copies of the texts have been issued variously as SGML (TCP schema; ASCII text with mnemonic sdata character entities); displayable XML (TCP schema; characters represented either as UTF-8 Unicode or text strings within braces); or lossless XML (TEI P5, characters represented either as UTF-8 Unicode or TEI g elements).
Keying and markup guidelines are available at the Text Creation Partnership web site.
This file is the EEBO-TCP transcription with editorial layers added inline; nothing of the transcription has been removed.

choice/orig holds the text as printed; choice/reg holds the modern reading. reg/@resp says who decided it (#auto = machine, #editor = reviewed by hand); reg/@type is spelling, case, punctuation, spacing, grammar (an archaic form modernized: thou, hath, -eth) or emendation (another word, or a word added or removed). Where the editor overrode the machine, the editor's reg comes first and the machine's proposal follows as a second reg[@resp='#auto'].
choice/abbr + choice/expan: macron abbreviations (e.g. frō = from) and superscript contractions (yᵉ = the).
supplied: letters or words lost to illegible print, with @cert and a comment giving the evidence; the TCP gap element is kept inside.

Spelling regularized: u/v, i/j, silent final e, doubled consonants, -ie to -y, -nesse to -ness, and a word list. Grammatical forms (hath, doth, thou, thee, thy, ye, shalt, wilt, art, hast, dost) are retained. Footnote text is left in original spelling.
list[@change='#review']: run-in enumerations (I. ... II. ...) set out as numbered lists; the printed numerals are kept in label.
head[@type='edition']: section title used by this edition; the printed heading is kept in the preceding head. @change='#review' points at the revisionDesc entry for these structural changes.
Line breaks are those of the TCP transcription (newlines in the text; g[@ref='char:EOLhyphen'] marks a word hyphenated at line end). pb/@n is the printed page, pb/@facs the page image.
note/@target points at the anchor where this edition places the note; the note itself stays where it was printed.
reg[@type='spacing']: a space this edition adds (empty orig) or removes (empty reg) between words.
hi inside reg: words of this edition's reading set in italic.
list[@subtype='printed']: a list printed as one that this edition numbers; the printed numerals are kept in label.

This is the mainemain end of my calling, and the markemark, which, as in the ordinary courſecourse of my MiniſtryMinistry, ſoso in the publiſhingpublishing of theſethese Eight TreatiſesTreatises of DomeſticallDomestical Dutiesduties, and dedicating them to you, I hauehave aimed at. Thus ſhallshall you gainegain much profit, and my ſelfeself much comfort by my painespains. Oh if the head and ſeuerallseveral members of a family would be perſwadedpersuaded eueryevery of them to be conſcionableconscionable in performing their owneown particular duties, what a ſweetsweet ſocietysociety, and happy harmony would there be in houſeshouses? What excellent ſeminariesseminaries would families be to Church and Commonwealthcommonwealth?

The firſtfirst TreatiſeTreatise (which is a fourth part of the bookebook) containeth a Commentary on that part of Scripture out of which DomeſticallDomestical Dutiesduties are raiſedraised: wherein the ApoſtleApostle ſettingsetting forth ChriſtChrist and the Church as patternespatterns to husbands and wiueswives, liuelylively declareth the great louelove of ChriſtChrist to his Church, and the neerenear vnionunion betwixt them, together with other deepedeep myſteriesmysteries, the vnfoldingunfolding whereof hath a little the longer detained me. But as I hauehave a while inſiſtedinsisted on mainemain matters of much moment, ſoso hauehave I very briefly paſſedpassed ouerover other points. The other TreatiſesTreatises, wherein the Dutiesduties themſeluesthemselves are handled, are eueryevery of them much ſhortershorter then the firſtfirst. For many that hearehear the duties thinkethink all well enough, till they hearehear alſoalso the contrary vices, whereby in their conſciencesconsciences they are moſtmost conuincedconvinced. Concerning the many faults and vices of bad Husbandshusbands, Wiueswives, Parentsparents, Childrenchildren, Maſtersmasters and Seruantsservants, taxed in theſethese TreatiſesTreatises, let me intreatentreat you, not to apply them too generally to all Husbandshusbands, Wiueswives, Parentsparents, Childrenchildren, Maſtersmasters and Seruantsservants. Hath not wiſewise Solomon much taxed the lightneſſelightness, ſhrewiſhneſſeshrewishness, pride, flattery, and other vices of women? And ſhallshall ſobersober, meekemeek, humble, honeſthonest women thinkethink themſeluesthemselves taxed thereby? By like reaſonreason might vnchaſteunchaste ſtrumpetsstrumpets, vntruſtyuntrusty goſsipsgossips, vnquietunquiet ſhrewesshrews, and proud dames thinkethink themſeluesthemselves commended by thoſethose excellent commendations which behe giuethgiveth of good women. Let eueryevery
one, as their conſcienceconscience (an impartiallimpartial IudgeJudge) ſhallshall bearebear them witneſſewitness, make a right application of eueryevery thing to themſeluesthemselves. Thus ſhallshall we MiniſtersMinisters be freed from many euillevil ſurmizessurmises. I remember that when theſethese DomeſticallDomestical Dutiesduties were firſtfirst vttereduttered out of the pulpit, much exception was taken againſtagainst the application of a wiueswives ſubiectionsubjection to the reſtrainingrestraining of her from diſpoſingdisposing the common goods of the family without, or againſtagainst her husbands conſentconsent. But ſurelysurely they that made thoſethose exceptions did not well thinkethink of the Cautions and LamitationsLimitations which were then deliuereddelivered, and are now againeagain expreſlyexpressly noted: which are, that the foreſaidforesaid reſtraintrestraint be not extended to the Paraphernalia. Treat. 3. §. 21. proper goods of a wife, no nor ouerſtrictlyoverstrictly to ſuchsuch Ibid. goods as are ſetset apart for the vſeuse of the family, nor to Treat. 3. §. 22. extraordinary caſescases, nor alwaiesalways to an Treat. 3. §. 19. expreſſeexpress conſentconsent, nor to the Treat. 3. §. 18. conſentconsent of ſuchsuch husbands as are impotent, or farrefar and long abſentabsent. If any other warrantable caution ſhallshall be ſhewedshowed me, I will be as willing to admit it, as any of theſethese. Now that my meaning may not ſtillstill be peruertedperverted, I pray you, in reading the reſtraintrestraint of wiueswives power in diſpoſingdisposing the goods of the family, euerever bearebear in mindemind thoſethose Cautions. Other exceptions were made againſtagainst ſomesome other particular duties of wiueswives. For many that can patiently enough hearehear their duties declared in generallgeneral termesterms, cannot endure to hearehear thoſethose generals exemplified in their particular branches. This commethcometh too neerenear to the quickequick, and pierceth too deepedeep. But (to interpret all, according to the rule of louelove, in the better part) I take the mainemain reaſonreason of the many exceptions which were taken, to be this, that wiueswives duties (according to the ApoſtlesApostles method) being in the firſtfirst place handled, there was taught (as muſtmust hauehave beenebeen taught, except the truth ſhouldshould hauehave beenebeen betrayed) what a wife, in the vttermoſtuttermost extent of that ſubiectionsubjection vnderunder which God hath put her, is bound vntounto, in caſecase her husband will ſtandstand vponupon the

But when I came to deliuerdeliver husbands duties, Treat. 4. §. 18. I ſhewedshowed, that he ought not to exact whatſoeuerwhatsoever his wife was bound vntounto (in caſecase it were exacted by him) but that he ought to make her a ioyntjoint GouernourGovernor of the family with himſelfehimself, and referrerefer the ordering of many things to her diſcretiondiscretion, and with all honourable and kindekind reſpectrespect to carriecarry himſelfehimself towards her. In a word, I ſoso ſetset downedown an husbands duties, as if he be wiſewise and conſcionableconscionable in obſeruingobserving them, his wife can hauehave no iuſtjust cauſecause to complainecomplain of her ſubiectionsubjection. That which maketh a wiueswives yoakeyoke heauyheavy and hard, is an husbands abuſeabuse of his authority: and more preſsingpressing his wiueswives dutieduty, then performing his owneown: which is directly contrary to the EpheſEphes. 5. 33. Now that in all thoſethose places where a wiueswives yoke may ſeemeseem moſtmost to pinch, I might giuegive ſomesome eaſeease, I hauehave to eueryevery head of wiueswives duties made a reference, in the margin ouerover againſtagainst it, to the duties of husbands anſwerableanswerable thereunto, and noted the reference with this markemark *, that it might the more readily be turned vntounto. Yea I hauehave further parallel'd, and laid eueneven one againſtagainst another in one view, the heads of husbands and wiueswives duties, as they anſweranswer each other: and in like manner the contrary aberrations: with a reference made vntounto the particular ſectionssections where they are handled: that ſoso on the one ſideside it may appeareappear, that if both of them be conſcionableconscionable and carefullcareful to performeperform their owneown duty, the matrimoniallmatrimonial yoke will ſoso equally lie on both their necks, as the wife will be no more pinched therewith then the husband, but that it will be like ChriſtsChrists ſpirituallspiritual yoke, light and eaſieeasy: and that on the Mat. 11. 30.
other ſideside it may be manifeſtmanifest that there is commonly as much failing by husbands in their duties, as by wiueswives in theirs. This parallel and eueneven-ſettingsetting out of each of their duties, and of the contrary aberrations, I hauehave annexed next to this epiſtleepistle. And further I hauehave added thereto a table of the ſeuerallseveral heads of thoſethose points that are handled in the eight following TreatiſesTreatises, that by this helpehelp you may the more readily findefind out ſuchsuch particular points as you deſiredesire moſtmost eſpeciallyespecially to read. To ſhewshow that the duties preſcribedprescribed to Husbandshusbands, Wiueswives, Parentsparents, Childrenchildren, Maſtersmasters, and Seruantsservants, are ſuchsuch as in conſcienceconscience they are bound vntounto, I hauehave endeuouredendeavoured to ſhewshow how they are grounded on the word of God, and gathered from thence. To auoidavoid prolixity, I hauehave referred moſtmost of the quotations to the margin. If your leiſureleisure will ſerueserve you, you may doedo well to ſearchsearch them out. Two things hauehave beenebeen eſpeciallespecial helpeshelps to me for finding out the many duties noted in theſethese TreatiſesTreatises, & vices contrary thereunto: ObſeruationObservation and DiſpoſitionDisposition. ObſeruationObservation both of ſuchsuch duties as the Scripture commendeth and contrary vices as it condemneth: and alſoalso of ſuchsuch commendable virtues as I well liked in thoſethose Husbandshusbands, Wiueswives, Parentsparents, Childrenchildren, Maſtersmasters, and Seruantsservants, that I came among, and ſuchsuch vnſeemelyunseemly vices as I diſlikeddisliked in them: and DiſpoſitionDisposition of one point after another in the beſtbest order that I could. My method and manner of proceeding brought many things to my mindemind, which otherwiſeotherwise might hauehave ſlippedslipped by. For by method ſundrysundry and ſeuerallseveral points appertaining to one matter are drawnedrawn forth, as in a chainechain one linkelink draweth vpup another. There is no better way to findefind out many obſeruationsobservations in a text, then by a methodicallmethodical reſolutionresolution thereof. As method is an helpehelp to InuentionInvention, ſoso alſoalso to retention. It is as the thread or wierwire whereon pearlespearls are put, which keepeth them from ſcatteringscattering. And if a man by abundance of matter be caſtcast into a labyrinth, by the helpehelp of method he may eaſilyeasily and readily findefind
out the way againeagain. In which reſpectsrespects method is fitly ſtiledstyled the MethodusintelligentiaeMethodus intelligentiae parens eſtest, & magiſtramagistra memoriae. If you well markemark the order and dependance of points one vponupon another, you will findefind as great an helpehelp in conceiuingconceiving and remembringremembering Ordo memoriae maximè, lumen affert. Cic. 2. de Orat. them, as I did in inuentinginventing and diſpoſingdisposing them.

div.head: §. 1. Of the ApoſtlesApostles tranſitiontransition from generallgeneral duties to particulars.
div.p:
ASAs there are two vocations whereunto it hath pleaſedpleased God to call eueryevery one; one Generallgeneral, by vertuevirtue whereof certainecertain common duties which are to be performed of all men, are required, (as knowledge, faith, obedience, repentance, louelove, merciemercy, iuſticejustice, truth, &etcc.) the other Particularparticular, by vertuevirtue whereof certainecertain peculiar duties are required of ſeuerallseveral perſonspersons, according to thoſethose diſtinctdistinct places wherein the DiuineDivine ProuidenceProvidence hath ſetset them in Commoncommon-wealth, Church, or family; ſoso ought Gods MiniſtersMinisters to be carefullcareful in inſtructinginstructing
Gods people in both kindeskinds of duties; both thoſethose which concerneconcern their generallgeneral, and thoſethose alſoalso which concerneconcern their particular calling. Accordingly S. Paul (who, as Num. 12. 7. MoſesMoses, was faithfullfaithful in all the houſehouse of God) after he had ſufficientlysufficiently inſtructedinstructed Gods Church in ſuchsuch generallgeneral duties, as belong to all ChriſtiansChristians, of what ſexsex, ſtatestate, degree, or condition ſoeuersoever they be, proceedeth to lay downedown certainecertain particular duties, which appertaineappertain to particular callings and conditions: among which, he maketh choiſechoice of thoſethose which God hath eſtabliſhedestablished in a family. With excellent Art doth he paſſepass from thoſethose generals, to theſethese particulars: laying downedown a tranſitiontransition betwixt them, in theſethese words, Submitting your ſeluesselves one to another in the fearefear of God; which words hauehave reference both to that which goeth before, and alſoalso to that which followeth after. The formeform and manner of ſettingsetting downedown this verſeverse, with a participle thus, ſubmittingsubmitting, ſhewethshoweth that it dependeth on that which went before, and ſoso hath reference thereunto. AgaineAgain, the word it ſelfeself being the very ſamesame which is vſedused
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 , ſubmittingsubmitting. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 , ſubmitsubmit. in the next verſeverse following, ſhewethshoweth, that this verſeverse containeth the ſummesum of that which followeth, and ſoso hath reference thereunto, as a generallgeneral vntounto particulars. This manner of paſſingpassing from one point to another, by a perfect tranſitiontransition which looketh both wayesways, both to that which is paſtpast, and to that which commethcometh on, as it is very elegant, ſoso is it frequent with this our ApoſtleApostle. Whereby he teacheth vsus, Note. ſoso to giuegive heed to that which followeth, as we forget not that which is paſtpast: as we muſtmust giuegive diligent attention to that which remaineth, ſoso we muſtmust well retaineretain that which we hauehave heard, and not let it ſlipslip: otherwiſeotherwise, if (as one nailenail driuethdriveth out another) one precept maketh another to be forgotten, it will be altogether in vainevain to addeadd line vntounto line, or precept vntounto precept.

div.head: §. 2. Of ioyningjoining ſeruiceservice to men with our praiſingpraising of God.
div.p: As this verſeverse hath reference to that which was deliuereddelivered before, concerning our dutieduty to God, it teacheth vsus this leſſonlesson:

It is the dutieduty of ChriſtiansChristians as to ſetset forth the praiſepraise of God, ſoso to be ſeruiceableserviceable one to another. For this purpoſepurpose in the Doct. Decalogue to the firſtfirst table, which preſcribethprescribeth that duty which we owe to God, is added the ſecondsecond table, which declareth the ſeruiceservice that we owe one to another: and he that ſaidsaid, Matt. 22. 38, 39. The firſtfirst and great CommandementCommandment is this, Thou ſhaltshalt louelove the Lord, &etcc. ſaidSaid alſoalso, The ſecondsecond is like to this, Thou ſhaltshalt louelove thy neighbour, &etcc. whereuponWhereupon the Heb. 13. 15, 16. ApoſtleApostle declaring what thoſethose ſacrificessacrifices be wherewith God is well pleaſedpleased, ioynethjoinethjoyneth theſethese two together, to giuegive thankesthanks to God, and to doedo good to man. The ſeruiceservice which in the fearefear of God we performeperform one to another, is an euidentevident and reallreal demonſtrationdemonstration of the reſpectrespect we bearebear vntounto God. PſalPsal. 16. 2. To God our goodneſſegoodness extendeth not.
IobJob 22. 3. & 35. 7. He is ſoso high aboueabove vsus, ſoso perfect and compleatcomplete in himſelfehimself, that neither can we giuegive to him, nor he receiuereceive of vsus. But in his owneown ſteadstead he hath placed our brother like to our ſeluesselves; to whom, IobJob 35. 8. as we may doedo hurt, ſoso by our faithfullfaithful ſeruiceservice we may doedo much PſalPsal. 16. 3. good: in doing whereof God is much honoured.

This diſcouerethdiscovereth their hypocriſiehypocrisy, who make great pretence 1. VſeUse. A note of hypocriſiehypocrisy. of praiſingpraising God, and yet are ſcornfullscornful, and diſdainfulldisdainful to their brethren, and ſlothfullslothful to doedo any ſeruiceservice to man: TheſeThese mens religion is vainevain. By this note did the Prophets IamJam. 1. 26. IſaIsa. 58. 3 &etcc. Mic. 6. 6. &etcc. Matt. 23. 14. 1 IohJoh. 4. 20. in their time, and ChriſtChrist and his ApoſtlesApostles in their time alſoalso, diſcouerdiscover the hypocriſiehypocrisy of thoſethose among whom they liuedlived: and ſoso may we alſoalso in our times. For many there be, who frequently in their houſeshouses, and in the middeſtmiddest of the Congregation ſingsing praiſepraise vntounto God, and performeperform other parts of Gods outward worſhipworship, but towards one another, are proud, ſtoutstout, enuiousenvious, vnmercifullunmerciful, vniuſtunjust, ſlanderousslanderous, and very backward to doedo any good ſeruiceservice. Surely, that outward ſeruiceservice which they pretend to performeperform to God, doth not ſoso much wipe out the ſpotspot of prophaneſſeprofaneness, as their neglect of dutieduty vntounto man brandeth their foreheads with the ſtampestamp of hypocriſiehypocrisy. 2. VſeUse. Put not off one dutieduty with another. Matt. 23. 23.

For our parts, let vsus not vponupon pretext of one dutieduty, though it may ſeemeseem to be the waightierweightier, thinkethink to ſhiftshift off another; leſtlest that fearefullfearful woe which ChriſtChrist denounced
againſtagainst the Scribes and PhariſiesPharisees fall vponupon our pates. As God is carefullcareful to inſtructinstruct vsus how to carriecarry our ſeluesselves both to his owneown MaieſtieMajesty, and alſoalso one to another, ſoso let vsus in both approueapprove our ſeluesselves to him: remembringremembering what ChriſtChrist ſaidsaid to the PhariſiesPharisees, TheſeThese ought ye to hauehave done, and not to leaueleave the other vndoneundone. The ſamesame Lord that requireth praiſepraise to his owneown MaieſtieMajesty, inioynethenjoineth mutuallmutual ſeruiceservice one to another; the neglect of this, as well as of that, ſhewethshoweth too light reſpectrespect of his will and pleaſurepleasure: What therefore God
Matth. 19. 6. hath ioynedjoined together, let not man put aſunderasunder.

div.head: §. 3. Of eueryevery ones ſubmittingsubmitting himſelfehimself to another.
div.p:
AgaineAgain, as this verſeverse hath reference to that which followeth, it declareth the generallgeneral ſummesum of all, which is mutually to ſubmitsubmit our ſeluesselves one to another in the fearefear of God. The parts hereof are two:
1. An Exhortation.
2. A Direction.
In the exhortation is noted, both the dutieduty it ſelfeself in this word ſubmitsubmit, and alſoalso the parties to whom it is to be performed, one to another.
Both branches of the exhortation, viz. theThe dutieduty, and the parties ioynedjoined together, afford this doctrine, that

It is a generallgeneral mutuallmutual dutieduty appertaining to all ChriſtiansChristians, 2. Doct.
to ſubmitsubmit themſeluesthemselves one to another: For this precept is as generallgeneral as any of the former, belonging to all ſortssorts and degrees whatſoeuerwhatsoever: and ſoso much doth this word one another
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . imply: in which extent the ApoſtleApostle in another place exhorteth to ſerueserve one another: and againeagain, eueryevery man to ſeekeseek
Gal. 5. 13. 1 Cor. 10. 24. anothers wealth.

Concerning inferioursinferiors, it is without queſtionquestion cleareclear, that QueſtQuest. they ought to ſubmitsubmit themſeluesthemselves to their ſuperiourssuperiors: yea, concerning equals no great queſtionquestion can be made, but they in giuinggiving honour muſtmust goego one before another, and ſoso ſubmitsubmit Rom. 12. 10. How ſuperiourssuperiors ought to ſubiectsubject themſeluesthemselves. themſeluesthemselves: but concerning ſuperiourssuperiors, iuſtjust queſtionquestion may be made, whether it be a dutieduty required of them to ſubmitsubmit themſeluesthemselves to their inferioursinferiors.
To reſolueresolve this doubt, we muſtmust firſtfirst diſtinguiſhdistinguish betwixt AnſwAnsw. ſubiectionsubjection of reuerencereverence, and ſubiectionsubjection of ſeruiceservice.

SubiectionSubjection of reuerencereverence is that whereby one teſtifiethtestifieth an eminencieeminency and ſuperioritiesuperiority in them whom he reuerencethreverenceth, and that in ſpeechspeech, by giuinggiving them titles of honour; or in geſturegesture, by ſomesome kindekind of obeyſanceobeisance; or in action, by a ready obeying of their commandementcommandment. This is proper to inferioursinferiors.

SubiectionSubjection of ſeruiceservice is that whereby one in his place is Difference betwixt ſubiectionsubjection of ReuerenceReverence and SeruiceService. ready to doedo what good he can to another. This is common to all ChriſtiansChristians: a dutieduty which eueneven ſuperiourssuperiors owe to inferioursinferiors, according to the fore-named extent of this word one another: in which reſpectrespect eueneven the higheſthighest gouernourgovernor on earth is called a miniſterminister, for the good of ſuchsuch as
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . Rom. 13. 4. are vnderunder him.

Secondly, we muſtmust put difference betwixt the workework it Difference betwixt the workework and manner of doing it. ſelfeself, and the manner of doing it. That workework which in it ſelfeself is a workework of ſuperioritiesuperiority and authoritieauthority, in the manner of doing it may be a workework of ſubmiſſionsubmission, viz. ifIf it be done in humilitiehumility and meekneſſemeekness of mindemind. The MagiſtrateMagistrate by ruling with meekneſſemeekness and humilitiehumility, ſubmittethsubmittethsubmiteth himſelfehimself to his ſubiectsubject. In this reſpectrespect the ApoſtleApostle exhorteth that nothing (no not the higheſthighest and greateſtgreatest workesworks that Phil. 2. 3. can be) be done in vainevain-glory, but in meekneſſemeekness.

Thirdly, we muſtmust diſtinguiſhdistinguish betwixt the ſeuerallseveral places wherein men are: for eueneven they who are ſuperiourssuperiors to ſomesome, EueryEvery one vnderunder ſomesome authoritieauthority. Matth. 8. 9. are inferioursinferiors to others: as he that ſaidsaid, I hauehave vnderunder me, and am vnderunder authoritieauthority. The maſtermaster that hath ſeruantsservants vnderunder him, may be vnderunder the authoritieauthority of a MagiſtrateMagistrate. Yea, God hath ſoso diſpoſeddisposed eueryevery ones ſeuerallseveral place, as there is not any one, but in ſomesome reſpectrespect is vnderunder another. The wife, though a mother of children, is vnderunder her husband. The husband, though head of a family, is vnderunder publikepublic MagiſtratesMagistrates. PublikePublic MagiſtratesMagistrates one vnderunder another, and all vnderunder the King. The King himſelfehimself vnderunder God and his word deliuereddelivered by his AmbaſſadoursAmbassadours, whereunto the higheſthighest are to ſubmitsubmit themſeluesthemselves. And MiniſtersMinisters of the word, as ſubiectssubjects, are vnderunder their Kings and GouernoursGovernors.
He that ſaithsaith, Let eueryevery ſoulesoul be ſubiectsubject to the higher powers,
Rom. 13. 1. excepteth not MiniſtersMinisters of the word: and he that ſaithsaith, obey them that hauehave the ouerſightoversight of you, and ſubmitsubmit your ſeluesselves,
Heb. 13. 17. Difference betwixt MagiſtratesMagistrates and MiniſtersMinisters authoritieauthority. excepteth not kings: only the difference is in this, that the authoritieauthority of the king is in himſelfehimself, and in his owneown name he may command obedience to be performed to himſelfehimself: but the authoritieauthority of a MiniſterMinister is in ChriſtChrist, and in ChriſtsChrists name only may he require obedience to be performed to ChriſtChrist.

The reaſonreason why all are bound to ſubmitsubmit themſeluesthemselves one ReaſonReason. EueryEvery ones Office for the good of another. to another is, becauſebecause eueryevery one is ſetset in his place by God, not ſoso much for himſelfehimself, as for the good of others: whereupon the ApoſtleApostle exhorteth, that none ſeekeseek his owneown, but eueryevery man anothers wealth. EuenEven GouernoursGovernors are aduancedadvanced 1 Cor. 10. 24. to places of dignitiedignity and authoritieauthority, rather for the good of their ſubiectssubjects then for their owneown honour. Their callings are in truth offices of ſeruiceservice, yea burdens vnderunder which they muſtmust willingly put their ſhouldersshoulders, being called of God, and of which they are to giuegive an account concerning the good which they hauehave done to others: for the effecting whereof, it is needfullneedful that they ſubmitsubmit themſeluesthemselves.

Let eueryevery one therefore high and low, rich and poorepoor, 1. VſeUse. ExhòrtationExhortation vntounto all to doedo ſeruiceservice. ſuperioursuperior and inferiourinferior, MagiſtrateMagistrate and ſubiectsubject, MiniſterMinister and people, husband and wife, parent and childechild, maſtermaster and ſeruantservant, neighbours and fellowesfellows, all of all ſortssorts in their ſeuerallseveral places take notice of their dutieduty in this point of ſubmiſſionsubmission, and make conſcienceconscience to put it in practice: MagiſtratesMagistrates, by procuring the wealth and peace of their people, as Mordecai: MiniſtersMinisters, by making themſeluesthemselves ſeruantsservants EſtEst. 10. 3. vntounto their people, not ſeekingseeking their owneown profit, but the 1 Cor. 9. 19. & 10. 33. profit of many, that they may be ſauedsaved, as Paul: Fathersfathers, by well educating their children, and taking heed that they prouokeprovoke them not to wrath, as DauidDavid: Husbandshusbands,
ProuProv. 4. 3, 4. by dwelling with their wiueswives according to knowledge; giuinggiving honour to the wife as to the weaker veſſellvessel, as Abraham:
Gen. 16. 6. Maſtersmasters, by doing that which is iuſtjust and equallequal to their ſeruantsservants, as the Centurion: EueryEvery one, by being of like Luke 7. 2. affection one towards another, and by ſeruingserving one another
in louelove, according to the ApoſtlesApostles rule. Let this dutieduty of Rom. 12. 16. Gal. 5. 13. ſubmiſſionsubmission be firſtfirst well learned, and then all other duties will better be performed.

Be not high minded, nor ſwellswell one againſtagainst another. 2. VſeUse. Dehortation from ſwellingswelling one againſtagainst another. Though in outward eſtateestate ſomesome may be higher than other, yet in ChriſtChrist all are one whether bond or free: all members of one and the ſamesame body. Now conſiderconsider the mutuallmutual affection (as I may ſoso ſpeakespeak) of the members of a naturallnatural body one towards another: not any one of them will puffepuff it ſelfeself vpup, Gal. 3. 28. and riſerise againſtagainst the other: the head which is the higheſthighest 1 Cor. 12. 27. and of greateſtgreatest honour will ſubmitsubmit it ſelfeself to the feet in performing the dutieduty of an head, as well as the feet to the head in performing their dutieduty; ſoso all other parts. Neither is it hereby implied that they which are in place of dignitiedignity and authoritieauthority ſhouldshould forget or relinquiſhrelinquish their place, dignitiedignity, or authoritieauthority, and become as inferioursinferiors vnderunder authoritieauthority, no more than the head doth: for the head in ſubmittingsubmitting it ſelfeself doth not goego vponupon the ground and bearebear the body, as the feet; but it ſubmittethsubmittethsubmiteth it ſelfeself by directing and gouerninggoverning the other parts, and that with all the humilitiehumility, meekneſſemeekness, and gentleneſſegentleness that it can. So muſtmust all ſuperiourssuperiors: much more muſtmust equals and inferioursinferiors learnelearn with humilitiehumility, and meekneſſemeekness, without ſcornescorn or diſdainedisdain, to performeperform their dutieduty: this is that which was before by the ApoſtleApostle EpheſEphes. 4. 2. expreſlyexpressly mentioned, and is here againeagain intimated; none are exempted and priuilegedprivileged from it. We know that it is vnnaturallunnatural, and vnbeſeemingunbeseeming the head to ſcornescorn the feet, and to ſwellswell againſtagainst them, but more than monſtrousmonstrous for one hand to ſcornscorn another: what ſhallshall we then ſaysay if the feet ſwelswellswel againſtagainst the head? Surely ſuchsuch ſcornescorn and diſdainedisdain among the members, would cauſecause not only great diſturbancedisturbance, but alſoalso vtterutter ruineruin to the body. And can it be otherwiſeotherwise in a politiquepolitic body? But on the contrariecontrary, when all of all ſortssorts ſhallshall (as hath beenebeen before ſhewedshowed) willingly ſubmitsubmit themſeluesthemselves one to another, the whole body, and eueryevery member thereof will reapereap good thereby: yea, by this mutuallmutual ſubmiſſionsubmission, as we doedo good, ſoso we ſhallshall receiuereceive good.

div.head: §. 4. Of the fearefear of God.
div.p:
Hitherto of the exhortation. The direction followeth. In the fearefear of the Lord. This clauſeclause is added, to declare partly the meanesmeans, how men may be brought to ſubmitsubmit themſeluesthemselves readily one to another: and partly the manner, how they ought to ſubmitsubmit themſeluesthemselves. The fearefear of the Lord is both the efficient cauſecause that mouethmoveth a true ChriſtianChristian willingly to performeperform all dutieduty to man, and alſoalso the end whereunto he referrethreferrethrefereth eueryevery thing that he doth. For the better conceiuingconceiving whereof, I will briefly declare
1. What this fearefear of the Lord is.
2. How the Lord is the proper obiectobject of it.
3. What is the extent thereof.
4. Why it is ſoso much vrgedurged.

First, fearefear of God is an awfullawful reſpectrespect of the diuinedivine MaieſtieMajesty. 1. What the fearefear of God is. The cauſescauses of it. Sometimes it ariſethariseth from faith in the mercy and goodneſſegoodness of God: for when the heart of man hath once felt a ſweetsweet taſtetaste of Gods goodneſſegoodness, and found that in his fauourfavour only all happineſſehappiness conſiſtethconsisteth, it is ſtruckenstrucken with ſuchsuch an inward awe and reuerencereverence, as it would not for any thing diſpleaſedisplease Two effects of a filiallfilial fearefear of God. his MaieſtieMajesty, but rather doedo whatſoeuerwhatsoever it may know to be pleaſingpleasing and acceptable vntounto him. For theſethese are two effects which ariſearise from this kindekind of fearefear of God:

1. A carefullcareful endeuourendeavour to pleaſeplease God, in which reſpectrespect Deum timere eſtest nulla mala facere, & nulla bona quae faci endafacienda ſuntsunt praete rirepraeterire. Bernar. de modo benè viuen. ſerser. 4. good king IehoſaphatJehosaphat hauinghaving exhorted his IudgesJudges to execute the iudgementjudgment of the Lord aright, addeth this clauſeclause as a motiuemotive thereunto, Let the fearefear of the Lord be vponupon you: implying thereby that Gods fearefear would make them endeuourendeavour to approueapprove themſeluesthemselves to God.

2. A carefullcareful auoidingavoiding of ſuchsuch things as offend the MaieſtyMajesty of God, and grieuegrieve his ſpiritspirit: in which reſpectrespect the WiſemanWiseman 2 Chro. 19. 6, 7. ſaithsaith, The fearefear of the Lord is to hate euillevil: and of IobJob it is ProuProv. 8. 13. ſaidsaid that he fearing God departed from euillevil.
Job. 1. 1.

Sometimes againeagain, awe and dread of the diuinedivine MaieſtieMajesty ariſethariseth from diffidence: For when a mans heart doubteth of Gods mercy, and expecteth nothing but vengeance, the very thought of God ſtrikethstriketh an awe or rather dread into him, and ſoso maketh him fearefear God.

From this double cauſecause of fearefear, whereof one is contrary Difference betwixt filiallfilial and ſeruileservile fearefear. to another, hath ariſenarisen that vſuallusual diſtinctiondistinction of a filiallfilial or ſonneson-like fearefear, and a ſeruileservile or ſlauiſhslavish fearefear: which diſtinctiondistinction is grounded on theſethese words of the ApoſtleApostle, ye hauehave not receiuedreceived the ſpiritspirit of bondage againeagain to fearefear (this is Bernard. loc. citat. a ſeruileservile fearefear) but ye hauehave receiuedreceived the ſpiritspirit of adoption
Rom. 8. 15. whereby we cry, Abba, father: this cauſethcauseth a filiallfilial fearefear. The filiallfilial fearefear is ſuchsuch a fearefear as dutifulldutiful children bearebear to their fathers. But the ſeruileservile fearefear is ſuchsuch an one as bondſlauesbondslaves bearebear to their maſtersmasters. A ſonneson feareth ſimplysimply to offend or diſpleaſedisplease his father: ſoso as EſtEst timor ne amittatur gratia beneficij. Hic timor caſtcast uscastus eſtest, non eum charitas eijcit, ſedsed aſciſcitasciscit. AuguſtAugust. epiſtepist. 120. it is accompanied with louelove. A bondſlauebondslave feareth nothing but the puniſhmentpunishment of his offence; ſoso as it is ioynedjoined with hatred: and ſuchsuch an one feareth not to ſinnesin, but to burneburn in hell for ſinnesin. By fearefear of man, may one be brought to ſubmitsubmit himſelfehimself ObiectObject. to another: as a magiſtratemagistrate may be mouedmoved to dealedeal iuſtlyjustly and mildly with his people through fearefear of inſurrectionsinsurrections and rebellions: ſubiectssubjects may by ſeueresevere laweslaws and tyrannietyranny be brought to ſubmitsubmit themſeluesthemselves: and ſoso other inferioursinferiors alſoalso by threats, by hard vſageusage, and other by-reſpectsrespects.

1. Though fearefear of man be a motiuemotive, yet it followeth AnſwAnsw. not, that therefore fearefear of God ſhouldshould be no motiuemotive: it may be another motiuemotive, and a better motiuemotive.

2. The ſubmiſſionsubmission which is performed through fearefear of Difference betwixt doing a thing for fearefear of God and fearefear of man. man is a forced and a ſlauiſhslavish ſubmiſſionsubmission, nothing acceptable to God: but that which is performed through a true filiallfilial fearefear of God, is a free, willing, ready, cheerefullcheerful, conſcionableconscionable ſubmiſſionsubmission: ſuchsuch a ſubmiſſionsubmission as will ſtirrestir vsus vpup to doedo the beſtbest good we can thereby vntounto them, to whom we ſubmitsubmit our ſeluesselves, and ſoso is more acceptable to God, by reaſonreason of the cauſecause thereof, and more profitable vntounto man, by reaſonreason of the effect and fruit thereof.

For a true fearefear of God maketh vsus more reſpectrespect what ReaſonReason. The power of a fearefear of God. God requireth and commandeth, than what our corrupt heart deſirethdesireth and ſuggeſtethsuggesteth: It ſubduethsubdueth our vnrulyunruly paſſionspassions, and bringeth them within compaſſecompass of dutieduty: It maketh vsus deny our ſeluesselves and our owneown deſiresdesires: and though through the corruption of our nature and inborneinborn pride we be loth to ſubmitsubmit, yet will Gods fearefear bring downedown that proud mindemind, and make vsus humble and gentle. It will keepekeep thoſethose who are in authoritieauthority from tyranny, crueltiecruelty, and ouerover-much ſeueritieseverity: and it will keepekeep thoſethose who are vnderunder ſubiectionsubjection from diſſimulationdissimulation, deceit, and priuieprivy conſpiraciesconspiracies.

Behold how neceſſarienecessary it is, that a true fearefear of the Lord VſeUse. The neceſſitienecessity of a fearefear of God. be planted in mens hearts, in the hearts of Kings and all GouernoursGovernors, in the hearts of ſubiectssubjects and all people, whether ſuperiourssuperiors or inferioursinferiors. Where no fearefear of God is, there will be no good ſubmiſſionsubmission vntounto man. Abraham
Gen. 20. 11. thought that the men of Gerar would hauehave no reſpectrespect to him or his wife, nor make conſcienceconscience of common honeſtiehonesty, nor abſtaineabstain from innocent bloudblood, becauſebecause he ſawsaw no fearefear of God in that place: and the ApoſtleApostle hauinghaving reckoned vpup Rom. 3. 11, &etcc. many notorious effects of mans naturallnatural corruption, concludeth all with this, as the cauſecause of all, There is no fearefear of God before their eyes. Wherefore let MagiſtratesMagistrates, Parentsparents, Maſtersmasters, and all in authoritieauthority, hauehave eſpeciallespecial care that their ſubiectssubjects, children, ſeruantsservants, and all vnderunder them may be taught and brought to fearefear the Lord. I dare auouchavouch it, that ſuchsuch inferioursinferiors which are taught to fearefear God, will doedo better ſeruieeserviceseruiee to their ſuperiourssuperiors, than ſuchsuch as fearefear their ſuperiourssuperiors only as men, and fearefear not God. Let MiniſtersMinisters eſpeciallyespecially vrgeurge and preſſepress vponupon the conſciencesconsciences of men a fearefear of God. Let all inferioursinferiors pray that the fearefear of the Lord may be planted in the hearts of their ſuperiourssuperiors, that ſoso they may liuelive a quiet and peaceable life in all godlineſſegodliness and honeſtiehonesty vnderunder them. HappieHappy is that kingdomekingdom where MagiſtratesMagistrates and ſubiectssubjects fearefear the Lord. HappieHappy is that Church where MiniſtersMinisters and people fearefear the Lord. HappieHappy is that family where husband and wife, parents and children, maſtermaster and ſeruantsservants fearefear the Lord. In ſuchsuch a KingdomeKingdom, Church, and family, will eueryevery one, to the mutuallmutual good one of another, ſubmitsubmit themſeluesthemselves one to another. But if ſuchsuch as fearefear not God ſubmitsubmit themſeluesthemselves, whether they be ſuperiourssuperiors or inferioursinferiors, it is for their owneown ends and aduantagesadvantages, and not for their good to whom they ſubmitsubmit themſeluesthemselves.

div.head: §. 6. Of limiting all dutieduty to man, within the compaſſecompass of the fearefear of God.
div.p: AgaineAgain, as this clauſeclause (In the fearefear of the Lord) declareth the manner of ſubmiſſionsubmission, it ſhewethshoweth, that

No ſubmiſſionsubmission is to be performed vntounto man, but that which Doct. may ſtandstand with the fearefear of God. Such ColoſſColoss. 3. 22. phraſesphrases as theſethese, For the Lords ſakesake, As vntounto the Lord, In the 1 Pet. 2. 13. Great reaſonreason there is that all ſeruiceservice ſhouldshould be limited 1. ReaſonReason. God the higheſthighest Lord. with the fearefear of God: for God is the higheſthighest Lord to whom all ſeruiceservice primarily and principally is due: whatſoeuerwhatsoever ſeruiceservice is due to any man, high or low, is due in and for the Lord. The Lord hath ſetset ſuperiourssuperiors in the places of eminencieeminency, wherein they bearebear the image of God. The Lord alſoalso hath ſetset inferioursinferiors in their places, and commended them as his charge to the gouernmentgovernment of thoſethose who are ouerover them. He that obeyeth not thoſethose who are ouerover him in the fearefear of God, ſhewethshoweth no reſpectrespect of Gods image: and he who gouernethgoverneth not thoſethose who are vnderunder him in the fearefear of God, ſhewethshoweth no reſpectrespect of Gods charge.

The fearefullfearful iſſueissue of this their ſubmiſſionsubmission, not ſeaſonedseasoned with a fearefear of God, but contrary thereunto, may be a warning to all ſuperiourssuperiors, to take heed how they ſeekeseek to pleaſeplease them that are vnderunder them, more than God who is aboueabove them. All the places in Scripture which require family-duties, are proofs of the truth of this doctrine.

The reaſonsreasons of this doctrine are cleereclear; for the family is ReaſonReason. The familiefamily a ſeminarieseminary. a ſeminaryseminary of the Church and common-wealth. div.head: §. 14. How an husband is his wiueswives head.

div.p: THeThe place of an husband intimated in the laſtlast clauſeclause of the former verſeverse, is more plainly expreſſedexpressed, and fully explained in this verſeverse. His place is expreſſedexpressed vnderunder the metaphor of an head: and amplified by his reſemblanceresemblance therein vntounto ChriſtChrist.

The particle of connexionconnection (FOR) ſhewethshoweth that this verſeverse is added as a reaſonreason: which may fitly be referred both to the duty it ſelfeself: and to the manner of performing it.

A wife muſtmust ſubmitsubmit her ſelfeself to an husband, becauſebecause he is her head: and ſheshe muſtmust doedo it as to the Lord, becauſebecause her husband is to her, as ChriſtChrist is to the Church.
The metaphor of an head declareth two points:
1. As an head is more eminent and excellent than the body, and placed aboueabove it, ſoso is an husband to his wife.

div.head: §. 27. Of the example of ChriſtsChrists louelove.
div.p:
The note of compariſoncomparison (
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . EuenEven as) requireth no equality, as if it were poſſiblepossible for an Husbandhusband in that meaſuremeasure to louelove his wife, as ChriſtChrist louedloved his Church; (for as ChriſtChrist in excellency and greatneſſegreatness exceedeth man, ſoso in louelove and tenderneſſetenderness) But it noteth an equity, and like quality.

An equitieequity, becauſebecause there is as great reaſonreason that Husbandshusbands by vertuevirtue of their place ſhouldshould louelove their Wiueswives, as that ChriſtChrist by vertuevirtue of his place ſhouldshould louelove the Church.

A like quality, becauſebecause the louelove which ChriſtChrist beareth to the Church is eueryevery way without exception: and a louelove which turneth to the good and benefit of the Church. Hence note two points.

1. Husbands muſtmust come as nearenear as they can to ChriſtChrist in louingloving their wiueswives. In which reſpectrespect, becauſebecause they can neuernever louelove ſoso much as ChriſtChrist did, they muſtmust neuernever thinkethink they hauehave louedloved enough.

2. Though their louelove in meaſuremeasure cannot equallequal ChriſtsChrists louelove, yet in the manner thereof it muſtmust be like ChriſtsChrists, a preuentingpreventing, true, free, pure, exceeding, conſtantconstant louelove.

div.p: The Act (he gauegave) ſhewethshoweth that his louelove was in deed and truth: not only in ſhewshow and pretence.

The Object (himſelfehimself) ſhewethshoweth that he louedloved his Church more then his owneown life. A greater euidenceevidence of louelove could not be giuengiven: for greater louelove hath no man then this, that a man
IohnJohn 15. 13. lay downedown his life for his friend.

The end of ChriſtsChrists louelove (ſetset forth verſvers. 26, 27.) is noted to ſhewshow that he ſoso louedloved his Church for her good and happineſſehappiness, rather then for any aduantageadvantage to himſelfehimself.
As this example of ChriſtsChrists louelove to his Church is ſetset before husbands: ſoso it may and ought alſoalso to be applied to all ChriſtiansChristians: and that in a double reſpectrespect.
1. As a motiuemotive to ſtirrestir them vpup to louelove both ChriſtChrist himſelfehimself, and alſoalso their brethren.
2. As a patternepattern to teach them how to louelove.

A motiuemotive it is to louelove ChriſtChrist, becauſebecause louelove deſeruethdeservethdeserueth louelove: eſpeciallyespecially ſuchsuch a louelove, of ſuchsuch a perſonperson as the louelove of ChriſtChrist is. Yea, our louelove of ChriſtChrist is an euidenceevidence that we are louedloved of ChriſtChrist, as ſmoakesmoke is a ſignesign of fire. Wherefore both in thankfulneſſethankfulness to ChriſtChrist, for his louelove to vsus, and for aſſuranceassurance to our owneown ſoulessouls of ChriſtsChrists louelove to vsus, we ought in all things that we can to teſtifietestify our louelove to ChriſtChrist.

A motiuemotive it is alſoalso to louelove our brethren, becauſebecause ChriſtChrist being in heauenheaven, our PſalPsal. 16. 2. goodneſſegoodness extendeth not to him: but our brethren on earth ſtandstand in his ſteadstead, and the louelove we ſhewshow to them, we ſhewshow to him; and he accepteth it as done to him: Matth. 25. 35, 40. Ye fed me, yeeye viſitedvisited me, ſaithsaith ChriſtChrist to them that fed and viſitedvisited his brethren. This louelove alſoalso, eueneven the 1 Joh. 4. 20. louelove of our brethren, is an euidenceevidence that we are louedloved of God. Wherefore & verſvers. 11. if ChriſtChrist ſoso louedloved vsus, we ought alſoalso to louelove one another.
How the louelove of ChriſtChrist is a patternepattern, I will TreatTreat. 44. §. 61. &etcc. afterwards ſhewshow.

div.head: §. 36. Of the Churches IuſtificationJustification.
div.p: The two particular parts of the forenamed end, which are CleanſingCleansing, and ſanctifyingsanctifying, doedo more diſtinctlydistinctly ſetset forth the puritiepurity of the Church eueneven in this world. div.head: §. 40. Of SacramentallSacramental waſhingwashing of water.
div.p: One of the meanesmeans which ChriſtChrist vſethuseth for the cleanſingcleansing and ſanctifyingsanctifying of his Church, is expreſſedexpressed vnderunder this phraſephrase, with the waſhingwashing of water. Water ſettethsetteth forth ChriſtsChrists bloudblood: WaſhingWashing noteth out the application and efficacieefficacy thereof, which is the purging and cleanſingcleansing of our ſoulessouls. As water without waſhingwashing maketh nothing cleaneclean: ſoso the bloudblood of ChriſtChrist, without a right application thereof, cleanſethcleanseth no mans ſoulesoul.

This waſhingwashing of water here mentioned, being applied to an inward ſpirituallspiritual cleanſingcleansing, what can it elſeelse ſetset forth but the Sacrament of BaptiſmeBaptism, wherein both water and waſhingwashing is vſedused?

div.head: §. 44. Of the neceſſitienecessity of BaptiſmeBaptism.
div.p: III. A meanesmeans of working a thing may be ſaidsaid to be neceſſarienecessary Things neceſſarienecessary two wayesways. two wayesways.

1. AbſolutelyAbsolutely, ſoso as the thing cannot poſſiblypossibly be without it. Ex HypotheſiHypothesi. div.head: QueſtQuest. Is it not then lawfulllawful to adminiſteradminister BaptiſmeBaptism without 1 Tim. 4. 5. a Sermon?
div.p: AnſwAnsw. Though it be a very commendable, and honourable manner of adminiſtringadministering that Sacrament, then to adminiſteradminister it when the word is preached, yet I thinkethink not a Sermon at that time to be ſoso neceſſarynecessary, as it ſhouldshould be vnlawfullunlawful without one, to adminiſteradminister BaptiſmeBaptism. For the ioyningjoining of the word and Sacrament here ſpokenspoken of is, that they who are baptiſedbaptised, or who preſentpresent children to be baptiſedbaptised, and anſweranswer for them, or are preſentpresent at the adminiſtringadministering of BaptiſmeBaptism, or liuelive in the places where it vſethuseth to be adminiſtredadministered, ſhouldshould be inſtructedinstructed in the GoſpellGospel, and taught the couenantcovenant which BaptiſmeBaptism ſealethsealeth vpup. BeſidesBesides, the liturgieliturgy and publikepublic formeform preſcribedprescribed for the adminiſtringadministering of BaptiſmeBaptism both in our Church and other reformed Churches, laiethlayeth downedown the nature, efficacy, end, vſeuse, and other like points appertaining to that Sacrament, & plainly declareth the couenantcovenant of God ſealedsealed vpup thereby: ſoso as in our and other like Churches where ſuchsuch formesforms are preſcribedprescribed to be alwaiesalways vſedused, the word is neuernever ſeparatedseparated from BaptiſmeBaptism, though at the adminiſtringadministering of BaptiſmeBaptism there be no Sermon.

The Church of Rome doth directly tranſgreſſetransgress againſtagainst the PapiſtsPapists ioynejoin not the word and ſealeseal. forenamed rule of ioyningjoining the word and BaptiſmeBaptism together. For though they hauehave a publikepublic formeform preſcribedprescribed, yet it being in an vnknowneunknown tongue, not vnderſtoodunderstood of the people, nor expounded to them, it is all one as if there were no formeform at all, no word at all: for that which is not vnderſtoodunderstood is all one 1 Cor. 14. 9. &etcc. as if it were not vttereduttered.

div.head: §. 53. Of the application of the things which ChriſtChrist hath done for the Church, vntounto husbands.

epigraph.q: So ought men to louelove their wiueswives, &etcc.

div.p: THEThe firſtfirst clauſeclause of this verſeverse ſeruethserveth both for an application of the former argument, and alſoalso for a tranſitiontransition to another argument.

The particle of relation (So) ſhewethshoweth that that which hath

AnſwAnsw. No, See §. 27. not for meaſuremeasure, but for likeneſſelikeness. For in this large declaration of ChriſtsChrists louelove, there are two generallgeneral points to be noted.
1. That the Church in her ſelfeself was no way worthieworthy of louelove.
2. That ChriſtChrist ſoso carried himſelfehimself towards her that he made her worthieworthy of much louelove.
This ought to be the mindemind of husbands to their wiueswives.
1. Though they be no way worthieworthy of louelove, yet they muſtmust louelove them.

2. They muſtmust endeuourendeavour with all the wit and wiſdomewisdom they hauehave, to make them worthieworthy of louelove. I ſaysay endeuourendeavour becauſebecause it is not ſimplysimply in the husbands power to doedo the deed. Yet his faithfullfaithful endeuourendeavour ſhallshall on his part be accepted for the deed.
Of theſethese points I ſhallshall hereafter more fully ſpeakespeak.

div.head: §. 54. Of the application of the louelove which a man beareth to himſelfehimself, vntounto an husband.

p.hi: So ought men to louelove their wiueswives as their owneown bodies.

div.p: THeThe forenamed particle (So) hath alſoalso relation to another patternepattern, namely, of a mans ſelfeself to his bodiebody: and ſoso it is a tranſitiontransition from one argument to another.
There is ſomesome more EmphaſisEmphasis here vſedused in ſettingsetting downedown an husbands dutieduty, then was before, verſvers. 25.
There it was laid downedown by way of exhortation, Husbandshusbands louelove your wiueswives.

Here it is laid downedown with a ſtraiterstraiter charge: Husbandshusbands ought to louelove their wiueswives. So as this dutieduty is not a matter arbitrariearbitrary, left to the husbands will to doedo it, or leaueleave it vndoneundone:
there is a neceſſitienecessity laid vponupon him: he muſtmust louelove his wife. Woe therefore vntounto him if he doedo it not.

In ſettingsetting downedown this argument taken from a mans ſelfeself, the ApoſtleApostle reſemblethresembleth a mans wife vntounto his bodiebody: wherein he hath relation to verſvers. 23. whereWhere he ſaidsaid, the husband is the head of the wife. Whereby he ſhewethshoweth, that as an husbands place is a motiuemotive to his wife, for her to performeperform her dutieduty: ſoso to himſelfehimself, See Treat. 4. §. 7474. 76. Why the patternepattern of a mans ſelfeself is added to the patternepattern of ChriſtChrist. for him to performeperform his dutieduty.
He is her head, therefore ſheshe muſtmust be ſubiectsubject to him.
She is his bodiebody, therefore he muſtmust louelove her.
This example of a mans ſelfeself is both a reaſonreason, the more to mouemove husbands to louelove their wiueswives, and alſoalso a rule to teach them how to louelove them.

The reaſonreason is implied vnderunder that neerenear vnionunion that is betwixt Sicut corpus nunquam à ſese diſſidetdissidet, ne

ChryſChrys. in Gen. hom. 45. a man and his wife: ſheshe is as neerenear to him as his owneown bodiebody: therefore ſheshe ought to be as deeredear to him. The bodiebody neuernever diſſentethdissenteth from it ſelfeself, nor the ſoulesoul againſtagainst it ſelfeself. So neither ſhouldshould man and wife.
The rule is noted vnderunder the manner of a mans louingloving his owneown bodiebody: as intirelyentirely as he louethloveth his bodiebody, ſoso intirelyentirely he ought to louelove his wife.
Of the manner of a mans louingloving himſelfehimself, ſeesee Treat. 4. §. 74. 76.

The more to enforce this compariſoncomparison, the ApoſtleApostle addeth, He that louethloveth his wife, louethloveth himſelfehimself.

By this clauſeclause two things are implied.

1. That a wife is not only as a mans bodiebody, namely, his outward fleſhflesh, but as his perſonperson, his bodiebody and ſoulesoul. She is as his bodiebody, becauſebecause ſheshe was taken out of his bodiebody: and becauſebecause Gen. 2. 23. ſheshe is ſetset vnderunder him, as his bodiebody vnderunder his head. She is as himſelfehimself, by reaſonreason of the bond of mariagemarriage, which maketh one of two. In which reſpectrespect a wife is commonly called a mans Matth. 19. 5, 6. ſecondsecond ſelfeself.
2. That an husband in louingloving his wife louethloveth himſelfehimself: ſoso as the benefit of louingloving his wife will redound to himſelfehimself, as well as to his wife.

div.head: §. 55. Of the amplification of a mans louelove of himſelfehimself.

div.p: THeThe former patternepattern of a mans ſelfeself is here further amplified. For firſtfirst the ApoſtleApostle prouethproveth, that a man louethloveth himſelfehimself: and then he ſhewethshoweth how he louethloveth himſelfehimself.
Two arguments are vſedused to proueprove the point.
One is taken from the contrariecontrary: No man euerever yet hated his owneown fleſhflesh. Therefore he louethloveth it.

The other is taken from the effects of louelove: To nouriſhnourish and cheriſhcherish ones fleſhflesh is a fruit of louelove: But euerieevery man nouriſhethnourisheth and cheriſhethcherisheth his fleſhflesh. Therefore he louethloveth it.
This latter argument ſhewethshoweth the manner of a mans louingloving himſelfehimself: and therein a mans louelove of himſelfehimself is a rule to teach him how to louelove his wife.

This indefinite particle (no man) is to be reſtrainedrestrained to ſuchsuch as hauehave the vnderſtandingunderstanding and affection of a man in them: as if he had ſaidsaid, no man in his right wits: for furious, frantickefrantic, mad, deſperatedesperate perſonspersons will cut their armesarms, legs, and other parts, mangle their fleſhflesh, hang, drownedrown, ſmothersmother, choakechoke, and ſtabstab themſeluesthemselves. ChriſtChrist. lib. 1. cap. 25. hate, or any way hurt their wiueswives: yea, it is the part of a mad man to doubt of louingloving, and doing good to himſelfehimself.

That he may yet further preſſepress this point, he returneth againeagain to the example of ChriſtChrist (eueneven as the Lord the Church) The ApoſtleApostle thought that this nailenail of louelove had need be faſtfast beaten into the heads and hearts of husbands, and therefore addeth blow to blow to knockeknock it vpup deepedeep, eueneven to the head: before he confirmed ChriſtsChrists example with the example of our ſeluesselves: here he confirmeth the example of our ſeluesselves with the example of ChriſtChrist againeagain. To giuegive husbands a better direction for their prouidenceprovidence towards their wiueswives, whom they muſtmust nouriſhnourish and cheriſhcherish, not only as their bodies, but as ChriſtChrist nouriſhethnourisheth and cheriſhethcherisheth his Church, not only with things temporalltemporal, but alſoalso with things ſpirituallspiritual and eternalleternal.

div.p:
That which is naturallnatural is in all by the very inſtinctinstinct of nature: and it was at firſtfirst created, and ſtillstill is by Gods prouidenceprovidence preſeruedpreserved in our nature, and that for the preſeruationpreservation of nature. Were there not ſuchsuch a naturallnatural louelove of himſelfehimself in eueryevery one, man would be as careleſſecareless of himſelfehimself, as of others, and as loth to take painespains for himſelfehimself, as for others. Wherefore that eueryevery one might hauehave care at leaſtleast of one, eueneven of himſelfehimself, and ſoso the world be better preſeruedpreserved, God hath reſeruedreserved in man this naturallnatural affection, notwithſtandingnotwithstanding his corruption by ſinsin. Yea further becauſebecause eueryevery one is not able to lookelook to himſelfehimself, at leaſtleast when he is young, ſickesick, old, or any other way impotent, God by his wiſewise prouidenceprovidence hath extended this naturallnatural affection towards otheralſoother alsootheralso as they are neerelynearly linked vntounto vsus by the bonds of nature. The next to a mans ſelfeself are (by bloudblood and bond of nature) children. Admirably much is that which parents doedo for their children, which they would neuernever doedo, if there were not a naturallnatural affection in them to their children. From children againeagain this affection ariſethariseth towards their parents, that when parents grow old, impotent, or any way vnableunable to helpehelp themſeluesthemselves, they might hauehave ſuccoursuccour from their children. And becauſebecause parents and children are not alwaiesalways together, or not able to helpehelp one another, or vnnaturallunnatural, God hath yet further extended this naturallnatural affection to brethren, couſinscousins, and other kindred. And for a further extent thereof hath inſtitutedinstituted mariagemarriage betwixt ſuchsuch as are not of the ſamesame bloudblood, and by vertuevirtue of that bond raiſedraised a naturallnatural affection not only in husband and wife one to another, but alſoalso in all the alliance that is made therbythereby. MoreouerMoreover this affection is wrought in neighbours, friends, fellowesfellows, and other by like bonds knit together, that the bow of Gods prouidenceprovidence might hauehave many ſtringsstrings, and if one breakebreak, another might hold. In all theſethese kinds, the neerernearer a man commethcometh to himſelfehimself, the more doth this affection ſhewshow it ſelfeself, according to the prouerbeproverb, NeareNear is my coat, but nearer is my skin. God hauinghaving wrought this naturallnatural affection in the ſeuerallseveral
kindeskinds thereof, and there being good ends and vſesuses thereof, it is not to be condemned.

div.head: §. 61. Of well vſingusing naturallnatural affection.
div.p:
Let vsus labour to cheriſhcherish this naturallnatural affection in vsus, and to 2. It is not, becauſebecause there is no matter of hatred in the Church, ReaſonReason. that ChriſtChrist hateth it not: for by nature all are of one and the ſamesame curſedcursed ſtockestock, EpheſEphes. 2. 3. children of wrath: and after our ſanctificationsanctification is begun, the fleſhflesh abiding in vsus, we daily giuegive much

div.head: §. 69. Of ChriſtsChrists nouriſhingnourishing and cheriſhingcherishing his Church.
div.p:
2. That The Lord nouriſhethnourisheth and cheriſhethcherisheth his Church, is euidentevident by his continuallcontinual prouidenceprovidence ouerover her in all ages. When firſtfirst he created man, he Gen. 1. 28, 29. prouidedprovided before hand all things needfullneedful to nouriſhnourish and cheriſhcherish him. When he was mouedmoved to deſtroydestroy the earth and all liuingliving things thereon, he had care of his Church, and prouidedprovided an ArkeArk to keepekeep her out of Gen. 6. 14. 21. the waters, and ſtoredstored vpup in the ArkeArk all things needfullneedful for

Exo. 16. 15. and 17. 6. his Church was in a barren and driedry wilderneſſewilderness, he gauegave them bread from heauenheaven, water out of the rockerock, and kept their raiment from waxing old, and their feet from ſwellingswelling. After this Deut. 8. 4. he brought his Church into a land flowing with milkemilk and honiehony: and ſoso long as it remained faithfullfaithful he preſeruedpreserved it in that pleaſantpleasant and plentifullplentiful land. Thus he dealt with the Church in her non-age: and thus alſoalso hath he dealt with her in her riper age vnderunder the GoſpellGospel, as experience of all ages may witneſſewitness. Neither hath he only nouriſhednourished and cheriſhedcherished her with temporalltemporal bleſſingsblessings, but alſoalso with all needfullneedful ſpirituallspiritual bleſſingsblessings: his word and Sacraments, his Spirit and the graces thereof hath he in all ages giuengiven her for that purpoſepurpose: yea with his owneown fleſhflesh and bloudblood hath he fed her, and with IohJoh. 6. 55. his owneown righteouſneſſerighteousness hath he clothed her. IſaIsa. 61. 10.

VſeUse. ſpirituallspiritual and temporalltemporal, for ſoulesoul and bodiebody, that accordingly AſcribeAscribe all to ChriſtChrist. we may giuegive him the praiſepraise of all. And let vsus not be like the vngratefullungrateful IſraelitesIsraelites who Ezek. 20. 11, 12. regarded not the meanesmeans of ſpirituallspiritual OſeOse. 8. 12. nouriſhmentnourishment, and IerJer. 44. 17. OſeOse. 2. 5, 8. aſcribedascribed the meanesmeans of their temporalltemporal nouriſhingnourishing and cheriſhingcherishing to their Idols. In this reſpectrespect the Prophet maketh them IſaIsa. 1. 3. worſeworse then the oxeox, and the aſſeass, two of the moſtmost bruitiſhbruitish beaſtsbeasts that be. Oh take we heed that the like be not vpbraidedupbraided to vsus. The Lord hath not ſparinglysparingly, but moſtmost liberally and bountifully nouriſhednourished and cheriſhedcherished vsus in this land, and that both with temporalltemporal and ſpirituallspiritual bleſſingsblessings, ſoso as he may iuſtlyjustly ſaysay, what could hauehave beenebeen done
