ChriſtChrist will not ſuffersuffer his Church to famiſhfamish for want of food, nor ſtaruestarve for want of cloathing, whether temporalltemporal for body, or ſpirituallspiritual for ſoulesoul. He that can and will performeperform it hath ſaidsaid, I will neuernever leaueleave thee nor forſakeforsake thee. Lazarus was not Heb. 13. 5. forſakenforsaken; witneſſewitness the Angels that cariedcarried his ſoulesoul into AbrahamsAbraham's
Luk. 16. 22. boſomebosom. If any of ChriſtsChrists Church doedo periſhperish for want
of outward meanesmeans, it is becauſebecause ChriſtChrist by that meanesmeans will aduanceadvance them to that place where they ſhallshall ſtandstand in need of nothing: ſoso as he doth not forſakeforsake them.

div.head: §. 70. Of the vnionunion betwixt ChriſtChrist and the Saints.

epigraph.q: For we are members of his body, of his fleſhflesh, and of his bones.

div.p: THeThe reaſonreason of the forenamed louelove of ChriſtChrist, and fruits Inference. thereof to his Church, is here laid downedown, as both the cauſallcausal particle (FOR) and the inference of this verſeverse vponupon the former doedo ſhewshow. This reaſonreason is that neerenear vnionunion which is betwixt ChriſtChrist and his Church, ſetset forth by a metaphor of the members of our bodiebody. Whereby he implieth, that though there were no other reaſonreason to mouemove an husband to louelove his wife then the neerenear vnionunion which is betwixt them (they being VerſVers. 23. one bodiebody, VerſVers. 31. one fleſhflesh, VerſVers. 28. one ſelfeself) that were enough, for thereby only is ChriſtChrist mouedmoved to louelove his Church.

The myſteriemystery of our ſpirituallspiritual vnionunion with ChriſtChrist is here laid downedown, and that as fully, and diſtinctlydistinctly (though very ſuccinctlysuccinctly) SummeSum, as in any place of Scripture. I will endeuourendeavour to open it as plainly as I can.

We are] The ApoſtleApostle here changeth both perſonperson and number:
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . Paul ranketh himſelfehimself among the members of ChriſtChrist. for before he ſpakespake of the Church as of another in the third perſonperson, and of one in the ſingularsingular number: but here he ſpeakethspeaketh of the ſamesame in the firſtfirst perſonperson including himſelfehimself, and in the plurallplural number, including all others like himſelfehimself (elect of God, and Saints by calling) whereby he giuethgiveth vsus to vnderſtandunderstand what he meaneth by the Church, namely the companiecompany of Saints, to which, though he were a Preacher of the GoſpellGospel, an extraordinarieextraordinary Preacher, an ApoſtleApostle, he aſſociatethassociateth and ioynethjoinethjoyneth himſelfehimself: noting thereby that he was made partaker of the ſamesame grace, and ſauedsaved by the ſamesame meanesmeans that others were. Well might he in this priuiledgeprivilege not thinkethink much to rankerank himſelfehimself, becauſebecause it is the higheſthighest degree of honour that can be ObſerObser. to be a member of the bodiebody of ChriſtChrist: much more then to be a Preacher, a Prophet, an ApoſtleApostle, or of any other eminent calling.

The metaphor here vſedused (members of his body) ſettethsetteth Metaphors which ſetset forth our vnionunion with ChriſtChrist. forth the neerenear vnionunion which is betwixt ChriſtChrist and the Saints. Many other metaphors are vſedused in Scripture for the ſamesame purpoſepurpose, as 1 Pet. 2. 4, 5, 6. foundation and edifice,
IohJoh. 15. 5. vine and branches, 2 Cor. 11. 2. husband and wife, with the like, which are all of them very fit, but none more proper and pertinent to the point then this of a body, the Head and members thereof. What neerernearer vnionunion can there be then betwixt the head and members of the ſamesame body?

If the ApoſtleApostle had here ſtaidstaid, we might hauehave thought that he had here meant no other thing then he meant Eph. 1. 23. and 4. 16. and 5. 23. before, where he ſtiledstyled ChriſtChrist an head, and the Church a body: but in that he addeth (Of his fleſhflesh and of his bones) he declareth yet a further myſteriemystery.

In the generallgeneral there is a difference betwixt this phraſephrase (
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . OF his body) and theſethese (OF
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . his fleſhflesh; and OF his bones) the former is a note of the Corporis. genetiuegenitivegenetive caſecase, the two latter are a Ex. praepoſitionpraeposition: for diſtinctiondistinction ſakesake the two latter might hauehave beenebeen tranſlatedtranslated, out of his fleſhflesh, out of his bones, or from his fleſhflesh, from his bones (for ſoso a like phraſephrase is tranſlatedtranslated Eph. 4. 16. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . before, From whom) but ſeeingseeing theſethese particles out of, or from are ambiguous, the former tranſlationtranslation may ſtandstand as the beſtbest, ſoso as a difference be made in the ſenſesense though there be none in the words.
The former (members of his body) declareth the vnionunion it ſelfeself.

The latter (of his fleſhflesh and of his bones) declareth the meanesmeans How we are of ChriſtsChrists fleſhflesh. of making that vnionunion. This latter hath relation to that which Adam ſaidsaid of EueEve, This is now bone of my bones, and fleſhflesh of my fleſhflesh, (Gen. 2. 23.) which is manifeſtmanifest by the next verſeverse which the ApoſtleApostle taketh out of the ſamesame place. It implieth then, that as EueEve was made a woman out of AdamsAdam's fleſhflesh and bones, ſoso the Church is made a Church out of ChriſtsChrists fleſhflesh and bones.
1. QueſtQuest. Was the very ſubſtancesubstance of the Saints, their fleſhflesh and bones taken out of ChriſtChrist, as the ſubſtancesubstance of EueEve was taken out of Adam?

AnſwAnsw. Not ſoso, if the words be literally taken. For ſoso may ChriſtChrist rather be ſaidsaid to be of our fleſhflesh, and of our bones, becauſebecause he tooketook our nature, and that from a daughter of Adam: in
which reſpectrespect he is ſaidsaid to be 2 Tim. 2. 8. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . of the ſeedseed of DauidDavid, and Rom. 9. 5. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . of the IewesJews, as concerning the fleſhflesh. BeſidesBesides, the ApoſtleApostle expreſlyexpressly ſaithsaith (verſvers. 32.) that This is a great myſteriemystery. The myſteriemystery therefore muſtmust be ſearchedsearched out. For this end ChriſtChrist muſtmust be conſideredconsidered as another Adam (and ſoso the holy GhoſtGhost ſtilethstyleth him 1 Cor. 15. 45, 47. The laſtlast Adam, The ſecondsecond man) that is, a ſtockestock, a root that giuethgiveth a being to branches ſproutingsprouting out of him.

div.head: 2. QueſtQuest. What being is that which we receiuereceive from ChriſtChrist? What being we receiuereceive from ChriſtChrist.
div.p:
AnſwAnsw. Not our naturallnatural being (that we hauehave of the parents of our fleſhflesh) but a ſupernaturallsupernatural, and ſpirituallspiritual being, which the Scripture termeth Tit. 3. 5. a new birth,
EpheſEphes. 4. 24. a new man, 2 Cor. 5. 17. a new creature. This ſpirituallspiritual being is not in regard of the ſubſtancesubstance of our ſoulesoul, or bodiebody, or of any of the powers or parts, faculties or members of them (for all theſethese we hauehave by linealllineal deſcentdescent from Adam, and all theſethese hauehave all ſortssorts of men, as well they who are not of the Church, as they who are of it) but in regard of the integritieintegrity, goodneſſegoodness, and diuinedivine qualities which are in them 2 Pet. 1. 4. EpheſEphes. 4. 24. eueneven that holineſſeholiness and righteouſneſſerighteousness wherewith the Church is endued and adorned. As we are naturallnatural men we are of Adam, as we are ſpirituallspiritual men we are of ChriſtChrist.

div.head: 3. QueſtQuest. Why is mention made of fleſhflesh and bones in this Why we are ſaidsaid to be of ChriſtsChrists fleſhflesh. Gen. 2. 23. ſpirituallspiritual being?
div.p: AnſwAnsw. 1. In alluſionallusion to the creation of EueEve, that by comparing this with that, this might be the better conceiuedconceived.

2. In regard of the Lords Supper, where the fleſhflesh of ChriſtChrist is myſticallymystically ſetset before vsus to be ſpirituallspiritual food vntounto vsus. That as before (verſvers. 26.) he ſhewedshowed the myſteriemystery of one Sacrament, BaptiſmeBaptism; here he might ſhewshow the myſteriemystery of the other Sacrament, The Lords Supper.

3. In relation to ChriſtsChrists humane nature, by vertuevirtue whereof we come to be vnitedunited vntounto ChriſtChrist. For the diuinedivine nature of ChriſtChrist is infinite, incomprehenſibleincomprehensible, incommunicable, and Diuinitas vnigeniti facta eſtest particeps mortalitatis noſtraenostrae, vt & nos participes eius immortalitatis eſſemusessemus. Aug. EpiſtEpist. 57. there is no manner of proportion betwixt it and vsus, ſoso as we could not be vnitedunited to it immediately. But ChriſtChrist by taking his humane nature into the vnitieunity of his diuinedivine nature, made himſelfehimself one with vsus, and vsus one with him: ſoso as by his partaking of our mortalitiemortality, we are made partakers of his immortalitieimmortality.

div.head: 4. QueſtQuest. Are we then vnitedunited only to his humane nature?
div.p: AnſwAnsw. No: we are vnitedunited to his perſonperson, God-Manman. For as We are vnitedunited to ChriſtsChrists perſonperson. the diuinedivine nature, in and by it ſelfeself, is incommunicable; ſoso the humane nature ſinglysingly conſideredconsidered, in and by it ſelfeself, is vnprofitableunprofitable. The DeitieDeity is the fountainefountain of all life and grace: the fleſhflesh quickneth not: but that ſpirituallspiritual life which originally and primarily floweth from the DeitieDeity, as from a fountainefountain, is by the humanitiehumanity of ChriſtChrist, as by a conduit-pipe, conueyedconveyed into vsus.

div.head: 5. QueſtQuest. How can we who are on earth, be vnitedunited to his How Saints on earth are vnitedunited to ChriſtChrist in heauenheaven. humane nature, which is contained in the higheſthighest heauenheaven?
div.p: AnſwAnsw. This vnionunion being ſupernaturallsupernatural and ſpirituallspiritual, there needeth no localllocal preſencepresence for the making of it. That eternalleternal Spirit which is in ChriſtChrist is conueyedconveyed into euerieevery of the Saints (as the ſoulesoul of a man is into euerieevery member and part of his bodiebody) by vertuevirtue whereof they are all made one with ChriſtChrist, and with one another: by one Spirit we are all baptized into one bodiebody, 1 Cor. 12. 12, 13. which bodiebody is ChriſtChrist.

This is to be noted againſtagainst theſethese two errourserrors. The firſtfirst is I. Error. this, We are vnitedunited firſtfirst to the diuinedivine nature of ChriſtChrist which is euerieevery where, and by vertuevirtue thereof to his humane nature.
AnſwAnsw. 1. The DeitieDeity (as we ſhewedshowed) is immediately incommunicable: ſoso as this cannot be.
2. Our vnionunion with ChriſtChrist is ſpirituallspiritual, not phyſicallphysical or naturallnatural, ſoso as this localllocal preſencepresence needeth not.
The ſecondsecond errourerror is this,

The humane nature of ChriſtChrist hath all the diuinedivine properties in it, II. Error. ſoso as it is euerieevery where preſentpresent, and by reaſonreason thereof we are vnitedunited vntounto ChriſtChrist.

AnſwAnsw. This alſoalso is impoſſibleimpossible and needleſſeneedless. The properties of a true bodiebody cannot poſſiblypossibly admit the incommunicable properties of the DeitieDeity: that implieth direct contradiction, which is, that finite ſhouldshould be infinite. NeedleſſeNeedless alſoalso this is, becauſebecause the vnionunion we ſpeakespeak of, is (as we ſaidsaid) ſpirituallspiritual.

div.head: 6. QueſtQuest. What kindekind of vnionunion is this ſpirituallspiritual vnionunion? Our vnionunion with ChriſtChrist a true and reallreal vnionunion.
div.p:
AnſwAnsw. A true, reallreal vnionunion of our perſonspersons (bodies and ſoulessouls) with the perſonperson of ChriſtChrist (God and man.) For as the holy GhoſtGhost did vniteunite in the virgins wombewomb the diuinedivine and humane
natures of ChriſtChrist, and made them one perſonperson, by reaſonreason wherofwhereof ChriſtChrist is of our fleſhflesh & of our bones: ſoso the ſpiritspirit vnitethuniteth that perſonperson of ChriſtChrist with our perſonspersons, by reaſonreason whereof we are of his fleſhflesh, and of his bones. A great difference there is betwixt the kindeskinds of theſethese vnionsunions: for the vnionunion of ChriſtsChrists two natures is hypoſtaticallhypostaticall and eſſentiallessential, they make one perſonperson: but the vnionunion of ChriſtsChrists perſonperson, and ours, is ſpirituallspiritual and myſticallmystical: they make one myſticallmystical body: yet is there no difference in the reality and truth of theſethese vnionsunions: our vnionunion with ChriſtChrist is neuernever a whit the leſſeless reallreal and true becauſebecause it is myſticallmystical and ſpirituallspiritual: they who hauehave the ſamesame ſpiritspirit are • as truly one, as thoſethose parts which hauehave the ſamesame ſoulesoul. The effects which proceed from this vnionunion doedo ſhewshow the truth thereof: for that ſpiritspirit which ſanctifiedsanctified ChriſtChrist in his mothers wombewomb ſanctifiethsanctifieth vsus alſoalso, that which quicknedquickened him quickneth Rom. 8. 11. Eph. 2. 6. vsus, that which raiſedraised him from death, raiſethraiseth vsus, that which exalted him exalteth vsus. The many reſemblancesresemblances which the Scripture vſethuseth to ſetset forth this vnionunion, doedo ſhewshow the truth thereof: but moſtmost liuelylively is it ſetset forth by that reſemblanceresemblance which ChriſtChrist maketh betwixt it and his vnionunion with his Fatherfather. I pray (ſaithsaith he of all his Saints) That they may all
IohJoh. 17. 21, 22. be one, as thou Fatherfather art in me, and I in thee, that they alſoalso may be one in vsus: that they may be one, as we are one. This note of compariſoncomparison (as) is not to be taken of the kindekind, but of the truth of theſethese vnionsunions, our vnionunion with ChriſtChrist is as true as ChriſtsChrists vnionunion with his Fatherfather.

So true is this vnionunion, as not only IeſusJesus himſelfehimself, but all the UnuſquiſqueUnusquisque ChriſtianusChristianus non incongruè ſuſtinetsustinet perſonampersonam ChriſtiChristi. Aug. de Gen. l. 2. c. 24. vide eundem quaeſtquaest. 69. Saints which are members of this body together with IeſusJesus the head thereof are called CHRIST, 1 Cor. 12. 12. Gal. 3. 16.

This is to be noted againſtagainst their conceit, who imagine this vnionunion to be only in imagination and conceit: or elſeelse only in conſentconsent of ſpiritspirit, heart, and will: or at the moſtmost, in participation of ſpirituallspiritual graces.

div.head: 7. QueſtQuest. What is the bond whereby this vnionunion is made: With what bonds we are vnitedunited to ChriſtChrist. 1 Joh. 4. 13. namely whereby ChriſtChrist and the Saints are made one?
div.p:
AnſwAnsw. There is a double bond, one on ChriſtsChrists part, eueneven the ſpiritspirit of ChriſtChrist (for hereby know we that we dwell in him, and he in vsus, becauſebecause he hath giuengiven vsus of his ſpiritspirit) another on the
Saints part, eueneven faith (for ChriſtChrist dwelleth in our hearts by faith)
Eph. 3. 17. The ſpiritspirit is conueyedconveyed into vsus when we are dead in ſinnessins, wholly fleſhflesh, but being in vsus, it breedeth this bleſſedblessed inſtrumentinstrument of faith whereby we lay hold on ChriſtChrist, and grow into him as the ſciencescience into the ſtockestock. Thus ChriſtChrist laying hold on vsus by his ſpiritspirit, and we on him by faith, we come to be incorporated into him, and made one body, as the ſciencescience and ſtockestock one tree.

div.head: 8. QueſtQuest. To what end hath ChriſtChrist thus truly and neerelynearly Why ChriſtChrist made the Saints one with himſelfehimself. vnitedunited vsus vntounto himſelfehimself?
div.p: AnſwAnsw. Not for any benefit vntounto himſelfehimself: but meerelymerely for the honour and good of the Church. By this vnionunion the honour of ChriſtChrist is communicated to the Church, as the honour of an husband to his wife, and of an head to the body. Great alſoalso is the benefit which the Church reapeth thereby: for by this meanesmeans is ChriſtChrist made more fit to doedo good to the Church, as an head to the body, and the Church is made more capable of receiuingreceiving good from ChriſtChrist, as a body from the head, being knit to it by the ſoulesoul, and by veinesveins, ſinewessinews, neruesnerves, arteries, and other like ligaments.

Thus hauinghaving as plainly as I can by queſtionsquestions and anſwersanswers laid open this great myſteriemystery, I will further note out ſomesome of thoſethose excellent priuiledgesprivileges which by vertuevirtue thereof appertaineappertain to the Saints, and alſoalso ſomesome of the principallprincipal duties which in regard thereof the Saints are bound vntounto.

div.head: §. 71. Of the priuiledgesprivileges appertaining to the Saints eueneven in this life by reaſonreason of their vnionunion with ChriſtChrist.
div.p: The priuiledgesprivileges of the Saints which ariſearise from their vnionunion with ChriſtChrist reſpectrespect this life, the time of death, and the life to come.
In this life theſethese,

1. A moſtmost glorious condition, which is to be a part of ChriſtChrist, a 1. Saints are members of a glorious body. member of his body. All the glory of Adam in ParadiſeParadise, or of the Angels in heauenheaven is not comparable to this. In this reſpectrespect the Saints are ſaidsaid to be crowned with glory and honour, and to hauehave all things put vnderunder their feet. Compare PſalPsal. 8. 4, 5. &etcc. with Heb. 2. 6, 7. &etcc. and ye ſhallshall findefind the ApoſtleApostle apply that to ChriſtChrist, which the Prophet ſpakespake indefinitlyindefinitely of man.
Now thoſethose two places cannot be better reconciled, then by Coelo, & Angelis, & omni creatura honorabilior eſtest ecclesia. ChryſChrys. de PentecoſtPentecost. ſermserm. 26. this vnionunion of ChriſtChrist and Saints: for ſeeingseeing both make one body, which is ChriſtChrist, that which is ſpokenspoken of the body may be applied to the head, and that which is ſpokenspoken of the head may be applied to the body: for the ſamesame honour appertaineth to both. In which reſpectrespect the Church is more honourable then HeauenHeaven, Angels, and eueryevery other creature.

2. The attendance of good Angels, who are ſentsent forth to miniſterminister 2. Saints attended by Angels. for them who ſhallshall be heiresheirs of ſaluationsalvation, becauſebecause thoſethose heiresheirs are of the body of ChriſtChrist, who is their Lord. TheſeThese are thoſethose horſeshorses, and charets of fire which were round about EliſhaElisha:
Heb. 1. 14. 2 King. 6. 17. which are alſoalso round about eueryevery of Gods Saints in all their diſtreſſesdistresses, though we ſeesee them no more then the ſeruantservant of the man of God ſawsaw them, till the Lord opened his eieseyes. That charge which is giuengiven to the Angels ouerover the Sonneson of God to keepekeep him in all his waiesways, and to bearebear him in their hands leſtlest
PſalPsal. 91. 11, 12. he daſhdash his foot againſtagainst a ſtonestone, hath relation to this body which is ChriſtChrist.

3. An honour to make ChriſtChrist himſelfehimself perfect: for as the ſeuerallseveral 3. Saints make ChriſtChrist perfect. members make a naturallnatural body perfect, ſoso the ſeuerallseveral Saints, this bodiebody which is ChriſtChrist. In this reſpectrespect the Church is ſaidsaid to be the fulneſſefulness of him that filleth all in all.
Eph. 1. 23. ChriſtChrist filleth all things, and yet the Church maketh him full: which is to be vnderſtoodunderstood of that voluntary condition whereunto ChriſtChrist ſubiectedsubjected himſelfehimself, to be the head of a body: ſoso as without the parts of the body he is imperfect, as a naturallnatural body is maimed and imperfect if it want but the leaſtleast member thereof. How can we now thinkethink but that he will preſeruepreserve and keepekeep ſafesafe all his Saints? Will he reſtorerestore to vsus all the parts of our naturallnatural body at the generallgeneral reſurrectionresurrection, and will he loſelose any of the parts of his owneown myſticallmystical bodiebody?

4. A kindekind of poſſeſſionpossession of heauenheaven while we are on earth: for 4. Saints aſſuredassured of ſaluationsalvation: and how. that which the head hath a poſſeſſionpossession of, the body and ſeuerallseveral members hauehave alſoalso a poſſeſſionpossession of. In this reſpectrespect it is ſaidsaid, he hath raiſedraised vsus vpup together, and made vsus ſitsit together in

div.head: §. 72. Of the priuiledgeprivilege of our vnionunion with ChriſtChrist in the time of death.
div.p: The priuiledgeprivilege which the Saints receiuereceive by their vnionunion with ChriſtChrist in the time of death (eueneven all that time that paſſethpasseth from the departure of the Saints out of this world vntounto the generallgeneral ReſurrectionResurrection) is admirable: for when body and ſoulesoul are ſeueredsevered one from another, neither ſoulesoul nor body are ſeparatedseparated from ChriſtChrist, but both remaineremain vnitedunited to him: eueneven as, when ChriſtsChrists body and ſoulesoul were by death ſeueredsevered one from another, neither his ſoulesoul, nor his body were ſeparatedseparated from the DeitieDeity, but both remained vnitedunited thereunto. This inuiolableinviolable bond that holdeth the Saints, (yea, eueneven their very bodies as well as their ſoulessouls) vnitedunited to ChriſtChrist in death, is the benefit of a ſpirituallspiritual vnionunion. If our vnionunion with ChriſtChrist were corporeallcorporeal, it could not be ſoso.

Ob. Is it poſſiblepossible that the body which is dead ſhouldshould remaineremain Corruption of the body no hinderancehindrance to our vnionunion with ChriſtChrist. vnitedunited to ChriſtChrist, when as it receiuethreceiveth no vertuevirtue from him?

AnſwAnsw. 1. If a member of a naturallnatural body may doedo ſoso, why not a member of the myſticallmystical bodiebody? That a member of a naturallnatural body may doedo ſoso, is euidentevident by thoſethose who hauehave an hand, armearm, foot, leg, or any other member taken, with a dead palſiepalsy: they are ſometimessometimes ſoso taken, as thoſethose parts receiuereceive no manner of ſenſesense, or any vigor, or life from head or heart at all: and yet remaineremain true members of that body.

2. The very dead bodies conſumedconsumed with wormesworms or otherwiſeotherwise, doedo receiuereceive a great preſentpresent benefit from their vnionunion with ChriſtChrist: for by vertuevirtue thereof there is a ſubſtancesubstance preſeruedpreserved, and they are kept from deſtructiondestruction: there is nothing deſtroieddestroyed in the Saints by death, but that which if it were not deſtroieddestroyed, would make them moſtmost miſerablemiserable, namely ſinnesin: that is vtterlyutterly, totally, finally deſtroieddestroyed in them, and all the concomitances thereof, which are all manner of infirmities: but the rotting of the body, is but as the rotting of cornecorn in the earth, 1 Cor. 15. 36. that it may ariſearise a more glorious bodiebody. The metaphor of ſleepesleep, 1 TheſThes 4. 13. attributed to the Saints when they die, ſhewethshoweth that their bodies are not vtterlyutterly deſtroieddestroyed.

ObiectObject. The bodies of all men, eueneven of thoſethose that are not Difference betwixt the preſeruationpreservation of the Saints bodies and others in the grauegrave. of this vnionunion, are preſeruedpreserved from vtterutter deſtructiondestruction. This therefore is no benefit of our vnionunion with ChriſtChrist.

AnſwAnsw. Though in the generallgeneral thing it ſelfeself, which is a preſeruationpreservation of the ſubſtancesubstance of the body, the ſamesame thing befalleth the Saints and the wicked: yet the meanesmeans whereby both are preſeruedpreserved, and the end why they are preſeruedpreserved is farrefar different.

1. The Saints are preſeruedpreserved by a ſecretsecret influence proceeding 1 TheſThes. 4. 14, 16. from ChriſtChrist, as an head: in which reſpectrespect they are ſaidsaid to ſleepesleep in IeſusJesus, and to be dead in ChriſtChrist. But the wicked are reſeruedreserved by an AlmightieAlmighty power of ChriſtChrist, as a terrible Lord and ſeueresevere IudgeJudge.
2. The bodies of the Saints are preſeruedpreserved to enioyenjoy eternalleternal glory together with their ſoulessouls: but the bodies of the wicked are reſeruedreserved to be tormented in hell.

In regard of theſethese differēcesdifferences, the grauegrave is as a bed to the Saints, IſaIsa. 57. 2. for them quietly to ſleepesleep therein free from all diſturbancedisturbance till the day of reſurrectionresurrection: but it is a priſonprison to the wicked to hold them faſtfast againſtagainst the great Day of AſſiſeAssise, that at DoomesDooms day they may be brought to appeareappear at the barre of Gods iudgementjudgment ſeatseat, and there receiuereceive the ſentencesentence of condemnation.

div.head: §. 73. Of the priuiledgeprivilege of our vnionunion with ChriſtChrist after death.
div.p:
The priuiledgeprivilege which the Saints by vertuevirtue of their vnionunion with ChriſtChrist receiuereceive after death, farrefar ſurpaſſethsurpasseth all before. It may be drawnedrawn to two heads.

That which was before ſaidsaid of the difference betwixt the preſeruationpreservation of the bodies of the Saints and wicked in death, may be applied to the difference of their ReſurrectionResurrection.

div.head: § 75. Of their regeneration who are members of ChriſtChrist.

div.p: This clauſeclause declareth the meanesmeans whereby we come to be members of ChriſtChrist, namely by receiuingreceiving a new being from ChriſtChrist, which is to be, not of the fleſhflesh, and of the bones of Adam, but of the fleſhflesh and of the bones of ChriſtChrist, which being ſpirituallyspiritually taken, as hath beenebeen expounded §. 70. before, ſhewethshoweth that

neither is expreſſedexpressed, but either, or both may be vnderſtoodunderstood. As many of you as have been baptized into ChriſtChrist (that is, made Gal. 3. 27. members of this body) hauehave put on ChriſtChrist, (that is, hauehave beenebeen borne againeagain) the firſtfirst branch noteth out our incorporation into ChriſtChrist, the latter our regeneration.

This ſecondsecond man, and laſtlast Adam ChriſtChrist IeſusJesus is a quickningquickening ReaſonReason. ſpiritspirit: he diffuſethdiffuseth life and grace into all his members: if his 1 Cor. 15. 45. Rom. 8. 11. ſpiritspirit be in vsus, it will quicken our mortallmortal bodies. If the head of our naturallnatural bodies conueigh ſenſesense into all our members: if the root of a tree diffuſediffuse ſapsap into all the branches: ſhallshall not ChriſtChrist much more giuegive life to all his members?

div.head: §. 76. Of the author of our regeneration ChriſtChrist.
div.p:
This relatiuerelative particle (HIS) twice repeated (of HIS fleſhflesh,
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . and of HIS bones) ſhewethshoweth that

p.hi: Regeneration is of ChriſtChrist.
The Sonneson quickneth whom he will.

div.p: Object. This workework is attributed in Scripture to the 1 Pet. 1. 3. Fatherfather, to the IohJoh. 3. 5. Spirit, to the IamJam. 1. 18. word, and to the 1 Cor. 4. 15. MiniſtersMinisters of the word.

AnſwAnsw. ChriſtChrist may very well ſtandstand with all theſethese. The three perſonspersons in TrinitieTrinity are all one: One in nature and eſſenceessence: Philem. verſvers. 10. The workework of the three perſonspersons in our regeneration. One in will and conſentconsent: One in vertuevirtue and power: what the one doth the other doth alſoalso. Yet becauſebecause there is a difference in their manner of working, this workework (as other workesworks) is diſtinctlydistinctly attributed to each of them.

The Fatherfather is (as I may ſoso ſpeakespeak) the beginner of this
workework. His will it was that his Sonneson ſhouldshould be the head of a bodiebody, and that there ſhouldshould members be made fit for that head, and hauehave a new being (of his owneown will begat he vsus) for IamJam. 1. 18. this end he ſentsent his Sonneson into the world to be made fleſhflesh. The Sonneson put in execution the will of his Fatherfather: he tooketook fleſhflesh vponupon him, that we might be of his fleſhflesh. Thus ſaithsaith ChriſtChrist of himſelfehimself, I came downedown from heauenheaven to doedo the will of him that
Joh. 6. 38, 39. ſentsent me; And this is the Fathersfathers will which hath ſentsent me, that of all which he hath giuengiven me I ſhouldshould loſelose nothing, but ſhouldshould raiſeraise it vpup againeagain at the laſtlast day. The Spirit applieth vntounto vsus the vertuevirtue and efficacieefficacy of the fleſhflesh of ChriſtChrist, and ſoso finiſherhfinisherh this bleſſedblessed workework. It is the Spirit that quickneth: the fleſhflesh profiteth nothing,
IohJoh. 6. 63. namely, of it ſelfeself without the Spirit.

Thus we ſeesee that the applying of this workework of regeneration vntounto ChriſtChrist, excludeth not the workework of the Fatherfather, or of the Holy GhoſtGhost therein, but excludeth the workework of man: ſoso as it is not of our ſeluesselves, nor of our parents, nor of any other man: for we are borne not of bloudblood, nor of the will of the fleſhflesh, nor of the will of man, but of God: in which reſpectrespect our new birth IohJoh. 1. 13. is ſaidsaid to be
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . from aboueabove.
ObiectObject. How is it then attributed to the word, and to the IohJoh. 3. 3. miniſterieministry of man? How regeneration is attributed to the word, and to MiniſtersMinisters thereof.

AnſwAnsw. As vntounto inſtrumentsinstruments which the Lord is pleaſedpleased to vſeuse: Of the word it is ſaidsaid, God hath begotten vsus with the word: of himſelfehimself a MiniſterMinister thus ſaithsaith the ApoſtleApostle, In ChriſtChrist IeſusJesus I hauehave begotten you: ſoso as God and ChriſtChrist are ioynedjoined IamJam. 1. 18. with theſethese inſtrumentsinstruments, or elſeelse they are no whit powerfullpowerful and 1 Cor. 4. 15. effectualleffectual for ſoso great a workework: for neither is he that planteth any 1 Cor. 3. 7. thing, nor he that watreth: but God that giuethgiveth the increaſeincrease.

div.head: §. 79. Of the ancient Law of mariagemarriage.

epigraph.q: For this cauſecause ſhallshall a man leaueleave his father and mother, and ſhallshall be ioynedjoined vntounto his wife: and they two ſhallshall be one fleſhflesh.

div.p: THeThe ſamesame points which were before laid downedown, concerning the neerenear vnionunion of man and wife, and of ChriſtChrist and the Church, are here further confirmed by the ancient law of mariagemarriage: which the ApoſtleApostle doth the rather mention, becauſebecause it followeth vponupon that text, whereunto he alluded in the former verſeverse. For when MoſesMoses had alledgedalleged theſethese words of Adam concerning EueEve, This is bone of my bones, and fleſhflesh of my fleſhflesh, he Gen. 2. 23, 24. addeth this law, Therefore ſhallshall a man leaueleave his father, &etcc. In this place theſethese words hauehave both a literallliteral and a myſticallmystical ſenſesense. A literallliteral of man and wife. A myſticallmystical of ChriſtChrist and the Church. The mainemain thing which the ApoſtleApostle aimeth at, is to Inference. ſhewshow how neerelynearly man and wife are linked together: that thereby they may the rathet be mouedmoved to performeperform thoſethose mutuallmutual and ſeuerallseveral duties which they owe each to other. But becauſebecause he propounded to husbands and wiueswives the examples of ChriſtChrist and the Church, as patternespatterns and motiuesmotives to them, to doedo their dutieduty, he applieth that which was firſtfirst ſpokenspoken of man and wife, vntounto ChriſtChrist and his Church, to ſhewshow that there being ſoso fit a reſemblanceresemblance betwixt theſethese two couples, the patternepattern propounded is the more pertinent to the purpoſepurpose, and the reaſonreason enforced from thence the more forcible.
BecauſeBecause the opening of the literallliteral ſenſesense will giuegive great light to the myſteriemystery, I will firſtfirst handle this text according to the meaning of the letter.

The firſtfirst clauſeclause (for this cauſecause) implieth a neceſſarienecessary connexionconnection
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . with that which went before. The neerenear vnionunion of man and wife, as well as of ChriſtChrist and his Church, was before noted. A wife was ſaidsaid to be as the VerſVers. 28. Gen. 2. 23. bodiebody of a man, yea as VerſVers. 28. Gen. 2. 23. himſelfehimself. Adam called her his fleſhflesh and bones. Hereupon both MoſesMoses and Paul inferreinfer, Therefore, or, For this cauſecause ſhallshall a man leaueleave father. BecauſeBecause man and wife are ſoso neerenear by Gods
inſtitutioninstitution, they muſtmust alſoalso be moſtmost dearedear each to other in their mutuallmutual affection.

The Manman (meaning an husband) is here in particular mentioned, Meaning of the words. becauſebecause at the firſtfirst making of this Law the woman was brought to him to ſeesee how he would like her: and hauinghaving caſtcast his affection on her, he was to be bound hereby to continue that good liking towards her: as alſoalso becauſebecause of the preheminenciepreheminency which man hath aboueabove his wife. Yet is not the man only tied hereby, but the wife alſoalso: the nature and rule of relation requireth as much: if a man muſtmust inſeparablyinseparably cleauecleave to his wife, the wife muſtmust anſwerablyanswerably cleauecleave to her husband.

TheſeThese words (ſhallshall leaueleave father and mother) are neither generally to be taken of all duties, as if no dutieduty were to be performed to parents by children after they are mariedmarried: nor ſimplysimply, as if indeed parents were vtterlyutterly to be forſakenforsaken: but they are meant,

1. Of that daily ſeruiceservice which children vnderunder their parents gouernmentgovernment performeperform vntounto them, ſeekingseeking to pleaſeplease them in all things. When children are mariedmarried, then their daily attendance muſtmust be vponupon their wiueswives, or husbands, taking care how 1 Cor. 7. 33, 34. to pleaſeplease them.
2. Of erecting a new family: for which end their parents houſehouse muſtmust be left, and the husband and wife muſtmust dwell each with other.

3. Of the difference to be put betwixt parents, and wife or huſbandhusband. So as if by any ineuitableinevitable occaſionoccasion it ſhouldshould ſoso fall out, that a man muſtmust leaueleave his parent, or his wife (as in caſecase parent and wife were both giuinggiving vpup the GhoſtGhost, and in places ſoso farrefar remote, as the husband could not poſſiblypossibly be with both, yet both inſtantlyinstantly deſireddesired his companiecompany) by this Law he muſtmust leaueleave his parent, and cleauecleave to his wife.

Hereby then the bond of mariagemarriage is declared to be the moſtmost inuiolableinviolable bond that can be. For all men know, that the bond betwixt parent and childechild is a firmefirm and inuiolableinviolable bond: but the bond betwixt husband and wife is more firmefirm and inuiolableinviolable.

To ſetset forth the firmneſſefirmness of the mariagemarriage bond he addeth this Emphacicall phraſephrase, ſhallshall be ioynedjoined, (or as the word properly,
cording to the naturallnatural notation thereof ſignifiethsignifieth, ſhallshall be glued)
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . Glue. to his wife. Things well glued together are as faſtfast, firmefirm, and cloſeclose as if they were one intireentire peece. Yea we obſerueobserve by experience that a table will oft times cleauecleave in the whole wood, before it will part aſunderasunder where it is glued: ſoso as an husband ought to be as firmefirm to his wife as to himſelfehimself: and ſheshe to him.

Fitly doth this agree with that which followeth (they two ſhallshall be one fleſhflesh) Our EngliſhEnglish cannot well expreſſeexpress the GreekeGreek
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . in good ſenſesense word for word (which is thus, they two ſhallshall beinto, or in one fleſhflesh) the meaning is, They which were two before mariagemarriage, by the bond of mariagemarriage are brought into one fleſhflesh, to be eueneven as one fleſhflesh: as neerelynearly vnitedunited, as the parts of the ſamesame body, and the ſamesame fleſhflesh. This vnitieunity is not in regard of carnallcarnal copulation (for if they be mariedmarried they are one fleſhflesh,
Matrimonium non facit coitus, ſedsed voluntas. ChryſoſtChrysost. in Mat. hom. 32. though they neuernever know one another) nor in regard of procreation, because one childechild commethcometh from them both (for though they neuernever hauehave childechild, yet are they one fleſhflesh) but in regard of Gods inſtitutioninstitution, who hath ſetset it downedown for a law, and as another nature, that man and wife ſhouldshould be ſoso neerenear one to another. Their conſentconsent in mariagemarriage (by vertuevirtue of Gods inſtitutioninstitution) maketh them to be one fleſhflesh.

Well doth our EngliſhEnglish note the emphaſisemphasis of the originalloriginal in this particle THEY (they two) which ſhewethshoweth that the bond
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . of mariagemarriage knittethknittethkniteth only two together: one man, and one woman, and no more.
This Law ſettethsetteth forth the VnionUnion betwixt man and wife. SummeSum.
Therein three things are noted concerning the ſtatestate of mariagemarriage.
1. The praeeminenciepraeeminency of it (a man ſhallshall leaueleave father and mother.)
2. The firmneſſefirmness of it (and be ioynedjoined to his wife.)
3. The neereneſſenearness of it (they two ſhallshall be one fleſhflesh.)

div.head: §. 80. Of preferring husband or wife before parents.
div.p: The firſtfirst point ſhewethshoweth, that
A wife, or an husband muſtmust be preferred before parents. The Doct. examples of Gen. 31. 14. Leah and Rachel, yea and of 1 Sam. 19. 11 Micol, are commendable in this reſpectrespect.

1. The bond of mariagemarriage is more ancient, more firmefirm, more ReaſonReason. neerenear. There was husband and wife before there was parent and child: and there is a time when parents & children may depart one from another, and that while both liuelive: but no time, wherein man and wife may part aſunderasunder till death part them. And children though they come from the fleſhflesh of their parents, yet are made two (ſoso as of one are two) but husbands and wiueswives though they were two before, yet are made one (ſoso as of two is one.)

What wrong then doedo ſuchsuch parents vntounto their children, as VſeUse. keepekeep them, eueneven after they are mariedmarried, ſoso ſtraitstrait vnderunder ſubiectionsubjection, Parents may not keepekeep their children being mariedmarried too ſtraightstraight. as they cannot freely performeperform ſuchsuch duty as they ought to their husband, or their wife? This is more then a parents authority reacheth vntounto. Yet many thinkethink that their children owe as much ſeruiceservice to them after they are mariedmarried as before: which is directly againſtagainst this law.

Greater is the wrong, and more ſinfullsinful is the practiſepractise of Nor keepekeep them from husband or wife. ſuchsuch as keepekeep their children from their husbands, or from their wiueswives. The match (ſaysay they) falleth out much worſeworse then we looked for. But this ſhouldshould hauehave beenebeen looked to more carefully before hand. After mariagemarriage it is too late to ſeekeseek ſuchsuch a redreſſeredress.

On the other ſideside, there be many children who ſoso reſpectrespect Children may not preferreprefer their parents before huſbandhusband or wife. Apud Romanos ſponſasponsa obtecta flammeo capite quum extuliſſetextulisset pedem è paternis aedibus, vertebatur in gyrum, itaque duceba • tur in domumſponſidomumsponsi, neſc • iretnesciret redeundi viam ad aedes parentum. EraſmErasm. their parents, as they neglect their husband or their wife. Some husbands will beſtowbestow what they can on their parents, and keepekeep their wiueswives very bare, ſufferingsuffering them to want neceſſariesnecessaries; not caring how they vex and grieuegrieve them ſoso they pleaſeplease their parents. Some wiueswives alſoalso will priuilyprivily purloinepurloin from their husbands to beſtowbestow on their parents.

Others can neuernever tarrietarry out of their parents houſeshouses, but as oft as they can, goego thither. The ancient Romans, to ſhewshow how vnmeetunmeet this was, had a cuſtomecustom to couercover the brides face with a yellow veileveil, and ſoso ſoonesoon as ſheshe was out of her fathers houſehouse to turneturn her about and about, and ſoso to carriecarry her to the houſehouse of her husband, that ſheshe might not know the way to her fathers houſehouse againeagain. All thoſethose pretenſespretenses of louelove to parents are more prepoſterouspreposterous then pious: and naturallnatural affection beareth more ſwaysway in ſuchsuch, then true religion. Their pretence
of piety to parents is no ruſtrust excuſeexcuse for that iniuryinjury they doedo to husband and wife.

div.p: The ſecondsecond point concerning the firmneſſefirmness of the mariagemarriage knot in theſethese words (ſhallshall be ioynedjoined to his wife) affor deth two doctrines.

1. Man and wife muſtmust aſſociateassociate themſeluesthemselves together by continuallcontinual See Treat. 2. part. 2. §. 14. cohabitation: for this end they leaueleave their parents family, and erect a new family.

2. Man and wife are ioynedjoined together by an inuiolableinviolable bond. It See Treat. 2. part. 2 §. 2. muſtmust neuernever be cut aſunderasunder till death cut it. Body and ſoulesoul muſtmust be ſeueredsevered one from another before husband and wife.
Be carefullcareful therefore to preſeruepreserve this indiſſolubleindissoluble knot: and ſoso liuelive together, as with comfort you may liuelive together, becauſebecause you may not part.

div.head: §. 82. Of two only to be ioynedjoined together in mariagemarriage.
div.p: The third point concerning the neereneſſenearness of man and wife, in theſethese words (they two ſhallshall be one fleſhflesh) affordeth two other doctrines.

1. MariageMarriage can be but betwixt two, one man, and one woman: for it is impoſſibleimpossible that more then two ſhouldshould ſoso neerelynearly, and firmelyfirmly be ioynedjoined together, as man and wife are. EueryEvery word almoſtalmost in this law prouethproveth this doctrine. For it ſaithsaith a man, not men: to a wife, not to wiueswives: to his wife, not to anothers wife: two, not more then two: they two, not any two: one fleſhflesh, not many fleſhesfleshes.

div.head: ObiectObject. This particle (two) is not in the law as MoſesMoses recordeth Gen. 2. 24. it.

The ſamesame ſpiritspirit that guided MoſesMoses, guided alſoalso the Mat. 19. 5. EuangeliſtsEvangelists, and the 1 Cor. 6. 16. Mat. 4. 10. him only ſhaltshalt thou ſerueserve.

div.p: AnſwAnsw. The Mal. 2. 15. Prophet anſwerethanswereth, that he might ſeekeseek a godly ſeedseed.
If therefore there be more then two, it is an adulterous ſeedseed which proceedeth from thence.

div.p: Can Polygamy (the hauinghaving of many wiueswives) or Bigamy (the hauinghaving of two wiueswives at once) hauehave any good warrant againſtagainst ſuchsuch an expreſſeexpress law? div.p: AnſwAnsw. It was their ſinnesin, and a great blemiſhblemish in them. The common error of the time, & their vnſatiableunsatiable deſiredesire of increaſeincrease made them fall into it. Many inconueniencesinconveniences followed thereupon: neither can it be thought but that much miſchiefemischief muſtmust needesneeds follow vponupon hauinghaving more wiueswives then one: for whereas God at firſtfirst made a wife to be as an helpehelp vntounto man, two, or more wiueswives cannot but be a great griefegrief and vexation vntounto him by reaſonreason of that emulation that is betwixt them. Through Hagars meanesmeans was Sarah ſtirredstirred againſtagainst Abraham, and Abraham grieuedgrieved at Sarahs words. Though Leah and Rachel were ſiſterssisters, yet great were their emulations: the like whereof is noted of Peninnah and many others.

div.head: §. 84. Of the neerenear coniunctionconjunction of man and wife together.
div.p: 2. The neereſtnearest of all other are husband and wife one to another. Doctr. EueryEvery clauſeclause in the forenamed law prouethproveth as much.
1. Parents muſtmust be left for wife: who neerernearer then parent and childechild? ifIf man and wife be neerernearer then the neereſtnearest, then they are the neereſtnearest of all.

2. A man is glued to his wife. This metaphor ſettethsetteth forth the neerneſſenearnessneerness of a thing as well as the firmneſſefirmness of it: for things glued together are as one intireentire thing.

As God hath limited a propinquity, and vnityunity of things, so ReaſonReason. are they to be accounted: but God hath thus neerelynearly knit man and wife together, and made them one fleſhflesh. ThoſeThose whom

div.head: §. 92. Of the falſefalse Sacrament of MariageMarriage.
div.p:
The other error is, that Mariagemarriage is a Sacrament: the mainemain ground whereof they hauehave taken from this text, which ground by the ApoſtlesApostles application of this myſteriemystery to ChriſtChrist and the Church, is as plainly remouedremoved, as if the ApoſtleApostle had purpoſelypurposely ordered his ſtilestile, to preuentprevent this erroneous collection: as if he had ſaidsaid, That none may miſtakemistake this myſteriemystery, and apply it to a matrimoniallmatrimonial coniunctionconjunction of man and woman together, know that I meanemean no ſuchsuch thing: the myſteriemystery which I ſpeakespeak of, is concerning ChriſtChrist and the Church. I maruellmarvelmarvell how they dare miſapplymisapply that which is ſoso plainly expreſſedexpressed. Though the ApoſtleApostle had not ſoso clearelyclearly ſhewedshowed his mindemind and meaning, yet the verievery thing it ſelfeself would lead vsus ſoso to iudgejudge of it. For, that which in ChriſtChrist

que quibuſquequibusque viris & vxoribusuxoribus minimum. Aug. de nupt. & concup. lib. 1. cap. 21. and the Church is a great myſteriemystery, in man and wife is but a ſmallsmall matter. The vulgar LatineLatin tranſlationtranslation firſtfirst led them into this error, for it tranſlatethtranslateth the word myſteriemystery, a Sacrament. But a tranſlationtranslation is no ſufficientsufficient ground to proueprove a doctrine. BeſidesBesides the word Sacrament vſedused by that TranſlatorTranslator, hath as large an extent as a myſteriemystery: if they ſhouldshould make euerieevery thing which he tranſlatethtranslateth Sacrament, a proper Sacrament of the Church, there would be many more Sacraments then the PapiſtsPapists themſeluesthemselves doedo make.

1. As for this ſuppoſedsupposed Sacrament, no PapiſtPapist could euerever
ſhewshow when or where God ordained it to be a Sacrament. Nay, they agree not among themſeluesthemselves about the time, how long it hath beenebeen a Sacrament. Some of them hold, that euerever ſincesince the firſtfirst inſtitutioninstitution of mariagemarriage in ParadiſeParadise, it hath beenebeen a Sacrament. But the greater number of PapiſtsPapists hold it to be a Sacrament Petrus à Soto de Matr. lect. 2. Concil. Trident. SeſſSess. 24. Can. 1. of the new TeſtamentTestament vnderunder the GoſpellGospel, becauſebecause their Tridentine CouncellCouncil hath ſoso decreed it. 2. As they cannot ſhewshow where it was ordained for a Sacrament, ſoso neither can they ſhewshow what is the SacramentallSacramental ſignesign thereof. Some make carnallcarnal copulation to be it. But there may be a true mariagemarriage, though the parties mariedmarried neuernever know each other.

Others the PrieſtsPriests bleſſingblessing. Yet they hold the mariagemarriage of Infidels and HeretiquesHeretics who hauehave no PrieſtsPriests, to be a true mariagemarriage.
Others, the conſentconsent of the parties themſeluesthemselves. Thus ſhallshall a partieparty adminiſteradminister a Sacrament to himſelfehimself.
Others, other things. Thus they wanting the light of Gods word, one ſtrayethstrayeth in one by-path, another in another, and none of them hit vponupon the right.

4. If other poſitionspositions deliuereddelivered by them concerning matrimoniematrimony be noted, a man would thinkethink that they ſhouldshould be farrefar from making it a Sacrament. They preferreprefer virginitievirginity before it. Yea, they account it a kindekind of pollution. They hold it vnlawfullunlawful for PrieſtsPriests, Monks, Nuns, and ſuchsuch like holy orders (as they eſteemeesteem them) to mariemarry: ſoso as there is a Sacrament, whereof their holy ones may not partake. The order of

div.head: §. 94. Of applying the word to our ſeluesselves.
div.p: The direction for a particular application of their owneown proper duties to either of them is here eſpeciallyespecially to be noted. In this direction two things are to be obſeruedobserved.

1. That eueryevery particular perſonperson apply to himſelfehimself that which by a MiniſterMinister is indefinitlyindefinitely deliuereddelivered to all. EueryEvery one

2. That eueryevery one apply his owneown peculiar dutieduty vntounto himſelfehimself. LoueLove being peculiar to an husband, to him he ſaithsaith, Let him louelove his wife: and reuerencereverence being peculiar to a wife, to her he ſaithsaith, let the wife ſeesee that ſheshe reuerencereverence her huſbandhusband.

The direction in eueryevery of thoſethose ſeuerallseveral EpiſtlesEpistles which were ſentsent to the ſeuenseven Churches of AſiaAsia, (in theſethese words, He that

The life and power of Gods word conſiſtethconsisteth in this particular ReaſonReason. The life of Gods word in application. application thereof vntounto our ſeluesselves. This is to mixemix faith with hearing: faith, I ſaysay, whereby we doedo not only beleeuebelieve the truth of Gods word in generallgeneral, but alſoalso beleeuebelieve it to be a truth concerning our ſeluesselves in particular: and thus will eueryevery precept thereof be a good inſtructioninstruction and direction
on to vsus to guide vsus in the way of righteouſneſſerighteousness: eueryevery promiſepromise therein will be a great incouragementencouragement, and conſolationconsolation to vsus to vpholduphold vsus, and to make vsus hold on: and eueryevery iudgementjudgment threatnedthreatened therein will be a curbecurb, and bridle to hold vsus in, and to keepekeep vsus from thoſethose ſinnessins againſtagainst which the iudgementsjudgments are threatnedthreatened. But otherwiſeotherwise, if we bring not the word home to our own ſoulessouls, it will be as a word ſpokenspoken into the aireair, 1 Cor. 14 9. vaniſhingvanishing away without any profit to vsus. Nothing maketh the word leſſeless profitable, then the putting of it off from our ſeluesselves to others, thinking that it concernesconcerns others more then our ſeluesselves.

That we may make the better vſeuse of this doctrine, let vsus obſerueobserve both what are generallgeneral duties belonging to all ChriſtiansChristians, and apply them as particular to our ſeluesselves: and alſoalso what duties appertaineappertain to ſuchsuch perſonspersons as are of our place, calling, and condition, and more eſpeciallyespecially apply them to our ſeluesselves: let all manner of husbands, and all manner of wiueswives of what rankerank or degree ſoeuersoever they be that ſhallshall read the duties hereafter following, know that they are ſpokenspoken to them in particular. Let Kings and QueenesQueens, Lords and Ladies, MiniſtersMinisters and their wiueswives, Rich men and their wiueswives, PoorePoor men and their wiueswives, Old men and their wiueswives, Young men and their wiueswives, all of all ſortssorts take them as ſpokenspoken to them in particular. It is not honour, wealth, learning, or any other excellency, nor meanesmeans of place, pouertypoverty, want of learning, or any other like thing that can exempt an husband from louingloving his wife, or a wife from reuerencingreverencing her husband. He that ſaithsaith eueryevery one, excepteth not any one. Therefore eueryevery one in particular doedo yeeye ſoso. The like application may be made to all Parentsparents and children, Maſtersmasters and ſeruantsservants, concerning their duties.

div.p: In the forenamed application an eye muſtmust be had rather to the dutieduty which we owe, and ought to be performed by vsus to others, then to that which is due to vsus, and others ought to performeperform to vsus: for the ApoſtleApostle ſaithsaith not to the husband, ſeesee that thy wife reuerencereverence thee, but ſeesee that thou louelove her: ſoso to the wife.

div.head: QueſtQuest. Why is obedience put for all the reſtrest?
div.p: AnſwAnsw. 1. BecauſeBecause it is the hardeſthardest of all the reſtrest, and that which children are loatheſtloathest to performeperform they who willingly yeeldyield to this, will ſtickestick at no duty.
2. BecauſeBecause it is the ſureſtsurest euidenceevidence of that honour which a childechild oweth to his parent: and ſoso of performing the fiftfifth commandementcommandment.

3. BecauſeBecause children are bound to their parents: the duties which they performeperform are not of curteſiecourtesy, but neceſſitynecessity. Their parents hauehave power to command, and exact them.

The clauſeclause added (in the Lord) is in effect the ſamesame which
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . was vſedused Chap. 5. verſvers. 22. before (as vntounto the Lord) and it noteth forth a limitation, direction, and inſtigationinstigation: a limitation ſhewingshowing that childrens obedience to their parents is to be reſtrainedrestrained to the obedience which they owe to ChriſtChrist, and may not goego beyond the limits thereof: a direction ſhewingshowing that in obeying their parents, they muſtmust hauehave an eye to ChriſtChrist, and ſoso obey them as ChriſtChrist may approueapprove thereof: an inſtigationinstigation ſhewingshowing that parents bearebear the image of ChriſtChrist, and in that reſpectrespect children muſtmust the rather obey their parents.

The laſtlast clauſeclause of this verſeverse (for this is right) is an expreſſeexpress

The former phraſephrase (in the Lord) implying one reaſonreason, this plainly noteth out another, as the firſtfirst particle (for) declareth.

div.head: §. 97. Of the meaning of the ſecondsecond verſeverse.

epigraph.q: Honour thy father and mother (which is the firſtfirst commandementcommandment with promiſepromise.)

div.p:
THeThe very words of the fiftfifth commandementcommandment are here alleagedalleged Why the morallmoral law is alleagedalleged. by the ApoſtleApostle as a confirmation of the forenamed reaſonreason, that, it is iuſtjust and right to obey parents, becauſebecause God in the morallmoral law enioynethenjoineth as much. The law is more generallgeneral then
the ApoſtlesApostles precept: for the law compriſethcompriseth vnderunder it all thoſethose duties which all kindekind of inferioursinferiors owe to their ſuperiourssuperiors, whether they be in family, church, or common wealth: but the ApoſtlesApostles precept is giuengiven only to one kindekind of inferioursinferiors in the family: yet the argument is very ſoundsound and good from a generallgeneral to a particular, thus, All inferioursinferiors muſtmust A genere ad ſpeciemspeciem. honour their ſuperiourssuperiors, therefore children their parents.

By adding the expreſſeexpress words of the law the ApoſtleApostle ſhewethshoweth that the ſubiectionsubjection which he required of children is no yoke which he of his owneown head put on their neckesnecks: but that which the morallmoral law hath put on them: ſoso as this may be noted as a third reaſonreason, namely Gods expreſſeexpress charge in his morallmoral law.

If I ſhouldshould handle this law according to the full extent thereof, I ſhouldshould wander too farrefar from the ApoſtlesApostles ſcopescope. I will therefore open it no further then it may concerneconcern the point in hand, viz. the duty of children.

Honour compriſethcompriseth here all thoſethose duties which children in Honour compriſethcompriseth all childrens duties. any reſpectrespect owe to their parents. It implieth both an inward reuerendreverend eſtimationestimation, and alſoalso an outward dutifulldutiful ſubmiſſionsubmission. Yea it implieth alſoalso recompencerecompense, and maintenance.
Honour in relation to parents, is vſedused for two reaſonsreasons eſpeciallyespecially.
1. To ſhewshow that parents bearebear Gods image: for honour is properly due to God alone: to the creature it is due, only as it ſtandethstandeth in Gods roomeroom, and cariethcarrieth his image.
2. To ſhewshow, that it is an honour to parents to hauehave dutifulldutiful children: eueneven as it is a diſhonourdishonour to them to hauehave diſobedientdisobedient children.

Both father and mother are expreſlyexpressly mentioned, to take away Why both father and mother expreſſedexpressed. all pretence from children of neglecting either of them: for through the corruption of nature we are prone to ſeekeseek after many ſhiftsshifts to exempt vsus from our bounden dutieduty; and if not in whole, yet in as great a part as we can. Some might thinkethink if they honour their father, who is their mothers head, they hauehave done what the law requireth: others may thinkethink they hauehave done as much, if they honour their mother who is the weaker veſſellvessel: but the law expreſſingexpressing father and mother,
condemneth him that neglecteth either of them. Yet to ſhewshow that if oppoſitionopposition ſhouldshould ariſearise betwixt them, and by reaſonreason thereof both could not be obeyed together, the father commanding what the mother forbiddeth, the father is to be preferred, (eſpeciallyespecially if it be not againſtagainst the Lord) the father is ſetset in the firſtfirst place.

TheſeThese words following (which is the firſtfirst commandementcommandment How the fiftfifth commandementcommandment is the firſtfirst with promiſepromise. with promiſepromise) are fitly included in a parentheſisparenthesis, becauſebecause they are not the words of the law, but inſertedinserted by the ApoſtleApostle as a reaſonreason to inforceenforce the law, and ſoso make a fourth reaſonreason.

div.head: QueſtQuest. In what reſpectrespect is this commandementcommandment called the firſtfirst with promiſepromise?
div.p:
AnſwAnsw. 1. The * word here vſedused by the ApoſtleApostle properly
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . ſignifiethsignifieth an affirmatiueaffirmative precept, as our EngliſhEnglish word (commandementcommandment) doth. Now then of the affirmatiueaffirmative precepts it is the firſtfirst with promiſepromise.

2. The Scripture oft appropriateth the law to the ſecondsecond table, as where he ſaithsaith he that louethloveth another hath fulfilled the
Rom. 13 8. law, and ſoso in other places.
Now this is the firſtfirst commandementcommandment of the ſecondsecond table.
3. It is generally true of all the commandementscommandments: for among the ten it is the firſtfirst with promiſepromise.

div.head: ObiectObject. The ſecondsecond commandementcommandment hath a promiſepromise annexed Difference betwixt the promiſepromise in the ſecondsecond, and fiſtfist commandementcommandment. to it.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. 1. That which is annexed to the ſecondsecond CommandementCommandment, is not expreſlyexpressly a promiſepromise, but rather a declaration of Gods IuſticeJustice, in taking vengeance of tranſgreſſorstransgressors, and of his merciemercy in rewarding obſeruersobservers of the Law: yet I deniedeny not but that a promiſepromise by conſequenceconsequence is implied: but here it is expreſſedexpressed.

2. The promiſepromise there implied is only a generallgeneral promiſepromise made to obſeruersobservers of the whole Law, and therefore he vſethuseth the plurallplural number, CommandementsCommandments: but here is a particular promiſepromise made to them that keepekeep this CommandementCommandment in particular.

div.head: 2. QueſtQuest. Why is it then ſaidsaid the firſtfirst, when no other CommandementsCommandments with promiſepromise follow? FirſtFirst ſimplysimply taken.
div.p:
AnſwAnsw. This particle (firſtfirst) hath not alwayesalways reference to
ſomesome other following, but is oft ſimplysimply taken, to ſhewshow that none was before it: ſoso is the word firſtfirst-borne vſedused in the Law: Exod. 13. 2. Matth. 1. 25. and ſoso ChriſtChrist is called the firſtfirst-borne Sonneson of MarieMary.

The word promiſepromise ſhewethshoweth, that this fourth reaſonreason includeth ſomesome benefit redounding to thoſethose children themſeluesthemselves that honour their parents: the benefit is expreſlyexpressly mentioned in the next verſeverse, which we will afterwards diſtinctlydistinctly conſiderconsider.

div.head: §. 98. Of aiming at our owneown, in ſeekingseeking the good of others.
div.p: Here in generallgeneral we may note, that

It is not vnlawfullunlawful to aimeaim at our owneown good and benefit in doing the duties which God requireth at our hands to others: for that which God himſelfehimself propoundeth and ſettethsetteth before vsus, we may ſeekeseek and aimeaim at. Many like promiſespromises there be in Scripture, and many approuedapproved prayers grounded on thoſethose promiſespromises whereby the truth of the doctrine is confirmed vntounto vsus. Hezekiah
IſaIsa. 38. 2, 3. maketh the good ſeruiceservice he had done to God and his Church, a ground to obtaineobtain longer life: ſoso others.

For God layeth no dutieduty on any man, but therein he aimeth at the good of him who performeth the dutieduty as well as of him to whom the dutieduty is performed. Whereby he would ſhewshow that his CommandementsCommandments are no ſtraitstrait yokes and heauieheavy burthens, but meanesmeans of procuring their good who fulfill them.

How highly doth this commend the good reſpectrespect that 1. VſeUse. God beareth to all the ſonnessons of men: ſeekingseeking their good in euerieevery place wherein he ſettethsetteth them, either of authoritieauthority, or ſubiectionsubjection?

How ought this to ſtirrestir vsus vpup willingly and cheerefullycheerfully to 2. VſeUse. obſerueobserve the LawesLaws which God commandeth vsus, and performeperform the ſeruicesservices he requireth of vsus, ſeeingseeing thereby we procure our owneown good?

How fully may this ſatisfiesatisfy, and eueneven ſtopstop the mouthesmouths of 3. VſeUse. all ſuchsuch as are diſcontentdiscontent with their places, and mutter againſtagainst that ſubiectionsubjection which God enioynethenjoineth to them?

What a good direction and reſolutionresolution may this be to many, 4. VſeUse. who being mouedmoved in conſcienceconscience to ſeekeseek the good of others, doubt whether therein they may aimeaim at their owneown good or no? To make this caſecase cleareclear by an inſtanceinstance, which may ſerueserve in ſteadstead of many. A MiniſterMinister faithfullfaithful in his place, and verievery
painfullpainful, and in that reſpectrespect of a good conſcienceconscience, but withallwithal of a tender and weakeweak conſcienceconscience, doubteth whether thereby he may ſeekeseek maintenance to himſelfehimself, fearing that ſoso he ſeekethseeketh himſelfehimself, and not ſimplysimply the edification of Gods Church. But by the forenamed doctrine we ſeesee that both may be aimed at: for God commandeth the one, and promiſethpromiseth the other. As we hauehave one eye on Gods CommandementCommandment for direction, ſoso we may hauehave another on his promiſepromise for incouragementencouragement.

Yet becauſebecause through the corruption of our nature, we are too Cautions in ſeekingseeking our owneown good. prone to ſeekeseek our ſeluesselves, ſomesome cautions are in this point carefully to be obſeruedobserved.
1. That we ſeekeseek not our owneown good by any tranſgreſſiontransgression, for it is promiſedpromised vntounto obedience.
2. That we doedo not ſoso wholly ſeekeseek our ſeluesselves and our owneown good, as we neglect others: for God hauinghaving ioynedjoined both together, no man may put them aſunderasunder.
3. That we aimeaim at our owneown good, as a reward following vponupon the dutieduty which God commandeth, and ſoso be as willing to doedo the dutieduty, as deſirousdesirous of the reward.

4. That our owneown benefit be not the only, no nor the chiefeſtchiefest thing we aimeaim at in doing our dutieduty, but rather come as a motiuemotive to addeadd an edge, and to ſharpensharpen other motiuesmotives of greater moment. And thus much the order which the ApoſtleApostle obſeruethobserueth in ſettingsetting downedown his reaſonsreasons, noteth vntounto vsus: for the three former hauehave reſpectrespect to God, and to that good conſcienceconscience which children ought to carriecarry towards him: the firſtfirst pointeth at Gods image which parents cariecary (in the Lord:) the ſecondsecond ſettethsetteth forth that right which God hath preſcribedprescribed to children: the third declareth Gods charge: this fourth only, which is the laſtlast, hath reſpectrespect to the profit and benefit of children themſeluesthemselves.

div.head: §. 99. Of preferring honeſtiehonesty before commoditiecommodity.
div.p:
From the forenamed order we may further gather, that EquitieEquity and good conſcienceconscience ought more to mouemove vsus to doedo our dutieduty then our owneown profit, and the benefit that thereby redoundeth to vsus. If there ſhouldshould come ſuchsuch an oppoſitionopposition betwixt theſethese that they could not both ſtandstand togethet, but that for doing that which is right, and which God hath commanded, our
proſperitieprosperity muſtmust be hindredhindered and life ſhortnedshortened, we ſhouldshould ſoso ſtandstand to that which is right and commanded of God, as proſperitieprosperity, life and all be let goego. To this purpoſepurpose tend all the exhortations in Scripture, to forſakeforsake goods, lands, life, and euerieevery thing elſeelse for righteouſneſſerighteousness ſakesake. So cleareclear is this point, Cic. lib. 2. de Offic. & Paradox. 1. that the Heathen diſcerneddiscerned it by the glimpſeglimpse of that light of nature which they had: for they could ſaysay, that that which is honeſthonest and right, is to be preferred before that which is commodious and profitable.

There is no compariſoncomparison betwixt honeſtiehonesty and commoditiecommodity, right and profit. The one is abſolutelyabsolutely neceſſarienecessary for attaining to eternalleternal ſaluationsalvation, the other giuethgiveth but a little quiet and contentment in this world: nay, if profit be without right, it can giuegive no true contentment or quiet at all.

VnworthieUnworthy therefore they are of the name of ChriſtiansChristians, who VſeUse. ſoso wholly and only aimeaim at their outward profit and proſperitieprosperity, as they regard not what is right, and what God hath commanded. If by obeying God, and doing that which is right they may reapereap ſomesome benefit to themſeluesthemselves they can be content Nihil bonum Scriptura niſinisi quod honeſtumhonestum aſſeritasserit. Ambr. Offic. lib. 2. cap. 3. to yeeldyield thereunto: but if not, farewell all right, farewell all Gods commandementscommandments. Though they thinkethink eueryevery thing that is profitable, be it right or wrong, to be good, yet Gods word accounteth nothing good but that which is honeſthonest: ſuchsuch therefore can lookelook for no bleſſingblessing from the Lord.

div.head: §. 100. Of the meaning of the third verſeverse.

p.hi: That it may be well with thee, and thou maiſtmaist liuelive long on the earth.

div.p:
THeThe promiſepromise mentioned before in generallgeneral, is here particularly ſetset downedown. The firſtfirst words (that it may be well with thee) are not in the Hebrew text Exod. 20. 12. there where the Law is firſtfirst recorded, and thereupon not ſetset in that vſuallusual formeform of the ten CommandementsCommandments, which is in vſeuse among vsus: but yet in Deut. 5. 16. another place where the Law is repeated, they are ſetset downedown: and the GreekeGreek tranſlationtranslation, commonly called the Septuagint (which (as is probable) the Church in the ApoſtlesApostles time vſedused) hath expreſlyexpressly noted it in both places. Now this part of the promiſepromise
(that it may be well with thee) is prefixed as an amplification of the other part concerning long life, which is the moſtmost principallprincipal thing intended, as appeareth in that it only is mentioned where the Law is firſtfirst recorded. It ſhewethshoweth that the long life Longlife and proſperitieprosperity ioynedjoined together. which God promiſethpromiseth, ſhallshall not be a life of woe and miſeriemisery, (for then were it no bleſsingblessing, but the longer life laſtedlasted, the worſeworse it would be) but a life full of comfort and happineſſehappiness: therefore MoſesMoses fetteth this former clauſeclause in the latter place after long life thus (that thy dayesdays may be prolonged, and that it
Deut. 5. 16. may goego well with thee) to ſhewshow that the well being here ſpokenspoken of, is an amplification of the benefit of long life.

Whereas the ApoſtleApostle ſettethsetteth downedown the place where the benefit of this promiſepromise is to be enioyedenjoyed in a moſtmost large phraſephrase, thus (on earth) the Law bringeth it to a more narrow compaſſecompass thus (in the land which the Lord thy God giuethgiveth thee) meaning the land of Canaan which was giuengiven of God as a peculiar inheritance to the IewesJews: ſoso that the promiſepromise (as the Law ſettethsetteth it downedown in peculiar to the IewesJews) implieth long life, and proſperitieprosperity in their owneown inheritance: for long life to the IewesJews was counted no life out of their owneown CountreyCountry. But the ApoſtleApostle writing to all nations, leauethleaveth out that deſcriptiondescription of Canaan, and retaineth only the generallgeneral ſubſtancesubstance in this word (on earth) which he ſettethsetteth downedown to ſhewshow that eueneven outward proſperitieprosperity, and a long life in this world is here promiſedpromised.

div.head: §. 101. Of proſperitieprosperity: how farrefar forth it may be a bleſſingblessing.
div.p: For further clearing of this text, and for better application thereof, I will reſolueresolve ſundriesundry queſtionsquestions ariſingarising out of it, and gather ſuchsuch profitable inſtructionsinstructions as it affordeth.
The promiſepromise conſiſtethconsisteth of two branches.

div.head: 1. QuſtQust. What may be the extent of this phraſephrase in this place? TemporallTemporal proſperitieprosperity promiſedpromised. 1 Tim. 4. 8.
div.p:
AnſwAnsw. It may generally be extended to all manner of good things. For GodlineſſeGodliness hath promiſepromise of the life that now is and of
that that is to come. But (as I take it) temporalltemporal proſperitieprosperity is here principally intended: and that for theſethese reaſonsreasons.
1. It is ioynedjoined with long life, which is a temporalltemporal bleſsingblessing.
2. The laſtlast word (on earth) may be referred to this branch of well-being, as well as to the other of long life.

3. In the Law (from whence this clauſeclause is taken) it is expreſlyexpressly ſetset downedown, thus, that it may goego well with thee in the
Deut. 5. 16. land, &etcc.

div.head: 2. QueſtQuest. Is then outward temporalltemporal proſperitieprosperity (as honour, ProſperitieProsperity a good thing. health, peace, libertieliberty, goods, &etcc.) a token of Gods louelove and fauourfavour?
div.p: AnſwAnsw. Yea: in it ſelfeself it is a bleſsingblessing, and fruit of Gods louelove: as appeareth by theſethese reaſonsreasons.
1. As at firſtfirst it was made and ordained of God, it is a good thing.
2. It tendeth to mans good, if it be rightly vſedused.
3. It was beſtowedbestowed on man before he had offended.
4. It is promiſedpromised of God as a reward to them that fearefear him LeuitLevit. 26. 4. &etcc. Deut. 28. 1. &etcc. and keepekeep his CommandementsCommandments.
5. The Saints hauehave prayed for it, and hauehave beenebeen thankfullthankful Gen. 28. 20. & 32. 10, 11. for it.

6. The contrariecontrary was firſtfirst inflicted as a puniſhmentpunishment of ſinnesin, LeuitLevit. 26. 15. &etcc. and is oft threatnedthreatened as a token of Gods wrath, and ſoso hath alſoalso beenebeen inflicted on tranſgreſſorstransgressors. Deut. 28. 16. &etcc.

div.head: §. 102. Of proſperitieprosperity beſtowedbestowed on the wicked, how it prouesproves a curſecurse.

div.p:
3. QueſtQuest. Why then is it beſtowedbestowed vponupon the wicked, eueneven ſuchsuch as are
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . haters of God, and are hated of him? And why are Gods friends, ſuchsuch as are
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . louedloved of him, and louelove him againeagain, depriueddeprived thereof? This ſoresore ſcruplescruple made DauidDavid ſtumblestumble, PſalPsal. 73. 13. IerJer. 12. 1. Hab. 1. 3. and mouedmoved other Prophets to complainecomplain. But the anſweranswer is readieready.

AnſwAnsw. Outward proſperitieprosperity is of that nature, as it may turneturn to the good or hurt of him that enioyethenjoyeth it. And herein is Gods admirable and vnſearchableunsearchable wiſdomewisdom ſeeneseen, in that he is able to turneturn bleſſingsblessings into curſescurses, and curſescurses into bleſſingsblessings. How proſperitieprosperity prouesproves a curſecurse to the wicked. He can workework by contraries.

div.head: 4. QueſtQuest. How is proſperitieprosperity a curſecurse to the wicked?
div.p:
AnſwAnsw. By meeremere conſequenceconsequence, through their abuſeabuse of it. God giuesgives it to them to ſhewshow the riches of his merciemercy: and that all may taſtetaste thereof, he doth good to the euillevil and the good. BeſidesBesides, Matth. 5. 45. div.head: §. 103. How both hauinghaving, and wanting proſperitieprosperity is a bleſſingblessing to the Saints.

div.p:
AnſwAnsw. God in wiſdomewisdom knowing what is beſtbest for them accordingly dealesdeals with them, he beſtowethbestoweth proſperitieprosperity on them ſoso farrefar as he ſeethseeth it will turneturn vntounto their good: and denieth it to them ſoso farrefar as he ſeethseeth it will turneturn to their hurt. WhenſoeuerWhensoever therefore God beſtowethbestoweth any temporalltemporal bleſſingblessing on his Saints, it is a token of his favour: and whenſoeuerwhensoever he denieth any, the very denialldenial is alſoalso a fruit of his fauourfavour. Herein is it verified that All things workework together for good to them
Rom. 8. 28. that louelove God, ſoso as, if they abound, it ſhallshall goego well with them: if they want, it ſhallshall goego well with them: if they be in high place, it ſhallshall goego well with them: if in meanemean place, it ſhallshall got well with them: if they be at libertieliberty, if in priſonprison: if they be in health, if ſickesick: in what eſtateestate ſoeuersoever, it ſhallshall goego well with them.

div.head: §. 104. Of long-life: how farrefar forth it is a bleſſingblessing.
div.p: Concerning the ſecondsecond branch of Gods promiſepromise (long-life) other queſtionsquestions are to be reſoluedresolved.

div.head: 1. QueſtQuest. Is long-life a bleſſingblessing? Long life a bleſſingblessing.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. Yea, elſeelse would not God here and in other places hauehave promiſedpromised it as a reward, nor hauehave beſtowedbestowed it on his Saints.
The reaſonsreasons to proueprove it to be a bleſſingblessing may be drawnedrawn to three heads. 1. Gods glorieglory. 2. the good of the Church where they liuelive. 3. their owneown good.

1. Gods glorieglory is much aduancedadvanced by the long life of the Saints: for the longer they liuelive the more they doedo themſeluesthemselves obſerueobserve Gods wonderfullwonderful workesworks, and the more they doedo make them knowneknown and declare them to others. But in the grauegrave all PſalPsal. 6. 5. IſaIsa. 38. 18. is forgotten.

Phil. 1. 24. you: In the Saints that is true which Elihu ſaithsaith ſhouldshould be, namely that daiesdays ſpeakespeak, and multitude of yeeresyears teach wiſdomewisdom.
IobJob. 32. 7. The longer the Saints liuelive, the more good they doedo: but after death they doedo none: when the night commethcometh no man can workework:
IobJob. 9. 4.
Gal. 6. 10. vponupon which ground the ApoſtleApostle exhorteth to doedo good while we hauehave time.

3. The Saints by long liuingliving purchaſepurchase to themſeluesthemselves great honour, and dignitiedignity among Gods people, and a ſtrongstrong ſtedfaſtstedfast confidence in God. Men regard a good old ſeruantservant: much more will God. Two ſtrongstrong props hauehave old Saints to eſtabliſhestablish them, and make them bold: one is a remembrance of Gods former fauoursfavours, whereby their hope of eternalleternal life is made more ſuresure vntounto them: another is a kindekind of preſentpresent expectation of the accompliſhmentaccomplishment of Gods promiſespromises which they hauehave long waited for.
By this it appearesappears that this particular promiſepromise is no light matter, of ſmallsmall moment: but a ſtrongstrong motiuemotive to ſtirrestir vpup children to obedience.

div.head: §. 105. Of long life prouingproving a curſecurse to the wicked.
2. QueſtQuest.

AnſwAnsw. Long life is of the ſamesame kindekind that proſperitieprosperity is: it may be turned to a curſecurse, as well as proueprove a bleſſingblessing.

The wicked by liuingliving long on earth make their ſinssins grow to the full (as is implied of the Amorite) they make their Gen. 15. 16. name to ſtinkestink the more on earth, as a carion the longer it remaineth aboueabove ground the more it ſtinkethstinketh: and they cauſecause the greater torment in hell to be inflicted vponupon them: for as Rom. 2. 5. ſinnesin is increaſedincreased, ſoso ſhallshall that torment be increaſedincreased.

The righteous hauehave their daiesdays ſhortnedshortened for their good, when they are ſhortnedshortened, and that in theſethese, and ſuchsuch like reſpectsrespects
