4. That their Gen. 5. 24. Heb. 11. 5. chiefeſtchiefest and greateſtgreatest reward might be haſtenedhastened.

div.head: §. 106. Of limiting the promiſespromises of temporalltemporal bleſſingsblessings.
div.p: Thus we ſeesee there may be iuſtjust cauſecause to alter, as the former branch of this promiſepromise, proſperitieprosperity, ſoso the latter branch of it, long-life, and yet no wrong thereby redound to the righteous, nor benefit to the wicked.

div.head: 3. QueſtQuest.
div.p: Is not the truth of the promiſepromise impeached thereby?

AnſwAnsw. No whit at all. For firſtfirst all promiſespromises of temporalltemporal bleſſingsblessings are limited with ſuchsuch a condition as this, if the performance of it may ſtandstand with Gods honour, and the good of the partieparty to whom it is made. 2. God doth neuernever ſimplysimply depriuedeprive his Saints of that which is promiſedpromised, but only in ſteadstead of it giuethgiveth a better: as in taking away wealth, he giuethgiveth the more ſtorestore of grace: in reſtrainingrestraining liberty of body, he giuethgiveth freedomefreedom of conſcienceconscience: with affliction he giuethgiveth patience: by taking away this temporalltemporal life, he giuethgiveth eternalleternal life. God herein dealeth, as if one who hauinghaving promiſedpromised ſoso much iron, ſhouldshould in ſteadstead thereof giuegive as much ſiluersilver: or for ſiluersilver giuegive gold: and ſoso for one pound giuegive the worth of hundreds or thouſandsthousands.

div.head: §. 107. Of appropriating proſperityprosperity and long-life to the obedience which children yeeldyield to their parents.
4. QueſtQuest. Why is long-life and proſperityprosperity appropriated to this kindekind of righteouſneſſerighteousness?
div.p: AnſwAnsw. It is not ſoso appropriated to this, as if it appertained to no other: for it is elſewhereelsewhere in generallgeneral promiſedpromised to the Deut. 6. 2. obſeruersobservers of the whole law, and to other particular branches thereof beſidebeside this: yet in theſethese and ſuchsuch like particular reſpectsrespects PſalPsal. 34. 12, 13, 14. is it applied to the obedience of children.

1. BecauſeBecause obedience to parents is one of the ſureſtsurest euidencesevidences of our conformity to the whole law: in that thereby we ſhewshow our reſpectrespect of Gods image, and lay a good foundation for the performing of all dutieduty to man.

2. BecauſeBecause a childes performing of his dutieduty to his parents is vnderunder God an eſpeciallespecial meanesmeans that they doedo well, and liuelive long (for as rebellious children make their parents with griefegrief to come the ſoonersooner to their grauesgraves, ſoso dutifulldutiful children make them to continue the longer in proſperityprosperity) the Lord in recompencerecompense promiſethpromiseth to ſuchsuch a childechild proſperityprosperity and long life.

3. BecauſeBecause parents are an eſpeciallespecial meanesmeans to procure the welfare and long life of their children, partly by their prouidentprovident
care, as Noami ſaidsaid to Ruth, ſhallshall I not ſeekeseek reſtrest for thee,

In this reſpectrespect the law thus ſettethsetteth forth the bleſſingblessing of the fiftfifth commandementcommandment, they ſhallshall prolong thy daiesdays.

4. BecauſeBecause diſobediencedisobedience to parents bringeth much miſchiefemischief on childrens heads, and oft ſhortenethshorteneth their daiesdays, and that many waiesways.

1. In that parents are oft prouokedprovoked by their childrens diſobediencedisobedience How diſobedientdisobedient children hinder their welfare and ſhortenshorten their daiesdays. to diſinheritdisinherit them, at leaſtleast to allow them the leſſeless portion, ſoso as hereby it goeth not ſoso well with them: yea ſomesome are prouokedprovoked to bring their rebellious children to the MagiſtrateMagistrate, who by Gods law was to cut them off, ſoso as Deut. 21. 21. thereby their life is ſhortenedshortened.

2. In that parents are prouokedprovoked to complainecomplain vntounto God of their childrens diſobediencedisobedience, and God thereby mouedmoved both to lay heauieheavy iudgementsjudgments vponupon ſuchsuch children in their life time, and alſoalso to ſhortenshorten their daiesdays: for parents complaint doth make a loud criecry in Gods earesears. InſtanceInstance the examples of 1 Sam. 2. 34. Hophni and Phinehas, 2 Sam. 18. 14. AbſolomAbsalom, and 1 King. 2. 25. Adonijah.

4. In that diſobediencedisobedience to parents, is a ſinnesin that ſeldomeseldom goeth alone: for an vndutifullundutiful childechild is commonly a verievery lewd perſonperson many other waiesways. ConſideringConsidering the proueneſſeproveness of our nature to all ſinnesin, it cannot be auoidedavoided but that they who in the beginning ſhakeshake off the yoakeyoke of gouernmentgovernment, ſhouldshould run headlong into all riot, looſeneſſelooseness, and licentiouſneſſelicentiousness: thus then ſinnesin being added vntounto ſinnesin, it muſtmust needs bring miſchiefemischief vponupon miſchiefemischief, till at length life be cut off.

Wherefore in that theſethese miſchiefesmischiefs are auoidedavoided by performing due obedience to parents, it may well be ſaidsaid that it ſhallshall be well with obedient children, and they ſhallshall liuelive long.

div.head: §. 108. Of Gods ordering his fauoursfavours ſoso as they may appeareappear to be true bleſſingsblessings.
div.p: The particular branches of Gods promiſepromise hauinghaving beenebeen How fitly proſperityprosperity and long life are ioynedjoined together. diſtinctlydistinctly opened, we will conſiderconsider them ioyntlyjointly together, for they doedo exceedingly amplifieamplify one another: proſperityprosperity ſweetenssweetens long life and makes it acceptable: otherwiſeotherwise to liuelive long, namely in miſerymisery and wretchedneſſewretchedness, is very irkſomeirksome and grieuousgrievous. AgaineAgain, long life added to proſperityprosperity maketh it ſoso much the greater bleſſingblessing. For a good thing the longer it continueth the better it is. If proſperityprosperity were but as a flower, ſoonesoon gone, the very thought of the vanity thereof would much diminiſhdiminish the ioyjoy and comfort of it. But both of them ioynedjoined together, doedo ſhewshow that this is no ſmallsmall bleſſingblessing which is promiſedpromised.
From the connexionconnection of them both together, I obſerueobserve that

God ſoso ordereth his fauoursfavours as they appeareappear to be true bleſſingsblessings, God makes his ſauourssavours true bleſſingsblessings. Gen. 17. 19. tending indeed to the good of thoſethose vponupon whom he beſtowethbestoweth them. Thus when God gauegave Abraham a ſonneson, he eſtabliſhedestablished his couenantcovenant with him, that this gift might be a true bleſſingblessing.

The like I might inſtanceinstance in all the children of promiſepromise, as SampſonSamson, SalomonSolomon, IohnJohn BaptiſtBaptist, &etcc. So in other fauoursfavours. When God added fifteenefifteen yearesyears to Hezekiahs life, he alſoalso promiſedpromised IſaIsa. 38. 5, 6. & 39. 8. him deliuerancedeliverance from his enemies, and peace, and truth all his daiesdays: And when God gauegave DauidDavid a kingdomekingdom, he gauegave him 2 Sam. 7. 9. &etcc. great victories and long life, and eſtabliſhedestablished his kingdomekingdom to his poſterityposterity: ſoso alſoalso dealt he with SalomonSolomon. But not to inſiſtinsist on any more particulars, excellently is this doctrine confirmed in the 28 PſalmePsalm.

Thus God will ſhewshow that in louelove he beſtowethbestoweth eueneven the temporalltemporal bleſſingsblessings which he giuethgiveth to his Saints, that accordingly they may eſteemeesteem them, and that their hearts may be the more inlargedenlarged both to admire his goodneſſegoodness, and to be thankfullthankful for the ſamesame.

This vſeuse we muſtmust make of thoſethose things which the Lord is 1. VſeUse. pleaſedpleased to beſtowbestow vponupon vsus, as of long life, good health, honour, peace, plenty, liberty, and all proſperityprosperity: we muſtmust receiuereceive and vſeuse them as God beſtowethbestoweth them, namely as tokens
of his fauourfavour: and thereby be the more ſtirredstirred vpup to performeperform the duties he requireth of vsus, and not abuſeabuse them to his diſhonourdishonour and our owneown hurt: but rather ſoso as he may hauehave honour, and we profit thereby.

div.head: §. 109. Of Gods high account of dutifulldutiful children.
div.p: More particularly by this promiſepromise we may learnelearn what high 2. VſeUse. eſteemeesteem, and great account God maketh of dutifulldutiful children, and of that obedience which they performeperform to their parents: which ought ſoso much the more to prouokeprovoke children to all obedience, if at leaſtleast they hauehave any care of Gods fauourfavour, and of the tokens of his louelove. Oh conſiderconsider this all yeeye that hauehave parents to honour: conſiderconsider how carefullcareful, how earneſtearnest God is eueryevery way by all meanesmeans to draw you to obedience: he contents not himſelfehimself to vrgeurge the equity of the point, the place of your parent, the charge that himſelfehimself hath giuengiven, but moſtmost preſſethpresseth your owneown profit: and that not only in hope for the time to come, but eueneven in preſentpresent fruition for this life: and that becauſebecause we through our childiſhneſſechildishness are moſtmost affected with things ſenſiblesensible and preſentpresent: dealing with vsus as a tender father who prouidethprovideth not only a good calling, and a fairefair in heritance for his childechild, but giuethgiveth him alſoalso plums, pearespears, and ſuchsuch things as for the preſentpresent he is delighted withallwithal, the more to allure him.

div.head: §. 110. Of childrens doing good to themſeluesthemselves by honouring their parents.
div.p:
Children may further learnelearn out of this promiſepromise, that in 3. VſeUse. performing their dutieduty they doedo good not only to their parents, but alſoalso to themſeluesthemselves: they procure their owneown welfare and long-life. What egregious foolesfools then are diſobedientdisobedient children: they regard neither God, their parents, nor themſeluesthemselves, but depriuedeprive themſeluesthemselves of their eternalleternal happineſſehappiness, hinder their welfare, and ſhortenshorten their daiesdays. Fitly hereupon I may applieapply to vndutifullundutiful children theſethese words of the PſalmiſtPsalmist, MarkeMark the obedient childechild, for the end of him is peace:
PſalPsal. 37 37, 38. but the rebellious ſhallshall be deſtroyeddestroyed: he ſhallshall be cut off: and theſethese of the wiſewise-man, I know that it ſhallshall be well with the dutifulldutiful
Eccl. 8. 12, 13. childechild, but it ſhallshall not be well with the diſobedientdisobedient, he ſhallshall not prolong his daiesdays: and theſethese of the Prophet, Say ye to the obedient
childechild, it ſhallshall be well with him, he ſhallshall eat the fruit of his doings,

div.head: §. 111. Of parents doing good to their children by keeping them vnderunder obedience.
div.p: Out of this promiſepromise parents may learnelearn how to doedo good 4. UſeUse. for their children, how to prouideprovide for their welfare, and long to preſeruepreserve their life on earth (a thing whereunto moſtmost parents are naturally giuengiven, and whereof they are much deſirousdesirous) namely by teaching children their dutieduty, by keeping them vnderunder obedience: thus hauehave they Gods promiſepromise to aſſureassure them, that it ſhallshall goego well with their children, and that they ſhallshall liuelive long. When parents are vponupon their death-beds they may reſtrest more ſecurelysecurely vponupon this promiſepromise then vponupon great ſtorestore of treaſuretreasure laid vpup for them, and great reuenuesrevenues reſeruedreserved for them. Many parents neglect themſeluesthemselves: they moilemoil and toile, they carkecark and care, they pinch and ſparespare, to leaueleave their children ſtorestore of wealth, thinking thereby to doedo good to their children, when as withallwithal they too much cocker their children, giuegive the reinesreins vntounto them, and care not how little dutieduty they performeperform. Gods curſecurse will lie vponupon all the ſtorestore that is laid vpup for ſuchsuch children, as a fire to conſumeconsume it all. Doth not daily experience verifieverify the truth hereof? The iudgementsjudgments which are laid on ſomesome ſuchsuch children, doedo euidentlyevidently manifeſtmanifest Gods iuſtjust indignation againſtagainst all. Let not rich men therefore thinkethink they hauehave left their children well enough if they leaueleave them a large portion, but rather if they hauehave obſeruedobserved them to be obedient children: and if poorepoor mens children be ſuchsuch, let them not fearefear but that it ſhallshall goego well with them.

It is ſaidsaid, that a good trade is better then houſehouse and land, but by vertuevirtue of this promiſepromise we may ſaysay that obedience in a childechild is better then trade and all: this is the trade of a childes
ProuProv. 22. 6. way which parents ſhouldshould teach children. Wherefore as parents are deſirousdesirous of their childrens good, ſoso they ought to be wiſewise in procuring it, which is by teaching them this trade of obedience: and ſoso they ſhallshall bring much comfort to themſeluesthemselves while they liuelive, and good to their children after them.

div.head: §. 112. Of the perpetuitieperpetuity of the ſubſtancesubstance of ſuchsuch things as in their circumſtancescircumstances reſpectingrespecting the IewesJews are vaniſhedvanished.
div.p: In laying downedown this particular promiſepromise, the ApoſtleApostle in ſteadstead of the limitation thereof vntounto the IewesJews in theſethese words (in the land which the Lord thy God ſhallshall giuegive thee) putteth a generallgeneral word, which extendeth it to all nations, namely this (in the earth) whence I gather that

The ſubſtancesubstance of theſethese things which in ſomesome circumſtancescircumstances were
Doctr. SubſtanceSubstance of promiſespromises made to the IewesJews ſtillstill remaineth. after a peculiar manner reſtrainedrestrained to the IewesJews, remaineth in force to all ChriſtiansChristians. The ſubſtancesubstance of this promiſepromise was, that it ſhouldshould goego well with obedient children, while here on earth they liuedlived, and in this welfare they ſhouldshould long liuelive. The circumſtancecircumstance was, that in Canaan they ſhouldshould inioyenjoy that bleſſingblessing. Though ChriſtiansChristians liuelive not in Canaan, which is the circumſtancecircumstance, yet well it ſhallshall goego with them, and long they ſhallshall liuelive, which is the ſubſtancesubstance. Thus though the circumſtancecircumstance of Gods couenantcovenant with Abraham (which was circumciſioncircumcision) be aboliſhedabolished, yet the ſubſtancesubstance (which is, to be our God, and the God of our ſeedseed) remaineth. This might further be exemplified in many hundred inſtancesinstances: for the ſubſtancesubstance of all the IewiſhJewish ſacrificessacrifices, and Sacraments, both ordinarieordinary, and extraordinarieextraordinary, of their Sabbaths, of their faſtsfasts, of their feaſtsfeasts, and the like, remaineremain, though the circumſtancescircumstances, as ſhadowesshadows, be vaniſhedvanished away. epigraph.q: And ye fathers, prouokeprovoke not your children to wrath: but bring them vpup in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.

div.p: THeThe ApoſtleApostle hauinghaving vrgedurged children to performeperform their duties to their parents, he turneth his ſpeechspeech to parents, ſayingsaying, AND ye fathers, &etcc. That copulatiuecopulative particle AND, ioyningjoining an exhortation to parents, for performing their duties to the forenamed exhortation made to children, giuethgiveth vsus to vnderſtandunderstand, that

Parents are as well bound to dutieduty as children. Their duties 1. ObſeruObseru. All the directions and exhortations throughout the Scripture giuengiven vntounto parents, concerning their dutieduty, and all the threatningsthreatenings denounced, and iudgementsjudgments executed on parents for neglect of their dutieduty, are pregnant proofesproofs of this point.

Though parents be ouerover their children, and by them cannot be commanded, yet they are vnderunder God: and he it is who hath enioynedenjoined them their dutieduty: ſoso as they are bound thereunto, as they will anſweranswer it to their Fatherfather in heauenheaven.

The authoritieauthority which parents hauehave, is not ſoso much for their owneown aduancementadvancement, as for the better gouerninggoverning of their children, which being ſoso, their verievery gouernmentgovernment is a dutieduty.

div.p:
AnſwAnsw. Parentsparents dutieduty (as many others duties) is by iuſtjust and neceſſarienecessary conſequenceconsequence implied, which is equiualentequivalent, and as
much bindeth, as if it were expreſſedexpressed. It is thus implied. They who hauehave honour, muſtmust carriecarry themſeluesthemselves worthieworthy of honour. Now the way to carriecarry themſeluesthemselves worthieworthy of honour, is to be carefullcareful in doing dutieduty to them that honour them. MiniſtersMinisters muſtmust prouokeprovoke parents to their dutieduty. and carriecarry an eueneven hand towards all of all ſortssorts: let them not be partiallpartial in laying all the burden of dutieduty on childrens necks, and none on parents: holding in children verievery ſtraitlystraitly, but leauingleaving parents to their owneown will. Parents are fleſhflesh and bloudblood as well as children, and as prone to tranſgreſſetransgress in their place, as children in theirs. Yea, MiniſtersMinisters ought of the two to be more earneſtearnest in vrgingurging parents to performeperform their dutieduty, becauſebecause they are vnderunder no ſuchsuch power and authoritieauthority as children are. FeareFear of parents authoritieauthority keepeth children much in awe. There is no ſuchsuch thing to keepekeep parents in awe. They will be more readieready therefore to take the greater libertieliberty, if by fearefear of God, and by a good conſcienceconscience, they be not kept in compaſſecompass.

Now ye (ô parents) as you lookelook for honour, carriecarry yourſeluesyourselves 2. UſeUse. worthieworthy of honour: as ye lookelook for dutieduty from your children, performeperform dutieduty to them. Know that another day, eueneven you ſhallshall be called to an account before the higheſthighest IudgeJudge: your authoritieauthority will then be no pretence to excuſeexcuse, but an euidenceevidence to aggrauateaggravate your fault. For you being elder in yeeresyears, and more eminent in place, of more experience, and hauinghaving a charge ouerover your children, ought to be a light to ſhewshow them the way, an example to allure them, that they ſeeingseeing you carefullcareful and conſcionableconscionable in performing your dutieduty, may be the more prouokedprovoked to performeperform theirs, or at leaſtleast made aſhamedashamed of their neglect of dutieduty. But if you be careleſſecareless of your dutieduty, how can ye expect dutieduty at their hands? nayNay if by your ill example they hauehave beenebeen made negligent, their bloudblood ſhallshall be required at your hands.

div.head: §. 123. Of the ſubiectionsubjection which beleeuingbelieving ſeruantsservants owe.
div.p: BecauſeBecause there is yet another order in the family beſidesbesides thoſethose which hauehave been noted before, namely the order of Maſtersmasters & ſeruantsservants, the ApoſtleApostle preſcribethprescribeth alſoalso vntounto them their dutieduty.

As he began with wiueswives and children, in the two former orders, ſoso here he beginnethbeginnethbegineth with ſeruantsservants who are the inferioursinferiors, for the ſamesame reaſonsreasons §. 10. Why the ApoſtleApostle is ſoso copious in vrgingurging ſeruantsservants to their dutieduty. before rendredrendered.

The ApoſtleApostle is ſomewhatsomewhat copious in laying forth the duties of ſeruantsservants, and in vrgingurging them to performeperform their dutieduty; and that for two eſpeciallespecial reaſonsreasons: One in reſpectrespect of thoſethose, whoſewhose maſtersmasters were infidels: another in reſpectrespect of thoſethose, whoſewhose maſtersmasters were Saints.

1. Many ſeruantsservants there were in thoſethose daiesdays wherein the Seruus beneuolentia proſequaturprosequatur dominum, quamuis impiūimpiun. Qui fidelem habet dominum, ſaluosaluo eius dominio, diligat vt patrem. ConſlitConslit. ApoſtApost. li. 4. ca. 12. Gal. 4. 28. GoſpellGospel was firſtfirst preached to the Gentiles, that by the preaching thereof were conuertedconverted, whoſewhose maſtersmasters embraced not the GoſpellGospel: whereupon thoſethose ſeruantsservants began to conceit that they being ChriſtiansChristians, ought not to be ſubiectsubject to their maſtersmasters that were infidels.

2. Other ſeruantsservants there were whoſewhose Maſtersmasters beleeuedbelieved the GoſpellGospel as well as they: now becauſebecause the GoſpellGospel taught, that there is neither bond nor free, but all are one in ChriſtChrist IeſusJesus: they thought that they ought not to be ſubiectsubject to their maſtermaster who was their brother in ChriſtChrist.

TheſeThese two prepoſterouspreposterous and preſumptuouspresumptuous conceits doth the ApoſtleApostle intimate, and expreſlyexpressly meet with in 1 Tim. 6. 1, 2. another
place. And becauſebecause they had taken too deepedeep rooting in the mindesminds of many ſeruantsservants, the ApoſtleApostle here in this place laboureth the more earneſtlyearnestly to root them out, and that by a thorowthorough preſſingpressing vponupon their conſcienceconscience that ſubiectionsubjection wherein they are bound to their maſtersmasters, as maſtersmasters, whatſoeuerwhatsoever their diſpoſitiondisposition were. Hereof more Treat. 7. §. 2, 3. afterwards.

Here by the way, note three points.
1. The GoſpellGospel doth not free inferioursinferiors from that ſubiectionsubjection 1. ObſerObser. to men whereunto by the morallmoral law they are bound.
2. Men are ready to turneturn the grace of God into libertieliberty. 2. ObſerObser.
3. As errors begin to ſproutsprout vpup in the Church, MiniſtersMinisters 3. ObſerObser. muſtmust be carefullcareful to root them out.

div.p:
THisThis title (Seruantsservants) is a generallgeneral title, which may be applied

SeruileServile, as being borne ſeruantsservants, or ſoldsold for ſeruantsservants, or taken in warrewar, or ranſomedransomed; For of old they were called ſeruantsservants, who being taken in warrewar, were ſauedsaved from death.

Wherefore whatſoeuerwhatsoever the birth, parentage, eſtateestate, or former condition of any hauehave beenebeen; being

SeruantsServants they muſtmust be ſubiectsubject, and doedo the dutieduty of ſeruantsservants: the 4. ObſerObser. ApoſtlesApostles indefinite title (ſeruantsservants) admittethadmittethadmiteth no exception of any.

The other title (Maſtersmasters) hath as large an extent compriſingcomprising
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . What maſtersmasters are meant. vnderunder it both ſexessexes, Maſtersmasters and Miſtreſſesmistresses: and of theſethese all ſortssorts, great and meanemean, rich and poorepoor, ſtrongstrong and weakeweak,
faithfullfaithful and infidels, true profeſſorsprofessors and profane; ſuperſtitioussuperstitious, idolatrous, hereticallheretical perſonspersons, or the like: ſoso as

from performing dutieduty to him.

div.p: Among other degrees and differences, moſtmost eſpeciallyespecially let it be noted that both ſexessexes, miſtreſſesmistresses as well as maſtersmasters, are here meant, that ſoso the duties which are enioynedenjoined to be performed to maſtersmasters may anſwerablyanswerably be performed to miſtreſſesmistresses (ſoso farrefar as they are common to both) and that both by maidſeruantsmaidservants, and alſoalso by men-ſeruantsservants that are vnderunder miſtreſſesmistresses. In families miſtreſſesmistresses are as ordinary as maſtersmasters, and therefore I thought good to giuegive an eſpeciallespecial item of this.

VnderUnder this word (obey) are compriſedcomprised all thoſethose duties which
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . ſeruantsservants owe to their maſtersmasters: it is the ſamesame word that was before vſedused in the firſtfirst verſeverse: and it hath as large an extent here being applied to ſeruantsservants, as it had there being applied to children: It ſhewethshoweth that

The rule of ſeruantsservants (as ſeruantsservants) is the will of their Maſtermaster. 6. ObſeruObseru.
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 .

This clauſeclause (according to the fleſhflesh) is by ſomesome referred to the action of obedience, as if it were added by the ApoſtleApostle to ſhewshow what kindekind of obedience ſeruantsservants owe to their maſtersmasters, namely a ciuillcivil, corporallcorporal obedience in temporalltemporal things, oppoſedopposed to that ſpirituallspiritual obedience which is due to God alone.

AnſAns. Though diſtinctiondistinction may be made betwixt that ſeruiceservice which is due to God, and that which is due to man, yet this application of this phraſephrase in this place may giuegive occaſionoccasion to ſeruantsservants to thinkethink that if they performeperform outward ſeruiceservice to their maſtersmasters all is well, they owe no inward fearefear, or honour, which is an error that the ApoſtleApostle doth here mainly oppoſeoppose againſtagainst.

But becauſebecause this clauſeclause (according to the fleſhflesh) is immediatlyimmediately Why maſtersmasters are ſaidsaid to be after the fleſhflesh. Dominis carnalibus. vet. tranſltransl. ioynedjoined to Maſtersmasters, I referrerefer it to the perſonspersons to whom obedience is to be giuengiven, and ſoso take it as a deſcriptiondescription of them, as if he had ſaidsaid, to fleſhlyfleshly or bodily Maſtersmasters.
The ApoſtleApostle thus deſcribethdescribeth maſtersmasters for theſethese reaſonsreasons.

1. For diſtinctiondistinction: to ſhewshow he meanesmeans ſuchsuch maſtersmasters as are of the ſamesame mould that ſeruantsservants are: ſoso diſtinguiſhingdistinguishing them from God who is a ſpiritspirit: thus doth the ApoſtleApostle diſtinguiſhdistinguish betwixt fathers of our fleſhflesh, and father of ſpiritsspirits.
Heb. 12. 9.

2. For preuentionprevention: leftlest ſeruantsservants might ſaysay, our maſtersmasters are fleſhflesh and bloudblood as we are, why then ſhouldshould we be ſubiectsubject to them? To meet with that conceit, the ApoſtleApostle expreſlyexpressly ſaithsaith that obedience is due to maſtersmasters after the fleſhflesh.

3. For mitigation of their ſeruitudeservitude: for their maſtersmasters being fleſhflesh, they hauehave no power but ouerover the bodies of their ſeruantsservants: their ſpiritsspirits are free from them: in which reſpectrespect the ApoſtleApostle calleth ChriſtianChristian ſeruantsservants the Lords freemen. 1 Cor. 7. 22.

4. For conſolationconsolation againſtagainst their preſentpresent condition, which is but for a time, becauſebecause their maſtersmasters are fleſhflesh: whatſoeuerwhatsoever is according to the fleſhflesh is of no long continuance, but hath his date.

5. For direction: to ſhewshow in what things eſpeciallyespecially that obedience which properly belongeth to a maſtermaster conſiſtethconsisteth: namely in ciuillcivil, outward things: for eueryevery one muſtmust be ſeruedserved according to his nature. As God being ſpiritspirit, muſtmust in ſpiritspirit be ſeruedserved: ſoso man being fleſhflesh muſtmust in fleſhflesh be ſeruedserved. Now this ſeruiceservice in the fleſhflesh is not oppoſedopposed to ſinceresincere and vprightupright ſeruiceservice, but to ſpirituallspiritual. Thus by conſequenceconsequence that may be intended, which ſomesome would hauehave principally to be meant.

div.head: ObiectObject. MaſtersMasters may command ſpirituallspiritual things, namely to worſhipworship God, and after ſuchsuch and ſuchsuch a manner.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. Of his owneown head he cannot command ſuchsuch things: there muſtmust be an higher warrant for the doing of them then the commandementcommandment of a man.
A mainemain point here intended is this, that

MaſtersMasters are not to be lightly reſpectedrespected becauſebecause they be after the 7. ObſeruObseru.
fleſhflesh: that is, weakeweak, frailefrail, of ſhortshort continuance, of the ſamesame nature that ſeruantsservants are.

LeſtLest vponupon the forenamed deſcriptiondescription of maſtersmasters, ſeruantsservants SeruantsServants fearefear of their maſtersmasters. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . ſhouldshould take to themſeluesthemselves too much heart, the ApoſtleApostle annexeth this clauſeclause (with fearefear and trembling, &etcc.) which hath relation to the manner of their obedience. No ſlauiſhslavish fearefear is here meant, as if ſeruantsservants ſhouldshould liuelive in continuallcontinual dread, or tremble at the ſightsight of their maſtersmasters: a ſeruantservant by the tyrannietyranny of ſomesome maſtermaster may be brought ſoso to doedo: but to doedo ſoso is no ChriſtianChristian dutieduty: that which the ApoſtleApostle here requireth is a
dutieduty belonging to all ChriſtianChristian ſeruantsservants towards all ſortssorts of maſtersmasters, eueneven the mildeſtmildest that be. It is therefore an awfullawful reſpectrespect of the authority of a maſtermaster, and a dutifulldutiful reuerencereverence to his perſonperson which is here required: and it is oppoſedopposed to ſawcineſſesaucinesssawciness, malepartneſſemalapertnessmalepartness, boldneſſeboldness, ſtoutneſſestoutness, anſweringanswering againeagain, murmuring and muttering againſtagainst their maſtersmasters, and other like vices. To ſhewshow how foulefoul thoſethose faults be, and what great reſpectrespect ſeruantsservants ought to bearebear to their maſtersmasters, theſethese two words (fearefear, and trembling) are ioynedjoined together: which in Difference betwixt fearefear and trembling. effect declare one and the ſamesame thing: but yet for explication ſakesake they may be diſtinguiſheddistinguished. For
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . VerſVers. 33. FeareFear ſignifiethsignifieth a reuerendreverend reſpectrespect of one: it is that which in the former Chapter was required of wiueswives: though the thing in generallgeneral which is required of wiueswives and ſeruantsservants is the ſamesame, yet the particular manner and meaſuremeasure of a ſeruantsservants fearefear is farrefar different.

〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . Trembling is more proper to ſeruantsservants: it is a dread of puniſhmentpunishment: and it is required of ſeruantsservants, not as if they ſhouldshould doedo all things ſimplysimply for fearefear of puniſhmentpunishment, but becauſebecause God hath put a ſtaffestaff into a maſtersmasters hands, ſeruantsservants muſtmust tremble at that power their maſtersmasters hauehave, and fearefear to prouokeprovoke them to ſtrikestrike. To this purpoſepurpose ſaithsaith the ApoſtleApostle to ſubiectssubjects in regard of the power which a MagiſtrateMagistrate hath, be afraid, for
Rom. 13. 3, 4. he beareth not the ſwordsword in vainevain.
Hence learnelearn that

p.hi: The authority of a Maſtermaster ought to ſtrikestrike a ſeruantsservants heart with
dread.

div.p:
The dread which ſeruantsservants ought to hauehave of their maſtersmasters power and authority maketh many to care for no more then to auoidavoid their maſtersmasters diſpleaſuredispleasure: wherefore the ApoſtleApostle addeth a further degree of a ſeruantsservants ſubiectionsubjection, namely that
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . it be in ſingleneſſesingleness of heart, that is, honeſthonest, intireentire, vprightupright: for this is oppoſedopposed to hypocriſiehypocrisy, diſſimulationdissimulation, and fraud: yea of YOVRYOUR heart, not anothers: another in the ſimplicitysimplicity of his heart may thinkethink you doedo a thing better then you doedo, by a charitable conſtructionconstruction of euerieevery thing, but if in ſingleneſſesingleness of your owneown heart you doedo it, it will in truth be as it appeareth to be. So as

p.hi: All the ſeruicesservices which ſeruantsservants performeperform to their maſtersmasters muſtmust
be done in truth and vprightneſſeuprightness.

div.p: The ApoſtleApostle giuesgives this direction to ChriſtiansChristians who hauehave to doedo not only with maſtersmasters according to the fleſhflesh (who only ſeesee the outward appearance) but alſoalso with the maſtermaster of ſpiritsspirits 1 Sam. 16. 7. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . who looketh on the heart: and therefore alſoalso he added this clauſeclause, as vntounto ChriſtChrist: teaching ſeruantsservants thereby that

p.hi: SeruantsServants in their obedience to their maſtersmasters, muſtmust approueapprove
themſeluesthemselves to IeſusJesus ChriſtChrist as well as to their maſtersmasters after the fleſhflesh.

div.p: This phraſephrase (as vntounto ChriſtChrist) implieth as much as that (in the Lord) whereof we ſpakespake §. 96. before.

div.head: §. 125. Of the meaning of the ſixtsixth verſeverse.

epigraph.q: Not with eieeye ſeruiceservice, as men-pleaſerspleasers, but as the ſeruantsservants of ChriſtChrist, doing the will of God from the heart.

div.p: THisThis and the verſeverse following are added as a further explication of the laſtlast clauſeclause of the former verſeverse. It ſhouldshould ſeemeseem that ſeruantsservants, howſoeuerhowsoever they might in ſomesome meaſuremeasure performeperform the mainemain dutieduty of obedience, yet failed exceedingly in the manner of performing it. BecauſeBecause maſtersmasters were but men, maſtersmasters according to the fleſhflesh, who neither had power ouerover the heart, nor could diſcernediscern the diſpoſitiondisposition thereof, ſeruantsservants thought they had well done their dutieduty, if they had outwardly performed what their maſtermaster required: now to root out this bitter weed, and to reformereform this corrupt conceit, the ApoſtleApostle is more large in cleeringclearing the point of ſinceresincere and vprightupright ſeruiceservice: therefore, the more fully to expreſſeexpress his mindemind and meaning, firſtfirst he layeth downedown the vice contrariecontrary to the foreſaidforesaid ſinceritysincerity (for contraries laid together doedo much ſetset forth one OppoſitaOpposita iuxta ſese poſitaposita magis eluceſcuntelucescunt. another) and then returneth more diſtinctlydistinctly to declare the vertuevirtue. Whence note

moſtmost failefail.

div.p:
The vice here noted to be contrariecontrary to ſinceresincere ſeruiceservice is termed

ParaſiticallParasitical ſeruiceservice is that which is indeed done, but in preſencepresence of the maſtermaster: ſuchsuch ſeruantsservants are they who will be very diligent and faithfullfaithful in doing ſuchsuch things as their maſtersmasters ſeesee, or ſhallshall come to their notice: but otherwiſeotherwise behindebehind their maſtersmasters backeback, and in things which they hope ſhallshall neuernever come to his knowledge, they will be as negligent, and vnfaithfullunfaithful as if they were no ſeruantsservants. Yet to ſatisfiesatisfy their maſtersmasters, and to ſoothsooth them, they will doedo any thing though neuernever ſoso vnlawfullunlawful.

ThoſeThose that content themſeluesthemselves with doing eieeye-ſeruiceservice the Men pleaſerspleasers. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉
ApoſtleApostle here termeth men-pleaſerspleasers: which title he giuethgiveth vntounto them for two eſpeciallespecial reaſonsreasons.

1. To ſhewshow the ground of eieeye-ſeruiceservice: which is becauſebecause all their care is to pleaſeplease their maſtermaster, who is a man: for well they know that man can ſeesee but the outward ſhewshow, or that which is done before his face.

2. To ſhewshow the hainouſneſſeheinousnesshainousness of that ſinnesin: for it is tainted with AtheiſmeAtheism, in that the man guilty thereof hath no reſpectrespect to God: but preferrethpreferrethprefereth his maſtermaster before God: he careth not to pleaſeplease God ſoso he pleaſeplease his maſtermaster: for this is the emphaſisemphasis of that word (men-pleaſerspleasers) It is ſpokenspoken in oppoſitionopposition to God,
as the ApoſtleApostle implieth in another place, ſayingsaying, If I yet pleaſedpleased

Tit. 2. 9. when the ApoſtleApostle aduiſethadvisethaduiseth ſeruantsservants to pleaſeplease their maſtersmasters in all things?

That generallgeneral particle (all things) muſtmust be reſtrainedrestrained How maſtersmasters are to be pleaſedpleased in all things. to the duties of a ſeruantservant, and to all the parts of obedience, which he there mentioneth in the words immediatlyimmediately going before. SeruantsServants therefore muſtmust pleaſeplease their maſtersmasters in all things that their maſtersmasters hauehave power to require at their hands, and they are bound to doedo. Men-pleaſingpleasing, here ſpokenspoken of, is oppoſedopposed to pleaſingpleasing of God. PleaſingPleasing of men there mentioned is ſubordinatesubordinate to our pleaſingpleasing of God: here to pleaſeplease men is to ſoothsooth them vpup in euerieevery thing good or euillevil: there to pleaſeplease them is conſcionablyconscionably to obey them in euerieevery lawfulllawful thing. Here is condemned a ſeekingseeking to pleaſeplease men in the firſtfirst place, and that only, and wholly in eueryevery thing, whereas we ought firſtfirst to ſeekeseek Gods approbation, then the teſtimonytestimony of a good conſcienceconscience, and after theſethese a pleaſingpleasing of men, but in, for, and vnderunder God. To auoidavoid the two forenamed ſinnessins, eieeye-ſeruiceservice, and men-pleaſingpleasing, the ApoſtleApostle giuethgiveth an excellent direction in theſethese words, as the ſeruantsservants of ChriſtChrist doing the will of God from the heart, where we may obſerueobserve Seruantsservants of ChriſtChrist to be oppoſedopposed to men-pleaſerspleasers, and doing Gods will from the heart to eieeye-ſeruiceservice.

div.head: §. 129. Of the meaning of this phraſephrase, DoeDo the ſamesame things.
div.p: TheſeThese two titles (Maſtersmasters, Seruantsservants) are ſoso taken here as they were §. 124. before in the fiftfifth verſeverse.

All the duties of maſtersmasters are compriſedcomprised vnderunder this phraſephrase, doedo the ſamesame things: which at firſtfirst ſightsight may ſeemeseem to be ſomewhatsomewhat

AnſwAnsw. 1. TheſeThese words are not to be referred to thoſethose particular duties which are proper to ſeruantsservants, but to thoſethose generallgeneral rules of equitieequity which are common to maſtersmasters as well as ſeruantsservants; namely, that in their ſeuerallseveral places, with ſingleneſſesingleness of heart, as vntounto ChriſtChrist, not with eieeye ſeruiceservice as men pleaſerspleasers, but as the ſeruantsservants of ChriſtChrist they doedo the will of God from the heart.

2. ThoſeThose words may be referred to the eight verſeverse, the verſeverse going immediatlyimmediately before, which laieth downedown a generallgeneral rule for all men in their ſeuerallseveral places to doedo the good things of their places. Now then as ſeruantsservants muſtmust hauehave an eieeye to their places to doedo the good things thereof, ſoso maſtersmasters muſtmust doedo the ſamesame things: that is, they muſtmust hauehave an eieeye to their places, to doedo the good things thereof.

3. ThoſeThose words may be taken without reference to any former words, and expounded of a mutuallmutual, reciprocallreciprocal, and proportionable dutieduty that ought to paſſepass betwixt maſtermaster and ſeruantservant: not in the particulars, as if the ſamesame duties were to be performed by each of them, for that were to ouerthrowoverthrow the order and degrees which God hath ſetset betwixt maſtermaster and ſeruantservant, to croſſecross Gods ordinance, and inferreinfer contradiction: but in generallgeneral, that duties are to be performed of each to other: in which reſpectrespect the ApoſtleApostle ſaidsaid §. 3. before of all ſortssorts, ſuperiourssuperiors, and inferioursinferiors, Submit your ſeluesselves one to another. And thus by this phraſephrase the doctrine before mentioned is confirmed, that Maſtersmasters are as well bound to dutieduty as ſeruantsservants.

None of theſethese anſwersanswers thwart another, but all of them may well be admitted, and all of them well ſtandstand together. They all imply a common equitieequity betwixt maſtersmasters and ſeruantsservants, but no equalitieequality: mutuallmutual duties, but diuersdivers and diſtinctdistinct duties, appertaining to their ſeuerallseveral places. Compare with this text, that which the ApoſtleApostle himſelfehimself hath more plainly and fully noted (Col. 4. 1.) and we ſhallshall obſerueobserve him to expound his own meaning, for that which here he implieth vnderunder this phraſephrase (the ſamesame things) that he expreſſethexpresseth there vnderunder theſethese two words, iuſtjust, equallequal: whereof we ſhallshall Treat. 8. §. 20, 44. hereafter more diſtinctlydistinctly ſpeakespeak.

PurpoſelyPurposely doth the ApoſtleApostle infold maſtersmasters duties vnderunder this generallgeneral phraſephrase (the ſamesame things) to preuentprevent a ſecretsecret obiectionobjection raiſedraised from the eminency and ſuperioritiesuperiority of maſtersmasters aboueabove ſeruantsservants, which maketh them thinkethink, that ſeruantsservants are only for the vſeuse of maſtersmasters, and that maſtersmasters are no way tied to their ſeruantsservants. But if in the generallgeneral maſtersmasters muſtmust doedo the ſamesame things, then they are for their ſeruantsservants good, as well as ſeruantsservants for theirs.

div.p: That great Maſtermaster, vnderunder whom all maſtersmasters on earth are, is here ſaidsaid to be in heauenheaven, the more to commend and ſetset forth his dignitiedignity and authoritieauthority: and to make maſtersmasters to ſtandstand in the more awe of him: To like purpoſepurpose DauidDavid hauinghaving ſetset forth God PſalPsal. 2. 4, 10, 11. ſittingsitting in the heauensheavens, inferrethinferrethinfereth this exhortation vntounto the great Commanders on earth, Be wiſewise now therefore, ôyeô ye Kings, be inſtructedinstructed, ye IudgesJudges of the earth: SerueServe the Lord with fearefear, and reioycerejoice with trembling.

div.head: §. 133. Of Gods hauinghaving no reſpectrespect of perſonspersons.
div.p:
The ApoſtleApostle further addeth of God the great maſtermaster of all, that with him there is no reſpectrespect of perſonspersons. The Hebrew word vſedused to ſetset forth this point ſignifiethsignifieth

Now we know that the face of a man is outward, and that which of all other parts maketh him moſtmost amiable in anothers eieeye. It is oppoſedopposed to that which is inward, eueneven the heart: in which reſpectrespect it is ſaidsaid that the Lord ſeethseeth not as 1 Sam. 16. 7. man ſeethseeth, for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart. Here by a Synecdoche, face or perſonperson is put for eueryevery outward quality, ſtatestate, or condition which maketh one to be preferred before another in mans approbation, as beautiebeauty, comelineſſecomeliness, ſtaturestature, wealth, honour, authoritieauthority, and the like. Now in that God receinethreceiveth not, or reſpectethrespecteth not perſonspersons, it ſhewethshoweth that God preferrethpreferrethprefereth not any one before another for any the forenamed outward reſpectsrespects, or any other like to them. Elihu plainly expoundeth this phraſephrase in theſethese words, he accepteth not the perſonperson of princes, nor regardeth the
IobJob. 34. 19. rich more then the poorepoor. After a liking is thus taken by one partieparty of a meet mate, that liking muſtmust be mouedmoved to the other partieparty ſoso liked, to know whether there be a reciprocallreciprocal affection of one towards another. Thus SampſonSamson went and IudgJudg. 14. 7. talked with that woman whom he liked to be his wife. If at firſtfirst there be a good liking mutually and thorowlythoroughly ſetledsettled in both their hearts of one another, louelove is like to continue in them for euerever, as things which are well glued, and ſetledsettled before they be ſhakenshaken vpup and downedown, will neuernever be ſeueredsevered aſunderasunder: but if they be ioynedjoined together without glue, or ſhakenshaken while the glue is moiſtmoist, they cannot remaineremain firmefirm.
MutuallMutual louelove and good liking of each other is as glue.
Let the parties to be mariedmarried be herein well ſetledsettled before they come to meet with trials through cohabitation, and that louelove will not eaſilyeasily be looſenedloosened by any trials.

ContrarieContrary is the adulterous and brutiſhbrutish practiſepractise of ſuchsuch as Too eager and haſtyhasty purſuingpursuing after mariagemarriage, a brutiſhbrutish thing. ſoso ſoonesoon as they caſtcast their eieeye on any whom they like, neuernever aduiſeadvise or conſultconsult about a right and due proceeding vntounto mariagemarriage, but inſtantlyinstantly with all the eagerneſſeeagerness and ſpeedspeed they can, like brute beaſtsbeasts, ſeekeseek to hauehave their deſiredesire and luſtlust ſatisfiedsatisfied. Though to keepekeep themſeluesthemselves free from the penalty of the laweslaws vnderunder which they liuelive, they procure meanesmeans to be mariedmarried, yet they declare a luſtfulllustful and adulterous mindemind. And their practiſepractise is too like to the practiſepractise of the BeniamitsBenjamites, who catchtcatched wiueswives from among the daughters of Shiloh as they were dancing: or elſeelse to the practiſepractise of the old world, which ſoso grieuedgrieved the Spirit of God, that it repented him that he had IudgJudg. 21. 23. made man, and thereupon he was mouedmoved to bring a generallgeneral deluge on the whole world. Their practiſepractise was this, that they
tooketook them wiueswives of all that they choſechose: that is, they raſhlyrashly and Gen. 6. 2. ſuddenlysuddenly mariedmarried whomſoeuerwhomsoever they liked, without any conſiderationconsideration of their condition.

div.head: §. 14. Of a contract what it is?
div.p: II. When both parties hauehave manifeſtedmanifested a mutuallmutual liking Ubi non eſtest conſenſusconsensus vtriuſquevtriusque, non poteſtpotest eſſeesse matrimonium. InſtitInstit. iur. can. lib. 2. de nupt. tit. 11. each to other, and vponupon mature deliberation and good aduiceadvice doedo conceiueconceive one to be a fit match for another, it is requiſiterequisite that a ioyntjoint conſentconsent and abſoluteabsolute promiſepromise of maryingmarrying one another before ſufficientsufficient witneſſeswitnesses be made. This rightly made is a contract, which is the beginning of a mariagemarriage.
The right making of a firmefirm contract conſiſtethconsisteth in two things:
1. In an actuallactual taking of each other for eſpouſedespoused man and wife.

2. In a direct promiſepromise of maryingmarrying each other within a conuenientconvenient time. So as a formeform of contract may be made to this purpoſepurpose; FirſtFirst the man taking the woman by the hand to ſaysay, I A. taketakeTake thee B. totoTo my eſpouſedespoused wife, and doedo faithfully promiſepromise to mariemarry thee in time meet and conuenientconvenient. And then the woman againeagain taking the man by the hand to ſaysay, I B. taketakeTake thee A. totoTo my eſpouſedespoused husband, and doedo faithfully promiſepromise to yeeldyield to be mariedmarried to thee in time meet and conuenientconvenient. This mutuallmutual and actuallactual taking of one another for eſpouſedespoused man and wife in the time preſentpresent, and a direct promiſepromise of maryingmarrying one another afterwards, ſetlethsettlethsetleth ſuchsuch a right and property of the one in the other as cannot be alienated without licence had from the great IudgeJudge of heauenheaven, who hath by his diuinedivine ordinance ſetledsettled that right.

div.head: §. 15. Of the grounds of a contract.
QueſtQuest. Is a contract abſolutelyabsolutely neceſſarynecessary?
div.p: AnſwAnsw. Though it hauehave beenebeen an ancient cuſtomecustom continued Mos ille vete ribusveteribus erat ante multum tempus ſponſaliasponsalia facere. ChryſChrys. in Gen. Hom. 43. in all ages, yet I dare not pronounce it to be ſoso abſolutelyabsolutely neceſſarynecessary, as the want thereof ſhouldshould nullifienullify a mariagemarriage, and make it to be no lawfulllawful mariagemarriage. But ſurelysurely it is ſoso meet and requiſiterequisite, as I would aduiſeadvise all ChriſtiansChristians that deſiredesire a bleſſingblessing and good ſucceſſesuccess on their mariagemarriage to be contracted before they are mariedmarried.

If there were no other ground for it but this, that God hath ſanctifiedsanctified it, and commended it vntounto vsus by his word, it were enough to perſwadepersuade ſuchsuch as fearefear God to vſeuse it.

For I demand, why doth God commend vntounto his Church any thing by his word, but that his Church ſhouldshould make conſcienceconscience of vſingusing it? Now that by Gods word it is commended, is without contradiction moſtmost euidentevident. For, not to inſiſtinsist on that argument which, not without good probability, is alleagedalleged for the antiquity of a contract, and thus collected from Gods ordering of that firſtfirst ancient mariagemarriage betwixt Adam and Gen. 2. 22. EuahEve, God brought EuahEve to Adam on the firſtfirst day that they were created to ſeesee how he would like her, and vponupon the ſightsight of her, and notice which withallwithal he had of her, by that wiſdomewisdom which God gauegave him, he then tooketook her to himſelfehimself: which taking is ſuppoſedsupposed to be but a contract, becauſebecause Gen. 4. 1. he did not know her till after his fall. If it be obiectedobjected that Adam and EuahEve are called Gen. 2. 25. man and wife in the time of their innocencieinnocency. It may beebe anſweredanswered that thoſethose titles Deut. 22. 24. Gen. 19. 14. ConſuetudineConsuetudine Scripturarum ſponſisponsi viri, & ſponſaesponsae vocantur vxores. Hier. in Mat. 1. are in Scripture giuengiven to ſuchsuch as are only contracted, to ſhewshow the neerenear and firmefirm coniunctionconjunction betwixt parties eſpouſedespoused.

But not to inſiſtinsist on that which is but probable, it is more then probable that Lots daughters were contracted: for it is ſaidsaid that Gen. 19. 14, 8. Quia iam deſponſatiodesponsatio facta erat, ideo vocat eos generos. ChryſChrys. in hunc loc.
Lot had ſonnessons in law which mariedmarried (or rather ſhouldshould mariemarry) his daughters: and withallwithal it is ſaidsaid that they had not knowneknown man: now then it muſtmust needs follow that they were called Lots ſonnessons in law becauſebecause his daughters were eſpouſedespoused to them. But moſtmost euidentevident for this purpoſepurpose is that difference which the Deut. 22. 22, &etcc. law putteth betwixt a pure virgin, an eſpouſedespoused maid, and a mariedmarried wife. So as contracted perſonspersons are in a middle degree betwixt ſinglesingle perſonspersons, and mariedmarried perſonspersons: they are neither ſimplysimply ſinglesingle, nor actually mariedmarried. To ſhewshow that this cuſtomecustom of a contract before mariagemarriage continued in Gods Church among the Saints, it is expreſlyexpressly noted that MarieMary the mother of the Lord Luk. 1. 27. IeſusJesus who liuedlived many hundred yearesyears after that law, was contracted.

div.head: §. 16. Of the reaſonsreasons which ſhewshow how requiſiterequisite a contract is.
div.p: Many good and weightieweighty reaſonsreasons may be alledgedalleged to ſhewshow how requiſiterequisite it is that a contract ſhouldshould go before mariagemarriage. For

1. It addeth much to the honour of mariagemarriage, that it ſhouldshould be deliberatlydeliberately and aduiſedlyadvisedly ſtepstep after ſtepstep, by one degree after another conſummatedconsummated and made vpup.

2. It putteth a difference betwixt ſuchsuch as intend mariagemarriage in the fearefear of the Lord, for ſuchsuch holy ends as are warranted in the word, and ſuchsuch as intend it only to ſatisfiesatisfy their luſtlust, or for other like carnallcarnal ends. For theſethese can admit no delay, as was noted In the end of §. 13. before. But they that vſeuse this ſolemnesolemn preparation by a contract before mariagemarriage, ſhewshow that they deſiredesire to hauehave all things fit for ſoso ſacredsacred a matter duly performed; and therefore they are content to make ſomesome ſtaystay for the better effecting thereof.

3. It is a meanesmeans of knitting the hearts of the two parties to be mariedmarried more firmelyfirmly and inuiolablyinviolably together before they come to dwell together. For a contract being the beginning of a mariagemarriage, it is an euidentevident demonſtrationdemonstration of Gods counſellcounsel concerning the parties contracted, that God hath prepared them each for other to be man and wife: ſoso as after the contract is made, they may ſimplysimply and abſolutelyabsolutely pray each for other, that God would bleſſebless them one to another, to liuelive comfortably and happily together. Before a contract is made, they can but vponupon ſuppoſitionsupposition (if God hauehave appointed them to be man and wife) pray one for another. For oft it falleth out that after many great hopes and likelihoods of proceeding in ſuchsuch or ſuchsuch a match, by ſomesome occaſionoccasion or other it is cleaneclean broken off: but a lawfulllawful contract knittethknittethkniteth ſoso firmefirm a knot as cannot be broken: ſoso as a man may conclude that being contracted to a woman ſheshe ſhallshall be his wife: and ſoso may a woman conclude of a man. The conſiderationconsideration hereof will further mouemove them more narrowly to obſerueobserve what good qualities, or what other things, which may make them more louelylovely one to another, are in each other.

4. It is a meanesmeans to make them before hand prepare themſeluesthemselves to perfomeperform ſuchsuch mariagemarriage duties as Gods word requireth of man and wife. For a contract giuethgiveth them aſſuranceassurance of
mariagemarriage if they liuelive vntounto it: ſoso as then they cannot but know that it is high time for them to thinkethink how they are to carriecarry themſeluesthemselves, when they come to liuelive in houſehouse together: and withallwithal to conſiderconsider, what croſſescrosses ordinarily doedo accompanieaccompany the mariedmarried eſtateestate, that they may be before hand prepared wiſelywisely to paſſepass them ouerover, or patiently to vndergoeundergo them.

5. It may be a meanesmeans of diſcoueringdiscovering many hidden and cloſeclose inconueniencesinconveniences, which otherwiſeotherwise would neuernever come to light. For many friends fearing leſtlest the diſcoueringdiscovering of ſomesome euilsevils which are carried cloſelyclosely, ſhouldshould make a breach betwixt themſeluesthemselves and their friends, will not make them knowneknown till they ſeesee ſomesome vrgenturgent neceſſitienecessity to mouemove them ſoso to doedo. Though the euillevil be ſuchsuch, as being knowneknown would hinder mariagemarriage, yet till they ſeesee ſomesome ſuresure euidenceevidence, that they ſhallshall indeed be mariedmarried (if no iuſtjust exception be put in) they will hope that ſomesome other occaſionoccasion may fall out to hinder the mariagemarriage, and in that reſpectrespect concealeconceal their exception. But becauſebecause a contract is the beginning of mariagemarriage, after they hauehave notice therofthereof, they will not forbeareforbear to diſcloſedisclose what they know. For this end is it, that the contract is three ſeuerallseveral times openly publiſhedpublished in the Church, that if any doedo know any iuſtjust cauſecause why ſuchsuch perſonspersons as are contracted may not lawfully proceed to mariagemarriage, they make knowneknown the ſamesame. A commendable cuſtomecustom: and great pittypity, that it is ſoso much neglected as it is.

6. It may preuentprevent many plots and practiſespractises of inueiglinginveigling, or ſtealingstealing away maids and widoweswidows. For it oft falleth out, that when parents or other friends hauehave prouidedprovided a good match for their daughter, or for ſomesome other vnderunder their gouernmentgovernment, and all things on all parts well concluded, the wedding day appointed, and all things fitted and prepared for the ſolemnizingsolemnizing of the wedding, ſomesome deſirousdesirous to foreſtallforestall that mariagemarriage, by ſecretsecret and cunning deuicesdevices get the bride away a few daiesdays before, if not on the very morning of the intended wedding day, and marymarry her out of hand to another. That which maketh men ſoso bold is, that they know a clandeſtineclandestine mariagemarriage being conſummateconsummate ſhallshall ſtandstand firmefirm in law. But a legalllegal contract preuentethpreventeth ſuchsuch miſchiefesmischiefs, becauſebecause it maketh ſuchsuch a furtiuefurtive mariagemarriage vtterlyutterly void. None therforetherefore knowing
that a contract is lawfully made before hand, will be ſoso bold, or rather ſoso mad, as to offer to fruſtratefrustrate a mariagemarriage after any ſuchsuch manner.

7. It is a meanesmeans to ſtirrestir vpup the parties which are to be mariedmarried, more carefully and diligently to prouideprovide all things fit for their dwelling together, and well ordering their houſholdhousehold before hand; that they be not to ſeekeseek for neceſſariesnecessaries when they ſhouldshould vſeuse them. For being contracted, they know that it cannot be long ere they muſtmust come to dwell together.

div.head: §. 17. Of abuſingabusing, or neglecting a contract.
div.p: There are two extremes contrariecontrary to the forenamed doctrine of a contract. One of attributing too much to it: another of derogating too much from it. Many make it a very mariagemarriage, and thereupon hauehave a greater ſolemnitiesolemnity at their contract, then Nonnullis ſponſissponsis tam impotens eſtest ardor libidinis, vt corpuſculocorpusculo puellari vim adferant. EraſEras. in InſtInst. Matr. at their mariagemarriage: yea many take libertieliberty after a contract to know their ſpouſespouse, as if they were mariedmarried: an unwarrantable and diſhoneſtdishonest practiſepractise. Lots daughters were See §. 15. contracted to husbands, and yet they are ſaidsaid to hauehave knowneknown no man. The law ſtilethstyleth her that is contracted Deut. 22. 24. a maid, to ſhewshow that ſheshe ought to keepekeep her ſelfeself a virgin till the mariagemarriage be conſummateconsummate. Therefore Mary is thus deſcribeddescribed, Luk. 1. 27. a virgin eſpouſedespoused. But it is the common courſecourse of moſtmost to make light account of this warrantable and honourable proceeding to mariagemarriage by a contract. Few there be in compariſoncomparison of the multitudes that are mariedmarried, who make any conſcienceconscience thereof. They thinkethink it needleſſeneedless, and vtterlyutterly neglect it. No maruellmarvelmarvell that they meet with many miſchiefesmischiefs and inconueniencesinconveniences, when the meanesmeans of preuentingpreventing the ſamesame are not vſedused. Let ſuchsuch duly weightweigh the reaſonsreasons rendredrendered in the former ſectionsection.

div.head: §. 18. Of the diſtancedistance of time betwixt the contract and mariagemarriage.
Quest. What diſtancedistance of time muſtmust paſſepass betwixt the making of a contract, and conſummatingconsummating of mariagemarriage?
div.p:
AnſwAnsw. This muſtmust be left to the wiſewise conſiderationconsideration of the parties contracted, and of their friends, for the ſamesame time cannot preciſelyprecisely be preſcribedprescribed to all. OccaſionsOccasions may fall out either of haſteninghastening, or putting off the mariagemarriage. Only extremes on both ſidessides muſtmust be auoidedavoided. Neither ought the mariagemarriage be
too ſuddenlysuddenly ſolemnizedsolemnized vponupon the contract: (then the ends and reaſonsreasons of a contract, before mentioned, are made void) nor yet too long put off (then may Satan take occaſionoccasion to tempt them for their incontinencieincontinency.) The laudable cuſtomecustom of our and other Churches ſhewethshoweth, that at leaſtleast three weekesweeks muſtmust paſſepass betwixt contract and mariagemarriage. For the contract is Rubr. before the formeform of ſolemnizingsolemnizing of matrimony. to be three times publiſhedpublished, and that but once a weekeweek before the wedding be celebrated. And we read that the virgin Mary was at leaſtleast three monethsmonths contracted before IoſephJoseph tooketook her to wife. For when the AngellAngel firſtfirst came to her ſheshe was Luk. 1. 27. 56. eſpouſedespoused: after that ſheshe went to her coſencousincosen Elizabeth, with whom ſheshe abode three monethsmonths: and then being returned home IoſephJoseph was warned by an AngellAngel to take her to wife. I Mat. 1. 20. note not this as a rule for eueryevery one preciſelyprecisely to follow. For the virgin Mary had a iuſtjust occaſionoccasion to tarrietarry three monethsmonths with her old coſencousincosen Elizabeth: and ſoso may others hauehave occaſionsoccasions to put off their mariagesmarriages: which may be lawfulllawful, ſoso the mariagemarriage be not put off too long, and that there be a mutuallmutual and ioyntjoint conſentconsent of both parties. For after the contract is made, neither the man nor the woman hauehave the power of their owneown body.

Contrary is that vnwarrantableunwarrantable courſecourse which many take, to VnlawfullUnlawful for parties contracted long to abſentabsent themſeluesthemselves each from other. Deut. 24. 5. be affianced and made ſuresure to a wife, and then to trauelltravel beyond ſeasea, or to any other place, and be abſentabsent from their ſpouſespouse a yeereyear, or two, or three, or it may be more yeeresyears. If a man might not goego to warrewar, nor be charged with any buſineſſebusiness that ſhouldshould draw him from his wife the firſtfirst yeereyear of his mariagemarriage, much leſſeless may he abſentabsent himſelfehimself for any long time after he is contracted but not mariedmarried. This may be a meanesmeans to alienate the heart of his ſpouſespouse from him for euerever.

div.head: §. 19. Of a religious conſecratingconsecrating of mariagemarriage.
div.p: III. The laſtlast degree of conſummatingconsummating a mariagemarriage, is the open and publikepublic ſolemnizationsolemnization thereof: which conſiſtethconsisteth

A religious conſecrationconsecration of mariagemarriage is performed by the bleſſingblessing of a publikepublic MiniſterMinister of the word in the open face of the Church in the day time. This of old hath beenebeen vſedused of
ChriſtiansChristians, and ſtillstill is continued among vsus. Though we hauehave neither expreſſeexpress precept, nor particular patternepattern in Gods word for this manner of ſolemnizingsolemnizing a mariagemarriage (for there is no particular formeform thereof ſetset downedown in the Scripture) yet it being agreeable to the generallgeneral rules thereof, we ought in conſcienceconscience to ſubiectsubject our ſeluesselves thereto.

The generallgeneral rules are theſethese, Let all things be done decently, 1 Cor. 14. 40. and in order. The Churches of God hauehave ſuchsuch a cuſtomecustom. Submit 1 Cor. 11. 16. your ſeluesselves to eueryevery ordinance of man for the Lords ſakesake, with 1 Pet. 2. 13. the like. But the foreſaidforesaid manner of conſecratingconsecrating mariagemarriage, is very decent and in good order, a laudable cuſtomecustom of the Churches, and an ordinance of thoſethose gouernoursgovernors vnderunder whom we liuelive. Therefore warrantable, and to be obſeruedobserved. Neither is this order, cuſtomecustom, and ordinance appointed without iuſtjust and weightieweighty reaſonsreasons. For

1. MariageMarriage is a kind of publikepublic action: the well or ill ordering therofthereof much tendeth to the good or hurt of family, Church, and common-wealth. For by mariagemarriage families are erected, and Church and common-wealth increaſedincreased and continued.
2. Heb. 1313. 4. MariageMarriage is honourable. Treat. 1. §. 80, 81, 82, &etcc. The moſtmost ſacredsacred and inuiolableinviolable bond that knittethknittethkniteth any two perſonspersons together.

3. MariageMarriage is ProuProv. 2. 17. Gods couenantcovenant, wherein he himſelfehimself hath a mainemain and principallprincipal ſtrokestroke. For God is the chiefeſtchiefest agent in ioyningjoining man and woman in mariagemarriage.

On theſethese grounds it hath beenebeen thought very requiſiterequisite that mariagemarriage ſhouldshould be ſolemnizedsolemnized in the day time (as a workework of light that need not be couertlycovertly and cloſelyclosely done) and that in a publikepublic place, whetherwhither any, that will, may hauehave free acceſſeaccess, either to except againſtagainst it, and hinder it (if there be iuſtjust cauſecause) or to be a witneſſewitness thereof, and to addeadd his bleſſingblessing thereto. And among publikepublic places the Church is thought the fitteſtfittest, becauſebecause it is the houſehouse of praierprayer, where perſonspersons and actions are moſtmost ſolemnlysolemnly bleſſedblessed. And of all perſonspersons a publikepublic MiniſterMinister is thought to be the meeteſtmeetest to celebrate mariagemarriage, and to ioynejoin Coniugium benedictione ſacersacer dotalisacerdotali ſanctificarisanctificari oportet. Ambr. epiſtepist. 70. the parties to be mariedmarried, together, becauſebecause he ſtandsstands in Gods roomeroom, and in and by his miniſterieministry God ioynethjoinethjoyneth them together, and bleſſethblesseth them: ſoso as after the miniſterminister hath rightly ioynedjoined man and wife together in matrimony, it may be well
ſaidsaid, ThoſeThose whom God hath ioynedjoined together, let no man put aſunderasunder. The formeform of conſecratingconsecrating mariagemarriage, which is preſcribedprescribed in our liturgieliturgy or common-prayer-bookebook, doth ſoso diſtinctlydistinctly, perſpicuouſlyperspicuously, and fully ſetset downedown whatſoeuerwhatsoever is to be obſeruedobserved and done by the parties to be mariedmarried, their parents, or other gouernoursgovernors, and the MiniſterMinister that ioynethjoinethjoyneth them together, that I can addeadd nothing thereunto. There are declared the grounds, ends, and vſesuses of mariagemarriage. There open proclamation is made whether any can except againſtagainst the intended mariagemarriage. There each partieparty is ſolemnlysolemnly charged, that if either of them doedo know any impediment, why they may not lawfully be mariedmarried, to diſcloſedisclose it. There alſoalso each partieparty is openly demanded if freely and willingly they will take one another for man and wife. There the duties of mariedmarried perſonspersons are declared, and they ſeuerallyseverally asked whether they will ſubiectsubject themſeluesthemselves thereto or no. All which being openly profeſſedprofessed, the parent or ſomesome in his ſteadstead is called forth to giuegive the Bridebride to the Bridegroomebridegroom. Then they two actually taking each other to be man and wife, and teſtifyingtestifying the ſamesame by expreſſeexpress words, and by mutuallmutual pledges, the MiniſterMinister in Gods name ioynethjoinethjoyneth them together, pronounceth them to be lawfulllawful husband and wife, and by prayer crauethcraveth Gods bleſſingblessing vponupon the action, and vponupon their perſonspersons. Thus is the mariagemarriage conſecratedconsecrated, and they two made one fleſhflesh, that is, lawfully ioynedjoined together by the inuiolableinviolable bond of mariagemarriage.

div.head: §. 20. Of clandeſtineclandestine mariagesmarriages.
div.p:
Contrary are clandeſtineclandestine mariagesmarriages, ſuchsuch as are made in priuateprivate houſeshouses, or other ſecretsecret places, or in Churches without a ſufficientsufficient number of witneſſeswitnesses, or in the night time, or without a lawfulllawful MiniſterMinister of the word, with the like. For preuentingpreventing of theſethese abuſesabuses, a ſeaſonableseasonable time for celebrating Direction for mariagemarriage feaſtsfeasts mariagemarriage muſtmust be choſenchosen out: and moderation vſedused both by him that maketh the feaſtfeast, and alſoalso by them that partake thereof: moderation I ſaysay in the meaſuremeasure of eating and drinking, and in the time ſpentspent therein: which time muſtmust be ſanctifiedsanctified with ſuchsuch communication as is good to the vſeuse of edifying, that it may miniſterminister grace vntounto the hearers. div.head: §. 23. Of the honour of mariagemarriage in regard of the firſtfirst inſtitutioninstitution thereof.
div.p: Great reaſonreason there is why mariagemarriage ſhouldshould with ſuchsuch honour be ſolemnizedsolemnized. For it is a moſtmost honourable thing. Honourable in the inſtitutioninstitution, ends, priuiledgesprivileges, and myſteriemystery thereof. No ordinance was more honourable in the firſtfirst inſtitutioninstitution thereof, as is euidentevident by the Author thereof, the Placeplace where it was inſtitutedinstituted, the Timetime when it was inſtitutedinstituted, the Perſonspersons who were firſtfirst mariedmarried, and the Manner of ioyningjoining them together.
1. The Author and firſtfirst InſtitutorInstitutor of mariagemarriage was the Lord Gen. 2. 18, 21, 22 God. Could there hauehave beenebeen a greater, or any way a more excellent Author?

2. The Placeplace was ParadiſeParadise; the moſtmost fairefair, glorious, pleaſantpleasant, honourable, commodious, and eueryevery way moſtmost excellent place that euerever was in this world,. PlacePlaceplace, though it be but a circumſtancecircumstance, addeth much to the honour of a thing. SolematSolemn ordinances are made in honourable places. Thus with vsus mariagesmarriages are ſolemnizedsolemnized in Churches, not in priuateprivate houſeshouses.

3. The Timetime was the moſtmost pure and perfect time that euerever was in the world, when no ſinnesin or pollution of man had ſtainedstained it, eueneven the time of mans innocencieinnocency. PuritiePurity addeth much to the honour of a thing.

4. The Perſonspersons were the moſtmost honourable that euerever were eueneven the firſtfirst father and mother of all mankindemankind, they who had an abſoluteabsolute power and dominion ouerover all creatures, and
to whom all were ſubiectsubject. None but they euerever had a true monarchy ouerover the whole world.

5. The Manner was with as great deliberation as euerever was vſedused in inſtitutinginstituting any ordinance. For firſtfirst the three glorious Gen. 2. 18. Cui hoc dicitur? non creatae alicui potentiae, ſedsed ei qui exſeex seexse natus eſtest, ConſiliarioConsiliario admirabili, &etcc. ChryſChrys. in Gen. hom. 14. perſonspersons in the Trinity doedo meet to aduiſeadvise about it. For The Lord God ſaidsaid, and to whom ſhouldshould he ſpeakespeak? notNot to any created power, but to him that was begotten of himſelfehimself, that WonderfullWonderful, CounſellerCounsellorCounseller, &etcc. In this conſultationconsultation this ordinance is found to be very needfullneedful: (It is not good for man to be alone) thereupon a determination is ſetset downedown, to make an helpehelp meet for man. For the better effecting hereof the Lord proceedeth thereto very deliberatlydeliberately, by ſundrysundry ſtepssteps, and degrees.
1. All the creatures that liuedlived on the earth, or breathed in the aireair, are brought before man, to ſeesee if an helpehelp meet for him might be found among them.
2. EueryEvery of them being thorowlythoroughly viewed, and found vnfitunfit, another creature is made and that out of mans ſubſtancesubstance and ſideside, and after his image.
3. This excellent creature thus made is by the maker therofthereof preſentedpresented to man, to ſeesee how he would like it.
4. Man manifeſtingmanifesting a good liking to her, ſheshe is giuengiven to him to be his wife.
5. The inuiolableinviolable law of the neerenear and firmefirm vnionunion of man and wife together is enacted.

Let all the forenamed branches concerning the firſtfirst inſtitutioninstitution of mariagemarriage expreſlyexpressly recorded by the holy GhoſtGhost be well weighed, and we ſhallshall eaſilyeasily ſeesee that there is no ordinance now in force among the ſonnessons of men ſoso honourable in the inſtitutioninstitution thereof, as this.

div.p: 2. The Ends for which mariagemarriage was ordained addeadd much to the honour thereof. They are eſpeciallyespecially three. Prima ſocietassocietas in ipſoipso coniugio eſtest &etcc. Id autēautemautemauten eſtest principium vrbis, & quaſiquasi ſeminariumseminarium reip. Cic. Offic. lib. 1.

1. That the world might be increaſedincreased: and not ſimplysimply increaſedincreased, but with a legitimate brood, and diſtinctdistinct families, which are the ſeminariesseminaries of cities and common-wealths. An helpehelp as for bringing forth, ſoso for bringing vpup children; and as for erecting, ſoso for well gouerninggoverning their family. An helpehelp alſoalso for well ordering proſperityprosperity, and well bearing aduerſityadversity. An helpehelp in health and ſickneſſesickness. Ut non ſolumsolum honeſtèhonestè, ſedsed & commodè viuatvivat. ChryſChrys. in Gen. 2. hom. 14. An helpehelp while both liuelive together, and when one is by death taken from the other. div.p: IIII. Great is that myſteriemystery which is ſetset forth by mariagemarriage, namely the ſacredsacred, ſpirituallspiritual, reallreal, and inuiolableinviolable vnionunion betwixt ChriſtChrist and his Church: which is excellently decipher • ed in SalomonsSolomon's Song, and in PſalPsal. 45. andAnd expreſlyexpressly noted, Eph. 5. 32.

Contrary to the forenamed ioyfulljoyful celebrating of mariagemarriage are all thoſethose indirect courſescourses which bring much griefegrief, trouble and vexation thereunto: as forced, ſtolnestolenstolne, vnequallunequal, or any other way vnlawfullunlawful mariagesmarriages: mariagesmarriages without parents, or

div.head: §. 2. Of MatrimoniallMatrimonial vnitieunity.
div.p: The firſtfirst, higheſthighest, chiefeſtchiefest, and moſtmost abſolutelyabsolutely neceſſarienecessary common-mutuallmutual dutieduty betwixt Manman and Wifewife, is MatrimoniallMatrimonial VnitieUnity, whereby husband and wife doedo account one another to be one fleſhflesh, and accordingly preſeruepreserve the inuiolableinviolable vnionunion whereby they are knit together. This is that dutieduty which the ApoſtleApostle inioynethenjoineth to husbands and wiueswives, in theſethese words, Let 1 Cor. 7. 10, 11. not the wife depart from her husband: Let not the husband put away his wife. He there ſpeakethspeaketh of renouncing each other, and making the matrimoniallmatrimonial bond fruſtratefrustrate, and of no effect: which bond he would hauehave to be kept firmefirm and inuiolableinviolable, and they two who are thereby made one, conſtantlyconstantly to remaineremain one, and not to make themſeluesthemselves two againeagain. This matrimoniallmatrimonial vnitieunity is ſoso neceſſarienecessary, as it may not be diſdis-united or diſſolueddissolved though one be a ChriſtianChristian, the other a Pagan. And the woman which hath an husband that beleeuethbelieveth not, let her not leaueleave him.
The reaſonsreasons of this inuiolableinviolable vnionunion are eſpeciallyespecially two: One taken from the Author of mariagemarriage: the other from the Naturenature thereof.

1. The Author of mariagemarriage is God. It is his ordinance: and Gen. 2. 18, 22, 24 he it is that by his ordinance hath made of two, one fleſhflesh. Now markemark the conſequenceconsequence which ChriſtChrist as a ruled caſecase, and vndeniableundeniable principle inferrethinfereth thereon, What God hath ioynedjoined together

div.head: §. 5. Of AdulterieAdultery.
div.p: The vice contrariecontrary to matrimoniallmatrimonial chaſtitiechastity is AdulterieAdultery, one of the moſtmost capitallcapital vices in that eſtateestate: a vice whereby way is made for DiuorceDivorce: as is cleareclear and euidentevident by the determination of ChriſtChrist himſelfehimself, concerning that point, firſtfirst Matth. 5. 32. propounded in his ſermonsermon on the mount, and againeagain Matth. 19. 9. And great reaſonreason there is thereof. For 1 Cor. 6. 16. the adulterer maketh himſelfehimself one fleſhflesh with his harlot. Why then ſhouldshould he remaineremain to be one fleſhflesh with his wife? Two (ſaithsaith the Law) ſhallshall be one fleſhflesh: not three. The like may be ſaidsaid of a wife committing adulterieadultery.

div.head: §. 6. Of pardoning adulterieadultery vponupon repentance.

div.p: QueſtQuest. For the law of diuorcedivorce did not neceſſarilynecessarily enioyneenjoin any to ſuesue out the bill, but only afforded them libertieliberty to vſeuse that puniſhmentpunishment if they ſawsaw cauſecause. div.head: §. 7. Of the difference of adultery in a man, and in a wife.

div.p: QueſtQuest. Is the bond of mariagemarriage as much violated on the Adultery as great a ſinnesin in a man as in his wife. Lex Jul. de Adult. l. 1. Orif. Codic. in l. IlluſtIllust. Greg. Sayr. I deniedeny not but that more inconueniencesinconveniences may follow vponupon the womans default then vponupon the mans: as, greater infamy before men, worſeworse diſturbancedisturbance More inconueniencesinconveniences of a womans adultery, then a mans. of the family, more miſtakingmistaking of legitimate, or illegitimate children, with the like. The man cannot ſoso well know which be his owneown children, as the woman; he may take baſebase children to be his owneown, and ſoso caſtcast the inheritance vponupon them; and ſuſpectsuspect his owneown to be baſelybasely borne, and ſoso depriuedeprive them of their patrimony. Accordingly the puniſhmentpunishment Tanto grauius viros puniri oportet, quanto magis ad eos pertinet & virtute vincere, & exemplo regere ſoeminasfoeminassoeminas. Aug. de adult.
