div.head: §. 10. Of mutuallmutual louelove betwixt man and wife.
div.p:
Hitherto of thoſethose common mutuallmutual duties which tend to the preſeruationpreservation of the very being of mariagemarriage, and are in that reſpectrespect abſolutelyabsolutely neceſſarienecessary. The other common mutuallmutual duties (though they be not of ſoso abſoluteabsolute neceſſitienecessity as the former) are in their kindekind neceſſarynecessary for the good eſtateestate of mariagemarriage, and for the better preſeruingpreserving of that knot: ſoso as, if they be not performed, the end and right vſeuse of mariagemarriage will be peruertedperverted, & that eſtateestate made vncomfortableuncomfortable, & very burdenſomeburdensome.
The firſtfirst of theſethese is Louelove. A louingloving mutuallmutual affection muſtmust paſſepass betwixt husband and wife, or elſeelse no dutieduty will be well performed: this is the ground of all the reſtrest. In ſomesome reſpectsrespects Louelove is proper and peculiar to an husband, as Treat. 4. §. 2. I purpoſepurpose to ſhewshow when I come to ſpeakespeak of an husbands particular duties. But Louelove is alſoalso required of wiueswives, and they are commanded to be louerslovers of their husbands, as well as husbands to louelove their wiueswives:
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . Tit. 2. 4. Col. 3. 19. ſoso as it is a common mutuallmutual dutieduty belonging to husband and wife too: and that is true wedlockewedlock, when man and wife are linked together by the bond of louelove. VnderUnder louelove all other duties Hoc verum eſtest coniugium, quando vinculo charitatis ſuntsunt concatenati. ChryſChrys. hom. 45. in Gen. are compriſedcomprised: for without it no dutieduty can be well performed. Rom. 13. 10. LoueLovelove is the fulfilling of the Law, that is, the very life of all thoſethose duties which the law requireth. It is the Col. 3. 14. bond of perfection, which bindeth together all thoſethose duties that paſſepass betwixt partieparty and partieparty. Where louelove aboundeth, there all duties will readily and cheerefullycheerfully be performed. Where louelove is wanting, there eueryevery duty will either be altogether neglected, or ſoso careleſlycarelessly performed, that as good not be performed at all: in which reſpectrespect the ApoſtleApostle willeth, that all things be done 1 Cor. 16. 14. in louelove. LoueLove as it prouokethprovoketh the partieparty in whom it ruleth to doedo all the good it can; ſoso it ſtirrethstirrethstireth vpup the partieparty louedloved to repay good for good. It is like fire, which is not only hot in it ſelfeself, but alſoalso conueighethconveyeth heat into that which is neerenear it: whence ariſethariseth a reflection of heat from one to another. Note how admirably this is ſetset forth betwixt ChriſtChrist and his SpouſeSpouse in the Song of SalomonSolomon: and it is further manifeſtedmanifested in the examples of all good husbands and wiueswives noted in the Scripture: they did mutually bearebear a very louingloving affection one to another.

Though louelove be a general duty which eueryevery one oweth to another, Matth. 5. 44. eueneven to his enemieenemy, yet the neerernearer that God hath linked any together, the more are they bound to this dutieduty, and the more muſtmust they abound therein. But of all others are Treat. 1. §. 79, 80. man and wife moſtmost neerelynearly and firmly linked together. Of all others therefore are they moſtmost bound hereunto, & that in the higheſthighest degree that may be, eueneven like to IonathansJonathans louelove, who louedloved DauidDavid 1 Sam. 18. 1. ProuProv. 18. 22. as his owneown ſoulesoul. SalomonSolomon ſaithsaith, He that findeth a wife findeth a good thing, and obtaineth fauourfavour of the Lord: which by the
rule of relation is alſoalso true of an husband, SheeShe that findeth an husband findeth a good thing, and obtaineth fauourfavour of the Lord. ManManman and wife therefore are each to other an eſpeciallespecial pledge of Gods fauourfavour, and in this reſpectrespect aboueabove all others vnderunder God to be louedloved. If this be the ground (as it ought to be) of their mutuallmutual That which in Treat. 4. §. 2. 9. 11. is ſpokenspoken of an husbands louelove and intireentire affection, may alſoalso be applied in ſomesome reſpectsrespects to a wife: and ſoso ſerueserve to amplifieamplify this common mutuallmutual dutieduty of louelove. louelove, their louelove will be feruentfervent and conſtantconstant. Neither will the want, or withering of any outward allurements, as beautiebeauty, perſonagepersonage, parentage, friends, riches, honours, or the like, with-hold or with-draw, extinguiſhextinguish or extenuate their louelove: neither will any excellencies of nature or grace in other husbands and wiueswives draw their hearts from their owneown to thoſethose other: nor yet will the louelove of a former yoakeyoke-fellow dead and gone, any whit leſſenlessen the louelove of the liuingliving mate.

This inſtanceinstance I hauehave the rather mentioned, becauſebecause in many, LoueLove of after venters to be as intireentire as of former. who are farrefar from ſettingsetting their affection on ſtrangestrange fleſhflesh, their louelove of a former husband or wife departed is ſoso faſtfast fixed in their heart, as they can neuernever againeagain ſoso intirelyentirely louelove any other. They who are ſoso minded are not fit to be ioinedjoined with another yoke-fellow after they are looſedloosed from one. If they marymarry againeagain, and manifeſtmanifest ſuchsuch a mindemind, they plainly ſhewshow that they reſpectrespect this or that perſonperson more then Gods ordinance. By Gods ordinance man and wife are no longer bound one to another then they liuelive together. Death is an abſoluteabsolute diremption, and maketh an vtterutter diſſolutiondissolution of the mariagemarriage bond. If the man
Rom. 7. 2, 3. be dead, the wife is deliuereddelivered from the law of the man, ſoso as ſheeshe may take another man. Which liberty is alſoalso giuengiven to the man. Being now free, if they marymarry another (that other being now a true husband or wife) their louelove muſtmust be as intireentire to that other as it was to the former: yea, and more intireentire, if there were any defect in the former. For as children mariedmarried out of their parents houſehouse muſtmust not retaineretain ſuchsuch a louelove of their parents as ſhallshall ſwallowswallow vpup their louelove of the partieparty to whom they are mariedmarried, but muſtmust according to the law, leaueleave father and
mother, and cleauecleave to their yoke-fellow: ſoso neither muſtmust the louelove of a former husband or wife be predominant when they are mariedmarried to another. This other muſtmust be as cloſeclose cleauedcleaved vntounto, as if they had neuernever beenebeen ioinedjoined to a former. The liuingliving husband or wife is the preſentpresent pledge of Gods fauourfavour. He is now thine owneown husband: and ſheshe is now thine owneown wife: and not the partieparty that is dead. I deniedeny not but the memoriememory of a vertuousvirtuous husband or wife ought to be pretiousprecious to the ſuruiuingsurviving partieparty: for the memoriallmemorial of the iustjust is bleſſedblessed.
ProuProv. 10. 7. But as the vertuevirtue of a perſonperson deceaſeddeceased may not be buried with the dead corpscorpse: ſoso neither may the perſonperson be kept aboueabove ground with the memoriememory of his or her vertuevirtue: which after a ſortsort is done, when louelove of the partieparty deceaſeddeceased either taketh away, or extenuateth the louelove of the liuingliving. This is to giuegive dominion to the dead ouerover the liuingliving: which is more then the law enioynethenjoineth.

div.head: §. 11. Of husbands and wiueswives mutuallmutual hatred contrary to louelove.
div.p:
There is a generation of ſoso crabbed and crooked a diſpoſitiondisposition * See Treat. 3. §§. 8. & Treat. 4. §. 10. as they cannot louelove, but rather hate one another becauſebecause they are man and wife: for many husbands hauinghaving wiueswives, and wiueswives husbands eueryevery way worthy to be louedloved, will notwithſtandingnotwithstanding ſaysay to the aſtoniſhmentastonishment of the hearers, I hauehave indeed a good husband, or I hauehave a good wife: but I cannot louelove him, or I cannot louelove her: and being demanded a reaſonreason, ſtickestick not openly and impudently to reply, I thinkethink I could louelove him if he were not mine husband, or I thinkethink I could louelove her if ſheshe were not my wife. O more then monſtrousmonstrous impudencieimpudency! Is not this directly to oppoſeoppose againſtagainst Gods ordinance, and againſtagainst that order which he hath ſetset betwixt man and woman? Is it not to trample vnderunder foot Gods fauourfavour? Though there were nothing elſeelse to mouemove louelove but this, that ſuchsuch an one is thine huſbandhusband, or ſuchsuch an one is thy wife, yet this ſhouldshould be motiuemotive enough. And ſhallshall this be the ground of thine hatred? AſſuredlyAssuredly ſuchsuch a ſpiritspirit is a plaineplain diabolicalldiabolical ſpiritspirit, contrary to that ſpiritspirit which is from aboueabove; and if it be not
caſtcast out, it will caſtcast thoſethose whom it poſſeſſethpossesseth into the fire of hell.

div.head: §. 12. Of mutuallmutual peace betwixt Man and Wife.
div.p:
Among other meanesmeans of maintaining an inward louingloving affection betwixt man and wife, outward mutuallmutual peace, concord, and agreement is one of the principallprincipal. Whereupon the ApoſtleApostle exhorteth to keepekeep the vnitieunity of the ſpiritspirit in the bond of
EpheſEphes. 4. 3. peace: for peace is a bond that tieth one to another, and maketh them to be as one, eueneven one in ſpiritspirit: as on the contrary ſideside outward diſcorddiscord diſunitesdisunites mens ſpiritsspirits. We are enioinedenjoined to follow peace with all men: how much more of all perſonspersons ought Heb. 12. 14. husbands to hauehave peace with their wiueswives, and wiueswives with their husbands? theyThey are neerernearer then brothers and ſiſterssisters. Behold then how good and pleaſantpleasant a thing it is for them to dwell together in vnityunity. §. 14. ProuProv. 21. 9. Dwell together they muſtmust: but without peace there is no dwelling together: It is better to dwell in a corner of the houſehouse top then with a contentious woman in a wide houſehouse. PerſonsPersonspersons at variance were farrefar better be out of ſightsight and place, then preſentpresent together. Out of ſightsight and place man and wife muſtmust not be, at peace therefore Portus eſtest mulier, & maximūmaximummaximummaximun ſecuritatissecuritatis remedium. MutuallMutual peace betwixt them is a great refreſhingrefreshing to their mindesminds, being beaten with the diſcordsdiscords of others. It is ſaidsaid that a wife is in this reſpectrespect as an hauenhaven to man (how much more man to his wife?) If the hauenhaven be calmecalm, and free from ſtormesstorms and tempeſtstempests, what a refreſhingrefreshing will it be to the Mariner that hath beenebeen toſſedtossed in the ſeasea with windeswinds and waueswaves?
For maintaining peace,

1. All offences ſoso much as poſſiblypossibly may be muſtmust be auoidedavoided. Directions for maintaining peace betwixt Man and Wife. The husband muſtmust be watchfullwatchful ouerover himſelfehimself that he giuegive no offence to his wife: and ſoso the wife on the other ſideside. Offences cauſecause contentions.

3. If both be incenſedincensed together, the fire is like to be the
greater: with the greater ſpeedspeed therefore muſtmust they both labour to put it out. That this fire may be the ſoonersooner quenched, they muſtmust both ſtriuestrive firſtfirst to offer reconciliation. Theirs is the glory who doedo firſtfirst begin, for they are moſtmost properly the bleſſedblessed peacemakers. Not Mat. 5. 9. to accept peace when it is offered is more then heatheniſhheathenish: but when wrath is incenſedincensed, to ſeekeseek atonement is the dutieduty of a ChriſtianChristian, and a grace that commethcometh from aboueabove.

div.head: §. 13. Of contentions betwixt man and wife.
div.p: Contrary to mutuallmutual peace are contentions betwixt man and wife: which are too frequent in moſtmost families, and by which Cùm vir & vxor domi diſſentiuntdissentiunt, nihilo melius naui iactata domus illa diſponiturdisponitur, cùm gubernator aduerſusaduersus prorae directo. remdirectorem diſſentiatdissentiat. ChryſChrys. loc. citat. Gen. 13. 8. the common good is much hindered. DiſcordDiscord betwixt man and wife in an houſehouse is as contention betwixt the maſtermaster and pilot in a ſhipship: may not great danger, and much miſchiefemischief be thence iuſtlyjustly feared? We heard before that man to his wife, and ſheshe to him, is as an hauenhaven. Now by experience we findefind that if the hauenhaven be tempeſtuoustempestuous it is much more troubleſometroublesome, and dangerous to the Mariner then the wide ſeasea. Wherefore let man and wife be of the ſamesame mindemind one to another as Abraham was to Lot, and when occaſionsoccasions of diſcorddiscord are offered, ſaysay, Let there be no ſtrifestrife betwixt thee and me, for we are man and wife: no more two, but one fleſhflesh.

div.head: §. 14. Of husbands and wiueswives dwelling together.
div.p:
From a mutuallmutual affection of louelove proceedeth a mutuallmutual prouidentprovident care in husband and wife one for another. In handling whereof we will firſtfirst note the meanesmeans whereby their mutuallmutual prouidenceprovidence may be the better effected and manifeſtedmanifested, and then the matter whereabout it muſtmust be conuerſantconversant. The meanesmeans in one word is cohabitation. For a dutieduty it is that man and wife dwell together. The power which the one hath of the others body, and ReaſonsReasons for cohabitation. the aduantageadvantage which by liuingliving aſunderasunder, they giuegive vntounto Satan, (both of which are expreſlyexpressly noted, 1 Cor. 7. 4, 5.) doedo ſhewshow the neceſſitynecessity of this dutieduty: and the many benefits ariſingarising from thence doedo further preſſepress the equity of it. By husbands and Benefits of cohabitation. wiueswives dwelling together all mariagemarriage duties are better performed: mutuallmutual louelove is better bred, preſeruedpreserved, and increaſedincreased: the good gifts of either of them are better obſeruedobserved by the other: better helpehelp and ſuccoursuccour is mutually by each afforded to the other: and in fine they are made more capable of doing good one to another, and of receiuingreceiving good one from another. Why then ſhouldshould they hauehave any mindemind of liuingliving aſunderasunder, vnleſſeunless they be forced by extraordinary occaſionsoccasions, as captiuitycaptivity, cloſeclose impriſonmentimprisonment, contagious ſickneſſesickness, and ſuchsuch like, which are no faults of theirs, but croſſescrosses to be borne with griefegrief; and inſtantinstant praierprayer, together with all other good meanesmeans, to be vſedused to bring them together againeagain? Yea if the impriſonmentimprisonment, baniſhmentbanishment, or other like kindekind of abſenceabsence, D. QueſtQuest. May there be any iuſtjust cauſescauses for man and wife willingly to liuelive aſunderasunder?
div.p: AnſwAnsw. There can nor ought to be any cauſecause of vtterutter relinquiſhingrelinquishing one another, which is a kindekind of §. 3. deſertiondesertion: but for liuingliving aſunderasunder for a time there may be iuſtjust cauſescauses, as

Weighty and vrgenturgent affairesaffairs which concerneconcern the good of the Church, or commonwealth: as when a man is ſentsent forth to warrewar, or on an ambaſſageambassage (in which caſecase though he may take his wife with him, yet is he not neceſſarilynecessarily bound there tothereto, eſpeciallyespecially if the place whither he is ſentsent be farrefar off, the paſſagepassage thereto difficult and dangerous, and his abode there not long.) div.head: §. 17. Of husbands and wiueswives vnlawfullunlawful abſentingabsenting themſeluesthemselves one from another.
div.p:
ContrarieContrary alſoalso to the forenamed dutieduty of cohabitation, is the practiſepractise of many men, who liuingliving themſeluesthemselves in one place (ſuppoſesuppose at London) ſendsend their wiueswives vntounto ſomesome countreycountry houſehouse, and there eueneven mew them vpup, as HawkesHawks, neuernever caring to come at them, but are then moſtmost merriemerry, when their wiueswives are fartheſtfarthest off. If their wiueswives liuelive at home they will be abroad, mealing and lodging where their wiueswives ſhallshall not know: their owneown houſehouse is as a priſonprison to them: they are not well, but when they are out of it. Of the like lewd conceit and practifepractise are many wiueswives, who on no other occaſionoccasion then meeremere lightneſſelightness, being eager in purſuingpursuing their pleaſurespleasures, and ſatisfyingsatisfying their luſtslusts, gad out of their owneown houſeshouses in the day, lie out of them in the night, and remaineremain in other company dayesdays and nights: or at leaſtleast are glad when their husbands hauehave occaſionoccasion to be from home; not vnlikeunlike to the light huſwifehuswife which SalomonSolomon deſcribethdescribeth, ProuProv. 7. 10. &etcc. I ſpeakespeak of matters too famous, or rather infamous. I would there were no iuſtjust cauſecause to taxetax this lightneſſelightness. But let ſuchsuch as deſiredesire to approueapprove themſeluesthemselves to God or man, take heed of theſethese hainousheinous and more then heatheniſhheathenish vices. Though IſraelIsrael play the harlot, yet let not IudahJudah
HoſHos. 4. 15. offend.

Too neerenear to the forenamed kindekind of vnlawfullunlawful ſeparationseparation Man and wifes fault in parting roomesrooms and beds in the ſamesame houſehouse. doedo they come, who though they liuelive both in one houſehouse, yet make that houſehouse by their eſtrangingestranging themſeluesthemselves one from another as two houſeshouses: the man abiding in one end thereof, his wife in another: and ſoso hauehave their ſeuerallseveral roomesrooms, ſeuerallseveral tables, ſeuerallseveral ſeruantsservants, all ſeuerallseveral: Or if the ſtraitneſſestraitness of their houſehouse will not ſuffersuffer them ſoso to part other roomesrooms, yet they will hauehave ſeuerallseveral bed-chambers, or at leaſtleast ſeuerallseveral beds: ſoso as they that ſhallshall call them bed-fellowesfellows, ſhallshall but nickenick-name them. Thus they rob each other of that due beneuolencebenevolence which they mutually owe one to another, they expoſeexpose themſeluesthemselves to the deuilsdevils ſnaressnares, they more and more eſtrangeestrange their
hearts one from another, and depriuedeprive themſeluesthemselves of ſuchsuch mutuallmutual comforts and helpeshelps, as by matrimoniallmatrimonial ſocietiesociety they might afford to, and receiuereceive from one another.

div.head: §. 18. Of husbands and wiueswives mutuallmutual prayers.
div.p:
The matter whereabout husbands and wiueswives mutuallmutual prouidenceprovidence ought to be conuerſantconversant, is in generallgeneral the good of one another; that each of them doedo that for the other, which SalomonSolomon in particular applieth to a wife, viz. good and not euillevil all
ProuProv. 31. 12. the dayesdays of their life. Now the good of man extendeth to his ſoulesoul, bodiebody, good name, and goods.

A generallgeneral dutieduty tending to the good of all theſethese is prayer. Prayer a mutuallmutual dutieduty. 1 PetPet. 3. 7. S. Peter requireth ſuchsuch a cariagecarriage of man and wife one towards another, as their prayers be not hindredhindered: whereby he taketh it for grant, that prayer is a mutuallmutual dutieduty which one oweth to the other: which dutieduty IſaakIsaac performed for his wife. Herein may Gen. 25. 21. man and wife be helpfullhelpful each to other in all things needfullneedful to either of them: for it is the meanesmeans which God in wiſdomewisdom Matth. 7. 7. I amJam. 5. 16. hath ſanctifiedsanctified for the obtaining of euerieevery needfullneedful bleſsingblessing for ourſeluesourselves or others. By many it is counted but a ſlightslight dutieduty and of ſmallsmall vſeuse; but the truth is, that to performeperform it aright, in truth and faith, is both difficult in the deed, and powerfullpowerful in the effect. It is the beſtbest dutieduty that one can performeperform for another, and the leaſtleast to be neglected. We heard before, that IſaakIsaac prayed for his wife: and to ſhewshow the good he did to her thereby, it is noted, that the Lord was intreatedentreated of him: ſoso as ſheshe, being Gen. 25. 21. barren before, by that meanesmeans conceiuedconceived. All the phyſickephysic in the world could not hauehave done her ſoso much good.
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . Luke 18. 1. AlwayesAlways therefore,
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . 1 TheſſThess. 5. 17. without ceasing is this dutieduty to be performed. WhenſoeuerWhensoever man and wife make any prayer, therein they muſtmust be mindfullmindful of one another: yea and oft muſtmust they of purpoſepurpose take occaſionoccasion to make prayers in ſpeciallspecial one for another: and that both in abſenceabsence, and alſoalso in preſencepresence of one another.

This latter doth eſpeciallyespecially concerneconcern the husband, who is as a PrieſtPriest vntounto his wife, and ought to be her mouth to God when they two are together: yet I doubt not, but that the wife may pray in the husbands preſencepresence when they two are alone, e • ither for trialltrial (that he may hauehave knowledge of her abilitieability and gift in that kindekind) or for helpehelp (if the wife be much better
able to performeperform that duty then the man is, as many wiueswives are.) Not without cauſecause therefore hauehave I reckoned this among common mutuallmutual duties.

div.head: §. 19. Of the things for which husbands and wiueswives are to pray alone.
div.p: There are ſundrysundry needfullneedful bleſſingsblessings which husbands and wiueswives are to pray for that appertaineappertain only to themſeluesthemselves, and are moſtmost meet to be mentioned in priuateprivate praierprayer betwixt themſeluesthemselves, as

1. That as they two are one fleſhflesh, ſoso they may be alſoalso one ſpiritspirit: that their hearts may be as one, knit together by a true, ſpirituallspiritual, matrimoniallmatrimonial louelove: alwayesalways delighting one in another, euerever helpfullhelpful one to another, and readieready with all willingneſſewillingness and cheerefulneſſecheerfulness to performeperform all thoſethose duties which they owe one to another.

2. That their mariagemarriage bed may be ſanctifiedsanctified: and as it is by Gods ordinance, ſoso it may remaineremain to them by their well vſingusing it, a bed vndefiledundefiled. There is no other thing, for which mutuallmutual prayer in priuateprivate betwixt man and wife is more needfullneedful: and that ſoso much the rather, becauſebecause of the naturallnatural heat of luſtlust which is in moſtmost: which if it be not by prayer (the beſtbest meanesmeans for that purpoſepurpose) aſſwagedassuagedasswaged, it may proueprove a defilement Intemperans in coniugio quid aliud niſinisi quidam adulter vxoris eſtest? Aug. ex Ambr. contr. Iulian. lib. 2. of the vndefiledundefiled bed: and man and wife become adulterers one to another. As other things, ſoso this alſoalso is ſanctifiedsanctified by the word and praierprayer. The word giuethgiveth a warrant and direction for the vſeuse of it: praierprayer both ſeaſonethseasoneth it, and procureth a bleſſingblessing vponupon it.

3. That they may hauehave children, and thoſethose ſuchsuch as may be heiresheirs of ſaluationsalvation, and liuelive in this world to their owneown and others good: that they may be comely and well proportioned children: nor ideotsidiots in vnderſtandingunderstanding, nor monſtersmonsters in bodily ſhapeshape, nor yet lewd and infamous in their liueslives: which could not but be a griefegrief to their parents, and might alſoalso open the mouthesmouths of the wicked againſtagainst them.

4. That God would giuegive them competenciecompetency of this worlds goods, and other good meanesmeans well to nouriſhnourish, nurture, and place forth their children: and a ſufficienciesufficiency for the maintenance
of their family, and of that eſtateestate wherein God ſettethsetteth them.
5. That ſuchsuch needfullneedful gifts and graces as are wanting in either of them may be wrought: and ſuchsuch vices and infirmities as they are ſubiectsubject vntounto may be redreſſedredressed.
TheſeThese and many other like things giuegive occaſionoccasion to man and wife in ſpeciallspecial manner to pray one for another, and one with another.

div.head: §. 20. Of husbands and wiueswives hatefullhateful imprecations and wiſheswishes one againſtagainst another.
div.p: Contrary to that holy and heauenlyheavenly dutieduty of praierprayer are thoſethose direfulldireful and helliſhhellish imprecations and execrations, which ordinarily doedo paſſepass out of the mouthesmouths of many husbands and wiueswives againſtagainst one another (and that many times for very light occaſionsoccasions) curſingcursing the day that euerever they knew one another, and wiſhingwishing that one of them had beenebeen vnderunder the ground before they came together. MoſtMost odious are theſethese and ſuchsuch like execrations in any mans mouth, but more then moſtmost odious in the mouth of man and wife againſtagainst one another.

div.head: §. 21. Of husbands and wiueswives neglect of mutuallmutual praierprayer.
div.p: The very neglect of mutuallmutual prayer in husbands and wiueswives for each other is alſoalso a ſinnesin contrary to the forenamed dutieduty of praierprayer: whereof if all that are guiltieguilty were as well knowneknown to man as to God, how many vnkindeunkind husbands and wiueswives careleſſecareless of one anothers good would be noted, more then are? Though in outward complements they may ſeemeseem very kindekind, and in the outward things of this world, very prouidentprovident, yet if they pray not one for another, they are neither kindekind, nor prouidentprovident. HeartieHearty, feruentfervent, frequent prayer is the greateſtgreatest token of kindneſſekindness, and beſtbest part of prouidenceprovidence that can be.

div.head: §. 24. Of husbands and wiueswives edifying one another.
div.p: The ſecondsecond dutieduty tending to the ſoulessouls ſaluationsalvation is, that two beleeuersbelievers being mariedmarried together, they endeuourendeavour mutually to build vpup one another more and more. 1 TheſſThess. 5. 1111. div.head: §. 25. Of husbands and wiueswives hindering ſinnesin one in another.
div.p: Two things are requiſiterequisite vntounto ſpirituallspiritual edification.
One reſpectethrespecteth the hinderanceshindrances of growth in grace.
The other the helpeshelps thereof.

The hinderanceshindrances of grace are all manner of ſinnessins. SinneSin to grace is as water to fire: it ſlakethslaketh the heat of it, and if without hoeho it be powredpoured on it, it will cleaneclean put it out. div.p: When either husband or wife is fallen into any ſinnesin, a mutuallmutual dutieduty it is for the other, to vſeuse what redreſſeredress may be of that ſinnesin: as if one of them were wounded, the other muſtmust take care for the healing of that wound. Naz. ad Olymp. to hearehear the word, partake of the Sacrament, and conſcionablyconscionably performeperform all the parts of Gods publikepublic worſhipworship.

div.p: The vices contrary to that generallgeneral mutuallmutual dutieduty of huſbandshusbands and wiueswives in procuring the SaluationSalvation of one another, and to the particular branches compriſedcomprised vnderunder it, are many: As

div.head: §. 29. Of husbands and wiueswives mutuallmutual care ouerover one anothers body.
div.p: After the good of the ſoulesoul followeth the good of the body, wherein husband and wife muſtmust ſhewshow their prouidentprovident care each ouerover other: and doedo what lieth in them to procure the well-fare of one anothers perſonperson, and to nouriſhnourish and cheriſhcherish one anothers body. This dutieduty the ApoſtleApostle layeth down vnderunder the compariſoncomparison of a body which he calleth fleſhflesh, ſayingsaying, Eph. 5. 29. No man hateth his owneown fleſhflesh, but nouriſhethnourisheth and cheriſhethcherisheth it: now man and wife are Eph. 5. 31. one fleſhflesh. div.head: §. 38. Of husbands and wiueswives mutuallmutual prouidenceprovidence about the goods of the family.
div.p: Yet there remaineth one thing more, whereabout husbands TreatiſeTreatise 3. §. 29. and wiueswives ought to manifeſtmanifest a mutuallmutual prouidentprovident care each ouerover other: and that is about the goods of this world. HowſoeuerHowsoever the husband, while he liuethliveth with his wife, hath the trueſttruest propertieproperty in them, and the greateſtgreatest title vntounto them, yet I referrerefer this to thoſethose mutuallmutual duties which man and wife owe each to other, in three reſpectsrespects.
FirſtFirst, becauſebecause in conſcienceconscience they appertaineappertain to the vſeuse of the wife, as well as of the husband.

Secondly, becauſebecause the wife is by Gods prouidenceprovidence appointed a ioyntjoint gouernourgovernor with the husband of the familiefamily, and in that reſpectrespect ought to be an helpehelp in prouidingproviding ſuchsuch a ſufficienciesufficiency of the goods of this world, as are needfullneedful for that eſtateestate wherein God hath ſetset them, and for that charge which God hath committed to them.
Thirdly, becauſebecause the wife, if ſheshe ſuruiuesurvive the husband, ought to hauehave ſuchsuch a portion of thoſethose goods, as are meet for her place and charge.

In theſethese reſpectsrespects we ſeesee it requiſiterequisite, yea a bounden dutieduty, that husband and wife, eueneven in a mutuallmutual regard one of another, be as prouidentprovident as they can be with a good conſcienceconscience in getting, keeping, and diſpoſingdisposing competent goods and riches for the mutuallmutual good one of another. Concerning the huſbandshusbands dutieduty in this reſpectrespect no queſtionquestion is made: the practiſepractise of all good husbands mentioned in Scripture, the care of prouidingproviding for their 1 Tim. 5. 8. See Treat. 4. §. 46. owneown enioynedenjoined to them, their place and office to be their wiueswives head, with many other like arguments, whereof we ſhallshall more diſtinctlydistinctly ſpeakespeak, when we come to declare the particular duties of husbands, doedo proueprove as much. The greateſtgreatest queſtionquestion is concerning the wife, whether ſheshe be bound to take any care about the goods. But if the Scripture be thor • owlythoroughly ſearchedsearched, we ſhallshall findefind proofeproof enough to ſhewshow that eueneven s • heshethe alſoalso is bound hereunto. For firſtfirst, the generallgeneral end which God aimed at in making the woman (namely to be Gen. 2. 18. an helpehelp t • o man) implieth as much: for herein may ſheshe be a verievery great helpehelp, as we ſhallshall ſeesee by and by in ſundrysundry particulars. 2. That
generallgeneral property attributed to a wife to be ProuProv. 18. 22. a good thing, confirmeth as much: for that which is profitable is called good: and it is one reſpectrespect wherein a wife is termed a good thing, that ſheshe may by her prouidenceprovidence and diligence bring much profit to her husband: and therefore in this, among other reſpectsrespects, the good wife which SalomonSolomon deſcribethdescribeth, is ſaidsaid ProuProv. 31. 12. to doedo good to her husband all the daiesdays of her life: for by her induſtryindustry and prouidenceprovidence ſheeshe did ſoso preſeruepreserve and increaſeincrease his goods, that VerſVers. 11. the heart of her husband truſtedtrusted in her, and he had no need of ſpoilespoil. If the particular actions whereby that good wife is deſcribeddescribed be well noted, we may eaſilyeasily obſerueobserve that ſheshe was an eſpeciallespecial helpehelp vntounto her husband, eueneven in his outward eſtateestate. From all which, we may inferreinfer theſethese two points. FirſtFirst, that this prouidentprovident care about outward temporalltemporal goods is lawfulllawful, not vnbeſeemingunbeseeming a ChriſtianChristian man or woman. Secondly, that it is a mutuallmutual dutieduty appertaining both to husband and wife.

For the firſtfirst, how needfullneedful the goods of this world are for preſeruationpreservation of life and health, eſtateestate of the family, good of Church and Commoncommon-wealth, releeferelief of the poorepoor, with the like vſesuses, no man can be ignorant. God hath giuengiven them as bleſſingsblessings to his children, and that often times in great abundance; and his children hauehave accordingly beenebeen thankfullthankful for them: ſoso as a prouidentprovident care about them is not vnlawfullunlawful, but very expedient and needfullneedful.

For the ſecondsecond, If there ſhouldshould not be a iointjoint care herein, the care and painespains of the one might be altogether in vainevain. For ſuppoſesuppose an husband be induſtriousindustrious, as Gen. 31. 40. IaakobJacob was, and get much abroad, if the wife either by her vnthriftineſſeunthriftiness, idleneſſeidleness, negligence, or the like vices, ſuffersuffer that which is brought home to be embeaſeledembezzledembeaseled and waſtedwasted; or by her prodigalitieprodigality, braueriebravery, or louelove of vainevain companiecompany, conſumeconsume it her ſelfeself, where will be the profit of the husbands painespains? Or on the other ſideside, if a wife ſhouldshould be as painfullpainful and proſperousprosperous in getting, as ProuProv. 31. 10. &etcc. the good houſwifehousewifehouswife before mentioned was, and the husband by carding, dicing, drinking, reuellingrevelling, or other like meanesmeans ſhouldshould waſtewaste all away, what fruit would remaineremain of the wiueswives prouidenceprovidence? In this mutuallmutual prouidentprovident care of husband and wife, each of them muſtmust hauehave an eye to their owneown place:
affairesaffairs abroad doedo moſtmost appertaineappertain to the man, and are eſpeciallyespecially Externa negotia viro permitte. Greg. Naz. ad Olymp. to be ordered by him: that which the wife is eſpeciallyespecially to care for, is the buſineſſebusiness of the houſehouse: for the ApoſtleApostle laiethlayeth it downedown as a rule for wiueswives (as we ſhallshall hereafter more particularly declare) that they Tit. 2. 5. keepekeep at home, and 1 Tim. 5. 14. gouernegovern the houſehouse. By this means may they be very profitable each to other.

div.head: §. 39. Of the vices contrary to the good prouidenceprovidence of huſbandhusband and wife, about the goods of the family.
div.p: Contrary to that dutieduty, are theſethese vices following.

1. CouetouſneſſeCovetousness, and ouermuchovermuch care for themſeluesthemselves: as Contrary vices. when an husband ſoso raketh, and ſcrapethscrapeth, and hoordethhoardeth vpup for himſelfehimself, as he neither affordeth vntounto his wife ſoso much as is 1. CouetouſneſſeCovetousness. meet for her place while he liuethliveth with her, nor thinketh of prouidingproviding ſufficientsufficient maintenance for her, if ſheeshe ouerover-liuelive him, but rather thinketh how to defraud her of that which the law caſtethcasteth vponupon her. Or when a wife ſecretlysecretly hoordethhoardeth vpup whatſoeuerwhatsoever ſheshe can get, either by her owneown induſtryindustry, or elſeelse by purloining from her husband: ſometimessometimes ſellingselling cornecorn, wares, houſholdhousehold-ſtuffestuff, or other like commodities, ſoso priuilyprivily as the husband ſhallshall neuernever know it: ſometimessometimes taking money out of his counter, box, baggebag, cheſtchest, or the like, ſoso as either it ſhallshall not be miſſedmissed, or if it be, it ſhallshall not be knowneknown who had it. Many there be who in miſtruſtmistrust of their husbands prouidenceprovidence, or in diſlikedislike of them, or on ſomesome other by-reſpectsrespects, commit whatſoeuerwhatsoever they can get to the truſttrust and cuſtodycustody of others, whereby it oft commethcometh to paſſepass, that they themſeluesthemselves, meeting with deceitfulldeceitful friends, are vtterlyutterly defeated, eueneven becauſebecause they dare not make their fraud knowneknown. As CouetouſneſſeCovetousness is in it ſelfeself an odious ſinnesin; ſoso it is made much more hainousheinous by defrauding husband or wife, who ought to be as dearedear each to other as themſeluesthemselves.

2. ProdigalitieProdigality, and too lauiſhlavish ſpendingspending vponupon themſeluesthemselves, 2. Prodigality. and thoſethose things which are moſtmost agreeable to their owneown corrupt humor: as when husbands without any meanemean or meas • ure, ſpendspend their goods abroad in hunting, haukinghawking, carding, d • icing, eating, drinking, or the like, and ſuffersuffer their wiueswives to want at home, and yet tooketook their wiueswives to maintainemaintain them, and therefore had their portion. Or when wiueswives bring their
husbands into debt, and weaken, if not cleaneclean ouerthrowoverthrow their eſtateestate, by gorgeous decking and adorning their houſeshouses, by brauebrave and coſtlycostly apparellapparel, by dainty fare, by goſſippinggossipping abroad, with the like. Many wiueswives are ſoso violent herein, that if their deſiredesire and humour be not ſatisfiedsatisfied, their husbands ſhallshall hauehave no reſtrest (forſoothforsooth they brought a portion, and maintained they muſtmust and will be; it skilleth not whether their husbands eſtateestate can bearebear it or no) in ſoso much as many are forced wittingly, for quietneſſequietness ſakesake, to ſuffersuffer their eſtateestate to ſinkesink. O fooliſhfoolish and wretched wiueswives! howHow little do they conſiderconsider that they were mariedmarried to doedo their husbands good, and not euillevil all the daiesdays of their life? isIs this to be an helpehelp to man? orOr rather is it not cleaneclean to thwart Gods counſellcounsel, and peruertpervert his purpoſepurpose? canCan we thinkethink that God will forbeareforbear, and not be auengedavenged of them? yetYet much more will God be auengedavenged of the forenamed husbands, becauſebecause of that image of himſelfehimself which he hath placed in them, and becauſebecause of that place and authority wherein he hath ſetset them. The ApoſtleApostle expreſlyexpressly ſaithsaith of them, that they are worſeworse then Infidels, which being ſoso, they muſtmust lookelook for 1 Tim. 5. 8. the greater iudgementjudgment.

3. IdleneſſeIdleness, and a careleſſecareless neglect of their eſtateestate. Many 3. IdleneſſeIdleness. men ſpendspend day after day, like a bird that flieth vpup and downedown, as it falleth out, from tree to tree, from twiggetwig to twiggetwig: they goego from place to place, but know not for what end: as they meet with any company, ſoso they abide as long as the company tarrieth, and then ſeekeseek after other company, and are ready to goego with any to Ale-houſehouse, TauerneTavern, Play-houſehouse, BowlingalleyBowling-alley, or other like places. Many women alſoalso ſpendspend all the forenooneforenoon in lying a bed and tyringtiring themſeluesthemselves, and the afternooneafternoon as occaſionoccasion is offered in ſittingsitting idly at home, or walking forth to little purpoſepurpose, but only to wearewear out time, little regarding their husbands eſtateestate, whether it increaſeincrease, or diminiſhdiminish. Thus by the idleneſſeidleness and careleſneſſecarelessness of husband and wife, come fairefair eſtatesestates many times to ruineruin, and both of thenthem brought to penury and beggerybeggary.

div.head: §. 40. Of husbands and wiueswives iointjoint care in gouerninggoverning the family.
div.p:
Hitherto I hauehave deliuereddelivered ſuchsuch common duties as mutually
reſpectrespect the husband and wife, and are to be performed of each to other. There are other common duties which they are both iointlyjointly bound to performeperform to other perſonspersons: and thoſethose either members of the family, or ſtrangersstrangers commingcoming to the family.

Concerning the members of the family, though there be ſomesome peculiar duties belonging to the maſtermaster, and ſomesome to the miſtreſſemistress, ſomesome to the father, and ſomesome to the mother, of which we ſhallshall ſpeakespeak in their due place; yet in generallgeneral the gouernmentgovernment of the family, and the ſeuerallseveral members thereof belongeth to the husband and wife both (if at leaſtleast they hauehave a family) and a iointjoint common dutieduty it is to be helpfullhelpful one to another therein.

ObiectObject. Seeing it is not neceſſarilynecessarily required, that a huſbandhusband and wife ſhouldshould hauehave a family to gouernegovern, for two may be mariedmarried and hauehave neither children nor ſeruantsservants (as many are) and yet be true husband and wife; why is this care of a family ranked among the duties of husband and wife?

AnſwAnsw. 1. BecauſeBecause ordinarily when two are mariedmarried they gather a family, and are the gouernoursgovernors thereof: ſoso as though it failefail in ſomesome particulars, yet for the moſtmost part it holdeth.

2. BecauſeBecause the iointjoint gouernmentgovernment whereof I ſpeakespeak in this place is by vertuevirtue of the mariagemarriage-bond: for if a man and a woman ſhouldshould liuelive together in an houſehouse, and by mutuallmutual conſentconsent hauehave a iointjoint authority and gouernmentgovernment, this would be very offenſiueoffensive to all that ſhouldshould know it, or hearehear of it: neither were they by any ordinance of God bound to be ſoso helpfullhelpful one to another as husband and wife: nor the members of a family ſoso bound to ſubiectsubject themſeluesthemselves to both.

3. The duty whereof I ſpeakespeak, though it be about the gouernmentgovernment of a family, yet hath it reſpectrespect to an huſbandhusband as he is an husband, and to a wife as ſheeshe is a wife; namely, that by vertuevirtue of their mariagemarriage-bond, and neerenear vnionunion, they be helpfullhelpful one to another in well-ordering the things of the family.

Whether the man ought to look to the good gouernmentgovernment of
his houſehouse is a queſtionquestion without all queſtionquestion. He is the higheſthighest in the family, and hath both authoritieauthority ouerover all, and the charge of all is committed to his charge: he is as a king in his owneown houſehouse: as a king is to ſeesee that land well gouernedgoverned where he is king, ſoso he that is the chiefechief ruler in an houſehouse. The dutieduty which the ApoſtleApostle applieth in particular to BiſhopsBishops & Deacons, in generallgeneral appertaineth to all husbands, 1 Tim. 3. 4. that they rule their owneown houſehouse honeſtlyhonestly: and againeagain, VerſVers. 12. that they be ſuchsuch as can rule their children well, and their owneown houſholdshouseholds. The care of many huſbandshusbands is in this reſpectrespect commended in Scripture, as of Gen. 18. 19. Abram, of & 35. 2, &etcc.
IaakobJacob, of Jo • ſ • Jos 4. 24. 15. IoſuahJoshua, of PſalPsal. 101. 2. &etcc.
DauidDavid, the IohJoh. 44. 53. Ruler at GalileGalilee, and of many other. That the wife alſoalso ought to be an helpehelp to him therein, is very euidentevident: for the ApoſtleApostle layeth it expreſlyexpressly to their charge, 1 Tim. 5. 14. that they gouernegovern the houſehouse: would the WiſeWise man hauehave ſoso highly commended a wife ProuProv. 31. 11, &etcc. for well gouerninggoverning her huſbandshusbands houſehouse if it had not appertained to her? It is very likely that wiſewise Abigail had a great hand in gouerninggoverning Nabals houſehouse, becauſebecause the ſeruantsservants made complaint to her of Nabals churliſhneſſechurlishness, and becauſebecause ſheshe had the ſeruantsservants at command, readily to doedo what ſheshe would hauehave them; yea alſoalso, becauſebecause ſheshe could ſoso readily prepare ſuchsuch ſtorestore of prouiſionprovision for DauidDavid and his men, as ſheshe did. Hence is it that the wife is called Mater-familias. miſtreſſemistress of the houſehouse, as well as the husband Pater-familias. maſtermaster of the houſehouse.

p.hi: ObiectObject.
A woman is not to teach, nor to vſurpeusurp authoritieauthority ouerover the man.

div.p: AnſwAnsw. 1. That branch of teaching hath reſpectrespect to publikepublic aſſembliesassemblies, and Churches, in which ſheshe may not teach: but not to priuateprivate families, in which ſheshe may, and ought to teach: for Pro. 31. 4. BarthſhebahBathshebaBarthshebah taught SalomonSolomon. When Acts 18. 26. Apollos was brought to the houſehouse of Aquila, PriſcillaPriscilla the wife of Aquila did helpehelp to expound to Apollos the way of God more perfectly.

2. The other branch concerning authoritieauthority, hath not reference to the inferiourinferior members in the family, ouerover which the wife of an houſholdhousehold gouernourgovernor hath authoritieauthority, but only to the husband, ouerover whom if ſheshe take any authoritieauthority, ſheshe vſurpethusurpeth it. TherforeTherefore neither this place of Scripture, nor any other doth exclude the wife, being iointlyjointly conſideredconsidered with the husband, to rule & gouernegovern thoſethose in the family which are vnderunder them both.
2. ObiectObject. This iointjoint gouernmentgovernment of the wife doth much impaireimpair the dignity and authority of the husband.

AnſwAnsw. Nothing leſſeless: for ſheshe is ſubordinatesubordinate to her husband, and muſtmust ſoso rule others as ſheshe be ſubiectsubject to her husband, and not command any thing againſtagainst his command, (prouidedprovided that his command be not againſtagainst the Lord, and his word.) We ſeesee that in all eſtatesestates the king or higheſthighest gouernourgovernor hath other MagiſtratesMagistrates vnderunder him, who hauehave a command ouerover the ſubiectssubjects, and yet thereby the kings ſupremesupreme authoritieauthority is no whit impaired, but rather the better eſtabliſhedestablished, and he the more honoured. So is it in a family. 1. ReaſonReason. Husbands and wiueswives by their mutuallmutual aſſiſtanceassistance bring great help one to another. Plus vident oculi quàm oculus. AriſtArist. Polit. li. 3. c. 7.

Let therefore husbands and wiueswives herein aſſiſtassist one another, for ſoso they may be very helpfullhelpful one to another, and bring, by their mutuallmutual helpehelp in gouerninggoverning, much good to the family. The husband by his helpehelp aiding his wife, addeth much authoritieauthority vntounto her, and ſoso cauſethcauseth that ſheshe is not deſpiſeddespised, nor lightly eſteemedesteemed. The wife by her helpehelp cauſethcauseth many things to be eſpiedespied, and ſoso redreſſedredressed, which otherwiſeotherwise might neuernever hauehave beenebeen found out: for two eieseyes ſeesee more then one, eſpeciallyespecially when one of thoſethose is more at hand, and in preſencepresence, as the 2. ReaſonReason. Many things in a family more fit for the one to meddle with, then for the other. wife is in the houſehouse.

BeſidesBesides there are many things in well gouerninggoverning a family more fit for one to meddle withallwithal then for the other: as for the husband to meddle with the great and weightieweighty affairesaffairs of the family (as performing Gods worſhipworship, appointing and ſetlingsettling good orders, prouidingproviding conuenientconvenient houſehouse-roomeroom, and other neceſſariesnecessaries for the family: keeping children when they grow In familia diſpertitadispertita ſuntsunt officia: ſunt
que ſuntquesuntque alia viri, alia vxoris propria. Pro▪ ſuntsuntProsunt ergo vter
que vterque alteri ſuasua in commune confe rentesconferentes: ob eam
que eamque cauſamcausam ſuauitassuauitas in hac tali amicitia ineſtinest, vtilitaſ
que vtilitaſquevtilitasque maxima. AriſtArist. Eth. li. 8. ca. 12. great, or waxewax ſtubbornestubborn, in awe: ruling men ſeruantsservants, with the likelike.) And for the wife to meddle with ſomesome leſſeless, but very needfullneedful matters, as nouriſhingnourishing and inſtructinginstructing children when they are young, adorning the houſehouse, ordering the prouiſionprovision brought into the houſehouse, ruling maid ſeruantsservants, with the like. Yea further, as the man eſpeciallyespecially is to performeperform the very actions of prayer, reading the word, catechizing, and other like duties in the family, ſoso the wife may be a great helpehelp in putting her husband in mindemind both of the dutieduty it ſelfeself, and of the time of performing it, and incouragingencouraging him to doedo it, in gathering the family together, and exhorting them to be forward,
in making her ſelfeself an example to the reſtrest by her diligent and reuerendreverend attention, in oft vrgingurging and preſſingpressing to her children and ſeruantsservants ſuchsuch points of inſtructioninstruction as her husband hath taught; yea, in praying, reading, teaching, and performing like exerciſesexercises her ſelfeself, ſoso farrefar as ſheshe is able, when her huſbandhusband is abſentabsent, or negligent and careleſſecareless, and will not himſelfehimself doedo them; or it may be, is not able to doedo them: or if ſheshe performeperform them not her ſelfeself, in getting ſomesome other to performeperform them.

div.head: §. 41. Of the vices contrary to a iointjoint care of gouerninggoverning the family.
div.p: The mindemind and practiſepractise of many, both husbands and wiueswives, Vices contrary. is contrary to this dutieduty.

Many a husband becauſebecause the wiueswives office is eſpeciallyespecially to 1. When huſbandshusbands put off all gouernmentgovernment to their wiueswives. abide at home, will put off all gouernmentgovernment to the wife: leauingleaving it to her not only to order the things in the houſehouse, but alſoalso to bring in all needful things, to order and gouernegovern the children both young and old, yea eueneven to prouideprovide for them alſoalso, to take in, to put out, to vſeuse all ſortssorts of ſeruantsservants as pleaſethpleaseth her: yea, if ſeruantsservants ſhallshall be ſtubbornestubborn and ſtoutstout againſtagainst her, he will take no notice of it, nor endure to be told of it, much leſſeless afford her his aſſiſtanceassistance, but ſuffersuffer her to be diſgraceddisgraced and deſpiſeddespised. As for religious duties, he will no way meddle with them. Oh baſebase minded men, vnworthyunworthy to be huſbandshusbands and heads of wiueswives! ſhallShall your wiueswives who were made to be an helpehelp to you, hauehave no helpehelp from you, n • onodo not in thoſethose things which eſpeciallyespecially belong to your charge? ſhallShall the weaker veſſelsvessels bearebear all the burden? AſſuredlyAssuredly as the man carrieth away the greateſtgreatest reputation and honour when a family is well gouernedgoverned (though it be by the ioyntjoint care and wiſdomewisdom of his wife) ſoso lieth he moſtmost open to the iudgementjudgment of God if the gouernmentgovernment thereof be neglected, and through the neglect thereof, children and ſeruantsservants grow impious: inſtanceinstance 1 Sam. 3. 12, 13. ElieEliEly, and 2 Sam. 15. DauidDavid. For as in a common-wealth, the greateſtgreatest honour of good gouernmentgovernment, victorious battelsbattles, happy peace, and proſperityprosperity, and the greateſtgreatest diſhonordishonor and dammagedamage of the contrary, redoundeth to the king, ſoso to the man who is chiefechief gouernourgovernor in a family: for it is preſuppoſedpresupposed, that all which doedo any good are inſtrumentsinstruments of
the higheſthighest gouernourgovernor: if any euillevil or miſchiefemischief fall out, that it is through his negligence.

On the other ſideside, becauſebecause the husband is the moſtmost principallprincipal, 2. When wiueswives refuſerefuse to addeadd their aideaid. many wiueswives thinkethink that the gouernmentgovernment of the family nothing at all appertainesappertains to them, and thereupon are careleſſecareless of the good thereof, and will not ſtirrestir their leaſtleast finger to order any thing aright: but, if any thing be amiſſeamiss, lay all the blame on their husbands. DoeDo not ſuchsuch peruertpervert that mainemain end for which God made them, eueneven to be an helpehelp? DoeDo they not carriecarry themſeluesthemselves moſtmost vnworthyunworthy of the place wherein God hath ſetset them, namely to be ioyntjoint-gouernoursgovernors with their husbands, and partakers of their dignities? As by their negligence they make themſeluesthemselves acceſſaryaccessary to all the euillevil which falleth out in the family, ſoso aſſuredlyassuredly ſhallshall they hauehave their part in thoſethose iudgementsjudgments which are executed on the head thereof.

MoſtMost contrary to the forenamed dutieduty is the practiſepractise of 3. When husbands or wiueswives are hinderanceshindrances each to other. ſuchsuch as are hindrances one to another in gouerninggoverning the family: as when wiueswives are not only negligent themſeluesthemselves in commingcoming to religious exerciſesexercises, but keepekeep backeback children and ſeruantsservants, and ſoso are a great griefegrief vntounto their religious huſbandshusbands: or when they vſeuse any of the children or ſeruantsservants to be inſtrumentsinstruments of iniquity; or are themſeluesthemselves diſquietdisquiet and troubleſometroublesome in the houſehouse, like to her of whom SalomonSolomon ſpeakethspeaketh in this prouerbeproverb, It is better to dwell in the corner of the houſehouse
Pro. 21. 9. top, then with a contentious woman in a wide houſehouse.

Husbands alſoalso are oft an hinderancehindrance to that good gouernmentgovernment which their wiueswives would helpehelp forward, when they ſcoffescoff and ſcornescorn at that good counſellcounsel which their wiueswives giuegive them for that purpoſepurpose, or when they will not ſuffersuffer their wiueswives to meddle with any thing at all, nor endure that they ſhouldshould findefind any fault, much leſſeless take in hand to redreſſeredress any thing that is amiſſeamiss. TheſeThese and ſuchsuch like peruerſeperverse diſpoſitionsdispositions are in husbands and wiueswives, whereby it commethcometh to paſſepass that they who were ioynedjoined together to be a mutuallmutual helpehelp each to other, proueprove heauyheavy, yea intolerable burdens.

div.head: §. 42. Of husbands and wiueswives mutuallmutual helpehelp in hoſpitalityhospitality.
div.p:
The next common duty of husband and wife reſpectethrespecteth
ſuchsuch as come to their houſehouse, but are no particular members thereof, whether they be kindred, alliance, acquaintance, or ſtrangersstrangers, eſpeciallyespecially if they be Saints, to whom Heb. 13. 2. Rom. 12. 13. hoſpitalityhospitality, that is, a kindekind and courteous entertainment, is due. Herein therefore muſtmust husbands and wiueswives be helpfullhelpful one to another: for as it is required of 1 Tim. 3. 2. husbands, ſoso alſoalso of & 5. 10. wiueswives to be harborous, namely while they are mariedmarried, together with their husbands, and when they are widoweswidows, of themſeluesthemselves. Gen. 1818. 6. &etcc.
Abraham and Sarah were herein an helpehelp one to another, when the three Angels in ſhapesshapes of men came to their houſehouse: ſoso were 2 King. 4. 8. the Shunemite and her husband when EliſhaElisha the Prophet came to their houſehouse.

For hoſpitalityhospitality, that it is a commendable dutieduty belonging ReaſonsReasons. 1. HoſpitalityHospitality a commendable dutieduty. to ſuchsuch as are houſehouse-keepers and able to giuegive entertainment, is euidentevident by the precepts and examples before ſpecifiedspecified, as alſoalso by the bleſſingblessing which God thereupon hath brought to the houſeshouses of them that were giuengiven thereunto, which the ApoſtleApostle intimateth in theſethese words, Heb. 13. 2. thereby ſomesome hauehave entertained Angels vnawaresunawares. Now therforetherefore husbands and wiueswives being (as we hauehave heard) ioyntjoint gouernoursgovernors, as in other things, ſoso in this they ought to lend an helping hand each to other, and that for theſethese reaſonsreasons.

1. BecauſeBecause in giuinggiving entertainment there are ſundrysundry 2. The entertainment will be the better by a mutuallmutual helpehelp. things to be done, whereof ſomesome are proper to the husbands place, and ſomesome to the wiueswives. To take order for the prouiſionprovision of things without dooresdoors is more fit for the husband, Gen. 18. 7. Abraham did it: to order the ſmallersmaller things within dooresdoors is more fit for the wife; that was left to VerſVers. 6. Sarah.

2. BecauſeBecause it is meet that gueſtsguests ſhouldshould know they are welcome 3. GueſtsGuests will be more cheerefullcheerful. both to the husband and to the wife, that ſoso they may be the more cheerefullcheerful.

3. BecauſeBecause a mutuallmutual conſentconsent, and cheerefullcheerful help herein will 4. MutuallMutual louelove will be more firmefirm. be an eſpeciallespecial means, as to manifeſtmanifest their mutuallmutual affection, ſoso to hold the hearts of man and wife firmefirm and cloſeclose together, and make them the better like and louelove one the other: eſpeciallyespecially if the husband ſhallshall ſhewshow himſelfehimself as ready and willing to entertaineentertain his wiueswives friends and kindred as his owneown, and ſoso the wife her husbands (as they ought.) div.head: §. 43. Of vices contrary to mutuallmutual helpehelp in hoſpitalityhospitality.
div.p: Contrary to this dutieduty is for the moſtmost part couetouſneſſecovetousness in the husband, and laſineſſelazinesslasiness in the wife. The man, becauſebecause the charge of the family lieth on him, diſtruſtfullydistrustfully feareth leſtlest he ſhouldshould want for his owneown.

I deniedeny not but that a prouidentprovident care for our owneown, & namely for them of the family, is needfullneedful and commendable, 1 Tim. 5. 8. he that prouidethprovideth not for them is worſeworse then an infidellinfidel: ſoso as a man may be ouerlauiſhoverlavish in giuinggiving entertainment, if he goego beyond his meanesmeans, impoueriſhimpoverish his eſtateestate, and diſabledisable himſelfehimself to prouideprovide for his owneown, as many doedo: yet when a man hath ſufficientsufficient, yea and abundance, when there is no iuſtjust cauſecause, but meerelymerely vponupon an vndueundue fearefear too carkingly, and diſtruſtfullydistrustfully to pinch, and grudge to giuegive entertaimententertainment to any, is vnbeſeemingunbeseeming a ChriſtianChristian, yea alſoalso to be worſeworse then an infidellinfidel; not worthy to hauehave an houſehouse, or any thing fit for entertainment; no nor worthy of common ſocietysociety.

The woman on the other ſideside grudgeth at the painespains ſheshe muſtmust take, and trouble ſheshe muſtmust vndergoeundergo about entertaining gueſtsguests, and thereupon is loth that any at any time ſhouldshould come to their houſehouse.

Concerning a wife, I deniedeny not but that an husband may be in this kindekind ouerburdenſomeoverburdensome to her, by being too iouealljovialjoveall, as they ſpeakespeak, and bringing gueſtsguests too often into the houſehouse, eſpeciallyespecially if they be gueſtsguests of no good name; and by that meanesmeans make her eueneven weary of her life: but yet for a wife to refuſerefuse all painespains in that kindekind, and to be diſcontenteddiscontented when her husband inuitesinvitesinuits any friends, or when any come (as the three Angels did to Abraham) vnawaresunawares, argueth not a louingloving affection, nor a wiuelikewivelike ſubiectionsubjection vntounto her husband, to be in her.

TheſeThese faults are ſoso much the greater when the husband, or wife, are free and forward in entertaining their owneown kindred
and friends: but are backward, and grudge at the entertainment of each others friends and kindred. Hence commonly ariſethariseth much heart-burning of one againſtagainst the other: yea much iarrejar and contention betwixt them: and from diſlikedislike of the practiſepractise of one another in this kindekind oft followeth a diſlikedislike of one anothers perſonperson: ſoso that as the fault is bad in it ſelfeself, it prouesproves to be much worſeworse in the miſchiefesmischiefs that follow vponupon it.

div.head: §. 44. Of husbands and wiueswives mutuallmutual helpehelp in releeuingrelievingreleeving the poorepoor.
div.p: The laſtlast common and ioyntjoint dutieduty wherein husband and wife ought to be helpfullhelpful each to other, reſpectethrespecteth thoſethose that are without the houſehouse, namely the poorepoor, and ſuchsuch as ſtandstand in need of their helpehelp, who are to be releeuedrelieved and ſuccouredsuccoured. BecauſeBecause man and wife vſuallyusually mealemeal together, and are ioyntjoint partakers of Gods good creatures, they muſtmust put one another in mindemind of that precept of charity which was giuengiven to the IewesJews when they were at their mealesmeals, Neh. 8. 10. ſendsend part vntounto them for whom none is prouidedprovided. The good wife which is ſetset forth by the holy GhoſtGhost for a patternepattern and example vntounto others to follow, together with her husband, are noted to be helpfullhelpful one to another in this dutieduty: for ſheshe is ſaidsaid Pro. 31. 20. to ſtretchstretch out her hand to the poorepoor, and to the needy: and he is ſaidsaid VerſVers. 28. to praiſepraise her, thereby incouragingencouraging her to hold on in doing thoſethose good things which ſheshe did. What liberty the wife hath, or howfarhow far forth ſheshe may be reſtrainedrestrained in caſecase her husband vtterlyutterly refuſerefuse to giuegive conſentconsent, we ſhallshall Treat. 3. §. 23. 33. hereafter declare in the particular duties of wiueswives: the point here noted is, that both the huſbandhusband himſelfehimself muſtmust according to his abilitieability be bountifullbountiful to the poorepoor, and ſuffersuffer his wife, yea prouokeprovoke her ſoso to be, and withallwithal allow her wherewithallwherewithal to be bountifullbountiful: and that the wife alſoalso muſtmust ſtirrestir vpup her husband to liberalitieliberality in this reſpectrespect, and her ſelfeself open her hand to the poorepoor in the things which lawfully ſheshe may giuegive.

There is nothing wherbywhereby a man or wife can bring more profit to the houſehouse, then by giuinggiving to the poorepoor: that which is giuengiven
to the poorepoor is ProuProv. 19. 17. lent to the Lord, and he will repay it with great increaſeincrease: it is as 2 Cor. 9. 6. ſeedseed, which being liberally ſowensownsowen, will bring forth a plentifullplentiful harueſtharvest: yea, it is a meanesmeans to make vsus Luke 16. 9. friends, to ſpeakespeak a good word for vsus at the barrebar of ChriſtsChrists iudgementjudgment ſeatseat: and it bringeth not only the IobJob 29. 13. & 31. 20. bleſſingblessing of men, but Matth. 5. 7. of God alſoalso, eueneven the greateſtgreatest bleſsingblessing of all, the Mat. 25. 34. bleſsingblessing of eternalleternal life: for it is Heb. 13. 16. a ſacrificesacrifice with which God is well pleaſedpleased. The ApoſtleApostle noteth this to be one of ChriſtsChrists oracles, which by word of mouth he left vntounto his DiſciplesDisciples, Acts 20. 35. It is more bleſſedblessed to giuegive then to receiuereceive.

BeſidesBesides, husbands and wiueswives in diſtributingdistributing almesalms, may receiuereceive 2. Husband and wife in place to giuegive good direction one to another. good direction one from another: the husband by telling the wife who are fit to be releeuedrelieved (for commonly huſbandshusbands better know thoſethose which are abroad out of the family) the wife by telling the husband what things are fitteſtfittest to be giuengiven away: for wiueswives commonly know of what things there is greateſtgreatest ſtorestore, and what may in the houſehouse be beſtbest ſparedspared.

div.head: §. 45. Of husbands and wiueswives vnmercifulneſſeunmercifulness to the poorepoor.
div.p: ContrarieContrary is the vnmercifulneſſeunmercifulness of many husbands, who Vices contrariecontrary. are not only hard-hearted themſeluesthemselves (neuernever giuinggiving any thing vnleſſeunless by the law of the land they be forced, & then they part 1. Binding his wiueswives hands. they bring both the cry of the poorepoor, and alſoalso the groanesgroans and griefegrief of a mercifullmerciful wife who is thus reſtrainedrestrained, vponupon their owneown necks, and aggrauateaggravate their ſinnesin in an high degree.

On the other ſideside, the vnmercifulneſſeunmercifulness of many wiueswives is alſoalso contrariecontrary to the forenamed dutieduty: for there are many, who though they hauehave libertieliberty to giuegive of the common goods, and alſoalso allowance of their owneown out of which they may giuegive, yet couetouſlycovetously hoordhoard vpup all they can get, giuegive not a pennies worth, outbut rather ſuffersuffer victuals and other things to periſhperish in the houſehouse, and when they are naught to fling them away, then that any thing whilſtwhilst it is good ſhouldshould be giuengiven out of the houſehouse. Shall not the creatures which are ſpoiledspoiled in an houſehouse,

Yea further, many wiueswives are grieuedgrieved at their husbands bountiebounty, and ſtillstill mouingmoving him to ſhutshut his hand, and giuegive no more. Are they not plaineplain deuilsdevils herein, oppoſingopposing againſtagainst that which is good?

div.head: The third TreatiſeTreatise. Of wiueswives particular duties.
§. 1. Of the generallgeneral heads of this treatiſetreatise.

epigraph.q: WiuesWives ſubmitsubmit your ſeluesselves vntounto your owneown husbands as vntounto the Lord.

VerſVers. 24. Therefore as the Church is ſubjectsubject to ChriſtChrist, ſoso let wiueswives be ſubiectsubject to their husbands in euerieevery thing.

div.p:
INIn the particular declaration of wiueswives duties, the ApoſtleApostle noteth two points,
1. The dutieduty required.
2. The reaſonreason to enforce it.

In ſettingsetting forth the dutieduty, he declareth

In the matter we may note,

To declare the qualitiequality of wiueswives ſubiectionsubjection to their huſbandshusbands, two rules are ſetset downedown.

2. That it be ſuchsuch a ſubiectionsubjection as the As the Church is ſubiectsubject to ChriſtChrist. Church performeth vntounto ChriſtChrist.

The extent of wiueswives ſubiectionsubjection doth ſtretchstretch it ſelfeself verievery farrefar, eueneven to

The reaſonreason to enforce all theſethese points is taken from that place of eminencieeminency and authoritieauthority, wherein the husband is ſetset aboueabove his wife: which is,
1. Propounded vnderunder the metaphor of an head (for the huſbandhusband is the head of the wife.)
2. Amplified by that reſemblanceresemblance which therein he hath vntounto ChriſtChrist.
In which reſemblanceresemblance two points are noted.

2. That the husband by vertuevirtue of his office is a protector of his wife (and he is the ſauioursaviour of the body.)

div.head: §. 2. Of a wiueswives Treat. 4. §. 2. ſubiectionsubjection in generallgeneral.
div.p: The firſtfirst point to be handled in the treatiſetreatise of wiueswives particular duties is the generallgeneral matter of all (Subiectionsubjection) vnderunder which all other particulars are compriſedcomprised, for it hath as large Maritum habere Dominum meruit mulieris culpa, quod tamen niſinisi ſerueturseruetur, deprauabitur ampliùs natura, & augebitur culpa. Aug. de Gen. ad lit. lib. 11. c. 37. Ante peccatum non aliter factam fuiſſefuisse decet credere mulierem niſinisi vt vir ei dominaretur. Ibid. an extent as that Honourhonour which is required in the firſtfirst commandementcommandment, being applied to wiueswives. When firſtfirst the Lord declared vntounto woman her dutieduty, he ſetset it downedown vnderunder this phraſephrase, Thy deſiredesire ſhallshall be ſubiectsubject to thine husband, Gen. 3. 16.

div.head: ObiectObject. That was a puniſhmentpunishment inflicted on her for her tranſgreſſiontransgression?
div.p:
AnſwAnsw. And a law too, for trialltrial of her obedience, which if it be not obſeruedobserved, her nature will be more depraueddepraved, and her fault more increaſedincreased. BeſidesBesides, we cannot but thinkethink that the woman was made before the fall, that the man might rule ouerover her. VponUpon this ground the Prophets and ApoſtlesApostles hauehave oft vrgedurged the ſamesame. Sarah is commended for this, that ſheshe was ſubiectsubject to her husband (1. Pet. 3. 6.) Hereby the holy GhoſtGhost would teach wiueswives, that Subiectionsubjection ought to be as ſaltsalt to ſeaſonseason
eueryevery dutieduty which they performeperform to their husband. Their very opinion, affection, ſpeechspeech, action, and all that concerneth the husband, muſtmust ſauoursavour of ſubiectionsubjection. Contrary is the diſpoſitiondisposition of many wiueswives, whom ambition hath tainted and corrupted within and without: they cannot endure to hearehear of ſubiectionsubjection: they imagine that they are made ſlauesslaves thereby. But I hope partly by that which hath beenebeen before deliuereddelivered concerning thoſethose common duties which man and wife doedo mutually owe each to other, and partly by the particulars which vnderunder this generallgeneral are compriſedcomprised, but moſtmost eſpeciallyespecially Quem vocavit ad culpam mulier, iuſtumiustum eſtest vt eum gubernatorem aſſumat • assumat, ne iterum foeminea facilitate labatur. Ambr. Hexaem. l. 5. c. 7. by the duties which the husband in particular oweth to his wife, it will euidentlyevidently appeareappear, that this ſubiectionsubjection is no ſeruitudeservitude. But were it more then it is, ſeeingseeing God requireth ſubiectionsubjection of a wife to her husband, the wife is bound to yeeldyield it. And good reaſonreason it is that ſheshe who firſtfirst drew man into ſinsin, ſhouldshould be now ſubiectsubject to him, leſtlest by the like womaniſhwomanish weakneſſeweakness ſheshe fall againeagain.

div.head: §. 3. Of an husbands Treat. 4. §. 6, 7. ſuperioritiesuperiority ouerover a wife, to be acknowledged by a wife.
div.p:
The ſubiectionsubjection which is required of a wife to her husband implieth two things.
1. That ſheshe acknowledge her husband to be her ſuperioursuperior.
2. That ſheshe reſpectrespect him as her ſuperioursuperior.

row.cell: That acknowledgementacknowledgment of the husbands ſuperioritiesuperiority is twofold,

div.p: The generallgeneral is the ground of the particular: for till a wife be informed that an husband, by vertuevirtue of his place, is his wiueswives ſuperioursuperior, ſheshe will not be perſwadedpersuaded that her owneown huſbandhusband is aboueabove her, or hath any authoritieauthority ouerover her.

FirſtFirst therefore concerning the generallgeneral, I will lay downedown ProofesProofs that the husband is aboueabove the wife ſomesome euidentevident and vndeniableundeniable proofesproofs, to ſhewshow that an husband is his wiueswives ſuperioursuperior, and hath authoritieauthority ouerover her. The proofesproofs are theſethese following.

1. God of whom, Rom. 13. 1. the powers that be ordained, are, hath power to place his Image in whom he will, and to whom God giuethgiveth ſuperioritiesuperiority and authority, the ſamesame ought to be acknowledged
to be due vntounto them. But God ſaidsaid of the man to the woman, he ſhallshall rule ouerover thee, (Gen. 3. 16.)

2. Nature hath placed an eminencieeminency in the male ouerover the Mari & foeminae aea natura tribuiumtributum eſtest, vt hi,hic praeſitpraesit, illa obediat, cum mas praeſtantiorpraestantior ſitsit. AriſtArist. Pol. lib. 1. female: ſoso as where they are linked together in one yoakeyoke, it is giuengiven by nature that he should gouernegovern, ſheshe obey. This did the heathen by light of nature obſerueobserve.

3. The titles and names, whereby an husband is ſetset forth, doedo implieimply a ſuperioritysuperiority and authority in him, as
