〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉
Maſtermaster, (EſtEst. 1. 17.)
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉
Guide, (ProuProv. 2. 17.)
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . Head, (1 Cor. 11. 3.)
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . Image and glory of God, (1 Cor. 11. 7.)

4. The perſonspersons whom the husband by vertuevirtue of his place, and whom the wife by vertuevirtue of her place, repreſentrepresent, moſtmost euidentlyevidently proueprove as much: for an husband repreſentethrepresenteth Christ, and a wife, the Church, (Eph. 5. 23.)

5. The circumſtancescircumstances noted by the holy GhoſtGhost at the womans creation implieimply no leſſeless, as that ſheshe was created after man, for mans good, and out of mans ſideside, (Gen. 2. 18, &etcc.)

6. The very SicapilliSi capilli pro velamine dati ſuntsunt, qua gratia aliud addendūaddendumaddendumaddendun eſtest velamen? Vt non tantum natura, ſedsed etiam voluntate ſubiectamsubiectam ſese eſſeesse confiteatur. ChryſChrys. in 1 Cor. hom. 26. attire which nature and cuſtomecustom of all times and places hauehave taught women to put on, confirmeth the ſamesame: as long hairehair, vailesveils, and other coueringscoverings ouerover the head: this and the former argument doth the ApoſtleApostle himſelfehimself vſeuse to this very purpoſepurpose, 1 Cor. 11. 7, &etcc.

The point then being ſoso cleereclear, wiueswives ought in conſcienceconscience to acknowledge as much: namely that an husband hath ſuperioritysuperiority 1. WiuesWives muſtmust acknowledge a ſuperioritiesuperiority in husbands. and authoritieauthority ouerover a wife. The acknowledgementacknowledgment hereof is a mainemain and principallprincipal dutieduty, and a ground of all other duties. Till a wife be fully inſtructedinstructed therein and truly perſwadedpersuaded thereof, no dutieduty can be performed by her as it ought: for ſubiectionsubjection hath relation to ſuperioritiesuperiority and authoritieauthority. The very notation of the word implieth as much. How then can ſubiectionsubjection be yeeldedyielded, if husbands be not acknowledged ſuperiorssuperiors? It may be forced, as one King conquered in battellbattle by another, may be compelled to yeeldyield homage to the conqueror, but yet becauſebecause he ſtillstill thinketh with himſelfehimself, that he is no whit inferiourinferior, he will hardly be brought willingly to yeeldyield a ſubiectssubjects dutieduty to him, but rather expect a time when he may free himſelfehimself and take reuengerevenge of the conqueror.

div.head: §. 4. Of a fond conceit, that husband and wife are equallequal.
div.p: Contrary to the forenamed ſubiectionsubjection is the opinion of many wiueswives, who thinkethink themſeluesthemselves eueryevery way as good as their husbands, and no way inferiourinferior to them.

The reaſonreason whereof ſeemethseemeth to be that ſmallsmall inequalitieinequality Of all that are inferioursinferiors, the wife commethcometh neereſtnearest to a pariticparity. which is betwixt the husband and the wife: for of all degrees wherein there is any difference betwixt perſonperson and perſonperson, there is the leaſtleast diſparitiedisparity betwixt man and wife. Though the man be as the head, yet is the woman as the heart, which is the moſtmost excellent part of the body next the head, farrefar more excellent then any other member vnderunder the head, and almoſtalmost equallequal to the head in many reſpectsrespects, and as neceſſarynecessary as the head. As an euidenceevidence, that a wife is to man as the heart to the head, ſheshe was at her Gen. 2. 21. firſtfirst creation taken out of the ſideside of man where his heart lieth; and though the woman was at firſtfirst 1 Cor. 11. 12. of the man created out of his ſideside, yet is the man alſoalso by the woman. EuerEver ſincesince the firſtfirst creation man hath beenebeen borne and brought forth out of the womans wombewomb: ſoso as neither the man is without the woman, nor the woman without the man: yea, as 1 Cor. 7. 4. Cùm de pudicitia ſermonemsermonem habet, magna paritas. ChryſChrys. hom. 19. in 1 Cor. 7. the wife hath not power of her owneown body, but the husband, ſoso the husband hath not power of his owneown body, but the wife. They are alſoalso 1 Pet. 3. 7. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . heiresheirs together of the grace of life. BeſidesBesides, wiueswives are mothers of the ſamesame children, whereof their husbands are fathers (for God ſaidsaid to both, Gen. 1. 28. multipliemultiply and increaſeincrease) and miſtreſſesmistresses of the ſamesame ſeruantsservants whereof they are maſtersmasters (for Sarah is called & 16. 4. ObiectObject. AnſwAnsw.
miſtreſſemistress) and in many other reſpectsrespects there is a common equitieequity betwixt husbands and wiueswives; whence many wiueswives gather that in all things there ought to be a mutuallmutual equalitieequality.
But from ſomesome particulars to inferreinfer a generallgeneral is a very weakeweak argument.

1. Doth it follow, that becauſebecause in many things there is a common equitieequity betwixt IudgesJudges of AſſiſeAssizeAssise, IuſticesJustices of peace, and ConſtablesConstables of townestowns, that therefore there is in all things an equalitieequality betwixt them?
2. In many things there is not a common equitieequity: for the husband may command his wife, but not ſheshe him.

3. EuenEven in thoſethose things wherein there is a common equity,
there is not an equality: for the husband hath euerever eueneven in all things a ſuperioritiesuperiority: as if there be any difference eueneven in the forenamed inſtancesinstances, the husband muſtmust hauehave the ſtroakestroke: as in giuinggiving the name of Rachels youngeſtyoungest childechild, where the wife would hauehave one name, the husband another, that name which the husband gauegave, ſtoodstood, (Gen. 35. 18.)

Though there ſeemeseem to be neuernever ſoso little diſparitiedisparity, yet God hauinghaving ſoso expreſlyexpressly appointed ſubiectionsubjection, it ought to be acknowledged: and PoſſuntPossunt coniuges per charitatem ſeruireseruire inuicem, ſedsed mulierem non permittit ApoſtolusApostolus dominari in virum. Aug. de Gen. ad lit. l. 11. c. 37. though husband and wife may mutually ſerueserve one another through louelove: yet the ApoſtleApostle ſufferethsuffereth not a woman to rule ouerover the man.

div.head: §. 5. Of a wiueswives acknowledgementacknowledgment of her Treat. 44. §. 9. owneown husbands ſuperioritiesuperiority.
div.p: The truth and life of that generallgeneral acknowledgementacknowledgment of husbands honour, conſiſtethconsisteth in the particular application therofthereof vntounto their owneown proper husbands.

The next dutieduty therefore is, that wiueswives acknowledge their All wiueswives muſtmust acknowledge their owneown husbands worthy of honour. owneown husbands, eueneven thoſethose to whom by Gods prouidenceprovidence they are ioynedjoined in mariagemarriage, to be worthy of an husbands honour, and to be their ſuperioursuperior: thus much the ApoſtleApostle intendeth by that particle of reſtraintrestraint (
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . Eph. 5. 22, 24. owneown) which he vſethuseth very often: ſoso likewiſelikewise doth 1 Pet. 3. 1, 5. S. Peter, exhorting wiueswives to be in ſubiectionsubjection 1 Cor. 7. 2. to their owneown husbands: and hereunto reſtrainingrestraining the commendation of the ancient good wiueswives, that they were in ſubiectionsubjection to their owneown husbands.

ObiectObject. What if a man of meanemean place be mariedmarried to a woman of eminent place, or a ſeruantservant be mariedmarried to his miſtreſſemistress, or an aged woman to a youth, muſtmust ſuchsuch a wife acknowledge ſuchsuch an husband her ſuperioursuperior?

AnſwAnsw. Yea verily: for in giuinggiving her ſelfeself to be his wife, and WiuesWives inferiourinferior to thoſethose ouerover whom they were before mariagemarriage. taking him to be her husband, ſheshe aduancethadvanceth him aboueabove herſelfeherself, and ſubiectethsubjecteth her ſelfeself vntounto him. It booteth nothing what either of them were before mariagemarriage: by vertuevirtue of the matrimoniallmatrimonial bond the husband is made the head of his wife, though the husband were before mariagemarriage a very beggerbeggar, and of meanemean parentage, and the wife very wealthy and of a noble ſtockestock; or though he were her prentiſeprentice, or bondſlauebondslave; which alſoalso holdeth in the caſecase betwixt an aged woman and a youth:
for the Scripture hath made no exception in any of thoſethose caſescases.

2. ObiectObject. But what if a man of lewd and beaſtlybeastly conditions, as a drunkard, a glutton, a profane ſwaggererswaggerer, an impious ſwearerswearer, and blaſphemerblasphemer, be mariedmarried to a wife, ſobersober, religious Matron, muſtmust ſheshe account him her ſuperioursuperior, and worthy of an husbands honour?

AnſwAnsw. Surely ſheshe muſtmust. For the euillevil qualitiequality and diſpoſitiondisposition SubiectionSubjection due to huſbandshusbands of euillevil qualities. of his heart and life, doth not depriuedeprive a man of that ciuillcivil honour which God hath giuengiven vntounto him. Though an husband in regard of euillevil qualities may carriecarry the Image of the deuilldevil, yet in regard of his place and office he beareth the i • mage of God: ſoso doedo MagiſtratesMagistrates in the common-wealth, MiniſtersMinisters in the Church, parents and maſtersmasters in the familiefamily. Note for our preſentpresent purpoſepurpose, the exhortation of S. Peter to ChriſtianChristian wiueswives which had infidellinfidel husbands, 1 PetPet. 3. 1, 2. Be in ſubiectionsubjection to them: let your conuerſationconversation be in fearefear. If Infidels carriecarry n • ot the deuilsdevils Image, and are not, ſoso long as they are Infidels, v • aſſalsvassals of Satan, who are? yetYet wiueswives muſtmust be ſubiectsubject to them, and fearefear them.

div.head: §. 6. Of wiueswives denying honour to their owneown husbands.
div.p: Contrary thereunto is a very peruerſeperverse diſpoſitiondisposition in ſomesome A peruerſeperverse opinion to thinkethink other husbands worthy of honour, and not their owneown. wiueswives, who thinkethink they could better ſubiectsubject themſeluesthemselves to any husband, then their owneown. Though in generallgeneral they acknowledge that an husband is his wiueswives ſuperioursuperior, yet when the application commethcometh to themſeluesthemselves they failefail, and cannot be brought to yeeldyield, that they are their husbands inferioursinferiors. This is a vice worſeworse then the former. For to acknowledge no husband to be ſuperioursuperior ouerover his wife, but to thinkethink man and wife in all things equallequal, may proceed from ignorance of hindemindhind, and error of iudgementjudgment. But for a wife who knoweth and acknowledgeth the generallgeneral, that an husband is aboueabove his wife, to imagine that ſheshe her ſelfeself is not inferiourinferior to her huſbandhusband, ariſethariseth from monſtrousmonstrous ſelfeself-conceit, and intolerable a • rrogancy, as if ſheshe her ſelfeself were aboueabove her owneown ſexsex, and m • ore then a woman.

Contrary alſoalso is the practiſepractise of ſuchsuch See Treat. 2. part. 1. §. 9. women, as purpoſelypurposely m • arymarry men of farrefar lower rankerank then themſeluesthemselves, for this very
end, that they may rule ouerover their owneown husbands: and of others who being See Ibid. aged, for that end marymarry youths, if not very boyesboys. A mindemind and practiſepractise very vnſeemelyunseemly, and cleanethclean wartingthwarting Gods ordinance. But let them thinkethink of ruling Indecens eſtest vt mulier magiſtramagistra viri fiat. Orig. in IſaIsa. hom. 7. what they liſtlist, the truth is, that they make themſeluesthemselves ſubiectssubjects both by Gods law and mans: of which ſubiectionsubjection ſuchsuch wiueswives doedo oft feelefeel the heauieſtheaviest burden. SalomonSolomon noteth this to be one of the things for which the earth is diſquieteddisquieted, when
ProuProv. 30. 21, 22. a ſeruantservant reigneth. Now when can a ſeruantservant more domineredomineer, then when he hath mariedmarried his miſtreſſemistress? As for aged women who are mariedmarried to youths, I may ſaysay (as in another caſecase it was ſaidsaid) woe to thee ô wife whoſewhose husband is a childechild. VnmeetUnmeet it is Eccle. 10. 16. that an aged man ſhouldshould be mariedmarried to a young maid, but much more vnmeetunmeet for an aged woman to be mariedmarried to a youth.

div.head: §. 7. Of a wiueswives Treat. 4. §. 1111. inward fearefear of her husband.
div.p: Hitherto of a wiueswives acknowledgementacknowledgment of her husbands ſuperioritiesuperiority. It followeth to ſpeakespeak of that anſwerableanswerable reſpectrespect which ſheshe ought to bearebear towards him.

row.cell: A wiuewive-like reſpectrespect of her huſbandhusband conſiſtethconsisteth in two points:
The reuerencereverence which ſheshe oweth to him is WiueWive-like fearefear.

div.p:
Inward reuerencereverence is an awfullawful reſpectrespect which a wife in her heart hath of her husband, eſteemingesteeming him worthy of all honour for his place, and office ſakesake, becauſebecause he is her husband. DoubtleſſeDoubtless Sarah had in her heart a reuerendreverend reſpectrespect and honourable eſteemeesteem of her husband, when Gen. 18. 12. being alone, and thinking of him in her very thought ſheshe gauegave him this title Lord. This inward reuerencereverence the Scripture compriſethcompriseth vnderunder this word FeareFear: as where our ApoſtleApostle ſaithsaith, Eph. 5. 33. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . Let the wife ſeesee that ſheshe fearefear her husband: and where 1 Pet. 3. 2. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . S. Peter exhorteth wiueswives to hauehave their conuerſationconversation in FeareFear. It is no ſlauiſhslavish fearefear of her husband which ought to poſſeſſepossess the heart of a wife, dreading blowesblows, frownesfrowns, ſpightfullspiteful words, or the like; but ſuchsuch an awfullawful reſpectrespect of him as maketh her (to vſeuse the ApoſtlesApostles word) 1 Cor. 7. 34. care how ſheshe may pleaſeplease him. This wiuewive-like FeareFear is manifeſtedmanifested
by two effects: one is IoyJoy, when ſheshe giuethgiveth contentment to her husband, and obſeruethobservethobserueth him to be pleaſedpleased with that which ſheshe doth: the other is griefegrief, when he is iuſtlyjustly offended and grieuedgrieved, eſpeciallyespecially with any thing that ſheshe her ſelfeself hath done.

VnleſſeUnless this inward reuerencereverence and due reſpectrespect of an huſbandhusband True fearefear a ground of other duties. be firſtfirst placed in the heart of a wife, either no outward reuerencereverence and obedience will be performed at all, or if it be performed, it will be very vnſoundunsound, only in ſhewshow, hypocriticallhypocritical and deceitfulldeceitful: ſoso that as good neuernever a whit as neuernever the better. For according to ones inward affection and diſpoſitiondisposition will the outward action and conuerſationconversation be framed. 2 Sam. 6. 16. Michal firſtfirst deſpiſeddespised DauidDavid in her heart, and thence it followed that ſheshe UerſVersUers. 20. How fearefear may be wrought in a wiueswives heart. vtteredmoſtuttered mostutteredmost vnreuerendunreverend and vile ſpeechesspeeches of him, eueneven to his face. Wherefore after the iudgementjudgment of a wife is rightly informed of an husbands ſuperioritiesuperiority, and her will perſwadedpersuaded to account her owneown husband her head and guide, it is very needfullneedful that her heart and affection be accordingly ſeaſonedseasoned with the ſaltsalt of good reſpectrespect, and high eſteemeesteem, which breedeth fearefear: and that thus her heart may be ſeaſonedseasoned, ſheshe ought oft and ſeriouſlyseriously to meditate of his place and office, and of that honour which the Lord by vertuevirtue thereof hath planted in him. And if he hauehave gifts worthieworthy his place, as knowledge, wiſdomewisdom, pietiepiety, temperance, louelove, and the like, ſheshe ought to take notice thereof, and to thinkethink him worthieworthy of double honour.

div.head: §. 8. Of a wiueswives baſebase eſteemeesteem of her husband.
div.p: Contrary to this inward reuerencereverence of the heart is a baſebase and wilevile eſteemeesteem which many hauehave of their husbands, thinking no better of them then of other men; nay worſeworse then of others; deſpiſingdespising their husbands in their heart, like Michal, of whom we heard before. This, as it is in it ſelfeself a vile vice, ſoso is i • t a cauſecause of many other vices, as of preſumptionpresumption, rebellion, A baſebase eſteemesteem which wiueswives hauehave of their husbands, ariſethariseth yea and of adultery it ſelfeself many times: and it is alſoalso a mainemain hinderancehindrance of all dutieduty.

It commonly riſethriseth either from ſelfeself-conceit (whereby wiueswives ouerweeneoverweenoverweene their owneown gifts, thinking them ſoso excellent 1. From ſelfeconceitself-conceitselfeconceit. isas they need no guide or head, but are rather fit to guide and
rule both their husband and all the houſholdhousehold: of which proud and preſumptuouspresumptuous ſpiritspirit IezabelJezebel ſeemethseemeth to be, who with an audacious and impudent face ſaidsaid to Ahab her husband, 1 King. 21. 7. DoſtDost thou now gouernegovern the kingdomekingdom of IſraelIsrael? Up, I will giuegive thee the vineyard of Naboth. So alſoalso all thoſethose wiueswives which are noted to draw away their husbands hearts from the Lord, as the wiueswives of 1 King. 11. 4. SalomonSolomon, 2 King. 8. 18. IehoramJehoram, and others: which they learned of their great grandmother Gen. 3. 6. EuahEve:) or elſeelse from ſomesome infirmities of mindemind or body, or of life, which they behold in their 2. From their husbands infirmities. husbands (whence it commethcometh to paſſepass, that many husbands who are highly honoured and greatly accounted of by others, are much deſpiſeddespised by their wiueswives, becauſebecause their wiueswives alwaiesalways conuerſingconversing with them are priuieprivy to ſuchsuch infirmities as are concealed from others:) or, which is worſtworst of all, from vniuſtunjust ſurmizessurmises 3. From vniuſtunjust ſuſpicionssuspicions. and ſuſpicionssuspicions, ſuſpectingsuspecting many euillevil things of their husbands whereof they are no way guiltieguilty, and miſinterpretingmisinterpreting, and peruertingperverting things well done, as 2 Sam. 6. 20. Michal peruertedperverted DauidsDavid's holy zealezeal.

For redreſſeredress of this enormous vice, wiueswives ought firſtfirst in regard How wiueswives may redreſſeredress a light eſteemeesteem of their huſbandshusbands. of themſeluesthemselves to purge out of their hearts pride, and ſelfeself-conceit, thinking humbly and lowly of themſeluesthemselves, and that eueneven in regard of their ſexsex and the weakneſſeweakness thereof: and if the Lord hauehave endued them with any gift aboueabove the ordinary ſortsort of women, to note well their owneown infirmities, and to lay them by their eminent gifts: thus by looking on their blackeblack feet, their proud-peacock-feathers may be caſtcast downedown. Yea alſoalso when they behold any infirmities in their husbands, they ought to reflect their eieseyes on their owneown infirmities, which it may be are eueneven as many and as grieuousgrievous, if not more in number, and more hainousheinous in their nature and kindekind: at leaſtleast let them conſiderconsider that they are ſubiectsubject to the ſamesame, if God leaueleave them to the ſwaysway of their owneown corruption.

Secondly, wiueswives ought in regard of their husbands to ſurmizesurmise no euillevil whereof they hauehave not ſuresure proofeproof and euidenceevidence: but rather interpret eueryevery thing in better part: and follow the rule of louelove, 1 Cor. 13. 7. which beareth all things, beleeuethbelieveth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things. If they note any defects of nature, and deformity of body, or any enormous and notorious vices
in their husband, then ought they to turneturn their eieseyes and thoughts from his perſonperson to his place, and from his vicious qualities to his honourable office (which is to be an husband) and this will abate that vile eſteemeesteem which otherwiſeotherwise might be occaſionedoccasioned from the forenamed meanesmeans.

div.head: §. 9. Of Treat. 4. §. 4. wiuewive-like ſobrietysobriety.
div.p: A wiueswives outward reuerencereverence towards her husband is a manifeſtationmanifestation of her inward due reſpectrespect of him. Now then ſeeingseeing A wiueswives outward reuerencereverence. the intent of the heart, and inward diſpoſitiondisposition cannot be diſcerneddiscerned by man ſimplysimply in it ſelfeself, that the husband may know his wiueswives good affection towards him, it is behouefullbehoveful that ſheshe manifeſtmanifest the ſamesame by her outward reuerencereverence.

row.cell: A wiueswives outward reuerencereverence conſiſtethconsisteth in her reuerendreverend

div.p: For the firſtfirst, that a reuerendreverend geſturegesture & carriage of her ſelfeself to A wiueswives reuerencereverence in her geſturegesture. her husband, and in her husbands preſencepresence, beſeemethbeseemeth a wife, was of old implied by the vaileveil which the woman vſedused to put on, when ſheshe was brought vntounto her husband, as is noted in the Gen. 24. 65. example of Rebekah: whereunto the ApoſtleApostle alludeth in theſethese words, 1 Cor. 11. 10. the woman ought to hauehave power on her head. That couercover on the womans head, as in generallgeneral it implied ſubiectionsubjection, ſoso in particular this kindekind of ſubiectionsubjection, viz. a reuerendreverend carriage and geſturegesture. But moſtmost expreſlyexpressly is this dutieduty ſetset downedown by 1 Pet. 3. 1. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . Saint Peter who exhorteth wiueswives to order their conuerſationconversation before their husbands, ſoso as it be pure, with reuerencereverence.
This reuerendreverend conuerſationconversation conſiſtethconsisteth in a wiuewive-like ſobrietiesobriety, mildneſſemildness, courteſiecourtesy, and modeſtiemodesty.

By ſobrietysobriety I meanemean ſuchsuch a comely, grauegrave, and gratiousgracious carriage, as giuethgiveth euidenceevidence to the husband that his wife reſpectethrespecteth his place & the authority which God hath giuengiven him. Sobriety in generallgeneral is required of all women by reaſonreason of their ſexesex; and ſurelysurely it doth well become them all: but much more doth it become wiueswives: moſtmost of all, in their husbands preſencepresence. 1 Tim. 3. 11. The ApoſtleApostle in particular enioynethenjoineth it to Deacons wiueswives, yet not ſoso as proper vntounto them, but in a further reſpectrespect appertaining to them not only as wiueswives, but as the wiueswives of Deacons.

Contrary to this ſobrietysobriety is lightneſſelightness and wantonneſſewantonness:
which vices in a wife, eſpeciallyespecially before her husband, argueth little reſpectrespect, if not a plaineplain contempt of him.
ObiectObject. Thus ſhallshall all delightfulldelightful familiarity betwixt huſbandhusband and wife be taken away.

AnſwAnsw. Though the forenamed ſobrietysobriety be oppoſedopposed to lightneſſelightness Difference betwixt wantonneſſewantonness and familiarity. and wantonneſſewantonness, yet not to matrimoniallmatrimonial familiarity: which is ſoso farrefar permitted to man and wife, as if any other man and woman ſhouldshould ſoso behauebehave themſeluesthemselves one towards another as an husband and wife lawfully may, it might iuſtlyjustly be counted lightneſſelightness and ſinnesin: inſtanceinstance the example of IſaakIsaac and Rebekah, who ſoso ſportedsported together, as Abimelech,
Gen. 26. 8, 9. knowing them to be ſuchsuch as feared God, gathered by that ſportingsporting that they were man and wife: for he thought that otherwiſeotherwise they would not hauehave beenebeen ſoso familiar together.

See Treat. 4. §. 42. This familiarity argueth both liking and louelove: and ſhewethshoweth that the man and wife delight in one anothers perſonperson. But the lightneſſelightness here condemned in a wife, is not ſoso much a mutuallmutual familiarity with her husband by his good liking, as a wanton dallying with others to his griefegrief and diſgracedisgrace.

div.head: §. 10. Of Treat. 4. §. 13, 22. wiuewive-like mildneſſemildness.
div.p: MildneſſeMildness in a wife hath reſpectrespect alſoalso to the ordering of her countenance, geſturegesture, and whole cariagecarriage before her husband, whereby ſheshe manifeſtethmanifesteth a pleaſingneſſepleasingness to him, and a contentedneſſecontentedness and willingneſſewillingness to be vnderunder him and ruled by him. Excellently is this ſetset forth in the ſpouſespouse of ChriſtChrist whoſewhose eieseyes are ſaidsaid to be as douesdoves eieseyes, her lips to drop as honiehoneyhony combs, and Cant. 4. & 6. & 7. ſheshe her ſelfeself eueryevery way pleaſantpleasant: whereupon it is noted that ſheshe appeared to her husband as the bright morning, and that his heart was wounded with her. AſſuredlyAssuredly the cleereclear skiesky is not more pleaſantpleasant in time of harueſtharvest, then a mildemild and amiable countenance and carriage of a wife in her husbands preſencepresence. Is cui leonum cura commiſſacommissa eſtest, blanda manu, mollique verborum ſonosono permulſospermulsos domat. Greg. Naz. ad Olymp. And though her husband ſhouldshould be of an harſhharsh and cruellcruel diſpoſitiondisposition, yet by this means might he be made meekemeek and gentle. For the keepers of Lions are ſaidsaid to bring them to ſomesome tameneſſetameness by handling them gently and ſpeakingspeaking to them fairelyfairly.

Contrary to this mildneſſemildness is a frowning brow, a lowringlouring eieeye, a ſullensullen lookelook, a powtingpouting lip, a ſwellingswelling face, a deriding
mouth, a ſcornefullscornful caſtcast of the armesarms and hands, a diſdainfulldisdainful turning of this ſideside and that ſideside of the body, and a fretfullfretful flinging out of her husbands preſencepresence: all which and other like contemptuous geſturesgestures are as thickethick clouds ouerſpreadingoverspreading the heauensheavens in a Summers day, which make it very vncomfortableuncomfortable. They oft ſtirrestir vpup much paſſionpassion in the man, and bring much miſchiefemischief vponupon the wife her ſelfeself.

div.head: §. 11. Of Treat. 4. §. 15. wiuewive-like courteſiecourtesy and obeyſanceobeisance.
div.p:
CourteſieCourtesy is that vertuevirtue whereby a wife taketh occaſionoccasion to teſtifietestify her acknowledgementacknowledgment of her husbands ſuperioritysuperiority by ſomesome outward obeyſanceobeisance to him. Rebekah, ſoso ſoonesoon as ſheshe ſawsaw IſaakIsaac, whom ſheshe had taken for her husband, lighted from her CamellCamel and came to him on foot, which was a kindekind of obeyſanceobeisance. This is not ſoso to be taken as if no difference were to be made betwixt the carriage of a ſeruantservant, or childechild, and a wife: or as if a wife ſhouldshould bow at eueryevery word that ſheshe ſpeakethspeaketh to her husband. Though in the kindekind and extent of many duties the ſamesame things are required of wiueswives which are required of children and ſeruantsservants, becauſebecause God hath made them all inferioursinferiors, and exacted ſubiectionsubjection of all: yet in the manner and meaſuremeasure of many duties there is great difference: as in this, the obeyſanceobeisance of children and ſeruantsservants ought to be more ſubmiſſiuesubmissive, and more frequent. Yet becauſebecause God hath placed authority in the husband ouerover his wife, ſheshe is eueryevery way to teſtifietestify her reuerendreverend reſpectrespect of her husband, and therefore at ſomesome times, on ſomesome occaſionsoccasions (as when he is going on a iourneyjourney for a time from her, or when he returneth home againeagain, or when ſheshe hath a ſolemnesolemn and great ſutesuit to make vntounto him, or when he offereth an eſpeciallespecial and extraordinary fauourfavour vntounto her, or (as I hauehave obſeruedobserved ſuchsuch wiueswives as know what beſeemethbeseemeth their place, and are not aſhamedashamed to manifeſtmanifest as much) when ſheshe ſittethsitteth 1. A wiuelikewivelike courteſiecourtesy worketh a good reſpectrespect in her huſbandhusband to her. downedown or riſethriseth vpup from table) to declare her reuerencereverence by ſomesome obeyſanceobeisance. This cannot but much workework on the heart of a good and kindekind husband, and make him the more to reſpectrespect his wife, when he beholdeth this euidenceevidence of her reſpectrespect to him. Yea it cannot but be a good patternepattern to children 2. It maketh her husband be honoured of others. and ſeruantsservants, and a motiuemotive to ſtirrestir them vpup to yeeldyield all ſubmiſſiuesubmissive obeyſanceobeisance both to her husband and to her ſelfeself.
For it may make them thus to reaſonreason with themſeluesthemselves, ſhallshall 3. It bringeth honour to her ſelfeself. we ſcornescorn or thinkethink much to yeeldyield that to our father or maſtermaster which our mother or miſtreſſemistress thinketh not much to yeeldyield to her husband? ſhallShall -ſheshe bow to him, and ſhallshall not we much more bow to her? Thus a wiueswives honouring of her husband by yeeldingyielding obeyſanceobeisance to him, maketh both him and her ſelfeself to be more honoured of others.

Contrarily minded are they, who not only altogether omit Contrary ſcornescorn in wiueswives. this dutieduty, but alſoalso gibe and ſcoffescoff at the very hearing thereof, ſayingsaying, thus wiueswives ſhallshall be made no better then children or ſeruantsservants. But though ſcornefullscornful dames deride theſethese outward euidencesevidences of their ſubiectionsubjection, yet ſuchsuch wiueswives as fearefear the Lord ought not to be hindered thereby from doing their dutieduty: for by ſuchsuch euillevil examples they might be diſcourageddiscouraged from eueryevery good dutieduty. It is ſufficientsufficient that ſuchsuch holy women as truſtedtrusted in God ſoso behauedbehaved themſeluesthemselves. But for this particular, we know that equals ſcornescorn not vponupon occaſionsoccasions to performeperform this kindekind of courteſiecourtesy in making obeyſanceobeisance one to another: how much leſſeless ought wiueswives, who are their husbands inferioursinferiors?

div.head: §. 12. Of Treat. 4. §. 49, 52. 1 Tim. 22. 9. 1 Pet. 3. 3. wife-like modeſtiemodesty in apparellapparel.
div.p: ModeſtieModesty appertaining to a wife is much manifeſtedmanifested in her apparellapparel. S. Paul requireth this modeſtiemodesty in generallgeneral of all ſortssorts of women: but S. Peter preſſethpresseth it in particular vponupon wiueswives. For as it well beſeemethbeseemeth all women, ſoso wiueswives after a peculiar manner, namely, in attiring themſeluesthemselves, to reſpectrespect rather their husbands place and ſtatestate, then their owneown birth and parentage, but much rather then their owneown mindemind and humour. A wiueswives modeſtiemodesty therefore requireth that her apparellapparel be neither for coſtlineſſecostliness aboueabove her husbands abilitieability, nor for curiouſneſſecuriousness vnun beſeemingbeseemingunbeseeming his calling. As a poorepoor mans wife muſtmust not affect coſtlycostly apparellapparel, ſoso neither MiniſtersMinisters, grauegrave CounſelloursCounsellorsCounsellours, ſagesage MagiſtratesMagistrates, no nor conſcionableconscionable ProfeſſoursProfessorsProfessours wiueswives, hunt after new faſhionsfashions, or in light and gariſhgarish apparellapparel attire themſeluesthemselves. It is a token of great reuerencereverence in a wife towards her husband, to hauehave an eye to his place and ſtatestate in her apparellapparel.

On the contrariecontrary, ſuchsuch proud dainesdames as muſtmust hauehave their
owneown will in their attire, and thinkethink it nothing appertaineth ContrarieContrary wiueswives attire not fitting their huſbandshusbands ſtatestate or place. to their husbands to order them therein, who care not what their husbands abilitieability, or what his place and calling be, they ſhewshow little reſpectrespect and reuerencereverence to their husbands. Such are they, who are no whit mouedmoved with their husbands example: but though the mans apparellapparel be plaineplain and grauegrave, yet the wiueswives ſhallshall be coſtlycostly and gariſhgarish. Yea many there be that ſtandstand in ſomesome more awe of their husbands ſightsight, but ſhewshow little more reſpectrespect vntounto him, who hauehave their ſilkensilken gownesgowns, BeauerBeaver hats, and other like attire not agreeable to their place and ſtatestate, lie in the countreycountry, if they be of the citiecity; or in the citiecity, if they be of the countreycountry, in a friends houſehouse where their husbands ſhallshall Quae ſese pingit comitque ſecussecus quàm viro gratum eſſeesse nouit, ſatissatis declarat ſeſesese pluribus velle placcreplacere quàm oportet mulierem pudicam, cuius praecipua laus eſtest vni placuiſſeplacuisse cui deſponſatadesponsata eſtest. Matr. not know it, and when their husbands are not with them, wearewear them, and paint their faces, lay out their hairehair, and in euerieevery thing follow the faſhionfashion. What can they which behold this thinkethink, but that ſuchsuch a wiueswives care is more to pleaſeplease other light vainevain perſonspersons, then her grauegrave, diſcreetdiscreet husband: or that her husband can nothing at all preuaileprevail with her: which as it ſtainethstaineth her owneown credit, ſoso it leauethleaveth a blot of diſhonourdishonour eueneven vponupon him. If the care of a wife were to giuegive euidenceevidence of the reuerencereverence which ſheshe beareth to her husband, his deſiredesire and example would in this reſpectrespect more preuaileprevail with her, then the humour of her owneown heart.

div.head: §. 13. Of a wiueswives Treat. 4. §. 24. reuerendreverend ſpeechspeech to her husband.
div.p:
As by geſturegesture, ſoso by ſpeechspeech alſoalso, muſtmust a wiueswives reuerencereverence be manifeſtedmanifested: this muſtmust be anſwerableanswerable to that. For by words as well as by deeds, the affection of the heart is manifeſtedmanifested, Matt. 12. 34. Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth ſpeakethspeaketh. A wiueswives reuerencereverence is manifeſtedmanifested by her ſpeechspeech, both in her husbands preſencepresence, and alſoalso in his abſenceabsence. For this end in his preſencepresence her words muſtmust be few, reuerendreverend and meekemeek. FirſtFirst few: For the A wiueswives words in her huſbandshusbands preſencepresence muſtmust be few. ApoſtleApostle enioynethenjoineth 1 Tim. 2. 12. ſilencesilence to wiueswives in their husbands preſencepresence, and inforcethenforceth that dutieduty with a ſtrongstrong reaſonreason in theſethese words: I permit not the woman to vſurpeusurp authoritieauthority ouerover the man, but to be in ſilencesilence: the inference of the latter clauſeclause vponupon the former ſhewethshoweth that he ſpeakethspeaketh not only of a womans ſilencesilence in the Church, but alſoalso of a wiueswives ſilencesilence before her husband: which is further cleared by another like place, where the ſamesame ApoſtleApostle
enioynethenjoineth wiueswives to 1 Cor. 14. 35. learnelearn of their husbands at home. The reaſonreason before mentioned for ſilencesilence, on the one ſideside implieth a reuerendreverend ſubiectionsubjection, as on the other ſideside too much ſpeechspeech implieth an vſurpationusurpation of authoritieauthority.
ObiectObject. Then belike a wife muſtmust be alwayesalways mute before her husband.

AnſwAnsw. No ſuchsuch matter: for ſilencesilence in that place is not oppoſedopposed to ſpeechspeech, as if ſheshe ſhouldshould not ſpeakespeak at all, but to loquacitieloquacity, to talkatiueneſſetalkativeness, to ouerover-much tatlingtattling: her husbands preſencepresence muſtmust ſomesome whatsomewhat reſtrainerestrain her tongue, and ſoso will her verievery ſilencesilence teſtifietestify a reuerendreverend reſpectrespect. OtherwiſeOtherwise ſilencesilence, as it is oppoſedopposed to ſpeechspeech, would imply ſtoutneſſestoutness of ſtomackestomach, and ſtubbornneſſestubbornness of heart, which is an extreme contrariecontrary to loquacitieloquacity. But the meanemean betwixt both, is for a wife to be ſparingsparing in ſpeechspeech, to expect a fit time and iuſtjust occaſionoccasion of ſpeechspeech, to be willing to hearken to the word of knowledge commingcoming out of her husbands mouth. This argueth reuerencereverence. IobJob 32. 6. Elihu manifeſtedmanifested thereuerendthe reverendthereverend reſpectrespect, which as a younger he bare to his elders, by for bearingforbearing to ſpeakespeak while they had any thing to ſaysay. How much more ought wiueswives in regard both of their ſexsex and of their place?

ContrarieContrary is their practiſepractise, who muſtmust and will hauehave all the ContrarieContrary too much prate. prate. If their husbands hauehave begun to ſpeakespeak, their ſlipperieslippery tongues cannot expect and tarrietarry till he hauehave done: if (as verievery haſtilehastyhastile and forward they are to ſpeakespeak) they preuentprevent not their husbands, they will ſurelysurely take the tale out of his mouth before he hauehave done: Thus -they diſgracedisgrace themſeluesthemselves, and diſhonourdishonour their husbands.

div.head: §. 14. Of the Treat. 4. §. 24. titles which wiueswives giuegive their husbands.
div.p: As their words muſtmust be few, ſoso thoſethose few words muſtmust be reuerendreverend and meekemeek: both which are alſoalso implied vnderunder the forenamed word 1 Tim. 2. 12. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . ſilencesilence: which in the originalloriginal ſignifiethsignifieth alſoalso 1 Tim. 2. 12. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . quietneſſequietness.

ReuerenceReverence hath reſpectrespect to the titles whereby a wife nameth her husband. MeekneſſeMeekness to the manner of framing her ſpeechspeech to him. ReuerendReverend titles to be giuengiven to huſbandshusbands.

For the titles which a wife in ſpeakingspeaking to her husband, or naming him, giuethgiveth vntounto him, they muſtmust be ſuchsuch as ſignifiesignify
ſuperioritiesuperiority, and ſoso ſauoursavour of reuerencereverence. Such are the titles wherewith husbands are named in the Scripture; See §. 3. they are titles of honour. Such alſoalso are the titles which the Church (who by our ApoſtleApostle is made a patternepattern for wiueswives in all ſubiectionsubjection) giuethgiveth to her SpouſeSpouse ChriſtChrist IeſusJesus, as may be gathered out of the Song of ſongssongs. It is likely that Sarah did vſuallyusually giuegive this title Lord to her husband. For hauinghaving occaſionoccasion to thinkethink of him, preſentlypresently this title Gen. 18. 12. Lord was in her heart: which would not ſoso ſuddenlysuddenly hauehave riſenrisen vpup, if ſheshe had not ordinarily vſedused it. According to the vſuallusual titles which we giuegive to any, doedo we in our hearts name them, when we hauehave occaſionoccasion to thinkethink of them. Among all other titles the name husband, as it is the moſtmost vſuallusual, ſoso it is the fitteſtfittest and meeteſtmeetest title. It intimateth reuerencereverence, and ſauourethsavoureth not of niceneſſeniceness & ſingularitiesingularity, as theſethese titles, Head, Guide, Maſtermaster, Manman, and the like doedo: which though they be lawfulllawful titles, becauſebecause the Scripture attributeth them to husbands, and they ſignifiesignify ſuperioritiesuperiority, yet becauſebecause they are vnuſuallunusual and ſauoursavour of ſingularitiesingularity, they are not ſoso meet. Common vſeuse and practiſepractise hath made the addition of the husbands ſurnamesurname to this title Maſtermaster, more meet.
1 Pet. 3. 6. Saint Peter by this argument prouethproveth that Sarah obeyed Abraham, becauſebecause ſheshe called him Lord.

ContrarieContrary are thoſethose compellations which argue equalitieequality or inferioritieinferiority rather then ſuperioritiesuperiority, as Brotherbrother, CoſenCousinCosen, Friend, Manman, &etcc. ifIf a ſtrangerstranger be in preſencepresence, how can he tell by this manner of compellation, that he whom thou ſpeakeſtspeakest vntounto is thy husband? If he eſpieespy any matrimoniallmatrimonial familiaritiefamiliarity betwixt you, what can he iudgejudge of it otherwiſeotherwise to be, lightneſſelightness and wantonneſſewantonness? Remember the fearefullfearful iſſueissue that had like to hauehave fallen out by reaſonreason of ſuchsuch compellations giuengiven by Gen. 12. 19. & 20. 2. Sarah and & 26. 9. Rebekah to their husbands. Not vnlikeunlike to thoſethose are ſuchsuch as theſethese, Sweet, Sweeting, Heart, Sweet-heart, Louelove, IoyJoy, DeareDear, &etcc. andAnd ſuchsuch as theſethese, DuckeDuck, ChickeChick, PigſniePigsny, &etcc. andAnd husbands ChriſtianChristian names, as IohnJohn, Thomas, William, Henry, &etcc. whichWhich if they be contracted (as many vſeuse to contract them thus, Iacke • Jack, Tom, Will, Hall) they are much more vnſeemlyunseemly: ſeruantsservants are vſuallyusually ſoso called.

But what may we ſaysay of thoſethose titles giuengiven to an husband by
his wife, not ſeldomeseldom in paſſionpassion, but vſuallyusually in ordinarieordinary ſpeechspeech, which are not fit to be giuengiven to the baſeſtbasest men that be, as Grub, Rogue, and the like, which I am eueneven aſhamedashamed to name, but that the ſinssins of women are to be caſtcast as dirt on their faces, that they may be the more aſhamedashamed?

div.head: ObiectObject. Many of the forenamed titles are titles of amitieamity and familiaritiefamiliarity.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. SubiectionSubjectionsubjection is that markemark which wiueswives are directed to aimeaim at in their thoughts, words, deeds, and whole conuerſationconversation towards their husband. Such tokens of familiaritiefamiliarity as are not withallwithal tokens of ſubiectionsubjection and reuerencereverence, are vnbeſeemingunbeseeming a wife, becauſebecause they ſwerueswerve from that markemark.

div.head: §. 15. Of wiueswives Treat. 4. §. 24. &etcc. meekneſſemeekness in their ſpeechesspeeches.
div.p:
MeekneſſeMeekness in a wiueswives manner of framing her ſpeechspeech to her husband, doth alſoalso commend her reuerendreverend reſpectrespect of him. This is an eſpeciallespecial effect of that meekemeek and quiet ſpiritspirit which S. Peter requireth of wiueswives; which dutieduty he doth ſtronglystrongly inforceenforce by this weighty argument, 1 Pet. 3. 4. which is before God a thing much ſetset by. Is a wiueswives meekneſſemeekness much ſetset by before God, and ſhallshall not wiueswives hold it both a bounden dutieduty, and comely ornament, and grace vntounto them? As the formeform of words which a wife vſethuseth in asking or anſweringanswering queſtionsquestions, or any other kindekind of diſcourſediscourse which ſheeshe holdeth with her husband, ſoso her moderation in perſiſtingpersisting, arguing and preſſingpressing matters, yea and the mildemild compoſitioncomposition of her countenance in ſpeakingspeaking, declare her meekneſſemeekness. If ſheshe be deſirousdesirous to obtaineobtain any thing of him, fairelyfairly ſheshe muſtmust intreatentreat it, as the 2 King. 4. 10., 22. Shunemite: If ſheshe would mouemove him to performeperform a bounden dutieduty, mildly ſheshe muſtmust perſwadepersuade him. If ſheshe would reſtrainerestrain and keepekeep him from doing that which is euillevil, eueneven that alſoalso ſheshe muſtmust doedo with ſomesome meekneſſemeekness, as Matt. 27. 19. PilatsPilates wife: If ſheshe hauehave occaſionoccasion to tell him of a fault, therein ſheshe ought to manifeſtmanifest humilitiehumility and reuerencereverence, by obſeruingobserving a fit ſeaſonseason, and doing it after a gentle manner as 21 Sam. 25. 31, 37. Abigail: who as ſheshe wiſelywisely behauedbehaved her ſelfeself in this reſpectrespect with her husband in obſeruingobserving a fit ſeaſonseason, ſoso alſoalso with DauidDavid by intimating his fault vntounto him, rather then plainly reprouingreproving him, when ſheshe ſaidsaid, It ſhallshall be no griefegrief nor offence vntounto my Lord, that he hath not ſhedshed bloudblood cauſeleſſecauseless. This
meekneſſemeekness requireth alſoalso ſilencesilence and patience, eueneven when ſheshe is reprouedreproved.

Contrary is the waſpiſhwaspish and ſhrewiſhshrewish diſpoſitiondisposition of many Contrary wiueswives ſhrewiſhshrewish ſpeechesspeeches to their huſbandshusbands. wiueswives to their husbands, who care not how haſtilyhastily and vnaduiſedlyunadvisedly they ſpeakespeak to them, like Gen. 30. 1. RahelRachel; nor how angerly and chidingly, like 1 King. 21. 7. IezabelJezebel; nor how diſdainfullydisdainfully, and ſpightfullyspitefullyspightfully, like Exo. 4. 25, 26. Zipporah; nor how ſcoffinglyscoffingly, and frumpingly, like 2 Sam. 6. 20. Michal; nor how reproachfully and diſgracefullydisgracefully, like IobJob 2. 9. IobsJobs wife. If they be reprouedreproved by their husbands, their husbands ſhallshall be reproached by them: & they are ready to anſweranswer again, not only word for word, but ten for one. Many wiueswives by their ſhrewiſhshrewish ſpeechesspeeches, ſhewshow no more reſpectrespect to their husbands, then to their ſeruantsservants, if ſoso much. The leaſtleast occaſionoccasion mouethmoveth them not only inwardly to be angry and fret againſtagainst them, but alſoalso outwardly to manifeſtmanifest the ſamesame by chiding and brawling. The very obiectobject whereupon many wiueswives vſuallyusually ſpitspit out their venomous words, is their husband; when their ſtomacksstomachsstomacks are full, they muſtmust needs eaſeease them on their husbands: wherein their fault is doubled.

Let wiueswives therefore learnelearn firſtfirst to moderate their paſſionpassion, and then to keepekeep in their tongues with bit and bridle, but moſtmost of all to take heed that their husbands taſtetaste not of the bitterneſſebitterness thereof, no not though they ſhouldshould by ſomesome ouerſightoversight of their husbands be prouokedprovoked. It is to be noted how SalomonSolomon calleth the iarresjars which are betweenebetween man and wife, the contentions of a wife, whereby he intimateth that ſheshe commonly ProuProv. 19. 13. is the cauſecause thereof, either by prouokingprovoking her husband, or not bearing with him.

div.head: §. 16. Of a wiueswives ſpeechspeech of her husband Treat. 2. Part. 2. §. 36. in his abſenceabsence.
div.p: The reuerencereverence which a wife beareth to her husband, muſtmust further be manifeſtedmanifested by her ſpeechesspeeches of him in his abſenceabsence. So did Sarah manifeſtmanifest her reuerencereverence, and ſoso muſtmust all ſuchsuch as deſiredesire Gen. 18. 12. to be accounted the daughters of Sarah. The Church ſpeakingspeaking of her SpouſeSpouse, doth it with as great reuerencereverence, as if ſheshe CantCant. 5. 10. &etcc. had ſpokenspoken to him. It was for honour and reuerencereverence ſakesake, that the Virgin Mary called IoſephJoseph the Fatherfather of IeſusJesus, when ſheshe Luke 2. 48. ſpakespake of him.

This ſhewethshoweth that a wiueswives reuerendreverend ſpeechesspeeches in preſencepresence of
her husband and to his face, are not in flatterieflattery to pleaſeplease him and fawnefawn vponupon him, but in ſinceritiesincerity to pleaſeplease God and performeperform her dutieduty.

Contrary therefore to their dutieduty dealedeal they, who in preſencepresence Contrary wiueswives bitter ſpeechesspeeches behind their huſbandshusbands backs. can afford the faireſtfairest and meek eſtestmeekest ſpeechesspeeches that may be to their husbands face, but See more hereof TreatTreat. 2. partpart. 2. §. 36. behindebehind their backs ſpeakespeak moſtmost reproachfully of them.

div.head: §. 17. Of a wiueswives obedience in generallgeneral.
div.p: Hitherto of a wiueswives reuerencereverence, it followeth to ſpeakespeak of her obedience: The firſtfirst law that euerever was giuengiven to woman ſincesince her fall, laid vponupon her this dutieduty of Obedienceobedience to her husband, in theſethese words, Gen. 3. 16. Thy deſiredesire ſhallshall be to thine husband, and he ſhallshall rule ouerover thee. How can an husband rule ouerover a wife, if ſheshe obey not him? The principallprincipal part of that ſubmiſſionsubmission which in this EpheſEphes. 5. 22. text, and in many other places is required of a wife, conſiſtethconsisteth in obedience: and therefore it is expreſlyexpressly commended vntounto wiueswives in the example of Sarah who 1 Pet. 3. 6. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . obeyed Abraham. Thus by Obedienceobedience doth the Church manifeſtmanifest her ſubiectionsubjection to ChriſtChrist.

The place wherein God hath ſetset an husband; namely, to be an EpheſEphes. 5. 23. head; the authoritieauthority which he hath giuengiven vntounto him, to be a 1 Pet. 3. 6. Lord and EſterEsther 1. 17. Maſtermaster; the duty which he requireth of him Gen. 3. 16. to rule, doedo all require obedience of a wife. Is not obedience to be yeeldedyielded to an Head, Lord, and Maſtermaster? Take away all authoritieauthority from an husband, if ye exempt a wife from obedience.

Contrary is the ſtoutneſſestoutness of ſuchsuch wiueswives as muſtmust hauehave their Contrary to obedience, ſtoutneſſestoutness. own will, and doedo what they liſtlist, or elſeelse all ſhallshall be out of quiet. Their will muſtmust be done, they muſtmust rule and ouerover-rule all, they muſtmust command not only children and ſeruantsservants, but husbands alſoalso, if at leaſtleast the husband will be at peace. LookeLook into families, obſerueobserve the eſtateestate and condition of many of them, and then tell me if theſethese things be not ſoso. If an husband be a man of courage, and ſeekeseek to ſtandstand vponupon his right, and maintainemaintain his authoritieauthority by requiring obedience of his wife, ſtrangestrange it is to behold what an hurly burly ſheshe will make in the houſehouse: but if he be a milkemilk-ſopsop, and baſelybasely yeeldyield vntounto his wife, and ſuffersuffer her to rule, then, it may be, there ſhallshall be ſomesome outward quiet. The ground hereof is an ambitious and proud humour in
women, who muſtmust needs rule, or elſeelse they thinkethink themſeluesthemselves ſlauesslaves. But let them thinkethink as they liſtlist: aſſuredlyassuredly herein they thwart Gods ordinance, peruertpervert the order of nature, deface the image of ChriſtChrist, ouerthrowoverthrow the ground of all dutieduty, hinder the good of the family, become an ill patternepattern to children and ſeruantsservants, lay themſeluesthemselves open to Satan, and incurreincur many other miſchiefesmischiefs which cannot but follow vponupon the violating of this mainemain duty of Obedienceobedience, which if it be not performed, how can other duties be expected?

div.head: §. 18. Of the caſescases wherein a wife hath power to order things of the houſehouse without her husbands conſentconsent.
div.p: SubmiſſionSubmission in yeeldingyielding to her husbands mindemind and will.
See §. 49. Contentment in reſtingresting ſatisfiedsatisfied and content with his eſtateestate and abilitieability.
That SubmiſſionSubmission conſiſtethconsisteth in two things.
FirſtFirst, in abſtainingabstaining from doing things againſtagainst her husbands mindemind.

Secondly, in doing what her husband requireth. The former of theſethese requireth that a wife hauehave her husbands conſentconsent for the things which ſheshe doth. For the better cleeringclearing whereof we are to conſiderconsider,
1. What kindekind of husbands they muſtmust be whoſewhose conſentconsent is required.
2. How many waiesways his conſentconsent may be giuengiven.
3. What are the things whereabout his conſentconsent is to be expected.

For the firſtfirst, as on the one ſideside it oft falleth out that a wifewise, In two caſescases a wife hath power to order things of her ſelfeself, without her husbands conſentconsent. prouidentprovident, and religious man is mariedmarried to a fooliſhfoolish woman, a very ideotidiot, that hath no vnderſtandingunderstanding, of whom there can be no queſtionquestion, but that ſuchsuch a wife is to doedo nothing of her ſelfeself, and of her owneown head, but altogether to be ordered by her husband: So on the other ſideside, it oft falleth out that a wiſewise, vertuousvirtuous, and gratiousgracious woman, is mariedmarried to an husband deſtitutedestitute 11. In caſecase of her husbands impotency. of vnderſtandingunderstanding, to a very naturallnatural (as we ſaysay) or a f • renzy man, or to one made very blockiſhblockish, and ſtupidstupid, vnfitunfit to manage his affairesaffairs through ſomesome diſtemperdistemper, wound, or ſickneſlesicknesssicknesle.
In ſuchsuch a caſecase the whole gouernmentgovernment lieth vponupon the wife, ſoso as her husbands conſentconsent is not to be expected.

QueſtQuest. What if the husband be a wicked and prophaneprofane man, and ſoso blinded and ſtupifiedstupefiedstupified in his ſoulesoul, doth not this ſpirituallspiritual blindneſſeblindness and blockiſhneſeblockishnessblockishnese giuegive a religious wife as great libertieliberty as naturallnatural ſtupiditiestupidity?
AnſwAnsw. No verily: For S. Peter exhorteth faithfullfaithful wiueswives 1 Pet. 3. 1, 2. that were mariedmarried to InfidellInfidel husbands to be ſubiectsubject to them, and that in fearefear.

The reaſonreason is cleareclear: For ſpirituallspiritual blindneſſeblindness diſablethdisableth not from ciuillcivil gouernmentgovernment: indeed nothing that ſuchsuch a man doth is acceptable to God, or auailableavailable to his owneown ſaluationsalvation; but yet it may be profitable to man: a wicked man may be prouidentprovident enough for wife, children, and whole family in outward temporalltemporal things.

AgaineAgain, it oft falleth out, that an husband is a long time In caſecase of impoſſibilitieimpossibility for her huſbandhusband to doedo it. farrefar off abſentabsent from the houſehouse: ſometimessometimes by reaſonreason of his calling, as an AmbaſſadourAmbassadorAmbassadour, SouldierSoldier, or Mariner; ſometimessometimes alſoalso careleſlycarelessly or wilfully neglecting houſehouse, goods, wife, children and all: and in his abſenceabsence hath left no order for the ordering of things at home: in this caſecase alſoalso there is no queſtionquestion, but that the wife hath power to diſpoſedispose matters without her husbands conſentconsent: prouidedprovided that ſheshe obſerueobserve thoſethose rules of Gods word concerning iuſticejustice, equitieequity, truth and merciemercy, which an husband in his diſpoſingdisposing of them ought to obſerueobserve.

The firſtfirst of theſethese caſescases declareth an impotencieimpotency in the huſbandhusband: the other an impoſſibilitieimpossibility for him to order matters: wherefore the wife being next to the husband, the power of ordering things is diuolueddevolveddivolued on her: ſheshe is not bound to hauehave his conſentconsent.

div.head: §. 19. Of diuersdivers kindeskinds of conſentconsent.
div.p:
II. A conſentconsent may be generallgeneral or particular. A generallgeneral 1. A generallgeneral conſentconsent. conſentconsent is giuengiven, when without diſtinctdistinct reſpectrespect to this or that particular, libertieliberty is granted to a wife by her husband to doedo all things as ſeemethseemeth good in her owneown eyes. ProuProv. 31. 10, &etcc. That excellent good wife, and notable good houſehouse-wife that is ſetset forth by the WiſeWise-man, had ſuchsuch a conſentconsent. For firſtfirst, it is ſaidsaid, VerſVers. 11. The heart of her husband truſtethtrusteth in her; and then it is inferred, that
ſheshe ordereth all the things of the houſehouse, whereof many particulars are there ſpecifiedspecified. Whence I gather, that her husband obſeruingobserving her to be a godly, wiſewise, faithfullfaithful, and induſtriousindustrious woman, gauegave her power and liberty to doedo in the houſehouse-hold affairesaffairs, what ſheshe thought good, (he being a publikepublic magiſtratemagistrate, for VerſVers. 23. he was knowneknown in the gates, ſittingsitting among the Elders of the land) and accordingly ſheshe vſedused her liberty.

A particular conſentconsent is that which is giuengiven to one or more particular 2. A particular conſentconsent. things, as that conſentconsent Gen. 16. 6. which Abraham gauegave to Sarah about Hagar; and 1 SamSam. 1. 23. that which Elkanah gauegave to HannaHannah about tarrying at home till her childechild was weinedweaned.

This particular conſentconsent may be expreſſedexpressed or implied. An expreſſedexpressed conſentconsent is when the husband manifeſtethmanifesteth his good liking by word, writing, meſſagemessage, or ſignesign, and that whether his conſentconsent be asked (as was noted in the example of Elkanah) or freely offered.

An implicit conſentconsent, when by any probable coniectureconjecture it may be gathered that the husbands will is not againſtagainst ſuchsuch a thing, 4. An implicit conſentconsent,. though he hauehave not manifeſtedmanifested his mindemind concerning that very particular. This implicit conſentconsent may be gathered either by his ſilencesilence when he is preſentpresent to ſeesee a thing done, or otherwiſeotherwise hath knowledge thereof: or elſeelse when he is abſentabsent, by his former cariagecarriage or diſpoſitiondisposition in other like caſescases. The Scripture accounteth an husbands ſilencesilence, when he knoweth a thing and may, but doth not forbid it, to be a conſentconsent: as NumNum. 30. 8. in the caſecase of a wiueswives vow. For any thing we read to the contrary 2 King. 4. 10, 23. the Shunemite had no other conſentconsent to prepare a chamber for the Prophet, and to goego vntounto him, then her husbands ſilencesilence, and not forbidding it when he knew it.

As for the other kindekind of implicit conſentconsent, it may be ſetset forth in this following inſtanceinstance: ſuppoſesuppose a good wife hath an husband whom ſheshe knoweth by his former cariagecarriage and diſpoſitiondisposition to be a pittifullpitiful and charitable man, taking all occaſionsoccasions to ſhewshow mercy, and in his abſenceabsence there falleth out a fit and needfullneedful occaſionoccasion of ſhewingshowing mercy; if ſheshe take that occaſionoccasion to ſhewshow mercy, ſheshe hath an implicit conſentconsent, for ſheshe may well thinkethink that if her husband knew it he would approueapprove what ſheshe doth. It is to be ſuppoſedsupposed that 1 Sam. 1. 11. AnnahHannah vponupon ſomesome ſuchsuch ground vowed her childechild to God.
For it is not likely that ſheshe who would not tarry at home to weinewean her childechild without her husbands conſentconsent, would much leſſeless vow him to the Lord (which was a farrefar greater matter) without ſomesome perſwaſionpersuasion of her husbands good liking thereof. Now that a wife may ſhewshow ſheshe dealeth vprightlyuprightly in this caſecase vponupon a true perſwaſionpersuasion of her heart concerning her husbands mindemind, ſheshe ought (when conuenientlyconveniently ſheshe can) to make known to her husband what ſheshe hath done: as without all queſtionquestion AnnahHannah did; and ſoso much may be gathered out of theſethese words which Elkanah vttereduttered to AnnahHannah, 1 Sam. 1. 23. the Lord eſtabliſhestablish his word.

div.head: §. 20. Of the things whereabout a wife muſtmust hauehave her huſbandshusbands conſentconsent.
div.p: The things whereabout an husbands conſentconsent is to be expected, are ſuchsuch as he by vertuevirtue of his place and authoritieauthority hath power to order: as for example, ordering and diſpoſingdisposing the goods, cattellcattle, ſeruantsservants, and children of the family, entertaining ſtrangersstrangers; yea, alſoalso ordering eueneven his wiueswives going abroad, and making of vowesvows, with the like: now then diſtinctlydistinctly to lay downedown a wiueswives dutieduty in this firſtfirst branch of obedience, it is this:

A wife muſtmust doedo nothing which appertaineth to her husbandhusbands authoritieauthority ſimplysimply without, or directly againſtagainst his conſentconsent. DoeDo not theſethese words of that old law (thy deſiredesire ſhallshall be to thy husband)
Gen. 3. 16. imply as much? I deny not but that there may be ſundrysundry things proper and peculiar to a wife, wherein I will not reſtrainerestrain her libertieliberty: and therefore I vſeuse this phraſephrase (which appertaineth to her husbands authoritieauthority.) And I grant the forenamed generallgeneral and implicit conſentconsent, to be a true conſentconsent, ſoso as there needeth not an expreſſeexpress particular conſentconsent for eueryevery thing, and therefore I hauehave added theſethese clauſesclauses (ſimplysimply without, or directly againſtagainst conſentconsent.)

That is done ſimplysimply without conſentconsent which is done without all warrant from the husband, and that ſoso couertlycovertly as ſheshe is afraid it ſhouldshould come to his notice, imagining he would by no meanesmeans like it: As Rahels taking her fathers idols without all Gen. 31. 32. conſentconsent of IaakobJacob.
That is done directly againſtagainst conſentconsent which is expreſlyexpressly forbidden and diſclaimeddisclaimed by the husband.

But to deſcenddescend to the particulars before mentioned: FirſtFirst concerning the goods of the family: It is a queſtionquestion controuertedcontroverted whether the wife hauehave power to diſpoſedispose them without or againſtagainst the husbands conſentconsent.
Before I determine the queſtionquestion, I thinkethink it needfullneedful to declare, 1. What goods, 2. What occaſionoccasion of giuinggiving the queſtionquestion is about.

div.head: §. 21. Of the things which a wife may diſpoſedispose without her husbands conſentconsent.
div.p: 1. For the goods, ſomesome are proper and peculiar to the wife: Quaedam bona ſuntsunt propria vxorisuxoris, vt ſuntsunt bona paraphernalia. Greg. Sayr. Clau. reg. l. 9. c. 16. others are common. Goods proper to the wife are ſuchsuch as before mariagemarriage ſheshe her ſelfeself, or her friends except from the huſbandhusband to her ſolesole and proper vſeuse and diſpoſingdisposing, whereunto he alſoalso yeeldethyieldeth: or ſuchsuch as after mariagemarriage he giuethgiveth vntounto her to diſpoſedispose as ſheshe pleaſeplease: ſuppoſesuppose it be ſomesome rent, annuity, fees, v • ailesveils, or the like.

TheſeThese kindeskinds of goods are exempted out of the queſtionquestion

bona apud iuriſconſultosiurisconsultos, dicuntur
