(i.) quae ſponſasponsa praeter dotem à parentibus pactam ſecumsecum fert: vel (vt Sayrus loc. citat.) habet legata ei, ſeuseu donata. in hand; the wife hath liberty to diſpoſedispose them as ſheshe pleaſeplease without any further conſentconsent then ſheshe had by vertuevirtue of her hausbandshusbands former grant.

To theſethese I may referrerefer other goods, but of another nature, namely ſuchsuch as ſomesome friend of hers, ſuppoſesuppose father, mother, brother, or any other, obſeruingobserving her husband to be a very h • ard man, not allowing ſufficientsufficient for her ſelfeself, much leſſeless to diſtributedistribute on charitable vſesuses, ſhallshall giuegive vntounto her to diſpoſedispose as sh • e pleaſeplease, charging her not to let her husband know thereof. HowNow becauſebecause it is in the power of a free doner to order his g • ift as he pleaſeplease, and becauſebecause he ſoso ordereth this gift as he will not hauehave her husband know of it, I doubt not but ſheshe may of her ſelfeself according to the doners mindemind without her huſbandshusbands conſentconsent, diſpoſedispose ſuchsuch goods. She is herein but as a fe • offee in truſttrust.

AgaineAgain of common goods ſomesome are ſetset forth by the huſbandhusband to be ſpentspent about the family, other he reſeruethreservethreserueth for a st • ockestock, or to lay forth as he himſelfehimself ſhallshall ſeesee occaſionoccasion.

Concerning thoſethose which are ſetset forth to be ſpentspent, I doubt n • ot but the wife hath power to diſpoſedispose them; neither is ſheshe b • ound to askeask any further conſentconsent of her husband. For it
is the wiueswives place and dutieduty to guide or gouernegovern the houſehouse, 1 Tim. 5. 14. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . by vertuevirtue whereof, prouidingproviding ſufficientlysufficiently for the family, ſheshe may, as ſheshe ſeethseeth good occaſionoccasion, of ſuchsuch goods as are ſetset apart to be ſpentspent, diſtributedistribute to poorepoor, or otherwiſeotherwise.

This I hauehave noted for ſuchsuch tender conſciencesconsciences as thinkethink they cannot giuegive a bit of bread, or ſcarpscrapscarp of meat to a poorepoor body, or make a meſſemess of broth or caudle for a ſickesick body, except they firſtfirst askeask their husbands conſentconsent.
ProuidedProvided that if her husband expreſlyexpressly forbid this liberty, ſheshe take it not except neceſſitynecessity require it.
But our queſtionquestion is concerning ſuchsuch goods as the husband hath not ſetset apart, but reſeruedreserved to his owneown diſpoſingdisposing.

div.head: §. 22. Of a wiueswives liberty in extraordinary matters.
div.p: Concerning ſuchsuch as are out of the family, if they be in great need, and require preſentpresent releeferelief, though the wife know her husband to be ſoso hard-hearted, as he will not ſuffersuffer her to releeuerelieve ſuchsuch an one, yet without his conſentconsent ſheshe may releeuerelieve him. The ground of this and other like caſescases is that rule laid downedown by the Prophets, and by ChriſtChrist himſelfehimself, viz. OſeOse. 6. 6. MatMat. 9. 13. & 12. 7. I will hauehave merciemercy and not ſacrificesacrifice. If God in caſecase of merciemercy diſpenſethdispenseth with a dutieduty due to himſelfehimself, will he not much more diſpenſedispense with a dutieduty due to an husband?

div.head: §. 23. Of a wiueswives Treat. 4. §. 54. reſtraintrestraint in diſpoſingdisposing goods without conſentconsent of her husband: and of the ground of that reſtraintrestraint.
div.p: Out of all theſethese things thus premiſedpremised I gather the true ſtatestate Non poteſtpotest vxor ex bonis communibus occulte accipere ad donandum vel ad erogandum in alios vſusvsus ſinesine expreſſaexpressa, aut praeſumptapraesumpta ſaltemsaltem viri licentia. Greg • . Sayr. loc. citat. of the queſtionquestion in controuerſiecontroversy concerning the power of wiueswives in diſpoſingdisposing the goods of the family to be this,

p.hi: Whether a wife may priuilyprivily and ſimplysimply without, or openly and directly againſtagainst her husbands conſentconsent diſtributedistribute ſuchsuch common goods of the family as her husband reſeruethreservethreserueth to his owneown diſpoſingdisposing, there being no extraordinary neceſſitynecessity?

div.p: The moſtmost ancient and common anſweranswer vntounto this queſtionquestion hath beenebeen negatiuenegative, namely, that a wife hath not power ſoso to doedo: whereunto I for my part ſubſcribesubscribe.

The ground of this anſweranswer is taken from that primary law of the wiueswives ſubiectionsubjection, Gen. 3. 16. Thy deſiredesire ſhallshall be vntounto thine husband. How is her deſiredesire ſubiectsubject to her husband, if in the caſecase propounded ſheshe ſtandstand not vponupon his conſentconsent? It is further confirmed both by the §. 17. forenamed, and alſoalso by all other proofesproofs that might be produced out of the Scripture concerning the ſubiectionsubjection of wiueswives vntounto their husbands. If in ordering the goods of the family ſheshe yeeldyield not ſubiectionsubjection, wherein ſhallshall ſheshe yeeldyield it?

AgainſtAgainst this ground-workework ſomesome obiectobject that Gen. 4. 7. the ſamesame law of ſubiectionsubjection is impoſedimposed vponupon a younger brother in the very ſamesame words, and yet a younger brother was not therbythereby bound How the law of ſubiectionsubjection is applied to younger brothers. to hauehave his elder brothers conſentconsent in diſpoſingdisposing his goods.

AnſwAnsw. The law of the regality (as I may ſoso ſpeakespeak) and preheminencypreeminence of the firſtfirst borne was vnderunder thoſethose words ordained: and therforetherefore a younger brother was made a ſubiectsubject to his elder, while he remained in the family, as a ſonneson to the father. The elder brother was as a lord ouerover his other brothers: whereupon when IſaakIsaac conferred the right of the firſtfirst borne vponupon IaakobJacob (thinking he had beenebeen his eldeſteldest ſonneson EſauEsau) he vſedused theſethese words, Be lord ouerover thy brethren, and let thy
Gen. 27. 29. mothers ſonnessons bow downedown to thee. Which being ſoso, queſtionleſſequestionless the younger brother might not ſimplysimply without or directly againſtagainst the elder brothers conſentconsent diſpoſedispose the goods of the family: ſoso as this obiectionobjection more ſtronglystrongly eſtabliſhethestablisheth the forenamed argument.
AgaineAgain it is obiectedobjected that that old law is to be expounded of weighty matters.

AnſwAnsw. The ApoſtleApostle who was guided by the ſpiritspirit of the Eph. 5. 24. law-maker, extendeth that law to eueryevery thing: But is not this matter of diſpoſingdisposing goods a weighty matter? The conſequencesconsequences which I ſhallshall by and by note to follow hereupon will ſhewshow it to be a matter of moment.

div.head: §. 24. Of the example of the Shunemite in asking her huſbandshusbands conſentconsent. 2 King. 4. 9, 22.
div.p: As another reaſonreason may be alleged the Shunemites patternepattern who asked her husbands conſentconsent before ſheshe prepared the things that were thought meet for the Prophets entertainment: and before ſheshe vſedused the things which were meet for her iourneyjourney.

div.head: ObiectObject. It is indeed commendable for wiueswives to ſeekeseek their husbands conſentconsent as ſheshe did, but where ſuchsuch conſentconsent cannot be had, it is not neceſſarynecessary.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. This example being grounded vponupon a law (as we ſhewedshowed §. 23. before) it doth not only declare what may be done, but alſoalso what ought to be done. And if a wife be bound to hauehave her husbands conſentconsent for doing of a thing, by conſequenceconsequence it followeth that ſheshe is bound from doing it, without her huſbandshusbands conſentconsent.

2. AnſwAnsw. They that except againſtagainst this reaſonreason taken from example, vſeuse themſeluesthemselves the like reaſonreason in other points, as the examples of Abigail, IoannaJoanna, and SuſannaSusanna for the contrariecontrary.

2. ObiectObject. In the Shunemites example there was more then a mercifullmerciful releeferelief of the Prophet, namely bringing him into the houſehouse to diet and to lodge, wherein the husband muſtmust hauehave a chiefechief ſtroakestroke.

AnſwAnsw. The word of God maketh not that difference betwixt releeuingrelievingreleeving and entertaining: it extendeth a wiueswives ſubiectionsubjection to eueryevery thing: wherefore the husband hath a chiefechief ſtroakestroke as well in the one, as in the other.

div.head: §. 25. Of the law of a wiueswives vow.
div.p:
A third reaſonreason is taken from the law of a wiueswives vow: whereby Num. 30. 7. &etcc. in generallgeneral is implied, that a wife might not make a vow
without her husbands conſentconsent: whence it followeth as an argument taken from the greater to the leſſeless, that ſheshe may not diſpoſedispose the goods without his conſentconsent. Yea, VerſVers. 13. the Law further expreſlyexpressly ſaithsaith, that though ſheshe hath vowed, yet her husband hath power to diſanulldisannul her vow. Note here, how the Lord will rather depart from his owneown right (as I may ſoso ſpeakespeak) then hauehave that order which he hath appointed betwixt man and woman broken. The Lords right, was to hauehave what was vowed to him performed: the order which he appointed, was to hauehave the wife ſubiectsubject to her husband: rather then the wife ſhouldshould doedo that which the husband would not hauehave done, the Lord remitted a wiueswives vow in caſecase her husband would not conſentconsent to hauehave it performed. Now then I demand, is the diſpoſingdisposing of goods a greater matter then the performing of a vow? orOr hath a wife in theſethese dayesdays more libertieliberty then in former? ifIf ſheshe hauehave, by what law? wasWas there euerever vnderunder the Law a ſtraiterstraiter charge laid vponupon wiueswives then this, Let wiueswives be ſubiectsubject to their husbands in euerieevery thing.

div.head: ObiectObject. That point of a womans ſubiectionsubjection in performing her vow, is a particular ruled caſecase: but not this of diſpoſingdisposing goods.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. The Scripture by particular LawesLaws and examples teacheth directions for other caſescases like to them: and arguments drawnedrawn by iuſtjust and neceſſarienecessary conſequenceconsequence, are counted as ſoundsound as expreſſeexpress teſtimoniestestimonies. Whereas it is ſaidsaid, that this particular in queſtionquestion is not expreſlyexpressly decided, I take the reaſonreason thereof to be this, that in former times they ſoso well marked the extent of the generallgeneral law of a wiueswives ſubiectionsubjection, as they made no queſtionquestion of doing this or other like things without their husbands conſentconsent. Neither did good wiueswives take that libertieliberty, neither had they any patrons of ſuchsuch libertieliberty.

2. ObiectObject. The caſecase of a wiueswives diſpoſingdisposing goods is vnlikeunlike to that of vowesvows, becauſebecause vowesvows are voluntarievoluntary, but diſpoſingdisposing goods, as a workework of merciemercy, is neceſſarienecessary.

AnſwAnsw. Though it were a voluntarievoluntary thing to make, or not to make a vow: yet a vow being made, it was not in the power of the partieparty that made it, not to performeperform it: it was a Num. 30. 3. Deut. 23. 21. EccleſEccles. 5. 4. neceſſarienecessary dutieduty to performeperform a vow, eueneven expreſlyexpressly commanded. As
for the pretended workework of merciemercy, I will §. 34. hereafter ſhewshow, that a wife is not neceſſarilynecessarily tied thereunto.

div.head: §. 26. Of humane laweslaws which reſtrainerestrain wiueswives from diſpoſingdisposing goods, without or againſtagainst their husbands conſentconsent.
div.p: A fourth is taken from the laweslaws of men whereunto we are ſubiectsubject, and which we muſtmust obey eueneven for conſcienceconscience ſakesake, ſoso farrefar as they thwart not Gods Law, which in this caſecase they doedo not, as the reaſonsreasons before gathered out of Gods word doedo ſhewshow.

Now our Law ſaithsaith, that 45. E. 3. Fitz. CouenCoven. 18. euerieevery gift, grant, or diſpoſitiondisposition of goods, lands, or other thing whatſoeuerwhatsoever made by a woman 1. H. 5. 12. b. Perk. cap. de Grant. Nat. Breu. fol. 120. G. couertcovert, and all and euerieevery obligation and feoffment made by her, and recouerierecovery ſufferedsuffered, if they be done without her huſbandshusbands conſentconsent, are void. Yea, Nat. Breu. fol. 188. H. if ſheshe doedo wrong to another, ſheshe hath not any thing to make ſatisfactionsatisfaction during couerturecoverture: either her husband muſtmust doedo it, or by impriſonmentimprisonment of her perſonperson muſtmust it be done. And Perk. fol. 2. a. though ſheshe hauehave inheritance of her owneown, yet can ſheshe not grant any annuitieannuity out of it during her couerturecoverture, without her husband: if any deed be made to that purpoſepurpose without his conſentconsent, or in her name alone, it is void in law. Yea, Perk. fol. 2. b. if there be debate betweenebetween the husband and his wife, whereby certainecertain lands of the husbands be aſſignedassigned to the wife with his conſentconsent, if out of ſuchsuch lands ſheshe grant an annuitieannuity to a ſtrangerstranger, the grant is void. And 27. H. 8. 27. p. 12. if he couenantcovenant to giuegive her yeerelyyearly ſuchsuch and ſuchsuch apparellapparel, ſheshe cannot diſpoſedispose it as ſheshe liſtlist without his conſentconsent, but only vſeuse and wearewear it her ſelfeself. Perk. fol. 3. a. Neither can ſheshe leaſelease her owneown land for yeeresyears, for life, &etcc. ifIf ſheshe doedo, it is void, and the LeſſeeLessee entringentering by force thereof, is a DiſſeiſorDisseisor to the husband, and TreſpaſſorTrespasserTrespassor. And 21. H. 7. 18. p. 29. Nat. Breu. fol. 120 G. if ſheshe ſellsell any thing, the ſalesale is void, except ſheshe be a merchant, where by the cuſtomecustom ſheshe is enabled to merchandize. Finally, Ognels caſecase, Coke Rep. 4. 3 • 3. Deu. 12. ſheshe cannot make executors without the conſentconsent of her huſbandhusband, nor a deuiſedevise, or will. Plowd. ComCom. 344. a. Bret and Rigdons caſecase. If ſheshe make a will, and thereby deuiſedevise her owneown inheritance, and her husband die, and ſheshe after die without any new publication of it, it is of no force, becauſebecause it was void at firſtfirst. TheſeThese and many other like caſescases which might be alleagedalleged euidentlyevidently ſhewshow that by law a wife hath not
power of her ſelfeself, without her husband, to diſpoſedispose the common goods of the familiefamily.

div.head: §. 27. Of the inconueniencesinconveniences which may follow vponupon a wiueswives diſpoſingdisposing goods without or againſtagainst her husbands conſentconsent.
div.p: A fit reaſonreason may be taken from the miſchiefesmischiefs which would 1. A mans eſtateestate may be waſtedwasted before he can tell how to redreſſeredress it. fall out if this liberty were giuengiven vntounto women: which are theſethese that follow:

1. The eſtateestate of the family might be waſtedwasted before any redreſſeredress could be thought of: for if the wife may diſpoſedispose the goods without her husbands conſentconsent, it muſtmust alſoalso be granted without his knowledge: for it is to be ſuppoſedsupposed that if he knew of the diſpoſingdisposing of that which he liketh not, he would hinder it: if without his knowledge, then may that which he thinketh to be remaining as a ſtockestock for the family, be laid out by the wife, and nothing left: whereas if he knew of the ſpendingspending of that ſtockestock, it might be he would be more thrifty and ſparingsparing in other expencesexpenses.

div.head: ObiectObject. This liberty is not granted to wiueswives beyond their husbands ability.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. WiuesWiveswives cannot alwaiesalways know their husbands ability: for their husbands may be much indebted, and yet to maintainemaintain his credit, whereby he hopeth to raiſeraise his eſtateestate, may allow liberallliberal maintenance for his houſehouse, if thereupon his wife ſhallshall gather that he is very rich, and accordingly be very bountifullbountiful in her gifts, ſheshe may ſoonesoon goego beyond his ability, and ſoso increaſeincrease his debt, as he ſhallshall neuernever be able to recouerrecover himſelfehimself.

2. PerſonsPersons of contrary religions and diſpoſitionsdispositions being 2. ProfeſſorsProfessors of contrariecontrary religions may be ſuſtainedsustained by the goods of the ſamesame family. out of the family, might be maintained by the goods of the ſamesame family: for if the husband were of one religion, and the wife of another, he without her knowledge might maintainemaintain thoſethose of his religion, and ſheshe without his knowledge might maintainemaintain them of her religion.

div.head: ObiectObject. This liberty of diſpoſingdisposing goods giuengiven to the wife is limited within the bounds of the houſholdhousehold of faith.
div.p:
AnſwAnsw. If DiuinesDivines grant them this liberty, they will themſeluesthemselves iudgejudge and determine who be of the houſholdhousehold of faith:
PopiſhPopish wiueswives will ſaysay (ſaysay we what we can to the contrary) that IeſuitesJesuits, PrieſtsPriests, and FriersFriars, are of the houſholdhousehold of faith, principallprincipal members thereof.

3. Many iarresjars and contentions would thence ariſearise betwixt 3. IarsJars would ariſearise betwixt man and wife. husband and wife: for if a wife ſhallshall perſiſtpersist to doedo that which her husband will not conſentconsent vntounto, aſſuredlyassuredly one of a thouſandthousand will not well brookebrook it, but will rather ſeekeseek all the wayesways he can to croſſecross her; thinking himſelfehimself deſpiſeddespised, if ſheshe, whether he will or no, hauehave her mindemind.

div.head: ObiectObject. WiuesWives muſtmust vſeuse this libertieliberty with all due reſpectrespect vntounto their husbands authoritieauthority.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. If the husband peremptorily ſtandstand vponupon his authoritieauthority, and by all the fairefair meanesmeans that can be vſedused, will not yeeldyield this libertieliberty, I know not what better reſpectrespect ſheshe can ſhewshow to this authoritieauthority, then to forbeareforbear and abſtaineabstain from doing that which otherwiſeotherwise ſheshe would moſtmost gladly doedo: But if when it commethcometh to the vttermoſtuttermost point, and ſheshe ſhallshall ſaysay it is her right, and if ſheshe cannot hauehave his conſentconsent, ſheshe will doedo it without his conſentconsent, ſheshe therein ſhewethshoweth no great reſpectrespect.

Many other inconueniencesinconveniences might be reckoned vpup, but I will not longer inſiſtinsist on them, only from theſethese let it be well conſideredconsidered, whether it were not better for a familiefamily, that the huſbandhusband ſhouldshould be bardbarred from diſpoſingdisposing the goods without conſentconsent of his wife (ſoso as there might be according to the prouerbeproverb, but Though ſheshe had a proprietiepropriety, yet hath ſheshe not thereupon libertieliberty to diſpoſedispose the goods. one hand in the purſepurse) then both husband and wife to hauehave libertieliberty to diſpoſedispose them without each others conſentconsent.

div.head: §. 28. Of propertieproperty in goods, whether it giuegive libertieliberty to diſpoſedispose them as a wife will.
div.p: To iuſtifiejustify a wiueswives libertieliberty in diſpoſingdisposing the common goods Licet vxor proprietatem habeat, adminiſtrationemadministrationem tamen, & vſumvsum. fructūfructunvsumfructum bonorum viuente marito non habet. Greg. Sayr. clau. reg. lib. 9. cap. 16. of the family without her husbands conſentconsent, it is ſaidsaid, that ſheshe hath a true right and propertieproperty in thoſethose goods.

1. AnſwAnsw. Though it were granted that a wife hath a true property in the goods, yet this concluſionconclusion would not follow thereupon, that ſheshe hath power of her ſelfeself to diſpoſedispose the goods without her husbands conſentconsent: for the authoritieauthority which God hath giuengiven an husband, and ſubiectionsubjection which he hath laid on a wife, reſtrainerestrain her power and libertieliberty in that
which is her owneown: as for example, ſuppoſesuppose See Doctr. & ſtudstud. fol. 13. that a woman at the time of her mariagemarriage hauehave a leaſelease for yeeresyears, or the wardſhipwardship of the body and lands of an infant, or hauehave it by gift or Perk. plito. 560. 26. H. 8. 7. p. 1. Plowd. comment. 418. b. purchaſepurchase after mariagemarriage, ſheshe cannot giuegive it away whatſoeuerwhatsoever the extremitieextremity be: but her husband may any time during couerturecoverture, diſpoſedispose of it: and ſuchsuch his diſpoſitiondisposition ſhallshall cut off the wiueswives intereſtinterest. Or ſuppoſesuppose that the only childechild of her father be an inheretrixinheritrix of land, and hauehave in her ſelfeself (her father being dead) the full poſſeſſionpossession thereof: or that a widow hauehave the right vntounto, and poſſeſſionpossession of her husbands eſtateestate, and thus poſſeſſedpossessed be mariedmarried to an husband, hath ſheshe being a wife liberty to diſpoſedispose that eſtateestate which ſheshe brought with her without or againſtagainst her husbands conſentconsent? I thinkethink none will ſaysay it. Sure I am that what ſheshe giuethgiveth, lendeth, ſellethselleth, or otherwiſeotherwise diſpoſethdisposeth without his conſentconsent, he if he will, may for his lifetime recouerrecover againeagain: and yet no man will deniedeny but that ſheshe hath the trueſttruest intereſtinterest and propertieproperty in the forenamed lands and inheritance.
ObiectObject. May ſheshe not as well diſpoſedispose of her owneown inheritance, as of thoſethose goods, or reuenuesrevenues which her husband giuethgiveth her?
AnſwAnsw. No, for the gift of the husband is a generallgeneral conſentconsent of his for her to diſpoſedispose that which is giuengiven her as ſheshe ſeethseeth meet.

div.head: §. 29. Of the reaſonsreasons againſtagainst a wiueswives propertieproperty in the common goods of the family.
div.p:
2. AnſwAnsw. It may ſafelysafely be denied that a wife hath a propertieproperty in the common goods of the family whereof ſheshe is no heireheir, for property in goods is a ciuillcivil matter, and to be limited according to the law of man vnderunder which we liuelive. Where the law, or cuſtomecustom of the place, make all the children coheirescoheirs, all hauehave an equallequal right to their ſeuerallseveral parts: where the eldeſteldest only is made heireheir, he hath a right to all: where the youngeſtyoungest only is made heireheir, he hath a right to all: but neither the law of nations, nor of the land where we liuelive giuegive the wife a property. 12. H. 7. 22. Coke rep. 5. fo. 36. 28. H. 6. Dier fol. 6. plito. 5 Doct. & ſtudstud. fo. 13. Plowd. Comment. Bracebriges CaſeCase. By the common law mariagemarriage is a gift of all the goods and chattels perſonallpersonal of the wife to her husband, ſoso that no kindekind of propertieproperty in the ſamesame remaineth in her. 4. H. 6. 31. And all
perſonallpersonal goods and chattels during mariagemarriage giuengiven to the wife are preſentlypresently ipſoipso facto transferred (as to the property of them) to the husband. So that by our law ſheshe is ſoso farrefar from gaining any property by her mariagemarriage in her husbands goods, as ſheshe loſethloseth all the property ſheshe formerly had in her owneown goods. Yea 18. E. 4. 11. p. 44. her neceſſarynecessary apparellapparel is not hers in property. While ſheshe remaineth a wife ſheshe is (to vſeuse the law-phraſephrase) vnderunder couertcovert baron. See §. 26. She can neither let, ſellsell, alien, giuegive, nor otherwiſeotherwise of right make any thing away, no nor yet make a will ſoso to diſpoſedispose any goods while her husband liuethliveth without his conſentconsent: which yet an husband may while his wife liuethliveth, and that without or againſtagainst her conſentconsent.

ObiectObject. The law ſtatesstates a wife in a great part of the husbands goods, prouidingproviding for her iointerjointurejointer or thirds which the husband cannot make away without her conſentconsent.

AnſwAnsw. This prouiſionprovision is only for the time of her widowhood in caſecase ſheshe ouerliueoverlive him: but for the time that ſheshe remaineth his wife he may make away all, and ſheshe can recouerrecover none, till he be dead.

div.head: ObiectObject. This reſtraintrestraint of wiueswives is only in the court of men.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. Seeing it is not againſtagainst the law of God, it muſtmust alſoalso hold good in the court of ConſcienceConscience. Nay it is agreeable to the law of God and grounded thereupon.

For (to omit the proofesproofs before alleagedalleged) what might be the reaſonreason that the daughters of Zelophehad, who were heiresheirs to their father, were forbidden to marymarry out of their fathers tribe, and that a law was made that no daughters that poſſeſſedpossessed any inheritance ſhouldshould marymarry out of their fathers tribe, but becauſebecause all that a woman had before mariagemarriage, paſſedpassed vponupon the husband and became his by vertuevirtue of mariagemarriage? This alſoalso for that purpoſepurpose is by ſomesome not vnfitlyunfitly, nor without probabilitieprobability noted, that it is the common phraſephrase of Scripture to termeterm huſbandshusbands Si quis abduxerit vxorem cum bonis familiae dicitur abducere vxorem cum bonis viri. Fitzherb. Nat. breutumbreuium fol. 89. (but not wiueswives) rich, implying thereby that riches by a property appertaineappertain to husbands: yea vſuallyusually in Scripture goods and lands are ſaidsaid to be the husbands.
ObiectObject. The wiueswives of IaakobJacob doedo termeterm the goods which their husbands had theirs, ſayingsaying, the riches which God hath taken from our Fatherfather is OVRSOURS, Gen. 31. 16.

AnſwAnsw. They vſeuse the word Ours in oppoſitionopposition to their fathers houſehouse, and in relation not to their perſonspersons, but to their Ut vinum temperatum licet maiori ex parte aquae conſtatconstat, vinum appellamus: ſicsic cenſuscensus quamuis plus contribuerit vxor, nuncupandus viri eſtest. Plut. in praec. connub. husbands family, and therefore they addeadd and our childrens: So as by that place no greater right can be prouedproved for wiueswives, then for children. When the holy GhoſtGhost ſpeakethspeaketh of the ſamesame goods, he ſaithsaith not in relation to husband and wiueswives both, their flockesflocks, their ſubſtancesubstance, but only in relation to the huſbandhusband, his flockesflocks, his ſubſtancesubstance. For as in mixture of wine and water, though the greater quantitiequantity be water, yet we call the whole, wine: ſoso in the common goods of the family, though the wife ſhouldshould bring the greater part, we call all the husbands.

div.head: §. 30. Of anſwersanswers to the reaſonsreasons for a wiueswives property.
div.p: To proueprove a wiueswives property in the common goods of the family the reaſonsreasons following are alledgedalleged.

div.head: 1. ObiectObject. MariageMarriage giuinggiving a wife right of her husbands body, Cor1 Cor. 7. 4. doth much more of his goods.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. I deniedeny the conſequenceconsequence. For the vſeuse of the body is a proper act of the matrimoniallmatrimonial bond, wherein the difference betwixt ſuperioritiesuperiority and ſubiectionsubjection appeareth not: the wife hath as great a power ouerover the husbands body as the husband ouerover the wiueswives: which is not ſoso in the goods: no one thing can be named, wherein the power and authoritieauthority of the husband more conſiſtethconsisteth, then in the goods.

div.head: 2. ObiectObject. In the formeform of mariagemarriage the man ſaithsaith to his wife, with all my worldly goods I thee indowendow.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. 1. ThoſeThose words are to be taken of the vſeuse of his goods, and not of a property in them.

2. If an husband ſhallshall intend a property by them, that property which ſheshe hath thereby, ſheshe hath not by vertuevirtue of the generallgeneral law of mariagemarriage, but of his particualarparticular free donation.

3. In all countries thoſethose words are not vſedused in the formeform of mariagemarriage. If thoſethose words giuegive the wife her property, then ſuchsuch wiueswives as are mariedmarried without thoſethose words vſedused, hauehave no property: ſoso as this cannot be a generallgeneral ground of liberty for all wiueswives.

3. ObiectObject. A wife hath as good an eſtateestate in her husbands
goods as the Church in ChriſtsChrists bloudblood: but there the Church hath a property.

AnſwAnsw. Neither of thoſethose points can be prouedproved. But if a wiueswives right in her husbands goods be as the Churches in ChriſtsChrists bloudblood, what is gotten thereby? The Church hath not power without or againſtagainst ChriſtsChrists conſentconsent to diſpoſedispose his bloudblood: The Church of Rome is counted a proud vſurpingusurping ſtrumpetstrumpet for taking vponupon her ſoso to doedo.

div.head: §. 31. Of the priuiledgesprivileges of wiueswives aboueabove Children and ſeruantsservants in and about the goods of the familiefamily.
QueſtQuest. Where then is the preferment of the wife aboueabove ſeruantsservants and children, if ſheshe hauehave not a property?
div.p: I anſweranswer, Much eueryevery manner of way.
1. Treat. 4. §. 52. 54. There is due to her a more free and plentifullplentiful vſeuse of all the goods, then vntounto them.
2. By her place ſheshe hath the ordering and diſpoſingdisposing of the goods allotted for the common vſeuse of the familiefamily: as was §. 21. before granted.
3. Her husband ought to giuegive her a portion to diſpoſedispose as ſheshe ſhallshall ſeesee good, Treat. 4. §. 54. as we ſhallshall after ſhewshow, when we come to the husbands duties.
4. She is a iointjoint gouernourgovernor with her husband ouerover the children and ſeruantsservants, as was ſhewedshowed §. 4. before.

AgaineAgain I anſweranswer, that this argument might as well be alledgedalleged againſtagainst that fearefear, ſubiectionsubjection, and obedience which the Scripture expreſlyexpressly requireth of wiueswives, and it might be demanded, if wiueswives muſtmust fearefear and obey their husbands and be ſubiectsubject vntounto them, where is their preferment aboueabove their children and ſeruantsservants. But §. 11. it hath beenebeen ſhewedshowed that though the ſamesame things for matter be required of wiueswives which are required of children and ſeruantsservants, yet there is a great difference in the manner of performing them.

div.head: §. 32. Of examples and other reaſonsreasons alleadgedalleged for libertieliberty of wiueswives to diſpoſedispose goods.

div.p: 2. Abigails example is alleadgedalleged for a wiueswives libertieliberty: and 2. ReaſonReason. Examples. 1 Sam. 25. 18. &etcc. Pro. 31. 11, &etcc. the example of the good houſehouse wife deſcribeddescribed by SalomonSolomon.

AnſwAnsw. 1. Abigails example was extraordinary; beſidesbesides, who can tell whether the heart of her husband ſoso truſtedtrusted not in her
as he referred the whole gouernmentgovernment of the houſehouse to her, and ſoso ſheshe had a generallgeneral conſentconsent for what ſheshe did.

2. It is cleereclear that the other good-wife had her husbands conſentconsent for what ſheshe did: for beſidesbesides that it is ſaidsaid the heart of her husband truſtedtrusted in her, it is alſoalso ſaidsaid, that he praiſedpraised her. Therefore he was neither ignorant of that which ſheeshe did, nor vnwillingunwilling ſheshe ſhouldshould doedo it: it was neither without nor againſtagainst his conſentconsent.

3. It is alleadgedalleged that wiueswives hauehave as great a care in getting 3. ReaſonReason. WiuesWives hauehave a like care in getting goods. goods, or in preſeruingpreserving them for the good of the familiefamily: therefore it is iuſtjust and equallequal, that they ſhouldshould hauehave a like power in diſpoſingdisposing them.

AnſwAnsw. Though queſtionquestion may be made of the former part, at leaſtleast for the greater ſortsort and number of wiueswives, yet for anſweranswer to this reaſonreason I need not queſtionquestion it; for the conſequenceconsequence doth not follow, though that be granted. The right of diſpoſingdisposing goods doth not ſimplysimply riſerise from the care and painespains of getting and preſeruingpreserving them: but from that order that the Lord hath beenebeen pleaſedpleased to ſetset downedown. A wiſewise and induſtriousindustrious childechild may be a meanesmeans to raiſeraise and increaſeincrease his fathers eſtateestate, when his father taketh little care and painespains about it: yea a faithfullfaithful and wiſewise ſtewardsteward or other ſeruantservant (as IaakobJacob and IoſephJoseph were) may doedo much more by his painespains and care in getting and preſeruingpreserving the goods of the familiefamily, then his maſtermaster: yet will it not thereupon follow, that ſuchsuch a childechild, or ſuchsuch a ſeruantservant hath as great a right and power to diſpoſedispose ſuchsuch goods as his father or his maſtermaster.

4. The neerenear coniunctionconjunction betwixt man and wife is alleagedalleged: 4. ReaſonReason. WiuesWives are yoakyoke-fellowesfellows with their husbands. they are ſaidsaid to be yoakeyoke-fellowesfellows, and thence is inferred that they hauehave a like power in diſpoſingdisposing goods.

AnſwAnsw. They are yoakyoke-fellowesfellows in mutuallmutual familiaritiefamiliarity, not in equallequal authoritieauthority; and in relation to others as children and ſeruantsservants, not in oppoſitionopposition each to other. In this reſpectrespect ſheshe is ſubiectsubject, not equallequal. If therefore he will one thing, and ſheshe another, ſheshe may not thinkethink to hauehave an equallequal right and power, ſheshe muſtmust giuegive place and yeeldyield.

div.head: §. 33. Of the Treat. 4. §. 54. ſubiectionsubjection of wiueswives in diſtributingdistributing goods to charitable vſesuses.
div.p: Some that grant that a wife is ſoso ſubiectedsubjected to her husband in a ciuillcivil manner, as ſheshe may not diſpoſedispose any part of his goods at her pleaſurepleasure to any ciuillcivil vſeuse, deniedeny this ſubiectionsubjection to extend to giuinggiving of almesalms, and ſuchsuch like charitable vſesuses.

Before I come to determine this queſtionquestion, let it be remembredremembered, that it was before granted, that §§. 22. ordinarieordinary dutieduty muſtmust giuegive place to extraordinarieextraordinary need, ſoso that releeferelief in preſentpresent neceſſitienecessity is not controuertedcontroverted. Let it be alſoalso remembredremembered that §. 21. a wife may hauehave goods proper to her ſelfeself, yea Treat. 4. §. 54. it ſhallshall be ſhewedshowed that an husband ought according to his abilitieability to commit ſomethingsomething to her diſcretiondiscretion and diſpoſitiondisposition: of theſethese and ſuchsuch like goods ſheshe is as much bound as her husband to expend ſomethingsomething to charitable vſesuses: and (as God offereth occaſionoccasion) Pro. 31. 20. to reach forth her hand to the poorepoor and needy.

Yea further let this be premiſedpremised, that in caſecase a wife be forbidden or reſtrainedrestrained by her husband, ſheshe ought to vſeuse all the good meanesmeans ſheshe can by her ſelfeself and her friends to mouemove her husband to grant her ſomesome libertieliberty, that ſheshe may hauehave ſomesome trialltrial of her mercifullmerciful and charitable diſpoſitiondisposition: if herein ſheshe cannot preuaileprevail, then ſheshe ought to make knowneknown vntounto her husband ſuchsuch perſonspersons caſescases as ſheshe thinkesthinks meet to be releeuedrelieved, and vſeuse all the motiuesmotives ſheshe can to perſwadepersuade him to afford them ſomesome releeferelief.

But put the caſecase a wiſewise, religious, mercifullmerciful wife, be mariedmarried State of queſtionquestion. to a couetouscovetous worldling, who though he hauehave wit, and vnderſtandingunderstanding enough to manage ciuillcivil affairesaffairs, and to prouideprovide for the outward temporalltemporal eſtateestate of the houſehouse, yet hath no heart to releeuerelieve the poorepoor, and is not only vnwillingunwilling himſelfehimself to doedo good in that kindekind, but will not ſuffersuffer his wife to doedo it, whether may a wife priuilieprivily take of ſuchsuch goods as he hath reſeruedreserved to his owneown diſpoſingdisposing, and ſimplysimply without any kindekind of conſentconsent diſtributedistribute them to charitable vſesuses, or though he expreſlyexpressly forbid her, yet directly againſtagainst his conſentconsent diſpoſedispose them?

With reuerendreverend reſpectrespect to better iudgementsjudgments, I thinkethink ſheshe may Non excuſa • bitexcusabit bona intentio vxoris, etiamſietiamsi ea acciperet ad eleemoſynameleemosynam faciendam. Greg. Sayr. clav. reg. lib. 9. cap. 16. not (except before excepted.) For it being before prouedproved in generallgeneral, that ſheshe had no ſuchsuch liberty in diſpoſingdisposing goods, I cannot ſeesee how this particular end of giuinggiving almesalms can diſpencedispense with her generallgeneral ſubiectionsubjection in eueryevery thing, except there were ſomesome particular warrant for it in Gods word.

div.head: §. 34. Of generallgeneral exhortations to works of mercy. How far they bindebind wiueswives.

div.p:
ObiectObject. The many generallgeneral exhortations vntounto workesworks of mercy, which without limitation to any particular perſonspersons, are indefinitely directed to all, doedo giuegive ſufficientsufficient warrant to wiueswives: ſuchsuch as theſethese, Luke 11. 41. GiueGive almesalms.
Gal. 6. 10. Let vsus doedo good.
Heb. 13. 16. To diſtributedistribute forget not, &etcc.

AnſwAnsw. All theſethese are ſtrongstrong motiuesmotives to prouokeprovoke wiueswives to be mercifullmerciful and charitable in ſuchsuch things as they may, by any means with their husbands conſentconsent, or in ſuchsuch things as by their huſbandshusbands are giuengiven to them. Yea alſoalso they are ſtrongstrong motiuesmotives to prouokeprovoke husbands to allow them liberty to giuegive almesalms. But in the caſecase propounded they giuegive no liberty to wiueswives: for it is a ruled caſecase laid downedown by ChriſtChrist himſelfehimself, that workesworks of charity muſtmust be done, and almesalms muſtmust be giuengiven of ſuchsuch things Luke 11. 41. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . as we hauehave, or which are in our power to giuegive. Now if the husband will not giuegive her that power, ſheshe hath not power to giuegive, and ſoso is excuſedexcused. Date quae habetis eleemoſynameleemosynam Tertul. contr. Marcion. l. 4. 2 Cor. 8. 12. In this caſecase her true will, and her faithfullfaithful and earneſtearnest deſiredesire ſhallshall be accepted for the deed, according to that which the ApoſtleApostle ſaithsaith, if there be firſtfirst a willing mindemind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not. Many caſescases may be giuengiven wherein inferioursinferiors are reſtrainedrestrained from workesworks of mercy; as ſuppoſesuppose a ſonneson or ſeruantservant be deſirousdesirous to viſitvisit one ſickesick o • r in priſonprison, but his Parentparent or Maſtermaster (though leaueleave be asked) will not ſuffersuffer him, but charge him not to ſtirrestir out of dooresdoors, or t • o goego with him another way, ſhallshall this ſonneson or ſeruantservant notwithſtandingnotwithstanding that charge, doedo that workework of mercy?

div.head: §. 35. Of obedience to an husband in ſuchsuch things as he ſinfullysinfully forbiddeth.

div.p: ObiectObject. 2. This reſtraintrestraint is not in the Lord, but rather againſtagainst him and his word, therefore a wife is not bound thereunto.

AnſwAnsw. Though the husband ſinnesin in reſtrainingrestraining his wife, yet
ſheeshe in that reſtraintrestraint may obey, and that in the Lord: becauſebecause the Lord who hath commanded her to be ſubiectsubject in eueryevery thing, hath no where warranted her not to be ſubiectsubject in this particular. It is expreſlyexpressly ſaidsaid in the law concerning a wiueswives vowesvows, that if her huſbandhusband breakebreak them after he hath heard them, he ſhallshall bearebear her iniquity.
Numb. 30. 16. Did not he then ſinnesin in reſtrainingrestraining her, and was not ſheshe guiltleſſeguiltless though ſheshe yeeldedyielded to his reſtraintrestraint? The condition betwixt husbands and wiueswives in this caſecase, is not vnlikeunlike the caſecase betwixt other ſuperiourssuperiors in authority, and their inferioursinferiors in ſubiectionsubjection. But other inferioursinferiors may lawfully abſtaineabstain from ſuchsuch things as their gouernoursgovernors doedo ſinfullysinfully charge them to abſtaineabstain from. For ſuppoſesuppose a ſonneson growengrown to be a man, liuelive in his fathers houſehouse at his fathers finding, and hauehave no ſetset portion of his owneown, and his father will not giuegive him leaueleave to beſtowbestow any thing on charitable vſesuses, is he now bound to giuegive almesalms? ſhallShall the curſecurse be executed on him if he giuegive not? A croſſecross indeed I acknowledge it to be, both to ſuchsuch a ſonneson, and alſoalso to a wife to be ſoso reſtrainedrestrained: but not a curſecurse or ſinnesin; the ſinnesin and curſecurse lieth on their head, who reſtrainerestrain them by vertuevirtue of their authority, wherein they abuſeabuse their authority: as other gouernoursgovernors may do and oft do, and yet neither liberty granted thereby to ſubiectssubjects, nor authority taken from gouernoursgovernors. In this reſemblanceresemblance betwixt a ſonneson and a wife I deſiredesire not to be miſtakenmistaken; for I alleadgeallege it not to make the ſtatestate of a wife and a ſonneson all one: but to ſhewshow that thoſethose generallgeneral precepts of giuinggiving almesalms, may hauehave their exceptions, as they which in particular handle that point, giuegive other examples. There muſtmust therefore be a further ground then the generallgeneral commandementcommandment of almesalms-giuinggiving to proueprove the forenamed liberty of wiueswives.

div.head: §. 36. Of Zipporahs caſecase in circumciſingcircumcising her ſonneson.

div.p: ObiectObject. 3. A wife was made to be an helpehelp to her husband: in thoſethose things therefore wherein he faileth, ſheshe muſtmust make ſupplysupply, as Zipporah who performed a duty which belonged to her Exod. 4. 25. husband, and not vntounto her.

AnſwAnsw. She may be an helpehelp in many other things, though this be out of her power: yea and in this alſoalso by counſellcounsel, perſwaſionpersuasion, and other like meanesmeans ſheshe may be a great helpehelp. The caſecase of Zipporah was extraordinary, and of an vrgenturgent preſentpresent neceſſitynecessity, eueneven to ſauesave the life of her husband. BeſidesBesides, MoſesMoses was of himſelfehimself
vnableunable to doedo it, but willing that ſheshe ſhouldshould doedo it. Now what is this to ordinarieordinary caſescases, and ſuchsuch caſescases as husbands are able enough themſeluesthemselves to doedo, but altogether vnwillingunwilling that it ſhouldshould be done by their wiueswives? Factum Zephorae ſingularesingulare eſtest, & extraordinarium, ne
que neque conſtatconstat illud ſimplicitersimpliciter à Deo approbatum fuiſſefuisse. Simler. in Exod. 4. Luke 8. 3.

But what if Zipporahs example herein be not warrantable? forFor it doth not appeareappear that it was ſimplysimply approuedapproved of God: God doth oft remoueremove temporary iudgementsjudgments for the very workesworks ſakesake that is done, though in the manner it be ſinfullysinfully done. InſtanceInstance the repentance of Ahab, 1. King. 21. 29.

div.head: §. 37. Of the wife of Chuzas caſecase in miniſteringministering to ChriſtChrist.

div.p: 4. ObiectObject. IoannaJoanna the wife of Chuza, Herods ſtewardsteward, miniſtredministered vntounto ChriſtChrist of her ſubſtancesubstance without her husbands conſentconsent.

AnſwAnsw. If this could be prouedproved it were ſomewhatsomewhat to the purpoſepurpose; but this clauſeclause without her husbands conſentconsent (wherein the mainemain ſtatestate of the queſtionquestion conſiſtethconsisteth) is not in the text, nor by any good probabilitieprobability can be gathered out of it. All the ſhewshow of probabilitieprobability that can be ſhewedshowed for it is, that IoannaJoanna is there ſaidsaid to be the wife of Chuza, Herods ſtewardsteward. But to ſhewshow that that is nothing, let it be noted,

1. That phraſephrase doth not imply that Chuza was then liuingliving. It is ſaidsaid that DauidDavid begat SalomonSolomon of the wife of VriahUriah, but Matth. 1. 6. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . VriahUriah was not then liuingliving: therefore the tranſlatorstranslators for perſpicuitieperspicuity ſakesake doedo inſertinsert theſethese words (her that had beenebeen) the wife of VriahUriah. So likewiſelikewise Onan is commanded to goego in to his Gen. 38. 8. brothers wife, yet doth not this imply that his brother was then liuingliving.
ObiectObject. Why ſhouldshould mention be made of Chuza, Herods ſtewardsteward, if he were not then liuingliving?

AnſwAnsw. To ſhewshow that IoannaJoanna was a woman of great place, whereby this fruit of her faith in following ChriſtChrist was the more commended. Thus in another kindekind Matthew is intitledentitled Matth. 10. 3. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . the Publican, after he had cleaneclean relinquiſhtrelinquishedrelinquisht that office, the more to commend his faith.
I doedo not here directly affirmeaffirm that Chuza was then dead, but for ought that this phraſephrase doth imply, he might be dead.

2. Some gather that this ſtewardsteward was that Ruler whoſewhose Chemnit. Harm. EuangEvang. cap. 33. IohJoh. 4. 53. ſonneson ChriſtChrist healed, who thereupon beleeuedbelieved with all his houſehouse.
Which if he were, then it cannot be doubted, but that his wife followed ChriſtChrist with his good liking and conſentconsent.

3. Chuza being Herods ſtewardsteward, and ſoso a man of great place, and publikepublic imploimentemployment, might, if he were then liuingliving, depute the managing of all affairesaffairs at home to his wife, as the ProuProv. 31. 11. husband of the good wife commended by SalomonSolomon, and ſoso ſheshe might hauehave at leaſtleast a generallgeneral conſentconsent.

I doedo not certainly determine any of theſethese expreſlyexpressly to be ſoso, I doedo but note them as probabilities, yet ſuchsuch as doedo ſufficientlysufficiently ouerthrowoverthrow the ſurmiſedsurmised libertieliberty of a wife in giuinggiving almesalms without any conſentconsent of her husband: for this of all other probabilities ſeemethseemeth to be moſtmost improbable. Into my heart it can neuernever enter to imagine that ChriſtChrist would giuegive ſuchsuch an occaſionoccasion of ſlanderslander vntounto his enemies, as to ſaysay he cariedcarried about with him other mens wiueswives, without or againſtagainst the conſentconsent of their husbands, and ſufferedsuffered them to ſpendspend the goods of their huſbandshusbands vponupon him. I had much rather thinkethink that either ſuchsuch women as followed him had no husbands liuingliving, or if they had, that they did that which they did with the conſentconsent of their husbands.

div.head: §. 38. Of the Treat. 4. §. 18. 52. reſtraintrestraint of wiueswives about allowance for themſeluesthemselves or families without their husbands conſentconsent.
div.p: That which hath hitherto beenebeen deliuereddelivered concerning a wiueswives ſubiectionsubjection in diſpoſingdisposing goods, may alſoalso be applied to other things concerning her ſelfeself, children, ſeruantsservants, &etcc. whereofWhereof I will giuegive ſomesome examples.

A wife hath not power to appoint what ſheshe liſtlist her ſelfeself without or againſtagainst her husbands conſentconsent, either for her owneown allowance, or for her family; ſheshe muſtmust rather reſtrest ſatisfiedsatisfied with that which he appointeth: for he being the head, muſtmust hauehave the ouerover-ruling ſtroakestroke therein. BeſidesBesides he better knoweth what may be afforded.
QueſtQuest. What if an husband make himſelfehimself poorer then he is: and the allowance which he appointeth be meaner then his meanesmeans, and vnbeſeemingunbeseeming his place and ſtatestate?

AnſwAnsw. She ought, if poſſibypossiblypossiby ſheshe can by her owneown inſtantinstant perſwaſionpersuasion, or any other fairefair meanesmeans, mouemove him to that which tendeth to his honour and reputation: but if ſheshe can
no way preuaileprevail, her ſubiectionsubjection requireth contentment and patience.

div.head: §. 39. Of a wiueswives TreatTreat. 4. §. 18. ſubiectionsubjection to her husband about children.
div.p: A wife may not ſimplysimply without, or directly againſtagainst her huſbandshusbands conſentconsent, order and diſpoſedispose of the children in giuinggiving them names, apparelling their bodies, appointing their callings, places of bringing vpup, mariagesmarriages, or portions.

1. For giuinggiving names to children, beſidesbesides that it is throughout 1. Names. the Scripture for the moſtmost part enioynedenjoined to the husband, as to Gen. 17. 19. Abraham, to Luk. 1. 13. Zacharias, and to others, and that accordingly husbands hauehave ordinarily done, as Gen. 5. 3. Adam, 29. Lamech,
& 21. 3. Abraham, and others. It is to be noted that when there was a difference betwixt the man and his wife in giuinggiving a childeschilds name, he giuinggiving one name, ſheshe another, the name which he gauegave, ſtoodstood; though Gen. 35. 18. Rachel named her youngeſtyoungest ſonneson Benoni, yet BeniaminBenjamin (which name IaakobJacob gauegave) was the childeschilds name. So alſoalso when Luk. 1. 62. Elizabeth told her friends that her childeschilds name muſtmust be IohnJohn, they would not reſtrest therein, till Zacharias had ratified that name. Yea though IoſephJoseph were but the ſuppoſedsupposed father of IeſusJesus, yet becauſebecause he was the huſbandhusband of Mary the mother of IeſusJesus,
Mat. 1. 21. he had this honour giuengiven him, to giuegive the name vntounto her childechild.

Whereas in Scripture it is ſometimessometimes ſaidsaid that the mothers named their children, as Gen. 29. 32. Leah,
& 30. 24. RahelRachel, and others, it is vponupon the forenamed ground to be ſuppoſedsupposed that they had their husbands conſentconsent.

2. For appointing place and mariagemarriage it is noted that Gen. 27. 43, &etcc.
Rebekah 2. Place and mariagemarriage. asked the conſentconsent of her husband: though ſheshe told her ſonneson IaakobJacob that he ſhouldshould goego to Haran to his vncleuncle Laban to be there kept in ſafetysafety from the fury of EſauEsau, yet ſheshe would not ſendsend him till Gen. 28. 1, 2. IſaakIsaac had giuengiven his conſentconsent for his abode there, and taking a wife from thence.

3. For deputing vntounto a calling, it is noted of 1 Sam. 1. 11. AnnahHannah, that 3. Calling. though before her childechild was borne ſheshe had by ſolemnesolemn vow dedicated him to the Lord, yet when the childechild was borne VerſVers.Vers 22. ſheshe asked her husbands conſentconsent about it. 4. ApparellApparel.

4. That which is noted of 1 Sam. 2. 19. AnnahsHannahs carrying a little coat to
her ſonneson yeareyear by yeareyear when ſheshe went vpup with her husband, ſhewethshoweth that ſheshe did it not without her husbands conſentconsent. Women are for the moſtmost part prone to prankeprank vpup their children aboueabove their husbands place and calling, and therefore good reaſonreason that therein they ſhouldshould be gouernedgoverned by their husbands.
What if husbands be more forward to hauehave their children attired vainly and vnſeemelyunseemly, then wiueswives?

AnſwAnsw. A wife muſtmust doedo what ſheshe can to hinder it: if ſheshe can no way preuaileprevail with him, ſheshe by reaſonreason of her ſubiectionsubjection is much more excuſedexcused, then he could be, if he would ſuffersuffer his wife therein to hauehave her will.

5. The law that layeth the charge vponupon husbands to giuegive 5. Portions. Deut. 21. 15, &etcc. ſuchsuch and ſuchsuch portions to his children, and the anſwerableanswerable practiſepractise of husbands from time to time, ſhewshow that the wife of her ſelfeself hath not power to order them.

div.head: §. 40. Of a wiueswives Treat. 4. §. 18. ſubiectionsubjection to her husband about ordering ſeruantsservants and beaſtsbeasts.
div.p: If wiueswives muſtmust hauehave their husbands conſentconsent in ordering and diſpoſingdisposing of their children which come out of her wombewomb, much more of their ſeruantsservants.

They may not take in, or thruſtthrust out ſeruantsservants againſtagainst their husbands mindemind. In this point, as in many other, Sarah manifeſtedmanifested her wiuewive-like obedience; in that Gen. 16. 5. ſheshe would not dealedeal roughly with her maid though ſheshe were prouokedprovoked: much leſſeless & 21. 10. put her out of dooresdoors till ſheshe had made the matter knowneknown to her husband. Though ſheshe failed in the manner, yet in the thing it ſelfeself ſheshe is a good example. It is further noted and approuedapproved in the 2 King. 4. 22. Shunemite that ſheshe asked her husbands conſentconsent about ſendingsending a ſeruantservant with her.

My meaning is not that ſuchsuch wiueswives as hauehave ſeruantsservants allowed them to attend vponupon them ſhouldshould askeask their husbands conſentconsent whenſoeuerwhensoever they hauehave occaſionoccasion to vſeuse them; for their husbands by allowing them men for their attendance manifeſtmanifest their will and conſentconsent that they may vſeuse them as they ſeesee occaſionoccasion: but that they ſhouldshould not vſeuse and imployemploy their ſeruantsservants in ſuchsuch things as they know their husbands would diſlikedislike, except they can gainegain their husbands conſentconsent.

AgainſtAgainst thoſethose particulars of children and ſeruantsservants it may be obiectedobjected, that wiueswives are parents of their children as well as husbands, and miſtreſſesmistresses of ſeruantsservants as well as they maſtersmasters, and therefore hauehave altogether as great power ouerover them as their husbands.

AnſwAnsw. Indeed if the authority of the husband come not betweenebetween, that may be granted in relation betwixt her and them: but her power being ſubordinatesubordinate to her husbands in relation to him ſheshe hath not ſoso great a power: the power of a wife that now we ſpeakespeak of is directly in relation to her husband.

The like may be ſaidsaid of their beaſtsbeasts and cattellcattle, a particular point noted alſoalso in the example of the Shunemite, who hauinghaving occaſionoccasion to vſeuse a beaſtbeast went to her husband, and ſaidsaid, ſendsend I pray thee with me one of the aſſesasses. 2 King. 4. 22.

div.head: §. 41. Of a wiueswives Treat. 4. §. 18. ſubiectionsubjection in entertaining ſtrangersstrangers iournyingjourneyingjournying abroad, and making vowesvows.
div.p: If wiueswives may not at their pleaſurepleasure vſeuse the things appertaining to the houſehouse, much leſſeless may they bring ſtrangersstrangers into the houſehouse and entertaineentertain them without or againſtagainst their huſbandshusbands conſentconsent. The good Shunemite ſoso often named as a preſidentprecedentpresident 2 King. 4. 10. for good wiueswives, firſtfirst asked her husbands conſentconsent, before ſheshe lodged a Prophet of the Lord.

The ſamesame patternepattern is alſoalso commended vntounto wiueswives to mouemove them not to iourneyjourney abroad without their husbands conſentconsent. For though that good wife had a very weighty and iuſtjust occaſionoccasion 2 King. 4. 22. to goego vntounto the Prophet, yet ſheshe would not before ſheshe knew her husbands mindemind.

As for a wiueswives power to make vowesvows, in that the law giuethgiveth an husband power to diſanulldisannul her vow when he knoweth it, it implieth that ſheshe ought to hauehave his conſentconsent in making it, if Num. 30. 9. at leaſtleast ſheshe deſiredesire to hauehave it eſtabliſhedestablished, which ſheshe ought to deſiredesire, or elſeelse ſheshe mocketh God.

I hauehave thought good to mention theſethese particular points for illuſtrationillustration of a wiueswives ſubiectionsubjection, becauſebecause they are all of them grounded on Gods word: many other might be added to them, but theſethese are ſufficientsufficient.

div.head: §. 42. Of aberrations contrary to a wiueswives ſubiectionsubjection in doing things without or againſtagainst their husbands conſentconsent.
div.p: Now conſiderconsider we the vſuallusual vices and aberrations contrary to thoſethose duties: the generallgeneral ſummesum of all is, for a wife to take on her to doedo what ſheshe liſtlist, whether her husband will or no, either not willing that he ſhouldshould know what ſheshe doth, or not caring though it be againſtagainst his mindemind and will. Of this ſortsort are

1. Such as priuilyprivily take money out of their husbands cloſetsclosets, 1. PriuyPrivy purloyningpurloining huſbandshusbands goods. counters, or other like places where he laiethlayeth it, neuernever telling him of it, nor willing that he ſhouldshould know it: likewiſelikewise ſuchsuch as after the like manner take ware out of the ſhopshop, cornecorn out of the garner, ſheepesheep out of the flockeflock, or any other goods to ſellsell and make money of: or to giuegive away, or otherwiſeotherwise to vſeuse ſoso as their husbands ſhallshall neuernever know, if they can hinder it. Such wiueswives herein ſinnesin hainouſlyheinouslyhainously, and that in many reſpectsrespects.
FirſtFirst they diſobeydisobey the ordinance of God in a mainemain branch of their particular calling, which is ſubiectionsubjection.

2. They ill repay the care and painespains which their husbands take for their good. Many ſuchsuch wiueswives recompencerecompense euillevil for good, which is a deuilliſhdevilishdevillish qualitiequality.
3. They are oft a meanesmeans to impaireimpair and impoueriſhimpoverish their husbands eſtateestate.

4. They ſhewshow themſeluesthemselves no better then Si vxor ex bonis communibus ſid • esineside viri licentia ſaltemsaltem praeſumptapraesumpta accipiat, verè furtum commis •• it. Greg. Sayr. clau. reg. l. 9. c. 16. pilfringpilfering theeuesthieves thereby. All that can be iuſtlyjustly and truly ſaidsaid for their right in the common goods, cannot defend them from the guilt of theft: they are the more dangerous by how much the more they are truſtedtrusted, and leſſeless ſuſpectedsuspected: and their fact is ſoso much the more hainousheinous by how much the more deeredear their husbands ought to be vntounto them.

5. They are a verievery ill example to other inferioursinferiors in the houſehouse, for ſeldomeseldom hath a man a deceitfulldeceitful wife, but ſomesome of the children or ſeruantsservants, are made acceſſarieaccessary thereunto, being made her inſtrumentsinstruments to take the goods, and beſtowbestow them as ſheshe ordereth, and ſoso are made vnfaithfullunfaithful.

6. They make themſeluesthemselves ſlauesslaves to their owneown children and
ſeruantsservants, whom they dare not diſpleaſedisplease, leſtlest they ſhouldshould tell what was done.

7. They teach their children and ſeruantsservants to be theeuesthieves: for beſidesbesides that ſuchsuch as are vſedused by their miſtreſſesmistresses to purloinepurloin for them, are thereby made acceſſarieaccessary to their ſinnesin, they will alſoalso purloinepurloin for themſeluesthemselves, when their miſtreſſesmistresses ſhallshall not know. So as what with the wiueswives purloining one way, and the childrens or ſeruantsservants another way, a mans eſtateestate may be waſtedwasted as dew before the SunneSun, and he not know which way.

2. Such as will hauehave what allowance they thinkethink beſtbest for 2. Taking what allowance they liſtlist. themſeluesthemselves and family, and ſcornfullyscornfully ſaysay, They will not be at their husbands finding: they know beſtbest what allowance is fitteſtfittest for the family, and that it ſhallshall hauehave. Many will make their huſbandshusbands eareear tingle againeagain, yea and make the whole houſehouse (if not the ſtreetstreet alſoalso) ring of it, if they thinkethink their allowance be not anſwerableanswerable to the vttermoſtuttermost extent of their husbands eſtateestate. This impatiencieimpatiency and inſolencieinsolency, as it croſſethcrosseth Gods ordinance, ſoso it maketh both their liueslives vncomfortableuncomfortable.

3. Such as cocker, attire, or any way bring vpup their children 3. Ordering children againſtagainst their husbands mindemind. otherwiſeotherwise then their husbands would, eueneven to the griefegrief and diſhonourdishonour of their husbands: keeping them at home when their husbands, for their better education, would hauehave them abroad: as theſethese ſinnesin in hindringhindering the good of their children, ſoso alſoalso in not yeeldingyielding to their husbands. 4. Ordering ſeruantsservants againſtagainst their husbands mindemind.

4. Such as will hauehave their owneown will about ſeruantsservants, taking in, and putting out whom they pleaſeplease, and when they pleaſeplease: vſingusing ſomesome ſeruantsservants whom they findefind for their turneturn to the preiudiceprejudice of their husbands: and caryingcarrying themſeluesthemselves ſoso ſharplysharply 5. Lending forth their husbands cattellcattle. and ſhrewiſhlyshrewishly to others that are for their husbands turneturn, as a good, truſtietrusty, faithfullfaithful ſeruantservant cannot long ſtaystay in the houſehouse.

5. Such as ſecretlysecretly lend out their husbands horſeshorses, or other 6. FeaſtingFeasting when their husbands ſhallshall not know it. AbſenteAbsente marito compotationes domi ne excita. Greg. Naz. ad Olymp. like cattellcattle, more reſpectingrespecting to pleaſurepleasure a vainevain friend, then to pleaſeplease a good husband. This fault is ſoso much the greater, when it is done to the dammagedamage and preiudiceprejudice of the husband.

6. Such as are then moſtmost frolickefrolic and iollyjolly, when their huſbandshusbands are furtheſtfurthest off and cannot know it. SalomonSolomon ſetssets it downedown as a note of a ſtrumpetstrumpet, ProuProv. 7. 19. then to tricketrick vpup her houſehouse and to ſeekeseek for gueſtsguests, when her husband is gone a iourneyjourney farrefar
off. Then ought ſheshe to be moſtmost ſolitariesolitary, and by abſtainingabstaining from merriemerry meetings, to ſhewshow that there can be no greater dampedamp to her mirth, then the abſenceabsence of her husband.

7. Such as thinkethink their houſeshouses a priſonprison vntounto them, that cannot 7. Gadding abroad at their owneown pleaſurepleasure. Noli pedem tuum limine crebro efferre. &etcc. Naz. loc. citat. long tarrietarry at home: they thinkethink they hauehave power to goego when and whither they will, and to tarrietarry out as long as they liſtlist, thinkethink their husbands of it what they will. 1 Tim. 5. 13. The ApoſtleApostle layeth downedown this as a markemark of a wanton wife, and an idle houſehouse-wife, being idle (ſaithsaith he) they goego about from houſehouse to houſehouse: therefore in Tit. 2. 5. another place he exhorteth them to be keepers at home. The WiſeWise-man goeth further, and maketh this to be another note of a ſtrumpetstrumpet, that ProuProv. 7. 11. her feet cannot abide in the houſehouse: which we may ſeesee verified in Judg. 19. 2. the LeuitesLevites adulterous wife, whoſewhose fearefullfearful end was a ſtampestamp of Gods iudgementjudgment on ſuchsuch looſeloose lewdneſſelewdness.

8. Such as care not how or what they bindebind themſeluesthemselves vntounto 8. div.head: §. 43. Of a wiueswives actiueactive Obedience.
div.p: It is a good proofeproof and trialltrial of a wiueswives obedience, to abſtaineabstain from doing ſuchsuch things as otherwiſeotherwise ſheshe would doedo, if her huſbandshusbands contrariecontrary will did not reſtrainerestrain her: but yet that is not ſufficientsufficient, there muſtmust be an actiueactive, as well as a paſſiuepassive obedience yeeldedyielded. 1. To his commandementscommandments, readily to doedo what he lawfully A wiueswives actiueactive obedience reſpectethrespecteth firſtfirst her husbands commandementcommandment. commands.

For the firſtfirst, ſoso farrefar ought a wife to be from thinking ſcornescorn to be commanded by her husband, that the very knowledge which by any meanesmeans ſheshe hath of her husbands mindemind and will, • oughtoughtsought to hauehave the force of a ſtraightstraight commandementcommandment with her. div.head: §. 44. Of a wiueswives willingneſſewillingness to Treat. 4. §. 18. dwell where her husband will.
div.p: To make this part of a wiueswives obedience ſomewhatsomewhat more cleareclear, I will exemplifieexemplify it by two or three particular inſtancesinstances, recorded and approuedapproved in Gods word.
The firſtfirst is, that a wife ought to be willing to dwell where her husband will hauehave her dwell.

The wiueswives of Abraham, IſaakIsaac, and IaakobJacob, herein manifeſtedmanifested their wiuewive-like obedience: though their husbands brought them from their owneown countreycountry, and from their fathers houſehouse, yet they refuſedrefused not to goego with them, but dwelt in a ſtrangestrange countreycountry, and that in tents.

Note in particular what IaakobsJacob's wiueswives ſaysay to their husband in this caſecase, Is there any portion or inheritance for vsus in our fathers
Gen. 31. 14. houſehouse? implying thereby, that ſeeingseeing it was their husbands pleaſurepleasure to be gone, they would not any longer tarry in their fathers houſehouse, to lookelook for any more portion or inheritance there.

TheſeThese examples doedo further ſhewshow that if an husband hauehave iuſtjust occaſionoccasion to remoueremove from one country to another, and in thoſethose countries from place to place, his wife ought to yeeldyield to goego with him, if he require it at her hands. Note what the ApoſtleApostle ſaithsaith, hauehave we not power to lead about a wife? That interrogation 1 Cor. 9. 5. implieth a ſtrongstrong aſſeuerationasseveration. The husband then hauinghaving power to lead about a wife from place to place, ſheshe ought to ſubmitsubmit her ſelfeself to that power. This clauſeclause (as well as other ApoſtlesApostles, and as the brethren of the Lord and Cephas) ſhewethshoweth, that this was not only a power which might be vſedused, but which was vſedused by huſbandshusbands, and yeeldedyielded vntounto by wiueswives.

div.head: ObiectObject. The forenamed examples are extraordinary, and that vponupon extraordinary occaſionsoccasions.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. Yet they may be patternespatterns for ordinary occaſionsoccasions which are lawfulllawful and warrantable. Was it not an extraordinary fact of EliahElijah to pray firſtfirst that there might be no rainerain, and IamJam. 5. 17. then againeagain that there might be rainerain? yetYet is this propounded as a generallgeneral patternepattern to mouemove vsus to pray for things lawfulllawful.

Now in laying downedown this dutieduty I added the clauſeclause and caueatcaveat of iuſtjust occaſionoccasion, to meet both with ſuchsuch as vponupon diſcontentdiscontent, or ſuperſtitionsuperstition, leaueleave the land where the true GoſpellGospel is maintained, and preached, and goego into idolatrous places: and alſoalso with ſuchsuch wandringwandering giddy heads as only to ſatisfiesatisfy their owneown humour, and to ſeesee faſhionsfashions, as we ſpeakespeak, can neuernever reſtrest in a place, but are continually remouingremoving from countreycountry to countreycountry, and from place to place: I thinkethink (to vſeuse the words of the ApoſtleApostle) a wife is not vnderunder bondage in ſuchsuch caſeſcases. 1 Cor. 7. 15.

But if a man be ſentsent of an ambaſſageambassage by his Prince, or countreycountry: or if a Preacher or ProfeſſorProfessor be called into another countreycountry, as Bucer and Peter Martyr were into England in King Edwards daiesdays (which to this day is vſuallusual in other countries) or if a man be adiudgedadjudged vntounto long impriſonmentimprisonment, and
vponupon theſethese and other like occaſionsoccasions ſhallshall require his wife to be with him, ſheshe ought in dutieduty to yeeldyield vntounto his demand.

Contrary is the mindemind and practiſepractise of many wiueswives, who Contrary, when a wife makes her huſbandhusband dwell where ſheshe will. being affected and addicted to one place more then another, as to the place where they were bred and brought vpup, where their greateſtgreatest, beſtbest, and moſtmost friends dwell, and where they hauehave good acquaintance, refuſerefuse to goego and dwell where their husbands calling lieth, though he require, and deſiredesire them neuernever ſoso much. Thus many husbands are forced to their great dammagedamage for peace ſakesake to yeeldyield vntounto their wiueswives, and ſoso either to relinquiſhrelinquish their calling, or to hauehave two houſeshouses; whence it followeth, that ſometimessometimes they muſtmust neglect their ſeruantsservants and calling, and ſometimessometimes be abſentabsent from their wiueswives, if not from their children alſoalso. Some wiueswives pretend that they cannot endure the ſmoakesmoke of the citiecity, other that they cannot endure the aireair of the countriecountry: whereas indeed their owneown humour and conceit ſtuffesstuffs them more then either citiecity ſmoakesmoke or countriecountry aireair. I cannot call ſuchsuch the daughters of Sarah herein: 1 Pet. 3. 5, 6. they are not like thoſethose forenamed holy women that truſtedtrusted in God, and were ſubiectsubject to their husbands, but rather like to that light houſewifehousewife of the LeuiteLevite, who would not dwell in her huſbandshusbands IudgJudg. 19. 2. houſehouse at mount Ephraim, but at her fathers houſehouse in Beth-lehem IudahJudah. Such wiueswives as I ſpeakespeak of, in matrimoniallmatrimonial chaſtitiechastity may be more honeſthonest, but in wiuelikewivelike ſubiectionsubjection are little more dutifulldutiful. div.head: §. 45. Of a wiueswives Treat. 4. §. 29. readineſſereadiness to come to her husband when he requires it.
div.p: Another particular inſtanceinstance of a wiueswives readineſſereadiness to yeeldyield vntounto her husbands commandementcommandment is, to come to her husband when her husband requireth it, either by calling her, or ſendingsending for her. The forenamed Gen. 31. 4. wiueswives of IaakobJacob being ſentsent for to their husband in the field where he was, made no excuſeexcuse, but came preſentlypresently. div.head: §. 47. Of a wiueswives Treat. 4. §. 34, 35. meekemeek taking a reproofereproof.
div.p:
The husband hauinghaving authoritieauthority ouerover his wife, by vertuevirtue thereof he hath power, yea it is his dutieduty as there is needfullneedful
cauſecause to rebuke her: By iuſtjust conſequenceconsequence therefore it followeth, A wiueswives actiueactive obedience to her husbands reproofereproof. The beſtbest trialltrial of obedience. that it is her dutieduty to yeeldyield obedience thereunto. Which ought the rather to be done becauſebecause the chiefeſtchiefest trialltrial of ſoundsound obedience lieth herein. For nothing goeth ſoso much againſtagainst ones ſtomachstomach as reproofereproof: ſheshe that yeeldsyields when ſheshe is rebuked, will much more when ſheshe is intreatedentreated. This point of obedience is manifeſtedmanifested two waiesways.
1. By meekneſſemeekness in taking a reproofereproof.

2. By endeuourendeavour to redreſſeredress what is iuſtlyjustly reprouedreproved. The very point of obedience eſpeciallyespecially conſiſtethconsisteth in this latter: the former is as a good preparatiuepreparative thereunto, without which it will hardly be done, at leaſtleast not well done.

MeekneſſeMeekness in this caſecase is one of the moſtmost principallprincipal fruits of 1. She muſtmust meekly take reproofereproof. 1 Pet. 3. 4. Gen. 30. 1. that meekemeek and quiet ſpiritspirit which S. Peter commendeth vntounto wiueswives. HowſoeuerHowsoever Rachel iuſtlyjustly deſerueddeserved blame for commingcoming in a fuming chafe, and with an imperious command to her husband, yet in that ſheshe meekly tooketook his ſharpesharpsharpe reproofereproof (for ſheshe replied not againſtagainst it, but meekly gauegave a direction for the better accompliſhmentaccomplishment of her deſiredesire) her example is commendable: commendable I ſaysay, not in the matter of her direction, but in her patient bearing of reproofereproof.

Much wiſdomewisdom may be learned hereby: for when any WiſdomeWisdom learned. meekly take a reproofereproof, thereby they ſuppreſſesuppress their paſſionpassion, and keepekeep it from riſingrising as a cloud before their vnderſtandingunderstanding and darkningdarkening it, and ſoso may they better iudgejudge of the matter reprouedreproved whether it be iuſtjust or no: and whether it need redreſſeredress or no: whereof they who are impatient of reproofereproof, and fret and fume againſtagainst it, cannot ſoso well iudgejudge. The virgin Mary made good vſeuse of ChriſtsChrists reprouingreproving her, and thereby Joh. 2. 4, 5. learned and taught a good point of wiſdomewisdom, namely ſoso to referrerefer our affairesaffairs to ChriſtChrist as we expect his pleaſurepleasure; and not preſcribeprescribe time, meanesmeans, manner, or any other like circumſtancescircumstances vntounto him.

div.p: 2. AnſwAnsw. Yet may not meekneſſemeekness be forgotten. In ſuchsuch a caſecase a wife may make a iuſtjust apologieapology to cleareclear her owneown innocencieinnocency, and manifeſtmanifest her husbands error: but if he refuſerefuse to hearehear her, or will not beleeuebelieve her, then (as S. The two reaſonsreasons which there he rendrethrendereth in that other caſecase may not vnfitlyunfitly be applied to this.
