div.head: §. 48. Of a wiueswives Treat. 4. §. 35. readineſſereadiness to redreſſeredress what her husband iuſtlyjustly reprouethreproveth in her.
div.p: A further degree of obedience in bearing reproofereproof is, that 22. She muſtmust redreſſeredress what is iuſtlyjustly reprouedreproved. a wife readily redreſſeredress what is iuſtlyjustly reprouedreproved by her husband: I ſaysay iuſtlyjustly, becauſebecause where no fault is, there needs no amendment: patience may be needfullneedful (as was before ſhewedshowed) but no repentance of that which is not amiſſeamiss. But where any thing is amiſſeamiss, there muſtmust be a redreſſeredress. Rachel did amiſſeamiss in Gen. 31. 19. bringing Idols into her husbands houſehouse: her husband in & 35. 2, 4. bidding her among others to put away their ſtrangestrange gods, reprouedreproved them all. Whereupon ſheshe with all the reſtrest gauegave to him all their ſtrangestrange gods. This was a good redreſſeredress.

A reproofereproof may be iuſtlyjustly giuengiven either for a good dutieduty omitted; or for an euillevil thing committed: and accordingly muſtmust the redreſſeredress or amendment be. A dutieduty formerly omitted muſtmust after the reproofereproof be more carefully obſeruedobserved and performed, if it be a continuallcontinual dutieduty, and may be againeagain performed: otherwiſeotherwise the redreſſeredress is a teſtificationtestification of true ſorrowsorrow for that fault. When an euillevil is committed, if any meanesmeans can be vſedused to make vpup the hurt, and redreſſeredress the miſchiefemischief that followed thereupon, it muſtmust be done: if not, ſorrowsorrow as before, muſtmust be teſtifiedtestified, and care taken that the ſamesame, or the like be not committed againeagain.

As a good conſcienceconscience requireth as much of all ChriſtiansChristians by whomſoeuerwhomsoever they be reprouedreproved, ſoso the reſpectrespect which a wife
oweth to an husband doth after an eſpeciallespecial manner require it. OtherwiſeOtherwise her fault is doubled, 1. byBy continuance in her ſinsin;
2. byBy diſobediencedisobedience to her husband.

Contrary is their ſpiritspirit who for reproofereproof waxewax the worſeworse: Contrary, to be worſeworse for reprouingreproving. ProuProv. 9. 8. being like thoſethose ſcornersscorners (of whom SalomonSolomon ſpeakethspeaketh) that hate thoſethose that reprouereprove them. It is the ſpeechspeech of ſomesome wiueswives, that if their husbands would let them alone they would doedo the better: but vponupon rebuke they will neuernever amend: the more their husbands findefind fault, the more will they goego on, in doing what they doedo. What other iudgementjudgment can be giuengiven of ſuchsuch, then that which the wiſewise man giuethgiveth, there is more hope
ProuProv. 26. 12. of a foolefool then of them.

div.head: §. 49. Of a wiueswives Treat. 4. §. 5050. contentment with her husbands preſentpresent eſtateestate. Of ſubmiſſionsubmission hitherto.
div.p:
Contentment is alſoalso a part of obedience: it hath reſpectrespect to a mans outward eſtateestate and abilitieability, in and with which a wife muſtmust reſtrest ſatisfiedsatisfied and contented, whether it be high or low, great or meanemean, wealthy or needy, aboueabove, equallequal, or vnderunder that eſtateestate wherein ſheshe was before mariagemarriage: yea though a man hauehave beenebeen ſometimessometimes great in eſtateestate, yet, if he decay therein, and be brought to a meanemean eſtateestate, ſheshe ought to reſtrest content. Thus much IobJob implieth in his repliereply to his wife, ſayingsaying, ſhallshall we receiuereceive
Job 2. 10. expounded. good at the hand of God, and not receiuereceive euillevil? The euillevil he ſpeakethspeaketh of was the loſſeloss of his goods, ſeruantsservants, and children, together with other miſeriesmiseries that Satan through Gods permiſſionpermission inflicted vponupon him: the receiuingreceiving of euillevil which he ſpeakethspeaketh of was a reſtingresting content with it, and a patient bearing of it. EuillEvil may be laid on any, and ſoso they forced to bearebear it: but they only receiuereceive it, who are content with it. Now in that he vſethuseth the plurallplural number (WE) and ſpeakingspeaking to his wife ſaithsaith (ſhallshall not we receiuereceive euillevil) he ſhewethshoweth that his wife ought as well as he to hauehave reſtrest contented in that poorepoor and miſerablemiserable eſtateestate: For

1. Man and wife being one fleſhflesh, by vertuevirtue of their matrimoniallmatrimonial vnionunion, both his aduancementadvancement, and alſoalso his abaſementabasement is hers: as ſheshe riſethriseth with him, ſoso ſheshe falleth with him. Wherefore as ſheshe is willing to be aduancedadvanced with him, ſoso ſheshe muſtmust be content to be abaſedabased with him.

2. If at the time of mariagemarriage her husband was of meaner eſtateestate
then ſheshe, ſheshe voluntarily put her ſelfeself into that meanemean eſtateestate: for a wife taketh her husband (as he her) for better for worſeworse, for richer for poorer. And ſhallshall ſheshe not be content with her own act? If after mariagemarriage his eſtateestate decay, and wax meaner then it was, ſheshe is to be perſwadedpersuaded that by God it was ſoso ordered, and that God aimed at her humiliation as well as his: and thereupon ſheshe ought in her dutifulldutiful ſubmiſſionsubmission to Gods ouerover-ruling prouidenceprovidence to be patient and content: this IobJob implieth vnderunder this phraſephrase, ſhallshall we not receiuereceive euillevil at the hand of God? and vnderunder this, The Lord taketh away.

3. A wiueswives contentment is a great eaſeease to her husband lying vnderunder a croſſecross: and it maketh the burden ſeemeseem much lighter then otherwiſeotherwise it would, if at leaſtleast he be a kindekind husband, and affected with his wiueswives paſſionpassion, as he ought to be. For a louingloving husband in eueryevery diſtreſſedistress is more perplexed for his wife, then for himſelfehimself.

div.head: §. 50. Of wiueswives diſcontentdiscontent at their husbands eſtateestate.
div.p: Contrary is the impatiencieimpatiency, and diſcontentdiscontent of wiueswives at DiſcontentDiscontent manifeſtedmanifested. the meanneſſemeanness, and (as they thinkethink) baſeneſſebaseness of their husbands eſtateestate: which is many waiesways manifeſtedmanifested.

1. Some when they are mariedmarried finding their husbands eſtateestate 1. By repenting their mariagemarriage. weaker then they imagined, repent their mariagemarriage, and ſtickestick not to tell their husbands, that if they had before knowneknown them to be no better men then they findefind them to be, they ſhouldshould hauehave beenebeen no husbands for them. Wherein firſtfirst they bewray their fooliſhfoolish indiſcretionindiscretion by ſayingsaying, when it is too late, if I had
Non eſtest ſapientissapientis dicere non putâram. Cic. Offic. lib. 1. thought this; and withallwithal they manifeſtmanifest their own raſhneſſerashness and vnaduiſedneſſeunadvisednessunaduisedness, in that they gauegave their hands and plighted their troth to thoſethose whom they knew not. If they ſaysay, they were deceiueddeceived by their friends whom they put in truſttrust, I anſweranswer that mariagemarriage is too weightieweighty a matter to be wholly referred ouerover to the truſttrust of friends: eueryevery one that yeeldethyieldeth to be mariedmarried, ought welwell to know the party vntounto whom in this caſecase they yeeldyield: and aboueabove all they ought to ſeekeseek direction, helpehelp, and bleſſingblessing from God. If notwithſtandingnotwithstanding all the meanesmeans which poſſiblypossibly they could vſeuse, they be deceiueddeceived, they are to lookelook vntounto God, and to behold his prouidenceprovidence therein: and duly to weigh whether the Lord hauehave croſſedcrossed their deſiredesire for their
humiliation, or for trialltrial of their patience, wiſdomewisdom and other like graces, or elſeelse to weinewean them from ſomesome vainevain and worldly delights, whereunto they were too much addicted.

2. Others obſeruingobserving their husbands eſtateestate to be decaieddecayed 2. By impatient cariagecarriage. and waſtedwasted, neuernever ſearchsearch after the occaſionoccasion, but lay all the blame vponupon their husbands, and with their diſcontenteddiscontented lookeslooks, paſſionatepassionate words, and impatient cariagecarriage, ſoso vex their hearts, as they make the croſſecross much more heauyheavy then otherwiſeotherwise it could be. Though the eſtateestate ſhouldshould be ouerthrowneoverthrown by the vnthriftineſſeunthriftiness of an husband, yet ought a wife to lookelook vntounto Gods prouidenceprovidence therein, as was noted before.

3. Others ſcorningscorning to ſtoopestoop, and to come downedown to their 3. By refuſingrefusing to ſtoopestoop. husbands preſentpresent condition, through their pride and vainegloryvainglory are a great means to make his eſtateestate much the worſeworse: for they, ſoso long as by any meanesmeans they can get it, will not abate any thing of their brauebrave apparellapparel, dainty cheerecheer, rich furniture, and other like things, which are cauſescauses of great expenceexpense to their husbands: hereby alſoalso it commethcometh oft to paſſepass that huſbandshusbands are thought to be wealthier then indeed they are, and ſoso greater taxations and charges then they can bearebear are laid vponupon them for King, CountreyCountry, Church, PoorePoor, and the like.

4. Others, through diſcontentdiscontent lie long lazing in their beds, 4. By refuſingrefusing to helpehelp. or idly ſitsit ſtillstill when they are vpup, and will not take any whit the more painespains to raiſeraise vpup and increaſeincrease their husbands eſtateestate: whereby God is prouokedprovoked more and more to weaken their eſtatesestates, that ſoso he may the more puniſhpunish ſuchsuch pride and lazineſſelaziness in wiueswives.

div.head: §. 51. Of Treat. 4. §. 26. caſescases wherein a wife ought not to forbeareforbear what her husband forbiddeth.
div.p: So much of the diſtinctdistinct branches of a wiueswives ſubiectionsubjection. The limitation and manner of performing it next followeth.

To know the limitation of a wiueswives obedience, and the manner how ſheshe ought to yeeldyield ſubiectionsubjection vntounto her husband, two things muſtmust be conſideredconsidered:
1. The place of an husband.
2. The place of a wife.

The husbands place is noted in this phraſephrase, as to the Lord:
Eph. 5. 22. whereby is ſhewedshowed that the husband eueneven by vertuevirtue of his
place is to his wife in ChriſtsChrists ſteadstead: which is further more plainly laid downedown in theſethese words following, the husband is
VerſVers. 23. the head of the wife, as ChriſtChrist is the head of the Church.

The wiueswives place is intimated in theſethese words, as the Church
VerſVers. 24. is ſubiectsubject vntounto ChriſtChrist, ſoso let wiueswives be to their owneown husbands: whereby it is cleereclear that the obedience which a wife performeth to her husband muſtmust be ſuchsuch an obedience as the Church performeth to ChriſtChrist.
From the place of an husband, I gather this generallgeneral ground concerning a wiueswives ſubiectionsubjection, that
SubiectionSubjection muſtmust be yeeldedyielded to the husband as to ChriſtChrist, whence will follow two concluſionsconclusions, one negatiuenegative, which is this,

p.hi: The wife muſtmust yeeldyield no other ſubiectionsubjection to her husband then what may ſtandstand with her ſubiectionsubjection to ChriſtChrist.

div.p: The other affirmatiueaffirmative, which is this,

p.hi: The wife muſtmust ſubiectsubject her ſelfeself to her husband in that manner that ſheshe would or ſhouldshould ſubiectsubject her ſelfeself to ChriſtChrist.

div.p: The former is a neceſſarynecessary condition required of all inferioursinferiors in their ſubiectionsubjection, and obedience (as I ſhewedshowed Treat. 1. §. 6. before) much more in a wiueswives ſubiectionsubjection to her husband, becauſebecause there is of all vnequalsunequals See §. 4. of this Treat. the leaſtleast diſparitydisparity betwixt husbands and wiueswives.
Hence for our preſentpresent purpoſepurpose, I gather theſethese two other more particular concluſionsconclusions, The firſtfirst whereof is this,

1. If God expreſlyexpressly command the wife any duty, and her huſbandhusband will not by any meanesmeans giuegive conſentconsent that ſheshe ſhallshall doedo it, but forbid her, ſheshe may and ought to doedo it without, or againſtagainst his conſentconsent.
Two cautions are warily to be obſeruedobserved about this concluſionconclusion: 2. Cautions for limiting a wiueswives perſiſtingpersisting to doedo that which her husband forbids.

The ſecondsecond caution is that ſheshe vſeuse all good meanesmeans ſheshe can to gainegain her husbands conſentconsent, before ſheshe doedo, eueneven that which is commanded, againſtagainst his conſentconsent. Thus ſhallshall ſheshe teſtifietestify her ſubiectionsubjection both to God and her husband. To God, in that nothing can keepekeep her from doing his expreſſeexpress commandementcommandment: ſheshe will rather offend her husband then God, when one of them muſtmust needs be offended. To her husband, in that ſheshe putteth it to the vttermoſtuttermost puſhpush, and vſethuseth all the meanesmeans ſheshe can to auoidavoid his offence, in ſoso much as he himſelfehimself might ſeesee (if the god of this world blinded not his eieseyes) that the offence is no way giuengiven on her part, but meerelymerely taken on his.

For proofeproof of this, it is without all contradiction true, that the wife is not bound to greater ſubiectionsubjection vntounto her huſbandhusband then the ſubiectsubject is vntounto the magiſtratemagistrate: but a ſubiectsubject ought not to forbeareforbear a bounden duty commanded of God, becauſebecause his gouernourgovernor forbids him. InſtanceInstance the example of Daniel,
Dan. 6. 7, &etcc. who daily made his praiersprayers to God, though the King had made a ſolemnesolemn decree that none ſhouldshould askeask any petition of God or man within thirty daiesdays but of the king. InſtanceInstance alſoalso the ApoſtlesApostles, Act. 4. 18, &etcc. who preached the GoſpelGospel, thoghthough they were expreſlyexpressly forbiddēforbidden.

Though the Scripture be plentifullplentiful in affording examples of wiueswives ſubiectionsubjection, yet it is very ſparingsparing in recording examples of thoſethose who in ſuchsuch warrantable caſescases refuſedrefused to be ſubiectsubject, leſtlest wiueswives from thence ſhouldshould take too great liberty.

Some are recorded, but ſuchsuch as are either extraordinary, or not eueryevery way inſtifiablejustifiableinstifiable. Abigails example was extraordinary, 1 Sam. 25. 18. and therforetherefore not imitable but in ſuchsuch like extraordinary caſescases.

The example of Rebekah, which may ſeemeseem ſomewhatsomewhat more Gen. 27. 6. pertinent, is not eueryevery way to be iuſtifiedjustified. For though the thing which ſheshe intended were for the ſubſtancesubstance of it very good, and ought to hauehave beenebeen done, namely the bleſſingblessing of IaakobJacob, (for God foreſhewedforeshowed that the bleſſingblessing appertained to IaakobJacob, in that he ſaidsaid, The elder ſhallshall ſerueserve the younger) yet Gen. 25. 23. becauſebecause ſheshe put not her husband in mindemind of Gods word, nor laboured to perſwadepersuade him to fulfill the ſamesame, but went about the matter deceitfully, ſheshe cannot therein be iuſtifiedjustified. But in
the generallgeneral this example ſhewethshoweth that Gods word muſtmust be yeeldedyielded vntounto rather then an husbands will.

For better application of this point I will lay downedown ſomesome particular inſtancesinstances agreeable to Gods word. SuppoſeSuppose a wife well inſtructedinstructed in the true religion be mariedmarried to an idolatrous or profane husband, and he without any iuſtjust cauſecause forbid her to goego to the Church, eſpeciallyespecially on the Lords daiesdays, to pray in EngliſhEnglish, to read the word, to teach her children the principles of religion, to reſtorerestore that which ſheshe hath vniuſtlyunjustly and fraudulently gotten, with the like, ſheshe may, and muſtmust doedo them notwithſtandingnotwithstanding.

div.head: ObiectObject. Why may not giuinggiving of almesalms be reckoned among theſethese?
div.p: AnſwAnsw. 1. BecauſeBecause the husband hath a greater power ouerover the goods, then ouerover theſethese things.

2. BecauſeBecause almesalms-giuinggiving is not ſimplysimply commanded to all, but to ſuchsuch as hauehave wherewithallwherewithal to giuegive: but theſethese things are ſimplysimply commanded to all.

div.head: §. 52. Of caſescases wherein a wife ought to forbeareforbear what her husband requireth.
div.p: The other particular concluſionconclusion is this, that

p.hi: If an husband require his wife to doedo that which God hath forbidden ſheshe ought not to doedo it.

div.p: Two cautions like the former are likewiſelikewise to be obſeruedobserved 2. Cautions for limiting a wiueswives refuſingrefusing to doedo that which her husband commands. about this point.
FirſtFirst, that ſheshe be ſuresure (being truly informed by Gods word) that that which ſheshe refuſethrefuseth to doedo at her husbands command, is forbidden by God.

Secondly, that ſheshe firſtfirst labour with all meekeneſſemeekness and by all good meanesmeans that ſheshe can to diſſwadedissuadedisswade her husband from vrgingurging and preſſingpressing that vponupon her, which with a good conſcienceconscience ſheshe cannot doedo.

A like proofeproof may be brought for this as was for the former: for we know that a wife is not bound vntounto greater ſubiectionsubjection to her husband then a ſonneson is vntounto a father: but a ſonneson may in the caſecase propounded forbeareforbear to doedo that which his father requireth and commandeth him to doedo: inſtanceinstance the approuedapproved example of IonathanJonathan, who refuſedrefused to bring DauidDavid 1 Sam. 20. 31.
vntounto Saul to be ſlaineslain, though his father commanded him ſoso to doedo. I might alſoalso inſtanceinstance the ſamesame in Sauls ſubiectssubjects and 1 Sam. 22. 17. ſeruantsservants, who refuſedrefused to ſlayslay the PrieſtsPriests of the Lord at his command. Though an husband be not reckoned in particular among thoſethose to whom we are forbidden to hearken if they Deut. 13. 6. inticeentice vsus to idolatry, yet by the rule of relation he is implied, and by iuſtjust conſequenceconsequence gathered from this clauſeclause, thy friend which is as thine owneown ſoulesoul; for who ſoso dearedear as an husband?

To exemplifieexemplify this in ſomesome particulars as I did the former, If an husband ſhallshall command his wife to goego to MaſſeMass, to a ſtagestage play, to play at dice, to proſtituteprostitute her body to vncleannesuncleanness, to goego gariſhlygarishly and whoriſhlywhorishly attired, to ſellsell by ſcantscant weights, ſhortshort meaſuresmeasures, or the like, ſheshe ought not to doedo ſoso.

div.head: §. 53. Of wiueswives faults in ſhewingshowing more reſpectrespect to their huſbandshusbands then to God.
div.p: Contrary to this limitation is on the one ſideside a fawning flattering diſpoſitiondisposition of ſuchsuch wiueswives as ſeekeseek to pleaſeplease their husbands, ſoso as they care not to diſpleaſedisplease God, (IezabelJezebel was ſuchsuch an one; to pleaſeplease her husband moſtmost lewdly ſheshe did 1 Ki. 21. 7. &etcc. practiſepractise Naboths death) and on the other ſideside a fainting timorous heart which maketh them fearefear their husbands more then they fearefear God. Good Sarah, that worthy preſidentprecedentpresident of Gen. 12. 13. &etcc. good wiueswives in other things, ſomewhatsomewhat failed herein. Did wiueswives duly conſiderconsider, and alwaiesalways remember that they hauehave an husband (namely ChriſtChrist) in heauenheaven, as well as on earth, and that there is greater difference betwixt that and this husband, then betwixt heauenheaven and earth, and that both in giuinggiving reward, and taking reuengerevenge, there is no compariſoncomparison betwixt them, their care of pleaſingpleasing, or their fearefear of offending their husband in heauenheaven would be much more then of pleaſingpleasing, or offending their husband on earth: if any thing were commanded or forbidden them by their husbands on earth againſtagainst ChriſtChrist, they would ſaysay, If I doedo this, or forbeareforbear that, I ſhouldshould workework falſhoodfalsehoodfalshood againſtagainst mine owneown ſoulesoul; for nothing can be hid from mine husband in heauenheaven: yea I ſhouldshould herein obey Satan, rather then God.

div.head: §. 54. Of the manner of a wiueswives ſubiectionsubjection to her husband.
div.p:
The ſecondsecond generallgeneral concluſionconclusion concerning the manner of a
wiueswives ſubiectionsubjection, which was gathered from the place of an husband, was this, that

The wife muſtmust ſubiectsubject her ſelfeself to her husband in that manner, that ſheshe would or ſhouldshould ſubiectsubject her ſelfeself to ChriſtChrist. The particle As in this clauſeclause (as vntounto the Lord) importeth ſoso much.

This verievery concluſionconclusion is alſoalso inferred out of the place of a wife: In the ſamesame place that the Church is to ChriſtChrist, a wife is to an husband: therefore ſuchsuch ſubiectionsubjection as the Church yeeldethyieldeth to ChriſtChrist, muſtmust a wife yeeldyield to her husband; which the verievery words of the ApoſtleApostle doedo expreſlyexpressly affirmeaffirm. Now we EpheſEphes. 5. 24. know that euerieevery ChriſtianChristian wife in her particular ought to yeeldyield that obedience to ChriſtChrist which the Church in generallgeneral doth: therefore alſoalso ſheshe muſtmust yeeldyield ſuchsuch ſubiectionsubjection to her huſbandhusband as ſheshe ſhouldshould to ChriſtChrist.

QueſtQuest. See §. 5. of this TreatiſeTreatise. What if an husband be an enemieenemy of ChriſtChrist? muſtMust ſuchsuch ſubiectionsubjection be yeeldedyielded to an enemieenemy of ChriſtChrist as to ChriſtChrist himſelfehimself?

AnſwAnsw. Yea: becauſebecause in his office he is in ChriſtsChrists ſteadstead, though in his heart an enemieenemy. In this caſecase will the wiſdomewisdom, patience, and obedience of a wife be beſtbest tried. It is noted of the Church, that ſheshe is a Lilly among thornesthorns. She remaineth Cant. 2. 2. Lilly-like, white, ſoftsoft, pleaſantpleasant, amiable, though ſheshe be ioynedjoined with thornesthorns, which are ſcraggiescraggy, prickly, ſharpesharpsharpe: ſoso a wife muſtmust be mildemild, meekemeek, gentle, obedient, though ſheshe be matched with a crooked, peruerſeperverse, profane, wicked husband: thus ſhallshall her vertuevirtue and grace ſhineshine forth the more clearelyclearly, eueneven as the ſtarsstars ſhineshine forth moſtmost brightly in the darkeſtdarkest night. Among wiueswives Abigail deſeruethdeservethdeserueth great praiſepraise, that forgot not her dutieduty, though ſheshe were mariedmarried to a churliſhchurlish, couetouscovetous, drunken ſotsot, a verievery Nabal in name and deed. As for thoſethose who take occaſionoccasion from the wickedneſſewickedness of their husbands to neglect their dutieduty, they addeadd to their croſſecross a curſecurse: for a croſſecross it is to hauehave a bad husband, but to be a bad wife is a ſinnesin, which pulleth downedown a curſecurse. Let wiueswives therefore remoueremove their eyes from the diſpoſitiondisposition of their husbands perſonperson, to the condition of his place: and by vertuevirtue thereof, ſeeingseeing he beareth ChriſtsChrists image, be ſubiectsubject to him as vntounto ChriſtChrist.

This generallgeneral concluſionconclusion might be applied to the matter of
ſubiectionsubjection as well as to the manner, for the Church acknowledgeth ChriſtChrist her ſuperioursuperior, feareth him inwardly, reuerencethreverenceth him outwardly, obeyeth him alſoalso both by forbearing to doedo what he forbiddeth, and alſoalso by doing what he commandeth, which points hauinghaving beenebeen before diſtinctlydistinctly and largely handled and applied to wiueswives, I will not repeat them againeagain. Wherefore now to inſiſtinsist in the manner only, there are fourefour FoureFour graces needfullneedful to ſeaſonseason a wiueswives ſubiectionsubjection. vertuesvirtues which are eſpeciallyespecially needfullneedful hereunto, whereby the Church ſeaſonethseasoneth her ſubiectionsubjection to ChriſtChrist, and wiueswives alſoalso may and muſtmust ſeaſonseason their ſubiectionsubjection to their husbands.
TheſeThese are the fourefour,
1. HumilitieHumility, 2. SinceritieSincerity, 3. CheerefulneſſeCheerfulness, 4. ConſtancieConstancy.

div.head: §. 55. Of wiueswives TreatTreat. 4. §. 15. humilitiehumility in eueryevery duty.
div.p: Humility is that grace that keepeskeeps one from thinking highly of himſelfehimself aboueabove that which is meet: and in regard of that meanemean conceit which he hath of himſelfehimself maketh him thinkethink reuerendlyreverendly, and highly of others: ſoso as if humility be placed in a wiueswives heart, it will make her thinkethink better of her husband then of her ſelfeself, and ſoso make her the more willing to yeeldyield all ſubiectionsubjection vntounto him. The ApoſtleApostle requireth it of all Phil. 2. 3. EpheſEphes. 4. 2. ChriſtiansChristians as a generallgeneral ſawcesauce to ſeaſonseason all other duties: but after a peculiar manermanner is it needfullneedful for inferioursinferiors: moſtmost of all for wiueswives, becauſebecause there are See before §. 4. many prerogatiuesprerogatives appertaining to their place, which may ſoonesoon make them thinkethink they ought not to be ſubiectsubject, vnleſſeunless they be humbly minded. That the Church doth herewith ſeaſonseason her ſubiectionsubjection, is cleareclear by the bookebook of Canticles, where oft ſheshe acknowledgeth her owneown meanneſſemeanness, and the excellency of her ſpouſespouse.

p.hi: Therefore as the Church is humbly ſubiectsubject to ChriſtChrist, ſoso let wiueswives be to their husbands.

div.head: §. 56. Of wiueswives pride.
div.p:
Contrary is pride, which puffeth vpup wiueswives, & maketh them thinkethink there is no reaſonreason they ſhouldshould be ſubiectsubject to husbands, they can rule themſeluesthemselves well enough, yea and rule their huſbandshusbands too, as well as their husbands rule them. No more peſtilentpestilent vice for an inferiourinferior, then this: it is the cauſecause of all rebellion, diſobediencedisobedience, & diſloyaltydisloyalty: only by pride, commethcometh contention.
Pro. 13. 10.

div.head: §. 57. Of WiuesWives Treat. 4. §. 63. ſinceritiesincerity in eueryevery dutieduty.
div.p: II. Sincerity is that grace that maketh one to be within eueneven in truth, what without he appeareth to be in ſhewshow. This is that EpheſEphes. 6. 5. SingleneſſeSingleness of heart which is expreſlyexpressly required of ſeruantsservants, and may be applied to wiueswives, for indeed it appertaineth to all ſortssorts. BecauſeBecause it is only diſcerneddiscerned by the Lord, who is the Acts 1. 24. ſearchersearcher of all hearts, it will mouemove a wife to hauehave an eye to him in all ſheshe doth, and to endeuourendeavour to approueapprove her ſelfeself to him aboueabove all: therefore vprightneſſeuprightness and walking before God are oft ioynedjoined together: he that is vprightupright will aſſuredlyassuredly walkewalk before God, that is, endeuourendeavour to approueapprove himſelfehimself to God, as Gen. 6. 9. Noah did, and as & 17. 1. God commanded Abraham to doedo.

Though there were no other motiuemotive in the world to mouemove her to ſubiectionsubjection, yet for conſcienceconscience ſakesake to ChriſtChrist ſheshe ſhouldshould yeeldyield it. 1 Pet. 3. 5. S. Peter teſtifiethtestifieth of holy women, that they truſtedtrusted in God and were ſubiectsubject to their husbands: implying thereby, that their conſcienceconscience to God made them be ſubiectsubject to their huſbandshusbands. Was not Sarahs ſubiectionsubjection ſeaſonedseasoned with ſinceritiesincerity, when Gen. 18. 12. within her ſelfeself, in her heart ſheshe called her husband Lord?
Great reaſonreason there is that wiueswives ſhouldshould in ſinceritysincerity ſubiectsubject ReaſonsReasons for ſinceritysincerity. themſeluesthemselves: for

1. In their ſubiectionsubjection eueneven to their husbands they hauehave to 11. BecauſeBecause wiueswives hauehave to doedo with ChriſtChrist. doedo with ChriſtChrist, in whoſewhose roomeroom their husbands ſtandstand: ſoso as, though their husbands who are but men, ſeesee only the face and outward behauiourbehaviour, yet ChriſtChrist ſeethseeth their heart and inward diſpoſitiondisposition: though their husbands ſeesee only the things which they doedo before their faces, and can hearehear only of ſuchsuch things as are done before others: yet ChriſtChrist ſeethseeth and knoweth the things that are done in the moſtmost ſecretsecret places that can be, when no creature beſidebeside themſeluesthemselves is priuieprivy thereunto: Now let it be granted that in their outward carriage they giuegive very good contentment vntounto their husbands, and pleaſeplease them eueryevery way, yet if ſinceritiesincerity hauehave beenebeen wanting, with what face can they appeareappear before ChriſtChrist? heHe will take another manner account of them: before ChriſtChrist all their outward complement will ſtandstand them in no ſteadstead at all.

2. Herein lyethlieth a mainemain difference betwixt true, ChriſtianChristian, 2. This maketh a difference betwixt holy women and others,. religious wiueswives, and meeremere naturallnatural women: theſethese may be ſubiectsubject on by-reſpectsrespects, as namely, that their husbands may the more louelove them, or liuelive the more quietly and peaceably with them, or that they may the more readily obtaineobtain what they deſiredesire at their husbands hands, or for fearefear of their husbands diſpleaſuredispleasure and wrath, knowing him to be an angry, furious man, ſoso as otherwiſeotherwise it might be worſeworse with them, they might want many needfullneedful things, or carry away many ſoresore blowesblows if they were not ſubiectsubject. But the other hauehave reſpectrespect to ChriſtsChrists ordinance, whereby their husbands are made their head, and to his word and will, whereby they are commanded ſubiectionsubjection. Thus 1 Pet. 3. 5. holy women ſubiectedsubjected themſeluesthemselves; they cannot be holy that doedo not thus ſubiectsubject themſeluesthemselves: for this is a ſweetsweet perfume that ſendethsendeth forth a good ſauoursavour into ChriſtsChrists noſtrilsnostrils, and maketh the things we doedo pleaſantpleasant and acceptable to him.
3. The benefit of this vertuevirtue being planted in a wiueswives heart 3. Great is the benefit hereof. is very great, and that both to her husband, and alſoalso to her ſelfeself.

To her husband, in that it will make her manifeſtmanifest her reſpectrespect of him before others, behindebehind his backeback, as well as before himſelfehimself in his preſencepresence: and alſoalso will make her faithfullfaithful to him, and carefullcareful to doedo his will whereſoeuerwheresoever he be, with her, or from her.

To her ſelfeself, in that it will miniſterminister inward ſweetsweet comfort vntounto her, though her husband ſhouldshould take no notice of her ſubiectionsubjection, or mifmis-interpret it, or ill requite it; for ſheshe might ſaysay as Hezekiah did, IſaIsa. 38. 3. Remember ô Lord how I hauehave walked before thee in truth, and with a perfect heart, and hauehave done that which is good in thy ſightsight.

That the Church doth ſeaſonseason all her ſubiectionsubjection with ſinceritiesincerity is cleareclear, in that ſheshe is ſaidsaid to be PſalPsal. 45. 13. all glorious within: (there is no glory within, without ſinceritiesincerity) and in that ſheshe is oft ſaidsaid Cant. 3. 1, 2. to ſeekeseek him whom her ſoulesoul louedloved: if her ſoulesoul louedloved him, in ſinceritiesincerity of heart ſheshe was ſubiectsubject to him: Therefore as the Church is ſincerelysincerely ſubiectsubject to ChriſtChrist, ſoso let wiueswives be to their huſbandshusbands.

div.head: §. 58. Of wiueswives complementallcomplemental ſubiectionsubjection.
div.p:
Contrary to ſinceritiesincerity is diſſimulationdissimulation, and meeremere outward, complementallcomplemental ſubiectionsubjection: when a wife doth eueneven deſpiſedespise her husband in her heart, as Michal did DauidDavid and yet carry a fairefair 2 Sam. 6. 16. Pro. 30. 20. face before him, as that adulterous woman, who eateth, and wipeth her mouth, and ſaithsaith I hauehave not committed iniquitieiniquity. SalomonSolomon maketh it a note of a lewd wife to flatter with her words.
Pro. 2. 16. Though ſuchsuch a wife ſhouldshould performeperform all the duties named before, yet would thoſethose all be nothing to God, if they were done with a double heart, and not in ſingleneſſesingleness of heart. For as many outward imperfections are pardoned by God, where ſinceritiesincerity is, ſoso no outward actions are accepted of him though they ſeemeseem neuernever ſoso fairefair, where there is no ſinceritiesincerity.

div.head: §. 59. Of wiueswives Treat. 4. §. 65, 74. cheerefulneſſecheerfulness in eueryevery dutieduty.
div.p: III. CheerefulneſſeCheerfulness is more apparantapparent then ſinceritiesincerity, and maketh ſubiectionsubjection the more pleaſingpleasing not only to God, but alſoalso to man, who by the effects thereof may eaſilyeasily diſcernediscern it.

For God, as he doth himſelfehimself all things willingly and cheerefullycheerfully, ſoso he expecteth that his children ſhouldshould therein follow him, and thereby ſhewshow themſeluesthemselves his children. God louethloveth a 2 Cor. 9. 7. cheerefullcheerful giuergiver: not only a cheerefullcheerful giuergiver of almesalms, but of all dutieduty to God and man.

For men, it maketh them alſoalso much better accept any dutieduty when they obſerueobserve it to be done cheerefullycheerfully: this did eueneven rauiſhravish DauidDavid with ioyjoy, to ſeesee his people offer their gifts willingly 1 Chro. 29. 9. vntounto the Lord: when an husband ſeethseeth his wife willingly and cheerefullycheerfully performeperform her dutieduty, it cannot but raiſeraise vpup louelove in him. This cheerefulneſſecheerfulness is manifeſtedmanifested by a ready, quickequick, and ſpeedyspeedy performance of her duty. Sarahs readineſſereadiness to obey, Gen. 18. ſhewethshoweth that what ſheshe did, ſheshe did willingly.

That thus the Church ſubiectethsubjecteth her ſelfeself to ChriſtChrist is euidentevident by that which DauidDavid ſaithsaith, They ſhallshall be willing in the day
PſalPsal. 110. 3. of thy power. Therefore as the Church is cheerefullycheerfully ſubiectsubject vntounto ChriſtChrist, ſoso let wiueswives be to their husbands.

div.head: §. 60. Of wiueswives ſullensullen and forced obedience.
div.p:
Contrary to this cheerefulneſſecheerfulness is the ſullensullen diſpoſitiondisposition of ſomesome wiueswives, who will indeed be ſubiectsubject to their husbands, and obey, but with ſuchsuch a lowringlouring and ſowresoursowre countenance,
with ſuchsuch powtingpouting and muttering, as they grieuegrieve their huſbandshusbands more in the manner, then they can be pleaſedpleased with the thing it ſelfeself that they doedo: herein they ſhewshow themſeluesthemselves like to a curſtcurst cow, which hauinghaving giuengiven a fairefair ſoapesoap of milkemilk, caſtethcasteth all downedown with her heeleheel, and ſoso verifieverify the prouerbeproverb, AAs good neuernever a whit as neuernever the better. Such ſubiectionsubjection is in truth no ſubiectionsubjection, it can neither be acceptable to God, nor profitable to their husbands, nor comfortable to their owneown ſoulessouls.

div.head: §. 61. Of wiueswives Treat. 4. §. 72. conſtancyconstancy in doing their dutieduty.
div.p:
IIII. ConſtancyConstancy is a vertuevirtue which maketh all the reſtrest perfect, and ſettethsetteth the crownecrown vponupon them; without which they are all nothing. This is in thoſethose who after they hauehave begun well, continue to doedo well vntounto the end, and thereby reapereap the fruit of all. It hath reſpectrespect both to continuance without intermiſſionintermission, and alſoalso to perſeueranceperseverance without reuoltingrevolting, and giuinggiving cleaneclean ouerover. So as it is not enough to be ſubiectsubject by ſtartsstarts and fits: one while yeeldingyielding all good obedience, another while ſtoutstout and rebellious: neither is it ſufficientsufficient in former times to hauehave beenebeen a good wife, and after proueprove bad: but there muſtmust be daily proceeding and holding on from time to time, ſoso long as husband and wife liuelive together. This grace was in her of whom it is ſaidsaid, She will doedo him good, and not euillevil all the daiesdays of her life. Such were all the holy wiueswives commended in Scripture: among other particulars, mention is made of the wife of Phinehas, who on her death-bed ſhewedshowed the reuerendreverend 1 Sam. 4. 21. good reſpectrespect ſheshe bare to her husband, though he were a wicked and lewd man. This grace doth the Church addeadd to all her other vertuesvirtues, ſheshe in all parts of her ſubiectionsubjection remaineth conſtantconstant, & faithfullfaithful vntounto the death, whereby it commethcometh to paſſepass, that at length ſheshe receiuethreceiveth the reward of her holy obedience, which is full and perfect communion and fellowſhipfellowship with her ſpouſespouse ChriſtChrist IeſusJesus in heauenheaven. In regard of her vnmoueableunmoveable conſtancyconstancy it is ſaidsaid, that the gates of hell ſhallshall neuernever preuaileprevail againſtagainst
Matth. 16. 18. her. Therefore as the Church is conſtantlyconstantly ſubiectsubject vntounto ChriſtChrist, ſoso let wiueswives be to their husbands.

div.head: §. 62. Of wiueswives repenting their former goodneſſegoodness. Contrary, 1. IntermiſſionIntermission.
div.p:
Contrary to this ConſtancieConstancy is firſtfirst intermiſſionintermission of duty, a returning
to it, and a leauingleaving it off by turnesturns: like one that is ſickesick of an ague, ſometimessometimes well, ſometimessometimes ill, one while hot, another while cold. That ſometimessometimes ceaſingceasing taketh away all the vertuevirtue, grace and glory, from ſometimessometimes doing. BeſidesBesides, it is twenty to one that through the corruption of nature, that diuerſitiediversity and entercourſeintercourseentercourse of fits at length will ceaſecease, and end in the worſeworse. It is very likely that Michal was ſuchsuch an one: for one while ſheshe ſhewedshowed her ſelfeself ſoso full of reſpectrespect to DauidDavid, as 1 Sam. 19. 11, &etcc. for his ſakesake ſheshe incurred the King her fathers diſpleaſuredispleasure: another while in her heart ſheshe deſpiſeddespised him, and with her tongue 2 Sam. 6. 16, 20. taunted him.

Contrary alſoalso to the forenamed ConſtancyConstancy is ApoſtaſieApostasy, 2. ApoſtaſieApostasy. that is, a cleaneclean relinquiſhingrelinquishing of the former good courſecourse, as if a wife repented her of her former good beginning. Such an one is ſheshe that is ſaidsaid to for ſakesakeforsake the guide of her youth, and forget the
Pro. 2. 17. couenantcovenant of her God. For ought we readeread to the contrary, IobsJobs wife was ſuchsuch an one. And ſuchsuch are many who in their younger yearesyears, while their religious parents liuedlived (as IoaſhJoash while 2 Chron. 24. 2. old good IehoiadaJehoiada liuedlived) hauehave behauedbehaved themſeluesthemselves very well like good dutifulldutiful wiueswives, but being grown to elder yeeresyears, hauehave grownegrown alſoalso ſoso ſtoutstout and rebellious, as if they cleaneclean repented themſeluesthemselves of their former good beginning. This reuoltrevolt ariſethariseth ſometimessometimes from the euillevil counſellcounsel of wicked GoſſipsGossips, and ſometimessometimes from their owneown proud humour. I may ſaysay of theſethese wiueswives ſubiectionsubjection, as the Prophet ſaithsaith of the righteouſneſſerighteousness of reuoltersrevolters, Ezek. 18. 24. their ſubiectionsubjection ſhallshall not be remembredremembered, but in their rebellion they ſhallshall die. Therefore as the Church is ſubiectsubject to ChriſtChrist, let wiueswives be to their husbands.

div.head: §. 63. Of the Treat. 4. §. 26. extent of a wiueswives obedience.
div.p:
The extent of a wiueswives ſubiectionsubjection (which remaineth now to be handled) is ſetset downedown vnderunder theſethese generallgeneral termesterms (in eueryevery thing) which are not ſoso generally to be taken as if they admitted no reſtraintrestraint or limitation, for then would they contradict ſuchsuch cautions as theſethese, in the fearefear of the Lord, as to the Lord, in
Eph. 5. 21. & 22. Col. 3. 18. the Lord. For man is ſoso corrupt by nature, and of ſoso peruerſeperverse a diſpoſitiondisposition, that oft he willeth and commandeth that which is contrary to Gods will and commandementcommandment: which when he
doth, that ChriſtianChristian principle laid downedown as a ruled caſecase by the ApoſtleApostle muſtmust take place, we ought rather to obey God then men.
Acts 5. 29.

div.head: QueſtQuest. Why then is this extent laid downedown in ſuchsuch generallgeneral termesterms?
div.p: AnſwAnsw. 1. To teach wiueswives that it is not ſufficientsufficient for them to obey their husbands in ſomesome things, as they themſeluesthemselves thinkethink meet, but in all things whatſoeuerwhatsoever they be wherein the husband by vertuevirtue of his ſuperioritiesuperiority and authoritieauthority hath power to command his wife. Thus this generallgeneral extent excludeth not Gods will, but the wiueswives will. SheeShe may doedo nothing againſtagainst Gods will; but many things muſtmust ſheshe doedo againſtagainst her owneown will if her husband require her.

2. To ſhewshow that the husbands authoritieauthority and power is very large: it hath no reſtraintrestraint but Gods contrary command, whereof if a wife be not aſſuredassured, ſheshe muſtmust yeeldyield to her husbands will.

div.head: §. 64. Of a wiueswives Treat. 4. §. 28, 29. labouring to bring her iudgementjudgment to the bent of her husbands.
div.p: From that extent I gather theſethese two concluſionsconclusions:
1. A wife muſtmust labour to bring her iudgementjudgment and will to her husbands.
2. Though in her iudgementjudgment ſheshe cannot thinkethink that moſtmost meet which her husband requireth, yet ſheshe muſtmust yeeldyield to it in practiſepractise.

In the former of theſethese, I ſaysay not ſimplysimply that a wife is bound to bring her iudgementjudgment to the bent of her husbands; for he may be deceiueddeceived in his iudgementjudgment, and ſheshe may ſeesee his error, and then vnleſſeunless her vnderſtandingunderstanding ſhouldshould be blinded, ſheshe cannot conceiueconceive that to be true which he iudgethjudgeth ſoso: but I ſpeakespeak of endeuourendeavour (when ſheshe hath not ſuresure and vndeniableundeniable grounds to the contrary) to ſuſpectsuspect her iudgementjudgment when itsit's contrary to her husbands, and to thinkethink ſheshe may be in an error, and thereupon not be too peremptory and reſoluteresolute in contradicting her husbands opinion. This ſubmiſſionsubmission eueneven of her iudgementjudgment reſpectethrespecteth not only things neceſſarienecessary, for which her husband hath an expreſſeexpress determinate warrant out of the Scripture, but alſoalso things doubtfulldoubtful & indifferent: for eueneven ſoso farrefar doth this clauſeclause (in eueryevery thing) extend: and the ſubiectionsubjection of a wife reſpectethrespecteth not her practiſepractise only, but her iudgementjudgment and opinion alſoalso: which if ſheshe can bring to the lawfulneſſelawfulness and meetneſſemeetness of that which her husband requireth,
ſheshe will much more cheerefullycheerfully performeperform it. To this purpoſepurpose (as I take it) may be applied that exhortation of the ApoſtleApostle vntounto women, that they learnelearn in ſilencesilence with all ſubiectionsubjection: 1 Tim. 2. 11. which though it be principally meant of learning in the Church, yet it excludeth not her learning at home of her husband: for in the next words he addeth, I ſuffersuffer not a woman to vſurpeusurp authoritieauthority ouerover the man, but to be in ſilencesilence.

div.head: §. 65. Of wiueswives ouerweeningoverweening conceit of their owneown wiſdomewisdom.
div.p: Contrary is the preſumptionpresumption of ſuchsuch wiueswives as thinkethink themſeluesthemselves wiferwiser then their husbands, and able better to iudgejudge matters then they can. I deniedeny not but that a wife may hauehave more vnderſtandingunderstanding then her husband: for ſomesome men are very ignorant and blockiſhblockish; and on the other ſideside, ſomesome women well inſtructedinstructed, who thereby hauehave attained to a great meaſuremeasure of knowledge, and diſcretiondiscretion; but many though they hauehave husbands of ſufficientsufficient and good vnderſtandingunderstanding, wifewise and diſcreetdiscreet men, yet thinkethink that that which they hauehave once conceiuedconceived to be a truth, muſtmust needs be ſoso: and ſuchsuch is their peremptorineſſeperemptoriness, that they wilwill not be brought to thinkethink that they may erreerr: but ſaysay they will neuernever be brought to thinkethink otherwiſeotherwise then they doedo, though all the husbands in the world ſhouldshould be of another opinion: not much vnlikeunlike to the WiſemansWisemans foolefool, who thinketh himſelfehimself wiſerwiser then ſeuenseven men Pro. 26. 16. that can render a reaſonreason.

div.head: §. 66. Of a wiueswives Treat. 4. §. 27. yeeldingyielding to her husband in ſuchsuch things as ſheshe thinketh not to be the meet eſtestmeetest.
div.p:
The latter concluſionconclusion concerning a wiueswives yeeldingyielding in practiſepractise to that which her husband requireth, though ſheshe cannot bring her iudgementjudgment to thinkethink as he doth about the meet • neſſemeetness of it, Si res aliqua occurrat, quae conſilioconsilio opus habeat, quin ipſaipsa quo
que quoque quid cenſeascenseas dic • asdicas minimè prohibeo • : ſedsed viri tui ſententiamsententiam vim maiorem ſempersemper obtinere volo. Greg • . Naz. ad Olymp. hath reſpectrespect to indifferent things, namely, to ſuchsuch as are neither in their particulars commanded, nor forbidden by God: as the outward affairesaffairs of the houſehouse, ordering it, diſpoſingdisposing goods, entertaining gueſtsguests, &etcc.

QueſtQuest. May ſheshe not reaſonreason with her husband about ſuchsuch matters as ſheshe thinketh vnmeetunmeet, and labour to perſwadepersuade her husband not to perſiſtpersist in the preſſingpressing thereof, yea endeuourendeavour to bring her husband to ſeesee the vnmeetneſſeunmeetness (as ſheshe thinketh) of that which ſheshe ſeethseeth?

AnſwAnsw. With modeſtymodesty, humilitiehumility, and reuerencereverence, ſheshe may ſoso
doedo: and he ought to hearken vntounto her, as the husband of the Shunemite did, 2. King. 4. 23, 24. butBut yet, if notwithſtandingnotwithstanding all that ſheshe can ſaysay, he perſiſtpersist in his reſolutionresolution, and will hauehave it done, ſheshe muſtmust yeeldyield.

FirſtFirst, her ſubiectionsubjection is moſtmost manifeſtedmanifested in ſuchsuch caſescases: herein ſheshe apparantlyapparently ſhewethshoweth, that what ſheshe doth, ſheshe doth in reſpectrespect of her husbands place, and power: were it not for that, ſheshe would not doedo it. Other things are not ſoso euidentevident proofesproofs of her ſubiectionsubjection to her husband: for if he command her to doedo that which God hath expreſlyexpressly commanded, and ſoso ſheshe ought to doedo it, whether her husband commanded it or no, it may be thought ſheshe doth it on Gods command, and not on her husbands. If her husband command her to doedo that which God hath expreſlyexpressly forbidden, then ought ſheshe by no meanesmeans to yeeldyield vntounto it: if ſheshe doedo, it may rather be termed a iointjoint conſpiracieconspiracy of husband and wife together againſtagainst Gods will (as S. Peter ſaidsaid to Sapphira the wife of Ananias, How is it that ye hauehave agreed together to tempt the
Acts 5. 9. ſpiritspirit of the Lord?) then ſubiectionsubjection to the image of God in her husband.

Secondly, her yeeldingyielding in indifferent things tendeth much to the peace of the family, as ſubiectssubjects yeeldingyielding to their MagiſtratesMagistrates in ſuchsuch caſescases maketh much to the peace of the Commoncommon wealth. For in differenciesdifferences and diſſentionsdissensionsdissentions one ſideside muſtmust yeeldyield, or elſeelse great miſchiefemischief is like to follow: now of the two, who ſhouldshould yeeldyield but the inferiourinferior?

div.head: §. 67. Of wiueswives making their owneown will their law.
div.p:
Contrary is the cuſtomecustom of many wiueswives, who neuernever will doedo any more then they themſeluesthemselves thinkethink meet, though their huſbandshusbands require it neuernever ſoso much: ſurelysurely they come farrefar ſhortshort of this ApoſtolicallApostolicalApostolicall extent (in eueryevery thing) though in their own eieseyes they may ſeemeseem to be very much ſubiectsubject. But when wiueswives will no further be ſubiectsubject, then their owneown iudgmentsjudgments, wilswills and affections concurreconcur with their husbands, what can be thought but that they are ſubiectsubject rather to their owneown wilswills, then to the will of their husbands? Many ſuchsuch wiueswives, from the leaſtleast difference in iudgementjudgment & opiniōopinion, eueneven in the ſmalleſtsmallest matters, take occaſionoccasion to refuſerefuse ſubiectionsubjection, and thinkethink they hauehave warrant enough ſoso to doedo: whence oftentimes there ariſethariseth much contention, the fault whereof lieth
eſpeciallyespecially on the wiueswives neckeneck, though the occaſionoccasion may ariſearise from the husband: and I thinkethink that wiueswives themſeluesthemselves would ſoso iudgejudge of the like caſescases betwixt them and their children.

div.head: §. 68. Of care in chooſingchoosing ſuchsuch husbands as wiueswives may without See Treat. 2. Part. 1. §. 11. griefegrief be ſubiectsubject vntounto.
ObiectObject. If the caſecase be ſuchsuch betwixt man and wife, it is not good to marry.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. This is no good inference; for all the ſeemingseeming hardneſſehardness of a wiueswives caſecase is in the lewdneſſelewdness of an husband, who abuſethabuseth his place and power: and not in that ſubiectionsubjection which is required by God. For if an husband carry himſelfehimself to his wife as TutūTutumTutumTutun obſequiumobsequium eſtest, quoties qui dux eſtest, ipſeipse Dei Spiritu ducitur. God requireth, ſheshe will findefind her yoke to be eaſieeasy, and her ſubiectionsubjection a great benefit eueneven vntounto her ſelfeself. Wherefore I would exhort parties that are vnmariedunmarried, whether maidens or widoweswidows, to be very carefullcareful in their choiſechoice of husbands: and in their choiſechoice to reſpectrespect aboueabove all, their good qualities and conditions, therein bearing the image of ChriſtChrist, as well as in their office, and authoritieauthority: ſoso as their wiueswives may with ioyjoy and comfort, not with griefegrief and anguiſhanguish, be ſubiectsubject vntounto them: then will ſubiectionsubjection proueprove a vexation, when the husband is an ignorant, profane, idolatrous, worldly, wicked man: wiueswives of ſuchsuch husbands are oft brought into many ſtraitsstraits. Ye widoweswidows and maidens who are free, be not too free and forward in giuinggiving your conſentconsent to whom you know not: among other motiuesmotives, oft thinkethink of this point of ſubiectionsubjection, to which all wiueswives are bound: this I ſaysay, both of the ſeuerallseveral branches, and alſoalso of the extent thereof. After you are mariedmarried it is in vainevain to thinkethink of freedomefreedom from ſubiectionsubjection. By taking husbands, and giuinggiving your ſeluesselves to be wiueswives, you bindebind your ſeluesselves to the law of the man, as long as he liuethliveth. Then as you deſiredesire to be accepted of God, and to findefind mercy and comfort from him, you muſtmust bearebear this yoke, how heauyheavy and grieuousgrievous ſoeuersoever it ſeemeseem to be.

div.head: §. 69. Of the reaſonsreasons to mouemove wiueswives to doedo their duties.
div.p: Hitherto of wiueswives duties: The reaſonsreasons noted by the ApoſtleApostle to enforce thoſethose duties now follow. They are laid downedown in theſethese words.

p.q: VerſVers. 23. For the husband is the head of the wife, eueneven as ChriſtChrist is the head of the Church: and he is the SauiourSaviour of the bodiebody.
VerſVers. 24. Wherefore as the Church is ſubiectsubject, &etcc.

div.p: THeThe mainemain ground of all the reaſonsreasons which the ApoſtleApostle here intimateth, is taken from the place wherinwherein God hath ſetset an husband, which is firſtfirst by conſequenceconsequence implied in theſethese words, as to the Lord: and then more plainly and directly expreſſedexpressed in theſethese, the husband is the head of the wife. The particle prefixed before theſethese words (for) being a cauſallcausal coniunctionconjunction, doth ſhewshow, that they are here ſetset downedown as a reaſonreason, which is firſtfirst propounded vnderunder a metaphor (head) and then amplified by that reſemblanceresemblance which an husband hath therein vntounto ChriſtChrist (eueneven as ChriſtChrist, &etcc.) which reſemblanceresemblance is further commended by the vertuevirtue and benefit that proceedeth from the head-ſhipship of ChriſtChrist properly, and of an husband alſoalso by conſequenceconsequence, in theſethese words (and is the SauiourSaviour of the bodiebody.) VponUpon an husbands reſemblanceresemblance vntounto ChriſtChrist, he inferrethinfereth that a wife ſhouldshould hauehave a reſemblanceresemblance vntounto the Church, and ſoso concludeth, Therefore as the Church is in ſubiectionsubjection to ChriſtChrist, ſoso let wiueswives be to their husbands.

Out of the forenamed ground of a wiueswives ſubiectionsubjection, and the ſeuerallseveral amplifications thereof, and the inference thereupon made, fiuefive ſeuerallseveral and diſtinctdistinct reaſonsreasons may be gathered to enforce a wineswives ſubiectionsubjection to her husband.
The firſtfirst is taken from an husbands place: he is in the Lords ſteadstead to his wife (as to the Lord.)
The ſecondsecond from his office: he is an head to his wife.
The chirdthird from the image he beareth, or from the reſemblanceresemblance betwixt him and ChriſtChrist (eueneven as ChriſtChrist &etcc.)
The fourth from the benefit that his wife receiuethreceiveth from him (he is the SauiourSaviour &etcc.)
The fiftfifth from the example and patternepattern of the Church (as the Church is in ſubiectionsubjection, &etcc.)

div.head: §§. 70. Of an husbands place.
div.p: The place wherein God hath ſetset an husband as it ſeruethserveth 1. ReaſonReason. to direct a wife in the manner of her ſubiectionsubjection, whereof I hauehave ſpokenspoken §. 51. before, ſoso alſoalso it ſeruethserveth to mouemove a wife to yeeldyield ſuchsuch ſubiectionsubjection as is required: which will euidentlyevidently appeareappear by theſethese two concluſionsconclusions following from thence.
1. A wife by ſubiectingsubjecting her ſelfeself to her husband, therein is ſubiectsubject vntounto ChriſtChrist.
2. A wife by refuſingrefusing to be ſubiectsubject vntounto her husband, therein refuſethrefuseth to be ſubiectsubject vntounto ChriſtChrist.

That theſethese two concluſionsconclusions are rightly and iuſtlyjustly gathered from the forenamed ground I proueprove by like concluſionsconclusions which the holy GhoſtGhost inferrethinfereth vponupon the like ground. It is euidentevident that ChriſtChrist IeſusJesus, eueneven incarnatincarnate and made fleſhflesh, was in the roomeroom and ſteadstead of his father, whereupon ChriſtChrist ſaidsaid to Philip that deſireddesired to ſeesee the father, he that hath ſeeneseen me hath ſeeneseen the father: Now markemark what ChriſtChrist thence inferrethinfereth both on IohJoh. 14. 9. Mat. 10. 40. IohJoh. 5. 23. the one ſideside (he that receiuethreceiveth me receiuethreceiveth him that ſentsent me) and on the other (he that honoureth not the ſonneson, honoureth not the father that ſentsent him.) It is alſoalso euidentevident that MiniſtersMinisters of the GoſpellGospel ſtandstand in the roomeroom and ſteadstead of ChriſtChrist: for thus ſaithsaith the ApoſtleApostle of himſelfehimself and other MiniſtersMinisters, we are ambaſſadorsambassadors for ChriſtChrist, as though God did beſeechbeseech you by vsus, we pray you in ChriſtsChrists ſteadstead, &etcc. Now markemark againeagain the concluſionsconclusions inferred thereupon by ChriſtChrist, on the one ſideside, he that heareth
Luk. 10. 16. you, heareth me, and on the other, he that deſpiſethdespiseth you, deſpiſethdespiseth me. On this ground it was that God ſaidsaid to Samuel concerning the people that reiectedrejected his gouernmentgovernment, they hauehave not caſtcast thee away, but they hauehave caſtcast me away. 1 Sam. 8. 7.

To apply this reaſonreason, I hope ſuchsuch wiueswives as liuelive vnderunder the GoſpellGospel hauehave ſoso much religion and piety in them as to acknowledge, it becommethbecometh them well to be ſubiectsubject vntounto the Lord ChriſtChrist IeſusJesus: here then learnelearn one eſpeciallespecial and principallprincipal part of ſubiectionsubjection vntounto ChriſtChrist, which is to be ſubiectsubject
vntounto your husbands: thus ſhallshall you ſhewshow your ſeluesselves to be the wiueswives of the Lord ChriſtChrist, as the ApoſtleApostle ſaithsaith of obedient ſeruantsservants, they are the ſeruantsservants of God. 1 Pet. 2. 16.

AgaineAgain I hope none are ſoso void of all religion and piety as to refuſerefuse to be ſubiectsubject vntounto ChriſtChrist: here then take notice, that if wilfully yeeye refuſerefuse to be ſubiectsubject to your husbands, yeeye wilfully refuſerefuse to be ſubiectsubject to ChriſtChrist: fitly on this ground may I apply that to wiueswives, which the ApoſtleApostle ſpeakethspeaketh of ſubiectssubjects, whoſoeuerwhosoever reſiſtethresisteth the power and authority of an husband,
Rom. 13. 2. reſiſtethresisteth the ordinance of God: and they that reſiſtresist ſhallshall receiuereceive to themſeluesthemselves iudgementjudgment.

A ſtrongstrong motiuemotive is this firſtfirst motiuemotive. If it were duly conſideredconsidered of wiueswives, they would more readily, and cheerefullycheerfully be ſubiectsubject, then many are; they would not ſoso lightly thinkethink of their husbands place, nor ſoso reproachfully ſpeakespeak againſtagainst Gods MiniſtersMinisters who plainly declare their duty vntounto them, as many doedo.

div.head: §. 71. Of an husbands office.
div.p: The ſecondsecond reaſonreason is like vntounto this taken from an husbands 2. ReaſonReason. 1 Cor. 11. 3. office, he is the wiueswives head: which is alſoalso vrgedurged to this very purpoſepurpose in other places.

This metaphor ſhewethshoweth that to his wife he is as the head of a naturallnatural body, both more eminent in place, and alſoalso more excellent in dignity: by vertuevirtue of both which, he is a ruler and gouernourgovernor of his wife. Nature teacheth vsus that this is true of the head of a naturallnatural body: and the ApoſtleApostle by intitulingentitling an husband, an head, teacheth vsus that it is as true of an husband: whence it followeth, that it ſtandethstandeth with common equity, and with the light of nature, that the wife ſhouldshould be ſubiectsubject to her husband. This argument doth the ApoſtleApostle in plaineplain termesterms vrgeurge in another place, ſayingsaying, doth not nature teach you, &etcc. 1 Cor. 11. 14.

GoeGo therefore, ô wiueswives, vntounto the ſchooleschool of nature, lookelook vponupon the outward parts and members of your bodies. DoeDo they deſiredesire to be aboueabove the head? areAre they loth to be ſubiectsubject vntounto the head? Let your ſoulesoul then learnelearn of your body. Were it not monſtrousmonstrous for the ſideside to be aduancedadvanced aboueabove the head? If the body ſhouldshould not be ſubiectsubject to the head, would not deſtructiondestruction
follow vponupon head, body, and all the parts thereof? As monſtrousmonstrous, and much more monſtrousmonstrous is it for a wife to be aboueabove her husband: and as great, yea and greater diſturbancedisturbance and ruineruin would fall on that family. The order which God hath ſetset therein would be cleaneclean ouerthrowneoverthrown thereby: and they that ouerthrowoverthrow it would ſhewshow themſeluesthemselves oppugners of Gods wiſdomewisdom in eſtabliſhingestablishing order. This reaſonreason drawnedrawn from nature is of force to mouemove very Pagans, and SauagesSavages to yeeldyield ſubiectionsubjection, how much more ChriſtianChristian wiueswives, it being alſoalso agreeable to Gods word, and ratified thereby?

div.head: §. 72. Of the reſemblanceresemblance betwixt ChriſtChrist and an husband.
div.p: The third reaſonreason taken from an husbands reſemblanceresemblance vntounto 3. ReaſonReason. ChriſtChrist herein, addeth an edge vntounto that former reaſonreason: in being an head, he is like ChriſtChrist. So as there is a kindekind of fellowſhipfellowship and copartnerſhipcopartnership betwixt ChriſtChrist, and an husband: they are brethren in office, as two kings of ſeuerallseveral places.
ObiectObject. There is no equality betwixt ChriſtChrist the Lord from heauenheaven, and an earthly husband: the diſparitydisparity betwixt them is infinite.

AnſwAnsw. Yet there may be ſimilitudesimilitude, reſemblanceresemblance, and fellowſhipfellowship: inequality is no hinderancehindrance to theſethese. Two kings may be more different in eſtateestate then a ſubiectsubject and a king; yet thoſethose two kings brethren and fellowesfellows in office. There may be a reſemblanceresemblance where there is no parity, and a likeneſſelikeness where there is no equality. The glorious and bright SunneSun in the firmament, and a dimmedim candle in an houſehouse, hauehave a kindekind of fellowſhipfellowship, and the ſamesame office, which is to giuegive light: yet there is no equality betwixt them. So then an husband reſemblethresembleth not only the head of a naturallnatural body, but alſoalso the glorious image of ChriſtChrist, and is that to his wife which ChriſtChrist is to his Church.
To apply this point, markemark how from it two poſitionspositions (worthy to be noted) doedo ariſearise.
1. SubiectionSubjection is due to an husband as well as to ChriſtChrist. SubiectionSubjection due to an husband as well as to ChriſtChrist.

I ſaysay not as great, becauſebecause of the difference in glory: but as well, becauſebecause of the likeneſſelikeness in office. A ConſtableConstable (though a poorepoor meanemean man) muſtmust be obeyed as well as an high ſherifesheriffsherif: A beggars childechild muſtmust obey his father, as well as a kings
childechild. Such wiueswives therefore who are not ſubiectsubject, wrong their husbands, as well as they wrong ChriſtChrist who are not ſubiectsubject to him.

2. They who by their ſubiectionsubjection maintainemaintain the honour of their husbands place, maintainemaintain thereby the honour of ChriſtsChrists place: and againeagain by the rule of contraries, They who by refuſingrefusing to be ſubiectsubject impeach the honour of their husbands place, impeach thereby the honour of ChriſtsChrists place.

The obedience of a poorepoor mans childechild or ſeruantservant iuſtifiethjustifieth that obedience which kings children and ſeruantsservants owe their father and ſoueraignesovereign: and ſoso on the contrary, diſobediencedisobedience in meanemean ones, diſhonourethdishonoureth the place of great ones.

The argument of Memucan drawnedrawn from the greater to the EſtEst. 1. 16. leſſeless (in theſethese words, VaſhtyVashtiVashty the QueeneQueen hath not done wrong to the king only, but alſoalso to all the princes, and all the people) may be applied from the leſſeless to the greater. DiſobedientDisobedient wiueswives doedo wrong not only to their owneown particular husbands, but alſoalso to all heads, eueneven to ChriſtChrist the head of the Church.

If a naturallnatural body, and the Church were flexible, and could be ſeducedseduced, and drawnedrawn to preſumepresume, and rebellrebel againſtagainst their heads, the ill example of wiueswives were enough to mouemove them thereunto, for, as much as in them lieth, they by example ſeduceseduce them.

From the laſtlast forenamed poſitionspositions (viz. thatThat the obedience of a good wife maintaineth the honour of ChriſtsChrists place, and on the contrary ſideside that the diſobediencedisobedience of an ill wife impaireth the honour thereof) I may iuſtlyjustly inferreinfer two other concluſionsconclusions.

1. That ChriſtChrist will aſſuredlyassuredly reward the good ſubiectionsubjection of ChriſtChrist will reward the good ſubiectionsubjection, and reuengerevenge the rebellion of wiueswives. good wiueswives: for he hath ſaidsaid (and what he hath ſaidsaid he can and will performeperform) them that honour me will I honour.
2. That he will ſorelysorely reuengerevenge the rebellion of euillevil wiueswives: for againeagain he hath ſaidsaid, they that deſpiſedespise me, ſhallshall be deſpiſeddespised.

We know that fellowesfellows in office are ready to ſtandstand for the 1 Sam. 2. 30. credit of one anothers place, and to maintainemaintain the honour thereof: and that not without good reaſonreason: for thereby they maintainemaintain their owneown honour and credit.

Wherefore as good wiueswives may well expect a reward at ChriſtsChrists hands, howſoeuerhowsoever their husbands reſpectrespect their obedience,
whether well or ill: (a great incouragementencouragement for wiueswives to performeperform their duties, though their husbands be neuernever ſoso ill) ſoso euillevil wiueswives hauehave iuſtjust cauſecause to fearefear reuengerevenge at ChriſtsChrists hand, how ſoeuersoever their husbands bearebear with them.
They who duly weigh this reaſonreason taken from that reſemblanceresemblance which is betwixt ChriſtChrist and the Church, cannot but hold it to be a motiuemotive of great moment.

div.head: §. 73. Of the benefit which a wife hath by an husband.
div.p: The fourth reaſonreason taken from the benefit which a wife receiuethreceiveth 4. ReaſonReason. from her husband, doth yet further preſſepress the point in hand. Though ChriſtChrist be properly the SauiourSaviour of the bodiebody, yet eueneven herein an husband cariethcarrieth a reſemblanceresemblance of ChriſtChrist, and is after a manner a SaniourSaviour: for by vertuevirtue of his place and office he is on the one ſideside her protector, to defend her from hurt, and preſeruepreserve her from danger; and on the other ſideside, a proniderprovider of all needfullneedful and neceſſarienecessary things for her: in which reſpectrespect ſheshe is taken from her parents and friends, and wholly committed Gen. 31. 14. to him: (as IaakobsJacob's wiueswives ſaidsaid, HaueHave we any more portion or inheritance in our fathers houſehouse?) yea ſheshe her ſelfeself, and all ſheshe hath is giuengiven to him: and he againeagain communicateth what ſoeuersoever he hath to her good, and for her vſeuse. DauidDavid compareth a wife to PſalPsal. 128. 3. a Vine, in relation to her husband: intimating thereby, that by him ſheshe is raiſedraised to that height of honour ſheshe hath, as a vine by the tree, or frame neerenear vntounto which it is planted. By his honour is ſheshe dignified, by his wealth is ſheshe enriched. He is, vnderunder God, all in all to her; in the family he is a King to gouernegovern and aid her, a PrieſtPriest to pray with her and for her, a Prophet to teach and inſtructinstruct her. As the head is placed in the higheſthighest place ouerover the bodiebody, and vnderſtandingunderstanding placed in it, to gouernegovern, direct, protect, and euerieevery way ſeekeseek the good of the bodiebody, and as ChriſtChrist is vnitedunited to the Church as a ſpouſespouse, and made her head, that ſheshe might be ſauedsaved, maintained, and prouidedprovided for by him; ſoso for this end was an husband placed in his place of ſuperioritiesuperiority; and his authoritieauthority was committed to him, to be a SaniourSaviour of his wife. Wherefore if none of the former motiuesmotives preuaileprevail with wiueswives, and mouemove them to be ſubiectsubject to their husbands, yet ought this.

For from this reaſonreason flow theſethese two concluſionsconclusions.
1. The ſubiectionsubjection required of a wife is for her owneown good.
2. In refuſingrefusing to obey ſheshe ſhewethshoweth her ſelfeself both vngratefullungrateful to her husband, and alſoalso iniuriousinjurious to her ſelfeself.

That her ſubiectionsubjection is for her owneown good, is euidentevident by this A wiueswives ſubiectionsubjection tendeth to her owneown good. end for which an husband is made an head, to be a SaniourSaviour: not to puffepuff him vpup, to make him inſultinsult and tyrannize ouerover his wife. So as if ſheshe be ſubiectsubject vntounto him, ſheshe may reapereap much good from him. As the Church is wiſelywisely gouernedgoverned, and ſafelysafely protected by ſubiectingsubjecting her ſelfeself to her head ChriſtChrist IeſusJesus; and as the body partaketh of much good, and is preſeruedpreserved from much euillevil by ſubiectingsubjecting it ſelfeself to the head, ſoso if a wife be ſubiectsubject to her huſbandhusband, ſheshe will fare much the better thereby, all the eaſeease, profit, and benefit thereof will be hers. If therefore ſheshe tender her owneown good, this is a way and meanesmeans ordained of God for this end; let her herein ſeekeseek it.

If notwithſtandingnotwithstanding this ſheshe refuſerefuse to be ſubiectsubject vntounto her huſbandhusband, doth ſheshe not (as we ſaysay) ſtandstand in her owneown light? She being by her ſexsex the weaker, and the more vnableunable to helpehelp her ſelfeself, i • fifof ſheshe ſhallshall reiectreject this good helpehelp which God hath prouidedprovided for her, is ſheshe not moſtmost iniuriousinjurious to her owneown ſelfeself? And conſideringconsidering Gratitude requireth a wife to be ſubiectsubject. the care and pains her husband vndergoethundergoeth for her ſakesake, is it not moſtmost vnnaturallunnatural and monſtrousmonstrous ingratitude, inwardly to des • piſedespise, or outwardly to ſcornescorn ſuchsuch an head? No better teſtimonytestimony o • f a gratefullgrateful heart can be giuengiven by a wife to her husband, then c • heerefullcheerful and ready ſubiectionsubjection: and no greater ingratitude can b • e ſhewedshowed, then rebellion, and diſdainedisdain. Now among vices ing • ratitude is one of the moſtmost odious to God and man: ſoso as both t • o auoidavoid the blackeblack ſpotspot of ingratitude, and to carry away the n • ame of gratefulneſſegratefulness, ought wiueswives to be ſubiectsubject.

div.head: §. 74. Of the example of the Church ſetset before wineswives.
div.p:
The laſtlast reaſonreason taken from the example of the Church is alſoalso 5. ReaſonReason.
o • f good force to perſwadepersuade wiueswives vntounto ſubiectionsubjection. ExampleExampleexample more p • reuailesprevails with many then precept. If any example may be of f • orce, then this moſtmost of all: for it is not the example of one only, b • ut of many; not of many ignorant, and wicked perſonspersons, but of underſtandingunderstanding, wiſewise, holy and righteous perſonspersons, eueneven all the s • aints that euerever were, are, or ſhallshall be: for the Church compriſethcompriseth al •• l vnderunder it, eueneven that whole ſocietysociety of Saints, which are choſenchosen
of God in his eternalleternal counſellcounsel, redeemed of ChriſtChrist by his precious bloudblood, and effectually called by the GoſpellGospel of faluationsalvation, Gods ſpiritspirit working inwardly and powerfully vponupon them, thoſethose very ſoulessouls of iuſtjust and perfect men now triumphing in heauenheaven, not excepted: note how this Church is deſcribeddescribed in the 26, and 27. verſesVerses. Let this example therefore be oft thought of: it will neuernever repent any to follow it: for it treadeth the only right path to eternalleternal glory, whereunto they ſhallshall aſſuredlyassuredly come that follow it.
But to ſhewshow the force of this reaſonreason a little more diſtinctlydistinctly, note theſethese two concluſionsconclusions following from it.

1. WiuesWives are as much bound to be ſubiectsubject to their husbands, as the Church to ChriſtChrist. ElſeElse why ſhouldshould this example be thus ſetset before them, and preſſedpressed vponupon them? whyWhy are husbands ſetset in ChriſtsChrists ſteadstead, and reſembledresembled to him?

2. A wiueswives ſubiectionsubjection to her husband, anſwerableanswerable to the Churches ſubiectionsubjection vntounto ChriſtChrist, is an euidenceevidence that ſheshe is of the Church, guided by the ſamesame Spirit that the Church is. For it cannot be performed by the power of nature, it is a ſupernaturallsupernatural workework, and ſoso an euidenceevidence of the Spirit.

Wherefore, ô ChriſtianChristian wiueswives, as your husbands by their place reſembleresemble ChriſtChrist, ſoso doedo you by your practiſepractise reſembleresemble the Church. Of the two this is the more commendable: for that is a dignitiedignity, this a vertuevirtue: but true vertuevirtue is much more glorious then any dignitiedignity can be.

The ApoſtleApostle compriſethcompriseth the whole matter of them all vnderunder Louelove, which is the ſummesum and head of all.
