div.head: §. 2. Of that Treat. 3. §. 2. 1. Husbands muſtmust louelove their wiueswives. louelove which husbands owe their wiueswives.
div.p: This head of all the reſtrest, Louelove, is expreſlyexpressly ſetset downedown, and alone mentioned in this, and in many other places of Scripture, whereby it is euidentevident, that all other duties are compriſedcomprised vnderunder it.

To omit other places, where this dutieduty is vrgedurged in Eph. 5. 25, 28, 33. this place, Louelove is fourefour times by name expreſſedexpressed, beſidebeside that it is intimated vnderunder many other termesterms and phraſesphrases.

WhoſoeuerWhosoever therefore taketh a wife, muſtmust, in this reſpectrespect that ſheshe is his wife, louelove her: as it is noted of IſaakIsaac (the beſtbest patternepattern of husbands noted in the Scripture) Gen. 24. 67. he tooketook Rebekah, ſheshe was his wife ana he louedloved her.
Many good reaſonsreasons hereof may be rendredrendered. No dutieduty well performed without louelove.

1. BecauſeBecause no dutieduty on the husbands part can be rightly performed except it be ſeaſonedseasoned with louelove. The ApoſtleApostle exhorteth all ChriſtiansChristians to doedo all their things in louelove: much more 1 Cor. 16. 14. ought husbands: though in place they be aboueabove their wiueswives, yet louelove may not be forgotten.

2. BecauſeBecause of all perſonspersons on earth a wife is the moſtmost proper 2. A wife the moſtmost proper obiectobject of louelove. Deut. 13. 6. obiectobject of louelove: nor friend, nor childechild, nor parent ought ſoso to be louedloved as a wife: ſheshe is termed, the wife of his boſomebosom, to ſhewshow that ſheshe ought to be as his heart in his boſomebosom.

3. BecauſeBecause his place of eminency, and power of authority 3. LoueLove keepeskeeps a man from abuſingabusing his authority. may ſoonesoon puffepuff him vpup, and make him inſultinsult ouerover his wife, and trample her vnderunder his feet, if a intireentire louelove of her be not planted in his heart. To keepekeep him from abuſingabusing his authority is louelove ſoso much preſſedpressed vponupon him.

4. BecauſeBecause wiueswives through the weakneſſeweakness of their ſexsex (for 4. LoueLove maketh him bearebear with her infirmities. 5. His louelove draweth louelove from her. they are the weaker veſſelsvessels) are much prone to prouokeprovoke their husbands. So as if there be not louelove predominant in the huſbandhusband, there is like to be but little peace betwixt man and wife. Louelove couerethcovereth a multitude of imperfections.

5. BecauſeBecause as ChriſtChrist by his louelove firſtfirst manifeſtedmanifested prouokethprovoketh
the Church to louelove him, ſoso an husband by louingloving his wife ſhouldshould prouokeprovoke her to louelove him againeagain: ſhewingshowing himſelfehimself like the SunneSun which is the fountainefountain of light, and from which the MooneMoon receiuethreceiveth what light ſheshe hath: ſoso he ſhouldshould be the fountainefountain of louelove to his wife.
ObiectObject. LoueLove was before laid downedown as a common dutieduty appertaining both to man and wife: how is it then here required as a particular and peculiar dutieduty of an husband?

AnſwAnsw. In regard of the generallgeneral extent of louelove it is indeed a common dutieduty belonging to the one as well as to the other, yea How louelove is an husbands particular dutieduty. 1 Cor. 13. 5. belonging to all ChriſtiansChristians, to all men: for it is the very nature of louelove, and an eſpeciallespecial property thereof, to ſeekeseek not her owneown things, but the good of others, which all are bound to doedo by vertuevirtue of the bond of nature; more then others, ChriſtiansChristians by vertuevirtue of the bond of the ſpiritspirit: among ChriſtiansChristians, eſpeciallyespecially wiueswives and husbands by vertuevirtue of the matrimoniallmatrimonial bond: of mariedmarried couples, moſtmost of all husbands by vertuevirtue of their place and charge. Their place is a place of authoritieauthority, which without louelove will ſoonesoon turneturn into tyrannietyranny. Their charge is eſpeciallyespecially and aboueabove all, to ſeekeseek the good of their wiueswives: as wiueswives are the chiefeſtchiefest, and greateſtgreatest charge of husbands, ſoso their chiefeſtchiefest and greateſtgreatest care muſtmust be for them: the parents and friends of wiueswives as they giuegive ouerover all their authority to their husbands, ſoso they caſtcast all care vponupon them: wherefore that husbands may take the more care of their wiueswives, and the better ſeekeseek their good, they ought after a peculiar manner to louelove them. Husbands are moſtmost of all bound to louelove: and bound to louelove their wiueswives moſtmost of all.

Thus this affection of louelove is a diſtinctdistinct dutieduty in it ſelfeself, peculiarly LoueLove a common condition to be annexed to euerieevery dutieduty. appertaining to an husband: and alſoalso a common condition which muſtmust be annexed to eueryevery other dutieduty of an huſbandhusband, to ſeaſonseason and ſweetensweeten the ſamesame. His lookelook, his ſpeechspeech, his carriage, and all his actions, wherein he hath to doedo with his wife, muſtmust be ſeaſonedseasoned with louelove: louelove muſtmust ſhewshow it ſelfeself in his commandementscommandments, in his reproofesreproofs, in his inſtructionsinstructions, in his admonitions, in his authoritieauthority, in his familiaritiefamiliarity, when they are alone together, when they are in company before others, in ciuillcivil affairesaffairs, in religious matters, at all times, in all
things: as ſaltsalt muſtmust be firſtfirst and laſtlast vponupon the table, and eaten with eueryevery bit of meatemeat, ſoso muſtmust louelove be firſtfirst in an husbands heart, and laſtlast out of it, and mixed with eueryevery thing wherein he hath to doedo with his wife.

div.head: §. 3. Of an husbands hatred and want of louelove.
div.p: Contrary hereunto is hatred of heart: which vice as it is Contrary, 1. Hatred. very odious and deteſtabledetestable in it ſelfeself, ſoso much more when the wife is made the obiectobject thereof. As louelove prouokethprovoketh an huſbandhusband to doedo his wife what good he can, ſoso hatred, to doedo her what miſchiefemischief he can. Neither is it ſufficientsufficient for an husband not to hate his wife, 2. Want of louelove. for eueneven the want of louelove, though it be only a priuationprivation, yet is it a great vice, and contrary alſoalso to the forenamed dutieduty of louelove. Where this want of louelove is, there can be no duty welwell performed, eueneven as when the great wheelewheel of a clockeclock, the firſtfirst mouermover of all the reſtrest, is out of frame, neuernever a wheelewheel can be in good order. They that thinkethink lightly hereof, plainly diſcouerdiscover that there is little or no louelove of God in them at all: for if the ApoſtlesApostles inference be good, taken from a mans neighbour or brother whom 1 IohJoh. 4. 20. he hath ſeeneseen, it will much more be good hauinghaving relation to a wife: for how can he who louethloveth not his wife, (whom God hath giuengiven to him as a token of his fauourfavour, and as an helpehelp meet for him, to be in his boſomebosom, and euerever in his ſightsight, yea to be no more two, but one fleſhflesh) louelove God whom he hath not ſeeneseen? If any man ſaithsaith, he louethloveth God, and hate his wife, he is a lier. Let
husbands therefore by louingloving their wiueswives giuegive euidenceevidence that they louelove God.

div.head: §. 4. Of an husbands Treat. 3. §. 9. Branches of louelove. wiſewise maintaining his authoritieauthority.
div.p:
All the branches which grow out of this root of louelove, as they hauehave reſpectrespect to husbands duties, may be drawnedrawn to two heads:
1. A wiſewise maintaining of his authoritieauthority.
2. A right managing of the ſamesame.

That theſethese two are branches of an husbands louelove, is euidentevident by the place wherein God hath ſetset him, which is a place of authoritieauthority; for the beſtbest good that any can doedo, and ſoso the beſtbest fruits of louelove which he can ſhewshow forth to any, are ſuchsuch as are done in his owneown proper place, and by vertuevirtue thereof. If then an husband relinquiſhrelinquish his authoritieauthority, he diſablethdisableth himſelfehimself from doing that good, and ſhewingshowing thoſethose fruits of louelove which otherwiſeotherwise he might. div.p: Contrary is their practiſepractise who by their profaneneſſeprofaneness, riotouſneſſeriotousness, Contrary, 1. baſebase carriage drunkenneſſedrunkenness, lewdneſſelewdness, lightneſſelightness, vnthriftineſſeunthriftiness, and other like baſebase carriage, make themſeluesthemselves contemptible, and ſoso loſelose their authoritieauthority: though a wife ought not to take theſethese occaſionsoccasions to deſpiſedespise her husband, yet is it a iuſtjust iudgementjudgment on him to be deſpiſeddespised, ſeeingseeing he maketh himſelfehimself contemptible.

div.head: §. 11. Of husbands Treat. 3. §. 7. V. Husbands muſtmust intirelyentirely delight in their wiueswives. intireentire affection to their wiueswives.
div.p:
An husbands affection to his wife muſtmust be anſwerableanswerable to his opinion of her: he ought therefore to delight in his wife intirelyentirely, that is, ſoso to delight in her as wholly and only delighting in her: In this reſpectrespect the Prophets wife is called the Ezec. 24. 16. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉
deſiredesire, or delight, or pleaſurepleasure of his eyes: that wherein he moſtmost of all delighted, and therefore by a propriety ſoso called.

Such delight did IſaakIsaac take in his wife as it drouedrove out a contrary ſtrongstrong paſſionpassion, namely the griefegrief which he tooketook for the departure of his mother: for it is noted that he
Gen. 24. 67. louedloved her, and was comforted after his mothers death.

This kindekind of affection the wiſewise-man doth elegantly ſetset forth in theſethese words, ReioyceRejoice with the wife of thy youth: Let her
Pro. 5. 18, 19. expounded. be as the louingloving HindeHind, and pleaſantpleasant Roe, and be thou rauiſhtravishedravisht alwaiesalways with her louelove. Here note both the metaphors, and alſoalso the hyperbole which are vſedused to ſetset forth an husbands delight in his wife. In the metaphors againeagain note both the creatures whereunto a wife is reſembledresembled, and alſoalso the attributes giuengiven to them. The creatures are two, an Hind and a Roe, which are the females of an Hart and a Roe-BuckeBuck: now it is noted of the Hart and Roe-BuckeBuck, that of all other beaſtsbeasts they are moſtmost inamored (as I may ſoso ſpeakespeak) with their mates, and eueneven mad againeagain in their heat and deſiredesire after them.

TheſeThese metaphors hath SalomonSolomon vſedused to ſetset forth that vnfainedunfeignedunfained
and earneſtearnest, intireentire and ardent affection which an husband ought to bearebear vntounto his wife: which being taken in a good ſenſesense, and rightly applied, ſoso as they exceed not the bonds of chriſtianchristian modeſtymodesty and decency, are very fit, and pertinent to the purpoſepurpose: if we ſtretchstretch them beyond modeſtymodesty, we wrong the pen-man of them, or rather the Holy GhoſtGhost that directed him, and propound a pernicious patternepattern vntounto husbands.

The attributes giuengiven to the forenamed creatures much amplifieamplify the point: the former is termed a louingloving Hind, the latter

TheſeThese compariſonscomparisons applied to a wife, doedo liuelylively ſetset forth that delight which an husband ought to take in her, and yet is it much further amplified by the hyperbole vſedused in this phraſephrase, be thou rauiſhtravishedravisht with her louelove, word for word erreerr thou in her louelove,

Secondly, ſoso highly to eſteemeesteem, ſoso ardently to affect, ſoso tenderly to reſpectrespect her, as others may thinkethink him eueneven to doatdote on her. div.p:

There can be no courteſiecourtesy in yeeldingyielding, when it is againſtagainst their mindemind and will forced from them: their wiueswives muſtmust askeask, and intreatentreat againeagain and againeagain, yea be forced to vſeuse the mediation of others to perſwadepersuade their huſbandshusbands to yeeldyield to their requeſtrequest before they will yeeldyield, if at all they yeeldyield. div.head: §. 23. Of husbands bitterneſſebitterness.
div.p: Contrary is bitterneſſebitterness, a vice expreſlyexpressly forbidden, and that in particular to husbands. A vice that cannot ſtandstand with an huſbandhusband-like louelove: whereupon the ApoſtleApostle commanding the one forbiddeth the other, Louelove (ſaithsaith he) and be not bitter. Nothing Col. 3 19. more turneth the edge of his authority, peruertethperverteth the vſeuse of his gouernmentgovernment, prouokethprovoketh the ſtomackestomach of his wife, maketh his words and deeds leſſeless regarded, then bitterneſſebitterness. It is as gall and wormwood mixed with ſweetsweet and wholeſomewholesome meats, which cauſethcauseth that they cannot be well digeſteddigested, but with violence are ſpitspit out againeagain ſoso ſoonesoon as euerever they be taſtedtasted. Men in authority are much prone hereunto: and therefore O husbands be ſoso much the more watchfullwatchful againſtagainst it, louelove your wiueswives and be not bitter vntounto them.

I doedo not deny but that in the Song of SalomonSolomon, and in other places of Scripture many titles are giuengiven and ſpeechesspeeches vſedused by ChriſtChrist to the Church which are not meet to be vſedused by husbands to their wiueswives, becauſebecause they are metaphoricallmetaphorical, and hyperbolicallhyperbolical: but yet in them all we may obſerueobserve tokens of amiableneſſeamiableness, kindneſſekindness, and mildneſſemildness, which is the end for which I hauehave alledgedalleged his example.

Note the vnderſtandingunderstanding and capacity of thy wife, and accordingly fit thine inſtructionsinstructions: if ſheshe be of meanemean capacity, giuegive precept vponupon precept, line vponupon line, here a little and there a little: a little at once oft giuengiven (namely eueryevery day ſomethingsomething) will ariſearise in time to a great meaſuremeasure, and ſoso ariſearise, as, together with knowledge of the thing taught, louelove of the perſonperson that teacheth will increaſeincrease.

div.head: §. 26. Of an husbands manner of Treat. 3. §. 43, 51, 52. 63, 64. &etcc. CommandementsCommandments to be ordered with mildneſſemildness. commanding his wife any thing.
div.p: 3. The commandementscommandments which an husband giuethgiveth to his wife, whether they be affirmatiueaffirmative (bidding her to doedo ſomethingsomething) or negatiuenegative (forbidding her to doedo this or that) muſtmust all be ſeaſonedseasoned with mildneſſemildness. For which end reſpectrespect muſtmust be had to the matter and manner of his commandementscommandments.

In regard of the matter the things which he commandeth What things he may command his wife. his wife to doedo, muſtmust be
1. Such as are indeed lawfulllawful and honeſthonest.
2. Such as ſheshe is perſwadedpersuaded to be ſoso.
3. Such as beſeemebeseem her place.
4. Such as are of weight and moment.

And on the contrary, the things which he forbiddeth muſtmust be
1. Such as are indeed vnlawfullunlawful to be done. What things he may forbid his wife.
2. Such as he can euidentlyevidently proueprove vntounto her to be vnlawfullunlawful.
3. Such as are vnbeſeemingunbeseeming her place.
4. Such as will hauehave ſomesome euillevil and miſchieuousmischievous effect if they be done.

1. To command a thing vnlawfullunlawful, or forbid a thing which ought to be done, is to bring his owneown authority into oppoſitionopposition with Gods: in which caſecase he bringeth his wife into this ſtraitstrait, either to reiectreject Gods commandementcommandment or his. How then can ſheshe thinkethink that her husband louethloveth her, when he bringeth her into ſuchsuch ſnaressnares and ſtraitsstraits, that ſheshe muſtmust needs fall into the gulfegulf of Gods diſpleaſuredispleasure, or knockeknock againſtagainst the rockerock of her husbands offence? MildneſſeMildness is farrefar from ſuchsuch commandementscommandments.

The like may be ſaidsaid of ſuchsuch things as to a wiueswives conſcienceconscience Such things as a wife maketh doubt of, not to be preſſedpressed vponupon her. ſeemeseem to be ſinnefullsinnefull, if they be enioynedenjoined to her; or her bounden duty, if they be forbidden: eſpeciallyespecially if ſheshe hauehave any ground for her conſcienceconscience out of Gods word. The conſcienceconscience is ſubiectsubject to God alone: if it be forced it will be a fearefullfearful horror, and a very hell in that party whoſewhose conſcienceconscience is forced: She that doubteth is condemned if ſheshe doedo that whereof Rom. 14. 23. ſheshe maketh doubt.

1. ObiectObject. In doubtfulldoubtful matters the commanding power Of what doubtfulldoubtful things the commanding power of a gouernourgovernor may be a warrant. of a gouernourgovernor is ſufficientsufficient warrant and ground to reſolueresolve the conſcienceconscience of them that are vnderunder authority.

AnſwAnsw. 1. In things meerelymerely doubtfulldoubtful concerning which the partieparty in ſubiectionsubjection hath not warrant out of Gods word one way or other, it may be ſoso. But when the conſcienceconscience doth not doubt and hang in ſuſpencesuspence, but is out of ſomesome ground taken from Gods word perſwadedpersuaded that that which is commanded is vnlawfullunlawful, or that which is forbidden is a bounden dutieduty, then to doedo this, or to leaueleave that vndoneundone, is to the party ſoso perſwadedpersuaded a ſinnesin: and this is the doubting (whereof the
ApoſtleApostle ſpeakethspeaketh) that condemneth a man. In this caſecase to vrgeurge a wife to doedo this, or not to doedo that, is to vrgeurge her to ſinnesin: which a mildemild ſpiritspirit and louingloving heart will not doedo.

2. Though the husbands command be ſufficientsufficient warrant to the wife, and if he peremptorily preſſepress her to this or that, ſheshe ought to yeeldyield, yet the louelove and mildneſſemildness required of an husband ſhouldshould make him ſoso to tender her as to remit ſomethingsomething of his power, and when he ſeethseeth her conſcienceconscience troubled about his command, to releeuerelieve her conſcienceconscience by for bearing to preſſepress that which ſeemethseemeth ſoso burthenſomeburdensomeburthensome to her. A husband may ſinnesin in preſſingpressing that too much vponupon his wife, which ſheshe vponupon his preſſingpressing may without ſinnesin yeeldyield vntounto.

He muſtmust firſtfirst labour to reſolueresolve her conſcienceconscience by a plaineplain diſcouerydiscovery of her error; which is a true and a great token of louelove: if notwithſtandingnotwithstanding all that he can doedo in that kindekind ſheshe cannot be brought to yeeldyield to that which he would hauehave, then he muſtmust carefully obſerueobserve theſethese two things.
1. Whether her refuſingrefusing to yeeldyield, be an obſtinacyobstinacy, or weakeneſſeweakness.
2. Whether it be about a ſleightslight or weighty matter.

By the reaſonsreasons which ſheshe rendrethrendereth, and her manner of preſſingpressing How a wiueswives refuſingrefusing to yeeldyield may be diſcerneddiscerned to be on obſtinacyobstinacy or weakeneſſeweakness. them, he may diſcernediscern whether weakeneſſeweakness or obſtinacyobstinacy make her ſtandstand out againſtagainst him: if the reaſonreason which ſheshe reſtethresteth on taken from Gods word be doubtfulldoubtful, and to one that hath not a good ſoundsound iudgementjudgment, and a ſharpesharpsharpe diſcerningdiscerning wit, it may appeareappear to make ſomethingsomething for her, it is to be preſuppoſedpresupposed that there is more weakeneſſeweakness then ſtoutneſſestoutness in her. But if ſheshe can render no good reaſonreason, but only take eueryevery ſhewshow that any way ſeemethseemeth to incline to her words, and peremptorily holdeth the concluſionconclusion, and ſtiflystifly ſtandethstandeth on her owneown reſolutionresolution, though the vanity of her pretences be euidentlyevidently diſcouereddiscovered to her, ſoso as ſheshe hath not any thing further to obiectobject;
or if ſheshe render no reaſonreason at all but her owneown thought, conceit and will, and yet refuſethrefuseth to yeeldyield, ſurelysurely obſtinacyobstinacy poſſeſſethpossesseth her heart. In caſecase of obſtinacyobstinacy it is very expedient that an husband ſtandstand vponupon his power to maintainemaintain his authority, and by the beſtbest wiſdomewisdom he can (vſingusing only ſuchsuch meanesmeans as are lawfulllawful) bring her to yeeldyield from her ſtoutneſſestoutness to that which he requireth: eſpeciallyespecially if the matter be weighty: as in caſecase a religious man hauehave been mariedmarried to a PopiſhPopish wife, and ſheshe by no reaſonreason will be mouedmoved to forbeareforbear going to MaſſeMass, or yeeldyield to goego to the preaching of the GoſpellGospel. But if through weakeneſſeweakness ſheshe cannot be perſwadedpersuaded of the lawfulneſſelawfulness of that her husband requireth, and the matter required be of no great conſequenceconsequence, nor the weakeneſſeweakness of her conſcienceconscience cauſecause any great error, an husband ought ſoso farrefar to manifeſtmanifest his mildneſſemildness as to forbeareforbear to preſſepress her conſcienceconscience.

div.p: 3. Things vnbeſeemingunbeseeming the place of a wife are diſhonourabledishonourable vntounto her: for an husband to vrgeurge his wife by ſtrictstrict charge to doedo them, implieth more rigorouſneſſerigorousness then mildneſſemildness. Had the ſpiritspirit of that ſtoutstout Monarch AhaſhueroſhAhashuerosh beenebeen more mildemild towards his wife, he would not hauehave ſoso farrefar preſſedpressed his wife vntounto ſoso vnſeemlyunseemly a thing as he did, namely, to come before all his Princes and people to make ſhewshow of her beautiebeauty. It is true indeed (as we ſhewedshowed Treat. 3. §. 28. before) that ſheshe offended in refuſingrefusing to yeeldyield thereunto, he peremptorily requiring it; but that offence on her part doth not juſtifiejustify his fact, and free him from all blame: it is noted, that he was merry with wine, when he gauegave that commandementcommandment, EſtEst. 1. 10. whereby is intimated, that his practiſepractise was more beſeemingbeseeming a drunken, then a ſobersober man: ſuchsuch is their practiſepractise who exact of their wiueswives to doedo ſuchsuch buſineſſesbusinesses as beſeemebeseem maid-ſeruantsservants rather then wiueswives, or ſtrumpetsstrumpets rather then honeſthonest women; as to goego to tauernestaverns, ale-houſeshouses, play-houſeshouses, and ſuchsuch places where light companions be.

div.head: §. 29. Of an husbands preſſingpressing his authoritieauthority in weighty matters.
div.p:
4. To vſeuse a mans authoritieauthority about weightieweighty matters, matters of moment, maketh it to hauehave ſuchsuch weight in it, as it will much better
be regarded: for thus a wife will either be brought to yeeldyield vntounto that which is commanded, or to condemnecondemn her ſelfeself for not yeeldingyielding: yea thus a wife may ſeesee, that it is not his owneown will ſoso much which maketh him to vſeuse his authoritieauthority in commanding, as the neceſſitienecessity of the thing it ſelfeself, which redoundeth eſpeciallyespecially to her good that doth it: for the performance of a dutieduty is for the moſtmost part moſtmost aduantageable to the partieparty that performeth it, ſoso as hereby an husband ſhewethshoweth louelove to his wife in preſſingpressing that which he preſſethpresseth.

This token of louelove that it may the better appeareappear, it is behouefullbehoveful ReaſonsReasons of preſſingpressing a cōmandementconmandement to be rendredrendered. that an husband addeadd to his commandementcommandment iuſtjust & weightieweighty reaſonsreasons, that thereby his wife may the better diſcernediscern the meetneſſemeetness, lawfulneſſelawfulness, expediencieexpediency, and neceſſitienecessity of the things commanded. We know that all the things which God commandeth are weightieweighty and neceſſarienecessary: yea his will (being the very rule, and ground of all goodneſſegoodness) maketh things abſolutelyabsolutely neceſſarienecessary, yet vntounto his commandementscommandments he vſethuseth to addeadd weightieweighty reaſonsreasons; ſhewingshowing on the one ſideside the benefit and bleſſedneſſeblessedness that will come to ſuchsuch as obey his commandementscommandments; and on the other ſideside, the miſchiefemischief and miſeriemisery that will fall on their pates who refuſerefuse to obey; whereby he ſhewethshoweth the great good reſpectrespect which he beareth to vsus, and the earneſtearnest deſiredesire he hath of our good. Thus may an husband eueneven in his commandementscommandments ſhewshow much louelove and kindneſſekindness.

div.head: §. 30. Of husbands too great pride in commanding.
div.p:
Contrary is the peremptorieperemptory pride of husbands, when they will hauehave their owneown will done: it booteth not whether the thing commanded be lawfulllawful or vnlawfullunlawful, whether their wiueswives conſciencesconsciences can yeeldyield vntounto it or no, whether it ſtandstand with the honour of their places or no, and whether it be weightieweighty or light; their will it is it ſhouldshould be done, and done it ſhallshall be, there is all the reaſonreason they will giuegive. Some thinkethink it a glory to command what they liſtlist; and thinkethink that there is no proofeproof of their authoritieauthority, and of their wiueswives ſubiectionsubjection, but in ſuchsuch things as vponupon their own will, without any further ground or reaſonreason, they command. If ſuchsuch husbands meet with confronts; if though they command much, they findefind not anſwerableanswerable performance; they may thankethank themſeluesthemselves,
who runnerun the ready courſecourse to hauehave their authoritieauthority contemned and eueneven troden vnderunder foot.

div.head: §. 31. Of husbands rare and mildemild vſingusing their commanding power.
div.p: ReſpectRespect muſtmust be had by husbands to the manner of vſingusing their authoritieauthority in commanding as well as to the matter.

In regard of the manner his commandementscommandments muſtmust be
1. Rare, not too frequent.
2. By way of intreating, not too peremptorieperemptory.

AuthoritieAuthority is like a ſwordsword, which with ouerover much vſingusing will 1. Commanding muſtmust be rare. be blunted, and ſoso failefail to doedo that ſeruiceservice which otherwiſeotherwise it might when there is moſtmost need. A wiſewise, grauegrave, peaceable man, may alwayesalways hauehave his ſwordsword in readineſſereadiness, and that alſoalso very bright, keenekeen, and ſharpesharpsharpe: but he will not be very ready to pluckepluck it out of his ſcabberdscabberd; he rather keepeth it for a time of need, when it ſhouldshould ſtandstand him in moſtmost ſteedsteed. Such husbands therefore as are too frequent in their commands, ſhewshow themſeluesthemselves nor grauegrave, nor wiſewise, nor louerslovers of peace.

As the vſeuse of an husbands authoritieauthority in commanding muſtmust be 2. Commanding muſtmust be by way of intreating. Philem. 9. rare, ſoso when there is occaſionoccasion to vſeuse it, it muſtmust be with ſuchsuch mildneſſemildness and moderation tempered, ſoso as (according to Saint Pauls example) though he hauehave power to command that which is conuenientconvenient, yet for louesloves ſakesake he rather intreatentreat it. Notenote how mildly Abram frameth his ſpeechspeech to his wife, Say I pray thee
Gen. 12. 13. (ſaithsaith he) thou art my ſistersister. Though the thing he required fauouredfavoured of too much weakneſſeweakness, yet his manner of requiring it was well beſeemingbeseeming a kindekind husband.

div.head: §. 32. Of husbands inſolencieinsolency and peremptorineſſeperemptoriness.
div.p:
Contrary is the inſolencieinsolency of many, who cannot ſpeakespeak to their wiueswives, but in commanding-wiſewise. Their authoritieauthority is like a ſwaggerersswaggerers ſwordsword, which cannot long reſtrest in the ſheathsheath, but vponupon eueryevery ſmallsmall occaſionoccasion is drawnedrawn forth. This frequent vſeuse of commanding, maketh their commandementscommandments nought regarded. The like may be ſaidsaid of them who are too peremptorieperemptory in commanding: there muſtmust be no ſayingsaying of nay, to that which they ſaysay: vponupon command they will hauehave their mindemind done, and no other way: no perſwaſionpersuasion, no intreatieintreaty ſhallshall be vſedused: they will rather not at all hauehave their will done, then not vponupon abſoluteabsolute command: nay they
will not ſuffersuffer others, in caſecase of any refuſallrefusal, to intreatentreat, or perſwadepersuade, but will try what abſolutelyabsolutely they can doedo by authoritieauthority. Thus as by trying to bend ſteelesteele how farrefar it will goego, it oft breaketh; ſoso by putting their authoritieauthority to the vttermoſtuttermost trialltrial, they oft loſelose all their authoritieauthority: in which caſecase the mends (as we ſpeakespeak) is in their owneown hands.

div.head: §. 33. Of an husbands Treat. 3. §. 47. Husbands ought to reprouereprove. reprouingreproving his wife.
div.p:
4. The authoritieauthority and charge which God hath giuengiven to an husband ouerover his wife, doedo require that as good and iuſtjust occaſionoccasion is offered, he ſhouldshould reprouereprove her: for this is an eſpeciallespecial meanesmeans to draw her from thoſethose ſinnessins, wherein otherwiſeotherwise ſheeshe might liuelive and lie, yea and die alſoalso; and ſoso liuelive, lie, and die vnderunder Gods wrath: out of which miſeriemisery and wretchedneſſewretchedness to free a wife, is as great a token of louelove, as to pull her out of the water when ſheshe is in danger of drowning, or out of the fire when ſheshe is in danger of burning. Solomon thus ſtilethstyleth reproofesreproofs, Pro. 15. 31. reproofesreproofs of life, and expreſlyexpressly noteth & 6. 23. reproofesreproofs to be the way of life, a meanesmeans to breed and preſeruepreserve ſpirituallspiritual life, and to bring one vntounto eternalleternal life, and ſoso to eſcapeescape death and damnation. In theſethese reſpectsrespects rebukes are called a pretiousprecious balmebalm, or excellent oyleoil, which may healeheal a wound, but make none: it PſalPsal. 141. 5. See the fruits of reproofereproof, Treat. 3. §. 47. breaketh not the head, as the PſalmiſtPsalmist ſpeakethspeaketh. VponUpon this ground, no doubt, it is noted of many good husbands, who were without all queſtionquestion, louingloving, kindekind, meekemeek, and mildemild husbands, that they reprouedreproved their wiueswives: as Gen. 30. 2. IaakobJacob,
IobJob 2. 10. IobJob, 2 Sam. 6. 21, 22. DauidDavid, and others.

div.head: §. 34. Of neglecting reproofereproof.
div.p:
Contrary is a ſeruileservile and timorous mindemind of many husbands, who are loth to offend, and (as they thinkethink) to prouokeprovoke their wiueswives; and thereupon chuſechoose rather to let them continue in ſinnesin, then tell them of it. Wherein they both diſhonourdishonour their place, and the image of God, which by vertuevirtue of their place they carry, and alſoalso in effect and in truth hate their wiueswives; which the Law implieth, where it ſaithsaith, Thou ſhaltshalt not hate thy brother in thine heart,
LeuitLevit. 19. 17. but ſhaltshalt plainly rebuke thy neighbour, and not ſuffersuffer ſinnesin vponupon him.

div.head: §. 35. Of Treat. 3. §. 47 An husbands reproofereproof muſtmust be ſweetnedsweetened with mildnesmildness. well ordering reproofereproof in the matter thereof.
div.p:
That an husband may euidentlyevidently demonſtratedemonstrate that his reprouingreproving of his wife is indeed a fruit of his louelove, he muſtmust hauehave an eſpeciallespecial
care to ſweetensweeten it, eſpeciallyespecially with mildneſſemildness: for it is the bittereſtbitterest pill that by an husband can be giuengiven to a wife. It is a verballverbal correction, & in that reſpectrespect a middle meanesmeans (as I may ſoso ſpeakespeak) betwixt admonition and correction; partaking ſomewhatsomewhat of both: it goeth no further then words, and ſoso is an admonition: the words of a reproofereproof are ſharpesharpsharpe, and ſoso it is a correction: though it be but a mildemild correction, yet it is a ſharpesharpsharpe admonition; and all the correction which by himſelfehimself an husband can giuegive his wife: for we ſhallshall §. 44. after ſhewshow that he may not proceed to blowesblows, and ſtrokesstrokes.
To ſweetensweeten reproofereproof with mildneſſemildness reſpectrespect muſtmust be had (as before was noted of commanding) both to the matter, and alſoalso to the manner thereof.

row.cell: The matter of reproofereproof muſtmust be Matter of reproofereproof. 1. IuſtJust.

div.p: IuſticeJustice requireth that it be a truth, and a knowneknown truth, eueneven a thing whereof he is aſſuredassured, for which he reprouethreproveth his wife. ChriſtChrist in giuinggiving direction for reprouingreproving aright, layeth downedown this as a ground, If thy brother ſhallshall treſpaſſetrespass, &etcc. a treſpaſſetrespass Matth. 18. 15. therefore muſtmust goego before reproofereproof: where no treſpaſſetrespass is, there reproofereproof is vniuſtunjust.

AgaineAgain, the ApoſtleApostle aduiſethadvisethaduiseth that an accuſationaccusation ſhouldshould not 1 Tim 5. 19. be receiuedreceived but vnderunder two, or three witneſſeswitnesses; whereby he implieth that a light report muſtmust not be receiuedreceived, but where blame is laid, there muſtmust be two or three witneſſeswitnesses to confirmeconfirm it, ſoso as he that cenſurethcensureth may hauehave good and ſuresure ground for that which he doth: indeed that aduiſeadvise was in particular giuengiven about an elder, but from the leſſeless to the greater it will follow to be a good aduiſeadvise concerning wiueswives: for no kindekind of perſonperson muſtmust be more wariewary in laying blame vponupon another and reproouingreprooving for the ſamesame, then an husband on his wife.

EquitieEquity further requireth that the matter for which an huſbandhusband 2. Weigh. y. reprouethreproveth his wife be weightieweighty; namely for ſomesome fault that is dangerous to her ſoulesoul, hurtfullhurtful to their eſtateestate, contagious by reaſonreason of ill example to children, and others in the family, but moſtmost of all for ſinnesin againſtagainst God which prouokethprovoketh his wrath, and pulleth downedown his heauieheavy curſecurse vponupon him, her, and the whole family.

When that for which a wife is reprouedreproved is a truth, a knowneknown
truth, and a weightieweighty truth, the husband in performing this dutieduty iuſtifiethjustifieth his deed, ſhewethshoweth that there was need thereof, and ſoso giuethgiveth euidenceevidence of his louelove, maketh his reproofereproof to pierce the more deeply, and ſoso maketh her the more aſhamedashamed of her fault; whence it will follow, that either ſheshe will amend her fault or at leaſtleast will hauehave her mouth ſtoppedstopped, ſoso as ſheshe ſhallshall hauehave nothing to except againſtagainst it. The reproofereproof of the three Saints before mentioned, Gen. 30. 2. IaakobJacob,
IobJob 2. 10. IobJob, and 2 Sam. 6. 21, 22. DauidDavid, were anſwerableanswerable to theſethese points of IuſticeJustice and wiſdomewisdom: and the effects thereof anſwerableanswerable to thoſethose which we hauehave noted in this reaſonreason, as the ſilencesilence of the three wiueswives implieth: for none of them replied againeagain.

div.head: §. 36. Of vndueundue reproofereproof.
div.p: Contrary to the forenamed IuſticeJustice and equitieequity are ouerlightoverlight Contrary, 1. CredulitieCredulity. credulitiecredulity and vndueundue ſuſpicionsuspicion. CredulitieCredulity is when credence is giuengiven to eueryevery light report, and thereupon blame laid vponupon the wife before any iuſtjust proofeproof be made of that for which ſheshe is blamed: whereby it oft commethcometh to paſſepass, that ſheshe is wrongfully and vniuſtlyunjustly blamed: which if ſheshe be, what good fruit can proceed from ſuchsuch reproofesreproofs? yeaYea what euillevil fruits are not like to proceed from thence, as ſecretsecret diſcontentdiscontent (if not malice and hatred) and open contentions and brawlings?

The like may be ſaidsaid of light and cauſeleſſecauseless ſuſpicionsuspicion, which 2. SuſpicionSuspicion. is the mother of iealouſiejealousy, and the very bane of mariagemarriage, from whence the deuilldevil taketh great aduantageadvantage againſtagainst them both, ſeekingseeking thereby to vnlooſeunloose that knot which God hath ſoso firmly knit betwixt them. SuſpicionSuspicion to the mindemind is as a coloured glaſſeglass to the eieeye, which repreſentethrepresenteth things to the ſightsight not as indeed they are in their owneown true colour, but as the colour of the glaſſeglass is. SuſpicionSuspicion will make a man peruertpervert eueryevery thing that his wife doth, and blame her many times for ſuchsuch things as are praiſepraise-worthy: in which caſecase what can be thought, but that an husband ſeekethseeketh aduantageadvantage againſtagainst his wife, rather then any good vntounto her?

If to thoſethose two forenamed vices (credulity and ſuſpicionsuspicion) he 3. RaſhneſſeRashness. a • ddeadd raſhneſſerashness and haſtineſſehastiness in reprouingreproving, and make eueryevery s • mall and light matter which any way he diſlikethdisliketh, matter of
reproofereproof, doth he not proclaimeproclaim to all that ſhallshall know it, that he louesloves chiding more then he louesloves his wife? Yea is not this the ready way to make all his reproofereproof (if not ſcornedscorned) lightly regarded? What then will be the profit of them?

div.head: §. 37. Whether an husband may reproouereproove his wife for ſuchsuch things as he is guilty of.
div.p:
To the matter of reproofereproof ſomesome addeadd, that an husband ought not to reprouereprove his wife for that fault whereof he himſelfehimself is guiltieguilty: but I make doubt of this direction. I deniedeny not but that he ought to hauehave an eſpeciallespecial care that he be not guiltieguilty of that crime for which he blameth his wife; otherwiſeotherwise, 1. heHe blunteth the edge of his reproofereproof, ſoso as readily it cannot peirce into her heart. 2. He cauſethcauseth it to rebound backeback againeagain vponupon himſelfehimself with theſethese reproches, PhyſitianPhysician healethy
Luk 4. 23. Mat. 7. 5. Rom. 2. 21. Rom. 2. 1. ſelfeself: Hypocrite firſtfirst caſtcast the beamebeam out of thine owneown eye. Thou that teacheſtteachest another teacheſtteachest thou not thy ſelfeself? 3. He is an heauyheavy witneſſewitness againſtagainst himſelfehimself; for in that he iudgethjudgeth another he condemneth himſelfehimself. But thereupon to infer, that becauſebecause he is guiltieguilty of ſuchsuch vices as are in his wife, he ought not to reprouereprove her though ſheshe be worthy to be reprouedreproved, is ſcarſescars ſoundsound and good diuinitiedivinity: for thus he maketh himſelfehimself guilty of a double fault, one of committing the ſinnesin himſelfehimself, the other of ſufferingsuffering his wife to lie therein: whereas if he reprouedreproved his wife, he might thereby reclaimereclaim both her and himſelfehimself: for I doubt not but his reprouingreproving of his wife would ſtrikestrike deeper into his owneown conſcienceconscience then if a third ſhouldshould reprouereprove them both. How were IudahJudah and DauidDavid ſtrokenstroken to Gen. 38. 26. 2 Sam. 12. 13. the heart after they had giuengiven ſentencesentence againſtagainst ſuchsuch crimes as they themſeluesthemselves were guiltieguilty of? It is a good aduiceadvice that no man be guiltieguilty of that which he reprouethreproveth in his wife, but it is no good rule to ſaysay, no man ought to reprouereprove his wife of that whereof he is guiltieguilty.

div.head: §. 38. Of well ordering reproofereproof in the manner thereof,
div.p: Like directions to thoſethose which were giuengiven for the manner Manner of reprouingreproving. of commanding muſtmust be obſeruedobserved in the manner of reprouingreproving.

When reproofesreproofs are ſeldomeseldom vſedused, not but vponupon vrgenturgent and 1. SeldomeSeldom.
neceſſarynecessary occaſionoccasion, 1. It ſhewethshoweth that an husband taketh no delight in rebuking his wife, but is eueneven forced thereto. 2. It maketh his wife much more regard it. 3. It is like to workework a more perfect cure, for ſeldomeseldom and rare reproofesreproofs doedo commonly peirce moſtmost deeply.

Contrary is continuallcontinual chiding, and finding fault with a Contrary, continuallcontinual chiding. wife for eueryevery thing amiſſeamiss: if not only the wife her ſelfeself, but a childechild, or ſeruantservant, or any elſeelse in the houſehouse doedo amiſſeamiss, the wife ſhallshall be blamed for it. This is too common a fault in huſbandshusbands: whereby they much prouokeprovoke their wiueswives; yea and many times make them no more regard a reproofereproof then any other word. For as birds which alwaiesalways abide in Belfries where much ringing is, are not a whit afrighted with their lowd ſoundsound; ſoso wiueswives who hauehave their earesears from time to time filled with their husbands rebuke, by vſeuse are brought, nothing at all to be mouedmoved therewith.

2. That a reproofereproof muſtmust be giuengiven in meekneſſemeekness is cleereclear by 2. ReproueReprove mildly. Gal 6. 1. the ApoſtlesApostles generallgeneral precept of reſtoringrestoring one in the ſpiritspirit of meekneſſemeekness: for a right manner of reprouingreproving is thereby particularly intended. Now of all with whom we hauehave to doedo, no fitter obiectobject for meekneſſemeekness then a wife, who in a more peculiar manner then any other is thine owneown fleſhflesh.
MeekneſſeMeekness hath reſpectrespect both to ſecreciesecrecy of place, and to ſoftneſſesoftness of words.

When an husband is alone with his wife, then is the fitteſtfittest 3. ReproueReprove in ſecretsecret. Mat. 18. 15. ſeaſonseason for reproofereproof: thus will reproofereproof be anſwerableanswerable to ChriſtsChrists direction: tell him his fault betweenebetween thee and him alone (ſaithsaith ChriſtChrist of a brother:) but no brother muſtmust be tendredtendered more then a wife. Thus will it alſoalso ſoakesoak better into her ſoulesoul, when no conceit of diſhonourdishonour and diſcreditdiscredit ſhallshall ariſearise vpup to hinder the workework of it: which conceits will be ready to ariſearise when a reproofereproof is giuengiven in publikepublic before others. Thus likewiſelikewise will occaſionoccasion be taken away from children and ſeruantsservants of deſpiſingdespising her: which otherwiſeotherwise they would quickly take, o • f before them ſheshe ſhouldshould be rebuked; gathering from thence, t • hat ſheshe is kept vnderunder as much as they: now becauſebecause ſheshe is with him a ioyntjoint gouernourgovernor of them, he ought by all meanesmeans to maintainemaintain her reputation before them.

div.head: 1. QueſtQuest. What if ſheshe regard not a rebuke in ſecretsecret? Direction for reprouingreproving ſuchsuch a wife as regardeth not a ſecretsecret reproofereproof. Mat. 18. 15.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. He may follow ChriſtsChrists direction, Take one or two more, namely wiſewise, grauegrave, faithfullfaithful friends, if it may be, of her kindred, as her parents (if ſheshe hauehave any liuingliving) or ſuchsuch as are in courſecourse of nature next to parents (if they be not partiallpartial on her ſideside) and before them rebuke her: but by no meanesmeans before any of the houſehouse vnderunder her gouernmentgovernment.

2. QueſtQuest. What if her fault be publickepublic, ſuchsuch an one as Direction for reprouingreproving a wife whoſewhose offence is publikepublic. may be an ill example to them of the houſehouse, it being committed in their ſightsight, or brought ſomesome other way to their knowledge?

AnſwAnsw. WiſelyWisely he muſtmust ſoso manifeſtmanifest his diſlikedislike of her fault, as he no way impaireimpair her honour: he may therefore declare that ſuchsuch a thing was not well done, and fore-warnewarn his houſholdhousehold of committing the like; yea roundly threaten them that if any of them doedo the like they ſhallshall dearely repent it; and if ſuchsuch as are vnderunder correction offend therein, the more ſurelysurely and ſeuerelyseverely correct them, eueneven becauſebecause they hauehave taken example. Thus ſhallshall he teſtifietestify a great good reſpectrespect of his wife, and alſoalso a thorowthorough diſlikedislike and hatred of her ſinnesin.

2. A ſoftsoft tongue (as SalomonSolomon noteth) breaketh the bones, 4. ReproueReprove gently. Pro. 25. 15. that is, ſoftnethsoftneth an hard heart, and beateth downedown a ſtoutstout ſtomackestomach. How will it then workework vponupon a ſoftsoft heart, and gentle diſpoſitiondisposition? If therefore an husband lookelook to doedo good by reprouingreproving his wife, his reproofereproof muſtmust be ſoso ordered, as it may ſeemeseem to be rather a gentle admonition, then a ſharpesharpsharpe rebuke. He may and ought plainly to declare her fault vntounto her, but in mildemild and meekemeek tearmesterms, without reuilingreviling, opprobrious and ignominious words.

div.head: QueſtQuest. What if her fault be an heinous notorious ſinnesin?
div.p:
AnſwAnsw. In an extraordinary caſecase ſomesome ſharpneſſesharpness may be A reproofereproof may be ſharpesharpsharpe not bitter. Gen. 30. 2. IobJob 2. 10. vſedused: as the reproofesreproofs of IaakobJacob, IobJob, and DauidDavid doedo ſhewshow, for they were eueryevery one of them ſharpesharpsharpe: but yet this ſharpneſſesharpness muſtmust not be made bitter by any euillevil language. A womans wickedneſſewickedness may not mouemove an husband to be froward, and 2 Sam. 6. 21, 22. Rebuke neuernever to be giuengiven by a man in paſſionpassion. outragious; but rather to be the more watchfullwatchful ouerover himſelfehimself, that he containecontain himſelfehimself within the bounds of diſcretiondiscretion and moderation. For which end it is meetemeet that husbands lay it
downedown for a rule, neuernever to rebuke their wiueswives when they are in paſſionpassion. PaſſionPassion raiſethraiseth a darkedark miſtmist before the eieseyes of reaſonreason; which, while it remaineth, keepeth reaſonreason from giuinggiving any good direction. Yea paſſionpassion is as a fire, and it ſoso incenſethincenseth a man, and diſtemperethdistempereth him, that in his diſorderdisorder he can keepekeep no meanemean or meaſuremeasure. HowſoeuerHowsoever a man be not able to rule himſelfehimself when paſſionpassion is ſtirredstirred vpup, yet, if before hand while his eieeye is ſinglesingle, and his whole body light, while he is in tune (as we Mat. 6. 22. ſpeakespeak) and well tempered, he reſoluedlyresoluedly determine with himſelfehimself not to doedo ſuchsuch or ſuchsuch a thing in his paſſionpassion; that fore-going reſolutionresolution will be an eſpeciallespecial means to make him forbeareforbear doing that in paſſionpassion, which if he ſhouldshould doedo, he could not in paſſionpassion well order and moderate. For if once he begin to doedo a thing in paſſionpassion, the leaſtleast prouocationprovocation that can be, will be as bellowesbellows to blow vpup that fire into a flame.

In regard of the violence of paſſionpassion (wherein women by Rebuke to be put off while a wife is in paſſionpassion. reaſonreason of the weakneſſeweakness of their iudgementjudgment are for the moſtmost part moſtmost violent) it is alſoalso the part of a wiſewise man to forbeareforbear this duty of reprouingreproving his wife eueneven when ſheshe is in paſſionpassion. For as it is needfullneedful that he ſhouldshould be in caſecase well to giuegive a reproofereproof, ſoso as needfullneedful it is that ſheshe ſhouldshould be in caſecase well to take a rebuke. PaſſionPassion both filleth and feſterethfestereth ones heart. The heart then being full of paſſionpassion, what roomeroom is left for good aduiceadvice? willWill a man powrepour wine into a veſſellvessel full of water, or ſtaystay, till all the water be dreaned out?
The heart alſoalso being ſoso feſteredfestered as it ſauourethsavoureth of nothing but paſſionpassion, what good can then good aduiceadvice doedo?

It is therefore an eſpeciallespecial point of wiſdomewisdom, and ſhewethshoweth a good reſpectrespect that a man beareth to his wife, yea it ſauourethsavoureth of much meekneſſemeekness and moderation for an husband, well to weigh both his owneown and his wiueswives temper when he reprouethreproveth her, and to forbeareforbear doing it while either he or ſheshe be in paſſionpassion.

div.head: §. 39. Of vndiſcreetundiscreet reproouingreprooving a wife.
div.p:
Contrary is the indiſcretionindiscretion of husbands who regard nor place, nor perſonspersons, nor time, nor temper of themſeluesthemselves or their wiueswives, nor any other circumſtancecircumstance in reprouingreproving, but like Saul (who at a table where a great feaſtfeast was, in preſencepresence of his Nobles
and CaptainesCaptains, when he was inraged with anger, with moſtmost virulent and bitter ſpeechesspeeches not rebuked onelyonly but reproached alſoalso his ſonneson, and that with ſuchsuch words as he ſparedspared not his owneown wife; for in his paſſionpassion he called his ſonneson, ſonneson 1 Sam. 20. 30. of the peruerſeperverse rebellious woman:) like this fooliſhfoolish and furious Saul, I ſaysay, they take the moſtmost open place of the family before children, ſeruantsservants, and whole houſehouse, to reprouereprove their wiueswives; and that with ſuchsuch bitter and diſgracefulldisgraceful termesterms, as either they prouokeprovoke their wiueswives to anſweranswer againeagain for maintaining (as they thinkethink) their owneown credit and reputation, (thus IonathanJonathan 1 Sam. 20. 32. was prouokedprovoked to anſweranswer his father againeagain:) or elſeelse giuegive them of the houſehouse that behold her thus trampled vnderunder foot, occaſionoccasion to ſetset their feet alſoalso vponupon her.

MoſtMost husbands are forward enough to reprouereprove, but few doedo it in meekneſſemeekness, and moderation. They cannot doedo it but in company, nor without bitter words. Many in rebuking their wiueswives, ſtickestick not to vſeuse all the euillevil termesterms that they can thinkethink of, eueneven ſuchsuch as tend not only to their wiueswives diſhonourdishonour, but alſoalso to their owneown and their childrens infamy. The reaſonreason whereof is, becauſebecause they neuernever rebuke but when they are in paſſionpassion, and ſoso ſcarſescars know what they doedo: whereby alſoalso they ſtirrestir vpup paſſionpassion in their wiueswives, and yet for all that refrainerefrain not any whit the more, but rather grow more violent: as when the heat of two fires meet together, the flame muſtmust needs be the greater. This being the prepoſterouspreposterous practiſepractise of many husbands, is it any maruellmarvelmarvell that ordinarily ſoso little good, and ſoso much hurt is done by reprouingreproving? Nay, would it not be a wonder, if any good, and no hurt ſhouldshould be done thereby? This therefore though it be a duty, yet a dutieduty rarely and with great moderation to be vſedused.
Thus farrefar of an husbands mildneſſemildness in his ſpeechesspeeches to his wife.

div.p: An husbands cariagecarriage towards his wife muſtmust be anſwerableanswerable An husbands cariagecarriage muſtmust be mildemild. to his ſpeechspeech, or elſeelse all the mildneſſemildness thereof will ſeemeseem but complementallcomplemental.

1. His countenance in his wiueswives preſencepresence, and towards his 1. A mildemild countenance. wife, muſtmust be compoſedcomposed to an amiable pleaſantneſſepleasantness. His authority ouerover her, and eminencieeminency aboueabove her, may not make him forget the neerenear coniunctionconjunction and vnionunion betwixt them.

VnderUnder the face and countenance I compriſecomprise head, brow, eieseyes, lips and ſuchsuch other parts which are, according as they are framed, ſignessigns of amiableneſſeamiableness, or diſcontentedneſſediscontentedness. Now among, and aboueabove other parts of the body, the outward compoſitioncomposition of the countenance doth ſooneſtsoonest and beſtbest declare the inward diſpoſitiondisposition of the heart. By EſausEsaus pleaſantpleasant countenance IaakobJacob perceiuedperceived that he was pacified in his heart towards him, and thereupon ſaidsaid, I hauehave ſeeneseen thy face as though I had
Gen. 33. 10. ſeeneseen the face of God, that is, an amiable, gracious countenance. On this ground DauidDavid deſireddesired God, to lift vpup the light of his
PſalPsal. 4. 6. countenance vponupon him, that thereby he might know the fauourfavour and louelove of God towards him. On the other ſideside by a frowning and lowringlouring face, by hanging downedown the head, putting out the lips, with the like, anger, malice, griefegrief, with other like affections of heart, are manifeſtedmanifested: by CainesCains caſtingcasting downedown Gen. 4. 6. of his countenance God diſcerneddiscerned anger and enuyenvy to be in his heart: by Labans countenance IaakobJacob obſeruedobserved that his affection Gen. 31. 2. was turned from him. A wife then beholding mildneſſemildness and amiableneſſeamiableness in her husbands face, beholds it as the face of God, and therein as in a looking glaſſeglass beholds the kindneſſekindness and louelove of his heart, and ſoso hath her heart thereby the more firmelyfirmly knit vntounto him, and is mouedmoved the more to reſpectrespect him.

div.p: Contrary is 1. A loftielofty proud countenance, as of an imperious Contrary. 1. A lofty brow. Lord ouerover his vaſſalsvassals.
2. A grim ſternesterne countenance, as of a iudgejudge ouerover poorepoor priſonersprisoners. 2. A grim lookelook.

TheſeThese and ſuchsuch like countenances as they manifeſtmanifest a proud, ſtoutstout, furious diſcontenteddiscontented diſpoſitiondisposition of heart, ſoso they cannot but giuegive great diſcontentdiscontent to a wife, yea and much affright her being but a weakeweak veſſellvessel, and alienate her heart and affection from him.

div.head: §. 42. Of an husbands familiar geſturegesture with his wife.
div.p: II. An husbands geſturegesture ought to be ſoso familiar, and amiable 2. Mild geſluregeslure. towards his wife, as others may diſcernediscern him to be her husband, and his wife may be prouokedprovoked to be familiar with him. They which this way are ready to ſhewshow themſeluesthemselves kind and mildemild husbands, are prone to exceed and ſoso to fall into an extreame on the right hand: for ſomesome are neuernever well but when they hauehave their wiueswives in their laps, euerever colling, kiſſingkissing, and dallying with them, they care not in what company; thus they ſhewshow more lightneſſelightness, fondneſſefondness, and dotage, then true kindneſſekindness and louelove, which forgettethforgeteth not an husband-like grauitygravity, ſobrietysobriety, modeſtymodesty and decency.
Some ſtickestick not to alledgeallege IſaacksIsaacks ſportingsporting with RebeckahRebekah, to ObiectObject. countenance their laſciuiouſneſſelasciviousness. Gen. 26. 8.

But they forget that what IſaakIsaac did, was when he and his AnſwAnsw. wife were alone: he was ſeeneseen through a window. Much greater liberty is granted to man and wife when they are alone, then in company. BeſidesBesides there are many other waiesways to ſhewshow kindneſſekindness and familiarity, then by lightneſſelightness and wantonneſſewantonness.

div.head: §. 43. Of an husbands ſtrangeneſſestrangeness to his wife.
div.p:
Contrary to the familiaritiefamiliarity I ſpeakespeak of, is (as we ſpeakespeak) ſtrangeneſſestrangeness, when an husband ſoso carrieth himſelfehimself towards his wife as if ſheshe were a ſtrangerstranger to him: if he come in cōpanyconpany where his wife is, of all other women he will not turneturn to her, nor take notice of her. This fault is ſoso much the greater if ſuchsuch a man be of a free pleaſantpleasant cariagecarriage, and vſeuse to be merry and familiar with other women. Though his mirth and familiarity be ſuchsuch as is not vnbeſeemingunbeseeming a ChriſtianChristian, yet his cariagecarriage being of another temper towards his wife, it may be a meanesmeans to breed iealouſiejealousy in her. Many thinkethink outward kindekind geſturegesture towards
wife to be fondneſſefondness, but if they knew what a meanesmeans it is to ſtirrestir vpup, increaſeincrease, and preſeruepreserve louelove in a wiueswives heart to her husband, they would be otherwiſeotherwise minded.

div.head: §. 43. Of an husbands giuinggiving fauoursfavours to his wife.
div.p: III. Actions are of all other the moſtmost reallreal demonſtrationsdemonstrations of true kindneſſekindness, wherein an husband muſtmust not failefail, as he would hauehave his kindekind ſpeechspeech, countenance, and geſturegesture to be taken in the better part. KindneſſeKindness and mildneſſemildness in action conſiſtethconsisteth in giuinggiving fauoursfavours (as we ſpeakespeak) vntounto his wife. This is expreſlyexpressly noted in Elkanah, who eueryevery yeereyear gauegave fauoursfavours to 1 Sam. 1. 4, 5. his wiueswives. Thus an husband as he teſtifiethtestifieth his louelove to his wife, ſoso he will much prouokeprovoke her to doedo all duty to him. A ſmallsmall gift, as an action of kindneſſekindness freely giuengiven, not vponupon any debt, but in teſtimonytestimony of louelove, doth more workework on the heart of her to whom it is giuengiven, then much more giuengiven vponupon contract, or for a workework done, whereby it may ſeemeseem to be deſerueddeserved.

In giuinggiving fauoursfavours to a wife, an husband ought to be more bountifullbountiful and liberallliberal, then to others, that ſoso ſheshe may ſeesee thereby he louesloves her aboueabove all; as it is noted that Elkanah gauegave AnnahHannah a worthy portion, becauſebecause he louedloved her. And in giuinggiving 1 Sam. 1. 4. fauoursfavours it is beſtbest to beſtowbestow them with his owneown hands, vnleſſeunless he be abſentabsent from her.

div.head: §. 44. Of husbands beating their wiueswives.
div.p: Contrary are the furious, and ſpightfullspiteful actions of many vnkindeunkind husbands (heads too heady) whoſewhose fauoursfavours are buffets, Vipera virus ob venerationem nuptiarum euomit. Et tu duritiem animi, tuferitatem, tu crudelitatem ob vnionis reuerentiam non deponis? BaſilBasil. Hexaem. hom. 7. Ambr. Hexaem. l. 5. c. 7. vrget hanc ipſamipsam ſimilitudinemsimilitudinem. blowesblows, ſtrokesstrokes, & ſtripesstripes: wherein they are worſeworse then the venemous viper. For the viper for his mates ſakesake caſtethcasteth out his poiſonpoison: and wilt not thou, ô husband, in reſpectrespect of that neerenear vnionunion which is betwixt thee and thy wife, lay aſideaside thy fierceneſſefierceness and cruelty? Many wiueswives by reaſonreason of their huſbandshusbands furiefury, are in worſeworse caſecase then ſeruantsservants: for
1. Such as will not giuegive a blow to a ſeruantservant, care not what load they lay vponupon their wiueswives.
2. Where ſeruantsservants hauehave but a time and termeterm to be vnderunder the tyranny of ſuchsuch furious men, poorepoor wiueswives are tied to them all their life long.
3. WiuesWives can not hauehave ſoso good remedy by the helpehelp of law againſtagainst cruellcruel husbands, as ſeruantsservants may hauehave againſtagainst cruellcruel maſtersmasters.

4. MaſtersMasters hauehave not ſuchsuch opportunity to exerciſeexercise their cruelty ouerover ſeruantsservants as husbands ouerover wiueswives, who are to be continually at boord and bed with their husbands.

5. The neerernearer wiueswives are, and the dearer they ought to be to their husbands, the more grieuousgrievous muſtmust ſtroakesstrokes needs be when they are giuengiven by an husbands hand, then by a maſtersmasters. HuiuſmodiHuiusmodi virum (ſiquidemsiquidem vir appellandus eſtest potius quàm fera) & patricidae, & matricidae ſimilemsimilem dixeris. ChryſChrys. hom. 26. in 1 Cor. 11.

6. The leſſeless power and authority that an husband hath to ſtrikestrike his wife, then a maſtermaster to ſtrikestrike a ſeruantservant, the more heauieheavy doedo his ſtroakesstrokes ſeemeseem to be, and the worſeworse doth the caſecase of a wife ſeemeseem to be in that reſpectrespect, then of a ſeruantservant. Not vnfitlyunfitly therefore is ſuchsuch a man (if he may be thought a man rather then a beaſtbeast) ſaidsaid to be like a father-queller and mother-queller.

div.head: QueſtQuest. May not then an husband beat his wife? An husband may not beat his wife.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. With ſubmiſſionsubmission to better iudgementsjudgments, I thinkethink he may not: my reaſonsreasons are theſethese.

1. There is no warrant thorowoutthroughout the whole Scripture ReaſonsReasons. 1. No warrant in the word. by precept, or example for it: which argument though it be negatiuenegative, yet for the point in hand is a forceableforcible argument in two reſpectsrespects. 1. BecauſeBecause the Scripture hath ſoso plentifully and particularly declared the ſeuerallseveral duties of husbands and wiueswives: and yet hath deliuereddelivered nothing concerning an huſbandshusbands ſtrikingstriking and beating his wife. 2. BecauſeBecause it hath alſoalso plentifully and particularly ſpoakenspoaken of all ſuchsuch as are to correct, and of their manner of correcting, and of their bearing correction who are to be corrected, and of the vſeuse they are to make thereof; and yet not any thing at all concerning an husbands puniſhingpunishing, or a wiueswives bearing in this kindekind. The Scripture being ſoso ſilentsilent in this point, we may well inferreinfer that God hath not ranked wiueswives among thoſethose in the family who are to be corrected.

2. That ſmallsmall diſparitydisparity which (as I hauehave §. 4. before ſhewedshowed) is 2. Small diſparitydisparity. betwixt man and wife, permittethpermiteth not ſoso high a power in an husband, and ſoso low a ſeruitudeservitude in a wife, as for him to beat her. Can it be thought reaſonablereasonable that ſheshe who is the mans
perpetuallperpetual bed-fellow, who hath power ouerover his body, who Summa iniuria eſtest vitae ſociamsociam, & in rebus neceſſarijsnecessarijs tibi coniunctam, taquàm mancipium ignominia affioere. ChryſChrys. ibid. is a ioyntjoint parent of the children, a ioyntjoint gouernourgovernor of the family, ſhouldshould be beaten by his hands? What if children or ſeruantsservants ſhouldshould know of it? (as they muſtmust needs: for how can ſuchsuch a thing be done in the houſehouse and they of the houſehouse know it not?) can they reſpectrespect her as a mother, or a miſtreſſemistress who is vnderunder correction as well as they?

3. The neerenear coniunctionconjunction, and very vnionunion that is betwixt 3. NeereNear coniunctionconjunction. man and wife ſufferethsuffereth not ſuchsuch dealing to paſſepass betwixt them. The wife is as a mans ſelfeself, Eph. 5. 31. They two are one fleſhflesh. No man but a frantike, furious, deſperatdesperat wretch will beat himſelfehimself. Two ſortssorts of men are in Scripture noted to cut and lanch their owneown fleſhflesh, idolaters, as the 1 King. 18. 28. Baalites, and Daemoniacks, as Mar. 5. 5. he that was poſſeſſedpossessed with a legion of deuilsdevils. Such are they who beat their wiueswives, either blinded in their vnderſtandingunderstanding, or poſſeſſedpossessed with a deuilldevil.
ObiectObject. He that is beſtbest in his wits will ſuffersuffer his body to be pinched, pricked, lanched, and otherwiſeotherwise pained, if it be needfullneedful and behoofull.

AnſwAnsw. 1. A mans heart will not ſuffersuffer him to doedo any of theſethese himſelfehimself: their are Chirurgions whoſewhose office it is to doedo ſuchsuch things: if the ChirurgionSurgeon himſelfehimself hauehave need of any ſuchsuch remedy for his owneown body, he will vſeuse the helpehelp of another ChirurgionSurgeon. If the caſecase ſoso ſtandstand as a wife muſtmust needs be beaten, it is fitter for an husband to referrerefer the matter to a publikepublic MagiſtrateMagistrate (who is as an approuedapproved and licenſedlicensed ChirurgionSurgeon) and not to doedo it with his owneown hands.
2. Though ſomesome parts of the body may be ſoso dealt withallwithal, yet eueryevery part may not, as the heart, which the wife is to the man.

3. The compariſoncomparison holdeth not. For the fore-named pinching, lanching, &etcc. is no puniſhmentpunishment for any fault, as the beating of a wife in queſtionquestion is, there is no queſtionquestion but a man that hath skill may if need be open a veinevein, lanch a boileboil, ſplintersplinter a broken bone, or diſioynteddisioynted ioyntjoint in his wiueswives body, which may be more painfullpainful then correction: and herein the compariſoncomparison holdeth, but not in the other.

2. ObiectObject. There is as neerenear a coniunctionconjunction betwixt ChriſtChrist
and his Church, as betwixt man and wife: yet ChriſtChrist for beareth not to correct and puniſhpunish his Church.

AnſwAnsw. There is a double relation betwixt ChriſtChrist and the Church: he is an husband vntounto it, hauinghaving made it of his fleſhflesh, and of his bones: and a ſupremesupreme Lord ouerover it, hauinghaving all power
Eph. 5. 30. Mat. 28. 18. in heauenheaven and earth committed vntounto him. In this latter reſpectrespect he puniſhethpunisheth, not in the former. An husband is not ſuchsuch a ſupremesupreme Lord ouerover his wife: therefore ChriſtsChrists example, is no warrant to him.

4. There is no hope of any good to proceed from an huſbandshusbands 4. No profit: much miſchiefemischief. beating of his wife: for where the party corrected is perſwadedpersuaded that the party which correcteth hath no authority or right ſoso to doedo, it will not be brought patiently to take it: but will reſiſtresist, and ſtriuestrive if it be poſſiblepossible to get the maſterymastery. Let a ſtrangerstranger ſtrikestrike ſuchsuch a childechild of yeeresyears or a ſeruantservant as will patiently bearebear many ſtroakesstrokes at a parents or maſtersmasters hand, they will turneturn againeagain at that ſtrangerstranger, and indeauourindeavour to giuegive him as good as he brings: now a wife hauinghaving no ground to be perſwadedpersuaded that her husband hath authority to Adhibitis verberibus morbus non tollitur, ſedsed augetur, & exaſperaturexasperatur. Melch. Iun. quaeſtquaest. Polit. par. 2. beat her, what hope is there that ſheshe will patiently bearebear it, and be bettered by it? Or rather is it not likely that ſheshe will, if ſheshe can, riſerise againſtagainst him, ouerover-maſtermaster him (as many doedo) and neuernever doedo any duty aright? A fault in a wife is not taken away but increaſedincreased by blowesblows.

div.head: ObiectObject. Smart and painepain may make her dread her husband, ſtandstand in awe of him, and doedo her duty the better.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. Such dread and awe beſeemesbeseems neither the place of an husband to exact it, nor the place of a wife to yeeldyield it. Though perforce ſheshe may be brought to yeeldyield ſomesome outward ſubiectionsubjection, yet inward hatred of her husbands perſonperson may be ioynedjoined therewith, which is as bad, if not worſeworse then outward diſobediencedisobedience.

div.head: ObiectObject. She may be of ſoso outragious a diſpoſitiondisposition, as, but by Nullum ſitsit tam magnum peccatum, quod ad verberandum vxorem compellat. ChryſChrys. hom. 26. in 1 Cor. 11. force, ſheshe will not be kept in any compaſſecompass.
div.p: 1. AnſwAnsw. It hath beenebeen of old time anſweredanswered, that no fault ſhouldshould be ſoso great, as to compellcompel an husband to beat his wife.

2. AnſwAnsw. Other forceableforcible meanesmeans may be vſedused beſidesbesides beating by her husbands hands: ſheshe may be reſtrainedrestrained of libertieliberty, denied ſuchsuch things as ſheshe moſtmost affecteth, be kept vpup, as it were, in hold;
and, if no other meanesmeans will ſerueserve the turneturn, be put ouerover to the MagiſtratesMagistrates hands, that if ſheshe be of ſoso ſeruileservile a diſpoſitiondisposition, as by no other meanesmeans ſheshe will be kept vnderunder then by fearefear and force, by ſmartsmart and painepain, ſheshe may fearefear the MagiſtrateMagistrate, and feelefeel his hand, rather then her husbands.
ObiectObject. If a wife waxewax ſoso manniſhmannish, or rather mad, as to offer to ſtrikestrike and beat her husband, may he not in that caſecase beat her to make her ceaſecease her outrage?

AnſwAnsw. I doubt not but that that good prouiſionprovision which is made in law to preſeruepreserve a mans life, may be applied to this purpoſepurpose. The law ſimplysimply condemnescondemns all murthermurder; yet if a man be ſoso aſſaultedassaulted, as there is no way to preſeruepreserve his owneown life, but by taking away his life that aſſaultsassaults him, it condemneth not him as a murtherermurderer, becauſebecause he did it in defence of himſelfehimself. So if an huſbandhusband Sedefendendo. be ſetset vponupon by his wife, it is lawfulllawful and expedient that he defend himſelfehimself, and if he can doedo it no other wayesways but by ſtrikingstriking her, that is not to be reckoned an vnlawfullunlawful beating her.

div.head: §. 45. Of an husbands bearing with his wines infirmities.
div.q: Hither to of the husbands auoidingavoiding of offence, a word concerning his bearing with offence.
div.p:
A generallgeneral dutieduty it is, common to all of all ſortssorts, to bearebear one
Gal. 6. 2. anothers burden: in which extent eueneven a wife is to bearebear her huſbandshusbands burden, becauſebecause he, as eueryevery one elſeelse, is ſubiectsubject to ſlipslip and fall, and ſoso hath need to be ſupportedsupported. Yet after a more ſpeciallspecial and peculiar manner doth this dutieduty belong to an husband, and that in two reſpectsrespects.

1. Of the two, he is more bound then his wife, becauſebecause in relation to his wife he is the ſtrongerstronger: for ſheshe is the weaker veſſellvessel,
ConſideraConsidera mulierem debile vas eſſeesse: tu autem vir propterea princeps factus es, vt ſubditaesubditae feras imbecillitatem. ChryſChrys. hom. 26. in 1. Cor. 11. 1. Pet. 3. 7. But the ſtrongstrong are moſtmost bound to bearebear with the infirmities of the weakeweak, Rom. 15. 1.

2. He is bound to bearebear with his wife more then with any other, becauſebecause of that neerenear coniunctionconjunction which is betwixt them: he that cannot bearebear with his wife, his fleſhflesh, can bearebear with no bodiebody. The reaſonreason alleagedalleged by the ApoſtleApostle to mouemove a man to dwell with his wife according to knowledge, and to giuegive honour to her, intimated in this phraſephrase, as to the weaker veſſellvessel, ſhewethshoweth that this is a peculiar dutieduty belonging to an husband, wherein, and whereby he 1. Pet. 3. 7.
may both manifeſtmanifest his knowledge and wiſdomewisdom, and alſoalso doedo honour to his wife. For why is he put in mindemind of her weakneſſeweakness, but to ſhewshow he ſhouldshould bearebear with her?

As that phraſephrase intimateth the dutieduty, ſoso alſoalso it intimateth a good reaſonreason to inforceenforce it. For pretiousprecious things, whereof we make high account, the weaker they be, the more tenderly, and charily are they handled, as Cheney diſhesdishes, and chriſtallchristall glaſſesglasses: and of all parts of the bodiebody, the eye is moſtmost tenderly handled. Now what things, what perſonspersons are more dearedear and pretiousprecious then a wife? yetYet withallwithal ſheshe is a weakeweak veſſellvessel: therefore ſheshe is much to be borne withallwithal.

For an husbands better direction herein, difference muſtmust be Directions to husbands for bearing with their wiueswives infirmities. made betwixt infirmities: for ſomesome are naturallnatural imperfections, other are actuallactual tranſgreſſionstransgressions. NaturallNatural imperfections are inward, (as ſlowneſſeslowness in conceit, dulneſſedulness in apprehenſionapprehension, ſhortneſſeshortness of memoriememory, haſtineſſehastiness in paſſionpassion, &etcc.) or outward, (as lameneſſelameness, blindneſſeblindness, deafneſſedeafness, or any other defect, and deformitiedeformity of bodiebody.) TheſeThese infirmities ſhouldshould breed pitiepity, compaſſioncompassion, commiſerationcommiseration, yea and greater tenderneſſetenderness and reſpectrespect, but no offence. Note AbrahamsAbraham's example in this caſecase: his wife was barren, yet he deſpiſeddespised Neque Saram tanquam ſterilemsterilem contempſitcontempsit Abraham: ne •
