Uxor iracunda &etcc. admonenda & adiuvanda conſilioconsilio, & omni conatu anniten. dum, vt illis liberetur affectibus, Ibid. her not for it, nor vpbraidedupbraided her with any ſuchsuch thing.

ActuallActual tranſgreſſionstransgressions are breaches of Gods law: whereof ſuchsuch are here ment, as are moſtmost directly tending to his owneown diſquietdisquiet, and diſaduantagedisadvantage, as ſhrewiſhneſſeshrewishness, waiwardneſſewaiwardness, niceneſſeniceness, ſtubbornneſſestubbornness, &etcc. In the bearing of theſethese muſtmust an husband eſpeciallyespecially ſhewshow his wiſdomewisdom, and that ſundrysundry wayesways.

1. By vſingusing the beſtbest and mildeſtmildest meanesmeans he can to redreſſeredress them, as meekemeek admonition, ſeaſonableseasonable aduiceadvice, gentle intreatieintreaty, and compaſſionatecompassionate affection. Elkanah ſuppoſingsupposing that his wife offended in her paſſionpassion, thus dealt with her and ſupportedsupported her.

2. By remouingremoving the ſtonestone whereat ſheshe ſtumblethstumbleth, by taking away the occaſionoccasion (ſoso far as conuenientlyconveniently he can) which maketh her offend. Thus Abram, and that by Gods aduiceadvice, put Hagar and her ſonneson out of the houſehouse, becauſebecause they were an offence to Sarah.

3. By turning his eyes away (if the matter be not great, but 1 Sam. 1. 8. Gen. 21. 14. ſuchsuch as may be tolerated) and taking no notice of the offence, but rather paſſingpassing by it, as if he perceiuedperceived it not. Solomon ſaithsaith, that
it is a mans glory to paſſepass ouerover a tranſgreſſiontransgression: and he exhorteth a ProuProv. 19. 11. Eccl 7. 23. man not to giuegive his heart to all the words that men ſpeakespeak.

4. By forgiuingforgiving and forgetting it (if notice be taken thereof.) IaakobJacob tooketook notice of Rachels raſhrash, and froward demand, for he Gen. 30. 1. 2, &etcc. rebuked her for it: yet in that he readily yeeldedyielded to that which afterwards ſheshe mouedmoved him vntounto, it appeareth that he forgaueforgave the offence, if not forgat it.

The beſtbest trialltrial of a mans affection to his wife, and of his wiſdomewisdom ReaſonReason. BeſtBest tryalltrial of a mans wiſdomewisdom & louelove. in ordering the ſamesame, is in this point of bearing with offences. Not to be offended with a wife that giuethgiveth no offence is not praiſepraise-worthy: heathen men may goego ſoso farrefar. Note what ChriſtChrist ſaithsaith of this caſecase, If yeeye louelove them which louelove you, and doedo good to
Matth. 5. 46. Luk. 6. 32, 33. them that doedo good to you, what thanks and reward hauehave ye? forFor publicans, and ſinnerssinners doedo the ſamesame: but gently to forbeareforbear, and wiſelywisely to paſſepass ouerover offences when they are giuengiven, not to be prouokedprovoked when there is cauſecause of prouocationprovocation miniſtredministered, is a true ChriſtianChristian vertuevirtue, a vertuevirtue beſeemingbeseeming husbands better then any other kindekind of men.

div.head: §. 46. Of husbands teſtineſſetestiness.
div.p:
Contrary is teſtineſſetestiness, and peeuiſhneſſepeevishness, when husbands are mouedmoved with the leaſtleast prouocationprovocation, like tinder catching fire at the leaſtleast ſparkespark that falleth vponupon it: yea many are like gunpowder, which not only taketh fire, but alſoalso breaketh out into a violent flame, vponupon the leaſtleast touch of fire: as gunpowder is dangerous to be kept in an houſehouse, ſoso ſuchsuch husbands to be ioynedjoined ſoso neerelynearly to wiueswives as mariagemarriage ioynethjoinethjoyneth them. If it be ſaidsaid, that as gunpowder doth no hurt, if fire come not at it; ſoso they are good and kindekind, if they be not prouokedprovoked and diſpleaſeddispleased. I anſweranswer, that we hauehave a prouerbeproverb that ſaithsaith, The deuilldevil is good while he is pleaſedpleased, yet it is not ſafesafe to hauehave the deuilldevil too neerenear. It is as impoſſibleimpossible (conſideringconsidering mans weakneſſeweakness) that he ſhouldshould liuelive and conuerſeconverse with any, and not giuegive offence, as for flint ſtonesstones long to beat and daſhdash againſtagainst one another, & no ſparkespark of fire to come from them. How then may it be thought poſſiblepossible for a wife, who is ſoso continually conuerſantconversant with her husband, and the weaker veſſellvessel, to liuelive without giuinggiving him offence? It is no very kindekind ſpeechspeech, which huſbandshusbands vſeuse, eſpeciallyespecially if they be told of their vnkindneſſeunkindness, Let my wife deſeruedeserve fauourfavour, and ſheshe ſhallshall hauehave it. How little fauourfavour would
ſuchsuch husbands hauehave of ChriſtChrist their husband, if he ſhouldshould be of that mindemind towards them?
Thus farrefar hath beenebeen handled the firſtfirst part of an husbands well managing his authoritieauthority, by a tender reſpectrespect of his wife.
The ſecondsecond is a prouidentprovident care for her.

div.head: §. 46. Of an husbands prouidentprovident care for his wife.
div.p: An husband that tenderly reſpectethrespecteth his wife, but prouidentlyprovidently careth not for her, ſhewethshoweth more affection then diſcretiondiscretion: he may hauehave a kindekind heart, but he wants a wiſewise head. How then can he be a good head vntounto his wife? Some preſentpresent contentment ſheshe may hauehave by him: but ſmallsmall profit and benefit can ſheshe reapereap from him. ThoſeThose duties therefore which hauehave beenebeen deliuereddelivered muſtmust be done, but theſethese that follow muſtmust by no meanesmeans be left vndoneundone.

An husbands prouidentprovident care is noted in that office of ChriſtChrist, wherein an husband reſemblethresembleth him, namely, to be a SauiourSaviour of
Eph. 5. 23. the bodiebody, as hath beenebeen Treat. 1. §. 15. & Treat. 3. §. 73. before declared. It conſiſtethconsisteth
1. In prouidingproviding things needfullneedful for his wife.
2. In protecting her from things hurtfullhurtful.

1. A carefullcareful prouidingproviding of things needfullneedful, is a principallprincipal part of 1. ProuidingProviding things needfullneedful. that honour, which husbands are to giuegive vntounto their wiueswives. For where the ApoſtleApostle ſaithsaith, that Elders are worthy of double honour, 1 Pet. 3. 7. 1 Tim. 5. 17. he meaneth maintenance as well as reuerencereverence. The ApoſtleApostle counteth him worſeworse then an InfidellInfidel, that prouidethprovideth not for his owneown, and ſpeciallyspecially for thoſethose of his owneown houſehouse. Who are of an husbands houſehouse, 1 Tim. 5. 8. if not his wife? inIn his houſehouse, who more properly his owneown, then his wife? If then an husband prouideprovide not for his wife, what is he Recordare quòd pater vxoris tāquamtanquam depoſitumdepositum quoddam filiam tibi tradidit, & omnibus relictis, matre, domo, & ſeipſoseipso, omnem eius curācuran tuae dexterae commiſitcommisit. ChryſChrys. hōhon. 26. in 1. Cor. 11. to be accounted?

Great reaſonreason he ſhouldshould prouideprovide for her, becauſebecause he hath taken her from her parents and friends, and hath receiuedreceived that portion which they allotted her, and hath authoritieauthority committed vntounto him ouerover her, and ſheshe is put in ſubiectionsubjection vnderunder him: her friends hauinghaving giuengiven away her portion, and their power ouerover her, and committed all to him, will take no further care for her: ſheshe being in ſubiectionsubjection vnderunder him cannot without him prouideprovide for her ſelfeself. Who then ſhallshall prouideprovide for her if he doedo not, whoſewhose wholy and only ſheshe is?

Contrary is their mindemind, who take a wife only for their owneown Contrary, to take a wife only for himſelfehimself. content, or delight, or gainegain, and neuernever thinkethink of that charge which together with a wife they take vponupon them. According to their mindemind is their practiſepractise: for when they hauehave a wife they neglect her in eueryevery thing but what may ſtandstand with their owneown ends. Much hauehave they to anſweranswer for: and ſoso much the more, becauſebecause a wife is an eſpeciallespecial pledge of Gods fauourfavour. Pro. 18. 22.

div.head: §. 47. Of an husbands prouidingproviding meanesmeans of ſpirituallspiritual ediſicationedisication for his wife.

div.p: For her SouleSoul, meanesmeans of ſpirituallspiritual edification muſtmust be provided, and thoſethose both priuateprivate and publikepublic. PriuatePrivate meanesmeans, are PriuatePrivate means of edification. holy and religious exerciſesexercises in the houſehouse, as reading the word, praierprayer, catechiſingcatechising, and ſuchsuch like; which being the ſpirituallspiritual food of the ſoulesoul are to be eueryevery day, as our bodily food, prouidedprovided and vſedused. An husband as a maſtermaster of a family muſtmust provide theſethese for the good of his whole houſehouse; but as an husband, in ſpeciallspecial for the good of his wife: for to his wife, as well as to the whole houſehouse he is a King, a PrieſtPriest, and a Prophet.

By himſelfehimself therefore, for his wiueswives good, ought he to performeperform theſethese things, or to prouideprovide that they may be done by ſomesome other. The care of an husband for his wife in this reſpectrespect is, ſoso to order his habitation, and prouideprovide other needfullneedful things, as his wife may be made partaker thereof. It is expreſlyexpressly noted of Elkanah that he ſoso prouidedprovided for his 1 Sam. 1. 7. & 2. 19. Luk. 2. 41. wiueswives, that they went with him eueryevery yeereyear to the houſehouse of God: the like is intimated of IoſephJoseph the husband of the virgin
Mary. In thoſethose daiesdays there was a publikepublic place and houſehouse of God, whither all Gods people (how farrefar ſoeuersoever they dwelt from it) were to reſortresort eueryevery yeereyear: the places where Elkanah and IoſephJoseph dwelt, were farrefar remote from the houſehouse of God, yet they ſoso prouidedprovided, as not only themſeluesthemselves, but their wiueswives alſoalso went to the publikepublic worſhipworship of God. Now there are many houſeshouses of God, places for the publikepublic worſhipworship of God, but yet through the corruption of our times, the miniſteryministery of the word (the moſtmost principallprincipal meanesmeans of ſpirituallspiritual edification) is not eueryevery where to be enioyedenjoyed: therefore ſuchsuch ought an huſbandshusbands care for his wife in this reſpectrespect to be, as to dwell where ſheshe may hauehave the benefit of preaching the word, or elſeelse ſoso to prouideprovide for her, as ſheshe may weekly goego where it may be had.

If men of wiſdomewisdom and abilitieability make a purchaſepurchase, or build an houſehouse for their habitation, they will be ſuresure it ſhallshall be where ſweetsweet riuersrivers and waters are, and good paſturepasture ground, and where all needfullneedful prouiſionprovision may be had. Gods word preached is a ſpringspring of water of life; the place where it is preached a pleaſantpleasant, profitable paſturepasture; all needfullneedful prouiſionprovision for the ſoulesoul may there be had. Let this therefore be moſtmost of all inquired after: and no habitation ſetledsettled but where this may be had.

div.head: §. 48. Of neglecting their wiueswives edification.
div.p: Contrary is their practiſepractise, who hauinghaving their calling in places where the word is plentifullplentiful, yet vponupon outward reſpectsrespects of pleaſurepleasure, delight, eaſeease, and profit, remoueremove their families into remote places where preaching is ſcarcescarce, if at all; and there leaueleave their wiueswives to gouernegovern the family, not regarding their want of the word, for as much as they themſeluesthemselves oft commingcoming to London or other like places by reaſonreason of their calling, enioyenjoy the word themſeluesthemselves. Many Citizens, Lawyers, and others are guiltieguilty of great neglect of their wiueswives in this reſpectrespect.

So alſoalso are they, who abandon all religious exerciſesexercises out of their houſeshouses, making their houſeshouses rather ſtewesstews of the deuilldevil, then Churches of God. If for want of meanesmeans, either publikepublic or priuateprivate, a wife liuelive and die in ignorance, profaneneſſeprofaneness, infidelitieinfidelity, and impenitencieimpenitency, which cauſecause eternalleternal damnation,
aſſuredlyassuredly her bloudblood ſhallshall be required at his hands: for an huſbandhusband Ezek. 3. 18. &etcc. is Gods watchman to his wife.

div.head: §. 49. Of an husbands prouidingproviding things needfullneedful for his wiueswives boay.
div.p: To the body alſoalso muſtmust an husbands prouidentprovident care of his wife extend: and that both in health and ſickneſſesickness. In health by prouidingproviding ſuchsuch things as are needfullneedful to preſeruepreserve health, as competent food, raiment, and the like neceſſariesnecessaries. Where the JſaJsa. 4. 1. Prophet to aggrauateaggravate the miſerymisery of the people ſaithsaith, SeuenSeven women ſhallshall take hold of one man, ſayingsaying, We will eat our owneown bread, and wearewear our owneown apparellapparel, only let vsus be called by thy name, intimateth, that it was an husbands dutieduty to prouideprovide bread and apparellapparel, that is, all neceſſariesnecessaries for his wife. Which the Exo. 21. 10. law alſoalso implieth, where it inioynethenjoineth him that taketh one wife vponupon another, not to diminiſhdiminish the food and raiment of the former. In ſickneſſesickness ſuchsuch things are to be prouidedprovided as are needfullneedful either to recouerrecover her health, or to comfort, cheriſhcherish and refreſhrefresh her in her ſickneſſesickness.

This was Treat. 2. Part. 2. §. 29. before noted among common mutuallmutual duties; for by vertuevirtue of the matrimoniallmatrimonial bond it belongeth both to man and wife: but to the man it appertaineth by vertuevirtue of that power and charge which he hath ouerover his wife: and therefore it was needfullneedful here to be touched.

div.head: §. 50. Of an husbands Treat. 3. §. 49. prouidentprovident care for his wife about her child-bearing.
div.p: MoſtMost proper to this place is that prouidentprovident care which huſbandshusbands ought to hauehave of their wiueswives both before and in the time of their trauelltravel and child-bed: and that in two things eſpeciallyespecially.

1. In procuring for their wiueswives to the vttermoſtuttermost of their power and abilitieability, ſuchsuch things as may ſauesave their longing, in caſecase they doedo long (as in all ages women in the time of breeding and bearing childechild, hauehave beenebeen ſubiectsubject thereunto.) For it is well knowneknown, that it is very dangerous both for mother and childechild to want her longing: the death ſometimessometimes of the one, ſometimessometimes of the other, ſometimessometimes of both hath followed thereupon.

2. In prouidingproviding ſuchsuch things as are needfullneedful for their trauelltravel
and lying in childbed. This time is eſpeciallyespecially to be prouidedprovided for, in many reſpectsrespects.
1. BecauſeBecause it is a time of weakneſſeweakness, wherein the woman cannot well prouideprovide for her ſelfeself.

2. BecauſeBecause her weakneſſeweakness is ioynedjoined with much painepain: the The painespains of womens trauelltravel. painepain of a women in trauelltravel is the greateſtgreatest painepain that ordinarily is endured by any for the time: none know it ſoso well as they that feelefeel it: and many husbands becauſebecause they are not ſubiectsubject thereto, thinkethink but lightly of it: but if we duly weigh PſalPsal. 48 6. IſaIsa. 13. 8. & 21. 3 IerJer. 4. 31. & 30. 6. Mic. 49. that the holy GhoſtGhost when he would ſetset forth the extremitieextremity of any painespains and pangs, reſemblethresembleth them to the painespains of a woman in trauelltravel, we may well gather, that of all they are the greateſtgreatest: which is further manifeſtedmanifested by the ſcreekesscreekes and outcries which not only weakeweak, and faint-hearted women vtterutter in the time of their trauelltravel, but alſoalso are forced from the ſtrongeſtstrongest, and ſtouteſtstoutest women that be, and that though before hand they reſolueresolve to the contrary. Neither may we wonder thereat; for their body is as it were ſetset on a rackerack (if at leaſtleast the trauelltravel be ſharpesharpsharpe) and all their parts ſoso ſtretchedstretched, as a wonder it is they ſhouldshould euerever recouerrecover their health and ſtrengthstrength againeagain: or that they ſhouldshould hold out the brunt, and not die with their trauelltravel, as Rachel, and the wife of Phinchas, and many in all ages hauehave Gen. 35. 16, &etcc. 1 Sam. 4. 19. 20. done. Surely among ordinary deliuerancesdeliverances I know none ſoso neerenear a miracle, none wherein the Almighty doth ſoso euidentlyevidently manifeſtmanifest his great power and good prouidenceprovidence, as in the ſafesafe deliueriedelivery of women. BeſidesBesides the great pang of trauelltravel, women are alſoalso after their deliueriedelivery ſubiectsubject to many after-throws which are very painfullpainful. From all theſethese painespains and great weakneſſeweakness which befalleth women in childbed, eſpeciallyespecially if they nurſenurse their children, men by reaſonreason of their ſexsex are freed: Now then to apply this point, ſeeingseeing women are brought to ſuchsuch painespains and weakneſſeweakness in bringing forth thoſethose children which are the mans as well as hers, and he freed from all; is it not very iuſtjust and meet that he ſhouldshould prouideprovide all things needfullneedful for her welfare, eaſeease, and recoueryrecovery of ſtrengthstrength?
3. BecauſeBecause the want of things needfullneedful is at that time very dangerous: dangerous to the health and life of the woman and childechild alſoalso.

div.head: §. 51. Of neglecting wiueswives in their weakneſſeweakness.
div.p: Contrary to an husbands prouidentprovident care in generallgeneral are thoſethose vices which were taxed in the treatiſetreatise of common duties, * See Treat 2. Part. 2. § 30. 39. as grudging at the charges beſtowedbestowed on a wife: CouetouſneſſeCovetousness, Prodigality, and IdleneſſeIdleness.

But contrary in particular to an husbands care for his wife in childbed, is the inhumane and more then barbarous vnkindneſſeunkindness of many husbands, who no whit conſiderconsider the weakneſſeweakness of their wiueswives in this caſecase, to helpehelp, eaſeease, and comfort them, but rather make their burden much more heauyheavy. For,

1. Some through couetouſneſſecovetousness refuſerefuse before hand to afford meanesmeans to their wife to prouideprovide ſuchsuch things as are needfullneedful for her ſelfeself and child: & when the time commethcometh, if their wife be deſirousdesirous of a Midwife that requireth ſomwhatsomwhat more charges then ſheshe that is next, ſheshe ſhallshall hauehave none if ſheshe will not hauehave the next. And as for a nurſenurse to tend her, they thinkethink their Maid will ſerueserve the turneturn welwell enough: they need not be at the charges to bring a NurſeNurse into the houſehouse. In regard of conuenientconvenient lodging ſomesome will not ſtickestick to ſaysay, Cannot my wife be brought to bed in a roomeroom without a chimney as well as the Virgin Mary? Why ſhouldshould my wife need more things then ſheshe did? Yea further there be many that whēwhen the time that their wife ſhouldshould be deliuereddelivered approacheth neerenear, cariecary her from alall her friends into a place where ſheshe is not knowneknown, leſtlest her friends ſhouldshould by importunity draw him to expend and lay out more vponupon his wife then he is willing. In the time while their wife is weakeweak in childbed, many are loath to allow them any other diet then is for themſeluesthemselves and children prouidedprovided in the houſehouse, not conſideringconsidering that her ſtomachstomach cannot be like theirs.

Many other ſuchsuch bitter fruits of vnkindeunkind husbands ariſingarising from couetouſneſſecovetousness might be reckoned vpup, whereby husbands plainely ſhewshow that they louelove their wealth better then their wiueswives: they had rather loſelose them, then part with that.

2. Others through iealousjealous ſuſpicionsuspicion forbeareforbear not eueneven in Si quid vxor peccauerit conſolareconsolare & noli moerorem augere. ChryſChrys. hom. 26. in 1 Cor. 11. the time of their wiueswives painepain and weakneſſeweakness, to vpbraidupbraid them with lightneſſelightness, and to ſaysay that the childechild is none of theirs. To lay this to a wiueswives charge vniuſtlyunjustly, is at any time a moſtmost ſhamefullshameful and odious reproach: but in the time of childebirth
whether iuſtjust or vniuſtunjust, a thing too too ſpightfullspiteful and reuengefullrevengeful. Some wiueswives are ſoso farrefar ouercomeovercome thereby, (eſpeciallyespecially in the time of their weakneſſeweakness) as they are not able to bearebear it, but eueneven faint and die vnderunder the reproach: others more ſtoutstout vow neuernever to know their husbands againeagain. Many like miſchiefesmischiefs follow on ſuchsuch vnkindneſſeunkindness.

div.head: §. 52. Of an husbands Treat. 3. §. 38. prouidingproviding for his wife according to his eſtateestate and abilitieability.
div.p: In an husbands prouidingproviding for the body of his wife reſpectrespect muſtmust be had to the meaſuremeasure, and to the manner.

The meaſuremeasure muſtmust extend to his ability: for an husband ought to maintainemaintain his wife in as good an eſtateestate and faſhionfashion as himſelfehimself; by mariagemarriage ſheshe is aduancedadvanced to as high an eſtateestate, and dignity in relation to others as he is: and for her owneown vſeuse ſheshe is made a partner of all his goods, and accordingly ought to partake thereof.

For the manner, he muſtmust ſuffersuffer her (if at leaſtleast he obſerueobserve her to hauehave any competent diſcretiondiscretion) to order ſuchsuch things as are needfullneedful for her ſelfeself according to her beſtbest liking: as Elkanah in another caſecase ſaidsaid to his wife, DoeDo what ſeemethseemeth thee beſtbest. 1 Sam. 1. 23.

Both in the meaſuremeasure and in the manner of prouidingproviding, there muſtmust be a difference put betwixt a wife, and ſeruantsservants or children. TheſeThese may hauehave their portions of meat, apparrellapparel, and like neceſſariesnecessaries, proportioned out and ſtintedstinted vntounto them, which is vnmeetunmeet to be done to a wife. Neither is it needfullneedful that ſoso plentifullplentiful a prouiſionprovision be made for them as for her.

div.head: §. 53. Of an husbands nigardlyneſſenigardlyness to his wife.
div.p:
Contrary is an husbands nigardly dealing with his wife: when the allowance ſheshe hath is both farrefar vnderunder his eſtateestate, and alſoalso ſoso giuengiven her by little and little, as if ſheshe were a childechild. Many husbands make their wiueswives drudge at home, fare hardly, and goego meanly; who are themſeluesthemselves brauebrave in apparrellapparel, frolickefrolic in their feaſtingfeasting abroad, and ſoso exceed their wiueswives as they are aſhamedashamed to be ſeeneseen in company with them. They who marry their maids, or others of meaner rankerank then themſeluesthemselves, oft ſoso dealedeal with them: eſteemingesteeming them but as ſeruantsservants and meanemean perſonspersons though they be their wiueswives. But it hath beenebeen §. 6. before ſhewedshowed, that wiueswives by marriage are aduancedadvanced to their
husbands dignity, how meanemean ſoeuersoever they were before.

div.head: §. 54. Of husbands Treat. 3. §. 23. 29. 33. allowing their wiueswives to beſtowbestow on others, as they ſeesee good occaſionoccasion.
div.p: So farrefar ought the prouidentprovident care of an husband for his wife to extend, as ſheshe may hauehave (beſidebeside things needfullneedful to her ſelfeself) to beſtowbestow on ſuchsuch as it is requiſiterequisite for her to giuegive vntounto: as namely, on children and ſeruantsservants in the houſehouse, and others alſoalso out of the houſehouse. For ſoso much is noted in SalomonsSolomon's deſcriptiondescription Pro. 31. 15. &etcc. VerſVers. 21. UerſUers. 28. of a good wife; She giuethgiveth meat to her houſholdhousehold, and a portion to her maidens: all her houſholdhousehold is clothed with ſcarletscarlet (namely, by her ordering and diſpoſingdisposing the matter.) Her children riſerise vpup and call her bleſſedblessed, as for her generallgeneral cariagecarriage in the family, ſoso for her particular fauoursfavours beſtowedbestowed on themſeluesthemselves. As for VerſVers. 20. others out of the houſehouse, it is alſoalso noted, that ſheshe ſtretchethstretcheth out her hand to the poorepoor, and reacheth forth her hands to the needieneedy. TheſeThese things ſheshe did by virtue of that power and liberty which her husband gauegave her: as appeareth by two points there noted:
1. In that before any mention is made of thoſethose things VerſVers. 11. which ſheshe did, it is ſaidsaid, The heart of her husband doth ſafelysafely truſttrust in her.
2. In that, after all her good deedesdeeds are reckoned vpup, it is UerſUers. 28. ſaidsaid, Her husband praiſethpraiseth her.

After this patternepattern it is meetemeet that other husbands (whoſewhose wiueswives are wiſewise and faithfullfaithful) ſhouldshould dealedeal with their wiueswives: that in the houſehouse they might hauehave the more honour of children and ſeruantsservants: and that out of the houſehouse they might giuegive the better tryalltrial of their charity.

For conſideringconsidering the many excellent promiſespromises that are made to workesworks of mercy and charity, and the many terrible threatningsthreatenings that are denounced not onelyonly againſtagainst ſuchsuch as exerciſeexercise cruelty, but alſoalso againſtagainst ſuchsuch as ſhewshow no mercy: conſideringconsidering alſoalso that wiueswives together with their husbands, are heiresheirs of the 1 Pet. 3. 7. grace of life, it is very needfullneedful yea eueneven neceſſarynecessary, that they ſhouldshould manifeſtmanifest their faith by ſomesome workework of mercy and charity. Now vnleſſeunless her husband doedo giuegive vntounto her ſomethingsomething at her owneown diſcretiondiscretion to beſtowbestow on others, true and through
try all of her mercifullmerciful and charitable mindemind cannot be made. If ſheshe giuegive of that which her husband hath reſeruedreserved to himſelfehimself, as her giuinggiving is vnlawfullunlawful, ſoso ſheshe may be thought liberallliberal, not becauſebecause ſheshe is mercifullmerciful, but becauſebecause notwithſtandingnotwithstanding her liberality ſheshe parteth with nothing of her owneown: yea though ſheshe hauehave a generallgeneral conſentconsent to giuegive as ſheshe ſeethseeth cauſecause of the common goods of the family, yet is not that ſoso ſuresure and ſoundsound a tryalltrial of her charity, and mercifulneſſemercifulness, as if ſheshe had ſomethingsomething of her owneown which ſheshe might retaineretain or giuegive away as pleaſethpleaseth her ſelfeself; and what ſheshe giuesgives not away, lay vpup as her owneown ſtockestock proper to her ſelfeself. For there is naturally ſuchsuch a ſelfeself louelove in man, and a deſiredesire to keepekeep that which is proper to ones ſelfeself, that he is very loath to part with any of it, vnleſſeunless conſcienceconscience and grace alter this corruption of nature, and ſoso mouemove him readily to lay out ſomethingsomething on charitable vſesuses. But otherwiſeotherwise of that which in whole or in part belongeth to another (be that other, husband, parent, maſtermaster, friend, or any elſeelse) he is eaſilyeasily mouedmoved to be liberallliberal and bountifullbountiful: a man will willingly cut a large thong (as we ſpeakespeak) out of anothers leather.

It is knowneknown that many children and ſeruantsservants, who, when they come to be poſſeſſerspossessers of their owneown, are very niggards and miſersmisers, hauehave beenebeen liberallliberal of their parents and maſtersmasters goods vntounto the poorepoor. Yea parteners in a ſtockestock will be much more forward in giuinggiving away that which is common with another, then that which is proper to each of them. The trueſttruest trialltrial of a mercifullmerciful and charitable heart lieth in the diſtributiondistribution of that which is proper to ones ſelfeself.

It is therefore meet vponupon this very ground, that an husband ſhouldshould according to his ability let his wife hauehave ſomesome ſtockestock, and portion of her owneown, free to her ſelfeself to diſpoſedispose as ſheshe ſeethseeth good: intimating vntounto her that the principallprincipal end why he prouidethprovideth ſoso plentifully for her, is, that ſheshe may ſhewshow forth the fruits of her faith by ſomesome workesworks of charity: and exhorting her ſoso to doedo. Many religious, wiſewise, kindekind husbands thus doedo: ſomesome giuinggiving quarterly allowance in money to their wiueswives, others giuinggiving their wiueswives power to receiuereceive a certainecertain portion of rent out of certainecertain lands or houſeshouses; others making
their wiueswives an abſoluteabsolute eſtateestate of ſomesome inheritance, and ſufferingsuffering them to receiuereceive the profits and reuenewesrevenewes thereof; others giuinggiving them certainecertain fees of their offices, or of their trade; others, that are poorepoor, ſufferingsuffering them to workework for themſeluesthemselves, & diſpoſedispose their earnings as they ſeesee cauſecause: ſomesome one way, ſomesome another: eueryevery one in his place beſtbest knoweth the meanesmeans how to gratifiegratify his wife in this kindekind: it ſhallshall be ſufficientsufficient for me to hauehave laidelaid downedown the generallgeneral rule.

div.head: §. 55. Of husbands too great ſtraitneſſestraitness ouerover their wiueswives.
div.p: Contrary is their ſtraitstrait-handedneſſehandedness to their wiueswives, who allow them no more then may be for their owneown priuatprivat vſeuse. They thinkethink it a great matter and as much as an husband is bound to doedo, to let her hauehave apparrellapparel, meat and drinkedrink, and ſuchsuch neceſſariesnecessaries as are befitting her rankerank, but all other ouerplusoverplus they thinkethink needleſſeneedless. Thus their wiueswives are not only depriueddeprived of meanesmeans to gainegain reſpectrespect of their children and ſeruantsservants at home, and to gratifiegratify ſuchsuch as are obedient and ready to doedo ſeruiceservice to them, but alſoalso to performeperform ſuchsuch workesworks of merciemercy as both opportunity requireth, and alſoalso their conſcienceconscience mouethmoveth them to doedo. Yea many wiueswives of rich huſbandshusbands are brought to great ſhameshame hereby, in that being in places where there is iuſtjust occaſionoccasion of contributing to ſomesome charitable vſeuse, and by reaſonreason of their rich and coſtlycostly apparellapparel it is expected they ſhouldshould be bountiful, they hauehave not any thing at all to beſtowbestow. The fault of ſomesome husbands in this reſpectrespect is great many waiesways. As 1. inIn that they bring ſhameshame and griefegrief to their wiueswives, whom they ought with all tenderneſſetenderness to reſpectrespect. 2. In that they diſhonourdishonour their owneown places: for they who take notice of this ſtraitneſſestraitness to their wiueswives, will be ready to iudgejudge them both couetouscovetous, and vnkindeunkind. 3. The omitting of that workework of merciemercy which their wiueswives ſhouldshould hauehave done ſhallshall be laid to their charge: they ſhallshall hearehear that dreadfulldreadful doomedoom; GoeGo yeeye curſedcursed into euerlaſtingeverlasting fire, for I was an hungred and yeeye fed me not &etcc. and if they anſweranswer, When ſawsaw we thee an hungred &etcc. it ſhallshall be replied, In that yeeye ſufferedsuffered not your wiueswives to doedo it, you did it not.

Thus much of the extent of an husbands prouidentprovident care
for the good of his wife. It followeth to ſpeakespeak of the continuance thereof.

div.head: §. 57. Of an husbands care to prouideprovide for his wife ſoso long as ſheshe ſhallshall liuelive.
div.p: The continuance of an husbands prouidentprovident care for his wife muſtmust be ſoso long as ſheshe liuethliveth, yea though ſheshe out-liuelive him: not that he can actually when he is dead prouideprovide for her, but that he may before his death ſoso prouideprovide for her, as ſheshe may hauehave wherewithallwherewithal to maintainemaintain her ſelfeself, and to liuelive according to that place whereunto by him ſheshe is aduancedadvanced: at leaſtleast that he leaueleave her not only ſoso much as he had with her, but ſomethingsomething more alſoalso in teſtimonytestimony of his louelove to her, and care for her. Husbands hauehave the example of ChriſtChrist to preſſepress this duty vponupon them: for when he went away from his Church here on Eph 4. 8. earth, he left his ſpiritspirit, which furniſhedfurnished it with gifts as plentifully, as if ChriſtChrist had ſtillstill remained with her, if not more aboundantly.
For the better performance of this duty, husbands which die before the wiueswives, muſtmust obſerueobserve among other things two eſpeciallyespecially.

1. That plainly and expreſlyexpressly they declare their mindemind and Husbands before they die muſtmust make their will eueneven for their wiueswives good. will before they die, leſtlest their wiueswives ſhouldshould be circumuentedcircumvented and defrauded of that which they intended them. Thus did DauidDavid vponupon the motion of BathſhebahBathshebah, he ſetledsettled his eſtateestate, and cauſedcaused BathſhebahsBathshebahs ſonneson to be actually crowned before he himſelfehimself gauegave vpup the GhoſtGhost: which he did, as for other weighty reaſonsreasons, ſoso in particular for his wiueswives good, as may be gathered from that reaſonreason ſheshe alleagedalleged to the King in theſethese 1 King. 1. 21. Husbands on their deathbed muſtmust commend their wiueswives to ſomesome faithfullfaithful friend. IobJob. 19 26, 27. ReaſonReason. div.head: §. 58. Of an husbands protecting his wife from danger.
div.p: HauingHaving ſhewedshowed how an husband is to prouideprovide things needfullneedful for his wife: It remaineth to ſhewshow how he is to protect her from things hurtfullhurtful.

In regard of that protection which an husband oweth his wife, he is called the veileveil of her eieseyes: which phraſephrase as it implieth Gen. 20 16. Subiectionsubjection on the wiueswives part, ſoso alſoalso Protection on the huſbandshusbands: to protect one, is as it were, to couercover them, namely, from danger; to be negligent and careleſſecareless of them, is, as it were, to lay them open to danger. The ſamesame duty is implied vnderunder another like phraſephrase of ſpreadingspreading his wing ouerover his wife. Ruth 3. 9. The metaphor is taken from winged fowles, which to keepekeep their young ones from hurt, vſeuse to ſpreadspread their wings ouerover them: this phraſephrase and metaphor is alſoalso attributed to God, to Ruth 2. 12. ſetset forth his protection.
But moſtmost pertinent to this purpoſepurpose is the title, Treat. 1. §. 15. and treat. 3. §. 73. SaniourSaviour, giuengiven to an husband in relation to his wife.

For this end the Lord who ſubiectedsubjected a woman vntounto her husband, gauegave to his ſexesex greater ſtrengthstrength, courage and boldneſſeboldness then to hers, that he might protect her which is the weaker veſſellvessel. In this duty of protection ChriſtChrist ſhewethshoweth himſelfehimself an excellent patternepattern and preſidentprecedentpresident vntounto husbands.

div.head: §. 59. Of an husbands maintaining his wife againſtagainst children of a former venter, and ſeruantsservants.

div.p: ObiectObject. Mothersmothers in law often proueprove vnkindeunkind, and vniuſtunjust ſtepmothersstepmothers, and dealedeal vnmercifullyunmercifully with their husbands children: muſtmust an husband in ſuchsuch caſescases aſſiſtassist his wife againſtagainst his children?

AnſwAnsw. The protection, I ſpeakespeak of, is in caſecase a wife be wronged, then her husband is to doedo what he can to right her (as we ſpeakespeak.) But if ſheshe be the wrong-doer, he may by no meanesmeans boulſterboulster

As this beſeemethbeseemeth not any ChriſtianChristian to ſuffersuffer his neighbour to be wronged, (for it is noted as a commendable matter in MoſesMoses, that Exod. 2. 13. when he ſawsaw two HebrewesHebrews ſtriuingstriving together, he tooketook his part that had wrong done to him, and reprouedreproved the other) ſoso much l • eſſeless an husband, to whoſewhose ſafesafe-guard his wife is committed. As the wrong which is done by thoſethose who are in ſubiectionsubjection i • n the houſehouse vnderunder the wife, is greater then that which is done by s • trangers: ſoso is the husbands fault the greater in ſufferingsuffering it: for h • e hath more power ouerover them in his houſehouse, then ouerover others. Si illam quae ſecundumsecundum poſtpost te locum obtinet contumelia afficis, non parum tui principatus honori derogas. ChryſChrys. loc. cit. What then may we thinkethink of ſuchsuch, as either by their conniuenceconnivence, o • r by taking part againſtagainst their wiueswives, ſuffersuffer both children and ſeru • antsservants to inſultinsult ouerover them? on their owneown perſonspersons, both by their wiueswives (who cannot thinkethink them meet heads to gouernegovern others) but alſoalso by their children and ſeruantsservants, who thereby will take occaſionoccasion to waxewax proud, and preſumptuouspresumptuous againſtagainst him. By deſpiſingdespising the weaker, men grow by little and little to deſpiſedespise the ſtrongerstronger. This men of wiſdomewisdom and experience well know: whereupon in Commoncommon-wealths and Policies gouernedgoverned by wiſewise men, the authoritieauthority of inferiourinferior MagiſtratesMagistrates is vpheldupheld and maintained: ſuperioursuperior MagiſtratesMagistrates will not ſuffersuffer them who are in authoritieauthority vnderunder them to be deſpiſeddespised: for it is well knowneknown, that it tends not to the honour and eaſeease only, but to the ſafetiesafety alſoalso of the ſupremesupreme MagiſtrateMagistrate, to hauehave the power and authoritieauthority of inferiourinferior MagiſtratesMagistrates reſpectedrespected, and not trampled vnderunder feet. It argueth therefore both want of affection, and of diſcretiondiscretion and vnderſtandingunderstanding in husbands, to ſuffersuffer childechild, ſeruantservant, or any other in the houſehouse, to inſultinsult ouerover their wiueswives, who are ioyntjoint gouernoursgovernors with them ouerover the houſehouse.

div.head: §. 61. Of an husbands firſtfirst beginning to louelove his wife.
div.p: The generallgeneral matter together with the particular kindeskinds of husbands duties being thus farrefar handled, The manner alſoalso of performing them is to be deliuereddelivered.

row.cell: To inſtructinstruct an husband in the manner of performing his duties to his wife, the ApoſtleApostle laiethlayeth downedown two patternespatterns,

div.p: As ChriſtChrist louethloveth his Church, and as we louelove our ſeluesselves, ſoso muſtmust men louelove their wiueswives.

That we may the better follow theſethese patternespatterns, we muſtmust diſtinctlydistinctly note how ChriſtChrist louethloveth his Church, and how we The manner of an husbands louelove ſetset forth by ChriſtsChrists manner of louingloving his Church in ſixsix branches. 1. I. For the Order, ChriſtChrist began to louelove his Church: he mafeſtedmafested his louelove to her before ſheshe louedloved him: as the aireair heated by the SunneSun is hotehot, and a wall on which the Sun-beamesbeams

div.head: §. 62. Of husbands repaying vnkindneſſeunkindness for louelove.
div.p: Contrary, is their diſpoſitiondisposition, who hauinghaving louingloving and dutifulldutiful wiueswives, are notwithſtandingnotwithstanding nothing mouedmoved to louelove them againeagain: but are as vnkindeunkind and churliſhchurlish as if they had the moſtmost p • eeuiſhpeevish, and peruerſeperverse wiueswives that could be. div.head: §. 63. Of the Treat. 3. §. 57. 2. ChriſtChrist louethloveth in truth. truth of husbands louelove.
div.p:
II. The truth of ChriſtsChrists louelove was manifeſtedmanifested by the fruits thereof to his Church: He gauegave himſelfehimself for it. It was therefore not in word only, no nor only in heart, but in deed alſoalso. Thus his louelove prouedproved profitable, and beneficiallbeneficial to his Church, which thereby was clenſedclensed, and made a glorious
VerſVers. 26, 27. Church. Had he only borne a tender compaſſioncompassion and pittifullpitiful affection towards it, or laboured only with comfortable and ſweetsweet words to vpholduphold and ſuccoursuccour it, it had ſtillstill lainelain polluted with ſinnesin, in the power of the deuilldevil, and vnderunder Gods wrath, and ſoso receiuedreceived no profit and benefit at all.

So muſtmust husbands louelove their wiueswives in truth and in deed. Husbands muſtmust louelove in deed.
1 IohJoh. 3. 18. Such a louelove is required of a man to his brother: much more therefore to his wife, who is not only a ſiſtersister (as 1 Cor. 9. 5. the ApoſtleApostle expreſlyexpressly ſtilethstyleth her) but neerernearer then ſiſtersister, mother, daughter, friend, or any other whatſoeuerwhatsoever. This therefore ſeruethserveth to preſſepress the practiſepractise of all the forenamed duties appertaining to an husband.

div.head: §. 64. Of husbands diſſimulationdissimulation.
div.p: Contrary is their diſſimulationdissimulation and hypocriſiehypocrisy, who make great ſhewshow of much louelove, and pretence of earneſtearnest affection, vſingusing many outward complements, but failefail when they come to the trueſttruest trialltrial, the deed. Some like ſuterssuters or wooers, will promiſepromise mountainesmountains, but not performeperform moul-hills: others will coll and kiſſekiss their wiueswives much, but truſttrust them with nothing, nor prouideprovide for them things requiſiterequisite: there be that will weepeweep much when their wiueswives are ſickesick, yet not afford phyſickephysic and ſuchsuch like things for their recoueryrecovery: yea many will carriecarry a fairefair face all their life long towards their wiueswives, and at their death leaueleave them nothing to liuelive by.

Hence it is that many who by others are accounted to be very kindekind husbands, are by their wiueswives found to be farrefar otherwiſeotherwise. If trialltrial be made of husbands louelove by their practiſepractise and performance of the forenamed duties, it will be found that they for the moſtmost part come as farrefar ſhortshort in louelove, as wiueswives in ſubiectionsubjection.

div.head: §. 65. Of the freeneſſefreeness of husbands louelove.
div.p:
III. The cauſecause of ChriſtsChrists louelove, was his louelove, as MoſesMoses noteth, 3. ChriſtChrist louethloveth freely. Deut. 7. 7, 8. He ſetset his louelove on you, becauſebecause he louedloved you. His louelove aroſearose only, and wholly from himſelfehimself, and was eueryevery way free: as there was nothing in the Church, before ChriſtChrist louedloved her to mouemove him to louelove her, ſoso can there be nothing that he could hope for afterwards, but what himſelfehimself beſtowedbestowed. Indeed he delighteth in that righteouſneſſerighteousness wherewith, as with a glorious robe, ſheshe is clothed; and with thoſethose heauenlyheavenly graces, wherewith as with pretiousprecious IewelsJewels ſheshe is decked: but that righteouſneſſerighteousness, and thoſethose graces are his owneown, and of his free gift, He preſentspresents it to himſelfehimself a glorious Church.
Eph. 5. 27. Husbands louelove muſtmust be free.

In imitation hereof husbands ſhouldshould louelove their wiueswives, though there were nothing in wiueswives to mouemove them ſoso to doedo, but only that they are their wiueswives: yea though no future benefit could after be expected from them: true louelove hath reſpectrespect to the obiectobject which is louedloved, and the good it may doedo thereunto, rather then to the ſubiectsubject which louethloveth, and the good that it may receiuereceive. For louelove ſeekethseeketh not her owneown. 1 Cor. 13. 5.

ChriſtsChrists louelove in this branch thereof ſhouldshould further mouemove husbands to doedo what lieth in their power, to make their wiueswives worthy of louelove: thus will it be in truth ſaidsaid, that they dwell with their wiueswives according to knowledge: and thus will their 1 Pet. 3. 7. l • ouelove appeareappear to be as ChriſtsChrists louelove, free.

div.head: §. 66. Of husbands louingloving for aduantageadvantage.
div.p: Contrary is their louelove which is only for their owneown content a • nd aduantageadvantage. Many can louelove no further then they may hauehave s • ome bait to allure their affections, as beauty, wealth, honour, o • r the like by-reſpectsrespects; or at leaſtleast hope of ſomesome inheritance or p • ortion aboueabove that which they hauehave, or of ſomesome fauourfavour that they e • xpect from their wiueswives friends. This cannot be a true ſoundsound lo •• uelove: ſuchsuch a man may be thought to louelove his wiueswives beautiebeauty, in •• heritance, and friends rather then his wife. This louelove cannot laſtlast.

div.head: §. 67. Of the puritiepurity of husbands louelove.
div.p:
IIII. ChriſtsChrists louelove for the qualitiequality is an holy, pure, chaſtechaste, 4. ChriſtsChrists louelove pure. Eph. 5. 26, 27. lo •• uelove: as he himſelfehimself is, ſoso is his louelove, as is euidentevident by the ef •• fect thereof: for it mouedmoved him to ſanctifiesanctify and clenſeclense his
Church, to make it a glorious Church without ſpotspot: he did therefore no way pollute or defile his SpouſeSpouse: and that his louelove might the better appeareappear to be chaſtechaste louelove, caſtcast only vponupon one SpouſeSpouse and not many, he vnitedunited all his Saints together by the 1 Cor. 12. 12, 13 bond of his Spirit, and made them all one body.

Hereby husbands muſtmust learnelearn ſoso to be affected towards Husbands louelove muſtmust be chaſtechaste. Heb. 13. 4. their wiueswives as may ſtandstand with holineſſeholiness, and chaſtitiechastity: though much louelove be required, yet it may not ouerover-floweflow thoſethose banks. Mariagemarriage is honourable and a bed vndefiledundefiled. It muſtmust therefore be vſedused as an vndefiledundefiled thing. This indeed appertaineth to the wife as well as to the husband. But becauſebecause he is the head, and guide of his wife, and ought to be as a patternepattern and preſidentprecedentpresident before her, as ChriſtChrist is before him, therefore is it more ſpeciallyspecially applied to him. The puritiepurity of an husbands louelove here ſpokenspoken of, hath a double vſeuse,

1. It reſtrainethrestraineth an husbands louelove to his owneown wife. There is a generallgeneral ChriſtianChristian louelove whereby all occaſionsoccasions of doing good are taken, with which an husband may, and ought to louelove others: and a particular matrimoniallmatrimonial louelove, whereby he is mouedmoved to preferreprefer his wife before all, and to hauehave his heart ſetset and fixed on her, and ſoso proper and peculiar to her.
2. It orders and moderates his louelove, ſoso as it turneth not into ſinfullsinful luſtlust, whereby that eſtateestate, (which in it ſelfeself by vertuevirtue of Gods ordinance, is holy) is polluted.

div.head: §. 68. Of husbands lightneſſelightness.
div.p:
Contrary, is not only adulterieadultery, whereof we hauehave ſpokenspoken Treat. 2. part. 2. §. 5, 8. before, but alſoalso wantonneſſewantonness, lightneſſelightness, and vncleanneſſeuncleanness with his wife. For many intemperate and vnchaſteunchaste husbands, giuinggiving the rainesrains to their headſtrongheadstrong luſtslusts, manifeſtmanifest as much vnſeemlineſſeunseemliness and plaineplain filthineſſefilthiness in their words, geſturesgestures, and actions (to ſaysay nothing of their thoughts which are not ſeeneseen) to their wiueswives, as other doedo to ſtrumpetsstrumpets and harlots which is a moſtmost ſhameleſſeshameless thing, and I am eueneven aſhamedashamed to • mention: but becauſebecause it is mentioned, let ſuchsuch know, that • they ſhallshall be accounted among ſuchsuch whoremongers and adulte • rers
Heb. 13. 4. as God will iudgejudge.

div.head: §. 69. Of husbands louingloving their wiueswives more then themſeluesthemselves.
div.p:
The quantity of ChriſtsChrists louelove cannot be expreſſedexpressed: for the 5 ChriſtsChrists louelove extended to the giuinggiving of himſelfehimself meaſuremeasure of it was aboueabove meaſuremeasure. EpheſEphes. 5 25. He gauegave himſelfehimself for his Church, and in that reſpectrespect he calleth himſelfehimself that IohnJohn. 10. 11. Good ſheepheardsheepheard that gauegave his life for his ſheepesheep.
& 15. 13. Greater louelove then this hath no man. What will not he doedo for his ſpouſespouse, that gauegave his life for her?

This may ſeemeseem to be too high a ſtrainestrain, and pitch of louelove for an husband to attaineattain vntounto: a matter wherein he is to How huſbandshusbands muſtmust louelove their wiueswives more then themſeluesthemselves. 1 IohnJohn. 3. 16. l • eaueleave his patternepattern, and not to follow ChriſtChrist: but yet S. IohnJohn addeth eueneven this extent to the louelove of our brethren: We ought ſaithsaith he) to lay downedown our liueslives for the brethren: therefore by m • uſtmust conſequenceconsequence for our wiueswives. But that this extent be not ſtretchedstretched too farrefar, and husbands caſtcast into a pit of needleſſeneedless p • erillperil, two cautions muſtmust be noted,

1. That there be an abſoluteabsolute neceſſitynecessity, to bring vsus to this Cautions about an huſbandshusbands louingloving his wife more then himſelfehimself. st • raitestrait of parting with our life: which is, when the good we t • ime at in the behalfebehalf of our wiueswives cannot any other way be e • ffected, but by venturing our life. There was no other way to •• redeemeredeem the Church, but by the bloudblood of ChriſtChrist.

2. That the good we intend in this caſecase to our wiueswives be of g • reater valewvalue then our temporalltemporal life: as is the good of her r • ule, the ſauingsaving of it. Thus the ApoſtleApostle ſaithsaith, I will moſtmost gladly beſtowedbestowed for your ſoulessouls. Which mindemind men muſtmust much more 2 Cor. 12. 15. ca • riecary towards their wiueswives. It was for our ſaluationsalvation that ChriſtChrist ga • uegave himſelfehimself.

div.head: §. 70. Of husbands vnkindneſſeunkindness.
div.p: Contrary is their vnkindneſſeunkindness that preferreprefer eueryevery trifle of th •• eir owneown before the good of their wiueswives: their profit, their m • eaſuremeasure, their promotion, cleaneclean draw away their hearts and af •• fections from their wiueswives. If any extraordinary charge muſtmust be • laid out, or pains taken for their wiueswives good, little louelove wi • ll then appeareappear: whereby it appearesappears that there was no true an •• d ſoundsound louelove ſetledsettled in their hearts towards their wiueswives. As g • ld and other like mettals are tryed by the fire, ſoso louelove by affl •• ictions and croſſescrosses.

div.head: §. 71. Of combats in pretence of wiueswives honour.
div.p:
Contrary in another extreme is the ouerover-bold and ouerover-heady
pretended manhood of ſuchsuch husbands as vponupon eueryevery iealousjealous ſurmizesurmise and ſleightslight report, are ready to make challenges of fight, and to enter into ſinglesingle combats and duels, on pretence of maintaining their wiueswives honour. This being no warrantable courſecourse of righting a wrong, no honour can redound to the wife thereby, but much diſhonourdishonour and danger to the husband. If he preuaileprevail ouerover his aduerſarieadversary and kill, he is made guilty of murthermurder thereby, and ſoso reproach and ſhameshame muſtmust needs come to himſelfehimself, wife, and whole family: if he be ouercomeovercome and ſlaineslain, ſheshe may be reputed more guilty then ſheshe was before. And oft it falleth out that God in iuſtjust iudgementjudgment giuethgiveth ouerover the challenger into his aduerſariesadversaries hand, becauſebecause he hath vndertakenundertaken ſoso indirect a courſecourse.

div.head: §. 72. Of husbands Treat. 3. §. 6. 6 ChriſtsChrists louelove perpetuallperpetual. ConſtancyConstancy in louelove.
div.p:
VI. The continuance of ChriſtsChrists louelove was without date: IohJoh. 13. 1. HauingHaving louedloved his owneown, he louedloved them vntounto the end. His louelove was conſtantconstant (not by fits, now louingloving, then hating) and HoſHos. 2. 19. euerlaſtingeverlasting (neuernever repenting thereof, neuernever changing or altering his mindemind) no prouocationsprovocations, no tranſgreſſionstransgressions could euerever make him forget to louelove, and ceaſecease to doedo that good which he intended for his Church: note what he ſaidsaid to her eueneven when ſheshe reuoultedrevoulted from him, Thou haſthast played the harlot with many
IerJer. 3. 1. 2 Sam. 7. 15. louerslovers, yet returnereturn againeagain to me: and againeagain, My mercy ſhallshall not depart away.

For his louelove reſtethresteth not on the deſertdesert of his Church, but on the vnchangeableneſſeunchangeableness of his owneown will. As this manifeſtedmanifested ChriſtsChrists louelove to be true ſoundsound louelove, ſoso it made it profitable and beneficiallbeneficial to the Church, which, notwithſtandingnotwithstanding her many frailties, by virtue hereof is glorified.

This laſtlast branch muſtmust be added to all the former branches Husbands muſtmust be conſtantconstant in their louelove. of an husbands louelove, or elſeelse they will be all in vainevain and to no purpoſepurpose. This giuethgiveth the trueſttruest tryalltrial of ſoundsound louelove. Such was the louelove betwixt DauidDavid and IonathanJonathan: the ſoundeſtsoundest louelove that euerever was, betwixt partieparty and partieparty. This bringeth the greateſtgreatest glory to the partieparty which louethloveth: and the greateſtgreatest benefit to the partieparty which is louedloved. That a mans louelove may thus remaineremain firmefirm and inuiolableinviolable,

1. He muſtmust be ſuresure to lay a good foundation; he muſtmust
ground his louelove on Gods ordinance: and louelove his wife in regard of the matrimoniallmatrimonial bond which knittethknittethkniteth them together, and that neerenear vnionunion which thence ariſethariseth; and ſoso it will laſtlast ſoso long as that knot laſtethlasteth.

2. He muſtmust further ſupportsupport and ſtrengthenstrengthen it with an inuiolableinviolable reſolutionresolution to be changed and altered with no prouocationprovocation, but rather to paſſepass by all infirmities; indeauouringindeavouring in louelove to redreſſeredress them if poſſiblypossibly he can: if not, to bearebear with them.

div.head: §. 73. Of husbands variableneſſevariableness.
div.p: Contrary is their variableneſſevariableness, whoſewhose louelove is ready to turneturn as a weather cockecock with eueryevery blaſtblast of a contrary windewind: now t • ender-hearted, then againeagain hard-hearted: now ſmilingsmiling, then l • owringlouring: now giuinggiving this and that fauourfavour, then denying eueryevery thing, eueneven ſuchsuch things as are needfullneedful.

Many whoſewhose louelove was as hot as fire while their wiueswives were y • oung, or their friends liuedlived, or while they pleaſedpleased them, when t • hoſethose occaſionsoccasions are taken away, proueprove in their louelove as cold a • s ice.

AgaineAgain others by ſomesome continuance in doing good to their wiueswives, thinkethink it a burden: and waxing weary cleaneclean leaueleave off t • heir former good courſecourse; which plainly ſhewethshoweth that they neu • ernever truly and intirelyentirely louedloved their wiueswives.

By this patternepattern of ChriſtChrist here propounded to husbands, w • e hauehave on the one ſideside a good direction to teach vsus how to lo •• uelove our wiueswives, as hath beenebeen particularly declared; and on the o • ther ſideside, matter of humiliation, in that it ſhewethshoweth vsus how far •• refar ſhortshort we come of our bounden duty. HowſoeuerHowsoever, wiueswives m • ay moſtmost complainecomplain of their burden, becauſebecause it is a Subiectionsubjection w • hereunto by nature we are all loath to yeeldyield: yet I am ſuresure See Treat. 1. §. 10. th •• e heauieſtheaviest burden is laid vponupon the husbands ſhouldersshoulders: and m • uch more eaſieeasy it is to performeperform the part of a good wife, then a good husband.

div.head: §. 74. Of husbands louingloving their wiueswives Treat. 3. §. 59. as themſeluesthemselves.
div.p:
To the example of ChriſtChrist the ApoſtleApostle annexeth the patter •• nepattern of ones ſelfeself, in theſethese words: So ought men to louelove their
Eph. 5. 28.
wiu •• eswives as their owneown bodies.

div.head: QueſtQuest. Is not the former patternepattern ſufficientsufficient? Is this latter more excellent, or more perfect?
div.p: AnſwAnsw. ChriſtsChrists example is a full, compleatcomplete, perfect, and To ChriſtsChrists example, the patternepattern of ones ſelfeself is added. eueryevery way ſufficientsufficient patternepattern; farrefar more excellent then this of a mans ſelfeself: this is not annexed to addeadd any thing to that, or in regard of the excellency hereof, but only in regard of our dulneſſedulness, to make the point ſomewhatsomewhat more plaineplain and perſpicuousperspicuous. 1. BecauſeBecause it is more ſenſiblesensible. For this patternepattern is more ſenſiblesensible and better diſcerneddiscerned. EueryEvery one knoweth how he louethloveth his owneown body: but few or none know how ChriſtChrist louethloveth his Church. BeſidesBesides, 2. BecauſeBecause it is more imitable. that example of ChriſtChrist may ſeemeseem too high and excellent for any to attaineattain vntounto, eueneven inimitable; therefore to ſhewshow that he requireth no more then a man may performeperform, if he will ſetset himſelfehimself with care and conſcienceconscience to doedo his duty, he addeth the patternepattern of ones ſelfeself; that which one doth to his body, if he will, he may doedo to his wife.

No direction can be taken from this latter patternepattern, but The patternepattern of louingloving ones ſelfeself ſettethsetteth forth the ſamesame things that ChriſtsChrists louelove doth. might be referred to the former, as moſtmost of the former (though in a farrefar meaner manner) may be referred to the latter. For the louelove which a man beareth to himſelfehimself is true, and intireentire without all diſſimulationdissimulation: the moſtmost diſſemblingdissembling wretch in the world (who in his dealings with other men doth nothing vprightlyuprightly) nor will nor can diſſembledissemble with himſelfehimself; though other men ſhallshall neuernever know the depth of his heart, yet the ſpiritspirit 1 Cor. 2. 11. which is in him, eueneven himſelfehimself, knoweth it: ſoso as this patternepattern alſoalso preſſethpresseth truth and ſinceritysincerity on husbands in their affection towards their wiueswives: of all other they may not diſſembledissemble and dealedeal doubly with them; but let them know the intireneſſeintireness of their affection towards them: and ſeesee they neither faunefaun on • them, nor flatter them. They which pretend great louelove to their wiueswives in ſhewshow only, offend againſtagainst nature it ſelfeself. As the foreſaidforesaid louelove of a mans owneown ſelfeself is for manner intireentire and true, ſoso alſoalso free not forced: and for meaſuremeasure as great as poſſiblypossibly it • can be, and for continuance, conſtantconstant, and ſoso like to ChriſtChrist louelove. But there are two points eſpeciallyespecially to be conſideredconsidered in the louelove of ones ſelfeself which aboueabove others are moſtmost ſenſiblysensibly diſcerneddiscerned Man is tender towards himſelfehimself. in this patternepattern. 1. TenderneſſeTenderness. 2. CheerefulneſſeCheerfulness.

No other man will or can ſoso tenderly handle a mans hand
armearm, leggeleg or any other part of his body, as himſelfehimself: he is very ſenſiblesensible of his owneown ſmartsmart.

The metaphors which the ApoſtleApostle vſethuseth in theſethese words, He nouriſhethnourisheth and cheriſhethcherisheth it, doedo liuelylively ſetset forth this tenderneſſetenderness: Eph. 5. 29. for they are taken from fowles and birds which very charily, and tenderly houerhover ouerover their young ones, coueringcovering them all ouerover with their wings and feathers, but ſoso bearing vpup their bodies as no weight lieth vponupon them.

Thus ought husbands with all tenderneſſetenderness, and mildneſſemildness Husbands muſtmust dealedeal tenderly with their wiueswives. to dealedeal with their wiueswives, as we hauehave before noted in many particulars: only this example of a mans ſelfeself I thought good to ſetset before husbands, as a liuelylively patternepattern wherein they might behold a preſidentprecedentpresident without exception, going before them, and whereby they might receiuereceive excellent direction for the better performing of the particulars before noted.

AgaineAgain, no friend, no parent, no other party will or can ſoso Man is cheerefullcheerful in doing himſelfehimself good. willingly and cheerefullycheerfully doedo any kindneſſekindness for one, as a man for himſelfehimself. This among other is one eſpeciallespecial point which the law aimeth at, when it enioynesenjoins a man to louelove his neighbour
Leu. 19. 18. as himſelfehimself, namely, as willingly and readily as himſelfehimself. WhatſoeuerWhatsoever a man doth for himſelfehimself he doth much more cheerefullycheerfully then for another. There needeth no other proofeproof then experience. Let men take notice of their owneown mindemind and diſpoſitiondisposition when they doedo things for themſeluesthemselves, and this will be as cleereclear as the light when the SunneSun ſhinethshineth forth at s • oonesoon day.

Such an affection ought husbands to hauehave to their wiueswives: Husbands muſtmust be cheerefullcheerful in ſeekingseeking their wiueswives good. they ought more willingly and cheerefullycheerfully to doedo any thing f • or their wiueswives then for parents, children, friends or any other. Though this cheerefulneſſecheerfulness be an inward diſpoſitiondisposition of the h • eart, yet may it be manifeſtedmanifested by a mans forwardneſſeforwardness and re •• adineſſereadiness to doedo his wife good: when his wife ſhallshall no ſoonersooner deſiredesire a kindneſſekindness, then he will be ready to grant it: as b • oozBoaz ſaithsaith to Ruth, I will doedo to thee all that thou requireſtrequirest; yea, Ruth 3. 11. by any meanesmeans he may know that this or that will be beh • oofull to her, though ſheshe deſiredesire it not, yet to effect it for her: which was the mindemind of the ſaidsaid BoozBoaz to Ruth, as the hiſtoryhistory in •• many particulars ſhewethshoweth.

Contrary is the diſpoſitiondisposition of thoſethose husbands who ſoso grudgingly, repiningly, and diſcontentedlydiscontentedly doedo thoſethose things which they doedo in their wiueswives behalfebehalf, as their wiueswives had rather they were not done at all. The manner of doing them cauſethcauseth more griefegrief to tender hearted wiueswives, then the things themſeluesthemselves can doedo good.
Hitherto of the manner which husbands ought to obſerueobserve in performing their duties. The reaſonsreasons to inforceenforce the ſamesame remaineremain to be handled.

div.head: §. 75. Of ChriſtsChrists example, a motiuemotive to prouokeprovoke husbands to louelove their wiueswives.
div.p: The forenamed examples of ChriſtChrist and of our ſeluesselves as GenerallGeneral reaſonsreasons. 1. ChriſtsChrists example. they are patternespatterns for our direction, ſoso generallgeneral motiuesmotives to prouokeprovoke and ſtirrestir vsus vpup the more to performeperform all the forenamed duties after the manner preſcribedprescribed.

A greater, and ſtrongerstronger motiuemotive cannot be yeeldedyielded then the ChriſtsChrists example the greateſtgreatest motiuemotive that can be. example of ChriſtChrist. Example in it ſelfeself is of great force to prouokeprovoke vsus to doedo any thing: eſpeciallyespecially if it be the example of ſomesome great one, a man of place and renoune.

But who greater then ChriſtChrist? What more worthy patternepattern? If (as was Treat. 3. §. 74. ſhewedshowed) the example of the Church be of great force to mouemove wiueswives to be ſubiectsubject to their husbands, the example of ChriſtChrist muſtmust needs be of much greater force to mouemove husbands to louelove their wiueswives. A great honour it is to be like vntounto ChriſtChrist: and his example is a perfect patternepattern.

Two things there be which in ChriſtsChrists example are eſpeciallyespecially Two things in ChriſtsChrists patternepattern prouokeprovoke huſbandshusbands to louelove their wiueswives. to be noted to mouemove husbands to louelove their wiueswives.
1. That great inequality which is betwixt him and his ſpouſespouse.
2. That ſmallsmall benefit which he reapeth by louingloving her.

For the better diſcerningdiscerning of that inequality, the greatneſſegreatness of 1. The great inequality betwixt ChriſtChrist and his ſpouſespouse. ChriſtChrist on the one ſideside, and the meaneſſemeaness of the Church on the other, are duly to be weighed.

ChriſtsChrists greatneſſegreatness is in Scripture ſetset forth by comparing him with creatures, and the Creator. Compared with creatures he is farrefar more excellent then the moſtmost excellent, as the ApoſtleApostle by many arguments prouethproveth in the firſtfirst chapter to Hebr. that whole chapter is ſpentspent in proofeproof of this point: And in

Compared with the Creator he is no whit inferiourinferior to him, but Phil. 2. 6. equallequal:
Heb. 1. 3. Being the brightneſſebrightness of glory, and the expreſſeexpress image of his perſonperson: and that IobJob. 1. 1, 3. word of whom it is ſaidsaid, In the beginning was the word, and the word was with God, and the word was God: All things were made by him &etcc. So as he is the very Creator himſelfehimself, eternalleternal, infinite, incomprehenſibleincomprehensible. Thus is ChriſtsChrists greatneſſegreatness inexplicable.

The meaneſſemeaness of the Church is as low on the other ſideside: ſheshe is a creature, faſhionedfashioned out of the earth, proceeding from the loinesloins of corrupt Adam, not only finite, but in it ſelfeself vile and baſebase: The Prophet Ezec. 16. 1. &etcc.
Ezechiel doth ſetset her forth in her liuelylively colours as ſheshe is in her ſelfeself. Compared therefore vntounto ChriſtChrist ſheshe is IſaIsa. 40. 17. nothing, leſſeless then nothing. What equality, what proportion can there then be betwixt ChriſtChrist and her?

But if man and woman be compared together, we ſhallshall findefind a neerenear equality: and that both in the points of their humiliation, and alſoalso of their exaltation. In regard of the former, they are both of the ſamesame mould, of the ſamesame corrupt nature, ſubiectsubject to the ſamesame infirmities, at length brought to the ſamesame end. In regard of the latter the beſtbest and greateſtgreatest priuiledgesprivileges are common to both of them: they are both made after the ſamesame image, redeemed by the ſamesame price, partakers of the ſamesame grace, and heiresheirs together of the ſamesame inheritance.

div.head: QueſtQuest. What is then the preferment of the male kindekind? What is the excellency of an husband?
div.p: AnſwAnsw. Only outward and momentany. Outward, in the things of this world only: for Gal. 3. 28. in ChriſtChrist IeſusJesus they are both one. Momentany, for the time of this life only: for Mat. 22. 30. in the reſurrectionresurrection they neither mariemarry, nor are giuengiven in mariagemarriage, but are as the Angels of God in heauenheaven: then all ſubiectionsubjection of wiueswives to husbands ceaſethceaseth.

To conclude this point, the inequality betwixt ChriſtChrist and the Church, and equality betwixt man and wife being ſuchsuch as hath beenebeen declared; ſeeingseeing ChriſtChrist vouchſafethvouchsafeth to louelove his Church, ought not man thereby be mouedmoved to louelove his wife?

The other point concerning the ſmallsmall benefit which ChriſtChrist 2. The ſmallsmall benefit that ChriſtChrist reapeth by louingloving his Church. reapeth by his Church, will yet further inforceenforce the point: for illuſtrationillustration whereof we will note the great benefit which man reapeth by his wife.

The benefit which ChriſtChrist reapeth from the Church is in one word nothing. For ChriſtChrist is in himſelfehimself AlAll-ſufficientsufficient: he neither needeth any thing, nor can receiuereceive any thing: IobJob 35. 7. If thou be eſtest righteous, what giueſtgivest thou to him? Or what receiuethreceiveth he of thine hand? Yet abundantly he beſtowethbestoweth all manner of gifts, temporalltemporal, and ſpirituallspiritual, earthly and heauenlyheavenly. It was not therefore his owneown good that he reſpectedrespected in louingloving the Church, but her good: for he being 1 Tim. 3. 16. God became man; being Lord of heauenheaven and earth, he tooketook vponupon him Phil. 2. 6, 7. the formeform of a ſeruantservant; being 2 Cor. 8 9. rich he became poorepoor: hauinghaving the Reu. 1. 18. KeyesKeys of hell and of death, and being Act. 3. 15. the Lord of life, he Phil. 2. 8. humbled himſelfehimself, and became obedient vntounto the death: thus to ſhewshow louelove to his Church he left much for her ſakesake, but receiuedreceived nothing of her.

But the benefit which man reapeth from a wife is very great: for Gen. 2. 18. It was not good for a man to be alone: in ſoso much as Pro. 18. 22. He who findeth a wife findeth a good thing; and that in all the points of goodneſſegoodness, a profitable thing, a comfortable thing, a delightfulldelightful thing. They know not the benefit of the mariedmarried eſtateestate, who See Treat. 2. Part. 1. §. 27. prefer ſinglesingle life before it, eſpeciallyespecially if the mariedmarried eſtateestate be ordered by Gods word, and man and wife carefullcareful to performeperform their owneown duty each to other.

To apply this point alſoalso, and to bring it to the concluſionconclusion: ChriſtsChrists example remouethremoveth all pretences which men make for not louingloving their wiueswives. If ChriſtChrist who can receiuereceive nothing from the Church notwithſtandingnotwithstanding louelove her, ought not men much more to louelove their wiueswives, who many waiesways receiuereceive much good from them, and without whom they cannot well be?

This example of ChriſtChrist is the rather to be noted, becauſebecause it cleaneclean wipeth away all thoſethose falſefalse colours, and vainevain pretences which many alledgeallege as reaſonsreasons, to ſhewshow that there is little reaſonreason they ſhouldshould louelove their wiueswives: ſomesome of their pretences are theſethese.

1. Their wiueswives are of a farrefar meaner rankerank then 1. ObiectObject. themſeluesthemselves; ſhouldshould they then performeperform duty to their inferioursinferiors?
They commonly who marriemarry their kitchinkitchen maids, or others farrefar vnderunder their degree, alledgeallege this pretence.

AnſwAnsw. I might reply, That mariagemarriage aduancethadvanceth a wife to the degree of her husband: and that it was his owneown folliefolly to marriemarry one ſoso meanemean: but for the purpoſepurpose and point in hand, let any tell me, whether the ſuppoſedsupposed diſparitiedisparity betwixt them & their wiueswives, be in any degree comparable to that which is betwixt ChriſtChrist and the Church: yet ChriſtChrist thinketh not much to doedo duties of louelove to his Church.
2. There is nothing in their wiueswives worthy to be louedloved. 2. ObiectObject.

AnſwAnsw. This very thing, that ſuchsuch an one is thy wife, is matter enough to make her worthy of louelove. But what was there in the Church to make her worthy of ChriſtsChrists louelove? If it be ſaidsaid that ſheshe is endued with many excellent graces, which make her amiable in ChriſtsChrists ſightsight: I anſweranswer, that of her ſelfeself ſheshe hath none of thoſethose graces, ChriſtChrist hath beſtowedbestowed them vponupon her, and ſoso made her a • miable: and thus oughteſtoughtest thou to endeuourendeavour by vſingusing all good meanesmeans thou canſtcanst to make thy wife anſwerableanswerable to thy louelove: but howſoeuerhowsoever, to louelove her.

3. Their wiueswives giuegive iuſtjust occaſionoccasion to be hated by reaſonreason of their 3. ObiectObject. beeuiſhneſſebeevishness, ſtoutneſſestoutness, inſolencieinsolency, and other like intolerable v • ices.

AnſwAnsw. No occaſionoccasion may ſeemeseem iuſtjust to mouemove an husband to hate his wife: nor any vice ſeemeseem to him intolerable: with goodnesgoodness he ou •• ughtovught to ouercomeovercome euillevil. If notorious ſinssins ſeemedseemed intolerable to ChriſtChrist, or that he thought any occaſionoccasion iuſtjust to cauſecause hatred, many t • hat are of his Church would oft draw his hatred vponupon them: but ChriſtChrist hateth neuernever a member of his Church.
4. There is no hope that euerever I ſhallshall receiuereceive any helpehelp of my 4. ObiectObject. wife, or benefit from her.

AnſAns. There is little charitiecharity in ſuchsuch as can conceiueconceive no hope: for lo • uelove hopeth all things: but yet the caſecase ſoso ſtandethstandeth with ChriſtChrist. The 1. Cor. 13. 7. Church is ſoso vtterlyutterly vnableunable to help or benefit him, as he may iuſtlyjustly sa • y, he cannot hope to receiuereceive any thing frōfron her. ChriſtChrist louethloveth the c • hurch for her own good, not for his; ſoso ought husbands. Thus if ChriſtsChrists example be well weighed, & obſeruedobserved of husbands, it will af • ford matter enough to remoueremove eueryevery doubt or ſcruplescruple raiſedraised to ali • enate their affections from their wiueswives. Fitly therefore hath the
ApoſtleApostle ſetset it before husbands, both to direct them how to louelove their wiueswives, and alſoalso to mouemove them ſoso to doedo.

div.head: §. 76. Of a mans louelove to himſelfehimself, a motiuemotive to prouokeprovoke him to louelove his wife.
div.p: To the ſamesame purpoſepurpose that ChriſtsChrists example tendeth, tendeth alſoalso the patternepattern of a mans ſelfeself. Great is the affection that a man beareth to himſelfehimself, to his owneown fleſhflesh, his owneown bodiebody: he neuernever hateth, but euerever louethloveth himſelfehimself: no ſoresore, no diſeaſedisease, no painepain, no ſtinchstinch that the fleſhflesh bringeth to a man, can make him hate it: but rather all manner of infirmities doedo make him the more to pittypity, tender, and cheriſhcherish it. This is a workework of nature: the moſtmost heatheniſhheathenish, and barbarous, that euerever were, doedo it. Now a wife being to a man as his bodiebody and his fleſhflesh (for they two are one fleſhflesh) and God hauinghaving commanded men to louelove their wiueswives as their owneown bodies, theſethese concluſionsconclusions will neceſſarilynecessarily follow from this motiuemotive:

1. He that louethloveth not his wife is more cariedcarried with the inſtinctinstinct of nature, then with the expreſſeexpress charge of the God of nature. Natures inſtinctinstinct mouethmoveth him to louelove his bodiebody. But Gods expreſſeexpress charge mouethmoveth him not, to louelove his wife.

2. He that louethloveth not his wife is worſeworse then an infidellinfidel and a barbarian, yea then a very beaſtbeast: for all theſethese louelove their owneown bodies, and their owneown fleſhflesh: but a wife (by Gods ordinance) is as ones bodiebody, and his fleſhflesh.

3. He that louethloveth his wife louethloveth himſelfehimself: the ApoſtleApostle himſelfehimself verſvers. 28. in theſethese very words layeth downedown this concluſionconclusion: from whence by the rule of contraries this alſoalso will follow, He that louethloveth not his wife, louethloveth not himſelfehimself.

4. He that louethloveth not his wife cannot but bring woe and miſchiefemischief vponupon himſelfehimself. For the damage and miſchiefemischief which followeth on a wife, through any neglect of dutieduty on her husband part, followeth alſoalso on him: as the miſchiefemischief which followeth on the bodiebody through any negligence of the head, lighteth alſoalso on the head.
If theſethese be not motiuesmotives ſufficientsufficient to prouokeprovoke an husband to louelove his wife, I know not what can be ſufficientsufficient.
