div.head: §. 2. Of Childrens louelove to their Parents.
div.p: I make the fountainefountain of childrens duties to be a mixed and compound diſpoſitiondisposition, in reſpectrespect of that authoritieauthority and affection which is mixed together in parents. The authoritieauthority of parents requireth fearefear in children: and their affection, louelove. So intireentire and ſoso ardent is parents affection towards their children, as it would make children too bold and inſolentinsolent if there were not authoritieauthority mixed therewith to workework fearefear: and ſoso ſupremesupreme and abſoluteabsolute is their authoritieauthority ouerover them, as it would make children like ſlauesslaves to dread their parents, if a fatherly affection were not tempered therewith to breed louelove. But both theſethese ioynedjoined together make a very good compoſitioncomposition: louelove like ſugarsugar ſweetnethsweetneth fearefear, and fearefear like ſaltsalt ſeaſonethseasoneth louelove: and thus, to ioynejoin them both together, it is a louingloving-fearefear, or a fearinglouefearing-lovefearinglove, which is the ground of childrens duties.

Where ChriſtChrist forbiddeth an exceſſiueexcessive louelove in children to Mat. 10. 37. their parents, he implieth that parents are a fit obiectobject for children to louelove (ſoso as their louelove be welwell moderated:) yea he implieth that it is an affection eueneven by nature ingraffed in children to louelove their parents. IoſephJoseph is commended vntounto children as a worthy patternepattern in louingloving his father, and that from his youth till the deceaſedecease of his father: in teſtimonytestimony whereof in his younger yeeresyears he brought to his father the euillevil report of his
Gen. 37. 2. brethren, whereby he incurred their enuieenvy and hatred, which he would neuernever hauehave done, if he had not louedloved his father: and hauinghaving beenebeen long abſentabsent from his father, when by Gods prouidenceprovidence there was offered an occaſionoccasion for him to meet with his brethren, one of his firſtfirst queſtionsquestions to them was about their father: Gen. 43. 7. and hearing that he was liuingliving, he thought it not enough to ſendsend him food for his need, but muſtmust alſoalso needs ſeesee his face, Gen. 45. 9. and hauehave him dwell with him: and while his father was in the way he went out to meet him, and at firſtfirst ſightsight fell on his neck, Gen. 46. 29. and wept a good while (a token of great affection.)

That louelove which naturally parents bearebear to their children, ReaſonsReasons. 1. EquitieEquity. ought in equitieequity to breed in children a louelove to their parents. For louelove deſeruethdeservethdeserueth louelove: and moſtmost vnworthyunworthy are they to be louedloved, who cannot louelove againeagain. The louelove of parents aboueabove all others is to be anſweredanswered with louelove on childrens part to the vttermoſtuttermost of their power, becauſebecause it is free, great, and conſtantconstant.

BeſidesBesides, there is a neceſſitienecessity of louelove in children to their parents, 22. NeceſſitieNecessity. leſtlest for want thereof, their ſubiectionsubjection (which of all others ought to be moſtmost free) ſhouldshould turneturn into ſlauiſhslavish ſeruitudeservitude.

This ought children the rather to labour after, becauſebecause by nature they are nothing ſoso prone to louelove their parents, as their parents are to louelove them. LoueLove is weightieweighty, and, as weighty things, it deſcendethdescendeth. Children therefore with conſcienceconscience of dutieduty muſtmust labour to make ſupplysupply of this defect, and helpehelp nature by grace. I deniedeny not but naturally there is in children a greater louelove to their parents, then to others: yet in compariſoncomparison of the heat of parents louelove to them, their louelove to their parents is but cold. WherforeWherefore as the heat of the Sun ſhiningshining much and long on a ſtonestone wall, draweth a reflection of heat from that wall: ſoso the hot beamesbeams of parents louelove, which with
feruencyfervency and conſtancyconstancy is caſtcast on children, ought to prouokeprovoke and ſtirrestir vpup children to ſendsend forth a reflection of louelove on their parents.
Two extreamesextremes are contrary to this affection of louelove.

One is want of naturallnatural affection, which is a vice moſtmost odious
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . Rom. 1. 30. 2 Tim. 3. 3. and abominable in all, but moſtmost of all in children. The ApoſtleApostle reckoneth this among the moſtmost heighnousheinous vices that be.

The other is hatred and deſpightdespight of parents: a vice more then monſtrousmonstrous, and vnnaturallunnatural. From thence commethcometh mocking and curſingcursing of parents, whereof we ſhallshall afterwards hearehear.

div.head: §. 3. Of a childes fearefear of his parent.
div.p: To the forenamed dutieduty of louelove, muſtmust fearefear be added, which is a childes awfullawful reſpectrespect of his parent.

This awfullawful reſpectrespect ariſethariseth from an honourable eſteemeesteem which a childechild in his iudgementjudgment and opinion hath of his parent, as he is his parent; and from it proceedeth on the one ſideside, a deſiredesire and indeauourindeavour in all things to pleaſeplease the parent, and on the other ſideside a loathneſſeloathness to offend him.

In this reſpectrespect the fearefear of a childechild is oppoſedopposed to the fearefear of a ſlaueslave. For a childes fearefear being mixed with louelove, hath reſpectrespect to the offence which a parent may take; but a ſlauesslaves fearefear, which is ordinarily mixed with hatred, hath reſpectrespect to nothing but the puniſhmentpunishment which his maſtermaster may inflict vponupon him. The forenamed fearefear is ſoso proper to children, as that awfullawful reſpectrespect which the Saints bearebear to God, is called a See Treat. 1. §. 4. ſiliallfilialsiliall or child-like fearefear.

This fearefear in a childechild is an eſpeciallespecial branch of that Exo. 20. 12. honour which the law requireth of children to their parents: and it is in Leu. 19. 3. expreſſeexpress termesterms inioynedenjoined to children by the law. That phraſephrase which God vſethuseth of Miriam ( Num. 12. 14. If her father had but ſpitspit in her face, ſhouldshould ſheshe not be aſhamedashamed ſeuenseven daiesdays?) ſhewethshoweth that there ought to be ſuchsuch a fearefear of the parent in a childes heart, as ſhouldshould workework ſhameshame in it when the parent is offended.
A worthy patternepattern we hauehave hereof in Gen. 27. 12. IaakobJacob, who was loath to gainegain the bleſſingblessing with offence of his father.

This fearefear keepeth louelove in compaſſecompass: and reſtrainethrestraineth a childechild ReaſonsReasons. 1. FeareFear ordereth louelove. from ouermuchovermuch ſaucineſſesauciness, and malipartneſſemalipartness.
And it is a cauſecause of a childes reuerendreverend and dutifulldutiful carriage 2. It well guideth the carriage. to his parent. For as the heart is affected the carriage will be ordered.

Contrary hereunto is that light, or (which is more abomi • nable) Contrary, light and baſebase eſteemeesteem of parents. that baſebase and vile eſteemeesteem of parents, which is in the heart of many children: eſpeciallyespecially if parents be poorepoor, of low degree, vnlearnedunlearned, ignorant, or ſubiectsubject to any infirmities. It cannot be but that Gen. 9. 22. Cham had too light, if not a baſebase eſteemeesteem of his father, when he derided him. A true filiallfilial fearefear would hauehave reſtrainedrestrained him from that extreme.

Wherefore to breed and cheriſhcherish this fearefear, and to preuentprevent, How to breed and cheriſhcherish a filiallfilial fearefear. o • r redreſſeredress the contrary extreme, let children well informeinform themſeluesthemselves of their parents place and authoritieauthority, how they are in Gods ſteadstead, and a meanesmeans vnderunder God of their childrens being: children hauehave receiuedreceived their very ſubſtancesubstance from the ſubs • tancesubstance of their parents. In which reſpectrespect though they ſhouldshould s • eemeseem contemptible to others, yet not to their children.

Thus much of a childes inward diſpoſitiondisposition towards his parent. The manifeſtationmanifestation thereof muſtmust be by his outward carriage: and that in two things; Reuerencereverence, and Obedienceobedience: both which reſpectrespect a parents authoritieauthority.

div.head: ObiectObject. Kneeling is a geſturegesture proper to Gods worſhipworship.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. It is not ſoso proper, but that it may be vſedused in ciuillcivil caſescases: elſeelse ChriſtChrist would hauehave reprouedreproved the young man for kneeling before him as well as for calling him good: for he conceiuedconceived Mar. 10. 17. It is not ſimplysimply the geſturegesture, but the occaſionoccasion of the geſturegesture, the mindemind of him that performeth it, and the end why he performeth it that maketh it diuinedivine, or ciuillcivil. Cornelius fell down before Peter with conceit of ſomesome diuinedivine excellency in him, and was not allowed: his manner of worſhipingworshiping was diuinedivine. The iaylorjaylor fell downedown before Paul and Silas in acknowledgementacknowledgment of ſomesome outward eminency in them, and was not reprouedreproved: his manner of worſhippingworshipping was meerelymerely ciuillcivil. Yet it followeth not that he maketh his parent a king. Neither will it follow that by kneeling to his parent he maketh him a God, becauſebecause men kneelekneel to God.

div.head: §. 12. Of childrens forbearing to doedo things without conſentconsent of parents.
div.p:
That children may the better know their dutieduty in this reſpectrespect, The parts of a childs obedience. I will diſtinctlydistinctly ſetset forth, both the parts, and alſoalso the extent of a childs obedience:
1. Wherein it conſiſtethconsisteth.
2. How farrefar it extendeth.
The generallgeneral parts wherein it conſiſtethconsisteth are two:
1. A forbearance from doing things without conſentconsent of parents. Of the ſeuerallseveral wayesways whereby conſentconsent may be giuengiven, ſeesee Treat. 3.
2. A performance of ſuchsuch things as parents will hauehave done.

The former of theſethese is a dutieduty whereunto children are muſtmostmust bound while they are vnderunder their parents gouernmentgovernment. For that §. 19. Num. 30. 17. time the conſentconsent of parents is not only meet, but neceſſarienecessary: and that for theſethese reaſonsreasons.

1. Children are as the goods of their parents, wholly in their power, to be ordered and diſpoſeddisposed by them. On this ground Satan hauinghaving all that IobJob had put into his hand, tooketook libertieliberty ouerover IobJob 1. 12, 19. his children as well as ouerover his goods and chattellchattel.
2. Children while they be vnderunder gouernmentgovernment, (eueneven the eldeſteldest that are heiresheirs) differ nothing from ſeruantsservants. Galat. 4. 1.
3. By Gods law giuengiven to the IewesJews, parents had power to ſellsell Exod. 21. 7. their children.

4. Parents had power to diſanulldisannul ſuchsuch things as children had done. InſtanceInstance the caſecase of a vow made to God, which was one of Num. 30. 4. the moſtmost inuiolableinviolable things that one could doedo.

Contrary is the opinion and practiſepractise of many, who hold parents conſentconsent at the moſtmost but a matter of conueniencieconveniencyconueniency: that it is good, if children will, to hauehave their parents conſentconsent: if they hauehave it not, the matter is not great: their contracts or other things which they doedo, are as firmefirm, and good, without, as with their conſentsconsents. If this were ſoso, wherein is the authoritieauthority of a parent more then of a wiſewise experienced friend? It is meet, and good to hauehave ſuchsuch an ones conſentconsent.

But that the power of parents, and dutieduty of children in this
point, may the better be ſeeneseen, I will exemplifieexemplify it in fiuefive particular caſescases. 1. EntringEntering into a calling. 2. Making mariagemarriage. 3. DiſpoſingDisposing of goods. 4. Ordering apparellapparel. 5. Making vowesvows.

div.head: §. 17. Of the equity of the point, and reaſonsreasons why children ſhouldshould hauehave their parents conſentconsent vntounto their marriage.
div.p:
1. By mariagemarriage children are put from their parents: for The reaſonsreasons alleadgedalleged §.
Gen. 2. 24. Manman muſtmust leaueleave his Fatherfather and Mothermother, and cleauecleave vntounto his wife. Is it not then great reaſonreason that they from whom children 12. may be applied to this particular. had their being, and by whom they hauehave beenebeen maintained and trained vpup till the time of their mariagemarriage, ſhouldshould hauehave notice of that kind of leauingleaving them, and conſentconsent thereto?

2. A parents power by the marriage of his childechild is paſſedpassed ouerover to the husband or wife of the childechild. And ſhallshall ſuchsuch a power be taken away without conſentconsent of parent?

3. Children for the moſtmost part being heady and raſhrash for want of experience; and ſeekingseeking more to ſatisfiesatisfy their preſentpresent carnallcarnal deſiredesire, then to prouideprovide a good laſtinglasting helpehelp for themſeluesthemselves: but parents by the inſtinctinstinct of nature louingloving their children as well as children louelove themſeluesthemselves, and hauinghaving by much experience better vnderſtandingunderstanding of a meetemeet helpehelp, and better able to vſeuse their diſcerningdiscerning gift in this caſecase, becauſebecause it is not their owneown caſecase, and yet the caſecase of one whom they louelove as themſeluesthemselves, and to whom they wiſhwish as much good as to themſeluesthemselves; is it not meetemeet eueneven for the childs good, that in a matter of ſuchsuch moment as mariagemarriage, the parent ſhouldshould hauehave a ſtroakestroke?

div.head: §. 18. Of a childs cariagecarriage in caſecase a parent prouideprovide an vnfitunfit mate or none at all.

div.p: QueſtQuest. What if parents vrgeurge their children to marry ſuchsuch Whether parents may force their children to marry, or no. as they can not affect and louelove: muſtmust children therein againſtagainst their mindemind and liking yeeldyield obedience?

AnſwAnsw. If there be no iuſtjust exception againſtagainst the partieparty commended, they ought with the vttermoſtuttermost of their power to endeauourendeavour See Treat. 6. §. 54. to bring their affection to the bent of their parents will: and as an helpehelp thereunto, be perſwadedpersuaded that their parents are as carefullcareful of their good as they themſeluesthemselves are, and
wiſerwiser then themſeluesthemselves: yea aboueabove all they ought to make inſtantinstant prayer vntounto God (in whoſewhose hand mans heart is to turneturn it
ProuProv. 21. 1. whither ſoeuersoever he will) that he would be pleaſedpleased to alter the courſecourse of their affection, and to ſettlesettle it on the party whom their parent hath choſenchosen for them; if at leaſtleast they ſeesee no iuſtjust cauſecause to the contrary. But if notwithſtandingnotwithstanding all the meanesmeans that they can vſeuse, they ſtillstill findefind their heart altogether auerſeaverse, they may in a reuerendreverend manner entreat their parent to forbeareforbear to preſſepress that match, and to thinkethink of ſomesome other.
2. QueſtQuest. What if the parent be negligent, and in due time prouideprovide no fit match, may not the childechild prouideprovide one for himſelfehimself?

AnſwAnsw. A parents negligence is not a ſufficientsufficient pretext to make a child caſtcast off that ſubiectionsubjection which he oweth to his parent. Yet I deny not but that a childechild knowing where a fit match is to be had, may make knowneknown as much to his parent (as SampſonSamson did) and crauecrave both his conſentconsent and help thereunto. IudgJudg. 14. 2. And if his parent giuegive no eareear to his humble ſuitsuit, he may vſeuse the mediation of his kindred or other friends. Yea if neceſſitynecessity require that the childechild be married, and his parent addeadd wilfulneſſewilfulness to negligence, and will not be mouedmoved at all, neither by the humble ſuitsuit of his childechild, nor by the earneſtearnest ſolicitationsolicitation of any friends, meanesmeans may be made to the MagiſtrateMagistrate (who is in Gods place ouerover the parent as well as ouerover Qui liberos iniuria prohibuerint ducere vx eresvxores vel nubere, per praeſidespraesides cogantur in matrimonium collocare Di eſtestDigest. lib. 23. tit. 2. § 19. the childechild, and ought to afford releeferelief vntounto the childechild) and what the MagiſtrateMagistrate doth in that caſecase is as good a warrant to the childechild as if the parent had done it.

The like meanesmeans may be vſedused if a parent be an Idolater, HeretickeHeretic, or AtheiſtAtheist, and will not yeeldyield that his childechild be married to any but to one of his owneown profeſſionprofession and diſpoſitiondisposition.

div.head: §. 19. Of the ſinnesin of Children in marrying without their parents conſentconsent.
div.p:
Contrary is the mindemind and practiſepractise of ſuchsuch children as ouerover lightly eſteemingesteeming their parents power, take matches of their owneown choice: and that ſometimessometimes priuilyprivily without giuinggiving any notice at all to their parents: and ſometimessometimes moſtmost rebelliouſlyrebelliously againſtagainst their parents mind and charge: not much vnlikeunlike thoſethose
who in the old world are condemned for taking wiueswives of all that
Gen. 6. 2. they choſechose (which was one branch of that wickedneſſewickedness for which the world was drowned) or rather like EſauEsau who tooketook Gen. 26. 35. ſuchsuch wiueswives as prouedproved a griefegrief to his parents. What bleſſingblessing can be expected to fall vponupon ſuchsuch mariagesmarriages? orOr rather what curſecurse may not be feared to follow them? Gods law is tranſgreſſedtransgressed thereby: his Image in parents deſpiſeddespised, that which is more proper to them then any goods; or fraudulently, or violently taken from them: their ſoulessouls grieuedgrieved thereat: and they See more miſchiefesmischiefs following ſuchsuch mariagesmarriages, §. 21. oft prouokedprovoked to caſtcast off their children, and curſecurse their mariagesmarriages. Now Gods curſecurse doth oft follow the iuſtjust curſecurse of a parent.

div.head: §. 20. Of obiectionsobjections for childrens marrying without parents conſentconsent, anſweredanswered.

div.p: 1. ObiectObject. Though IaakobJacob married one wife according to his parents direction, yet he married other three (at leaſtleast the two maidesmaids) without their conſentconsent.
1. AnſwAnsw. IaakobsJacob's example in marrying more wiueswives then one is not iuſtifiablejustifiable.

2. AnſwAnsw. IaakobJacob had a generallgeneral conſentconsent of his parents to Gen. 28. 2. take a wife of the daughters of Laban: if therefore his maryingmarrying of two wiueswives had beenebeen lawfulllawful, neither this nor that daughter had beenebeen taken without all conſentconsent of his parents. As for the two maids of whom he had children, neither of them was his wife: for long after they had children they are called his maids,
Gen. 32. 22. and diſtinguiſheddistinguished from his wiueswives.
2. ObiectObject. SeruantsServantsservants may marymarry without their maſtersmasters conſentconsent: why then not children without their parents?
1. AnſwAnsw. See Treat. 8. §. 17. It is not lawfulllawful for ſeruantsservants ſoso to doedo while the d • ate of their couenantcovenant laſtethlasteth.

2. AnſwAnsw. Though the ſeruitudeservitude of a ſeruantservant be greater t • hen of a childechild, yet a parent hath in many reſpectsrespects a greater p • ower ouerover his childechild, then a maſtermaster ouerover his ſeruantservant. The p • ower which a maſtermaster hath is by a mutuallmutual couenantcovenant betwixt him and his ſeruantservant, and by the voluntary ſubiectionsubjection of a ſeru • antservant vntounto his maſtermaster. But the power of a parent is by the bond of nature, in that a childechild hath his being from his parents. Bes • ides, this ſubiectionsubjection of a childechild to his parents in caſecase of marriage,
is not for ſeruitudeservitude but See the third reaſonreason in §. 17. for the good of the childechild.
3. ObiectObject. ChildrenChildrenchildren marry for themſeluesthemselves and not for their parents, why then ſhouldshould parents conſentconsent be ſoso much ſtoodstood vponupon?

1. AnſwAnsw. Though they mariemarry not for their parents, yet they mariemarry See the ſecondsecond reaſonreason in §. 17. PſalPsal. 127. 3. from their parents: by mariagemarriage they are freed from the power of their parents.

2. AnſwAnsw. ChildrenChildrenchildren are not their owneown: they are the inheritance of the Lord: the Lord hath giuengiven them to parents as an inheritance: a childechild therefore may no more marry for himſelfehimself without conſentconsent of parents, then alienate his parents goods for himſelfehimself.

div.head: §. 21. Of ſtealingstealing children from parents for mariagemarriage ſakesake.
div.p: To the §. 19. forenamed ſinnesin, and to the vengeance thereof, doedo they make themſeluesthemselves acceſſaryaccessary, who fraudulently allure, or violently take away children to marry them otherwiſeotherwise then their parents would. This is a worſeworse kindekind of felony then ſtealingstealing away the goods of a man. For children are much more properly a mans owneown, then his goods: and dearer to him then any goods can be: yea and ſoso much more highly to be eſteemedesteemed, by how much reaſonablereasonable creatures are to be preferred before ſenſeleſſesenseless, and ſenſuallsensual things. Our Anno 4. & 5. Phil. & Mar. ſtatstat. 8. ſtatutestatute law expreſlyexpressly condemneth this, and impoſethimposeth a ſeueresevere puniſhmentpunishment on ſuchsuch as ſhallshall offend therein. And iuſtlyjustly doedo ſuchsuch offenders deſeruedeserve to be ſeuerelyseverely puniſhedpunished, both in regard of the heinouſneſſeheinousness of the ſinnesin, and alſoalso in regard of the many MiſchiefesMischiefs ariſingarising from marriages without parents conſentconsent. miſchiefesmischiefs which follow thereon, as, Alienation of parents affection from their children, DiſinheritingDisinheriting heiresheirs, Enmity betwixt the friends of each party ſoso married, Litigious ſuitssuits in law, RuineRuin of families, and (if the perſonagespersonages, whoſewhose children are married without their parents conſentconsent, be great and noble) DiſturbanceDisturbance of whole townestowns, cities, and nations. InſtanceInstance the deſtructiondestruction of the Shechemites Gen. 34. CauſaCausa mali tanti coniux. Virg. Aeneid. 6. Qui rapta longum cum coniuge bellum Attulit in patriam. Ouid. Met. l. 12. lege. Hor. Carm. l. 1. Od. 15. This is ſaidsaid to hauehave beenebeen the cauſecause of the tennetentenn yearesyears warrewar betwixt the Grecians and TroianesTrojans, and of the ruineruin of Troy.

div.head: §. 22. Of miniſtersministers ſinnesin in maryingmarrying children without parents conſentconsent.
div.p:
Such miniſtersministers alſoalso as through CareleſneſſeCarelessness, not taking due
account of the parties whom they mariemarry, whether they hauehave their parents conſentconsent or no; or through bribery, being hired by reward, doedo mariemarry ſuchsuch children as they know hauehave not their parents conſentconsent; doedo in an high degree make themſeluesthemselves acceſſaryaccessary to the §. 19. forenamed ſinnesin. Their fact is as bad as the fact of the principals themſeluesthemselves. Their ſolemnizationsolemnization of ſuchsuch mariagesmarriages emboldneth both the parties that are ſoso mariedmarried, and alſoalso all the perſonspersons that are preſentpresent thereat. They highly diſhonourdishonour Gods holy ordinance, in that bearing the perſonperson of God they ſaysay of ſuchsuch as God hath forbidden to be ſoso ioynedjoined together, ThoſeThose whom God hath ioynedjoined together let no man put aſunderasunder. If miniſtersministers had not their hand in ſuchsuch vnlawfullunlawful mariagesmarriages, they could not be made: for our Church ratifieth no mariagemarriage but what is made by a miniſterminister. Wherefore ſomesome miniſterminister or other is guilty of this foulefoul ſinnesin, whenſoeuerwhensoever any childechild is mariedmarried without conſentconsent of parents. Well therefore doth our Church (to preuentprevent this ſinnesin) expreſlyexpressly forbid miniſtersministers to mariemarry any without parents conſentconsent: and inflict a ſeueresevere cenſurecensure on them that ſhallshall offend therein.

div.head: §. 23. Of childrens forbearing to diſpoſedispose any of their parents goods without conſentconsent.
div.p: A third branch of the ſubiectionsubjection of children in forbearing to doedo any thing without their parents conſentconsent, is about their parents goods.

That children though liuingliving in their parents houſehouse, ought not without their parents conſentconsent to diſpoſedispose their goods, is euidentevident by the extent of their obedience, in all things.

In that IſaakIsaac was pleaſedpleased to ſendsend IaakobJacob to Padan Aram without any great prouiſionprovision, it ſeemethseemeth that IaakobJacob made conſcienceconscience of taking any thing priuilyprivily, but went as his father ſentsent him Gen. 32. 10. with his ſtaffestaff. And the Gen. 31. 36. apology which he made to Laban his father in law concerning things taken away, ſhewethshoweth that he held it vnlawfullunlawful for children priuilyprivily to conueyconvey a • way their parents goods. What is my treſpaſſetrespass? whatWhat is my ſinnesin? (ſaithsaith he) what haſthast thou found of all my houſholdhousehold-ſtuffestuff?
Doth he not hereby imply, that if Labans daughters had t • aken away any of their fathers goods, it had beenebeen a treſpaſſetrespass a • nd ſinnesin?

The ApoſtleApostle ſaithsaith of the heireheir (who of all the children may ReaſonsReasons. 1. Children vnderunder parents are as ſeruantsservants. ſeemeseem to hauehave the greateſtgreatest right) that as long as he is a childechild (that is, vnderunder the gouernmentgovernment of his parents) he differeth nothing from a ſeruantservant, though he be Lord of all. If he differ not from a ſeruantservant, what right can he hauehave at his pleaſurepleasure Gal. 4. 1. to diſpoſedispose his parents goods? Hath a ſeruantservant any ſuchsuch right?
It is very requiſiterequisite that children herein ſhouldshould be tied to their parents conſentconsent, both for the good of parents, and of children themſeluesthemselves.

Of parents, that they may know what they hauehave, or hauehave 2. Good of parents. not, and accordingly order their expencesexpenses. How can parents tell what they hauehave, if children priuilyprivily without their knowledge purloin and diſpoſedispose their goods?

Of children, that their lauiſhlavish humor might by this meanesmeans 3. Good of children. be reſtrainedrestrained: (for youth is much prone beyond moderation to ſpendspend, if it hauehave wherewithallwherewithal) and that their parents may the better lay vpup for them. 2 Cor. 12. 14.

div.head: §. 24. Of the ſinnesin of children in purloining and waſtingwasting their parents goods.
div.p: Contrary is both the opinion and practiſepractise of many It is a ſinnesin for children. children.

For opinion, many thinkethink and ſaysay, that whatſoeuerwhatsoever is their 1. To mutter at their parents allowance. parents, is theirs alſoalso: and thereupon being through the watchfullwatchful eieeye and prouidentprovident care of their parents reſtrainedrestrained from ouerlauiſhoverlavish ſpendingspending, or from laying out any thing with their owneown hands, they murmuremurmur againſtagainst that reſtraintrestraint.
Knowledge and perſwaſionpersuasion of their ſubiectionsubjection in this caſecase, would be a good meanesmeans to ſuppreſſesuppress that repining humour.
For practiſepractise, 2. PriuilyPrivily to purloinepurloin their parents goods. Gen. 31. 19. Who counſellcounsel children to conueyconvey away parents goods are acceſſaryaccessary to theft.

1. Some priuilyprivily take away and purloinepurloin what goods, money, wares or any thing elſeelse they can come by of their parents. This the holy GhoſtGhost accounteth plaineplain theft: for Rachel hauinghaving priuilyprivily taken away her fathers idollsidols, the Scripture ſaithsaith that ſheshe ſtolestole them.

Hereunto doedo they make themſeluesthemselves acceſſaryaccessary, who counſellcounsel and incourageencourage children ſoso to doedo: as many buſibodiesbusybodiesbusibodies, and deceitfulldeceitful perſonspersons aduiſeadvise daughters, when God hath taken
away their mothers, to take away linnenlinen, and other-like houſholdhousehold-ſtuffestuff from their father, pretending that their father may mariemarry another wife, who will carriecarry all away: And vponupon like pretence alſoalso perſwadepersuade ſonssons when their fathers die, to conueyconvey away what they can from their mother. But ſuchsuch pretences are no ſufficientsufficient warrant vntounto children to deceiuedeceive their parents. It were better for children to be depriueddeprived of their parents goods, then to enioyenjoy them with ſuchsuch deceit: for they will be like that bread which is ſweetsweet to a man, and afterward his
Pro. 20. 17. mouth is filled with grauellgravel.

2. Others riotouſlyriotously ſpendspend their portion, like the prodigallprodigal 3. WaſtfullyWastefullyWastfully to ſpendspend. Luk. 15. 13. childechild, and runnerun into debt, and ſoso make their parents either to pay it, or to leaueleave them to the law. Many SchollersScholars at the VniuerſitiesUniversities, Gentlemen at InnesInns of Court, and ſuchsuch children as are ſomewhatsomewhat liberally trained vpup in their parents, or other friends houſeshouses, doedo much offend herein. Little doth this exceſſeexcess and riot differ from the forenamed kindekind of theft: and ordinarily it bringeth as many miſchiefesmischiefs as that doth.

3. Some alſoalso be ſoso vngraciousungracious and vngratefullungrateful, that being 4. To defeat their parents of their goods cunningly. come to yeeresyears, and their parents grownegrown old, ſeekeseek to defeat their parents of all they hauehave, and to bring their parents vnderunder them, to be ordered by them: labouring to get poſſeſſionpossession of all before their parents be dead, or before they be willing to reſigneresign any ſuchsuch right vntounto their children. Such were 2 Sam. 15. 10. &etcc.
AbſolomAbsalom, and Adoniah. How highly diſpleaſingdispleasing ſuchsuch practiſespractises are to God, the vengeance which fell vponupon the pates of 1 King. 1. 5. &etcc. thoſethose two Brethrenbrethren in euillevil, traiteroustraitorous, and diſloyalldisloyal children, doth ſhewshow.

All ſuchsuch children as ſeekeseek after the forenamed, or any other like meanesmeans to defraud their parents, doedo very ill repay their parents care ouerover them, and more like Barbarians, then ChriſtiansChristians, recompencerecompense euillevil for good: they oft bring pouertypoverty and ignominy vponupon their parents and themſeluesthemselves: they are worſeworse then other theeuesthieves, becauſebecause they are more deerelydearly accounted of, and more freely truſtedtrusted: yea they are a very bad example to ſeruantsservants in the houſehouse, or ſubiectssubjects in the commonwealth.

div.head: §. 25. Of childrens contentedneſſecontentedness to be apparelled after their parents mindemind and liking.
div.p:
IIII. A fourth branch of the foreſaidforesaid ſubiectionsubjection of children is about their apparellapparel, that it be no other, then may ſtandstand with their parents good liking. It is noted that IſraelIsrael
Gen. 37. 3. made IoſephJoseph a coat, doth not the particular mentioning of that circumſtancecircumstance ſhewshow, that parents muſtmust hauehave the ordering of their childrens apparellapparel? Which is alſoalso intimated in the reaſonreason giuengiven of Tamars garment of diuersdivers colours, namely becauſebecause 2 Sam. 13. 18. with ſuchsuch garments were the kings daughters, that were virgins, apparelled. And whereas Rebekah had the keeping of her Gen. 27. 15. ſonneson EſausEsaus clothes, it appeareth that his clothes were to the mindemind of his parents: elſeelse he would hauehave hid them from them: for further confirmation whereof it is noted that his apparellapparel was pleaſingpleasing to his father.

Contrary is the vainevain-glorious humour of many children, Childrens ſinsin in apparelling themſeluesthemselves to the griefegrief, and diſgracedisgrace of their parents. who to the griefegrief and diſcreditdiscredit of their parents, apparellapparel themſeluesthemselves both againſtagainst the mindemind, and alſoalso aboueabove the ability, and vnbeſeemingunbeseeming the place and calling of their parents. Among others, many miniſtersministers children bring much diſcreditdiscredit on their parents hereby. Let all ſuchsuch proud Youths note how the Lord hath threatnedthreatened to viſitvisit eueneven Kings children that are clothed
Zeph. 1. 8. with ſtrangestrange apparellapparel.

div.head: §. 26. Of childrens forbearing to bindebind themſeluesthemselves to doedo any thing againſtagainst their parents conſentconsent.
div.p: V. The fiftfifth and laſtlast branch wherewith I will exemplifieexemplify the forenamed ſubiectionsubjection of children, ſhallshall be that which is expreſlyexpressly noted in the law, namely a childes binding of it ſelfeself by a vow.
The law giuethgiveth the parent power to diſanulldisannul his childes Num. 30. 4. vow. It is therefore a childes dutieduty to abſtaineabstain from vowing without his parents conſentconsent.

Contrary are ſuchsuch vowesvows as PapiſtsPapists allure children to make, VnlawfullUnlawful vowesvows of children. namely, vowesvows of continenciecontinency, perpetuallperpetual virginitievirginity, regular obedience, voluntarievoluntary pouertiepoverty, with the like.

Though by theſethese they be not drawnedrawn to forſakeforsake their parents (which §. 14. before we prouedproved to be vtterlyutterly vnlawfullunlawful:) and though theſethese in their nature were lawfulllawful (which they are not, becauſebecause
they are againſtagainst Gods law and ordinance, and againſtagainst ChriſtianChristian libertieliberty, and ſauoursavour too rankly of IudaiſmeJudaism, yea of a worſeworse ſuperſtitionsuperstition,) yet without parents conſentconsent might they not be made.

As vnlawfullunlawful are oaths, and other like meanesmeans, whereby children bindebind themſeluesthemselves to the performance of ſuchsuch indifferent things, as their parents are not willing they ſhouldshould doedo. What doth this but bring a ſnaresnare vponupon the conſciencesconsciences of children, and cauſecause a neceſſitienecessity of breaking one of Gods commandementscommandments? eitherEither the third, in breaking their vow or oath; or the fiftfifth, in diſobeyingdisobeying their parents.

div.head: §. 27. Of childrens actiueactive obedience.
div.p: The affirmatiueaffirmative and actiueactive part of a childs obedience, conſiſtsconsists in yeeldingyielding himſelfehimself pliable to his parents will; which muſtmust be added to the forenamed negatiuenegative and paſſiuepassive part of obedience in forbearing to doedo things without conſentconsent of parents, for manifeſtationmanifestation of a true child-like affection and diſpoſitiondisposition toward the parent. PaſſiuePassive obedience may ariſearise from meeremere fullenneſſesullennessfullenness, and ſtoutneſſestoutness of ſtomachstomach. For there are many who will forbeareforbear to doedo this or that without conſentconsent of parents, becauſebecause they are loth to askeask their conſentconsent: they had rather hauehave their owneown wills croſtcrost in the things they deſiredesire, then be made ſubiectsubject to their parents will. What doth this argue, but a ſtoutstout ſtomachstomach, and a diſdainfulldisdainful heart? BeſidesBesides, to forbeareforbear the doing of an vnlawfullunlawful thing, is but to abſtaineabstain from euillevil. But it is required of ChriſtiansChristians PſalPsal. 34. 14. to doedo that which is good, as well as to abſtaineabstain from that which is euillevil. This is it which is commended in IaakobJacob: he did not only forbeareforbear to take ſuchsuch a wife as would be a griefegrief to his parents (wherein his Gen. 26. 34, 35. brother EſauEsau had offended) but alſoalso obeyed his parents in Gen. 28. 2. & 29. 18. taking ſuchsuch a wife as they willed him to take.

This generallgeneral point we will exemplifieexemplify in fourefour particular inſtancesinstances, namely, in a childs obedience to his parents commandementscommandments, inſtructionsinstructions, reproofesreproofs, corrections.

div.head: §. 28. Of childrens obedience to their parents commandementscommandments.
div.p: I. What lawfulllawful commandementscommandments ſoeuersoever parents giuegive to their children, they muſtmust be ready to the vttermoſtuttermost of their power to obey. EpheſEphes. 6. 1. Obey your parents, ſaithsaith the ApoſtleApostle to children.
Parents, by vertuevirtue of their place, hauehave power and authoritieauthority to command: Childrenchildren therefore muſtmust obey, or elſeelse that power is to no purpoſepurpose.
To demonſtratedemonstrate this by ſomesome particulars:

1. If a parent call his childechild, or ſendsend for him, he muſtmust readily A childechild muſtmust come at the parents call. come, yea though he know not the occaſionoccasion. Eli was in place of a parent to Samuel, whereupon the childechild ſuppoſingsupposing that Eli called him, 1 Sam. 3. 5, &etcc. ranneran to him once, and againeagain and againeagain. & 16. 12. DauidDavid when he was ſentsent for by his father out of the field to be anointed King, knew not the occaſionoccasion, yet came. Gen. 49. 1. The tweluetwelve ſonnessons of IaakobJacob, though men grownegrown, yet called for by their father, aſſembledassembled themſeluesthemselves together before him.

2. If a parent be diſpoſeddisposed to ſendsend his childechild any whither, or of A childechild muſtmust goego at his parents word. any errand, though it be farrefar off, and may ſeemeseem ſomewhatsomewhat troubleſometroublesome, yet he ought to goego, and doedo it. The §. 27. forenamed example of Gen. 28. 5. IaakobJacob, the example alſoalso of & 37. 14. IoſephJoseph (being ſentsent to ſeesee whether it were well with his brethren) and of the & 42. 2, 3. tennetentenn ſonnessons of IaakobJacob (being ſentsent by their father into Egypt,) and of 1 Sam. 17. 17, DauidDavid (ſentsent to viſitvisit his brethren in the hoſtehost) are in this caſecase commended by the holy GhoſtGhost. Of DauidDavid it is noted, that 20. he aroſearose vpup early and went as IſhaiIshai had commanded him: which ſettethsetteth forth his ready obedience.

3. If a parent require his childechild to attend vponupon him, he muſtmust A childechild at command muſtmust attend vponupon the parent. alſoalso doedo that. When Abram was going vpup to the top of Moriah his will was that his ſeruantsservants ſhouldshould tarrietarry behindebehind, and that his ſonneson IſaakIsaac ſhouldshould attend him, and carry the wood for the ſacrificesacrifice, and accordingly IſaakIsaac obeyed. Gen. 22. 6.

4. If a parent inioyneenjoin any tasketask, or commit any buſineſſebusiness to A child muſtmust do the meſſagemessage his parent will hauehave him doedo. his childechild, he ought faithfully to performeperform it. This kindekind of faithfullfaithful obedience is commended in Gen. 50. 5. IoſephJoseph, in the IerJer. 35. 8. Rechabites, and in 1 Sam. 17. 20. DauidDavid, with many others. IoſephJoseph, by reaſonreason of his great place, might not goego out of Egypt, yet to performeperform that which his father inioynedenjoined him, he asked leaueleave. The Rechabites were tempted to breakebreak their fathers charge, yet they would not. DauidDavid when he was ſentsent by his father, from the ſheepesheep which were committed to his cuſtodiecustody, was carefullcareful to leaueleave them with a keeper: 1 Sam. 17. 20. and againeagain, when a BeareBear at one time, and a Lion at another came verſvers. 34. to the flockeflock, he put his life in hazard to preſeruepreserve the flockeflock: all
theſethese circumſtancescircumstances are thus noted, to ſetset forth the great care that theſethese children had to diſchargedischarge that charge which their parents had committed to them.

div.head: §. 29. Of childrens diſobediencedisobedience to their parents commandementscommandments.
div.p: Contrary is a rebellious diſpoſitiondisposition in children, manifeſtedmanifested by theſethese and ſuchsuch like practiſespractises,
1. By refuſingrefusing to be at their parents call; or commingcoming (as we ſpeakespeak) at leiſureleisure, and making their parents wait for them.

2. By a lazielazy, ſluggiſhsluggish pretending of vainevain and friuolousfrivolous excuſesexcuses, when their parents would ſendsend them of an errand, like that ſluggardsluggard, who ſaithsaith, ProuProv. 22. 13. A lion is without, I ſhallshall be ſlaineslain in the ſtreetsstreets. Such pretences are as & 10. 26. vinegervinegar to the teeth, and ſmokesmoke to the eyes.

3. By ſcorningscorning to wait on their parents; and in that reſpectrespect they will ſlinkeslink out of dooresdoors, and abſentabsent themſeluesthemselves, when they imagine their parents will vſeuse their ſeruiceservice in that kindekind: they forſoothforsooth will not be their parents ſeruantsservants: andan impious conceit.

4. By refuſingrefusing to doedo what their parents inioyneenjoin them to doedo, and require at their hands, like Matt. 21. 30. the younger ſonneson, that went not to workework in the vineyard at his fathers command. Such children for the moſtmost part offend herein, as through pride thinkethink the buſineſſebusiness inioynedenjoined to them too meanemean, and baſebase to doedo. Had DauidDavid, or the daughters of Reguel beenebeen of this mindemind, the one would 1 Sam. 16. 13, 21. & 17. 15. not hauehave returned to his fathers ſheepesheep, after he was anointed to be King ouerover IſraelIsrael, and after he had beenebeen called to the Court; and the other would not hauehave watered their fathers ſheepesheep, eſpeciallyespecially Exo. 2. 16, 17. among ſuchsuch rude and bioſterousboisterousbiosterous clownesclowns, as without all reſpectrespect to their place and ſexsex, would driuedrive them away.

div.head: §. 30. Of childrens obedience to their parents inſtructioninstruction.
div.p: II. Such wholſomewholesome inſtructionsinstructions as parents giuegive their children for the well ordering of their cariagecarriage, children ought conſcionablyconscionably t • o obey: a point which Pro. 1. 8. 9. & 4. 1. Solomon much preſſethpresseth: My ſonneson, ſaithsaith • he, hearehear the inſtructioninstruction of thy father, and forſakeforsake not the law of thy anothermother, &etcc. And to mouemove children the rather to doedo ſoso, he ſetssets before them Pro. 4. 3. his owneown example, ſhewingshowing that he required no more of them then himſelfehimself had performed. Exo. 18. 24. MoſesMoses, though grownegrown to yeeresyears, and a prince among his people, teſtifiedtestified his obedience to his father in law hereby.

1. Parents hauehave an expreſſeexpress commandementcommandment to inſtructinstruct their ReaſonsReasons. 1. Parents ought to inſtructinstruct. children (as we ſhallshall Treat. 6. after ſhewshow.) Great reaſonreason therefore that their children hearehear and obey them therein. The good inſtructionsinstructions of any one are to be regarded, much more of parents.

2. Great wiſdomewisdom may be attained thereby: for the deſiredesire that §. 26, &etcc. parents hauehave of their childrens good, maketh them giuegive the beſtbest 2. Children get much wiſdomewisdom thereby. directions they can vntounto them, eueneven what themſeluesthemselves hauehave learned of others, or obſeruedobserved by their owneown experience: in this reſpectrespect, Solomon ſtilethstyleth him ProuProv. 13. 1. a wiſewise ſonneson that obeyeth the inſtructioninstruction of his father: and reſemblethresembleth the fruit and benefit thereof, to ProuProv. 1. 9. & 4. 9. acomelya comely ornament, to chaineschains, and bracelets, and to a crownecrown of glory.

3. Much ioyjoy and comfort is brought to parents by ſeeingseeing 3. Much ioyjoy is brought to parents. their children obſerueobserve their inſtructioninstruction: for ProuProv. 10. 1. a wiſewise ſonneson maketh a • glad father. Now this is a thing which children ought to aimeaim at, ProuProv. 27. 11. to reioycerejoice their parents heart. EſauEsau is taxed for Gen. 26. 35. grieuinggrieving his parents.

Contrary is their proud and fooliſhfoolish humour, who thinkethink they need no inſtructioninstruction, their parents are too iealousjealous of them, they are wiſewise enough of themſeluesthemselves; if their parents would but let them alone, they ſhouldshould doedo better: thus they ſhewshow themſeluesthemselves impious againſtagainst God, rebellious againſtagainst their parents, and iniuriousinjurious to themſeluesthemselves. Such were 1 Sam. 2. 25. EliesElis, and Gen. 19. 14. Lots ſonnessons. Now note the vengeance that fell vponupon them.

div.head: §. 31. Of childrens patience to their parents reproofereproof.
div.p:
III. The obedience of children muſtmust further Treat. 3. §. 47, &etcc. The reaſonsreasons alledgedalleged, and the directions giuengiven concerning a wiueswives ſubiectionsubjection to her husbands reproofereproof, may fitly be applied to this part of childrens obedience. Here therefore the ſamesame order is obſeruedobserved, and the ſeuerallseveral points confirmed by proofesproofs pertinent to children. extend it ſelfself to their parents reproofereproof: and that by patient bearing all manner of reproofesreproofs, and by amending what is iuſtlyjustly reprouedreproved. That ſhameshame, whereof the Lord ſpeakethspeaketh, which ſhouldshould be in a childechild, Num. 12. 14. when her father hath ſpetspet in her face, that is, by ſomesome outward ſignesign manifeſtedmanifested his anger, implieth a childs patient bearing of a parents reproofereproof. This patience in a childechild muſtmust be manifeſtedmanifested
to his parent, whether his reproofereproof be mildemild or bitter, iuſtjust or vniuſtunjust. In this reſpectrespect a childechild muſtmust more conſiderconsider the perſonperson who reprouethreproveth, then the matter or manner of the reproofereproof. IaakobsJacob's reproofereproof of IoſephJoseph, for his dreamesdreams which came of God, was vniuſtunjust: Gen. 37. 10. the manner of vtteringuttering it, with many ſhortshort pauſespauses, and that interrogatiuelyinterrogatively, implieth ſomesome tartneſſetartness: yet ſuchsuch was his patience, as we read not of one diſcontenteddiscontented word that he gauegave. But moſtmost memorable is the patience of IonathanJonathan in this kindekind. His father Sauls 1 Sam. 20. 30, &etcc. reproofereproof of him was directly vniuſtunjust, and out of meaſuremeasure bitter: yet with what patience did he bearebear it? allAll that he replied was to make ſomesome little apologieapology for DauidDavid: he replied nothing againſtagainst his fathers opprobrious ſpeechesspeeches.

Great wiſdomewisdom may be learned by this patience: for ſoso may a ReaſonReason. WiſdomeWisdom learned. childechild better iudgejudge of his parents reproofereproof, whether it be iuſtjust or no. Though it be vniuſtunjust, yet thereby may he obſerueobserve what is diſpleaſingdispleasing to his parents: at leaſtleast he may obſerueobserve his parents infirmitieinfirmity, and ſoso know the better how to carry himſelfehimself towards them.

Contrary is the practiſepractise of ſuchsuch children, as vponupon eueryevery reproofereproof of their parents are ready to * anſweranswer againeagain. Our parents See. §. 6. are wayward, ſaysay they, who can bearebear them? If none elſeelse could bearebear them, yet ſhouldshould children: for parents ordinarily bearebear ſuchsuch waywardneſſewaywardness, and vntowardneſſeuntowardness at their childrens hands, eſpeciallyespecially while they are young, as none elſeelse would or could.

div.head: QueſtQuest. If a parent be miſtakenmistaken in a matter, and vniuſtlyunjustly reprouereprove his childechild, may the childechild make no anſweranswer?
div.p: AnſwAnsw. Yes, he may, ſoso he doedo it mildly, reuerendlyreverendly, and ſeaſonablyseasonably: not too peremptorily croſſingcrossing or thwarting his parent.

div.head: ObiectObject. ChriſtChrist tooketook vpup his mother very roundly for reprouingreproving Luk. 2. 49. him vniuſtlyunjustly.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. ChriſtChrist as God-man was greater then his mother, and in that reſpectrespect with authoritieauthority blamed her for her vniuſtunjust reproofereproof. The Virgin MarieMary was not ignorant thereof, and therefore was ſilentsilent.

div.head: §. 32. Of childrens readineſſereadiness to amend what is iuſtlyjustly reprouedreproved by their parents.
div.p:
If a childechild be iuſtlyjustly for his fault reprouedreproved by his parents, See Treat. 3. §. 48.
both conſcienceconscience toward God, and obedience to his parent, requireth that he readily redreſſeredress that which is amiſſeamiss. VnleſſeUnless amendment of the thing iuſtlyjustly reprouedreproved be added to patient bearing of reproofereproof, that patience can be no better accounted of, then diſſimulationdissimulation, and plaineplain mockage. When the father Exo. 18. 17. in law of MoſesMoses told him, that what he did was not well, he forthwith amended it.

But contrarily many lewd and vngraciousungracious children continue to goego on in their wicked courſescourses, though their parents againeagain, and againeagain rebuke them for it. IuſtJust was EliesElis reproofereproof of his children, but yet no amendment followed. Now note the inference made thereupon by the holy GhoſtGhost, They obeyed 1 Sam. 2. 25. not the voice of their father, becauſebecause the Lord would ſlayslay them: whereby is implied, that to deſpiſedespise the iuſtjust reproofereproof of parents is an euidentevident ſignesign, and forerunner of Gods heauyheavy iudgementjudgment. SalomonSolomon calls the childechild which will hearehear no rebuke, a Scorner,
Pro. 13. 1. which noteth out a moſtmost obſtinateobstinate ſinnersinner that cannot be reclaimed, and in that reſpectrespect is ſcornedscorned of the Lord. Pro. 3. 34.

div.head: §. 33. Of Childrens ſubmiſſionsubmission to their parents correction.
div.p: IIII. Correction is a reallreal reproofereproof, a reproofereproof in the higheſthighest degree, eueneven the ſeuereſtseverest kindekind of reproofereproof: ſoso as by ſubiectionsubjection hereunto great tryalltrial of obedience is made. By the ſamesame meanesmeans muſtmust a childes ſubmiſſionsubmission to his parent in this kindekind of reproofereproof be manifeſtedmanifested, as in the former: namely,
1. By bearing patiently the correction which his parent ſhallshall giuegive him.
2. By amending readily that for which he is iuſtlyjustly corrected.

The former of theſethese is noted by the ApoſtleApostle as a ruled caſecase, a matter not to be denied, in theſethese words, Heb. 12. 9. We hauehave had fathers of our fleſhflesh which corrected vsus, and we gauegave them reuerencereverence. One ſpeciallspecial part of this reuerencereverence is a patient ſufferingsuffering: therefore he inferresinfers thereupon, ought we not to be in ſubiectionsubjection? &etcc.

The latter is ſetset forth by SalomonSolomon vnderunder an effect which followeth vponupon the performance thereof: for hauinghaving aduiſedadvised a parent to correct his childechild, he addeth this reaſonreason, Pro. 29. 17. He ſhallshall giuegive thee reſtrest, yea he ſhallshall giuegive delight vntounto thy ſoulesoul: how can
this reſtrest, and delight be giuengiven, but by the childes amendment of that for which he is corrected? A parent taketh no delight in the painepain, and ſmartsmart of his childechild, but in the fruit that followeth thereupon. As a childes tranſgreſſiontransgression is Gen. 26. 35. a griefegrief, and vexation to the parent, ſoso his amendment cauſethcauseth reſtrest and delight. Now this effect followeth not ſimplysimply vponupon correction, but vponupon the good vſeuse thereof which is made by the childechild. It lyethlieth therefore in the childechild, and ſoso lyethlieth vponupon him as a dutieduty, to giuegive this reſtrest and delight to his parent by amending the fault for which he is corrected, as he brought griefegrief to him by prouokingprovoking him to vſeuse correction. Thus ſhallshall neither parent repent the inflicting, nor the childechild repent the induring of correction.

That a childechild may attaineattain to this degree of obedience, he Direction for well vſingusing correction. muſtmust duly conſiderconsider both the CauſeCause whereby his parent is mouedmoved to correct him, and alſoalso the End which he aimeth at therein. The cauſecause is the Pro. 13. 24. louelove he beareth to his childechild. The end which he aimeth at, is his childes
& 22. 15. good. If theſethese motiuesmotives workework not obedience, what can?

div.head: §. 34. Of refuſingrefusing, or abuſingabusing correction.
div.p: Contrary is diſdainedisdain on the one ſideside, and obſtinacieobstinacy on the other. DiſdaineDisdain, when children ſcornescorn to be corrected by their parents: and in that reſpectrespect when by all the meanesmeans they can vſeuse, they cannot auoidavoid it, they will mutter and murmuremurmur, fret and fume, rage and rauerave againſtagainst their parents, and deſpiſedespise and hate them for it. ObſtinacieObstinacy, when they will be no whit bettered thereby, but ſtillstill runnerun on in their leaudlewd courſescourses, and rather waxewax the worſeworse for being corrected. This may be counted the higheſthighest pitch of a childes rebellion: for this is the laſtlast meanesmeans which a parent can vſeuse to reclaimereclaim his childechild from deſperatedesperate courſescourses. If this preuailethprevaileth not, the law of God requireth, Deut. 21. 18. &etc.c that a parent ſhouldshould giuegive vpup his childechild into the hand of the MagiſtrateMagistrate, that he may be put to death.

p.hi: Hitherto of the diſtinctdistinct branches of childrens Obedienceobedience.
The Extent thereof followeth.

div.head: §. 35. Of childrens conforming their iudgementsjudgments to their parents.
div.p:
The extent of childrens obedience is only implied in this EpiſtleEpistle to the EpheſiansEphesians, but it is expreſſedexpressed (Col. 3. 2020.) in theſethese words, ChildrenChildrenchildren obey your parents
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . IN ALL THINGSTHINGSthings. A large extent, but not ſimplysimply to be taken without any limitation: for the ApoſtleApostle himſelfehimself noteth a reſtraintrestraint in theſethese words, Eph. 6. 1. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . In the Lord. So farrefar forth as children tranſgreſſetransgress not any of Gods commandementscommandments in obeying their parents, they ought to obey. This is to obey in all things, in the Lord.

Treat. 3. §. 63, 64, &etcc. The extent of childrens obedience. The extent of childrens duties being the very ſamesame that was of wiueswives duties: and the reſtraintrestraint alſoalso the ſamesame, that order which was there obſeruedobserved ſhallshall here alſoalso be kept. Only other proofesproofs more pertinent to childrens place, ſhallshall be brought to confirmeconfirm thoſethose generallgeneral propoſitionspropositions which may be applied to any inferioursinferiors. Many generallgeneral reaſonsreasons there alledgedalleged for proofeproof of the propoſitionspropositions ſhallshall here be omitted. Wherefore compare this place with that.

Thus we ſeesee that parents authority is very large: there is no reſtraintrestraint of it but Gods contrary command, whereof a childechild muſtmust be aſſuredassured, if he refuſerefuse to obey his parent in any thing.

It is not enough for a childechild to ſaysay I hauehave thus long, and in thus many things obeyed my parent, I hope in ſomesome things if I hauehave mine owneown will, I may be excuſedexcused. No: All things compriſecomprise more then many things. Wherefore Many are not enough. And though Gods will be exempted, yet is not thine owneown will exempted: though thou maieſtmaiest doedo nothing againſtagainst Gods will, yet thou oughteſtoughtest to doedo many things againſtagainst thine owneown will, if it be contrary to thy parents.
Two things are to be laboured after by children for attaining to this extent of obedience in all things.

1. They muſtmust labour to bring their iudgementjudgment and will to the bent of their parents: to thinkethink that meet and conuenientconvenient for them to doedo which their parents will hauehave them doedo. Though IſaakIsaac thought it ſomewhatsomewhat ſtrangestrange that he ſhouldshould Gen. 22. 6, 7. carry wood vpup to an hill to offer ſacrificesacrifice where was nothing for a burnt offering, yet it being the will of his father that he
ſhouldshould doedo ſoso, he thought it meet enough for him to doedo ſoso.

This ſubiectionsubjection of iudgementjudgment and will is to be yeeldedyielded in all the particular caſescases of obedience which were §. 13. 14. &etcc. before propounded, as in their calling, mariagemarriage, apparrellapparel, allowance, &etcc. So as children are to thinkethink that kindekind of calling, that particular match, that apparrellapparel, and that allowance to be meeteſtmeetest for them, which their parents thinkethink meetemeet.

If the iudgementjudgment be perſwadedpersuaded of the meetneſſemeetness of a thing, ReaſonReason. and the will inwardly brought to yeeldyield vntounto it, outward obedience will more readily and cheerefullycheerfully beebe yeeldedyielded thereunto.

Contrary is the ouerweiningoverweeningoverweining conceiptconceit which many children Childrens ouerover-weiningweaning conceit of their owneown iudgementjudgment aboueabove their parents, cauſethcauseth much miſchiefemischief. hauehave of their owneown iudgementjudgment and will, who thinkethink they can better diſcernediscern what is fit and meetemeet for themſeluesthemselves, then their parents. They imagine their parents to be too ſtrictstrict and preciſeprecise, or too ſuſpicioussuspicious and iealousjealous, or too couetouscovetous and worldly. This maketh them take what callings, what matches, what apparrellapparel, what allowance they thinkethink beſtbest; whence many miſchiefesmischiefs ariſearise, which would all eaſilyeasily be auoidedavoided, if they would lay downedown that preſumptuouspresumptuous conceit, and labour to obſerueobserve the forenamed direction.

div.head: §. 36. Of childrens yeeldingyielding to practiſepractise at their parents command, ſuchsuch things as in their iudgementsjudgments they cannot thinkethink very meet.
div.p:
2. Though children cannot in their iudgementsjudgments thinkethink that which their parents require to be the fitteſtfittest and meeteſtmeetest, yet being preſſedpressed thereto by the peremptory command of their parents, in practiſepractise they ought to yeeldyield vntounto it, ſayingsaying to their parents as Peter to the Lord, NeuertheleſſeNevertheless at thy word I will doedo this,. Thus did Gen. 27. 6. &etcc.
IaakobJacob yeeldyield to Rebekah: he thought by doing that which his mother bid him, he ſhouldshould ſeemeseem a c •• ocker to his father, yet ſheshe vrgingurging him, he did it.

May not a childechild, yeeldingyielding better reaſonreason then his parent, refuſerefuse to doedo what he thinketh vnmeetunmeet, or at leaſtleast forb • eareforbear to doedo what he is commanded, till he be better informed o • f the meetneſſemeetness thereof?

AnſwAnsw. With reuerencereverence and humility he may render his
reaſonreason why he thinketh it not meetemeet, and deſiredesire his parent not to vrgeurge it vponupon him.

(This did Gen. 43. 3. IudahJudah one of the ſonnessons of IaakobJacob, and is not blamed for it:) and parents ought in ſuchsuch a caſecase to yeeldyield to their children (as VerſVers. 11. IaakobJacob did.) But yet if in things indifferent, parents be otherwiſeotherwise minded then their children, and will hauehave their children yeeldyield to them, they muſtmust yeeldyield.

For, 1. In in differentindifferent things the command of a parent is a warrant to the childechild, by reaſonreason of this extent (all things:) ſoso as the parent may ſinnesin in commanding that, in doing whereof the childechild may not ſinnesin. Who can cleareclear RebeckahRebekah of ſinnesin in commanding IaakobJacob to deceiuedeceive his father? yetYet I take it, that IaakobJacob cannot iuſtlyjustly be blamed for obeying.

2. Children doedo thus manifeſtmanifest an high eſteemeesteem of their parents, and very great reſpectrespect towards them: they ſhewshow how deſirousdesirous they are to pleaſeplease them, and how fearefullfearful to offend them. When the will of parent and childechild conſentconsent, there is no ſuchsuch trialltrial.

3. div.p: The reſtraintrestraint of childrens obedience is expreſſedexpressed in this clauſeclause, in the Lord: which phraſephrase affordeth a neceſſarynecessary limitation Heb. 12. 9. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . in obeying their parents, who are but parents of our fleſhflesh, men and women, ſubiectsubject to erreerr in their commandementscommandments, and to require ſuchsuch ſinfullsinful things as their children may not with a good conſcienceconscience performeperform. Children muſtmust performeperform no other obedience to their parents, then may ſtandstand with their obedience to God. The reaſonsreasons rendredrendered by the ApoſtleApostle proueprove as much: This is right, this is well pleaſingpleasing to

div.head: §. 39. Of childrens RecompenceRecompense.
div.p:
The generallgeneral head whereunto alall the duties which children owe to their parents in regard of their NeceſſityNecessity, is in one word RecompenceRecompense, which is a dutieduty whereby children indeauourindeavour as much as in them lieth, to repay what they can for their parents kindneſſekindness, care, and coſtcost towards them, and that in way

Ethic. l. 8. c. 14. of thankfulneſſethankfulness; which maketh a childechild thinkethink he cannot doedo too much for his parent, & well may he thinkethink ſoso, for a parent doth much more for his childechild before it is able to doedo for it ſelfeself, then the childechild poſſiblypossibly can doedo for the parent. So as if the parents authority were laid aſideaside, yet the law of equity requireth this dutieduty of RecompenceRecompense: ſoso alſoalso doth the law of piety and charity. As all ingratitude is odious to God and man, ſoso this moſtmost of all, and yet very many are guilty thereof. In them the prouerbeproverb is verified that louelove is weighty. For it is the property of weighty things to fall downedown apace, outbut to aſcendascend ſlowlyslowly, and that not without ſomesome violence. Thus louelove from the parent to the childechild falleth downedown apace, b • ut it hardly aſcendethascendeth from children to parents. In which reſpectrespect another prouerbeproverb ſaithsaith, One father will better nouriſhnourish nine children, then nine children one father. Many children in histhis kindekind doedo no more for their parents, then for ſtrangersstrangers. They either conſiderconsider not how much their parents hauehave done
for them; or elſeelse they conceit that what their parents did, was of meeremere dutieduty, and needeth no recompencerecompense. Fie vponupon ſuchsuch barbarous and inhumane children!

div.p: Children bearebear with their parents infirmities when they doedo not the leſſeless reuerendlyreverendly eſteemeesteem their place, or perſonperson, nor performeperform the leſſeless dutieduty to them becauſebecause of their infirmities.

div.head: §. 42. Of childrens coueringcovering their parents infirmities.
div.p:
Children couercover their parents infirmities both by paſſingpassing by

The Scripture noteth it to be a property of louelove to couercover a multitude 1 Pet. 4. 8. of ſinnessins: now in whom ſhouldshould louelove abound, if not in children? And who ſhouldshould more manifeſtmanifest this property of louelove then children?

Of paſſingpassing by and concealing from others a parents infirmity, we hauehave a worthy patternepattern in Shem and IaphetJaphet: when Noah their father being drunken lay vncouereduncovered in the midſtmidst of his tent, they went backward (that they might not themſeluesthemselves Gen. 9. 23. ſeesee their fathers infirmity) and coueredcovered his nakedneſſenakedness (that others might not ſeesee it.) The bleſſingblessing which vponupon this occaſionoccasion was then promiſedpromised to them and their poſterityposterity, ſhewethshoweth how acceptable this dutieduty was to God.

Too many AbſolomAbsalom-like ſeekeseek to raiſeraise a ſuppoſedsupposed More then monſtrousmonstrous for a childechild to raiſeraise a ſlanderslander of a parent. reputation and honour to themſeluesthemselves by vilifying and diſgracingdisgracing their parents: but let them note AbſolomsAbsalomsAbsoloms end. div.p:

div.head: §. 46. Of the decency wherewith children ought to ſeesee their parents buried.
div.p: The manner after which children ought to ſeesee their parents buried, muſtmust be with ſuchsuch decency as is agreeable to the commendable cuſtomecustom of the countriecountry and Church where their parents die, and with ſuchsuch honour as is in ſomesome meaſuremeasure anſwerableanswerable to the eſtateestate, and place of their parents while they liuedlived (at leaſtleast if it be not aboueabove the meanesmeans that the parent hath left, or aboueabove the abilitieability of the childechild that maketh the ſolemnitiesolemnity.) div.head: §. 47. Of childrens paying their parents debts after their death.
div.p: As children muſtmust hauehave reſpectrespect to the body of their parents Childrens reſpectrespect to the credit of their deceaſeddeceased parents. deceaſeddeceased, ſoso alſoalso to their credit and name, which is a thing of greater account, and honour: a thing wherein they may bring a kindekind of bleſſingblessing to their parents and make them liuelive after their death.

Parents themſeluesthemselves cannot doedo any thing when they are dead to preſeruepreserve the ſamesame: children therefore being the liuingliving Image of their parents muſtmust indeuourendeavour to doedo it.

Three things there be which children muſtmust make conſcienceconscience of, eueneven in regard of their deceaſeddeceased parents credit, and reputation; one, to pay their debts: another, to ſuppreſſesuppress ill rumors: a third, to imitate their good example.

I. If the eſtateestate of parents, their goods or lands come to their children, their dutieduty is to pay their debts, ſoso farrefar as they can: eſpeciallyespecially if by law thoſethose debts may be recoueredrecovered at their hands. For what law may force others to doedo in equitieequity and IuſticeJustice, conſcienceconscience muſtmust mouemove good children to doedo in charitiecharity, and recompencerecompense to their parents. Yea if children of themſeluesthemselves be well able, though their parents left not ſufficientsufficient to pay all their debts, they ought to pay them. Herein eſpeciallyespecially a childlike affection is manifeſtedmanifested to the parent.

Contrary is their practiſepractise who ſtriuestrive to get all they can of their parents, and yet make no conſcienceconscience of paying any debts at all, vnleſſeunless law force them thereto. What they doedo in this caſecase cannot be thought to be done for their parents ſakesake, but rather
