ſinnesin be committed againſtagainst God. Hereof alſoalso we ſpakespake §. 37. & 38. before.

6. ConſtancyConstancy muſtmust be added to all other vertuesvirtues. For as the 6. With perſeveranceperseverance. Lord himſelfehimself is conſtantconstant in all his waiesways and workesworks, ſoso he expecteth that children ſhouldshould be in the duties which he requireth at their hands. He that beginnethbegineth well, and holdeth not on, loſethloseth all the glory of his good beginning.

If the examples of all good children commended in Scripture be well weighed, we ſhallshall findefind their duties, ſoso farrefar forth as they were acceptable to God, performed after the foreſaidforesaid manner, in all the branches thereof.

div.head: §. 53. Of the aberrations of children in the manner of their obedience.
div.p: Contrary are theſethese aberrations.

1. When children performeperform their duties on by-reſpectsrespects: Faults in the manner of doing duty. 1. By-reſpectsrespects. for fearefear of parents wrath, and the puniſhmentpunishment following thereon: for hope and expectation of greater portion and allowa • nce: vponupon inſtantinstant perſwaſionpersuasion of friends, with the like: theſethese reſpectsrespects ſimplysimply in themſeluesthemselves are not for the Lord.

2. When they performeperform them only outwardly in ſhewshow, 2. ComplementallComplemental. complementally while parents are in preſencepresence, or may know thereof. This is not with reſpectrespect to God who ſearehethsearchethseareheth the h • eart.

3. When they performeperform them grudgingly, mutteringly, 3. RudelyGrudgingly. diſdainfullydisdainfully: as if their parents authority were an vſurpedusurped p • ower and not giuengiven them of God. Is this in the Lord?
4. When they performeperform them rudely and vnmannerlyunmannerly: 4. GrudginglyRudely. hisThis ſhewethshoweth they conſiderconsider not the glory of Gods Image ſhin • ingshining in their parents.
5. §. 38. When they care not how they ſinnesin againſtagainst God, ſoso 5. OnelyOnly to pleaſeplease man. th •• ey may pleaſeplease their parents.

6. When, as if they repented of what they hauehave well done, 6. VnſetledlyUnsettledlyUnsetledly. th •• ey refuſerefuse to doedo any more duty to their parents. They waxewax w • eary, thinking that God hath laid too heauyheavy a burden vponupon th •• em. Many ſhewshow themſeluesthemselves more dutifulldutiful in their younger •• then in their riper yearesyears. That which maketh children w • eary in doing duty, is commonly the great and long needeneed of th •• eir parents, as long ſickneſſesickness, long impotency, long pouertypoverty,
with the like. It appearesappears that ſuchsuch children lookelook only on their parents as men, which, as they imagine, can neuernever recompencerecompense their painespains and coſtcost: they lookelook not to God who is able abundantly to recompencerecompense all. TheſeThese therefore performeperform not their duty in the Lord.

div.head: §. 54. Of the equallequal reſpectrespect that children are to bearebear to both parents.
div.p: As the diſtinctdistinct duties of children hauehave beenebeen ſetset forth, ſoso I thinkethink it requiſiterequisite to declare diſtinctlydistinctly who the parties be to whom thoſethose duties are to be performed. TheſeThese principally are the naturallnatural parents, both Fatherfather and Mothermother. Secondarily ſuchsuch as are in the place of parents.

The firſtfirst point then to be noted is, that children bearebear an equallequal reſpectrespect to both their naturallnatural parents, and performeperform duty to both alike. The law expreſlyexpressly mentioneth both, Honourhonour thy Fatherfather and thy Mothermother. Well may we thinkethink that there was ſomesome iuſtjust and vrgenturgent cauſecause, that the law which ſoso briefly vnderunder as few words as well could be, compriſethcompriseth exceeding much matter, ſhouldshould expreſlyexpressly mention father and mother, when as there is one word, parent, which includeth both. Now what other reaſonreason can be rendredrendered then the point in hand?

It is worthy to be noted, how the ApoſtleApostle contenteth not himſelfehimself to hauehave named parents, which implieth both, but alſoalso annexeth the expreſſeexpress words of the law, which in particular ſettethsetteth downedown, father and mother. It is expreſlyexpressly ſetset downedown of IaakobJacob that he obeyed his father and his mother. Among other Gen. 28. 7. pen-men of Scripture SalomonSolomon expreſlyexpressly mentioneth both father and mother, eueneven almoſtalmost twenty ſeuerallseveral times in ProuProv.
Many reaſonsreasons there be to inforceenforce this point.
1. Both parents are vnderunder God a like meanesmeans of their childrens ReaſonsReasons. being. Children come out of the ſubſtancesubstance of both alike.

2. The care and pains of both for the good of the children is very great: I know not of whether the greater. The mothers painespains and care in bringing forth the childechild is indeed the greater, and it may be alſoalso the greater in bringing vpup the childechild, eſpeciallyespecially while it is young, at leaſtleast if ſheshe giuegive it ſuckesuck her ſelfeself: yet afterwards the fathers exceedeth in prouidingproviding fit calling,
ſufficientsufficient meanesmeans of maintenance, yea and portion or inheritance for it, and that after he himſelfehimself is dead. Thus one way or other the childechild is equally bound to both: and accordingly Gods law maketh no difference betwixt them.

div.head: ObiectObject. The wife is ſubiectsubject to her husband: therefore a childechild ought to preferreprefer his father before his mother.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. Though there be a difference betwixt father and Both parents to be of like account with children. mother in relation of one to another, yet in relation to their children they are both as one, and hauehave a like authority ouerover them. Now children are not to lookelook to that difference that is betwixt their parents in that mutuallmutual relation that is betwixt husband and wife, but to that authority which both parents hauehave ouerover their children: and ſoso to carry an equallequal reſpectrespect to both.

div.head: 2. ObiectObject. What if the fathers and mothers diſpoſitiondisposition Direction for a childechild when one parent commandeth one thing, the other another. be contrary: and the one command what the other forbids.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. The thing commanded or forbidden muſtmust be obſeruedobserved: if it be about a thing ſimplysimply good or euillevil, lawfulllawful, or vnlawfullunlawful, then the parent which would hauehave the thing lawfulllawful to be done, or vnlawfullunlawful to be for borneforborne (though it be the mother) muſtmust be obeyed: for in this caſecase ſheshe is backtbacked with Gods authority. But if the matter be meerelymerely indifferent, then I doubt not but the father muſtmust be obeyed: yet ſoso as the childechild no way ſhewshow any contempt to his mother, but with all reuerencereverence and humility make it knowneknown to her that it is beſtbest both for her-ſelfeself and himſelfehimself, that his father be obeyed. But if the fathers contrary authority be not interpoſedinterposed, or if the father be dead, then is a mother as ſimplysimply and abſolutelyabsolutely to be obeyed in all things, as a father.

div.head: §. 55. Of pretences alledgedalleged to obey father rather then mother.
div.p:
Contrary on the one ſideside is their childiſhchildish fondneſſefondness who ſoso wholly reſpectrespect their mother, and ſeekeseek to pleaſeplease her, as they little regard their father, vnleſſeunless through fearefear they be forced thereto: and on the other ſideside, their ſcornefullscornful ſpiritspirit who only bearebear reſpectrespect to their father, and altogether neglect their mother, if not deſpiſedespise her. For the moſtmost part, of the two, the mother is leſſeless regarded. The reaſonsreasons whereof I take to be theſethese
following, whereunto I will annex particular meanesmeans to remoueremove the ſeemingseeming force of thoſethose reaſonsreasons, as antidotes or remedies vntounto them.
1. The mother by reaſonreason of her ſexsex is commonly the weaker, and ſubiectsubject to more infirmities.

AnſwAnsw. ChildrenChildrenchildren ought rather to lookelook vponupon their mothers place and authority, then their perſonperson and infirmitieinfirmity: ſoso theſethese would no whit impaireimpair their reſpectrespect of the other.
2. The mother is more indulgent and tender to her children: and vſethuseth more familiarity towards them: now familiarity Familiaritas parit contemptum. Teren. in Andr. breedeth contempt.

AnſwAnsw. This is the abuſeabuse of familiarity: louelove ſhouldshould breed louelove: and louelove muſtmust be ordered according to the condition of the parties louingloving, and louedloved. As children with one eieeye behold the affection of the mother, ſoso with another they ſhouldshould behold Gods image in the mother; and then (that which is §. 2, 3. noted as the ground of all childrens dutieduty) a louingloving-fearefear would be wrought in their heart, which would caſtcast out all contempt.
3. The mother hath not that power to reward or reuengerevenge that a father hath.

AnſwAnsw. 1. This is not to obey in the Lord. No outward reſpectrespect ſhouldshould mouemove the childechild to obey his parents ſoso much as conſcienceconscience to God-wards. If children duly conſideredconsidered God, how he hath made no difference, but commanded them to obey both alike, and how he is able abundantly to reward, and ſeuerelyseverely to reuengerevenge, that reaſonreason would be no reaſonreason.
4. The mother is ſubiectsubject to the father.
AnſwAnsw. This was remouedremoved §. 54. before.

As a generallgeneral anſweranswer to theſethese and all other ſuchsuch pretences as can be alledgedalleged, let it be noted that the Lord doth not only in expreſſeexpress termesterms charge children to fearefear their mother, but alſoalso (the more to preſſepress this point) ſometimesometime ſettethsetteth the mother in the firſtfirst place, thus; YeeYe ſhallshall fearefear eueryevery man his mother,
Leu. 19. 3. and his father: which is not ſoso to be taken as if the mother of the two were the more excellent (in this reſpectrespect the father for the moſtmost part is firſtfirst named) but becauſebecause it is the trueſttruest trialltrial of a childes ſubiectionsubjection to be ſubiectsubject to his mother. He that
willingly and conſcionablyconscionably ſubiectethsubjecteth himſelfehimself to her, who is in relation to her husband the inferiourinferior, in ſexsex the weaker, in condition ſubiectsubject to more infirmities, in her affections leſſeless moderate, in power leſſeless able to reward, or to puniſhpunish, will much rather (no doubt) ſubiectsubject himſelfehimself to his father.

div.head: §. 56. Of the difference of childrens ſubiectionsubjection to naturallnatural parents, and to ſuchsuch as only are in the place of parents.
div.p: BeſideBeside naturallnatural parents, there are others by God ſoso ſetset ouerover children, as they owe in conſcienceconscience child-like dutieduty vntounto them. TheſeThese in generallgeneral are ſuchsuch as are in the place of parents, and ſoso performeperform, or at leaſtleast ought to performeperform, the dutieduty of parents to children.
They are of two ſortssorts.
1. Such as are ioynedjoined to a naturallnatural parent in mariagemarriage, commonly called Step-fathers, and ſtepstep-mothers, or fathers in law, and mothers in law.

2. Such as hauehave the gouernmentgovernment and tuition of children committed to them, commonly called Guardians, Tutors, GouernoursGovernors: yea alſoalso foſterfoster-fathers, and foſterfoster-mothers.

div.head: QueſtQuest. Is the ſamesame dutieduty in eueryevery reſpectrespect due to thoſethose who are in place of parents, as to naturallnatural parents themſeluesthemselves?
div.p: AnſwAnsw. Not ſoso. There is ſuchsuch a prerogatiueprerogative appertaining to naturallnatural parents from whom children hauehave receiuedreceived their being, that many things wherein children by an abſoluteabsolute neceſſitynecessity De neceſſitatenecessitate. are bound to them, are bound vntounto the other who are but in place of parents, only by the law of honeſtyhonesty, of meetneſſemeetness & De honeſtatehonestate. conueniencyconveniency. Whence it commethcometh to paſſepass that ſuchsuch things as being done by children rebelliouſlyrebelliously without, or againſtagainst the conſentconsent of naturallnatural parents proueprove meeremere nullities, will ſtandstand in force though they be done without or againſtagainst the conſentconsent of ſuchsuch as are only in the place of parents: inſtanceinstance contracts made about goods, lands and ſuchsuch other things as parents retaineretain a right in: whereunto many good DiuinesDivines addeadd See §. 16. contracts of mariagemarriage, of calling and the like.

Yet notwithſtandingnotwithstanding ſeeingseeing in conſcienceconscience we are bound to thoſethose things which the law of honeſtyhonesty, and conueniencyconveniency requiretyrequireth (for whatſoeuerwhatsoever things are honeſthonest, iuſtjust, and of good report,
Phil. 4. 8.
are to be done) great is that dutieduty which children owe to thoſethose who are in place of parents.

div.head: §. 57. Of childrens ſubiectionsubjection to fathers and mothers in law.
div.p: Fathers and mothers in law are to be ranked in the firſtfirst degree of thoſethose who are in the place of naturallnatural parents. Very good proofeproof there is in Scripture for childrens ſubiectionsubjection to them. The reſpectrespect which MoſesMoses bearebarebear to his father in law, Exo. 18. 7. Ruth. 1. & 2. Luk. 2. 51. and Ruth to her mother in law, and ChriſtChrist himſelfehimself to his ſuppoſedsupposed father, are commended for this very purpoſepurpose. SubiectionSubjectionsubjection is noted in ChriſtsChrists example: Reuerencereverence in MoſesMoses: RecompenceRecompense in Ruths.

The mariagemarriage bond maketh man and wife one fleſhflesh: whereupon 1. ReaſonReason. the naturallnatural parent that mariethmarrieth another, maketh that other one with him, and in that reſpectrespect is as a parent to the children, and by them ought to be accounted ſoso.

The law of God maketh it plaineplain ince •• ſtincest for a ſonneson to vncoueruncover
Leu. 18. 8, 17. the ſhameshame of his mother in law, or for a father in law to vncoueruncover the ſhameshame of his daughter in law. Whereby it appeareth that fathers and mothers in law, are by Gods law in the very place and ſteedsteadsteed of naturallnatural parents to their children, and accordingly as naturallnatural parents are to be honoured.

BeſidesBesides it is a great honour which a childechild doth to his naturallnatural 2. ReaſonReason. father or mother to reſpectrespect ſuchsuch as they hauehave made one fleſhflesh with themſeluesthemselves, as they doedo their owneown parent. So as to honour a father, or mother in law, is to honour a naturallnatural parent.

Contrary is the mindemind and cariagecarriage of moſtmost children. Very few bearebear a reuerendreverend, dutifulldutiful, and child-like reſpectrespect to ſtepfathersstepfathers, and ſtepstep-mothers: but for the moſtmost part deſpiſedespise them in heart, grumble at them in ſpeechspeech, and are very vndutifullundutiful in their behauiourbehaviour: whence it commethcometh to paſſepass that they bring much griefegrief to their naturallnatural parent, and oft cauſecause much diſcorddiscord and diſſentiondissensiondissention betwixt their naturallnatural, and step-parents • being herein ſetset on workework by Satan, who laboureth what he can to diſunitedisunite thoſethose whom God hath neerelynearly vnitedunited together and made one fleſhflesh. Lamentable experience ſhewethshoweth that the ſecondsecond, third, or any after-mariagesmarriages are ſeldomeseldom ſoso comfortable and peaceable as the firſtfirst: eſpeciallyespecially if either the one, or other,
or both hauehave children. The cauſecause thereof, for the moſtmost part, is in children, who brookebrook not fathers or mothers in law.

div.head: ObiectObject. Nature cannot ſoso well brookebrook a ſtepstep-parent, as a naturallnatural parent.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. 1. If not ſoso well, yet deſpiſedespise them not: there is a difference betwixt extremes.

2. ConſcienceConscience and religion ought to alter corrupt nature. LookeLook to Gods ordinance: and let Gods fearefear poſſeſſepossess thine heart, that that may bring thee to doedo what nature cannot.

div.head: 2. ObiectObject. Fathers and Mothers in law ſeldomeseldom reſpectrespect their husbands or wiueswives former children.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. This obiectionobjection more beſeemethbeseemeth the mouth of a barbarian then a ChriſtianChristian. The GoſpellGospel teacheth to be ſubiectsubject not 1 Pet. 2. 18. Rom. 12. 21. only to the good and gentle, but alſoalso to the froward: and not to be ouercomeovercome of euillevil, but to ouercomeovercome euillevil with goodneſſegoodness.

The Scripture reckoneth ſuchsuch as riſerise vpup againſtagainst their parents Mic. 7. 6. in law, among ſuchsuch as riſerise vpup againſtagainst their naturallnatural parents: ſhewingshowing thereby that the impietieimpiety of thoſethose, is as blame-worthy, as the impietieimpiety of theſethese.

div.head: §. 58. Of childrens ſubiectionsubjection to Guardians, Tutors, &etcc.
div.p:
For childrens ſubiectionsubjection to GouernoursGovernors, Guardians, and Tutors, the ApoſtleApostle ſaithsaith that a childechild is vnderunder them. If by the law Galat. 4. 2. children are vnderunder them, they ought in equitieequity to be ſubiectsubject to them. It is expreſlyexpressly noted of Esther, eueneven after the King had choſenchosen her for his wife, that ſheshe did the commandementcommandment of Mordecai
EſthEsth. 2. 20. (who was as a Guardian to her) like as when ſheshe was brought vpup with him. A memorable patternepattern for this purpoſepurpose. What pretences might ſheshe hauehave made to hauehave caſtcast off all manner of ſubiectionsubjection? Mordecai was but her coſencousincosen: ſheshe was now aduancedadvanced aboueabove him: a wife ſheshe was, and ſoso ſubiectsubject to her husband: yea a Kings wife, and ſoso her ſelfeself a QueeneQueen: yet ſheshe was ſubiectsubject, and her ſubiectionsubjection commended. We readeread that the children of the Prophets much 2 Kin. 2. 15, &etcc. & 6. 1. reſpectedrespected EliſhaElisha, did reuerencereverence to him, and were obedient to him, becauſebecause he was as a father and tutor vntounto them: in which reſpectrespect alſoalso EliſhaElisha was as a childechild ſubiectsubject to Eliah, whom he called 2 King. 2. 12. father.

Guardians, Tutors, and ſuchsuch like ouerover-ſeersseers of children, hauehave a parents charge laid vponupon them, as we ſhallshall Treat 6. §. 74, &etcc. after ſhewshow: great reaſonreason
therefore that child-like dutieduty ſhouldshould be yeeldedyielded to them. Their honour muſtmust be anſwerableanswerable to their charge and care.

Contrary is the conceit of many lawleſſelawless children, whoſewhose parents being dead, or they being ſentsent and placed abroad out of the gouernmentgovernment of their parents, thinkethink they are cleaneclean free from all gouernmentgovernment, and may liuelive as they liſtlist. Their practiſepractise being correſpondentcorrespondent to this opinion, they runnerun into all riot, and in time bring themſeluesthemselves to vtterutter ruineruin. It is the ouerthrowoverthrow of many children, that they regard not their Guardians, Tutors, and GouernoursGovernors: and God in iudgementjudgment bringeth many ſuchsuch refractarierefractoryrefractary children to ſomesome fearefullfearful & ſhamefullshameful end or other. Let children therefore be wiſewise, and not take too much libertieliberty to themſeluesthemselves.

Thus farrefar hauehave beenebeen handled the duties of children in their ſeuerallseveral kindeskinds, the manner of performing them, and the parties to whom they are to be performed. It remaineth to ſpeakespeak of the reaſonsreasons which the ApoſtleApostle alledgethallegeth to inforceenforce thoſethose duties.

div.head: §. 59. Of the place of parents, whereby children ought to be mouedmoved to obey them.
div.p:
The reaſonsreasons which the ApoſtleApostle vſethuseth to mouemove children to performeperform their dutieduty are fourefour:
The firſtfirst is taken from the place of the parent.
The ſecondsecond from the equitieequity of the thing.
The third from Gods expreſſeexpress charge.
The fourth from Gods promiſepromise.

I. The place of a parent is noted forth by this phraſephrase, IN THE LORD: which as it affordeth a
• .§. 37. limitation, and giuethgiveth a §. 52. direction to children, ſoso it addeth a ſpurspur vntounto them, to ſtirrestir them vpup to performeperform their dutieduty: for it ſhewethshoweth that parents are to thentheir children in the Lords ſteedsteadsteed: as an euidenceevidence thereof hath God Liberis ſuissuis pater Dei vice eſtest. Greg. Naz. ad Vitit. communicated to them this glorious and honourable title (FATHERfather) which is See §. 5. proper and peculiar to himſelfehimself. Now then parents being to their children in Gods ſteedsteadsteed, and by vertuevirtue of their place bearing Gods image, children in obeying their parents, obey God; in refuſingrefusing to obey them, refuſerefuse to obey God. A ſtrongstrong motiuemotive is this firſtfirst motiuemotive. For who is ſoso void of religion, but will thinkethink it moſtmost meet, that God ſhouldshould be honoured? orOr
who ſoso impious, as to refuſerefuse to yeeldyield dutieduty to God? Here then children may learnelearn in one mainemain point how to honour the Lord, & ſhewshow themſeluesthemselves children of God. And let them here byhereby know, that diſobedientdisobedient and vndutifullundutiful children, that reſiſtresist the authoritieauthority of parents, reſistresist the ordinance of God, and receiuereceive to themſeluesthemselves
Rom. 13. 2. damnation.

div.head: §. 60. Of the equitieequity whereby children ſhouldshould be mouedmoved to obey their parents.
div.p: II. The ſecondsecond reaſonreason in theſethese words, for this is right, though it be not of greater force, yet is it more plainly and expreſlyexpressly noted to be a reaſonreason, as the cauſallcausal particle (for) prefixed before it, ſhewethshoweth. It is a generallgeneral reaſonreason drawnedrawn from common equitieequity; a reaſonreason which may mouemove all ſortssorts, eueneven Infidels and Pagans: therefore much more ChriſtiansChristians.
In ſayingsaying, It is right, he implieth three things.

1. That it is agreeable to all law. To the law of God, which Right implieth three things. 1. It is agreeable to all law. is the fountainefountain of equitieequity. To the law of Naturenature, which proceeds from thence. And to the law of Nations, which is anſwerableanswerable in many reſpectsrespects. The forenamed proofesproofs out of Gods word, ſhewshow it to be agreeable to Gods law. The precepts which heathen men hauehave giuengiven of this point, ſhewshow it to be agreeable to the law of nature. And the many ConſtitutionsConstitutions of Law-makers, in all ages, ſhewshow it to be agreeable to the law of nations.

2. That the place of parents requireth as much. For RIGHT 2. It is due by vertuevirtue of parents place. requireth that eueryevery one hauehave his owneown, that which is his due. It being therefore right, that children obey their parents, that dutieduty i • s due to them.

3. That parents deſeruedeserve as much: for right preſuppoſethpresupposeth des • ert. 3. It is a debt. That which is done of right, is done by way of recompencerecompense. The cauſecause of this deſertdesert, is the louelove which parents bearebear to children, the painepain, painespains, care, and coſtcost they hauehave beenebeen at, in bringing them forth, and bringing them vpup.
TheſeThese things being implied vnderunder right, note what followeth f • rom the force of this reaſonreason,

1. DiſobedientDisobedient and vndutifullundutiful children, tranſgreſſetransgress againſtagainst Gods law, againſtagainst common equitieequity of all nations, and againſtagainst light o • f nature: ſoso as they are vnworthyunworthy of the name of ChriſtiansChristians, t • hey are worſeworse then Infidels, yea worſeworse then the brute beaſtsbeasts.

2. They hauehave no reſpectrespect to the place of their parents, they diſgracedisgrace the image of God, which their parents by vertuevirtue of their place carriecarry, and they diſturbedisturb that comely order and degree, which God hath ſetset among men.

3. They ill repay their parents care and painespains for their good, and ſhewshow themſeluesthemselves both vngratefullungrateful and vnnaturallunnatural: which are two moſtmost monſtrousmonstrous and odious ſinnessins.

div.head: §. 61. Of Gods accepting childrens obedience.
div.p: The forenamed reaſonreason is by this ſamesame ApoſtleApostle in another place thus ſetset downedown, This is well-pleaſingpleasing to the Lord. By comparing ColoſſColoss. 3. 20. that place with my text, I obſerueobserve, that
What is right is well-pleaſingpleasing to the Lord. And againeagain, What is well-pleaſingpleasing to the Lord is right.

TheſeThese two propoſitionspropositions, are (as we ſpeakespeak in SchoolesSchools) conuertibleconvertible and reciprocallreciprocal; either of them true of the other eueryevery way. Wherefore the ApoſtleApostle, in another place, ioynethjoinethjoyneth them both together. For hauinghaving exhorted children to recompencerecompense their parents, he ſaithsaith, That is good and acceptable before God.
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . Good or 1 Tim. 5. 4. honeſthonest is in effect the ſamesame that
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . right.

This ſhewethshoweth, that dutifulldutiful children, as they doedo that which is good, or honeſthonest, and right vntounto their parents; ſoso alſoalso therein they highly pleaſeplease God: ſoso as they may be ſuresure not to loſelose thereby. At Gods hand they ſhallshall receiuereceive a reward, though their parents ſhouldshould little regard their dutifulneſſedutifulness. Thus God dealt with IaakobJacob. His father in law ill repaid his faithfulneſſefaithfulness: but God looked Gen. 31. 7, &etcc. verſvers 42. vponupon him, and abundantly recompencedrecompensed all his painespains.

This ſhewethshoweth againeagain, that vndutifullundutiful children, as they doedo not that which is right, but rather wrong vntounto their parents; ſoso they highly diſpleaſedisplease God: they may be ſuresure therefore not to eſcapeescape vnpuniſhedunpunished, though their parents, through ouerover-much indulgencieindulgency, ſhouldshould let them alone: inſtanceinstance the two impious children of ElieEly, Hophni and Phinehas: and the two rebellious children of 1 Sam. 2. 34. 2 Sam. 18. 9. 1 King. 2. 25. DauidDavid, AbſolomAbsalom, and Adoniah.

This therefore addeth force to the ſecondsecond reaſonreason, and mouethmoveth children to doedo right to their parents, by obeying them, as they reſpectrespect God, his good pleaſurepleasure, or diſpleaſuredispleasure: as they lookelook for recompencerecompense, or fearefear vengeance from him.

div.head: §. 62. Of Gods charge, how inuiolableinviolable a bond it is to tie children to obey their parents.
div.p: III. The third drawnedrawn from Gods charge is not only in expreſſeexpress termesterms noted, but for more weight the very words of the morallmoral law are quoted (Honourhonour thy father and thy mother:) and it is added, that this is a commandementcommandment, yea the firſtfirst commandementcommandment, and that with promiſepromise, all which is for amplification of the point.
From the reaſonreason that it is Gods charge, I gather theſethese three points.

1. That it is no arbitrary matter left to childrens diſcretiondiscretion Childrens obedience to parents is, 1. No arbitrary thing. whether they will obey their parents or no: but a matter whereunto in conſcienceconscience they are bound, eueneven as they owe alleageanceallegiance to God himſelfehimself the great law-giuergiver: ſoso as in neglecting dutieduty to parents, children ſinnesin eueneven againſtagainst God himſelfehimself: for the ſamesame God who hath commanded vsus to honour himſelfehimself, hath commanded vsus to honour father and mother.

2. That this is a perpetuallperpetual and a generallgeneral law: a law whereunto 2. An eternalleternal law, and generallgeneral to all children. all children of all times, places, ſexessexes, eſtatesestates and degrees alwaiesalways hauehave beenebeen, ſtillstill are, and euerever ſhallshall be bound. For the morallmoral law is of that extent: it is generallgeneral for all perſonspersons: perpetuallperpetual for all times. Therefore no children may thinkethink to be exempted from it.

div.head: QueſtQuest. What if children be grownegrown to yeeresyears, and not vnderunder their parents gouernmentgovernment?
div.p: AnſwAnsw. There may be ſomesome difference both in ſomesome parts of ſubiectionsubjection, and alſoalso in the manner of ſubiectionsubjection betwixt ſuchsuch children as remaineremain vnderunder their parents gouernmentgovernment, and ſuchsuch as are freed from it: but yet ſoso long as a childechild hath a parent, of what age or eſtateestate ſoso euerever he be, he oweth an honour vntounto his parent. Gen. 47. 12. & 48. 12. & 50. 5. IoſephJoseph when he was a great GouernourGovernor of Egypt, a man grownegrown, hauinghaving wife and children, yet performed the honour of reuerencereverence, obedience, and recompencerecompense vntounto his father. 1 King. 2. 19. 3. IndiſpenſableIndispensable. SalomonSolomon when he was in an higher place then IoſephJoseph, eueneven an abſoluteabsolute King, did the honour of Reuerencereverence to his mother.

3. That no man can giuegive children any diſpenſationdispensation, or ex
emptionexemption from their dutieduty to parents. If any may, he muſtmust be either the law-maker himſelfehimself, or one greater then he, one that hath power ouerover him. Now God is the author and giuergiver of that law, God ſpakespake all theſethese words, &etcc. But is any greater then Exo. 20. 1. God? hathHath any power ouerover him? Who then can diſpencedispense with children in this kindekind?
Hence then I inferreinfer theſethese two concluſionsconclusions.
1. That the Popes diſpenſationdispensation is nothing worth: they who make it to be of force, muſtmust make him greater then God, which is a horrible blaſphemyblasphemy.

2. Though parents themſeluesthemselves ſhouldshould not exact dutieduty of their children, yet children were bound to performeperform dutieduty to them, becauſebecause of Gods charge. To this therefore are children to lookelook. This ſhewethshoweth that there is no leſſeless painepain hanging ouerover the heads of the tranſgreſſorstransgressors of this charge, then the curſecurse of the law, eternalleternal condemnation.

div.head: §. 63. Of the title FIRST giuengiven to the fiftfifth commandementcommandment.
div.p:
In the amplification of the forenamed reaſonreason, the ApoſtleApostle ſtilethstyleth the commandementcommandment of honouring parents the firſtfirst with promiſepromise, as to ſhewshow that it is the firſtfirst which hath a particular promiſepromise annexed to it; ſoso it is the firſtfirst that God gauegave of any dutieduty to be performed vntounto man. The very order of the decalogue manifeſtethmanifesteth the truth hereof. The reaſonreason is cleereclear: Honourhonour due to parents is the ground of all the duties required in the ſecondsecond table: for if dutieduty be not performed to ſuchsuch as we are bound vntounto by ſomesome peculiar bond, may we thinkethink that it will be performed to ſuchsuch as we are bound vntounto at large? Now of all to whom we are firſtfirst and moſtmost bound, and to whom we owe our firſtfirst dutieduty, our parents are the perſonspersons. They therefore who are rebellious againſtagainst their parents, and refuſerefuse to doedo their dutieduty to them, will hardly performeperform dutieduty to any other. Little hope that a diſobedientdisobedient childechild will proueprove a profitable member in Church or common-wealth. AbſolomAbsalom, who was a rebellious childechild, prouedproved but a traiteroustraitorous ſubiectsubject: and Hophni ••
and PhineasPhinehas that refuſedrefused to hearken to the voice of their father, prouedproved but ſacrilegioussacrilegious PrieſtsPriests. Wherefore if any precept of the ſecondsecond table be conſcionablyconscionably to be obſeruedobserved (as all are, for the ſamesame law-maker gauegave all, and ChriſtChrist hath ſaidsaid that
the ſecondsecond table is like the firſtfirst) then is this of honouring father
Mat. 22. 39. and mother, among the reſtrest, and aboueabove the reſtrest to be obſeruedobserved, at leaſtleast if difference of obſeruingobserving any may be made,.

But this particle (firſtfirst) being ſetset downedown, not ſimplysimply but with a connexionconnection of promiſepromise with it (The firſtfirst with promiſepromise) we are duly to conſiderconsider the promiſepromise thereof: whence a fourth reaſonreason ariſethariseth.

div.head: §. 64. Of Gods promiſepromise mouingmoving children to obey their parents.
div.p: The fourth reaſonreason taken from Gods promiſepromise, is both generally propounded and particularly exemplified. Propounded in this clauſeclause (firſtfirst with promiſepromise.) Exemplified in the third verſeverse.

For the Generallgeneral. Gods promiſepromise made to the performance of any duty, cannot but be a ſtrongstrong motiuemotive to ſtirrestir vsus vpup to performeperform it. Men hereby doedo ſtirrestir vpup, and prouokeprovoke one another PromiſePromise of reward a great motiuemotive. to performeperform any thing. Thus Kings when they would fainefain hauehave their ſubiectssubjects doedo this or that, promiſepromise ſuchsuch and ſuchsuch rewards vntounto them: Thus maſtersmasters incite their ſeruantsservants, parents their children, and one man another. If the promiſespromises of men incourageencourage vsus to performeperform the things which they giuegive vsus in charge, how much more ought the promiſepromise of God? Men How Gods promiſepromise is a ſtrongerstronger motiuemotive then any mans. a • re deceitfulldeceitful, and may dealedeal doubly, pretending one thing with their mouthesmouths, and intending another with their heart, a • nd neuernever meanemean to performeperform what they promiſepromise: But God is faithfullfaithful and true: his words are as deeds: his promiſespromises as performances; ſoso as he neuernever maketh ſhewshow of more then he means t • o performeperform. AgaineAgain, mans power is limited; though he truly in •• tend what he promiſethpromiseth, yet in the performance he may failefail e • ither in that he knew not his owneown power, but thought when h • e made the promiſepromise he could hauehave done more then in the eu • entevent he findeth he can doedo; or in that he is after wardsafterwards by ſomesome occaſionoccasion hindered, or diſableddisabled. But Gods power cannot be ſoso str • aitnedstraitened, or hindered. BeſidesBesides, men may be taken away before th • etimethe time of performing their promiſepromise is come: but God euerever liv •• ethlivethlieth, and changeth not. If then mans promiſespromises be any mouesmoves to any thing, much more Gods who euerever remaineth the sa • me. Betwixt God and man there is no proportion, no compa • riſoncomparison. How Gods promiſepromise commendeth Gods louelove.

This motiuemotive doth exceedingly commend Gods fatherly
indulgencieindulgency towards vsus, and the earneſtearnest deſiredesire he hath of our good. For he hath ſuchsuch power and authoritieauthority ouerover all his creatures, that the very knowledge of his will ought to prouokeprovoke them to performeperform any dutieduty which he ſhallshall command: and if they obey not, he might preſentlypresently execute vengeance vponupon them. But conſideringconsidering that we are his children, and need many allurements to draw vsus on by little and little, he accordingly dealeth with vsus. He ſtandethstandeth not wholly and only vponupon his authoritieauthority, but addeth promiſespromises thereto: (for this is a commandementcommandment with promiſepromise.) If notwithſtandingnotwithstanding all this, children refuſerefuse to obey their parents, may not the Lord iuſtlyjustly expoſtulateexpostulate the matter with them, as ſometimessometimes in another caſecase he did with the IſraelitesIsraelites, and ſaysay, IudgeJudge betweenebetween me and theſethese children:
IſaIsa. 5. 3, 4. what could I hauehave done more that I hauehave not done? I gauegave them an expreſſeexpress charge to honour their parents: I laid it downedown in the firſtfirst place as a mainemain and principallprincipal charge: to incourageencourage them to keepekeep it, I added a promiſepromise of good to redound to themſeluesthemselves: what could I doedo more? DoeDo not they iustlyjustly deſeruedeserve vengeance that regard none of theſethese? Thus, in that this is a commandementcommandment with promiſepromise, we ſeesee how children diſobedientdisobedient to their parents are both rebellious againſtagainst God in regard of the commandementcommandment which they tranſgreſſetransgress, and iniuriousinjurious to themſeluesthemselves in regard of the promiſepromise which they make to be void and of no effect. Of this particular promiſepromise ſeesee more in the firſtfirst treatiſetreatise, §. 97, 98, &etcc.

div.head: The ſixthsixth TreatiſeTreatise. The Duties of Parents.
§. 1. Of the heads of Parents duties.

epigraph.q: And ye Fathersfathers prouokeprovoke not your children to wrath, but bring them vpup in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.

div.p:
NExtNext to childrens, follow Parentsparents duties, which the ApoſtleApostle layeth down in this fourth verſeverse: where he noteth,
1. The duties
2. The parties
1. That are to performeperform the duties, Fathersfathers.
2. To whom they are to be performed, Childrenchildren.
The prohibition noteth out one extreme, which is ouermuchovermuch rigour, (ProuokeProvoke not to wrath)
The inference of the precept vponupon the prohibition noteth out another extreme, which is ouerover-much-remiſneſſeremissness.

The precept it ſelfeself enioynethenjoineth to parents three duties.
1. To nouriſhnourish children, namely with food, apparrellapparel, and other like neceſſariesnecessaries (NouriſhNourish them.)
2. To nurture them, namely with good diſciplinediscipline (In nurture.)

list.item: 3. To inſtructinstruct them, namely in the waiesways of God (And admonition of the Lord.)

div.p: To theſethese heads may all the ſeuerallseveral points which I ſhallshall deliuerdeliver concerning parents duties, be referred.
That Parentsparents may the better diſcernediscern how one dutieduty followeth another, I will proceed in this order.
The ſtreamesstreams ſhallshall be diuideddivided into two riuersrivers.
In the firſtfirst are thoſethose generallgeneral duties that are continually to be done.
In the ſecondsecond, ſuchsuch particular duties as are to be applied to the ſeuerallseveral ages of children.

There are two principallprincipal generallgeneral duties.
1. FaithfullFaithful prayer to God.
2. VprightUpright walking with God.

All the particulars may be compriſedcomprised vnderunder this one head, A prouidentprovident care. And this hath reſpectrespect,
1. To the Infancy of children,
2. To their Youth,
3. To the time of their placing forth,
4. To the time of parents departing out of this world.

div.head: §. 2. Of that LoueLove which parents owe to their children.
div.p:
The FountaineFountain of parents duties is Louelove.
Tit. 2. 4. This is expreſlyexpressly enioynedenjoined to them. Many approuedapproved examples are recorded hereof: as Gen. 22. 2. AbrahamsAbraham's,
& 25. 28. IſaacksIsaacsIsaacks, Ibid. Rebekahs, and others.

Great reaſonreason there is why this affection ſhouldshould be faſtfast fixed in the heart of parents towards their children. For great is that painepain, painespains, coſtcost, and care, which parents muſtmust vndergoeundergo
for their children. But if louelove be in them, no painepain, painespains, coſtcost, or care, will ſeemeseem too much. Herein appeareth the wiſewise prouidenceprovidence of God, who by nature hath ſoso faſtfast fixed louelove in the hearts of parents, as if there be any in whom it aboundeth not, he is counted vnnaturallunnatural. If louelove did not abound in parents, many children would be neglected and loſtlost. For if parents look not to their children, who will? If none lookelook to them, they muſtmust needs periſhperish: for they are not able to helpehelp themſeluesthemselves. As God by nature hath planted louelove in all parents, ſoso ChriſtiansChristians ought eueneven for conſcienceconscience ſakesake, to nouriſhnourish, increaſeincrease, and blow vpup this fire of louelove, that they may thereby be made more forward to doedo eueryevery duty with cheerefulneſſecheerfulness. The more feruentfervent louelove is, the more readily will eueryevery duty be performed. As I hauehave heretofore laid downedown LoueLove a fountainefountain of wiueswives, husbands, and childrens duties; ſoso muſtmust I continue my courſecourse, and ſetset it forth as the fountainefountain of parents duties. For the Scripture hath noted it as a dutieduty belonging to all and eueryevery of them: and therefore I might not omit it in any of them. Yet let not any thereupon thinkethink, that the ſamesame point is oft handled, and repeated againeagain and againeagain. For according to the ſeuerallseveral parties, and the ſeuerallseveral relation they hauehave to others, there are ſeuerallseveral fruits of louelove: eueneven as the ſamesame moiſturemoisture of the earth cauſethcauseth ſeuerallseveral and diuersdivers fruits, according to the ſeuerallseveral kindeskinds of plants that receiuereceive that moiſturemoisture. Compare the ſeuerallseveral places, where this generallgeneral duty of louelove hath beenebeen handled, and you will findefind the manner of handling to be different, and to afford new matter.

div.head: ObiectObject. As too much fire is dangerous, ſoso too much louelove.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. True. Wherefore as in other things, ſoso in this, the golden meanemean muſtmust be kept. No dutieduty ſoso holy and neceſſarienecessary, b • ut may be peruertedperverted. Let the extremes be auoidedavoided, and the meanemean will better be kept.

div.head: §. 3. Of the contraries to louelove.
div.p:
The extreme contrary to louelove in the defect is want of naturallnatural Want of naturallnatural affection in parents. affection, which is reckoned in the Rom. 1. 30. Tit. 3. 3. catalogue of notorious si •• nnessins. Though louelove of children be by nature engrauenengraven in mans heart, yet many cleaneclean put it out through couetouſneſſecovetousness, lu •• ſtlust, vainevain-glory, ſuperſtitionsuperstition, idolatry, and other vices: whereby it commethcometh to paſſepass that in ſteadstead of the good which they sh • ould doedo for their children, they bring much miſchiefemischief vponupon t • hem. Some ſparespare not the pretiousprecious life of their children.
Among theſethese, barbarous idolaters doedo moſtmost exceed in this kindekind of vnnaturallunnatural cruelty, ſacrificingsacrificing their children, and offering them vpup to deuilsdevils. To this the great bloudblood-sucker Satan of old brought not only the heathen, who being ignorant of God did ſeruiceservice to the diuelldevil, but alſoalso the 2 King. 16. 3. & 21. 6. Ezek. 16. 20. IſraelitesIsraelites to whom IehouahJehovah the true God made himſelfehimself knowneknown, and expreſlyexpressly Leu. 18. 21. forbid this cruelty, and that & 20. 2. vnderunder painepain of death. Behold how ſuperſtitionsuperstition and idolatry blindeblind the eieseyes of men. Purc. Pilgr. in Americ. cap. 7. & cap. 11. They who hauehave beenebeen among the SauadgesSavagesSavadges in VirgineaVirginia, Florida, India, and other like places teſtifietestify that ſuchsuch cruelty is vſedused to this day. And it is rendredrendered as a mainemain reaſonreason why, notwithſtandingnotwithstanding ſuchsuch ſpaciousspacious places as they hauehave, they increaſeincrease no more in multitude, becauſebecause many of their children from time to time are offered vpup in ſacrificesacrifice.

ReaſonableReasonable men herein ſhewshow themſeluesthemselves more vnreaſonableunreasonable then vnreaſonableunreasonable beaſtsbeasts, which doedo what poſſiblypossibly they can to preſeruepreserve their young ones.

Though not ſoso high, yet too high on this ladder of vnnaturalneſſeunnaturalness Haters of children for piety. doedo they climbeclimb, who hate their children, and that (which maketh the ſinsin to be out of meaſuremeasure ſinfulsinful) for piety and integrity; as many PopiſhPopish and profane parents, who hauehave children truly religious: and in that reſpectrespect ought ſoso much the more to be louedloved.

The extreme in the exceſſeexcess is too much doting vponupon children: Doting on children. as they doedo who ſoso vnmeaſurablyunmeasurably louelove them, as they make reckoning of nothing in compariſoncomparison of children. EuenEven God himſelfehimself is lightly eſteemedesteemed, his worſhipworship neglected, his word tranſgreſſedtransgressed, all dutieduty to others omitted, their owneown ſoulessouls forgotten thorowthrough care of children. Is not this meere •• mere apiſhapish kindneſſekindness? forFor Apes kill their young ones with hugging. This is no louelove, but plaineplain dotage. But what may be ſaidsaid of thoſethose that are ſoso helliſhlyhellishly enamoured with their children as to commit inceſtincest or buggery with them?

div.head: §. 4. Of Parents praying for their children.
div.p:
The firſtfirst and beſtbest ſtreamestream which iſſuethissueth out of the forenamed fountainefountain of louelove is faithfullfaithful and feruentfervent prayer. This extendeth it ſelfeself to all things, at all times, thorowoutthroughout the whole courſecourse of the childes life. It is the firſtfirst and it is the laſtlast
dutieduty which parents ought to performeperform to their children: 1 TheſThes.Thes 5. 17. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . eueneven that which they muſtmust doedo without intermiſſionintermission; Pray without ceaſingceasing.

Though praierprayer be a generallgeneral dutieduty which all ChriſtiansChristians owe PraierPrayer a peculiar dutieduty of parents. one to another, yet after a peculiar manner doth it appertaineappertain to parents: and of all others they are moſtmost bound to it. For the promiſepromise which God maketh to a parent is extended to his ſeedseed and children, as theſethese and ſuchsuch like Scriptures ſhewshow, Gen. 17. 7. I will be thy God, and the God of thy ſeedseed:
Deut. 5. 29. That it may be well with them and with their children:
Act. 2. 39. The promiſepromise is vntounto you, and vntounto your children. Parentsparents therefore with moſtmost aſſuranceassurance of faith may call vponupon God for their children. For Gods promiſepromise is the ground of faith: ſoso farrefar as Gods promiſepromise is extended, ſoso farrefar our faith may and ought to extend it ſelfeself. Hence hath ariſenarisen the commendable cuſtomecustom of childrens asking TreatTreat. 5. §. 9. their parents bleſſingblessing: which intimateth a deſiredesire that parents would pray for Gods bleſſingblessing on them.

This dutieduty of praierprayer muſtmust be performed before parents hauehave children (that they may hauehave ſomesome, as Gen. 25. 21. IſaakIsaac, 1 Sam. 1. 10. Paulam antè votis quàm vtero concepiſticoncepisti. Hier. ad 1 aetLaet.
AnnahHannah and others did Gen. 25. 21.) and ſoso ſoonesoon as children are conceiuedconceived, eſpeciallyespecially if they obſerueobserve them to be quickequick in the wombewomb (as Gen. 25. 22. Rebekah did) and againeagain when they are borne (as Luk. 1. 64. Zachariah did) and thorowoutthroughout the whole courſecourse of their life (as IobJob. 1. 5. IobJob did) and when they are going out of this world, and leauingleaving their children (as Gen. 27. 4. IſaakIsaac did.)

There is no one thing wherein and whereby parents may doedo more good for their children, then in and by true praierprayer. God hath ſanctifiedsanctified praierprayer as a meanesmeans to receiuereceive all needfullneedful bleſſingblessing from himſelfehimself the fountainefountain of all bleſſingblessing. If therefore Gods bleſſingblessing be of vſeuse to children (what AtheiſtsAtheists are they that beleeuebelieve it not?) then alſoalso is praierprayer by which it is obtained.

div.head: §. 5. Of vices contrary to parents praying for their children.
div.p:
The very neglect of this dutieduty is a ſinnesin contrary to the dutieduty Parents neglect of praierprayer. it ſelfeself: and many parents there be that ſtandstand guilty of this ſinnesin. Some thinkethink it needleſſeneedless to pray for a childechild before it be borne, not conſideringconsidering that in ſinnesin it is conceiuedconceived. When it is borne they referrerefer this dutieduty to the midwife, whereas it
properly appertaineth to the father. After it is grownegrown to any ripeneſſeripeness, they put it off to the childechild to pray for it ſelfeself. And when they are on their death-bed, they thinkethink it enough if they can pray for their owneown ſoulessouls. Such parents ſhewshow little true louelove to their children: but leſſeless faith in God.

But what may we ſaysay or thinkethink of ſuchsuch impious parents as Parents imprecations againſtagainst children. fearefear not to make fearefullfearful imprecations againſtagainst their children? God oft in wrath and vengeance heareth ſuchsuch imprecations to the woe of parent and childechild: whereby he ſhewethshoweth his great indignation againſtagainst them for the ſamesame.

div.head: §. 6. Of parents endeauouringendeavouring to be righteous that they may leaueleave Gods bleſſingblessing to their children.
div.p:
Another generallgeneral branch proceeding from parents louelove to their children, is, that for their childrens ſakesake they endeauourendeavour to walkewalk vprightlyuprightly before God, and to pleaſeplease him. This I doedo the rather note, becauſebecause I findefind the reward promiſedpromised to righteous parents to be extended vntounto their children PſalPsal. 1. 12112. 2. The generation of the righteous ſhallshall be bleſſedblessed, ſaithsaith DauidDavid. And SalomonSolomon,

Deut. 5. 29. This motiuemotive is therefore vrgedurged by the holy GhoſtGhost to prouokeprovoke parents vntounto all righteouſneſſerighteousness.

Thus doth the Lord extend the reward of righteous parents vntounto their children to ſhewshow his great good liking, and high approbation of righteouſneſſerighteousness. ReadeRead for this purpoſepurpose, 1 King. 11. 34. & 2 King. 10. 30.

1. ObiectObject.
Ezec. 18. 20. The righteouſneſſerighteousness of the righteous ſhallshall be vponupon himſelfehimself.

AnſwAnsw. That is meant rather of a mans perſonallpersonal righteouſneſſerighteousness, and grace it ſelfeself which is not communicated to children, then of the fruit thereof: That faith in ChriſtChrist, fearefear of God, obedience to Gods word, or any other perſonallpersonal grace which is in righteous parents, ſhallshall not iuſtifiejustify or ſauesave their children. For the iuſtjust ſhallshall liuelive by his owneown faith. Yet this hindereth Hab. 2. 4. not but that the benefit and bleſſingblessing of righteous parents may fall vponupon their children according to the extent of Gods promiſepromise.

2. ObiectObject. By experience we findefind it verified, that the children
of ſomesome righteous parents are curſedcursed: and the Scripture giuethgiveth vsus many examples thereof: as Gen. 4. 11. Cain,
& 9. 25. Cham, 2 Sam. 18. 15. AbſolomAbsalom, and others like them.

1. LeſtLest Gods gifts and bleſſingsblessings ſhouldshould otherwiſeotherwise ſeemeseem to come rather by naturallnatural propagation from the parent, then by free donation from God.
2. LeſtLest parents ſhouldshould thereby be drawnedrawn to neglect the meanesmeans of good education.
3. LeſtLest children alſoalso themſeluesthemselves, truſtingtrusting too much to their parents righteouſneſſerighteousness, ſhouldshould take too much liberty, and waxewax licentious.
4. LeſtLest Gods free election ſhouldshould ſeemeseem hereby to be reſtrainedrestrained.

div.head: 3. ObiectObject.
div.p: If this be ſoso, what motiuemotive can it be vntounto parents to labour after righteouſneſſerighteousness for their childrens ſakesake?

AnſwAnsw. Though God doedo reſeruereserve in himſelfehimself a freedomefreedom to order his bleſſingsblessings as it pleaſethpleaseth him, and to beſtowbestow them vponupon whom he will: and thereupon ſometimessometimes bleſſethblesseth the childechild of a wicked parent (inſtanceinstance 2 Chr. 28. 27. Hezekiah) & denieth his bleſſingblessing to the childechild of a righteous parent (inſtanceinstance 2 Sam. 13. 14, 29. Relinque bonam filijs memoriam magis quàm diuitias multas. BaſBas ſermserm. in Scrip. loc.
AmmonAmnon) yet in that it is a very vſuallusual courſecourse with him to extend his bleſſingblessing (according to his promiſepromise) to the children of the righteous, it is a ſtrongstrong motiuemotive to ſuchsuch as deſiredesire the good of their children, the rather for their childrens ſakesake to endeauourendeavour after righteouſneſſerighteousness: for thus doedo they vſeuse the meanesmeans which by Gods word is warranted and ſanctifiedsanctified for procuring Gods bleſſingblessing to their children. LeaueLeave therefore a good memory to thy children rather then much wealth.

div.head: §. 7. Of the prepoſterouspreposterous courſecourse which couetouscovetous and vniuſtunjust parents take for the good of their children.
div.p:
Contrary is the courſecourse of ſuchsuch parents as by vnrighteousunrighteous meanesmeans thinkethink to prouideprovide well for their children. For many
doedo not only too carkingly, and diſtruſtfullydistrustfully moilemoil and toiletoil to ſcrapescrape together great maſſesmasses of money, or great ſtorestore of land, or other ſtockesstocks for their children, neglecting duties of piety and mercy, but alſoalso by vniuſtunjust and wrongfullwrongful courſescourses defraud others to make their children rich. So common is this vndueundue courſecourse of prouidingproviding for children, as thence hath ariſenarisen this prouerbeproverb, Happy are thoſethose children whoſewhose parents goego to the deuilldevil. A curſedcursed prouerbeproverb. For what other thing can it intend, but this, that they who fearefear not God, nor take care for their owneown ſaulationsalvationsaulation, will hauehave moſtmost reſpectrespect to the outward eſtateestate of their children, and be moſtmost carefullcareful to make them great, and rich in this world? Wherein note how many waiesways they bewray their notorious folly.
1. They preferreprefer the outward eſtateestate of their children before the eternalleternal ſaluationsalvation of their owneown ſoulessouls. Yea and before God himſelfehimself.
2. They place the happineſſehappiness of their children in the goods of this world; Pro. 23. 5. then which nothing more vainevain.
3. They make themſeluesthemselves drudges to their children, and ſoso debaſedebase themſeluesthemselves below that dignity which by reaſonreason of Gods image on them, appertaineth to them.
4. They with much painespains, care, griefegrief, and fearefear are long gathering that which their children in ſhortshort time moſtmost riotouſlyriotously and prodigally will lauiſhlavish out.

5. They make themſeluesthemselves vaſſalsvassals to Satan and ſeekeseek by him to be made rich: whereas indeed TroPro. 10. 22. it is the bleſſingblessing of God that maketh rich. Thus they take a wrong courſecourse to get wealth. If it be ſaidsaid that many are thus made rich, I anſweranswer, that as HoſHos. 13. 11. Ne liberos praetexas. Qui enim filium fecit, & te fecit: qui etiam tibi occaſionesoccasiones nutriendnutriendi praebet, & filio praebebit vitae ſubſidiasubsidia. BaſilBasil. loc. c • it. God gauegave a King to IſraellIsrael, ſoso he giuethgiveth wealth to them, in wrath: and in wrath will he take it away.

6. They bring Gods curſecurse into their houſehouse, and leaueleave it vntounto their children: So as theſethese are the riches that are reſeruedreserved to the owners thereof for their euillevil. Let not therefore care for children draw thee to any coueteouscovetouscoveteous or vniuſtunjust courſescourses: but know that he who made thy ſonneson made thee alſoalso, and he who affoordedafforded thee meanesmeans of nouriſhmentnourishment, will alſoalso affoordafford thy children ſufficientsufficient ſuccoursuccour.

div.head: §. 8. Of Parents prouidenceprovidence for their children. How farrefar parents prouidenceprovidence extendeth it ſelfeself.
div.p: The head, whereunto all the particular duties, which parents owe to their children, may be referred, is A prouidentprovident care for their childrens good. This extendeth it ſelfeself to all times, and to all things.
To all times, as to the infancieinfancy, youth, and man-age of their children: and that not only while parents liuelive, but after their departure.
To all things, namely, tending both to the temporalltemporal good of their children, and alſoalso to their ſpirituallspiritual good.
Children are of the very ſubſtancesubstance of their parents, & therefore ought parents ſoso farrefar to ſeekeseek their childrens good as their owneown.
The patternespatterns of holy parents recorded and commended in Scripture, doedo liuelylively ſetset forth this prouidentprovident care.

But this generallgeneral we will exemplifieexemplify in the particulars: and in order declare how parents muſtmust prouideprovide both for the temporalltemporal, and alſoalso for the ſpirituallspiritual good of their children in eueryevery degree of their age.

They who at any time in any thing are negligent and careleſſecareless of their childrens good, offend in the contrary to this generallgeneral dutieduty. The heinouſneſſeheinousness of which offences will appeareappear in the particulars.

div.head: §. 9. Of a mothers care ouerover her childechild while it is in her wombewomb.
div.p: The firſtfirst age of a childechild is the infancieinfancy thereof. I will therefore firſtfirst ſhewshow how therein parents muſtmust procure the temporalltemporal good of their children, and then their ſpirituallspiritual good.

The firſtfirst part of a childs infancieinfancy is while it remaineth in the mothers wombewomb. Here therefore the dutieduty lieth principally vponupon the mother: who ſoso ſoonesoon as ſheshe perceiuethperceiveth a childechild to be conceiuedconceived in her wombewomb, ought to hauehave an eſpeciallespecial care thereof, that (ſoso much as in her lieth) the childechild may be ſafelysafely brought forth. ( Grauidae corpora curare debent. Mens item earum quietem deſideratdesiderat. Quae enim procreantur à matre in cuius aluo continentur, alimentum capiunt, vt à terra ea-quae gignantur ex ea. AriſtArist. Pol. lib. 7. The heathen PhiloſophenPhilosophersPhilosophen, by light of nature, obſeruedobserved this to be a dutieduty; and preſcribedprescribed it to mothers.) A mother then muſtmust hauehave a tender care ouerover her ſelfeself when ſheeshe is with childechild: for the childechild being lodged in her, and receiuingreceiving nouriſhmentnourishment from her (as plants from the earth) her well-being tendeth much to the good and ſafetiesafety of the childechild: but the hurt that commethcometh to her, maketh the childechild the worſeworse, if it be not a meanesmeans to deſtroydestroy it.
Why was the charge of IudgJudg. 13. 4. abſtainingabstaining from wine, ſtrongstrong drinkedrink, and vncleaneunclean things, giuengiven to Manoahs wife, but becauſebecause of the childechild which ſheshe conceiuedconceived?

In this caſecase there is a double bond to make mothers carefullcareful of themſeluesthemselves.
1. Their owneown,
2. Their childs good.

Husbands alſoalso in this caſecase muſtmust be very tender ouerover their wiueswives, and helpfullhelpful to them in all things needfullneedful, both in regard of that dutieduty which they owe to their wiueswives, and alſoalso of that they IudgJudg. 13. 11, &etcc. owe to their children. Why was Manoah ſoso deſirousdesirous to hearehear himſelfehimself the forenamed direction which the AngellAngel gauegave to his wife? andAnd why did the AngellAngel againeagain repeat it to him, but to ſhewshow it belonged to him to ſeesee her obſerueobserve it?

They who through violence of paſſionpassion, whether of griefegrief, or Contrary. anger, or through violent motion of the bodiebody, as by dancing, ſtriuingstriving, 1. To miſcarrymiscarry through negligence. running, galloping on horſebackehorseback, or the like: or through diſtemperdistemper of the bodiebody, by eating things hurtfullhurtful, by eating too much, by too much abſtinenceabstinence, by too much baſhfulneſſebashfulness in concealing their deſiresdesires and longings (as we ſpeakespeak) cauſecause any abortion or miſcariagemiscarriagemiscariage, fall into the offence contrary to the forenamed dutieduty. If women were perſwadedpersuaded that in conſcienceconscience they are bound to the forenamed dutieduty, they would, I thinkethink, be more carefullcareful of themſeluesthemselves. For if through their default, they themſeluesthemselves or their childechild miſcarrymiscarry, they make themſeluesthemselves guilty of that miſcariagemiscarriagemiscariage: if both miſcarrymiscarry, they make themſeluesthemselves guiltieguilty of the bloudblood of both; at leaſtleast in the court of conſcienceconscience before God.

But they who purpoſelypurposely take things to make away their children 2. To make away a childechild in the wombewomb.
