ApoſtApost. l. 7. c. 4. in their wombewomb, are in farrefar higher degree guiltieguilty of bloudblood: yea eueneven of wilfullwilful murthermurder. For that which hath receiuedreceived a ſoulesoul formed in it by God, if it be vniuſtlyunjustly caſtcast away, ſhallshall be reuengedrevenged.

So farrefar forth as husbands are careleſſecareless of their wiueswives being with childechild, denying them things needfullneedful, they are acceſſarieaccessary to the hurt, which the woman, or childechild taketh, guiltieguilty of the ſinsin, and liable to the iudgementjudgment.

div.head: §. 10. Of prouidingproviding things needfullneedful for the childechild, ſoso ſoonesoon as it is borne: and of crueltiecruelty contrary thereunto.
div.p:
The next degree of a childs infancieinfancy, is while it is in the ſwadlingswaddling
bands, and remaineth a ſuckingsucking childechild. In this alſoalso the care eſpeciallyespecially lieth vponupon the mother: yet ſoso as the father muſtmust afford what helpehelp he can.

The firſtfirst dutieduty here required is, that ſufficientsufficient prouiſionprovision of all things needfullneedful for a childechild in that weakneſſeweakness be before hand prouidedprovided. What the particulars be, women better know, then I can expreſſeexpress. For me, it is ſufficientsufficient, to lay downedown the dutieduty in generallgeneral: which is commended vntounto vsus in that worthy patternepattern of the Virgin MarieMary, who though ſheshe were very poorepoor, and forced to trauelltravel farrefar, and brought to bed in a ſtrangestrange place, where ſheshe was ſoso little reſpectedrespected, as ſheshe was not afforded a place meet for a woman in her caſecase, but was fainefain to content her ſelfeself with a ſtablestable in a common InneInn, yet ſheshe prouidedprovided for her childechild. For it is ſaidsaid, She wrapped him in ſwadlingswaddling clothes, Luk 2. 7.

Contrary is the practiſepractise of ſuchsuch lewd and vnnaturallunnatural women, as leaueleave their new-borne children vnderunder ſtallsstalls, at mens dooresdoors, in Church porches, yea many times in open field. It is noted as a point of vnnaturalneſſeunnaturalness in the OſtrichOstrich, to leaueleave her eggs in the earth, and in the duſtdust: in which reſpectrespect ſheshe is ſaidsaid to be hardnedhardened againſtagainst her young ones, as though they were not hers, IobJob 39. 14, 16. Much more hardnedhardened are the foreſaidforesaid lewd women. The Eagle is IniquiffimaIniquissima volucris Aquila dicitur, quiaequia taedio nutriendi pullum quem genuit, ipſaipsa fugat. Tales parentes ij ſuntsunt, qui liberos ſuossuos infantes exponunt. BaſilBasil. Hexam. hom. 8. Necare videtur qui partum abijcit, & qui publicis locis miſericordiaemisericordiae cauſacausa, quam ipſeipse non habet, exponit. DigeſtDigest. l,. 25. tit. 3. §. 4. 1 Pet. 2. 2. counted an vnnaturallunnatural bird, becauſebecause ſheshe thruſteththrusteth her young ones, which ſheshe hath brought forth, out of her neſtnest. Are not then ſuchsuch mothers much more vnnaturallunnatural? They oft lay their children forth in publikepublic places, for others to ſhewshow that mercy, which they themſeluesthemselves hauehave not. The CiuillCivil Law iudgethjudgeth this to be a kindekind of furthermurder.

div.head: §. 11. Of giuinggiving ſuckesuck to children.
div.p:
Among other needfullneedful things, the milkemilk of the breaſtbreast is fit for y • oung babes, and with it they are to be nouriſhednourished. I thinkethink none d • oubt of the equitieequity of this. It hath in all ages, and in all countr • ies, beenebeen accounted the beſtfoodbest foodbestfood that can be for young babes. The metaphor, which S. Peter vſethuseth, taken from young infants in theſethese words,, ( As new-borne babes deſiredesire the ſinceresincere milkemilk of the w • ord) confirmeth as much. So doth alſoalso the deſiredesire which ſuchsuch i • nfants hauehave to the milkemilk of the breaſtsbreasts: and the abilitieability, and pr • omptneſſepromptness which is in them to ſuckesuck: and Gods prouidenceprovidence in ca • uſingcausing a womans breaſtsbreasts to yeeldyield forth ſuchsuch milkemilk: and the conſtantconstant
manner of nouriſhingnourishing little infants after this manner, commended in the Scriptures: and (to conclude) the naturallnatural inſtinctinstinct which many vnreaſonableunreasonable creatures hauehave thus to nouriſhnourish their young ones.

They who on meeremere curioſitiecuriosity (where no vrgenturgent neceſſitienecessity requireth) try whether their children may not as birds be nouriſhednourished without ſuckesuck, offend contrary to this dutieduty; and reiectreject that meanesmeans which God hath ordained as the beſtbest: and ſoso oppoſeoppose their ſhallowshallow wit to his vnſearchableunsearchable wiſdomewisdom.

div.head: §. 12. Of mothers giuinggiving ſuckesuck to their owneown children.
div.p: Of nouriſhingnourishing children with breſtbreastbrest-milkemilk, there is no great queſtionquestion: therefore I hauehave with a touch paſſedpassed it ouerover. The chiefeſtchiefest queſtionquestion of doubt is concerning the partieparty who is bound to this dutieduty; namely, whether the mother be bound to doedo it her ſelfeself or no.

Many ſtrongstrong arguments there be to preſſepress it vponupon the conſciencesconsciences PoſtquamPostquam ablactaueris cameam, &etcc. dixit Hier. ad Laetam de filia ſuasua. of mothers, and to ſhewshow that (ſoso farrefar as they are able) they are bound to giuegive ſuckesuck to their owneown children. Some are taken from the light of Gods word; and ſomesome from the light of nature.

Gods word doth in many places by iuſtjust conſequenceconsequence imply, that it is a bounden dutieduty: in other places it doth expreſlyexpressly commend it by the practiſepractise of holy women: and againeagain in other places it taketh it for a granted truth, and ruled caſecase, not to be denied.
1I. The conſequencesconsequences whereby the word implieth this dutieduty are theſethese:

1. In the bleſſingblessing giuengiven to IoſephJoseph thus ſpeakethspeaketh old IaakobJacob, God ſhallshall bleſſebless thee with the bleſſingblessing of the breaſtsbreasts, and of the
Gen. 49. 25. wombewomb. By the bleſſingblessing of the wombewomb, what can be meant, but children? By the bleſſingblessing of the breaſtsbreasts, what, but milkemilk, whereby thoſethose children are nouriſhednourished? As if he had ſaidsaid; I will bleſſebless thee with ſuchsuch women, as ſhallshall both bearebear thee children, and alſoalso giuegive ſuckesuck to them which they bearebear. The conſequenceconsequence then is this: As it is a bleſſingblessing to hauehave children of a true lawfulllawful wife; ſoso to hauehave thoſethose children nurſednursed of the ſamesame wife their mother.

div.head: ObiectObject. They hauehave the bleſſingblessing of breaſtsbreasts that hauehave other women to nurſenurse their children.
div.p:
AnſwAnsw. By the ſamesame reaſonreason it may be ſaidsaid, they hauehave the bleſſingblessing
of the wombewomb who hauehave ſtrangestrange women to bearebear them children. But the ioyningjoining of theſethese two branches of bleſſingblessing together, ſhewethshoweth that both muſtmust be taken in the ſamesame kindekind: ſoso that as the bleſſingblessing of the wombewomb is to hauehave children of a mans wife, ſoso the bleſſingblessing of the breaſtsbreasts is to hauehave them nurſednursed of his wife. If it be a bleſſingblessing for the woman which beareth the childechild to giuegive it ſuckesuck, then mothers are bound to performeperform this dutieduty.

2. It is denounced as a curſecurse, that women ſhallshall hauehave a barren
OſeOse. 9. 14. wombewomb and driedry breaſtsbreasts. If it be a curſecurse for women to hauehave driedry breaſtsbreasts, then may not women wittingly make them driedry: which all mothers doedo, that giuegive not ſuckesuck to their children.

3. Manoahs wife being promiſedpromised to bearebear a ſonneson, had this charge giuengiven her, DrinkeDrink no wine, nor ſtrongstrong drinkedrink. &etcc. thoſeThose things were eſpeciallyespecially hurtfullhurtful for her milkemilk. It is therefore implied thereby, that ſheshe ſhouldshould ſoso order her diet, as ſheshe might well nurſenurse her childechild, and hauehave good milkemilk for him.

4. God by his good prouidenceprovidence brought it to paſſepass, that the mother of MoſesMoses (though ſheshe were forced to caſtcast out her Exo. 2. 7, &etcc. childechild) ſhouldshould nurſenurse her owneown childechild. Yea the mother her ſelfeself was deſirousdesirous to doedo it, and therefore appointed her daughter t • o watch who ſhouldshould take it vpup. TheſeThese two circumſtancescircumstances i • mplieimply that it appertaineth to a mother to nurſenurse her children.

5. The ApoſtleApostle layeth this downedown as a note of a good woman, 1. Tim. 5. 10. who in her place hath beenebeen carefullcareful to doedo her dutieduty, a • nd thereupon fit to doedo ſeruiceservice in Gods Church (If ſheshe hauehave
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 .
n • ouriſhednourished her children, or word for word, If ſheshe hauehave fed her children.) Now the proper food for young babes is breaſtbreast-milk, which, by the ApoſtlesApostles rule, the mother muſtmust giuegive.

6. The ſamesame ApoſtleApostle commandeth mothers to louelove their
Tit. 2. 4. children. How can a mother better expreſſeexpress her louelove to her y • oung babe, then by letting it ſuckesuck of her owneown breaſtsbreasts? As histhis is a teſtimonytestimony of louelove, ſoso it is a meanesmeans of preſeruingpreserving and increaſingincreasing louelove: for daily experience ſhewethshoweth that mothers lo • uelove thoſethose children beſtbest to whom they themſeluesthemselves giuegive ſuckesuck.

SummeSum theſethese ſeuerallseveral conſequencesconsequences together, and we sh • all findefind the dutieduty in queſtionquestion to be very ſtronglystrongly inforcedenforced hereby.
1. As a bleſſingblessing it is promiſedpromised, that mothers ſhallshall giuegive ſuckesuck to the children that they bearebear.
2. As a curſecurse it is threatnedthreatened, that women ſhallshall not be able to giuegive ſuckesuck.
3. An AngellAngel gauegave direction to a mother ſoso to carriecarry her ſelfeself as ſheshe might hauehave ſtorestore of good milkemilk for the childechild which ſheshe ſhouldshould bearebear.
4. God by his ſpeciallspecial prouidenceprovidence manifeſtedmanifested that the proper mother was the beſtbest nurſenurse for a childechild.
5. It is the note of a good woman to performeperform this part of her particular calling, namely to nurſenurse her owneown childechild.
6. Women ought to doedo all the beſtbest duties of louelove that they can to their children.
div.q: Therefore mothers ought to nurſenurse their owneown children.
div.p: II. Some of the moſtmost worthy patternespatterns, in whoſewhose example this dutieduty is commended to mothers, are theſethese.

1. Sarah gauegave ſuckesuck to IſaakIsaac. This example is to be noted Gen. 21. 7. eſpeciallyespecially of the greater ſortsort: as rich mens wiueswives, honourable mens wiueswives, and the like. For Sarah was an honourable woman, a princeſſeprincess, a rich mans wife, a beautifullbeautiful woman, aged and well grownegrown in yeeresyears, and a miſtreſſemistress of a family.
Are not theſethese excuſesexcuses pretended by many mothers for not nurſingnursing children themſeluesthemselves?

2. The virgin Mary gauegave ſuckesuck to IeſusJesus. This example is to be noted eſpeciallyespecially of the meaner ſortsort, for the virgin ManMaryman was young, poorepoor, perſecutedpersecuted, forced to remoueremove and fliefly with her childechild from countriecountry to countriecountry. Are not theſethese excuſesexcuses pretended by other mothers?
TheſeThese two patternespatterns doedo not only commend the duty, but alſoalso ſtrippestrip all mothers that are negligent therein, of all excuſeexcuse.

To theſethese may be added the examples of 1 Sam. 1. 22. AnnahHannah, of PſalPsal. 22. 9. DauidsDavid's mother, and of many others. What if alſoalso I addeadd the example of that true, naturallnatural, affectionate mother who ſtoodstood before SalomonsSolomon's throne to plead for her childechild? ſheShe thus ſaithsaith of her ſelfeself, 1 King. 3. 21. I aroſearose to giuegive my ſonneson ſuckesuck, &etcc. If this had not beenebeen a good motherly dutieduty, ſheshe would not then and there hauehave pleaded it.
III. The places of Scripture which take this dutieduty for a matter granted, and for a ruled caſecase, are ſuchsuch as theſethese.

1. Where Sarah ſaithsaith, Who would hauehave ſaidsaid to Abram that
Gen. 21. 7. Sarah ſhouldshould hauehave giuengiven children ſuckesuck? In this phraſephrase ſheshe ſettethsetteth forth Gods bleſſingblessing in giuinggiving Abram a ſonneson by her. Now in that ſheshe expreſſethexpresseth the bleſſingblessing vnderunder this phraſephrase of giuinggiving ſuckesuck, ſheshe taketh it for grant, that the mother which beareth children muſtmust giuegive them ſuckesuck.

2. Where DauidDavid ſaithsaith, thou diddeſtdidstdiddest make me hope vponupon my
PſalPsal. 22. 9. mothers breaſtsbreasts, he doth not onelyonly imply that his mother gauegave him ſuckesuck, but by the phraſephrase maketh it a ruled caſecase that the childechild which ſuckessucks muſtmust hang vponupon the mothers breaſtbreast.

3. Where SalomonSolomon ſaithsaith, O that thou wert as my brother that
Cant. 8. 1. ſuckedsucked the breaſtsbreasts of my mother, he taketh ifit alſoalso for grant, that brothers and ſiſterssisters, as they come out of the ſamesame wombewomb, ſoso they ſhouldshould ſuckesuck the ſamesame breaſtsbreasts, eueneven the breaſtsbreasts of her out of whoſewhose wombewomb they came, their owneown mothers breaſtsbreasts.

4. Where the woman ſaidsaid to ChriſtChrist, BleſſedBlessed is the wombewomb that
Luk. 11. 27. bare thee, and the paps which thou haſthast ſuckedsucked, ſheshe taketh it for grant (as it was an vſuallusual practiſepractise in thoſethose daiesdays) that the p • aps of that woman, whoſewhose wombewomb bearebarebear him, gauegave him IpſaIpsa ſuggeritsuggerit natura matribus ipſisipsis lactandos eſſeesse ſuossuos foetus. IdoircoIdcirco enim animanti enixae lactis alimentum omni praebuit▪. Sapiens verò etiam prouidentia mammas foeminis binas effinxit, &etcc. Plut. de JuſtitInstitJustit. lib. In ijs animantibus quae lacte aluntur, omnis ferè cibus lacteſcerelactescere incipit. Cic. de Nat. D. s • uckesuck.
TheſeThese arguments we hauehave from the light of Gods word: other we may hauehave from Gods workesworks and the light of nature, as

1. God hath giuengiven to women two breaſtsbreasts fit to containecontain a • nd hold milkemilk: and nipples vntounto them fit to hauehave milkemilk drawnedrawn from them. Why are theſethese thus giuengiven? toTo lay them fo • rth for oſtentationostentation? There is no warrant for that in all Gods w • ord. They are directly giuengiven for the childs food that commethcometh out of the wombewomb; for till the childechild be borne, there is n • o milkemilk in the breaſtsbreasts: anon after it is borne, milkemilk ordinarily •• floweth into the breaſtsbreasts: yea a great part of the meat which th •• ey eat turneth into milkemilk. They make this admirable workework o • f Gods prouidenceprovidence to be in vainevain, that driedry vpup this ſpringspring, an •• d ſuffersuffer not their children to partake of the benefit of it.

2. That nouriſhmentnourishment whereon the childechild fed in the moth •• ers wombewomb, and whereby it was there ſuſtainedsustained, turneth into
milkemilk, and commethcometh into the breaſtsbreasts when the childechild commethcometh out of the wombewomb. Whence we may gather, that of all womens milkemilk, that womans milkemilk is fitteſtfittest for the childechild, out of whoſewhose wombewomb the childechild came.

3. Together with the milkemilk paſſethpasseth ſomesome ſmackesmack of the Mater Bernardi liberos ſuossuos alienis vberibus nutriendos committere refugiebat, quaſiquasi cum lacte materno materni quodammodo boni infundens eis naturam. Guil. Abb. de vit. Bern. l. 1. c. 1. affection and diſpoſitiondisposition of the mother: which maketh mothers to louelove ſuchsuch children beſtbest as they hauehave giuengiven ſuckesuck vntounto: yea and oft times ſuchsuch children as hauehave ſuckedsucked their mothers breaſtsbreasts, louelove their mothers beſtbest: yea we may obſerueobserve many who hauehave ſuckedsucked others milkemilk, to louelove thoſethose nurſesnurses all the daiesdays of their life.

4. Other things are nouriſhednourished by the ſamesame that they are bred. The earth out of which plants grow, miniſtrethministreth nouriſhmentnourishment to the ſaidsaid plants: trees that bring forth fruit yeeldyield ſapsap to that fruit, whereby it groweth to ripeneſſeripeness: vnreaſonableunreasonable creatures, and among them the moſtmost ſauagesavage wildewild beaſtsbeasts, as Tigers and Dragons, yea ſeasea-monſtersmonsters giuegive ſuckesuck to their young ones; whereupon the Prophet ſaithsaith of women that giuegive not ſuckesuck Lam. 4. 3. to their Childrenchildren, that they are more cruellcruel then thoſethose ſeamonſterssea-monstersseamonsters, Like the OſtrichesOstriches in the wilderneſſewilderness: for the cruellcruel OſtrichOstrich, and the hatefullhateful CuccoCuckoo are the two kindekind of creatures which are noted to leaueleave their young ones for others to nouriſhnourish; the OſtrichOstrich leauethleaveth her eggs in the duſtdust: the CuccoCuckoo leauethleaveth hers in other birds neſtsnests. Other creatures (if nature afford them not milkemilk and duggesdugs, as to birds it doth not) feed their young ones other waiesways, yet by themſeluesthemselves.

5. Shall I addeadd another argument which daily experience confirmeth, namely Gods bleſſingblessing vponupon this motherly dutieduty: Matres maiore ſtudiostudio & cura nutrient, nempe ex ipſisipsis viſceribusvisceribus diligunt liberos ſuossuos. Cum nutrices vtpote quae mercedem ament, charitatem praebeant ſubditiciamsubditiciam. Plut. de InſtitInstit. lib. commonly ſuchsuch children as are nurſednursed by their mothers, proſperprosper beſtbest. Mothers are moſtmost tender ouerover them, and cannot indure to let them lie crying out, without taking them vpup., andandAnd ſtillingstilling them;: as nurſesnurses will let them criecry and criecry againeagain, if they be about any buſineſſebusiness of their owneown. For who are commonly choſenchosen to be nurſesnurses? euenEven poorepoor countriecountry women which hauehave much workework to doedo, and little helpehelp; and ſoso are forced to let the childechild lie and criecry, many times till it burſtburst againeagain. Children nurſednursed by their mothers are for the moſtmost part more cleanly, and neatly brought vpup, freer from diſeaſesdiseases;
not ſoso many die; I am ſuresure not ſoso many through negligence caſtcast away. The number of nurſenurse children that die eueryevery yeereyear is very great. It hath beenebeen obſeruedobserved in many countriecountry villages, that the moſtmost part, that from time to time die there, are nurſenurse children. Are not mothers that might hauehave nurſednursed their owneown children if they would, acceſſaryaccessary to the death of thoſethose that are caſtcast away by the nurſesnurses negligence?

On theſethese and other like reaſonsreasons heathen women, and very AriſtArist. Oecon. l. 2. c. 3. Plutarch. loc. citat. A. Gellius Noct. Attic. comment. li. 12. cap. 1. ſauagessavages, hauehave in all ages beenebeen mouedmoved to nurſenurse their owneown children: and ſomesome heathen PhiloſophersPhilosophers hauehave vrgedurged and preſſedpressed the neceſſitienecessity of this dutieduty. NeuerNever was it more neglected, then among thoſethose that bearebear the name of ChriſtiansChristians.

Let mothers know of what rankerank or degree ſoso euerever they be, that (out of the caſecase of neceſſitienecessity) they hauehave no warrant to put forth their children to others to nurſenurse. We read not in all the Scripture of any holy women that euerever did it.

div.head: §. 13. Of the obiectionsobjections for putting children forth to nurſenurse.

ObiectObject. Many nurſesnurses are mentioned in Scripture, as Rebekahs
Gen. 24. 59. 2 Sam. 4. 4. 2 King. 11. 2. nurſenurse, MephiboſhethsMephibosheths nurſenurse, IoaſhJoash his nurſenurse, and others.
div.p:
1. AnſwAnsw. Such nurſesnurses mentioned in Scripture were commonly driedry nurſesnurses. Rebekahs nurſenurse went with her before ſheshe was mariedmarried: how can it be thought that ſheshe was a milch nurſenurse? Could they tell when Rebekah ſhouldshould hauehave a childechild? orOr when Gen. 35. 8. heshe had one, that Deborah (the nurſenurse there mentioned) ſhouldshould hauehave milkemilk for her? It is ſaidsaid that Naomi became nurſenurse to Ruths
Ruth 4. 16. & 1. 12.
c • hildechild: now Naomi was old, long before this ſheshe was paſtpast c • hild-bearing, without an husband for many yeeresyears: how then was it poſſiblepossible that ſheshe ſhouldshould giuegive ſuckesuck? She was therefore a d • riedry nurſenurse, as other nurſesnurses mentioned in Scripture.

2. AnſwAnsw. The mothers of thoſethose children which are ſaidsaid to h • auehave nurſesnurses (if thoſethose nurſesnurses were milch-nurſesnurses) might be d • ead: or if liuingliving, not able to giuegive ſuckesuck for want of milkemilk, n • ipple, or for ſomesome other like defect: or if able, ſinnesin in putting forth their children.
3. AnſwAnsw. Though it be ſaidsaid that there were nurſesnurses, yet is no where ſaidsaid, that a mother put forth her childechild to ſuckesuck.

div.head: 2. ObiectObject. PharohsPharaohs daughter put forth the childechild which ſheshe Exod. 2. 7. to •• oketook for her owneown to nurſenurse.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. She bare not this childechild, nor was the naturallnatural mother of it, ſoso as this is nothing to the purpoſepurpose. Yea it maketh againſtagainst the obiectorsobjectors, in that the true mother of this childechild nurſednursed it.

div.head: 3. ObiectObject. The metaphor taken from nurſesnurses is oft vſedused, Num. 11. 12. 1 TheſThes. 2. 7. and applied to God, and to Gods miniſtersministers.
div.p: 1. AnſwAnsw. The vſingusing of a thing by way of compariſoncomparison and reſemblanceresemblance doth not ſimplysimply iuſtifiejustify it: inſtanceinstance the parable of the vniuſtunjust ſtewardsteward, and of a theefethief. Luke 16. 1. &etcc. Reu.. 16. 15. 16.

2. AnſwAnsw. The metaphor may be taken from a driedry nurſenurse as well as a milch nurſenurse: for the compariſonscomparisons are not vſedused of giuinggiving ſuckesuck, but of bearing and carrying in armesarms, as driedry nurſesnurses vſeuse to carry children.
3. AnſwAnsw. The metaphors are moſtmost fitly taken from mothers that are nurſesnurses to their owneown children.

div.head: 4. ObiectObject. Many mothers hauehave not ſuchsuch skill in giuinggiving ſuckesuck as nurſesnurses hauehave.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. Let them learnelearn ſeeingseeing it is their dutieduty.

div.head: 5. ObiectObject. Mothers that are of great wealth and high place cannot endure the painepain of nurſingnursing, nor take the painespains in handling young children as they muſtmust be handled.
div.p: 1. AnſwAnsw. The greateſtgreatest that be muſtmust ſetset themſeluesthemselves to doedo that duty which God requireth at their hands, though it be with painepain and painespains. Note Sarahs example before recorded.

2. AnſwAnsw. By this it appeareth, that if other women could bearebear their children in the wombewomb nine monethsmonths, and endure the painepain of trauelltravel for them, they would hire them to doedo it. But ſeeingseeing they doedo the one (namely bearebear and bring forth their owneown children with hard labour) why ſhouldshould they not doedo the other? If they ſaysay there is an vnauoidableunavoidable neceſſitynecessity of bearing and bringing forth their children; I anſweranswer, that conſcienceconscience ought to mouemove them to nurſenurse thoſethose children, which neceſſitynecessity forceth them to bring forth. God by this latter of • nurſingnursing children maketh trialltrial of women whether they will for conſcienceconscience ſakesake, doedo that duty which they may if they will put off. But becauſebecause God knew that many will doedo no more then neceſſitynecessity laieth vponupon them, he hath made it a matter of •
impoſſibilityimpossibility for women to bearebear and bring forth their children by another.
3. AnſwAnsw. If women would with cheerefulneſſecheerfulness ſetset themſeluesthemselves to performeperform this duty, much of the ſuppoſedsupposed painepain and painespains would be leſſenedlessened.
4. AnſwAnsw. Though they put not forth their children to nurſenurse, they may for their eaſeease entertaineentertain a nurſenurse, ſoso they giuegive ſuckesuck themſeluesthemselves.

div.head: 6. ObiectObject. A mother that hath a trade, or that hath the care of an houſehouse, will neglect much buſineſſebusiness by nurſingnursing her childechild: and her husband will ſauesave more by giuinggiving halfehalf a crownecrown a weekeweek to a nurſenurse, then if his wife gauegave the childechild ſuckesuck.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. No outward buſineſſebusiness appertaining to a mother can be more acceptable to God then the nurſingnursing of her childechild: this is the moſtmost proper workework of her ſpeciallspecial calling, therefore all other buſineſſesbusinesses muſtmust giuegive place to this, and this muſtmust not be left for any other buſineſſebusiness.
As for the husbands ſauingsaving by putting the childechild forth to nurſenurse, no gainegain may giuegive a diſpenſationdispensation againſtagainst a bounden duty.

div.head: 7. ObiectObject. It will breakebreak tender fairefair women, and make them lookelook old too ſoonesoon.
div.p: 1. AnſwAnsw. Gods ordinance muſtmust not giuegive place to womens n •• iceneſſeniceness. Sarah was fairefair and old: The Virgin Mary was fairefair and young.

2. AnſwAnsw. Drying vpup a womans milkemilk will more breakebreak her, then her childes ſuckingsucking of it: for it is a meanesmeans both of better health, and alſoalso of greater ſtrengthstrength, as to bearebear children, ſoso to giuegive them ſuckesuck. Barren women and bearing women which put forth their children to ſuckesuck, are moſtmost ſubiectsubject to ſickneſſesickness and weakneſſeweakness. The drawing forth of a womans milkemilk by her childechild is a meanesmeans to get and preſeruepreserve a good ſtomachstomach, which is a great preſeruatiuepreservative of good health.

div.head: 8. ObiectObject. Husbands are diſturbeddisturbed in the night time, and hindredhindered of their ſleepesleep by their wiueswives giuinggiving ſuckesuck to their children.
div.p:
1. AnſwAnsw. By this reaſonreason neither mothers nor other nurſesnurses
which hauehave husbands, ſhouldshould giuegive ſuckesuck to children.

2. AnſwAnsw. Seeing children come from the loinesloins of the father, as well as out of the wombewomb of the mother, they muſtmust be content to endure ſomesome diſturbancedisturbance as well as their wiueswives, and ſoso much the rather that they may the more pittypity their wiueswives, and afford vntounto them what helpehelp they can.

div.head: 9. ObiectObject. Many husbands will not ſuffersuffer their wiueswives to nurſenurse their children themſeluesthemselves.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. BecauſeBecause it is a bounden duty, wiueswives muſtmust vſeuse all the meanesmeans they can by themſeluesthemselves or others to perſwadepersuade their husbands to let them performeperform it: they muſtmust take heedeheed that they make not this a pretext to couercover their owneown ſlothsloth, and lothneſſelothness to this duty: they may not make themſeluesthemselves acceſſarieaccessary to their husbands fault by prouidingproviding a nurſenurse, and ſendingsending the childechild away themſeluesthemselves: if their husbands will ſtandstand vponupon their authority, and be perſwadedpersuaded by no meanesmeans to the contrary, they muſtmust be meeremere patients in ſufferingsuffering the childechild to be taken away.

div.head: 10. ObiectObject. Many poorepoor women maintainemaintain their houſehouse by nurſingnursing other folkesfolks children.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. If they were not that way imployedemployed, they might take painespains in ſomesome other thing. But the gainegain of one may not make another neglect her duty.

11. ObiectObject. Some mothers cannot giuegive ſuckesuck, they hauehave no milkemilk: others cannot very well, in that they hauehave no nipples, or they hauehave ſoresore breaſtsbreasts, or are ſicklysickly, or it may be that they hauehave ſuchsuch a diſeaſedisease, as the childechild, if it ſhouldshould ſuckesuck of their milkemilk, would draw to it ſelfeself, and ſoso the ſuckingsucking might proueprove very dangerous to the childechild.
1. AnſwAnsw. God requireth no impoſſibilitiesimpossibilities: wherefore in propounding the duty I put in this caution (ſoso far as they are able.)

2. God requireth merciemercy, and not ſacrificesacrifice: if therefore in HoſHos. 6. 6. Matt. 9. 13. truth it be ſoso that the mothers giuinggiving ſuckesuck to the childechild will be dangerous to her ſelfeself or to the childechild, ſheshe may and ought to forbeareforbear: for giuinggiving ſuckesuck is but as ſacrificesacrifice to preuentingpreventing of danger, which is merciemercy. But women muſtmust take heed that they pretend not inability, and danger without iuſtjust cauſecause. Some are themſeluesthemselves the cauſecause of wanting milkemilk becauſebecause they
will not let it be drawnedrawn downedown; or becauſebecause they will not vſeuse meanesmeans (for meanesmeans there are) to get and increaſeincrease milkemilk. There are meanesmeans alſoalso to raiſeraise nipples where the breaſtsbreasts are very flat. RefuſingRefusing to giuegive ſuckesuck many times cauſethcauseth ſomesome ſickiſhneſſesickishness in a woman, and ſoresore breaſtsbreasts, which might be preuentedprevented with the childes ſuckingsucking. If the foreneſſesorenessforeness be only in the nipples, a mother with enduring a little more painepain may ſafelysafely giuegive the childechild ſuckesuck. Many mothers hauehave giuengiven their children ſuckesuck when bloudblood hath runnerun by the mouth of the childechild by reaſonreason of ſoresore nipples, and yet both mother and childechild done very well.

div.head: 12. ObiectObject. DiuersDivers children being nurſednursed by the mother hauehave died one after another.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. Due and thorowthorough ſearchsearch muſtmust be made by thoſethose that are skilfullskilful: and if any cauſecause be found in the mother, then the rule holdeth, Mercy and not ſacrificesacrifice: but if none can be found, the iſſueissue muſtmust be referred to Gods prouidenceprovidence: and the vncertaineuncertain eueneventeven muſtmust not be an hinderancehindrance to a knowneknown dutieduty.
Thus the anſweringanswering of the forenamed obiectionsobjections maketh the point ſoso much the more cleereclear.

div.head: §. 14. Of the fathers dutieduty in incouragingencouraging his wife to nurſenurse her childechild.
div.p:
The dutieduty which on a fathers part in this reſpectrespect is required, is that he incourageencourage his wife, and helpehelp her with all needfullneedful things for the performance of this dutieduty. It is noted of Elkan • ah, that he ſufferedsuffered his wife to tarry at home while ſheshe gauegave ſuckesuck to her ſonneson, and would not force her to goego vpup to the tabernacle as his other wife did, but gauegave her all the eaſeease and content he could, ſayingsaying to her, DoeDo what ſeemethseemeth thee good. 1 Sam. 1. 23. And of Abraham it is noted, that after Sarah had done giuinggiving the childechild ſuckesuck, he made a great feaſtfeast, eueneven the day that
Gen. 21. 8. IſaakIsaac was weinedweaned: one end whereof was to teſtifietestify his reioycingrejoicing for Gods bleſſingblessing on her motherly dutieduty ſoso well performed.

div.head: §. 15. Of the faults contrariecontrary to a mothers nurſingnursing her childechild.
div.p:
Contrary to this dutieduty doedo all ſuchsuch mothers offend, as for
any by-reſpectsrespects when no neceſſitynecessity requireth put forth their children to be nurſednursed by others.
1. Some doedo it for eaſeease and quiet, becauſebecause they cannot endure to hauehave their ſleepesleep broken, or to hearehear their childechild wrangle and criecry.
2. Others doedo it for niceneſſeniceness, becauſebecause they are loth to open their breaſtsbreasts, or to ſoilesoil their cloathesclothes.
3. Others vponupon pride, conceiting that their beauty would be impaired, and they lookelook old too ſoonesoon.
4. Others vponupon gainegain, becauſebecause they can hauehave a childechild cheaper nurſednursed abroad then at home, where, at leaſtleast, they muſtmust hire a maid the more.
5. Others vponupon pleaſurepleasure, that they might more freely ride abroad, and meet their GoſſipsGossips.
6. Others vponupon other by-reſpectsrespects: all which doedo argue much ſelfeself-louelove: little louelove to their childechild, and little reſpectrespect to God. They can be counted but halfehalf-mothers: for nurſingnursing a childechild is as much as bearing and bringing it forth.

div.head: §. 16. Of a fathers fault in hindringhindering his wiueswives nurſingnursing of her child.
div.p: To the forenamed fault of mothers doedo all ſuchsuch fathers make themſeluesthemselves acceſſaryaccessary, as forbid their wiueswives to nurſenurse their children, or are a griefegrief to them by their complaints of trouble, diſquietdisquiet and expenceexpense: or afford not things needfullneedful, or doedo not incourageencourage them all they can to doedo it. The mothers both painepain and painespains is the greateſtgreatest: it is in compariſoncomparison but a ſmallsmall thing that fathers can endure therein. Their fault therefore muſtmust needs be the greater, if any way they be an occaſionoccasion of their childes putting forth to nurſenurse: which I hauehave the rather noted, becauſebecause husbands for the moſtmost part are the cauſecause that their wiueswives nurſenurse not their owneown children: and that partly by ſufferingsuffering, and partly by egging them on to put out their children. If husbands were willing that their wiueswives ſhouldshould performeperform this dutieduty, and would perſwadepersuade and incourageencourage them thereto, and afford them what helpeshelps they could, where one mother now nurſethnurseth her childechild, twenty would doedo it.

div.head: §. 17. Of parents ioyntjoint care about their childrens BaptiſmeBaptism.
div.p:
There is a further dutieduty to be performed of parents to their
children eueneven in their infancy, and that is in regard of their ſpirituallspiritual good, which is this,

p.hi: Parents ought to procure that their children be rightly baptized in due ſeaſonseason.

Some parents ſoso farrefar failefail in the defect, as they almoſtalmost ſtaruestarve their children through want of neceſſariesnecessaries: not affording them ſufficientsufficient wholeſomewholesome food, nor meet and comely appar • ellapparel, but ſuffersuffer them to goego tagged and ragged like beggars b • rats: if they be ſickesick, God may recouerrecover them if he pleaſeplease, but the parents will vſeuse no meanesmeans:means when they are well, they afford them no time of refreſhingrefreshing themſeluesthemselves by any recreation, but o • uerover-ſtrictlystrictly hold them in. There is not only want of charity, b • ut plaineplain vnnaturalneſſeunnaturalness in ſuchsuch parents: eueneven more then in th •• e moſtmost cruellcruel beaſtsbeasts. For the wildewild beaſtsbeasts doedo with much tend • erneſſetenderness prouideprovide for their young ones.

div.head: §. 25. Of parents too much lauiſhneſſelavishness and indulgency vponupon their children.
div.p:
Others ſurpaſſesurpass as much in the exceſſeexcess, feeding them too da •• intily: attiring them too gariſhlygarishly: tending them too
cockeringly: and letting them ſpendspend too much time in ſportsport and play. Many and great are the miſchiefesmischiefs that follow thereupon: as

1. They who are in their childhood daintily fed, and too much pampered, beſidesbesides that for the moſtmost part they are moſtmost ſicklysickly, they will in time grow ſoso ſqueamiſhsqueamish, and choice of meats, as their parents ſhallshall not know what to prouideprovide for them, or when to giuegive it them: The full ſoulesoul loatheth an honyhoneycomb
Pro. 27. 7. combe: yea if a ſtrangerstranger commethcometh to the table, where ſuchsuch a childechild ſittethsitteth, he may ſoonesoon obſerueobserve that he hath beenebeen too daintily fed. If at firſtfirst children be fed with ordinary moderate diet, they will afterwards both be in better health and liking, and alſoalso more contentedly, and thankfully accept whatſoeuerwhatsoever ſhallshall be prouidedprovided for them. But exceſſeexcess breedeth diſeaſesdiseases both in body and mindemind.

2. Vanity in apparellapparel doth alſoalso much corrupt young children: for there is in them eueneven from the cradle a naturallnatural diſpoſitiondisposition to outward brauerybravery: now for parents to prankeprank them vpup, what is it but to blow vpup the fire of that vanity, and make it ariſearise into ſuchsuch a flame as in time may much ſcorchscorch the parents themſeluesthemselves, and vtterlyutterly conſumeconsume the children: and yet how vſuallusual a fault is this? howHow monſtrouſlymonstrously doedo many parents offend therein? whatWhat fooliſhfoolish faſhionfashion is vſedused of the greateſtgreatest ſwaggerersswaggerers, and lighteſtlightest ſtrumpetsstrumpets, which they will not bring their children vntounto, and that when their children are not able to diſcernediscern betwixt ſtuffesstuffs or colours? whatWhat can this proclaimeproclaim but parents pride and folly? Proud maids are many times the inſtrumentsinstruments of pranking vpup children (eſpeciallyespecially when they are little ones) more then is meet: but yet the blame lieth on parents for ſufferingsuffering it.

3. Tending children too cockiſhlycockishly maketh them too long children, and too tender: and oft altereth a good conſtitutionconstitution of body. Some are ſoso ouerover-much tender of their children, as if a childechild neuernever ſoso little complainecomplain, or refuſerefuse the meatemeat (though for daintineſſedaintiness or fulneſſefulness) the PhyſicianPhysician muſtmust preſentlypresently be ſentsent for, and the Apothecary ſentsent vntounto, and the childechild with ſuppoſedsupposed and apiſhapish kindneſſekindness made much worſeworse.

4. Too much ſportsport maketh them wildewild, rude, vnfitunfit to be
trained vpup to any good calling, and ſpendethspendeth their ſpiritsspirits, and waſtethwasteth their ſtrengthstrength too much. Yet many parents care not how much time their children ſpendspend in ſportsport, and how little in learning: they thinkethink it dulsdulls their children too much to be held to ſchooleschool, or to any learning: whereas indeed too much play infatuates them more, and learning would much ſharpensharpen their wits.

div.head: §. 26. Of well nurturing children.
div.p:
I referrerefer good nurture in part to the temporalltemporal good of children, becauſebecause (as afterwards we ſhallshall hearehear in the particulars) it is an eſpeciallespecial meanesmeans of the outward temporalltemporal welfare of the childechild eueneven in this world. VnleſſeUnless this be added to nouriſhingnourishing, wherein doedo reaſonablereasonable men and women exceed vnreaſonableunreasonable beaſtsbeasts? theThe moſtmost cruellcruel beaſtsbeasts that be are very tender (as we heard before) towards their young ones, nouriſhingnourishing them, and prouidingproviding all things needfullneedful for them till they can ſhiftshift for themſeluesthemselves. But as God hath giuengiven to man a reaſonablereasonable ſoulesoul, an vnderſtandingunderstanding head, capacity, docility and aptneſſeaptness to learnelearn, ſoso ought parents to make vſeuse of thoſethose parts and gifts, leſtlest for want of vſingusing them, in time they be loſtlost: and ſoso children proueprove little better then bruits. In this reſpectrespect the prouerbeproverb is true, better be vnfedunfed then vntaughtuntaught. Experience ſhewethshoweth that good education is better then a great portion. The Holy GhoſtGhost doth very much preſſepress this point on parents, as we ſhallshall after hearehear in the particulars. For I will handle theſethese three points.
1. The kindeskinds of nurture.
2. The time when it is to be done.
3. The meanesmeans of well doing it.

div.head: §. 27. Of parents neglect in nurturing children.
div.p:
Contrary to good nurture is too much liberty: which oft bringeth much woe, and vtterutter ruineruin vponupon children: it is the greateſtgreatest enemy that can be of good education, and the nurſenurse of all vice Yet many parents care not to let their children liuelive as they liſtlist: all the care they take, is that they be fed and apparelled. This is a common fault both of rich, and of poorepoor parents. The rich pretend that their children need no education, becauſebecause they hauehave enough to leaueleave them: not knowing
that education is an eſpeciallespecial meanesmeans to make them keepekeep and well vſeuse that enough. The poorepoor pretend that they are not able to bring vpup their children to any thing: not conſideringconsidering that the Lord by his prouidenceprovidence hath ſoso ordered the affairesaffairs of men, that as there are fit imployments for the greateſtgreatest, ſoso alſoalso Si parentum incuria filij in intemperantiam labentur, genitores rei animarum illarum fient. ConſtitConstit. ApoſtApost. l. 4. c. 11. I. The kinds of nurture. for the meaneſtmeanest, which without much coſtcost may be vſedused. The fault therefore wholly reſtethresteth in the negligence of parents. And if thereupon children fall into any riot, their parents ſhallshall anſweranswer for it.

div.head: §. 28. Of parents teaching their children good manners.
div.p:
The nurturing of children before mentioned conſiſtethconsisteth
1. In teaching them good manners.
2. In training them vpup to a good calling.

Not only heathen men, and other moraliſtsmoralists which were but meeremere naturallnatural ciuillcivil men, but alſoalso the Holy GhoſtGhost himſelfehimself hath preſcribedprescribed many rules of good manners, and much vrgedurged and preſſedpressed the ſamesame.

1. The word
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . See Treat. 1. §. 110. nurture mentioned by the ApoſtleApostle in this text which we hauehave in hand, implieth as much: and the phraſephrase which Solomon vſethuseth, Pro. 22. 6. TraineTrain vpup a childechild in the way he ſhouldshould goego: that is, teach him how to order the courſecourse of his life.

2. The many Leu. 19. 32. Pro. 25. 6. Luke 14. 8. precepts of reuerencingreverencing our ſuperiourssuperiors, and caryingcarrying our ſeluesselves with reſpectrespect one to another, are rules of good manners. Hereof there be very many in ſcripturescripture.
3. ThoſeThose rules are Gen. 23. 7. & 43. 33. IobJob 32. 4, 6. commended by many examples of holy men recorded in Scripture.
4. Such as hauehave IobJob 30. 1, 12. Luke 14. 7. failed in the rules of good manners, and rudely carried themſeluesthemselves, are reprouedreproved by the Holy GhoſtGhost.
Neither is it without good reaſonreason that this point is ſoso ſetset forth. For

1. Good manners are a very comely and ſeemelyseemly thing. But 1. Cor. 14. 40. it beſeemethbeseemeth ChriſtiansChristians to doedo all things decently. That decency is not only to be applied to the affairesaffairs of Gods Church, but alſoalso to the whole courſecourse of our life, in which reſpectrespect we are commanded to walkewalk
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . Rom 13. 13. 1 TheſThes. 4. 12. decently, that is, to order all our actions and the whole courſecourse of our life mannerly.

2. They are a thing of good report, and that both to parents and children: Now we muſtmust doedo all things that are of good report.
Phil. 4. 8.

3. They workework a kindekind of delight, and louelove, and admiration, in thoſethose that behold them, as is noted of the QueeneQueen of 1 King. 10. 5. Sheba when ſheshe beheld the comely cariagecarriage of Solomons ſeruantsservants: and of the Egyptians when they beheld the orderly Gen. 43. 33. ſittingsitting of IoſephsJosephs brethren.

4. They are an outward ornament to piety and religion, and make it to be much more reſpectedrespected: in which reſpectrespect S. Peter exhorteth beleeuingbelieving wiueswives well to order their conuerſationconversation 1 Pet. 3. 1. before infidellinfidel husbands: and S. Paul exhorteth all ſortssorts of chriſtianschristians to walkewalk decently toward them that are without. 1 TheſThes. 4. 12.
The Holy GhoſtGhost hauinghaving thus vrgedurged the point of good manners, we may not thinkethink it a meeremere complementallcomplemental matter, and a needleſſeneedless point, but a bounden duty.

div.head: §. 29. Of the obiectionsobjections againſtagainst good manners.

div.p: 1. ObiectObject. Religion and grace conſiſtethconsisteth not in good manners: many that hauehave not a ſparkespark of Gods fearefear in their hearts, are able to carry themſeluesthemselves in their outward behauiourbehaviour very orderly and mannerly.

AnſwAnsw. Though grace conſiſtconsist not wholly in it, yet cannot grace well be without it: it is a great ornament and comelineſſecomeliness thereunto. And though mannerlineſſemannerliness may be ſeueredsevered from a fearefear of God, yet Gods fearefear will not be ſeueredsevered from it. ReſtrainingRestraining grace may be in him who hath no renewing grace: but renewing grace preſuppoſethpresupposeth reſtrainingrestraining grace, eueneven as reaſonreason preſuppoſethpresupposeth ſenſesense, though ſenſesense may be without reaſonreason. If ſuchsuch as fearefear not God can carry themſeluesthemselves comely and mannerly, what a ſhameshame is it for ſuchsuch as ſeemeseem to fearefear God, not to doedo ſoso? ſhallShall not thoſethose be a witneſſewitness againſtagainst theſethese?
2. ObiectObject. Good manners are an hinderancehindrance to grace: they who are moſtmost diligent in teaching or practiſingpractising the one, are commonly moſtmost negligent in the other.
AnſwAnsw. This is a meeremere cauillcavil. Sure I am that grace is no hinderancehindrance to good manners. If any make good manners an hinderancehindrance to grace, it is their fault.
3. ObiectObject. Good manners to grace are as mint, anniſeannise and cummin, to the great and weighty things of the law.

AnſwAnsw. Grant it to be ſoso: yet ſeeingseeing both may ſtandstand together, why ſhouldshould they be ſeueredsevered? ChriſtsChrists rule is this, TheſeThese
things ought ye to hauehave done, and not to leaueleave the other vndoneundone.
Matt. 23. 23.
4. ObiectObject. Many that make great ſhewshow of religion are very rude, and vnmannerlyunmannerly.

AnſwAnsw. If there be onelyonly a ſhewshow of religion in them, no maruellmarvelmarvell that they hauehave no manners. If ſomesome examples of ſuchsuch as are truly religious and want good manners ſhouldshould be ſhewedshowed, their patternepattern is no preſidentpresident, much leſſeless can it proueprove that to be no duty which Gods word hath ſetset downedown for a duty. Many that well performeperform ſomesome duties, much failefail in other duties. Who almoſtalmost followeth Gods word as he ſhouldshould in eueryevery thing?

div.head: §. 30. Of parents ſufferingsuffering their children to be rudely brought vpup.
div.p: Contrary to parents care in teaching their children good manners, is diſſoluteneſſedissoluteness: when parents ſuffersuffer their children to grow vpup in rudeneſſerudeness, not caring how they carry themſeluesthemselves at home or abroad, toward their parents, or toward others. Rude bringing vpup maketh children to be of a crooked, peruerſeperverse, ſtubbornestubborn, churliſhchurlish, furly, doggiſhdoggish diſpoſitiondisposition; as on the other ſideside, good nurture in this kindekind breedeth in genuity, amiableneſſeamiableness, curteſiecourtesy, and kindneſſekindness. If ſuchsuch as are rudely brought vpup be children of profeſſorsprofessors of the true religion, they bring a ſtainestain vponupon their profeſſionprofession: yea they diſhonourdishonour God, as if he were the author of vnmannerlineſſeunmannerliness and confuſionconfusion, againſtagainst which the Holy GhoſtGhost proteſtethprotesteth: and they make 1 Cor. 14. 33. themſeluesthemselves and their children a ſcornescorn in the eieeye and mouth of profane perſonspersons, who will be ready to point and ſaysay, Behold the children of profeſſorsprofessors, how rudely they are brought vpup, and ill taught: they hauehave not ſoso much as good manners in them.

For auoidingavoiding this blemiſhblemish, SchooleSchool-maſtersmasters and all ſuchsuch as Admonition to SchoolemaſtersSchoolmasters. hauehave the charge of trayning vpup young children, muſtmust bean helpehelp to parents in teaching children good manners.

div.head: §. 31. Of parents training vpup their children to ſomesome good calling.
div.p:
The ſecondsecond branch of good nurture is a training vpup of children vntounto a good calling. This charge (trainetrain vpup a child in
Pro 22. 6. the way that he ſhouldshould go • ) directly condeth to this purpoſepurpose. This duty hath from the beginning of the world beenebeen performed
by parents, and their performance thereof commended by the holy GhoſtGhost. Adam brought vpup his ſonnessons to ſeuerallseveral callings: one was a Gen. 4. 2. keeper of ſheepesheep, another a tiller of ground. The like is noted of Gen. 37. 12. IaakobsJacob's ſonnessons, Gen. 29. 9. Labans, and Exo. 2. 16. Reguels daughters, 1 Sam. 16. 7. IſhasIshas ſonneson, and many others.
Much good may from hence ariſearise to parents themſeluesthemselves, to their children, and to the people and places where ſuchsuch children Benefits of a good calling. ſhallshall liuelive.

1. A good calling is an eſpeciallespecial meanesmeans for children to maintainemaintain themſeluesthemselves and family, to releeuerelieve thoſethose that ſtandstand in need, to eaſeease their parents, and (if the need of parents require it) to releeuerelieve and maintainemaintain them.
2. It is that way wherein Gods Angels hauehave a charge to PſalPsal. 91. 11. keepekeep them while they walkewalk in it.
3. It is a meanesmeans wherein and whereby they may be ſeruiceableserviceable to the common wealth where they liuelive.
4. It is the beſtbest place wherein the generallgeneral duties of ChriſtianityChristianity may be moſtmost manifeſtedmanifested, and beſtbest performed.

5. It is the beſtbest ordinary meanesmeans that can be preſcribedprescribed to keepekeep a childechild from the vanities of youth, from immoderate purſuitpursuit of pleaſurespleasures, from vnlawfullunlawful games, from idleneſſeidleness, from ill company, and ſuchsuch like euilsevils; which, as they are ſinnessins in themſeluesthemselves, ſoso occaſionsoccasions and prouocationsprovocations to other moſtmost • grieuousgrievous and enormous ſinnessins, and proueprove to be the very • bane of youth.

div.head: ObiectObject. Many parents hauehave good lands to leaueleave to their children: what need is there of a calling to ſuchsuch?
div.p: AnſwAnsw. 1. Much land may ſoonesoon be conſumedconsumed by ſuchsuch as hauehave not skill well to vſeuse it.
2. Maintenance is but one end of a calling, and that not the chiefeſtchiefest and moſtmost principallprincipal.
3. More good may be done by skill in a calling, then by great ſtorestore of land.
4. We are borne for others as well as for our ſeluesselves: it is not therefore ſufficientsufficient to ſaysay I hauehave enough to maintainemaintain my ſelfeself.

div.head: §. 32. Of parents care in chooſingchoosing a fit calling for their children.
div.p: The point in generallgeneral being declared to be a dutieduty, I will Directions for choiſechoice of callings. 1. GenerallGeneral principles are to be taught. addeadd ſomesome directions for the better performing of it.

1. Children are to be trained vpup in thoſethose things which are the ground workework of all callings, as reading, writing, and principles of learning. WhatſoeuerWhatsoever the particular calling be, theſethese will be of great vſeuse to any one. Many that hauehave not beenebeen taught them at firſtfirst, would giuegive much for them afterwards. Parents at the firſtfirst might teach their children thoſethose things with much eaſeease and ſmallsmall charge, which afterwards cannot be Non ſuntsunt contemnenda quaſiquasi parua, ſinesine quibus magna conſtareconstare non poſſuntpossunt. Hier. ad Laet. 2. The calling muſtmust be lawfulllawful. ſoso well learned, partly for want of leaſureleisureleasure, and partly becauſebecause the parts of thoſethose who are grownegrown in yearesyears are not ſoso freſhfresh and fit to learnelearn, as in child-hood they were. ThoſeThose things are not to be contemned as ſmallsmall, without which great things cannot ſtandstand.

2. The calling whereunto children are trained vpup muſtmust be lawfulllawful, approuedapproved by Gods word, and not againſtagainst the generallgeneral rules thereof: ſoso may they keepekeep a good conſcienceconscience in the exerciſeexercise thereof.

3. The calling muſtmust be fit for the childechild that is trained vpup 3. The calling muſtmust be fit for the childes ability. to it. As there are diuersdivers callings, ſoso there are diuersdivers abilities of ſundrysundry children: ſomesome are fitteſtfittest for callings of wit and learning: others for callings that require an able and ſtrongstrong body. Wherein the wiſewise diſpoſingdisposing prouidenceprovidence of God is much commended: for thus are men much more vſefulluseful one to another. Now for choiſechoice of a fit calling, a childs beſtbest ability wherein eſpeciallyespecially it conſiſtethconsisteth, whether in the exerciſeexercise of mindemind or of body, is duly to be obſeruedobserved: and alſoalso his inclination, to what calling he is moſtmost diſpoſeddisposed.

4. Among fit callings (for there may be many) that which 4. The beſtbest callings muſtmust be preferred. 1 Cor. 12. 31. is beſtbest and the moſtmost excellent is to be preferred. To this purpoſepurpose not vnfitlyunfitly may I apply that of the ApoſtleApostle, ccuet earneſtlyearnestly the beſtbest gifts.

On this ground let parents be exhorted to trainetrain vpup ſuchsuch Children to be trained vpup to the miniſteryministery. children as they findefind fit, to the great and weighty calling of the miniſteryministery: no calling wherein any may doedo more good, and wherein (if they be able and faithfullfaithful MiniſtersMinisters) they can
receiuereceive more comfort and contentment. This exhortation is the more to be regarded, becauſebecause in compariſoncomparison of thoſethose who are trained vpup to other callings, ſoso few are trained vpup to this.

div.head: § 33. Of parents faults contrary to their dutieduty of training their children vpup to a calling.
div.p: On the contrary, many parents much offend in not training vpup their children to a calling as they ſhouldshould. And the offence in this kindekind is committed many waiesways. As

1. When parents ſuffersuffer their children to liuelive like little maſtersmasters at home, and paſſepass ouerover all their youth in idleneſſeidleness. Thus they proueprove very drones, and caterpillars in the common wealth: if they hauehave a patrimony, they ſoonesoon waſtewaste it: if they hauehave none, they oft proueprove either theeuesthieves or beggars: they are fit for all companies: the readieſtreadiest prey for the deuilldevil that can be: for they are like the houſehouse empty, ſweptswept and garniſhedgarnished, which Mat. 12. 44. when the euillevil ſpiritspirit eſpiethespieth, he preſentlypresently entereth into it with ſeuenseven other ſpiritsspirits worſeworse then himſelfehimself.

The wiſewise law-maker among the heathen is ſaidsaid to order Solon legibus cauiſſecauisse legitur, vt filius, quem parentes nullam artem docuiſſentdocuissent, non cogeretur illos alere ſeniosenio confectos, aut ad inopiam redactos. EraſEras. InſtitInstit. Matrim. that the childechild which by his parents had beenebeen taught no Art, ſhouldshould not be forced to nouriſhnourish them though they were old or poorepoor. This I all eage not to iuſtifiejustify the law (for it is againſtagainst the ChriſtianChristian rule of ouercommingovercomming euillevil with goodneſſegoodness) but to ſhewshow how the very heathen iudgedjudged the neglect of this dutieduty a great fault in parents.

2. When parents neglect to teach their children in their child-hood the generallgeneral and common grounds of all callings: ſomesome vponupon niggardlineſſeniggardliness; others vponupon careleſneſſecarelessness. Thus poorepoor men make their children vnfitunfit for many meanesmeans, whereby they might well maintainemaintain themſeluesthemselves: and rich men make theirs vnfitunfit for magiſtracymagistracy, and for good ſocietysociety. Yea poorepoor and rich are thus nouſlednousled vpup the more in ignorance, and made the more vnfitunfit to profit by the preaching of the word, and other meanesmeans of ſpirituallspiritual edification.

3. When parents bring vpup their children in vnwarrantableunwarrantable and vnlawfullunlawful callings, as to be of popiſhpopish and idolatrous orders; to attend vponupon papiſtspapists; to be ſtagestage-plaiers, keepers of dice-houſeshouses, &etcc. Some (which is horrible to thinkethink of) trainetrain
vpup their daughters to be common ſtrumpetsstrumpets: and ſomesome Phoenices Veneri donum dabant de proſtitationeprostitatione filiarum, antequam iungerent eas viris. Aug de Ciu. D. l. 4 c. 10. vide Lud. Uiu. in hunc loc. Recte dicuntur parentes filios daemoniorum ſacrilegijssacrilegijs obligare conantes, ſpirspir taliter homicidae. Aug. EpiſtEpist. 23. (which is yet more horrible) trainetrain vpup their children to be ſorcererssorcerers and witches. How can they in theſethese keepekeep a good conſcienceconscience, when the very workesworks of their calling are ſinnesin? Is not this to thruſtthrust them headlong into hell? They who thus bindebind their children to the deuilsdevils ſacrilegessacrileges are ſpirituallspiritual murtherersmurderers of them.

4. When parents hauehave no reſpectrespect at all to the fitneſſefitness of the calling: as when they trainetrain vpup children of able bodies, but dull and ſlowslow capacity, of a ſtutteringstuttering tongue and other like imperfections, to learning, wherein they proueprove very dunces, and loſelose all their time, or are not able to make vſeuse of the learning which they hauehave: or when they trainetrain vpup children which hauehave a great inclination to learning, and are very fit thereunto, in ſomesome other trade, which, after many yeeresyears ſpeutspeut therein, they are forced to leaueleave.

5. When parents only ſeekeseek after the moſtmost gainfullgainful trade, and neuernever thinkethink to educate their children moſtmost to the honour of God. How can ſuchsuch expect Gods bleſſingblessing vponupon the meanesmeans vſedused for their childrens good? Hence is it that among PapiſtsPapists ſoso many are trained vpup to EccleſiaſticallEcclesiastical orders and functions: and ſoso few among ProteſtantsProtestants. div.head: §. 34. Of parents teaching their children piety.
div.p: The ſpirituallspiritual good of children, and that in their childhood, is to be procured by parents as well as their temporalltemporal. Wherefore Parentsparents muſtmust trainetrain vpup their children in true piety. This is expreſlyexpressly commanded in my text vnderunder this phraſephrase admonition of the Lord. VnderUnder the law God did both ſimplysimply Deut. 4. 9. & 6. 7 & 11. 19. PſalPsal. 78. 5, 6. command it, and that very often, and alſoalso ordained diuersdivers outward Exo. 12 26. & 13. 14. rites, and cauſedcaused many viſiblevisible and extraordinary IoſJos 4. 6, 7, 21. monuments to be ſetset vpup, that thereby children might be occaſionedoccasioned to askeask of their parents the myſteriemystery of them, and that parents from that inquirieinquiry of their children might take occaſionoccasion to Deul. 6. 20. teach them the ordinances of the Lord.

This expreſſeexpress charge of the Lord is further commended by that practiſepractise which holy parents from time to time hauehave yeeldedyielded thereunto: inſtanceinstance the examples of Gen. 18. 19. Abraham,
Pro. 4 4. DauidDavid,
& 31. 1. BathſhebaBathsheba, 2 Tim. 1. 5. ReaſonsReasons. 1. Benefit of pietiepiety. Lois and Eunice, with many others.

1. PietiePiety is the beſtbest thing that a parent can teach his childechild: for as reaſonreason maketh a man differ from a beaſtbeast; and as learning and ciuilitiecivility maketh a wiſewise and ſobersober man differ from ſauagessavages and ſwaggerersswaggerers; ſoso pietiepiety maketh a ſoundsound ChriſtianChristian much more to differ from the moſtmost ciuillcivil and well ordered naturallnatural man that can be. Learning, ciuilitiecivility, calling, portion, are all nothing without pietiepiety. Now it is an eſpeciallespecial point of wiſdomewisdom, to ſeekeseek the beſtbest good that we can, as for our ſeluesselves, ſoso alſoalso for our children: yea this is an euidentevident ſignesign of a parents true louelove of his childechild.

2. There is a neceſſitienecessity that children be taught pietiepiety, becauſebecause 2. NeceſſitieNecessity of pietiepiety. Fiunt non naſcunturnascuntur ChriſtianiChristiani. Hier. ad Laet. they are not borne but made ChriſtiansChristians: by nature they are vtterlyutterly deſtitutedestitute of all pietiepiety: for by nature eueryevery imagination of the thoughts of mans heart is only euillevil continually (Gen. 6. 5.) and in that reſpectrespect man is borne like the wildewild aſſeass colt (IobJob 11. 12.) ſoso as a man were better be vnborneunborn then not taught pietiepiety.

3. The charge and office of parents bindeth them to teach their 3. Charge of parents. children pietiepiety: for they are by God made watchmen ouerover their children: if therefore their children liuelive and die in impietieimpiety through their parents negligence, their bloudblood ſhallshall be required at their parents hands: inſtanceinstance the example of 1 Sam. 3. 13. div.head: ObiectObject. This dutieduty appertaineth to MiniſtersMinisters. Why Parents as well as MiniſtersMinisters are bour • dbound to teach pietiepiety.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. 1. God hath giuengiven an expreſſeexpress charge hereof to parents, as we heard before.

2. In the familiefamily a parent is all in all ouerover his childechild: a King, a PrieſtPriest, and a Prophet. Therefore that which a MiniſterMinister is to doedo for matter of inſtructioninstruction in the Church, a parent muſtmust do at home.
3 Children hauehave need of daily inſtructioninstruction: the parents painespains in this kindekind muſtmust be added to the MiniſtersMinisters: and both are little enough.

4. Parents hauinghaving more familiaritiefamiliarity with their children then MiniſtersMinisters, muſtmust needs better know their capacitiecapacity, and their diſpoſitiondisposition: and ſoso may better know after what manner to inſtructinstruct them: whether to giuegive them milkemilk or ſtrongstrong meat, whether to dealedeal mildly or roughly with them.

5. InſtructionsInstructions from parents are commonly more kindly accepted then from others: and children will the better relliſhrelish them, when they come from their parents. They ſaysay that a plant will beſtbest grow in the ſoilesoil out of which it firſtfirst ſprungsprung: ſoso inſtructionsinstructions commingcoming from thoſethose who both brought vsus forth, and firſtfirst brought vsus vpup, are like to doedo moſtmost good.

6. There is no ſuchsuch meanesmeans to breed louelove in a childs heart, as to be an inſtrumentinstrument of bringing piety thereinto. Now who ſhouldshould more ſeekeseek the true louelove of a childechild then a parent? In this reſpectrespect a parent is more bound to this dutieduty then a MiniſterMinister.

7. It is impoſſibleimpossible, that a MiniſterMinister, who, it may be, hath many hundred children vnderunder his charge, ſhouldshould well inſtructinstruct them all: It is therefore requiſiterequisite, that each parent lookelook to his owneown children.

As theſethese diſtinctdistinct anſwersanswers ſatisfiesatisfy the obiectionobjection, ſoso they ſerueserve as ſoso many more reaſonsreasons to inforceenforce the dutieduty: wherefore to proceed in adding other reaſonsreasons,

4. Great equitieequity there is that parents teach their children piety, 4. EquitieEquity. becauſebecause they PſalPsal. 51. 5. conceiuedconceived and brought them forth in iniquitieiniquity. If they ſuffersuffer them to lie and die in that corrupt eſtateestate, they are more cruellcruel then the OſtrichOstrich and Dragon.

5. Children are moſtmost properly Gods: Ezec. 16. 20, 21. borne to God: he is the 5. Gods children. moſtmost proper parent of them: in compariſoncomparison of God, fathers and mothers of the fleſhflesh are but nurſesnurses. They muſtmust therefore nurture them in the admonition of the Lord.

6. PietiePiety is that, which of all other things, will make the childechild 6. CauſeCause of obedience. moſtmost obedient, and gratefullgrateful to his parents: for thus there is a double bond to bindebind him: 1. hisHis birth. 2. hisHis new birth: eſpeciallyespecially when the cauſecause of the one hath beenebeen alſoalso the cauſecause of the other.

7. Nothing can more ſettlesettle the heart of a wiſewise parent on his 7. Comfort of parents on their deathbed. death-bed concerning his children, then aſſuranceassurance that pietiepiety is planted in them: for then may he with ſtrongerstronger confidence commend them to Gods prouidenceprovidence, and with greater aſſuranceassurance expect his bleſſingblessing vponupon them after he is dead.

8. Parents, by teaching their children pietiepiety, are an eſpeciallespecial 8. Propagation of pietiepiety. meanesmeans of propagating true religion from age to age, and from generation to generation. No better meanesmeans can be thought of.
For if all parents were carefullcareful of their dutieduty in this kindekind, as there is a ſucceſſionsuccession of children, and thereby a preſeruationpreservation of mankindemankind, ſoso there would be a ſucceſſionsuccession of thoſethose that fearefear God, and thereby a preſeruationpreservation of true religion. My children that are taught by me, may be fathers of children, and ſoso teach that to their children, which they hauehave learned of me: yea after them may grandchildren proueprove fathers of other children, and they teach their children the ſamesame, and ſoso from age to age others after them. This is the meanesmeans on our part: and in our time we muſtmust doedo our part: and for thoſethose who come after vsus, leaueleave the iſſueissue to God.

Not only the great benefit of this point, but alſoalso the too much neglect thereof, in moſtmost families, hath mouedmoved me the longer to inſiſtinsist on it, and the more forcibly to preſſepress it. For the better performing thereof, I will addeadd ſomesome directions.

div.head: §. 35. Of directing parents how to teach their children true pietiepiety.
div.p: 1. WhatſoeuerWhatsoever principle of pietiepiety, parents doedo teach their children, 1. Principles of pietiepiety to be all taken out of Gods word. they muſtmust be ſuresure that it be grounded on Gods word: thus much this phraſephrase (admonition of the Lord) implieth.

Thus ſhallshall parents be ſuresure to feed them with good wholeſomewholesome ſpirituallspiritual food, ſuchsuch as ſhallshall make to their ſpirituallspiritual nouriſhmentnourishment, and eternalleternal life. In this reſpectrespect principles of religion grounded on Gods word are called ſoundsound, or wholſomewholesome, or healthfullhealthful words: 2 Tim. 1. 13. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . and that both in regard of their matter and ſubſtancesubstance, and alſoalso in regard of their effect; they cauſecause and preſeruepreserve good, ſoundsound, ſpirituallspiritual health. We know that naturallnatural men hauehave a care to giuegive their children ſuchsuch food as is wholſomewholesome for their bodiebody: (for will a father

ConſcienceConscience muſtmust mouemove religious parents, to hauehave the like care of the ſoulessouls of their children, as nature teacheth all parents to hauehave of their bodies. If parents be carefullcareful to draw thoſethose principles, wherein they inſtructinstruct their children, out of Gods word, they ſhallshall be ſuresure not to poyſonpoyson their ſoulessouls with any error, hereſieheresy, ſuperſtitionsuperstition, or idolatrieidolatry.

2. When children begin to read, let them read the holy Scripture: 2. Let children at firſtfirst read the Scripture. ſoso was TimothieTimothy trained vpup from a childechild (2 Tim. 3. 15.) It is the aduiceadvice of an ancient Fatherfather, that young children be made acquainted with the words and names of holy Scripture: and that, in ſteadstead of tales and fables, choice hiſtorieshistories of the Bible be made knowneknown to them: and that they be inſtructedinstructed in the ProuerbsProverbs of Solomon.

3. Let children be catechiſedcatechised conſtantlyconstantly from day to day: rehearſerehearse them continually vntounto thy children, ſaithsaith the Law. That which is daily done, is in Scripture ſaidsaid to be done continually: as the ſacrificesacrifice which was daily offered was called a continuallcontinual offering. Here let this caueatcaveat be noted, that in giuinggiving this ſpirituallspiritual food, parents dealedeal with their children, as skilfullskilful nurſesnurses and mothers doedo in feeding infants: they will not at once cram more into their mouthesmouths, then their ſtomachstomach is able to digeſtdigest, but they will rather oft feed them with a little: ſoso it is not meet, that parents be too tedious; that will but dull a childs vnderſtandingunderstanding, and breed weariſomneſſewearisomness, and make it loath to be againeagain inſtructedinstructed: but precept vponupon precept, precept vponupon precept, line vponupon line, line vponupon line,
IſaIsa. 28. 10. here a little, and there a little. Thus ſhallshall they learnelearn with caſecase and delight: and this being oft performed, in time a great meaſuremeasure of knowledge will be gained thereby. If a veſſellvessel hauehave a little mouth, we vſeuse not to fill it by powring whole pailepail-fuls vponupon it, for ſoso all may be ſpiltspilt, and it receiuereceive little or nothing: but we let the liquor fall in by little and little, according to the capacitiecapacity of the mouth; ſoso is nothing loſtlost, and the veſſellvessel filled the ſoonersooner. Thus are children to be dealt withallwithal.

div.head: §. 36. Of Parents faults contrary to their dutieduty of teaching their children piety.
div.p: Many are the aberrations contrary to the forenamed care of teaching pietiepiety. For

1. MoſtMost parents care only for the temporalltemporal and ciuillcivil good of their children: ſoso their children may be well fed and clothed, and brought vpup in ſomesome profitable calling, whereby they may well maintainemaintain themſeluesthemselves in this world, little thought is IobJob non tantum pro corpore filiorum ſollicitussollicitus erat, ſedsed plus de anima cogitabat. Orig. in IobJob. lib. 1. had, or care taken for their ſpirituallspiritual life in this world, or eternalleternal life in the world to come. Wherein are theſethese parents better then heathen? IobJob was otherwiſeotherwise minded: he was more carefullcareful for their ſoulessouls then for their bodies.

2. Many are ſoso farrefar from teaching piety, as they teach their children profaneneſſeprofaneness, pride, riot, lying, deceit, and ſuchsuch like principles of the deuilldevil. It had beenebeen better for ſuchsuch children to hauehave liuedlived among wildewild beaſtsbeasts, then vnderunder ſuchsuch parents. As the children hereby are thruſtthrust headlong to hell, ſoso their blood ſhallshall be required of their parents.

3. Others thinkethink it enough that their children be taught a religion, but what religion it skilleth not. Such are they as hauinghaving rich kindred but popiſhpopish, commend their children to the education of ſuchsuch kindred, in hope of ſomesome temporalltemporal benefit, that their children may reapereap from them. If they were as careleſſecareless of their childrens bodies, they would be accounted little better then murtherersmurderers: and is not the ſoulesoul more pretiousprecious then the body?

4. So farrefar are many from catechiſingcatechising their children and that daily, as they teach them not ſoso much as the Lords praierprayer, the BeleefeBelief, and the ten CommandementsCommandments. Wherein PapiſtsPapists ſhallshall riſerise vpup in iudgementjudgment againſtagainst them, that are very diligent in teaching their children, Pater noſternoster, AueAve Maria, and ſuchsuch like LatineLatin principles, as the children cannot poſſiblypossibly vnderſtandunderstand.

5. Few vſeuse the forenamed outward helpeshelps, as the holy rites appointed of God, the great and glorious workesworks of God, his extraordinary workesworks of mercy or iudgementjudgment, to inſtructinstruct their children thereby. As they themſeluesthemselves care not to take notice of any ſuchsuch thing, ſoso they care not whether their children doedo it or no.

6. So much doedo ſomesome preferreprefer a little pelfepelf before the true Alexander & in moribus, & in inceſſuincessu l. eonidis paedagogi ſuisui non potuit carere vitijs, quibus adbuc paruulus fuit infectus. Hier. ad Laet. good of their children, as they care not to what ſchoolemaſterschoolmaster they put their children, be he profane, or popiſhpopish, or vnlearnedunlearned, eſpeciallyespecially if he be a kinſmankinsman, or one of their friends. Few will ſoso doedo in caſecase of their health or outward eſtateestate: but will rather get the beſtbest PhyſitianPhysician, or the beſtbest Lawyer that they can. Children oft learnelearn ſuchsuch euillevil qualities of their ſchoolemaſtersschoolmasters as they can neuernever ſhakeshake off againeagain.

7. Many proueprove very bad patternespatterns to their children, and giuegive very ill example by profanenſſeprofanenss, riotouſneſſeriotousness, ſwearingswearing, drinking, playing at vnlawfullunlawful games, &etcc. TheſeThese parents as they brought forth their children in ſinnesin, ſoso they lead them on forward to hell. Their euillevil example is not only an hinderancehindrance to the good inſtructioninstruction of others, but alſoalso maketh all their owneown counſellscounsells (if at any time they doedo giuegive any good counſellcounsel) to be in vainevain: for the left hand of euillevil example Parentes non educant filios in eruditione domini quia ſollicitisolliciti non ſuntsunt pro ſalutesalute vel perditione eorum. To conclude, thoſethose parents whoſewhose children are not brought vpup in the inſtructioninstruction of the Lord, ſhewshow plainly that they regard neither the ſaluationsalvation or damnation of their ſoulessouls.

There are both priuatiueprivative, and poſitiuepositive reaſonsreasons to preſſepress this point. PriuatiuePrivative, in regard of the miſchiefesmischiefs that may be preuentedprevented thereby. PoſitiuePositive, in regard of the good that may be gained thereby.

1. Many are the euilsevils which children by nature are prone vntounto, eueneven as rankerank ground is ſubiectsubject to bring forth many weeds: for Gen. 8. 21. the imagination of mans heart is euillevil from his youth: and Pro. 22. 15. fooliſhneſſefoolishness is bound in the heart of a childechild. If therefore they be not well nurtured betimes, what can be looked for, but the fruits of euillevil, and folly. But timely nurture will preuentprevent ſuchsuch fruits, and be an excellent preſeruatiuepreservative againſtagainst their owneown naturallnatural corruption, againſtagainst Satans temptations and againſtagainst the allurements or diſcouragementsdiscouragements of the world

What creature can be tamed, if it be not begun with while it is young?

3. When children firſtfirst begin to be capable of inſtructioninstruction 3. Young children moſtmost pliable. they are moſtmost pliable to follow the direction of their parents as is euidentevident by the ordinary courſecourse of nature in all things Clay, wax, and ſuchsuch other things while they are ſoftsoft receiuereceive any impreſſionimpression: twigs while they are tender are bowed any way: birds and beaſtsbeasts are eaſilyeasily tamed when they are young: cornecorn ſownesown betimes bringeth a timely and plentifullplentiful harueſtharvest.

4. That which in childhood is learned, is longeſtlongest retained: 4. What firſtfirst learned beſtbest remembredremembered. ProuProv. 22. 6. Quo ſeme • leſtsemel estsemelest imbuta recens ſeruabitseruabit odo • rem TeſtaTesta diu. Hor.

ObiectObject. To teach children while they are young, is but as to teach a Parrot or ſuchsuch like vnreaſonableunreasonable creatures: they may learnelearn what is taught them, but they cannot conceiueconceive it.

1. AnſwAnsw. Though children hauehave not ſoso deepedeep an apprehenſionapprehension while they are young, as they hauehave when they come to riper yearesyears, yet ſoso ſoonesoon as they are capable of inſtructioninstruction, they doedo much better conceiueconceive what is taught them, then vnreaſonableunreasonable creatures can doedo.

2. Though that were granted, yet it would not thereupon follow, that it is better not to be taught while they are young. For, firſtfirst it is better that they ſhouldshould be framed and ſquaredsquared to a good courſecourse, before they can diſcernediscern betwixt good and euillevil, t • hen be ſufferedsuffered to runnerun on in euillevil, till they get an habit t • herein; which after it is got, will hardly be caſtcast off.
