Wherefore •• children are to be inſtructedinstructed betimes eueneven for the benefit at may be after reaped, as cornecorn is ſownesown in winter to receiuereceive cr •• op the harueſtharvest following: and to preuentprevent the miſchiefesmischiefs at may fall out, leſtlest they get head ouerover their parents againſtagainst the • ir mindemind.

div.head: §. 38. Of mothers peculiar care in nurturing young children.
div.p:
By the way let mothers eſpeciallyespecially note this point of timely nurture, as a point in peculiar appertaining to them. The Compare 2 Tim. 1. 5. with 3. 15. grandmother Lois, and mother Eunice, firſtfirst taught Timothy,
ProuProv. 31. 1. BathſhebaBathsheba taught SalomonSolomon when he was young. Oft doth SalomonSolomon warnewarn children & 1. 8. & 6. 20. not to forſakeforsake their mothers teaching.

Whereby he implieth that mothers ſhouldshould teach their children eſpeciallyespecially while they are young: which duty ſoso belongeth to a mother, as ProuProv. 29. 15. SalomonSolomon laieth the blame, and ſhameshame of the neglect thereof vponupon her: on the other ſideside the honour of well nurturing children redoundeth eſpeciallyespecially to the mother. To this purpoſepurpose is it, that the 1 King. 15. 2, 10. particular names of the mothers of the kings are recorded in Scripture: intimating thereby that mothers were a mainemain cauſecause of the piety, or impiety of ſuchsuch children. SalomonSolomon and AbſolomAbsalom had both one father, but diuersdivers mothers. May we not well thinkethink that SalomonsSolomon's mothers care to inſtructinstruct him was an eſpeciallespecial meanesmeans of his piety: and that AbſolomsAbsoloms mothers neglect of this duty, was ſomesome cauſecause of his impiety? It is expreſlyexpressly noted of Ahaziahs mother, that ſheshe was his counſellercounseller to doedo wickedly, which made him ſoso wicked 2 Chro. 22. 3. as he was. Home-experience confirmeth as much: for if father and mother be of diuersdivers religions, moſtmost of the children will follow the mother. For while children are young, their mother is moſtmost in their ſightsight: ſheshe feedeth, ſheshe apparellethappareleth them, ſheshe tendeth them when they are not well, (when the Shunemites childechild being ill, ſaidsaid to his father, my head, my head, he ſaidsaid to his ſeruantservant, carriecarry him to his mother.) Her precepts therefore 2 King. 4. 19. and practiſepractise in that reſpectrespect are beſtbest heeded by the children, and ſheshe hath the beſtbest opportunity to perſwadepersuade them to what ſheshe liketh beſtbest: ſoso as what they learnelearn in their younger yearesyears, commonly they learnelearn of their mothers: and that which then they learnelearn, for the moſtmost part ſtickethsticketh moſtmost cloſeclose vntounto them, and is longeſtlongest retained by them, as was noted §. 37. before.

I hauehave not thus in particular preſſedpressed this point vponupon mothers, as if I exempted fathers from all care of nurturing their children in the beginning: for in my text the ApoſtleApostle named Fathersfathers: and SalomonSolomon ſaithsaith, that his father taught him euen • even while he was tender: and DauidDavid felt the ſmartsmart of neglecting his •
other children. It is therefore (as hath before beenebeen prouedproved) a ioyntjoint duty belonging to both. Fathers therefore muſtmust doedo their beſtbest endeuourendeavour, and ſeesee that mothers doedo theirs alſoalso, becauſebecause he is a gouernourgovernor ouerover child, mother, and all.

div.head: §. 39. Of letting ſlipslip the beſtbest time for nurture.
div.p: Contrary is the negligence of moſtmost parents, who let the beſtbest yearesyears wherein their children are moſtmost docible paſſepass ouerover in wantonneſſewantonness, vanity, and folly: and ſoso loſelose that which can neuernever be recoueredrecovered againeagain, moſtmost precious time. Hence is it that when they goego about to reclaimereclaim their children, they findefind them exceedingly peruerſeperverse and head-ſtrongstrong: much like to a ſtrongstrong biggebig armearm of a tree, which if a man goego about to ſtraitenstraiten, he cannot eaſilyeasily make it bow: and though it bow, yet will it not continue to ſtandstand as he would hauehave it: nay it may be that it will rather breakebreak then bow much. Such a branch was Adoniah. It is apparent that in his childhood he was not well nurtured, for his father would not diſpleaſedisplease him from his childhood. 1 King. 1. 6.

The fathers putting off this duty to the mother, and the mothers putting it off to the father, is a great cauſecause of the neglect thereof. Were both of them perſwadedpersuaded that it belonged to them both, and in that reſpectrespect would to their power be helpfullhelpful each to other, children would much better be inſtructedinstructed.

div.head: §. 40. Of parents continuing to nurture their children.
div.p:
As parents muſtmust begin betimes to nurture their children, ſoso they muſtmust hold on therein, as long as they retaineretain any gouernmentgovernment ouerover them: yea ſoso long as they remaineremain to be parents vntounto them. Some difference there may be in the manner of performing this duty: for children are to be vſedused as children: and they who are grownegrown in yearesyears, and of riper vnderſtandingunderstanding, accordingly to be dealt withallwithal: yet ſtillstill muſtmust parents hauehave a care of their well doing. The word vſedused in my text and tranſlatedtranslated Childrenchildren, is a generallgeneral word which in Scripture and other
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . writers is vſedused to ſetset forth all ſortsort of children, of what ſexesex, of what age, of what degree ſoeuersoever they be. In handling the duty of children we Treat. 5. §. 62. ſhewedshowed, that children owed a ſubiectionsubjection to parents ſoso long as they liuedlived together: wherefore by the rule of relation, ſoso long alſoalso an authority remaineth in parents ouerover
their children, and accordingly they ought to hauehave a fatherly care for their good. On this ground Eli did well in admoniſhingadmonishing 1 Sam. 2. 25. IobJob 1. 5. Hoc faciebat ille beatus vir, non ſemelsemel, aut ſecundosecundo, neque vno anno, aut duobus, ſedsed ſicsic faciebat Iob omnibus diebus vitae eorum. Orig. in Iob lib. 1. his children after they were mariedmarried: his fault was that he went not farrefar enough in doing his duty: ſomewhatsomewhat he did, but not all that he ſhouldshould and might hauehave done. IobJob is commended for the care he had ouerover his children when they were grownegrown in yearesyears: for day by day he ſentsent for them and ſanctifiedsanctified them: and that after they had ſeuerallseveral houſeshouses of their owneown, and dwelt apart: and this all their daiesdays.

For the performance of that which is now vrgedurged, parents muſtmust ſoso carriecarry themſeluesthemselves from time to time towards their children, as they euerever keepekeep the reinesreins in their owneown hands, and Direction. retaineretain a power to curbecurb their children as they ſeesee occaſionoccasion. They may, as their children grow vpup in yearesyears, ſlakenslaken the reinesreins more and more, but neuernever let them cleaneclean goego, and caſtcast them looſeloose on their childrens neckeneck.

div.head: §. 41. Of parents folly in letting goego all their power ouerover their children.
div.p: Contrary is their folly who put themſeluesthemselves in their childrens power, and let goego all their authority ouerover them. Many Aegrè reprendas quod ſinissinis conſueſcereconsuescere. Hier. ad Laet. parents that hauehave thus done, hauinghaving by wofullwoful experience found the miſchiefemischief and inconuenienceinconvenience that hath followed thereupon, hauehave much repented their folly, and vſedused meanesmeans of redreſſeredress, but all too late. For a miſchiefemischief is much more eaſilyeasily preuentedprevented then redreſſedredressed. All the power that DauidDavid had could not hold in AbſolomAbsalom after he was permitted to hauehave 2 Sam. 15. 1. horſeshorses, and chariots, and men at his command. If DauidDavid, as he begun, had continued to keepekeep him within a compaſſecompass, and ſtillstill held him vnderunder, all the treaſonabletreasonable plots which he put in execution, might eaſilyeasily hauehave beenebeen preuentedprevented. Our times afford too many examples of parents folly in this kindekind, and of the miſchiefesmischiefs following thereupon.

div.head: §. 42. Of adding admonition to inſtructioninstruction.
div.p:
The meanesmeans of helping forward the good workework of nurture III. The means of nurture. are eſpeciallyespecially two.
1. Frequent admonition.
2. Due correction.

Both of them are implied in this text: one in the word tranſlatedtranslated admonition, which (according to the notation of the

Now both theſethese are to be ioynedjoined together, as being very helpfullhelpful each to other. For admonition without correction is like to proueprove but meeremere vanity: and correction without admonition will be too much auſterityausterity.
The dutieduty which the firſtfirst of theſethese ſettethsetteth forth, is this,

Parents muſtmust oft whet inſtructioninstruction vponupon their children: they Annuncia, praecipe, impera, ſuadesuade eis, &etcc. Aug. de ſalutsalut. docum. cap. 29. may not thinkethink it enough to tell their children what they ought to doedo, but to inſtructioninstruction they muſtmust addeadd admonition: and, as it were, beat into their childrens heads the leſſonslessons which they teach them: that ſoso they may make a deeper impreſſionimpression in their hearts. Thus ſhallshall their inſtructionsinstructions be like the words of the wiſewise which are as nailesnails faſtenedfastened, or faſtfast knocked Eccl. 12. 11. in: they remain firmefirm where they are once faſtenedfastened, and cannot eaſilyeasily be pluckt out: for as many blowesblows doedo knockeknock a nailenail vpup to the head (as we ſpeakespeak) ſoso many admonitions doedo ſettlesettle good inſtructionsinstructions in a childes heart, and cauſecause that the heart be eſtabliſhedestablished in that which is taught, Heb. 13. 9. which is a thing to be laboured after. The generallgeneral exhortation of being 2 Tim. 4. 2. inſtantinstant in ſeaſonseason and out of ſeaſonseason may be applied to this purpoſepurpose: but more pertinently that Deut. 6. 7. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉

To this purpoſepurpose is it that Solomon vſethuseth to double his inſtructionsinstructions, and vrgeurge them againeagain and againeagain, as Pro. 1. 8. hearehear the inſtructioninstruction, forſakeforsake not the law:

The apprehenſionapprehension of children is fickle, and their memory weakeweak: if they be but once, or ſeldomeseldom, or ſleightlyslightly inſtructedinstructed, that which is taught will ſoonesoon ſlipslip away, and doedo little or no good.

For the better performing of this dutieduty, parents muſtmust thinkethink of the beſtbest meanesmeans they can to faſtenfasten their inſtructionsinstructions vponupon their children: and obſerueobserve their inclination and diſpoſitiondisposition, and ſeesee with what they are moſtmost mouedmoved. div.head: §. 43. Of parents weariſomneſſewearisomness in inſtructinginstructing their children.
div.p:
Contrary is the practiſepractise of thoſethose parents who ſoonesoon waxewax weary in inſtructinginstructing their children. The ApoſtleApostle laieth it downedown as a generallgeneral caueatcaveat in good duties that we wax not
Gal. 6. 9. weary: if in no good thing we muſtmust wax weary, ſhallshall parents wax weary in doing good to their children? Yet how many be there that hauinghaving once taught their children, thinkethink they hauehave done dutieduty enough in that kindekind: if their children will take it, they may. They are loth to take too much painespains in often vrgingurging the points which they hauehave taught them.

Thus that teaching vaniſhethvanisheth away: and ſoso it falleth out, as we ſaysay in the prouerbeproverb, as good not at all as neuernever the better. This is one point wherein old Eli failed: for he gauegave very good inſtructioninstruction to his children: but becauſebecause he there ſtaiedstaied, neither was that accepted of God as a ſufficientsufficient diſchargedischarge of his duty, nor were his children any whit bettered thereby. If this were a fault in him notwithſtandingnotwithstanding his children were come to yearesyears of diſcretiondiscretion, and to ripeneſſeripeness of vnderſtandingunderstanding, how much greater is the fault in thoſethose whoſewhose children are but young?

ObiectObject. If a childechild take not inſtructioninstruction at firſtfirst, he is but of an vntowarduntoward and peruerſeperverse diſpoſitiondisposition: all the painespains that can be taken will be loſtlost.

AnſwAnsw. It may be childiſhneſſechildishness rather then peruerſneſſeperversenessperuersness, or ſomesome imperfection, rather then obſtinacyobstinacy. ConſideringConsidering the neceſſitynecessity of good nurture, no painespains may be thought too much. There is more peruerſeneſſeperverseness, and vntowardneſſeuntowardness in • ſuchsuch parents as wax weary in doing this dutieduty, then in ſuchsuch children as at firſtfirst are not wrought vponupon: for this is a means ordained of God to cure this vntowardneſſeuntowardness.

div.head: §. 44. Of parents reprouingreproving their children.
div.p: The other meanesmeans of helping nurture is correction.

The former is reprehenſionreprehension: and it muſtmust alwaiesalways goego before
the latter, which is moſtmost vſuallyusually and properly called Correction.
ReprehenſionReprehension is a kindekind of middle thing betwixt admonition and correction: it is a ſharpesharpe admonition, but a mildemild correction.

It is the rather to be vſedused becauſebecause it may be a meanesmeans to preuentprevent ſtrokesstrokes and blowesblows, eſpeciallyespecially in ingenuous, and good natured children (for Pro. 17. 10. a reproofereproof entereth more into him that is wiſewise, then a hundred ſtripesstripes into a foolefool) and becauſebecause it may be vſedused, when it is not ſoso meet to vſeuse ſtrokesstrokes and blowesblows: as when children are grownegrown to man-age.

The many good fruits which the holy GhoſtGhost noteth to proceed from due reproofereproof doedo ſhewshow that it is a dutieduty whereof parents ought to make conſcienceconscience as they deſiredesire to promote the good of their children: and ſoso much the rather becauſebecause many good fruits redound to the parents that reprouereprove, as well as to the children reprouedreproved. In regard of their good who are reprouedreproved, it is ſaidsaid, Pro. 6. 23. ReproofesReproofs for inſtructioninstruction are the way of life: they cauſecause & 15. 32. vnderſtandingunderstanding; and make & 15. 5. prudent. In regard of their good who reprouereprove, it is ſaidsaid, & 24. 25. To them that rebuke ſhallshall be delight (that is, much comfort and matter of reioycingrejoicing, ſoso as they ſhallshall not need to repent what they hauehave done) and a bleſſingblessing of good ſhallshall come vponupon them, that is, either a bleſſingblessing of good men, who will bleſſebless, praiſepraise and commend them: or a bleſſingblessing of good things, and that from the Lord who will reward them for this conſcionableconscionable performance of their dutieduty.

VponUpon theſethese grounds Gen. 9. 25. & 34. 30. & 49. 4. holy men hauehave not ſparedspared to rebuke their children as there was occaſionoccasion. Though 1 Sam. 2. 23. Eli dum filijs moleſtusmolestus eſſeesse ſeueraseuera increpatione recuſatrecusat, & illos & ſeipſumseipsum u • na perdidit, ChryſChrys. in 1 Tim. hom. 9. 1 King. 1. 6. Eli did ſomewhatsomewhat in this duty, yet becauſebecause he was not more ſeueresevere therein, • he brought deſtructiondestruction both vponupon himſelfehimself and his children.
The direction noted §. 40. andAnd 47. andAnd Treat. 4. §. 35. mayMay be here applied.

div.head: §. 45. Of parents cockering their children.
div.p:
Contrary is their too much doting on children, who are l • oth to giuegive them a foulefoul word. DauidDavid (though otherwiſeotherwise a e • very wiſewise man) herein manifeſtedmanifested much folly, for he diſpleaſeddispleased n • ot Adoniah at any time in ſayingsaying, why haſthast thou done ſoso? and like
enough it is, that alſoalso he ſoso cockered his other rebellious ſonneson AbſolomAbsalom. Notenote the fearefullfearful iſſueissue that followed thereupon both to father and children. Though their father would not diſpleaſedisplease them, yet they cared not to diſpleaſedisplease their father, yea to grieuegrieve his heart, and vex his ſoulesoul. The like may all fooliſhfoolish doting parents lookelook for at their childrens hands. For firſtfirst parents by neglect of this dutieduty highly diſpleaſedisplease God: therefore in iuſtjust reuengerevenge will God giuegive their children ouerover to Omnia quae deliquerint filij, de parentibus requiruntur qui non erudierint ſiliossilios ſuossuos. Orig. in Iob. lib. 1. diſpleaſedisplease and vex them. Secondly, neglect of reproofereproof is a meanesmeans to make children rude, preſumptuouspresumptuous, rebellious, and ſoso careleſſecareless to pleaſeplease their parents. Yea all things where in children offend through want of education ſhallshall be required at their parents hands.

div.head: §. 46. Of correcting children.
div.p: The latter and more proper kindekind of correction which is by ſtripesstripes and blowesblows is alſoalso a meanesmeans appointed by God to helpehelp the good nurture and education of children. It is the laſtlast remedy which a parent can vſeuse: a remedy which may doedo good when nothing elſeelse can.

It is by the holy GhoſtGhost both expreſlyexpressly commanded, and alſoalso very oft preſſedpressed vnderunder theſethese and ſuchsuch like phraſesphrases, Pro. 19. 18. Cha • ſtenChasten thy ſonneson:
& 29. 17. correct thy ſonneson:
& 23. 13. with-hold not correction from the childechild:
VerſVers. 14. thou ſhaltshalt ſmitesmite him with the rod. Were there no other motiuemotive, this were ſufficientsufficient. Gods charge was ſuchsuch a motiuemotive to Abraham, as at it he would hauehave ſacrificedsacrificed his ſonneson: Gen. 22. 2, 3. and wilt not thou at Gods command correct thy childechild?

It is further commended by Gods owneown example, which is not only ſetset forth in ſomesome particular inſtancesinstances, but by his generallgeneral conſtantconstant dealing with all, and that as an eſpeciallespecial token and fruit of his louelove. For whom the Lord louethloveth he chaſtenethchasteneth,
Heb. 12. 6, 8. and ſcourgethscourgeth eueryevery ſonneson whom he receiuethreceiveth. If ye be without chaſtiſementchastisement wherofwhereof all are partakers, then are ye baſtardsbastards and not ſonnessons. Let this example of God be well weighed, for it is of great weight. Who can better tell what kindekind of dealing is fitteſtfittest for children then God? Who can better nurture children then God? Who doth more truly aimeaim at, and procure the good of children then God? Yea who doth more tender children then God? If God the father of ſpiritsspirits in wiſdomewisdom and
louelove thus dealedeal with his children, fathers of the fleſhflesh may not thinkethink by the contrary to ſhewshow wiſdomewisdom or louelove. Their wiſdomewisdom will be folly, their louelove hatred. VponUpon theſethese grounds it is taken for a thing granted, that parents (who tender the good of their children as they ſhouldshould) doedo chaſtiſechastise their children as need requireth: for it is ſaidsaid, that the Pro. 3. 12. Lord correcteth whom he louethloveth, as a father the ſonneson in whom he delighteth. If parents vſedused it not, this were no good inference to ſaysay, as a father: againeagain, as a thing without controuerſiecontroversy it is ſaidsaid, Heb. 12. 9. we hauehave had fathers of our fleſhflesh which corrected vsus.

The grounds of the equitieequity of this dutieduty, reſpectrespect partly the ReaſonsReasons to mouemove parents to correct. children corrected, and partly the parents that correct. In regard of children, it freeth them from much euillevil, and worketh in them much good.

Correction is as phyſickephysic to purge out much corruption 1. Benefits of correction to the parties corrected. which lurketh in children, and as a ſaluesalve to healeheal many wounds and ſoressores made by their folly. In which reſpectrespect Solomon ſaithsaith, that Pro. 22. 15. FooliſhneſſeFoolishness is bound in the heart of a childechild, but the rod of correction ſhallshall driuedrive it farrefar from him: and againeagain, & 20. 30. The blewneſſeblewness of a wound is a purging medicine againſtagainst euillevil: ſoso doedo ſtripesstripes the inward parts of the belly. In regard of the inward operation of this phyſickephysic, correction is further ſaidsaid to preſeruepreserve a childechild from death, ( Pro. 23. 13. if thou beatest him he ſhallshall not die) and that not only from temporalltemporal death (as many children are thus preſeruedpreserved from the MagiſtratesMagistrates ſwordsword) but alſoalso from eternalleternal death ( VerſVers. 14. thou ſhaltshalt deliuerdeliver his ſoulesoul from hell.) Notenote this ye cockering parents, whoſewhose ouerover-much lenitielenity is very great crueltiecruelty. For may we not iuſtlyjustly count him a cruellcruel parent, that ſhouldshould ſuffersuffer diſeaſesdiseases, boilesboils, ſoressores, and wounds to remaineremain, increaſeincrease, and feſterfester in his childechild, and giuegive him no phyſickephysic, nor apply any plaiſtersplaisters, or medicines to him? Nay rather who ſeethseeth his ſonneson running into a flaming fire, or deepedeep water, and would not hold him backeback? EuenEven ſoso cruellcruel, and more cruellcruel are they, who ſuffersuffer their children to runnerun on in euillevil, rather then correct them.

div.head: ObiectObject. Who can endure to make his owneown childechild ſmartsmart, and to put him to painepain?
div.p:
AnſwAnsw. The future fruit is more to be conſideredconsidered, then the preſentpresent painepain. Potions, pills, and coraſiuescorasives, are fulſomefulsome, bitter,
and painfullpainful; but becauſebecause there is a neceſſitienecessity of vſingusing them, and great miſchiefemischief is preuentedprevented by the vſeuse of them, wiſewise parents will not forbeareforbear them for the ſenſiblesensible bitterneſſebitterness, and painepain. Fitly doth the ApoſtleApostle thus anſweranswer that obiectionobjection, No chaſtningchastning for the
Heb. 12. 11. preſentpresent ſeemethseemeth to be ioyousjoyous, but grieuousgrievous; neuertheleſſenevertheless, afterward it yeeldethyieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteouſneſſerighteousness. This may be applied to parents corrections as well as to Gods.

The good which correction bringeth to children, is by Solomon noted in this and ſuchsuch like phraſesphrases, The rod giuethgiveth wiſdomewisdom:
Pro. 29. 15. for it maketh children obſerueobserve, what is good, and what euillevil; what commendable, and what blame-worthy: and accordingly to doedo the good, and leaueleave the euillevil, which is a great point of wiſdomewisdom.

div.head: ObiectObject. InſtructionInstruction will better doedo this.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. InſtructionInstruction may giuegive them more knowledge, but it is correction which bringeth them to practiſepractise what they know, which is the Matt. 7. 24. chiefeſtchiefest point of wiſdomewisdom.

In regard of parents, due correcting of their children both freeth them of many inconueniencesinconveniences, and alſoalso bringeth to them 2. Benefits of correcting to him that correcteth. much quiet.

1. It ſparethspareth them much painespains. For many admonitions oft repeated, and inculcated againeagain and againeagain, will not make many children ſoso much to heed wholſomewholesome and good aduiceadvice, as a little correction. They are much more ſenſiblesensible of ſmartsmart, then of words.

2. It preuentethpreventeth much griefegrief, ſhameshame, and vexation: for Pro. 17. 25. a fooliſhfoolish ſonneson is a griefegrief to his father, and bitterneſſebitterness to her that bare him. But it is
& 22. 15. the rod of correction that driuethdriveth away fooliſhneſſefoolishness, and ſoso preuentethpreventeth that griefegrief and bitterneſſebitterness.

3. It freeth them from the guilt of their childrens ſinnesin, ſoso as they are not acceſſarieaccessary thereto, as Sam. 3. 13. Eli was. For correction is the laſtlast remedieremedy that a parent can vſeuse: if by that he can doedo no good, it is preſuppoſedpresupposed that he hath done his vttermoſtuttermost endeuourendeavour: in which reſpectrespect, though the childechild die in his ſinnesin, yet the parent hath deliuereddelivered his owneown ſoulesoul.

The quiet which is brought to parents by correcting their children, is thus noted out by Solomon,
Pro. 29. 17. Correct thy ſonneson, and he ſhallshall giuegive thee rest, yea he ſhallshall giuegive delight vntounto thy ſoulesoul. For children well nurtured, and by correction kept in a filiallfilial awe,
will ſoso carriecarry themſeluesthemselves, as their parents may reſtrest ſomewhatsomewhat ſecuresecure, and not diſquietdisquiet themſeluesthemselves (as they doedo with children ſetset at libertieliberty) yea, as trees well pruned, and ground well tilled, they will bring forth pleaſantpleasant and abundant fruit; and ſoso their parents will hauehave iuſtjust cauſecause to reioycerejoice in them.

div.head: §. 47. A direction to parents in correcting their children.
div.p: For well vſingusing this biting coraſiuecorasive of correction, parents muſtmust hauehave reſpectrespect to the matter for which they doedo correct, and to their manner of correcting.
In regard of the matter, theſethese three things muſtmust be noted. Three things noted in the matter, for which correction is to be giuengiven.

1. That they be ſuresure there is a fault committed: that ſoso there be iuſtjust cauſecause of correcting: elſeelse more hurt then good will proceed from thence. If a coraſiuecorasive be laid where there is no ſoresore, it will make one. If correction be vniuſtlyunjustly giuengiven, it may prouokeprovoke to wrath, but will doedo little good. This is it wherein earthly fathers are taxed, and made vnlikeunlike to God, for that many times they correct after their owneown pleaſurepleasure: which is a point of great iniuſticeinjustice. Heb. 12. 10.

2. That the fault be made knowneknown to the childechild corrected: and he apparantlyapparently conuincedconvinced thereof. Correction muſtmust be for inſtructioninstruction, which cannot be, except the childechild know why he is corrected: for it is all one to him, as if he were corrected for no fault, if he know not his fault. God thus a firſtfirst proceeded with the ſerpentserpent, Gen. 3. 11, &etcc. with EueEve, and with Adam. Thus IudgesJudges proceed in puniſhingpunishing malefactors. Yea thus will men dealedeal with a dog. Should they not much more with a childechild?

3. That the faults be ſuchsuch eſpeciallyespecially, as the parents can ſhewshow to their children (if at leaſtleast they be of ſoso much diſcretiondiscretion) to be againſtagainst Gods word; as ſwearingswearing, lying, pilfring, and the like: for 1. theſeThese are moſtmost dangerous faults, and therefore more carefully to be purged out. 2. theThe childechild corrected will thus be the better euictedevicted of his fault, the more condemnecondemn himſelfehimself, and more contentedly bearebear the correction.
In regard of the manner of correcting, fourefour generallgeneral, and fourefour FoureFour general rules for the manner of correcting. particular rules are to be obſeruedobserved.
The generallgeneral rules are theſethese.

1. An eye muſtmust be had to Gods manner of correcting his children, and in particular of Gods correcting the parent himſelfehimself:
no better generallgeneral direction can be giuengiven: for Gods patternepattern is a perfect rule.

2. Prayer muſtmust be made by parents for themſeluesthemselves and for their children: for themſeluesthemselves, to be directed in doing it: for their children, to be bettered by it. Thus will good PhyſitiansPhysicians in miniſtringministering phyſickephysic. In all duties is prayer to be vſedused; eſpeciallyespecially in this: for a parent is ready, partly through his owneown intemperate paſſionpassion, and partly through the childs impatiencieimpatiency, to fall into one extreme or other. This is not to impoſeimpose vponupon all, whenſoeuerwhensoever they take vpup the rod, to goego and make a ſolemnesolemn prayer, but to lift vpup the heart for direction and bleſſingblessing.

3. Correction muſtmust be giuengiven in louelove. All things muſtmust be done in 1 Cor. 16. 14. louelove: much more this, that cariethcarrieth a ſhewshow of anger and hatred. In louelove they will giuegive phyſickephysic to their children, and ſplintersplinter a ioyntjoint, if need be. God correcteth his children in louelove: ſoso muſtmust Reu. 3. 19. parents. LoueLove will make them doedo it with tenderneſſetenderness and compaſſioncompassion.

4. Correction muſtmust be giuengiven in a mildemild moodemood, when the affections Nunquam, iratus qui accedit ad poenam, mediocritatem tenebit, Cic. Offic. lib. 1. IerJer. 10. 11. DiſturbedDisturbed paſſionspassions caſtcast a miſtmist before the vnderſtandingunderstanding, ſoso as a man cannot diſcernediscern what is enough, what too much. When paſſionpassion is mouedmoved, correction muſtmust be deferred. God correcteth in meaſuremeasure.
The particular rules are theſethese.

1. Due order muſtmust be kept. Correction by word muſtmust goego before correction by the rod. Reu. 3. 19. Vt ad vrendum & ſecandumsecandum medici, ſicsic nos ad caſtigandūcaſtiganduncastigandun, rarò, inuitique veniamus, nec vnquam niſinisi neceſſarionecessario, ſinullasinulla reperietur alia medicina. Thus a parent will ſhewshow that he taketh no delight in ſmitingsmiting his childechild: it is neceſſitienecessity that forceth him thereunto. Thus a parent ſhewethshoweth himſelfehimself like to God, who doth not puniſhpunish willingly, Lam. 3. 33. PhyſitiansPhysicians, when they miniſterminister ſtrongstrong phyſickephysic, will giuegive a preparatiuepreparative: rebuke may be as a preparatiuepreparative. Good and pitifullpitiful Chirurgions will try all other meanesmeans before they come to launce and ſeereseer.

2. Due reſpectrespect muſtmust be had to the partieparty corrected: if he be young and tender, the lighter correction muſtmust be vſedused. Solomon oft mentioneth a rod, as meeteſtmeetest for a childechild; for that is the lighteſtlightest correction. So if the childechild be of a flexible and ingenuous diſpoſitiondisposition, ſoonesoon ſneaptsneapt, the correction muſtmust accordingly be moderated.
If he be well grownegrown, and withallwithal be ſtoutstout, and ſtubbornestubborn, the correction may be more ſeueresevere.

3. Due reſpectrespect muſtmust be had to the fault: SinnesSins directly CauendumCavendum ne maiormajor poena, quàm culpa ſitsit. Cic. loc. citat. againſtagainst God, open, notorious, ſcandalousscandalous ſinnessins, knowneknown ſinnessins, ſinnessins often committed, in which they are grownegrown vpup, and whereof they hauehave gotten an habit, are with greater ſeueritieseverity to be corrected.
4. A parent muſtmust behold his owneown faults in correcting his childes: ſoso more compaſſioncompassion will be wrought in him.

div.head: §. 48. Of parents too much indulgency.
div.p:
Contrary to this dutieduty of correcting are two extremes.
1. Too much lenitielenity.
2. Too much ſeueritieseverity.

Many ſoso cocker their children, as they will ſuffersuffer them to Qui non corripiunt filios ſuossuos, & eorum animas igni inextinguibili in interitum tradunt, & ſemetipſossemetipsos in furorem iudicij deme • rgunt. Orig. in Iob. lib. 1. 1 Sam. 2. 29. run into any miſdemeanourmisdemeanour, rather then correct them. They cannot endure to hearehear their children cry: and therefore their children muſtmust be pleaſedpleased in all their humours and euillevil deſiresdesires. TheſeThese parents bring ſhameshame to themſeluesthemselves, and miſchiefemischief vponupon their children: for God is oft forced to correct ſuchsuch. HeauyHeavy are Gods corrections: and oft light on parent and childechild both: as appeareth by the iudgementjudgment on Eli and his ſonnessons: for ſuchsuch parents make themſeluesthemselves acceſſaryaccessary to their childrens ſinnessins: yea alſoalso to the iudgementsjudgments laid vponupon their children. God ſaithsaith of ſuchsuch parents, that they honour their children aboueabove God. It is therefore a fond indulgency which maketh parents regard neither Gods honour, nor their owneown or childrens ſafetiesafety.

Mothers for the moſtmost part offend herein, who are ſoso farrefar from performing this dutieduty themſeluesthemselves, as they are much offended with their husbands if they doedo it. And to proclaimeproclaim their folly to all the world, they cannot commit their children to a Tutor or SchooleSchool-maſtermaster, but with a ſtraitstrait charge, that they correct them not.

div.head: ObiectObject. Correction maketh children ſotssots and blocks.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. If Gods ſpiritspirit deſeruedeserve to hauehave more credence then ſuchsuch fooliſhfoolish women, that obiectionobjection is moſtmost falſefalse, for we heard §. 46. before how correction giuethgiveth wiſdomewisdom, and driuethdriveth out fooliſhneſſefoolishness.

2. ObiectObject. Mothersmothers may be the more borne with herein,
becauſebecause with long trouble they did bearebear, and with great trauelltravel bring forth their children.

AnſwAnsw. That may be a good motiuemotive for them to ſeekeseek the true good of their children, that ſoso their trouble and trauelltravel may not be in vainevain: but not to vpholduphold them in the broad way that leadeth to deſtructiondestruction.

div.head: §. 49. Of parents too much ſeueritieseverity in correcting their children.
div.p: They who offend in the other extreme of ſeuerityseverity, of the Patres non oportet aſperosasperos eſſeesse circa filios. Cyp. TeſtimTestim. l. 3. c. 71. two are the more vnnaturallunnatural parents; they offend directly againſtagainst the firſtfirst branch of this text (ProuokeProvoke not to wrath.) Nothing more prouokethprovoketh then immoderate ſeuerityseverity: for
1. It argueth no louelove in the parent, but rather hatred, at leaſtleast wrath, and other ſuchsuch like diſtempereddistempered affections.
2. It ſoftenethsofteneth not the childes heart, but hardeneth it rather. Uerendum ne, ſisi parentesparents ob quaevis errata filios coarguant, frontem tandem ipſiipsi perfricent. Greg. Naz. ad Vital.
3. It maketh him dull, and ſtupidstupid, and cleaneclean peruertethperverteth the right and true end of correction.
4. It oft maketh a childechild thinkethink of doing ſomesome miſchiefemischief to his parent or himſelfehimself.
That parents may the rather take heed of this extreme, I will briefly note wherein exceſſeexcess in ſeueritieseverity is ſhewedshowed.
It is ſhewedshowed, when correction is giuengiven
1. For no fault. In this caſecase, though correction be neuernever ſoso light, it is too ſeueresevere.
2. For ſmallsmall faults, in wrath and furiefury, though the ſtripesstripes be few and light, yet the parents behauiourbehaviour is too much ſeueritieseverity.
3. To children that are young and tender, or ſoftsoft, mildemild and ingenuous, as if they were in ſomesome yeeresyears, the moſtmost obſtinateobstinate and peruerſeperverse that could be.

4. Too often: for eueryevery thing done amiſſeamiss: whereas parents Multa quae vident parentes videre ſese diſſimulentdissimulent; multa ſese minime audiſſeaudisse fingant quae auribus infixa habent. Greg. Naz. ad Vital. ſhouldshould ſeemeseem not to ſeesee or hearehear many things which they ſeesee, and hearehear.
5. Too ſorelysorely: ſoso as the childechild is lamed, or ſomesome way ſoso hurt as he ſhallshall feelefeel it as long as he liuethliveth.

div.head: §. 50. Of Parents care in prouidingproviding fit callings for their children.
div.p:
HauingHaving laid downedown ſuchsuch duties of parents as eſpeciallyespecially reſpectrespect
the childhood of children, I proceed to lay forth ſuchsuch as hauehave reſpectrespect to their riper yeeresyears wherein they are to be placed forth.
The kindeskinds may be drawnedrawn to two heads.
1. ProuidingProviding fit places and callings for them to exerciſeexercise their gifts.
2. ProuidingProviding fit mariagesmarriages for them.

We heard §. 31. before how children were to be trained vpup, and fitted to ſomesome good calling eueneven in their childhood. Now further, when by vertuevirtue of good education they are inabled to diſchargedischarge the functions and duties of a calling, and by yeeresyears they are well grownegrown vpup, ſoso as it is time they ſhouldshould be ſetset to ſomesome particular calling:

Parents ought to prouideprovide fit callings for their children, and fit Fit callings to be prouidedprovided. places for them to exerciſeexercise the gifts which by nature or education they hauehave gotten. For example, If children hauehave beenebeen brought vpup in learning, parents muſtmust vſeuse what lawfulllawful and honeſthonest meanesmeans they can to ſettlesettle them in ſuchsuch a place and courſecourse as they may profeſſeprofess and exerciſeexercise their gifts, according to their ſeuerallseveral kindeskinds, be it DiuinitieDivinity, Law, PhyſickePhysic, or the like: or if they hauehave beenebeen brought vpup in any trade, to prouideprovide that they may ſetset vpup (as we ſpeakespeak) and exerciſeexercise their trade. The two firſtfirst children that euerever were borne of woman, Gen. 4. 2. Cain and Abel, were placed forth in ſeuerallseveral callings; and without doubt their places were ſoso ordered by their parents. The like may be gathered out of theſethese phraſesphrases, & 25. 27. EſauEsau was a man of the field, and IaakobJacob dwelt intents. 1 Sam. 8. 1. It is noted of Samuel, that he made his two ſonnessons IudgesJudges. Had they beenebeen as faithfullfaithful in well vſingusing their places, as their father was carefullcareful in prouidingproviding them, they might hauehave liuedlived well themſeluesthemselves, and done much good to others. IſhaiIshai hauinghaving many ſonnessons, had a care hereof: for 1 Sam. 17. 13. he ſentsent his three eldeſteldest ſonnessons to the war; and placed them in a ſouldierssoldiers courſecourse of life: &. 16. 11. his youngeſtyoungest he made a ſhepheardshepheard, which was in thoſethose daiesdays and places a calling of greater reckoning then now it is with vsus.

1. Thus ſhallshall they make vſeuse of that abilitieability whereunto by The benefits of a fit calling.
their parents prouidenceprovidence, and their owneown diligence they hauehave attained: otherwiſeotherwise that abilitieability may ſoonesoon be loſtlost. Doth not daily experience ſhewshow that many who hauehave beenebeen well trained vpup by their parents in learning, ſoso farrefar as they hauehave beenebeen fit to hauehave entredentered into the miniſterieministry, for want of place and imploiment, hauehave in time ſoso forgotten all, as if they had neuernever beenebeen trained vpup in learning: and ſoso in other ſciencessciences.

2. Thus come they to doedo much more good in Church or Commoncommon-wealth: till men be placed in diſtinctdistinct callings, they are but fitting and preparing for future times. I deniedeny not but that both Church and Commoncommon-wealth may reapereap much benefit by the painespains and labour of the younger ſortsort, who are trained vpup vnderunder others: but moſtmost properly are they counted members of the Church and Commoncommon-wealth, and actuallactual inſtrumentsinstruments of the good thereof, who hauehave ſomesome particular diſtinctdistinct calling, whereby they doedo good to others.

3. Thus they come to liuelive of themſeluesthemselves, and to be able to releeuerelieve others alſoalso. All the time of their education, they are commonly at the charge of others: at leaſtleast, though by their painespains they may gainegain much, yet the gainegain returnesreturns to others: they themſeluesthemselves for the moſtmost part hauehave but a bare maintenance, meat, drinkedrink and cloth (as we ſaysay:) little hauehave they to lay vpup for themſeluesthemselves for the time to come, or to giuegive to others for the preſentpresent.

4. They thus come to trainetrain vpup others againſtagainst after times, as they themſeluesthemselves hauehave beenebeen trained vpup: whereby a continuallcontinual and perpetuallperpetual ſucceſſionsuccession of all kindeskinds of callings, is from time to time preſeruedpreserved: and thus Familyfamily, Church, and Commoncommon-wealth vpheldupheld and maintained. In ſhortshort time would all callings and functions vtterlyutterly decay, if a continuallcontinual ſuppliesupply were not thus made.

div.head: §. 51. Direction for parents in prouidingproviding callings for their children.
div.p: Two eſpeciallespecial cautions are to be obſeruedobserved by parents in Cautions in prouidingproviding callings. prouidingproviding callings for their children.

1. That ſuchsuch callings be prouidedprovided as their children hauehave beenebeen trained vpup vntounto, and are in ſomesome meaſuremeasure fitted and enabled to performeperform the duties thereof: as to prouideprovide a MiniſtersMinisters

They that by lawfulllawful meanesmeans are brought into a calling whereunto they are fitted, are ſetset therein by God, as is implied by this phraſephrase, as God hath called eueryevery one, &etcc. div.head: §. 52. Of the extremes contrary to a parents lawfulllawful care in prouidingproviding fit callings for his children. 1. Extreme in the defect.
div.p:
The extreme in the defect contrary to a parents prouidentprovident care in prouidingproviding a fit calling, is, a careleſſecareless neglect of children after they are well educated, a leauingleaving them to ſhiftshift for themſeluesthemselves. Imitari noli crudelitatem earum auium quibus vngues adunciſuntaduncisunt: hi cùm ſuossuos ſenſerintsenserint foetus volandi iom poteſtatempotestatem conſequutosconsequutos eſſeesse, alis eos verberantes ac impingentes nidis pellunt, nullam
que nullamque prorſusprorsus erga illos extruſosextrusos curam de • inceps adhibent. BaſilBasil. Hexam. hom. 8. It is noted of the rauenousravenous fowles that hauehave ſharpesharpe talents, that ſoso ſoonesoon as they perceiueperceive their young ones to be able to fly, they will flap and beat them with their wings, and driuedrive them out of their neſtsnests, and after that take no further care of them. We may not be like ſuchsuch cruellcruel birds: reaſonreason a • nd religion teacheth vsus otherwiſeotherwise. Good education is a good duty, but not a parents whole duty: the ſtaystay which is here made, may make all the former care and painespains to be of little v •• ſeuse.

div.head: ObiectObject. This is to be left to Gods prouidenceprovidence.
div.p:
AnſwAnsw. MeanesMeans rightly vſedused are ſubordinatesubordinate to Gods prouidenceprovidence, and by them doth God manifeſtmanifest his prouidenceprovidence and bring his counſellcounsel to paſſepass: to neglect meanesmeans is to thwart and
croſſecross the diuinedivine prouidenceprovidence. It is therefore well done to rely on Gods prouidenceprovidence: but ill done to neglect the meanesmeans of effecting it. Gods bleſſingblessing is beſtbest diſcerneddiscerned in the vſeuse of meanesmeans.

BeſidesBesides, though children be neuernever ſoso fit 〈◊〉 for theſethese callings, yet there is little hope of any bleſſingblessing from God, when the firſtfirst entrance is without him: yea againſtagainst his will and word. Who can thinkethink that God hath placed ſuchsuch an • one in his place? ifIf God hauehave not placed him, with what faith can he ſeekeseek a bleſſingblessing? withWith what hope can he expect a blessing? Much terror is by this meanesmeans brought to many men conſcienceconscience: and they are oft in a great ſtraitstrait, not knowing whether it be fitteſtfittest for them to retaineretain, or relinquiſhrelinquish their ••

then ſafeſtsafest for him to ſeekeseek pardon for the former offence, and reconciliation with God, and vponupon true and vnfainedunfained repentance to hold the place (if at leaſtleast the law vnderunder which he liuethliveth eſtabliſhestablish him therein) and be ſoso much the more faithfullfaithful in the diſchargedischarge of the duties thereof.

div.head: §. 53. Of parents care in prouidingproviding fit mariagesmarriages for their children.
div.p:
God hath further laid a charge vponupon parents to prouideprovide mariagesmarriages Date operam vt cùm ad adultāadultan aetatem filij peruenerint matrimenio iungantur. ConſtitConstit. If any man thinkethink that he behauethbehaveth himſelfehimself vncomelyuncomely toward his virgin, if ſheshe paſſepass the floureflour of her age, and need ſoso require, let them marry. This direction was giuengiven in times of perſecutionpersecution, when by reaſonreason of the preſentpresent neceſſitynecessity it was better not to marry: if then a parent ought to be carefullcareful (need requiring) to prouideprovide a mariagemarriage for his daughter, much more ought he in times of peace. Not only holy ApoſtlesApostles, but alſoalso Liberos qui voluptatibus nimis ſuntsunt dediti dabis operam vt coniugio aſtringasastringas: vinculum enim hoc eſtest tutiſſimumtutissimum inventutis.
