div.head: §. 54. Direction to parents in prouidingproviding mariagesmarriages.
div.p: Two cautions are to be obſeruedobserved of parents in prouidingproviding mariagesmarriages for their children.

1. That the match which they prouideprovide be meet: ſoso ſaidsaid God when he was about to prouideprovide a match for Adam, I will
Gen. 2. 18. make him an helpehelp meet for him. Therefore See Treat. 2. Part. 1. §. 9, 10 &etcc. the match prouidedprovided muſtmust not be too neerenear of kin, of a contrary religion, of too vnequallunequal an age, of too great diſparitydisparity in eſtateestate. TheſeThese things will hinder louelove, and cauſecause diſdainedisdain and hatred of one another.

2. Though the match may ſeemeseem meet in the parents eieeye, yet he may not force his childechild thereto. Could a fitter match hauehave beenebeen found out for Rebekah then IſaakIsaac? yet Rebekahs friends Gen. 24. 57. What to be done if children like not ſuchsuch a match as parents thinkethink meet. Non cogitur filius-familias vxorem ducere. DigeſtDigest. l. 23. c. 2. §. 21. asked her conſentconsent. I deniedeny not but parents may vſeuse all manner of fairefair meanesmeans to mouemove their children to yeeldyield to that which they ſeesee good for them: but if they cannot mouemove them to yeeldyield, to referrerefer the matter to God, and not againſtagainst their childrens minds to force them. When God had made a moſtmost meet match for Adam, he brought her to the man: namely to ſeesee how he would like her. For the neereſtnearest bond of all is betwixt man and wife; a man muſtmust leaueleave father and mother, and
Gen. 2. 22. Sacra in hoc negotio parentibus authoritas eſſeesse debet: ſedsed tenenda eſtest media ratio, vt ſpontesponte ac mutuo conſenſuconsensu inter ſese contrahant partesparts. Cal. in Gen. 24. verſvers. 57. cleauecleave vntounto his wife; man and wife muſtmust alwaiesalways liuelive together: great reaſonreason therefore that at the firſtfirst ioyningjoining them together there be a mutuallmutual liking of one another, leſtlest euerever after there be a perpetuallperpetual diſlikedislike: and though the authority of parents ought in this caſecase to be inuiolableinviolable, yet a middle courſecourse is ſoso to be held, as the parties may willingly with a mutuallmutual conſentconsent ioynejoin themſeluesthemselves together.

div.head: §. 55. Of the extremes contrary to parents care in prouidingproviding fit mariagesmarriages for their children.
div.p:
The extreme in the defect is, when parents careleſlycarelessly let their children paſſepass the floureflour of their age: and neuernever conſiderconsider whether need require that they ſhouldshould marymarry or no. Their children may ſitsit long enough before they ſeekeseek out a match for them, vnleſſeunless it be brought to them: and when one is offered though it be neuernever ſoso fit, yet except they may make an aduantageadvantage thereof to themſeluesthemselves, they will hardly yeeldyield to it. Thus they make their children to ſeekeseek out mariagesmarriages for themſeluesthemselves, and
without their conſentconsent to make them vpup: or elſeelse to liuelive in diſcontentdiscontent, Si filij innupti feruore aetatis in conſuetudinemconsuetudinem ſornicandisornicandi inciderint, vos parentesparents in die iudicij rationem deo eſtisestis reddituri. ConſtitConstit. ApoſtApost. l. 4. c. 11. if not in vncleanneſſeuncleanness. By the careleſneſſecarelessness of parents in this reſpectrespect are children oft made a prey to the deuilldevil: whereof at the day of iudgementjudgment parents ſhallshall giuegive an account to God.

The extreme in the exceſſeexcess is, See Treat. 2. Part. 1. §. 2. when parents through a couetouscovetous deſiredesire to get great and rich matches for their children, mariemarry them before they be of yearesyears of diſcretiondiscretion to like or diſlikedislike, to know what is meet or vnmeetunmeet; or able to performeperform eueneven the eſſentiallessential duties of mariagesmarriages: ſeldomeseldom doedo ſuchsuch vnlawfullunlawful mariagesmarriages proſperprosper.

In a like exceſſeexcess doedo they offend who for outward aduantagesadvantages match their children to ſuchsuch as by nature are vnfitunfit for mariagemarriage, to ideots, to See Treat. 2. Part. 1. §. 11, 12. idolaters, to profane perſonspersons, or they care not to whom. And if their children like not theſethese matches, they will doedo to the vttermoſtuttermost of their power what they can to force them thereunto. Many miſchiefesmischiefs ordinarily fall out vponupon ſuchsuch mariagesmarriages, as vtterutter diſlikedislike betwixt husband and wife, continuallcontinual complaining one of another, inquiring after diuorcedivorce, or any other ſeparationseparation, wiſhingwishing, yea practiſingpractising one anothers death. To all theſethese miſchiefesmischiefs doedo parents, the cauſecause thereof, make themſeluesthemselves acceſſaryaccessary.

div.head: §. 56. Of parents prouidingproviding a ſtockestock for callings and mariagesmarriages of their children.
div.p: An eſpeciallespecial outward meanesmeans whereby parents may be the better inabled to prouideprovide fit callings and mariagesmarriages for their children, is, before hand to lay vpup ſomesome ſtockestock, or competent portion for their children. This is compriſedcomprised vnderunder that generallgeneral prouiſionprovision, whereof he that is careleſſecareless is counted by the ApoſtleApostle 1 Tim. 5. 8. worſeworse then an inſidellinsidell: but more expreſlyexpressly is it noted in theſethese words, 2 Cor. 12. 14. Parentsparents ought to lay vpup for their children: and commended in Gen. 25. 5, 6. AbrahamsAbraham's example.

While children are vnderunder their parents they hauehave no meanesmeans to lay vpup for themſeluesthemselves: for all their ſeruiceservice is for their parents. But in regard of the times wherein we liuelive, it is needfullneedful for ſettingsetting vpup in a good calling, and for obtaining a fit match, that children hauehave ſomesome ſtockestock and portion. It
lieth therefore vponupon the parents, and their duty it is to prouideprovide it.

div.head: ObiectObject. ChriſtChrist forbiddeth to lay vpup treaſurestreasures on earth. Mat • . 6 19. expounded.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. If the ſcopescope of that place be rightly marked, it will appeareappear that ChriſtChrist there forbiddeth not ſimplysimply the thing it ſelfeself, but

1. The mindemind of him that layeth vpup: namely when it is filled full of carking, and diſtruſtfulldistrustful thoughts: fearing that in the time to come he ſhallshall not hauehave ſufficientsufficient. To this purpoſepurpose doth ChriſtChrist propound Gods prouidenceprovidence ouerover fowles and VerſVers. 26, 28. lillies.

2. The manner of laying vpup, when temporalltemporal things are preferred before ſpirituallspiritual and heauenlyheavenly: therefore he addeth this precept, but lay vpup treaſurestreasures in heauenheaven, &etcc.
UerſUers. 20.

3. The meaſuremeasure, when men neuernever thinkethink they hauehave laid vpup enough: but ſcrapescrape what they can come by iuſtlyjustly or vniuſtlyunjustly; and ſparespare more then needs, eueneven things neceſſarynecessary, from themſeluesthemselves and others, to make a great ſtockestock and portion for their children. The word of
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . Direction for laying vpup portions. treaſuringtreasuring vpup (which ChriſtChrist there vſethuseth) implieth an immoderate meaſuremeasure.
Among other needfullneedful cautions for parents to be obſeruedobserved in laying vpup for their children, theſethese three are eſpeciallyespecially to be noted.

1. That iuſtlyjustly they come by that which they lay vpup: and lay nothing towards a childs portion which is any way vniuſtlyunjustly gotten; for the treaſurestreasures of wickedneſſewickedness profit nothing: they may Pro. 10. 2. proueprove a fire to conſumeconsume parents themſeluesthemselves, their children, their houſehouse, and whole poſterityposterity.

2. That they couetcovet not too much to make their children rich, and for that purpoſepurpose liuelive meanly and baſelybasely themſeluesthemselves, yea and depriuedeprive themſeluesthemselves of many neceſſariesnecessaries. An egregious Eccl. 5. 12. point of folly is this, which Solomon hath much taxed.
3. That all needfullneedful duties of charity to the poorepoor, and of iuſticejustice to the Church and common-wealth be performed, and pretext of laying vpup for children hinder none of theſethese.

div.head: §. 57. Of the extremes contrary to a parents prouidingproviding portions for his children.
div.p: The extremes contrary to the forenamed dutieduty are theſethese:

1. When parents liuelive at the vttermoſtuttermost extent of their eſtateestate, and from time to time ſpendspend all their reuenuesrevenues or all their gaines, and ſoso are ſcarcescarce able to make eueneven at quarter day, or yearesyears end. What ſtockestock or portion can they lay vpup for children?

2. When parents liuelive aboueabove their eſtateestate, and ſpendspend riotouſlyriotously their ordinary gaines, or reuenuesrevenues, and for other neceſſarynecessary affairesaffairs are forced to runnerun into debt. Many are ſoso farrefar from helping their children in this kindekind, as they are mainemain hinderancehindrance vntounto them, vrgingurging their eldeſteldest ſonneson eſpeciallyespecially who is their heireheir, to be bound for them, and ſoso lay ſuchsuch a burden on his backeback, as (to vſeuse the common phraſephrase) they make it crackecrack againeagain.

3. When parents hauehave enough for themſeluesthemselves and their children, and yet ſoso couetouſlycovetously dote vponupon their wealth, as they will not beſtowbestow a groat to helpehelp them in calling and mariagemarriage, but ſaysay they keepekeep all for them. What a wretched and fooliſhfoolish diſpoſitiondisposition is this, that they ſhouldshould ſtillstill lay vpup more and more for their children, and yet refuſerefuse to beſtowbestow any part thereof vponupon them in their greateſtgreatest need, when it might redound to their greateſtgreatest benefit? God oft meeteth with ſuchsuch couetouscovetous miſersmisers, and croſſethcrosseth their purpoſespurposes, by making ſtrangersstrangers to enioyenjoy that which they greedily hoorded vpup.

div.head: §. 58. Of parents last ſpeechspeech to their children.
div.p: The laſtlast dutieduty which parents owe to their children, is, when they ceaſecease to be parents: that is, when they are going out of this world. Their dutieduty at that time in generallgeneral is to doedo what lieth in them, that it may goego well with their children after their departure. Both See §. 6. the reaſonsreasons which are oft vrgedurged by the Holy GhoſtGhost, to ſtirstir vpup parents to yeeldyield obedience to God, taken from extent of Gods bleſſingblessing (in this kindekind of phraſephrase, Pro. 20. 7. BleſſedBlessed ſhallshall their children be after them) and Gods Deut. 5. 29. promiſespromises made to that purpoſepurpose doedo proueprove as much.

For the better performing of this dutieduty, three generallgeneral points, tending both to the temporalltemporal, and alſoalso to the ſpirituallspiritual good of children, are to be obſeruedobserved: and two particular points moſtmost tending to their temporalltemporal eſtateestate.

The three generals are theſethese.
1. Good direction.
2. FaithfullFaithful prayer.
3. A wiſewise choiſechoice of ſomesome friends to be as parents to them.

1. Parents on their deathbed to leaueleave good leſſonslessons to their children. For direction. When parents obſerueobserve their time to draw neerenear, they ought to commend ſomesome wiſewise and wholſomewholesome precepts vntounto their children, the better to direct them in their ChriſtianChristian courſecourse. So did Gen. 28. 2, 4. IſaakIsaac, and & 49. 1. &etcc.
IaakobJacob.
Ob. TheſeThese Patriarchs had an extraordinarieextraordinary ſpiritspirit of prophecying, & by vertuevirtue thereof foretold their children things to come.

AnſwAnsw. See Treat. 5. §. 9. They ſuſtainedsustained a double perſonperson: one of a prophet, another of a father: as prophets, they had an extraordinarieextraordinary ſpiritspirit; as parents, they performed ordinarieordinary dutieduty: by their extraordinarieextraordinary ſpiritspirit, they foretold things to come: the ordinarieordinary dutieduty which they performed, was to direct their children how to carriecarry themſeluesthemselves in thoſethose times to come. For their propheſiesprophesies were not only predictions, but alſoalso inſtructionsinstructions, to direct and teach them what to doedo. What they did by an extraordinarieextraordinary ſpiritspirit in extraordinarieextraordinary things, we muſtmust doedo in ordinarieordinary duties by the ordinarieordinary ſpiritspirit of vnderſtandingunderstanding and wiſdomewisdom which the Lord giuethgiveth vsus. But the direction which Gen. 28. 2. &etcc.
IſaakIsaac gauegave to IaakobJacob, when he ſentsent him to Laban, was no extraordinarieextraordinary propheſieprophesy: nor that which 1 Chro 28. 9. DauidDavid, when he was old, gauegave to Solomon: and againeagain, 1 King. 2. 2, 3, &etcc. when he lay on his death-bed. Now theſethese things are thus written for our imitation. And great reaſonreason there is to imitate thoſethose holy men in theſethese things. For

1. The words of a dying parent are commonly moſtmost regarded: his laſtlast words doedo make a deepedeep impreſſionimpression ( Gen. 50. 16. this doedo the brethren of IoſephJoseph preſſepress vponupon him.) If euerever therefore there be a time ſeaſonableseasonable for a parent to giuegive good inſtructionsinstructions to his children, then is the time when parents are cleaneclean departing from their children.

2. Thus ſhallshall a parent manifeſtmanifest his true affection, and earneſtearnest deſiredesire of his childrens good: for now they cannot thinkethink that he ſeekethseeketh his owneown eaſeease, and profit, more then their good: as at other times ſomesome will be ready to ſaysay of their parents inſtructionsinstructions and admonitions, Our parents know what is good for themſeluesthemselves.

That the laſtlast words of parents may be the more ſeaſonablyseasonably and Direction. profitably deliuereddelivered to their children, they muſtmust note, on the one
ſideside, what euilsevils their children are moſtmost prone vntounto, what temptations they are moſtmost aſſaultedassaulted withallwithal, what ſnaressnares they are moſtmost like to fall into; and on the other ſideside, what vertuesvirtues and graces are moſtmost needfullneedful for them, and wherein they failefail moſtmost, and accordingly they muſtmust order and frame their laſtlast words. Note for a patternepattern herein Gen. 28, 2, &etcc.
IſaaksIsaaks counſellcounsel to IaakobJacob, when he ſentsent him to Laban, and thought he ſhouldshould neuernever ſeesee him againeagain: and 1 King. 2. 2, 3. DauidsDavid's to his ſonneson Solomon.

div.head: §. 59. Of Parents laſtlast bleſſingblessing to their children.
div.p:
II. Concerning the prayers of parents for their children, I noted it §. 4. before to be a generallgeneral dutieduty neuernever to be omitted: yet here in particular I mention it againeagain, becauſebecause a parents bleſſingblessing conſiſtethconsisteth therein eſpeciallyespecially: and then is the moſtmost proper time for parents to beſtowbestow a bleſſingblessing on their children, as Gen. 28. 3. IſaakIsaac,
& 48. 15. IaakobJacob, 1 Chro. 29. 19. DauidDavid, and others did. Let parents therefore as they commend their owneown ſoulessouls into Gods hand, ſoso commend their children vntounto Gods grace and bleſſingblessing. Gods prouidenceprovidence is a good inheritance: many children doedo thereby exceedingly proſperprosper, though they hauehave but ſmallsmall outward meanesmeans; whereas others that hauehave great meanesmeans vſedused for their good, come to ruineruin; Gods curſecurse following them. Now no ſuchsuch meanesmeans can be thought of to procure Gods bleſſingblessing, or to with-hold his curſecurse, as the faithfullfaithful prayers of parents for their children; eſpeciallyespecially when parents are leauingleaving their children, and going to God.

div.head: §. 60. Of parents care to commend their children to ſomesome faithfullfaithful friends.
div.p:
III. The third generallgeneral point of making choiſechoice of ſomesome faithfullfaithful friends to commend their children vntounto, is eſpeciallyespecially in behalfebehalf of ſuchsuch as are not of ſufficientsufficient age and diſcretiondiscretion to lookelook to themſeluesthemselves, or to thoſethose weightieweighty affairesaffairs which belong vntounto them. The friends, which in this caſecase are made choiſechoice of, ought to be ſuchsuch as the parents themſeluesthemselves by good experience hauehave found to be honeſthonest, wiſewise, faithfullfaithful, and louingloving to them and theirs; whom parents are to ſetset in their owneown place for the good of their children. This meanesmeans did DauidDavid vſeuse when he was old in the behalfebehalf 1 Chro. 22. 17. & 28. 21. of his ſonneson Solomon. Many children hauehave found much helpehelp thereby. Such may make a good ſupplysupply of the departure of parents. TheſeThese are ſoso much the more needfullneedful, by how much
the more vnſtableunstable, and vnbridledunbridled youth is; and by how much the leſſeless able children are to helpehelp and guide themſeluesthemselves.

div.head: §. 61. Of parents neglect of their children for the time to come.
div.p: Contrary to a parents prouidenceprovidence for the good of his children after his departure, is the careleſneſſecarelessness of parents for the time to come. They thinkethink the world is gone with them when they are gone, and therefore they will take no thought for the future times that ſhallshall be after them; as if it were enough for eueryevery one to lookelook to his owneown time. There may ſeemeseem to be more ſelfeself-louelove in ſuchsuch parents then louelove of their children, in that their care determineth with their owneown time, and extendeth not it ſelfeself to the time and continuance of their children. Hence is it, that not a word of direction and exhortation commethcometh out of their mouths to their children when they are departing, no bleſſingblessing that they will leaueleave behindebehind them, no friends ſhallshall be deputed by them, to be as parents to their children. Let God prouideprovide, ſaysay they. But where there is a referring of matters to Gods prouidenceprovidence, without the vſeuse of thoſethose meanesmeans which God hath warranted and commended by his word, there can be little hope that God ſhouldshould take care of that which is ſoso commended to him. Such men doedo not in faith depend vponupon Gods prouidenceprovidence, but make the very name thereof a pretext to caſtcast off that care, which God as a bounden dutieduty requireth of them. As there is little louelove of their children in ſuchsuch parents, ſoso there is leſſeless zealezeal of Gods glory: for a parents care of his childrens welfare, eſpeciallyespecially of their continuing to fearefear and ſerueserve the Lord after their owneown departure out of this world, is an eſpeciallespecial meanesmeans of preſeruingpreserving Gods fearefear in the world, and propagating it from age to age: ſoso as this neglect is a greater fault then many are aware of.

div.head: §. 62. Of parents making a Will before they die.
div.p:
The two particular things to be obſeruedobserved by parents for manifeſtationmanifestation of their prouidentprovident care ouerover their children for the time to come, eueneven after their departure, eſpeciallyespecially in regard of their temporalltemporal eſtateestate, are theſethese,
1. That they make a will.
2. That they leaueleave their eſtatesestates to their children.

1. It hath beenebeen an ancient commendable practiſepractise both among A Will to be made. Gods people, and others alſoalso, that hauehave beenebeen guided with
common ciuilitiecivility, when they who hauehave any eſtateestate, waxewax old, or ſickesick, and hauehave any occaſionoccasion of expecting death offered vntounto them, to make their laſtlast Will and teſtamenttestament. This is ſetset forth in the old TeſtamentTestament vnderunder this phraſephrase (Put thy houſehouse in order.) A dutieduty it is expreſlyexpressly 2 King. 20. 1. commanded by God: and that not without good reaſonreason. For

1. A parents Will is an eſpeciallespecial meanesmeans to ſettlesettle peace among children after his departure, and to make them content with that allowance which he hath ſetset out vntounto them, becauſebecause by the Will they know it was their fathers pleaſurepleasure they ſhouldshould hauehave ſuchsuch and ſuchsuch a portion. If controuerſiescontroversies ſhouldshould ariſearise, yet a Will is a meanesmeans for the law ſpeedilyspeedily to determine the ſamesame without any tedious and chargeable ſuitssuits: for the ApoſtleApostle taketh it for a ruled caſecase, that no man diſanullethdisannuleth or addeth any thing to a mans' teſtamenttestament.
Gal. 3. 15.

2. After a parent hath made his Will, he may the more quietly ſettlesettle himſelfehimself for heauenlyheavenly contemplations, and preparations to death: and thinkethink of ſuchsuch good inſtructionsinstructions as are moſtmost fit to giuegive as his farewell to his children: and the more willingly expect the moment of his diſſolutiondissolution: and the more patiently ſubmitsubmit himſelfehimself to the very ſtrokestroke of death.

In performing this dutieduty, a man muſtmust both obſerueobserve a fit time, Direction. and alſoalso take good aduiceadvice. The fit time is while his vnderſtandingunderstanding is good, and his memoriememory perfect: ſoso as he may call to mindemind his debts, what he oweth, and what is owing to him: as alſoalso what goods he hath to beſtowbestow, and with diſcretiondiscretion and wiſdomewisdom order his eſtateestate. And becauſebecause through the cauilscavils which many vnconſcionableunconscionable lawyers and others are like to make, his true meaning may be peruertedperverted, it is meet to hauehave the aduiceadvice of ſuchsuch as can in diſtinctdistinct words and phraſesphrases ſoso expreſſeexpress his meaning, as they ſhallshall be free from exception. Matters of weight are wiſelywisely to be managed.

div.head: §. 63. Of neglecting to make a Will.
div.p:
Contrary is the daily practiſepractise of too many parents who are not willing to make any will at all: or elſeelse on vainevain hope that they may liuelive longer, and when they are ſickesick, vponupon conceit that they may recouerrecover, or at leaſtleast longer continue to enioyenjoy the vſeuse of their vnderſtandingunderstanding and memory, put off the making of their Will till it be too late: and ſoso die without Will,
or make ſuchsuch a Will as miniſtrethministreth more matter of ſutesuit, then if they had no Will at all; either becauſebecause doubt is made whether he that made it had his vnderſtandingunderstanding and memory or no: or becauſebecause his Will is ſoso abrupt and ambiguous, as his meaning cannot be knowneknown. The miſchiefesmischiefs that follow theſethese neglects, InconuenienceInconvenience of dying without a Will. are many. As
1. DiſcreditDiscredit to the partieparty deceaſeddeceased.
2. Contentions among his ſuruiuingsurviving children.
3. WaſtingWasting a great part, if not his whole eſtateestate, in ſuitssuits of law.
4. Defeating many creditors of their due debt.

The reaſonreason which maketh many to put off the making of their Will is a fooliſhfoolish conceit, that if a mans Will be once made, then he muſtmust needs die out of hand. But what ground hauehave men for any ſuchsuch conceit? If ſicknessickness grow vponupon a man, ſoso long as his Will is vnmadeunmade his mindemind is vnſetledunsetled, his mindemind being vnſetledunsetled, the phyſickephysic that is miniſtredministered to him cannot ſoso kindly workework; ſoso as his death may be the more haſtenedhastened for not making a Will. BeſidesBesides, if his ſpeechspeech failefail before his vnderſtandingunderstanding, the thought that then he ſhallshall die without a Will may ſoso perplex him, as his departure will be very vnquietunquiet and troubleſometroublesome.

div.head: §. 64. Of parents leauingleaving their eſtateestate to their children when they die.
div.p:
It was §. 56. before ſhewedshowed that parents were to lay vpup a portion for their children againſtagainst their entrance into a calling, and mariagemarriage: There is a further duty required when they are going out of the world, namely that they leaueleave their whole eſtateestate The eſtateestate of parents to be left to their children. to their children. (Where I ſaysay whole, I exempt not workesworks of charity, nor payment of debts, which is a point of iuſticejustice, but I include more then is giuengiven as portions or ſtockesstocks in their life time.) That eſtateestate eſpeciallyespecially which parents hauehave receiuedreceived from their progenitors are they moſtmost bound to leaueleave vntounto their children. It is expreſlyexpressly recorded that Abraham gauegave all
Gen. 25. 5. that he had to IſaakIsaac. Gods law did prouideprovide for this among the IewesJews: for a man might not ſellsell his land to cut it off from Leu. 25. 23. his poſterityposterity. This was it that made Naboth refuſerefuse to ſellsell his vineyard to Ahab, as his anſweranswer implieth, God forbid that I 1 King. 21. 3.
ſhouldshould giuegive the inheritance of my fathers vntounto thee: becauſebecause it was the inheritance of his fathers, that is, he had receiuedreceived it from them, he thought it vnlawfullunlawful to depriuedeprive his children of it. This phraſephrase (if children, then heiresheirs) taketh it for a granted Rom. 8. 17. truth that children hauehave a right to their parents eſtateestate: and if they hauehave a right thereto, they may not be defeated thereof.

God giuethgiveth wealth vntounto parents but for their life time: in which time they are but as Guardians vntounto Gods children, and are accountable to God: ſoso as they hauehave not an abſoluteabsolute power to doedo with it what they will, but according to the directions of the great Lord and Maſtermaster they muſtmust vſeuse it, reſeruereserve it, and leaueleave it.

For this end parents muſtmust order their manner of liuingliving according Direction. to that portion which the Lord hath appointed vntounto them, and by his prouidenceprovidence beſtowedbestowed vponupon them; they muſtmust (as it is ſaidsaid in the prouerbeproverb) cut their coat according to their cloth. Of the two it is much better for parents to liuelive vnderunder, then aboueabove their meanesmeans. ProuidedProvided that they neglect no duty of charitiecharity, or iuſticejustice: nor through miſerableneſſemiserableness and niggardlineſſeniggardliness carry themſeluesthemselves vnbeſeemingunbeseeming the place wherein God hath ſetset them, and eſtateestate which he hath beſtowedbestowed vponupon them. He that liuethliveth ſomewhatsomewhat vnderunder his meanesmeans, hath opportunitieopportunity to lay vpup portions for other children (if he hauehave many) and to reſeruereserve his inheritance intireentire to his eldeſteldest (beſidebeside many other good workesworks of charity as God ſhallshall offer occaſionoccasion) which he that liuethliveth aboueabove his meanesmeans cannot doedo.

div.head: §. 65. Of the inconueniencesinconveniences which improuidentimprovident parents bring their children vntounto after their death.
div.p: Contrary to this branch of a parents prouidenceprovidence, are many courſescourses of improuidentimprovident parents: For

1. Some parents lauiſhlavish and bezellbezel out all their eſtateestate in their owneown life time, making it to determine in their perſonspersons. VnworthyUnworthy they are to receiuereceive any inheritance from anceſtorsancestors. Their fault is double.
1. In ſpendingspending prodigally aboueabove their eſtateestate.

2. In wronging their children, and depriuingdepriving them of their right: for particular perſonspersons ſuccedingsucceding one another are but as diuersdivers linkeslinks of a continued family, which are by Gods
prouidenceprovidence added one to another: this chainechain is not to be broken at any mans pleaſurepleasure; but for the preſeruationpreservation thereof, that which hath beenebeen receiuedreceived of the predeceſſorspredecessors, muſtmust be left to the ſucceſſorssuccessors.

2. Others leaueleave their eſtateestate to their children, but ſoso incumbred with debts, bonds, recognizances, and ſtatutesstatutes, as their children were better be without it, then hauehave it. For the hauinghaving it maketh them liuelive at an anſwerableanswerable rate, and bringeth many burdens vponupon them: beſidesbesides, the debts wherein they ſtandstand obliged make them as Pro. 22. 7. ſeruantsservants to their creditors: and in time they muſtmust be forced to ſellsell all, or as captiuescaptives lie in priſonprison.

3. Others though they dealedeal not ſoso hardly with their children, yet they dealedeal too hardly by peeling and polling their inheritance as much as they can: they wilwill not forbeareforbear to make any preſentpresent gainegain that they can, though it tend neuernever ſoso much to the preiudiceprejudice and dammagedamage of their children after them: as they who cut downedown all the timber and wood that they can, and take out all the heart of their land.

4. Among theſethese may be reckoned ſuchsuch parents as by meeremere negligence ſuffersuffer things to goego to decay for want of timely reparations: whereby it commethcometh to paſſepass, that ſuchsuch dammagesdamages as in the parents time might hauehave beenebeen preuentedprevented with laying out a few ſhillingsshillings, cannot be renewed with many pounds.

5. Such alſoalso as care not in their life time to cleereclear the titles of thoſethose things which they leaueleave to their children: but leaueleave all things ſoso vnſetledunsetled and litigious, as it oft coſtscosts children more in ſuitsuit of law to maintainemaintain the inheritance which their parents leaueleave them, then the inheritance is worth: and yet after all their painespains and coſtcost loſelose the inheritance too: whereas the parent that knew more then the childechild can, might with ſmallsmall painespains and charge hauehave well ſetledsettled and cleeredcleared all.

TheſeThese are miſchiefesmischiefs that many children hauehave beenebeen brought into by the improuidenceimprovidence of their parents: which are the rather to be made knowneknown, that ſuchsuch as come after, may proueprove the more prouidentprovident for their children.

div.head: §. 66. Of parents impartiallimpartial reſpectrespect to all their children.
div.p: Hitherto of parents duties. The perſonspersons to whom thoſethose duties are to be performed, are diſtinctlydistinctly to be conſideredconsidered.

The parties to whom parents are to performeperform all the forenamed duties are expreſſedexpressed vnderunder this word (Childrenchildren) which
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . hath not any ſpeciallspecial reſpectrespect to prioritiepriority of birth, to conſtitutionconstitution of body, to affection of parent, or any ſuchsuch thing, as if firſtfirst borne, proper, beautifullbeautiful, darling, or the like children were only meant, but all that are begotten and borne of parents, all their children are meant. Whence I obſerueobserve, that Parentsparents ought to hauehave an impartiallimpartial reſpectrespect to all their children, and performeperform dutieduty indifferently and equally to all. We hauehave for proofeproof hereof Gods patternepattern, who accounteth all his children dearedear or belouedbeloved children. The GreekeGreek word tranſlatedtranslated
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . Eph. 5. 1. dearedear is very emphaticall: it is properly attributed to an only childechild: the ſeuentieseventy that tranſlatedtranslated the Hebrew Bible into GreekeGreek, doedo with this word interpret that phraſephrase, Only Sonneson:
Gen. 22. 2. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . HeſychiusHesychius
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉
exponit
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . Plutarchus dicit
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉
vocari
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . for where in Hebrew it is thus ſaidsaid to Abraham, take thy ſonneson, thine only one, they thus tranſlatetranslate it, take thy ſonneson, thy dearedear one, or thy belouedbeloved one. Other GreekeGreek authors doedo ſoso attribute the ſamesame word to an only childechild, yea also and to an only eieeye: as when a man hath but one eieeye they call it a belouedbeloved eieeye. This word then ſhewethshoweth that God ſoso reſpectethrespecteth all his children, as if all were but one, all a firſtfirst-borne, all a darling childechild. So rare a vertuevirtue this impartiallimpartial reſpectrespect is (rare in the excellencieexcellency of it, rare alſoalso in the ſcarcitiescarcity of it) as thorowoutthroughout the Scripture I can ſcarcescarce findefind a perfect patternepattern thereof AriſtArist. Rhet. 1. vocat vnicumunicum oculum
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . among the ſonnessons of men. Many may be giuengiven of the contrary, as we ſhallshall after hearehear. But the more rare it is, the more we muſtmust labour after it, that ſoso we may reſembleresemble Gods fatherhood.

1. All our children come from our owneown ſubſtancesubstance and ReaſonsReasons. bowels. Why then ſhouldshould we reſpectrespect one childechild aboueabove another, more then we doedo one eieeye, or one eareear aboueabove another? We are as tender ouerover one as ouerover another, though it may be we hauehave more vſeuse of one then of another.

2. All our children are alike committed to vsus by God: the ſamesame precepts and directions giuengiven for all alike: the like account to be giuengiven for all. If a King ſhouldshould commit many of
his children to one nurſenurse, would not he be offended (and that iuſtlyjustly) if ſheshe ſhouldshould put ſuchsuch a difference betwixt them, through a fooliſhfoolish partialitiepartiality, as to reſpectrespect ſomesome, and neglect others?

div.head: §. 67. Of parents preferring a dutifulldutiful childechild before a diſobedientdisobedient childechild.

div.p: ObiectObject. What if one childechild be more pious to God and parent, another more rebellious, may not a parent reſpectrespect that more then this?

1. AnſwAnsw. He may take notice of their different carriage, and accordingly reward the one, and puniſhpunish the other, and yet carriecarry an equallequal deſiredesire of doing good to both of them alike: for the puniſhingpunishing of the rebellious childechild is a parents dutieduty; an euidenceevidence of louelove, and a meanesmeans of doing him good.

2. AnſwAnsw. It is no partialitiepartiality to like grace and goodneſſegoodness in a childechild, and for grace and goodneſſegoodness ſakesake to louelove his childechild ſoso much the more, as alſoalso for impietieimpiety and obſtinacyobstinacy in rebellion to hauehave his heart the more alienated from his childechild: this is rather a vertuevirtue in a parent. PartialitiePartiality is when on by and vndueundue reſpectsrespects one childechild is preferred before another.

div.head: §. 68. Of the prerogatiueprerogative of the firſtfirst-borne ſonneson.
QueſtQuest. May not a parent preferreprefer his firſtfirst-borne childechild, and heireheir before his other children?
div.p: AnſwAnsw. We muſtmust put difference betwixt a fathers diſpoſingdisposing his eſtateestate vponupon his children, and the ordering of his affection towards them. A parents affection, and care of good education, and deſiredesire of true good, and faithfullfaithful praiersprayers to God, may be as great towards his younger children, as towards his eldeſteldest ſonneson and heireheir, and yet may he beſtowbestow the greateſtgreatest patrimony vponupon the heireheir: which is no partialitiepartiality.

div.head: 2. QueſtQuest. Is it then iuſtjust and equallequal that the eldeſteldest ſonneson ſhouldshould hauehave a greater patrimony then any of the reſtrest?
div.p: AnſwAnsw. It is moſtmost iuſtjust and equallequal. For

1. God hath ſoso appointed it: yea Deut. 21. 17. he made this to be one of the prerogatiuesprerogatives of the firſtfirst-borne, to hauehave a double portion. VponUpon this ground 1 Chr. 5. 2. IoſephJoseph, who was the firſtfirst-borne of the true wife, had a double portion; and as a teſtimonytestimony thereof his poſteritieposterity made two tribes.
2. The laweslaws of all nations doedo order as much.

3. Our law giuethgiveth the whole inheritance of freeholds to the eldeſteldest ſonneson: in which reſpectrespect it is due vntounto him. For in ciuillcivil and temporalltemporal matters this rule is true, we liuelive by law. I take it to be a matter of conſcienceconscience for a parent to leaueleave that to eueryevery childechild which by law is due to him. Neither is it without good reaſonreason that the law ordaineth that a parents whole eſtateestate of freehold land ſhouldshould deſcenddescend: for

1. There is an excellency in the firſtfirst borne, as is euidentevident by IaakobsJacob's ſpeechspeech to his eldeſteldest ſonneson, Gen. 49. 3. thou art my firſtfirst borne, my might, and the beginning of my ſtrengthstrength, the excellency of dignity, and the excellency of power. And thereupon Exod. 13. 2. God tooketook the firſtfirst borne as peculiar to himſelfehimself.

2. HouſesHouses and families by this meanesmeans are vpheldupheld and continued from age to age. How needfullneedful it is for the eſtabliſhmentestablishment of a commonwealth that families ſhouldshould thus be continued, is euidentevident both by experience to all ſuchsuch as hauehave but halfehalf an eieeye to ſeesee wherein the ſtabilitystability of a common wealth conſiſtethconsisteth, and alſoalso by the many laweslaws which God ordained among the IewesJews for this purpoſepurpose: as
1. That Leu. 25. 23. no land ſhouldshould be quite cut off from a family.
2. That VerſVers. 25. if any through pouertypoverty were forced to ſellsell his land, the next of kin was to buy it.

3. That VerſVers. 28. if a man that had ſoldsold his land, could by no meanesmeans redeemeredeem it againeagain, at the yeereyear of IubileeJubilee he was to hauehave the poſſeſſionpossession of it againeagain.

4. That Num. 36. 8. if daughters were heiresheirs they ſhouldshould not marry out of their fathers tribe: and this reaſonreason is giuengiven, that eueryevery man may enioyenjoy the inheritance of his fathers.

div.head: ObiectObject. By leauingleaving the whole inheritance to the eldeſteldest, he may be made a Gentleman, and all the other beggars.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. In this reſpectrespect parents ought to be ſoso much the more prouidentprovident for their other children, in training them vpup to callings, or laying vpup portions, or ſetlingsettling other eſtatesestates vponupon them beſidebeside the mainemain inheritance, or in taking order that compet • ent portions be raiſedraised out of the inheritance of the eldeſteldest ſonson, in • n caſecase God take them away before they hauehave otherwiſeotherwise prou • idedprovided for their children.

Out of this anſweranswer may a third reaſonreason be gathered, to ſhewshow that it is a behouefullbehoveful law for the commonwealth that the heireheir ſhouldshould hauehave all the land. For this law maketh parents more carefullcareful in training vpup their younger ſonnessons to ſundrysundry callings which are profitable to a commonwealth. If eueryevery childechild ſhouldshould hauehave a part of his fathers lands, they would all ſoso depend thereupon, as none of them would exerciſeexercise themſeluesthemselves to ſuchsuch callings as are meanesmeans of mens maintenance.

div.head: §. 69. Of parents partiality towards ſomesome children.
div.p: Contrary to the forenamed duty of a parents equallequal reſpectrespect to all his children, is partiality in fathers and mothers, manifeſtedmanifested ſundrysundry waiesways. For

1. Many parents hauehave their darling children, to whom ſoso IniquiſſimaIniquissima volucris aquila in educanda ſuasua prole dicitur eſſeesse. Pullorum enim alterum alis percuſſumpercussum abigit: alterum ſolumsolum vti ſuumsuum educat. BaſilBasil. Hexaem. hom. 8. much affection is ſhewedshowed, as in compariſoncomparison none is ſhewedshowed to others. When ſomesome are hugged in the boſomebosom, others are neglected as if they were none of their owneown, but baſelybasely borne. The vnnaturalneſſeunnaturalness of the eagle is noted in this kindekind, that ſheshe flaps and driuesdrives out of the neſtnest one of her young ones, and feedeth only the other as her owneown. From ſuchsuch partiality in parents proceed many miſchiefesmischiefs: as theſethese,
1. They giuegive occaſionoccasion to ſuchsuch as obſerueobserve it, to ſuſpectsuspect that thoſethose children who are ſoso little reſpectedrespected, are none of their owneown.

2. They cauſecause enuyenvy, malice, and much contention to ariſearise among children. When IoſephsJosephs brethren ſawsaw that their father
Gen. 37. 4. louedloved him more then all them, they hated him, and could not ſpeakespeak peaceably vntounto him.
3. They prouokeprovoke God to inflict ſomesome iudgementjudgment on thoſethose children that are ſoso cockered, and preferred before the reſtrest: that ſoso they may the better ſeesee their folly.

This ſinnesin of parents partiality is ſoso much the greater, when vponupon outward reſpectsrespects they preferreprefer the wicked and vngodlyungodly children before pious and gracious children. IſaakIsaac herein much failed, for Gen. 25. 28. he louedloved EſauEsau (a Heb. 12. 16. profane wretch) becauſebecause he did eat of his VeniſonVenison.

2. Other parents ſoso ſetset themſeluesthemselves to raiſeraise their houſehouse, as all • their care is to aduanceadvance their eldeſteldest ſonneson, by education, by liberallliberal allowance, and by leauingleaving all they hauehave to him: and in •
the meanemean while neglect their younger children. Though (as was noted §. 68. before) the mainemain inheritance may iuſtlyjustly without ſhewshow of partiality be left to the heireheir, yet to be carefullcareful only for him, and to neglect the other, ſauourethsavoureth rankerank of partiality. It is moſtmost agreeable to naturallnatural reaſonreason, that as life is giuengiven to all ConſentaneumConsentaneum eſtest rationi naturae vt aequè tribuere cui
que cuique vitam, ſicsic etiam viuendi facultates praeſtarepraestare. BaſilBasil. loc. citat. children, ſoso meanesmeans of maintaining life ſhouldshould be giuengiven to all.

3. In the number of partiallpartial parents may they be reckoned, who vniuſtlyunjustly diſinheritdisinherit their firſtfirst borne. For the inheritance of right belonging to them, and they not deſeruingdeserving to be diſinheriteddisinherited, aſſuredlyassuredly it is ſomesome by reſpectrespect or other which maketh parents prefer the younger before the elder: and this is plaineplain partiality. This kindekind of partiality is commonly in ſuchsuch parents as hauehave had children by ſeuerallseveral wiueswives. Sometimes diſlikedislike of a former wife maketh a father diſlikedislike the children he hath by her, and through diſlikedislike to diſinheritdisinherit the heireheir by her. God gauegave the IewesJews an expreſſeexpress law againſtagainst this kindekind of Deu. 21. 15. &etcc. partiality.

Sometimes againeagain a gripulous ſeekingseeking of aduantageadvantage to themſeluesthemselves maketh parents to diſinheritdisinherit the right heireheir: as when a man after he hath buried the mother of his firſtfirst borne, hearing of another woman which is of great wealth, maketh ſutesuit for her. She refuſethrefuseth becauſebecause he hath an heireheir of a former wife. He to remoueremove that blockeblock entereth couenantcovenant to make the ſonneson which he hath by her (if he hauehave any) his heireheir: hereupon the mariagemarriage is conſummateconsummate: his ſecondsecond wife bringeth forth a ſonneson: he for his couenantcovenant ſakesake diſinheritethdisinheriteth the firſtfirst heireheir. An vniuſtunjust, and vnlawfullunlawful practiſepractise.

div.head: §. 70. Of the cauſescauses for which the firſtfirst-borne may be diſinheriteddisinherited.
QueſtQuest. May not then a firſtfirst-borne ſonneson be diſinheriteddisinherited?
div.p: AnſwAnsw. Yes, The Scripture noteth two cauſescauses wherein the firſtfirst-borne may be put from the inheritance.

1. If he be illegitimate: for ſuchsuch an one hath no good title: The ſonneson of the bondwoman ſhallshall not be heireheir with my ſonneson,
Gen. 21. 10. ſaithsaith Sarah, and that iuſtlyjustly. To like purpoſepurpose ſaysay the ſonssons of Gileads wife to IephthahJephthah, Thou ſhaltshalt not inherit in our fathers houſehouse,
IudgJudg. 11. 2. for thou art the ſonneson of a ſtrangestrange woman. IuſtJust was that blame which IothamJotham laid vponupon the men of Shechem for making Abimelech
IudgJudg. 9. 18.
the baſebase ſonneson of IerubbaalJerubbaal King: and iuſtjust was Gods vengeance vponupon them for that wrong done to IerubbaalsJerubbaals legitimate children.
2. If he be notoriouſlynotoriously wicked. Thus Gen. 49. 4. 1 Chro. 5. 1. Ruben for committing abominable inceſtincest loſtlost his birthright.
Many particular crimes are reckoned vpup by the Sum. SylueſtSyluest. part. 1. Tract▪ de haered. ciuillcivil Lawyers, which would be too long here to recite.

div.head: §. 71. Of the dutieduty of fathers and mothers in law.
div.p:
The extent of this title (Fathersfathers) is in the laſtlast place to be Who are in place of parents. conſideredconsidered. Not only naturallnatural parents themſeluesthemselves, but alſoalso all that are in their place are compriſedcomprised vnderunder it. As they who are in the place of parents,
1. By the bond of mariagemarriage.
2. By propinquity of bloudblood.
3. By voluntary appointment.
The firſtfirst ſortsort are fathers and mothers in law: who are ſoso reckoned either by the mariagemarriage of parents themſeluesthemselves, or by the mariagemarriage of their children.

That man or woman which is mariedmarried to a parent that had children before their mariagemarriage, is in the place of a naturallnatural parent: thus IoſephJoseph was a Luke 2. 48. father to IeſusJesus, and Gen. 25. 1. Keturah a mother to IſaakIsaac. So againeagain the naturallnatural parents of that ſonneson that hath mariedmarried a wife, or of that daughter that is mariedmarried to an husband, are in the place of parents to the wife of their ſonneson, and to the husband of their daughter. Thus Exod. 18. 1. IethroJethro was a father to MoſesMoses, and Ruth 3. 1. Naomi a mother to Ruth.

All theſethese are to account their children in law (that is, the Parents in law to performeperform like duties as naturallnatural parents. children of their husband and wife, or the wiueswives of their ſonssons, and the husbands of their daughters) as their owneown naturallnatural children, and according to the age and place of theſethese children to performeperform the forenamed duties, and eueryevery way to ſeekeseek their good (except in ſuchsuch duties as after a peculiar manner belong to naturallnatural parents, as nurſingnursing to a naturallnatural mother, leauingleaving the inheritance to a naturallnatural parent.)

For a patternepattern hereof take the forenamed examples of IoſephJoseph and Naomi. What naturallnatural parents could doedo more for their owneown children then IoſephJoseph did for IeſusJesus, and Naomi for Ruth? The hiſtoryhistory noteth how IoſephJoseph tooketook care to hauehave his wiueswives
childechild Luk. 2. 21, 22. circumciſedcircumcised, and preſentedpresented in the temple: how he Mat. 2. 14. fled from place to place to preſeruepreserve the childs life: how Luk. 2. 48. perplexed he was when he thought the childechild was loſtlost: how he UerſUers. 51. trained him vpup in his owneown houſehouse. The hiſtoryhistory alſoalso noteth how Ruth 1. 22. Naomi brought Ruth her ſonnessons wife into her own countreycountry, and retained her with her ſelfeself, and & 2. 22. directed her whither to goego, and & 3. 1. what husband to hauehave, and & 4. 16. became a nurſenurse to her childechild.

1. MariageMarriage maketh man and wife one fleſhflesh: in which reſpectrespect ReaſonsReasons. they ought to hauehave one mindemind, and the ſamesame affections, as mutually each to other, ſoso ioyntlyjointly to the children of each other. On which ground alſoalso the husband and wife of a childechild, being one fleſhflesh with the childechild, ought as the childechild to be reſpectedrespected. On this ground God counteth the Saints his Eph. 5. 1. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . dearedear children, becauſebecause they are 2 Cor. 11. 2. eſpouſedespoused to his naturallnatural ſonson.

2. To reſpectrespect the children of an husband or wife as their owneown, is a great euidenceevidence of intireentire louelove to the husband and wife. And to reſpectrespect the husband and wife of a childechild is a great euidenceevidence of louelove to the childechild it ſelfeself. If the worlds prouerbeproverb hold true (louelove me and louelove my dog) how much more true is this ChriſtianChristian rule, louelove me and louelove my childechild: or louelove me and louelove mine husband: or louelove me and louelove my wife.

3. This alſoalso is an eſpeciallespecial meanesmeans to kindle and preſeruepreserve mutuallmutual louelove betwixt man and wife, who hauehave children of former husbands and wiueswives: as alſoalso betwixt parents and children.

div.head: §. 72. Of the peruerſeperverse cariagecarriage of fathers and mothers in law to their children.
div.p:
Contrary is the cariagecarriage of moſtmost fathers and mothers in law: eſpeciallyespecially of thoſethose who are mariedmarried to husbands or to wiueswives that had children before mariagemarriage: ſoso farrefar they are from performing the forenamed duty, as rather they enuyenvy at the proſperityprosperity of their husbands and wiueswives children: and ſecretlysecretly endeuourendeavour to hinder it in what they can: and cunningly leekeleek to alienate the naturallnatural parents affection from them: whence SenecaeSeneca Hippolytus. fearefullfearful tragedies hauehave beenebeen made, and lamentable miſchiefesmischiefs hauehave followed. What other reaſonreason can be giuengiven hereof OuidOvid. Metamorph. l. 15. ſabsab. 45. but a plaineplain inſtigationinstigation of the deuilldevil, who thus laboureth to
diſunitedisunite thoſethose whom God hath ioynedjoined together? For auoidingavoiding this ſnaresnare note the miſchiefesmischiefs that follow from thence.
1. Such parents ſinnesin againſtagainst Gods ordinance: and as EueEve, leanelean more to Satans ſuggeſtionsuggestion then to Gods direction.
2. They alienate the hearts and affections of one from another: not only from their children, but from themſeluesthemselves.
3. They prouokeprovoke their children in law to contemnecontemn and deſpiſedespise them, and to yeeldyield no duty vntounto them.

Hence note into what an hell vnkindeunkind fathers and mothers in law doedo caſtcast themſeluesthemselves. If this were duly weighed, I thinkethink they would be otherwiſeotherwise minded. But the god of this world doth ſoso blindeblind their eieseyes with ſelfeself-louelove, and with enuyenvy, that they cannot ſeesee the miſchiefesmischiefs whereinto they implunge themſeluesthemselves.

This is a point the more to be weighed, becauſebecause the fault here taxed is ſoso common, and hath in all ages beenebeen too common. Lurida terribiles miſcentmiscent aconita nouercae. Ouid. Metam. l. 1. fab. 4. What grieuousgrievous complaints hauehave in former times beenebeen made, and ſtillstill are made by children againſtagainst fathers and mothers in law? Whence alſoalso direfulldireful imprecations hauehave followed. Let widowers and widoweswidows that hauehave children ſeriouſlyseriously thinkethink of it before hand: and be the more circumſpectcircumspect in taking a ſecondsecond or third husband or wife: and after they are mariedmarried let them take heed of Satans ſnaressnares: and let conſcienceconscience of dutieduty more preuaileprevail with them, then corruption of nature.

div.head: §. 73. Of the faults of parents to their childrens husbands and wiueswives.
div.p: Many parents to the husbands and wiueswives of their children doedo alſoalso much tranſgreſſetransgress and ſwarueswarue from their dutieduty: for

1. They will ſhewshow much more reſpectrespect to their owneown children then to the children of their husbands or wiueswives: as by commingcoming to their daughters when their husbands are abroad, and neuernever but then: and ſendingsending for their ſonnessons to their houſehouse, but not for their wiueswives.
2. In all differences they will take part with their owneown children, though it be in the worſeworse part, and ſhewshow great partiality.

3. They will oft giuegive very ill counſellcounsel: aduiſingadvising their ſonssons
to keepekeep their wiueswives ſhortshort: aduiſingadvising their daughters not to be too ſubiectsubject to their husbands, yea priuilyprivily to purloinepurloin from their husbands.

4. If they liuelive with their children, they will ſoso priepry into eueryevery thing that their childrens husband or wife doth, and ſhewshow ſuchsuch ſuſpicionsuspicion and iealouſlyjealously in eueryevery thing, as they cannot but cauſecause much diſcorddiscord: and hence it oft commethcometh to paſſepass, that either parent and childechild, or husband and wife muſtmust be parted: they cannot all in peace liuelive together.
TheſeThese faults I thus note, that they may the more carefully be auoidedavoided.

div.head: §. 74. Of their dutieduty who are in ſteadstead of parents to OrphantsOrphans.
div.p: The next ſortsort of thoſethose who are in ſteadstead of parents, are thoſethose who in bloudblood and kindred are next to parents: as grandfathers, grand-mothers, vnclesuncles, aunts, elder brothers, or ſiſterssisters, their husbands or wiueswives, and coſinscosins.

TheſeThese commonly are counted to be in the place of parents, The next of kin to OrphantsOrphans to be as naturallnatural parents. when God taketh away naturallnatural and immediate parents from their children: ſoso as they are parents to OrphantsOrphans.

The duties which were preſcribedprescribed to naturallnatural parents appertaineappertain to them (except §. 71. before excepted.) Their dutieduty is to ſeesee theſethese OrphantsOrphans well educated, well placed in ſomesome good calling, well mariedmarried, and (if the OrphantsOrphans be left deſtitutedestitute of meanesmeans) well prouidedprovided for.

Mordecai is a worthy preſidentpresident and patternepattern for this kindekind of parents. EſtEst. 2. 7. He brought vpup EſtherEsther his vnclesuncles daughter (for ſheshe had neither father nor mother) he tooketook her for his owneown daughter: when ſheshe was taken from him, VerſVers. 11. he went to know how ſheshe did, and what ſhouldshould become of her: and VerſVers. 20, 22. Chap. 4. verſvers. 13. he gauegave her aduiceadvice from time to time how to carriecarry her ſelfeself. Let ſuchsuch as are parents to OrphantsOrphans take this example as a direction, and as a motiuemotive to performeperform the other duties preſcribedprescribed to naturallnatural parents as need requireth, and occaſionoccasion is offered.

God by his prouidenceprovidence taking away naturallnatural parents committethcommittethcommiteth their OrphantsOrphans as a charge to the next of kin: that as their naturallnatural parents brought them forth, theſethese ſhouldshould bring them vpup: therefore for their recompencerecompense let them lookelook to God, (who taketh vponupon himſelfehimself to be PſalPsal. 68. 5. a father of the fatherleſſefatherless)
and for their incouragementencouragement remember the reward which Mordecai receiuedreceived of the Lord: yea alſoalso let them remember the bleſſingblessing that God beſtowedbestowed vponupon EſtherEsther. God doth oft ſoso bleſſebless the meanesmeans vſedused for the education of OrphantsOrphans, as they who take the care thereof hauehave no cauſecause to repent their painespains and coſtcost, but rather hauehave much matter of comfort, ioyjoy and thankſgiuingthanksgiving.

div.head: §. 75. Of the common neglect of OrphantsOrphans.
div.p:
Too too common is the contrary diſpoſitiondisposition of moſtmost kinſmenkinsmen, and kinſwomenkinswomen; they thinkethink they are bound to none but their owneown children, and if they hauehave no children, to none at all. Many are of Ruths kinſmanskinsmans mindemind, they fearefear to marremar
Ruth 4. 6. their owneown inheritance. Though they be themſeluesthemselves exceeding rich, and ſpendspend much in apparellapparel, paſtimespastimes and houſehouse-keeping, yet they can ſuffersuffer the OrphantsOrphans of their poorepoor kindred to want, and to beg for need.

This is it that maketh the loſſeloss of naturallnatural parents to be ſoso much the greater. And herein many ChriſtiansChristians are more inhumane then the heathen: which the ApoſtleApostle implieth, where he faith, they are worſeworse then infidels: for OrphantsOrphans next of kinnekin 1 Tim. 5. 8. are to be reckoned among thoſethose whom the ApoſtleApostle termeth a mans
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . OVVNE.

div.head: §. 76. Of the dutieduty of Guardians.
div.p: The laſtlast ſortsort of thoſethose who are in place of parents, are ſuchsuch as hauehave the charge of children committed to them by voluntary appointment of parents, or are choſenchosen by children themſeluesthemselves, or by the magiſtratemagistrate when parents are dead, or lunatike, or any other way impotent, and vnableunable to trainetrain vpup their owneown children.
Of theſethese care and conſcienceconscience is rather required, then coſtcost and charges: for commonly both their charges are allowed, and their painespains recompencedrecompensed.

They who by reaſonreason of the death or impotency of naturallnatural parents hauehave the charge of children committed to them, are commonly called Guardians: of whom two generallgeneral duties are required.

list.item: 1. That they lookelook to their Pupils good education.
2. That they preſeruepreserve their patrimony and inheritance.

div.p: For their education, the directions giuengiven before to naturallnatural parents are to be obſeruedobserved by them.

For preſeruationpreservation of their patrimoniepatrimony, they muſtmust doedo for their Pupils what they would doedo for their owneown children; and ſoso carry themſeluesthemselves, as with good conſcienceconscience they may giuegive that account to their Pupils, or any other, which the law requireth.

The two forenamed duties, are the rhaine ends for which Guardians are choſenchosen: in performing whereof, if they be faithfullfaithful, great redreſſeredress will be made of the vntimelyuntimely death of parents; and notwithſtandingnotwithstanding parents die before their children be of diſcretiondiscretion to manage their eſtateestate, yet will their houſeshouses and families be maintained, and young heiresheirs kept from cunniecunny-catchers and cheaters.
It is noted of IohnJohn, who had the mother of IeſusJesus commended IohJoh. 19. 27. to him, that he tooketook her to his owneown home: whereby is implied his prouidentprovident care for her good.

div.head: §. 77. Of the fraud of Guardians.
div.p: Contrary is the practiſepractise of moſtmost Guardians, who take Pupils Tutela ad vtilitatem eorum qui commiſſicommissi ſuntsunt, non ad corum quibus commiſſacommissa, gerenda eſtest. Cic. Offic. l. 1. for their owneown aduantageadvantage, and make a prey of them. The heathen could ſaysay, that GuardianſhipGuardianship is to be performed for the benefit of the PupillPupil, and not of the Guardian. Yet among ChriſtiansChristians is the forenamed fault of Guardians.

1. There are few children (that hauehave not naturallnatural parents to lookelook to their good education) but are exceedingly neglected therein, and brought vpup very rudely and licentiouſlylicentiously: yea many times too ſparinglysparingly and n • iggardly for diet, apparellapparel, and other needfullneedful things, though they hauehave ſufficientsufficient to diſchargedischarge all that ſhallshall be laid out vponupon them.

2. The mainemain eſtateestate & patrimoniepatrimony of many Pupils is much impaired: and if they hauehave lands, as much waſtewaste is made vponupon them as poſſiblypossibly can be: and when a reckoning is to be giuengiven, it ſhallshall be a large, vniuſtunjust, and moſtmost vnconſcionableunconscionable reckoning of the Guardian can but get a generallgeneral releaſerelease, it is all that the cauethcaveth for.

3. MariagesMarriages are after a for forced vponupon many Pupils: and ſuchsuch matches put vponupon them as they cannot like; yea ſuchsuch as are no way fit for them, neither for eſtateestate, nor yeeresyears, nor proportion of bodiebody, nor qualities of mindemind.

Little doedo theſethese Guardians thinkethink of that account where unto they ſhallshall be brought an other day before the Lord, who ſtilethstyleth
himſelfehimself the PſalPsal. 10. 14. helper of the fatherleſſefatherless, and who beholdeth miſchiefemischief to requite it. FearefullFearful is that iudgementjudgment which the Lord hath Exo. 22. 22, &etcc. threatnedthreatened againſtagainst thoſethose that oppreſſeoppress the fatherleſſefatherless. Let not therefore vniuſtunjust Guardians thinkethink, that the gainegain they get wrongfully from their Pupils ſhallshall proſperprosper: but rather let them lookelook for Gods curſecurse vponupon their owneown children, and goods.

If ſuchsuch as parents themſeluesthemselves hauehave vponupon their death-beds committed their children vntounto, in confidence of their faithfulneſſefaithfulness, ſhallshall dealedeal deceitfully with their Pupils, their ſinnesin is doubled, and trebled. For
1. They violate the bond of friendſhipfriendship, faithfulneſſefaithfulness, and truſttrust repoſedreposed vponupon them.
2. They ſinnesin directly againſtagainst iuſticejustice.
3. MoſtMost monſtrouſlymonstrously they tranſgreſſetransgress the rules of charitiecharity.

div.head: §. 78. Of the dutieduty of SchoolemaſtersSchoolmasters and Tutors.
div.p: Among thoſethose who are by voluntarievoluntary appointment ſetset in the place of parents, are SchoolemaſtersSchoolmasters and Tutors to be reckoned. The authoritieauthority and charge of a parent is for a time committed to them: therefore for that time they ought to performeperform a parents dutieduty.

Their dutieduty is appropriated to education: it appertaineth not to them to maintainemaintain the children committed to them: they are rather themſeluesthemselves by their painespains that way maintained.

All the duties which were before compriſedcomprised vnderunder nurture, belong to SchoolemaſtersSchoolmasters and Tutors. More particularly they are to inſtructinstruct children in three things.
1. In learning.
2. In ciuilitiecivility, and good manners.
3. In true pietiepiety, and religion.

I ſhallshall not need to ſpeakespeak more of theſethese points then hath §. 28, 34. before beenebeen deliuereddelivered: only to prouokeprovoke them to be diligent in well nurturing children in thoſethose three points, let the benefit of good SchoolemaſtersSchoolmasters and Tutors be well noted.

SchoolemaſtersSchoolmasters commonly caſtcast the firſtfirst ſeedseed into the hearts of The benefit of a good SchoolmaſterSchoolmaster. children: they firſtfirst ſeaſonseason them: as the ſeedseed is, ſuchsuch will the crop be: as the firſtfirst ſeaſoningseasoning is, ſoso will the ſauoursavour continue to be. If they ſowesow no good ſeedseed at all, what harueſtharvest can be looked for? If they ſowesow a corrupt ſeedseed of rudeneſſerudeness, licentiouſneſſelicentiousness, profaneneſſeprofaneness,
ſuperſtitionsuperstition, and any wickedneſſewickedness, the crop muſtmust needs be anſwerableanswerable thereto. But if they ſowesow the good ſeedseed of learning, ciuilitiecivility, and pietiepiety, there is great hope of a good crop.

Hence it followeth that they are of great vſeuse, and may bring much good, not only to the children themſeluesthemselves, and their parents, Scholas & phrontiſteriaphrontisteria virorum & mulierum philoſophiaephilosophiae ethnicae addictorum conſtrux • construx itconstruxit. Nicep. eccl. hiſthist. l. 10. c. 21. The benefit of a good Tutor. but alſoalso to the Church and Commoncommon-wealth. IulianJulian the ApoſtatApostat was not ignorant hereof: and therefore endeuouringendeavouring to root ChriſtianitieChristianity out of the world, he ſufferedsuffered no man that profeſſedprofessed himſelfehimself a ChriſtianChristian, to teach a ſchooleschool: but in ſteadstead of ChriſtianChristian SchoolemaſtersSchoolmasters, he ſetset vpup in eueryevery part of his dominions, heatheniſhheathenish SchoolemaſtersSchoolmasters.

Tutors, to whoſewhose gouernmentgovernment young ſchollersscholars, that are ſentsent to the VniuerſitiesUniversities, are committed, hauehave to dealedeal with children in their riper yeeresyears; eueneven when the time of ſetlingsettling them in a courſecourse is come: the very time wherein much good may be done to children, or elſeelse wherein they may be vtterlyutterly peruertedperverted. There will be little hope of bowing them, and drawing them into another courſecourse after they be freed from the gouernmentgovernment of a Tutor. Tutors therefore, as they hauehave need of great wiſdomewisdom, ſoso of good conſcienceconscience, that they may hauehave the greater care of their Pupils, and take the greater painespains in teaching them the three forenamed points, learning, ciuilitiecivility, and pietiepiety. A good Tutor may doedo much to repairerepair the negligence, and amend the defects of a SchoolemaſterSchoolmaster: but there remaineremain none to redreſſeredress the failings of a Tutor: children for the moſtmost part are paſtpast redreſſingredressing, when they ceaſecease to hauehave a Tutor.

div.head: §. 79. Of the negligence of SchoolemaſtersSchoolmasters and Tutors.
div.p: The vices contrary to the forenamed dutieduty of SchoolemaſtersSchoolmasters, are theſethese.

1. UnskilfulneſſeUnskilfulness. Many that are more fit to be taught then to teach, take vponupon them this weightieweighty calling. Some hauehave not ſufficientsufficient learning: ſomesome againeagain are rude, and know not themſeluesthemselves good manners: and ſomesome know not the firſtfirst principles of the oracles of God. No good can be expected from theſethese.

2. CouetouſneſſeCovetousness. All that many ſeekeseek, is to multiply the number of their ſchollersscholars, and to get as much as they can for boording, and teaching: they aimeaim more at their owneown gainegain then at their ſchollersscholars profit. Children are not like to thriuethrive well vnderunder them.

3. Negligence. Many are loth to take the painespains of a SchoolemaſterSchoolmaster, and thereupon come as little into the ſchooleschool as they can: take eueryevery ſmallsmall occaſionoccasion to be gone againeagain: care not how much their children play: if they be able to hire a poorepoor VſherUsher, all the burden ſhallshall be caſtcast vponupon him. Little is that fruit that can be looked for from them.

4. Want of pietiepiety. Many skilfullskilful and painfullpainful SchoolemaſtersSchoolmasters, vnderunder whoſewhose teaching children come forward exceeding well in learning, thinkethink it nothing appertaineth to them to teach the grounds of religion, ſoso as they altogether neglect pietiepiety. AſſuredlyAssuredly they want it themſeluesthemselves: for were their owneown hearts ſeaſonedseasoned with true pietiepiety, their conſciencesconsciences would mouemove them to teach it to their children. The things of the kingdomekingdom of God are like vntounto h • eauenheaven, which ſeaſonethseasoneth the whole batch of dough with that ſeaſonseason and ſauoursavour which it ſelfeself hath. When children ſpendspend almoſtalmost all their time with their SchoolemaſtersSchoolmasters, of whom ſhouldshould they learnelearn it, if not of them? What bleſſingblessing can be hoped from the painespains of ſuchsuch SchoolemaſtersSchoolmasters?

I might to theſethese addeadd the ouerover-much remiſneſſeremissness of ſomesome (whereby children get too great an head) and the too great ſeueritieseverity of others, either in frequenciefrequency of correcting, as if they delighted therein; or in the meaſuremeasure thereof, as if they had to doedo with beaſtsbeasts, whereby they affright children, make them dull, yea and impudent alſoalso. div.head: §. 33. Of the AnabaptiſtsAnabaptists arguments againſtagainst the authoritieauthority of maſtersmasters, and ſubiectionsubjection of ſeruantsservants.
div.p: Contrary to this firſtfirst ground of ſeruantsservants ſubiectionsubjection is the opinion of AnabaptiſtsAnabaptists, who teach that all are alike, and that there is no difference betwixt maſtersmasters and ſeruantsservants. Their reaſonsreasons, whereby they would make ſhewshow to proueprove their vnreaſonableunreasonable opinion, are theſethese.

1. ObiectObject. MaſtersMastersmasters are either Infidels or ChriſtiansChristians, and ſoso ſeruantsservants either one or other. If maſtersmasters be Infidels, and ſeruantsservants ChriſtiansChristians, how vnmeetunmeet is it that ChriſtiansChristians ſhouldshould be ſubiectsubject to Infidels? andAnd if maſtermaster and ſeruantservant be both ChriſtiansChristians, they are brothers: but brothers are equallsequals, and neither ſubiectsubject to other.

AnſwAnsw. RuleRulerule and ſubiectionsubjection are matters of outward policy, they tend to the outward preſeruationpreservation of Church, Commonwealthcommonwealth, and family, in this world: but faith, piety, and ſuchsuch graces are inward matters of the ſoulesoul, tending to a better life.

TheſeThese being thus different, one that is more excellent in the one, may be inferiourinferior in the other. Yea though there be an equality in the one, namely, in ſpirituallspiritual things, yet there may be a diſparitydisparity in the other, namely, in ciuillcivil and temporalltemporal matters. And though Saints may be farrefar inferiourinferior to infidels in outward eſtateestate, yet they are not a whit the leſſeless glorious before God. The honour proper and peculiar to Saints is inward, not viſiblevisible to the carnallcarnal eye of a naturallnatural man.

div.head: 2. ObiectObject. It is againſtagainst nature for one to be ſeruantservant, eſpeciallyespecially a bond-ſeruantservant to another. To grant that it is againſtagainst that abſoluteabsolute and perfect nature wherein at firſtfirst God created man, and that it came in by ſinnesin, yet is it not againſtagainst that order and courſecourse of nature wherein God hath now ſetledsettled man. div.head: 3. ObiectObject. It is the prerogatiueprerogative of ChriſtiansChristians to be Gal. 3. 28. all one: but ſubiectionsubjection of ſeruantsservants to maſtersmasters is againſtagainst that prerogatiueprerogative.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. That prerogatiueprerogative is meerelymerely ſpirituallspiritual: for in ChriſtChrist all are one, as they are members of ChriſtChrist, which is a ſpirituallspiritual body: not as they are members of a politiquepolitic body. That all their ſpeechesspeeches and anſwersanswers to their maſtermaster be true, not daring to tell a lie vntounto them: this argueth a very reuerendreverend reſpectrespect of a maſtermaster.
