div.head: §. 7. Of the vices contrary to a ſeruantsservants reuerencereverence in ſpeechspeech.
div.p: Offences contrary to the forenamed Reuerencereverence of ſeruantsservants to their maſtersmasters are theſethese.

1. SawcineſſeSaucinessSawciness and boldneſſeboldness in ſeruantsservants when they hauehave no more reſpectrespect to their maſtersmasters preſencepresence then to any others, but are full of prate, and loud in ſpeechspeech before their maſtermaster, or in the roomeroom next to him, where they may be heard as well as if they were in the ſamesame roomeroom: much offence is thus oft times giuengiven to maſtersmasters.

2. Importunity in ſpeakingspeaking, and replying againeagain and againeagain, though their maſtersmasters doedo not only ſhewshow their diſlikedislike thereof, but alſoalso expreſlyexpressly charge them to ſpeakespeak no more. Scolding maids that will hauehave the laſtlast words of their miſtreſſemistress much offend herein. This is directly againſtagainst the ApoſtlesApostles prohibition to ſeruantsservants, that they anſweranswer not againeagain.
Tit. 2. 9.
3. Impatiency, when they cannot endure to hearehear their maſtermaster make an end of his ſpeechspeech, but either they will interrupt him, or fling away.

4. StoutneſſeStoutness, when (as Solomon noteth) though they vnderſtandunderstand,
Pro. 29. 19. they will not ſpeakespeak: though they know very well that it is their maſtersmasters pleaſurepleasure they ſhouldshould ſpeakespeak, yea though they are bidden to ſpeakespeak, yet their ſtoutstout ſtomachstomach, and ſullensullen heart will not ſuffersuffer them to ſpeakespeak: no though it be neuernever ſoso behouefullbehoveful for their maſtersmasters: if they know that their maſtermaster goeth on in a courſecourse very preiudiciallprejudicial to him, yet will not they tell him of it: nay if their maſtermaster vniuſtlyunjustly ſuſpectsuspect any euillevil of them, they will let him abide in that iealouſlyjealousyjealously rather then ſpeakespeak to cleareclear themſeluesthemselves: and if their maſtermaster doedo not expreſlyexpressly
appoint them from time to time what to doedo, they will neuernever askeask: nor if they be doubtfulldoubtful of that which he giuethgiveth them in charge, will they further inquire to be reſoluedresolved thereof. This kindekind of ſilencesilence, in theſethese and ſuchsuch like caſescases, argueth more doggedneſſedoggedness then dutifulneſſedutifulness.
5. DiſdaineDisdain, when they See §. 5. ſcornescorn to giuegive the title Maſtermaster to him that is ſetset ouerover them, becauſebecause he is a poorepoor and meanemean man.

6. Arrogancy, when their words are high and lofty againſtagainst their maſtermaster, pretending that they are as good as he, though for a time they be vnderunder him. ClerkesClerks, prentiſesprentices, waiting women, and ſuchsuch like, being borne of gentlemen, and men of good degree, are for the moſtmost part guilty of this fault: the reaſonreason is, becauſebecause their birth and parentage maketh them forget their preſentpresent place and condition; or elſeelse (which is worſeworse) maketh them wilfully preſumepresume aboueabove it.

7. Muttering and murmuring vponupon eueryevery occaſionoccasion of diſcontentdiscontent: whereby it commethcometh to paſſepass that they oft prouokeprovoke much wrath (for grieuousgrievous words ſtirrestir vpup anger.)
Pro. 15. 1.

8. VnſeaſonableUnseasonable interruption of their maſtermaster: ſpeakingspeaking to him when he is ſeriouſlyseriously occupied in ſomesome weighty buſineſſebusiness (as they who told ChriſtChrist of his mother and brethren when he was preaching) or vnſeaſonablyunseasonably ſpeakingspeaking vntounto him while he Mar. 3. 32. is in paſſionpassion, whereby they oft bring much miſchiefemischief vponupon themſeluesthemselves.

9. AnſweringAnswering their maſtermaster at their owneown leiſureleisure, ſufferingsuffering him to call, and call againeagain and againeagain. This doth IobJob complainecomplain of, ſayingsaying, I called my ſeruantservant and he gauegave me no anſweranswer.
IobJob 19. 16.

10. Flapping their maſtermaster in the mouth with a lie: like Gehazi, who, when he had lewdly fetched money and apparellapparel of Naaman, and his maſtermaster asked him where he had beenebeen, ſaidsaid with a fairefair face, Thy ſeruantservant went no whither. Let the iudgementjudgment 2 King. 5. 25. executed on him make all ſeruantsservants take heed of the like ſinnesin. For Lying is in it ſelfeself an hainousheinous ſinnesin: yet ſoso much the more hainousheinous when it is told to one that hath authority ouerover vsus, and by reaſonreason thereof ſtandethstandeth in Gods place.

LaſtlyLastly, EuillEvil language of their maſtermaster behindebehind his backeback. This is a ſinnesin, though that which is ſpokenspoken to a maſtersmasters diſgracedisgrace
be true: for the infirmities of a maſtermaster ought rather to be coueredcovered, then reuealedrevealed and laid open by a ſeruantservant. How monſtrousmonstrous a ſinnesin is it then, to raiſeraise ſlanderousslanderous reports againſtagainst a maſtermaster which are vntrueuntrue? This was Zibas ſinnesin againſtagainst MephiboſhethMephibosheth his maſtermaster. 2 Sam. 16. 3.
Hitherto of ſeruantsservants Reuerencereverence in ſpeechspeech to their maſtersmasters.
Their Reuerencereverence in cariagecarriage followeth.

div.head: §. 8. Of ſeruantsservants reuerendreverend behauiourbehaviour to their maſtersmasters.
div.p:
For manifeſtationmanifestation of a ſeruantsservants reuerencereverence in cariagecarriage towards his maſtermaster, three things are eſpeciallyespecially required.
1. DutifullDutiful obeyſanceobeisance.
2. ReſpectfullRespectful behauiourbehaviour.
3. ModeſtModest apparellapparel.

I. Such dutifulldutiful and ſubmiſſiuesubmissive obeyſanceobeisance and curteſiecourtesy, as beſeemethbeseemeth their ſexsex and place, and that according to the moſtmost vſuallusual 1. SeruantsServants obeyſanceobeisance to their maſtersmasters. cuſtomecustom of the country and place where they are, muſtmust ſeruantsservants performeperform to their maſtersmasters, as they hauehave occaſionoccasion to goego to them, to come from them, to receiuereceive any charge of them, or to bring any meſſagemessage vntounto them. Where IſaakIsaac ſaithsaith in his bleſſingblessing giuengiven to IaakobJacob, Be lord ouerover thy brethren, and let thy mothers ſonnessons bowebow
Gen. 27. 29. downedown to thee, by that phraſephrase of bowing downedown, he noteth the condition of a ſeruantservant, and withallwithal implieth a ſeruantsservants dutieduty: on this ground, when the children of the Prophets ſawsaw that the ſpiritspirit of Eliah reſtedrested on EliſhaElisha, they taking it for an euidentevident ſignesign that God had made him a gouernourgovernor and maſtermaster ouerover them, they came to 2 King. 2. 15. meet him, and bowed themſeluesthemselves to the ground before him.

II. AnſwerableAnswerable to a ſeruantsservants obeiſanceobeisance muſtmust be his whole behauiourbehaviour 2. SeruantsServants dutifulldutiful behauiourbehaviour before their maſtersmasters. before his maſtermaster, ſeaſonedseasoned and ordered with ſuchsuch modeſtiemodesty and humilitiehumility, as may manifeſtmanifest an honourable reſpectrespect to his maſtermaster: as

1. To ſtandstand in his maſtersmasters preſencepresence; which teſtifiethtestifieth a readineſſereadiness to performeperform any ſeruiceservice which his maſtermaster ſhallshall appoint him to doedo: this was one thing noted, and commended by the QueeneQueen of Sheba in Solomons ſeruantsservants: ſheshe ſawsaw their 1 King. 10. 5, 8. ſtandingstanding, and ſaidsaid, happy are theſethese thy ſeruantsservants that ſtandstand before thee. Whereas it is ſaidsaid that ſheshe ſawsaw alſoalso their ſittingsitting, that phraſephrase ſhewethshoweth a ſeemlyseemly order which they obſeruedobserved eueneven when they were out of his preſencepresence, by giuinggiving and taking their right and due place.

2. By vncoueringuncovering their heads in their maſtersmasters preſencepresence: this in our dayesdays, and in the parts of the world where we dwell, is in the male kindekind a ſignesign and token of ſubiectionsubjection.

3. By ſobrietiesobriety and modeſtiemodesty both in countenance, and in the whole diſpoſitiondisposition of bodiebody, eſpeciallyespecially when ſeruantsservants are in their maſtersmasters preſencepresence: for to compoſecompose countenance and whole bodiebody ſoberlysoberly, becauſebecause of the preſencepresence of one, argueth a reuerendreverend reſpectrespect of that perſonperson, for whoſewhose ſakesake that ſobrietiesobriety is ſhewedshowed.

III. The apparellapparel alſoalso which ſeruantsservants wearewear muſtmust be ſoso faſhionedfashioned 3. SeruantsServants ſeemlyseemly apparellapparel. and ordered, as it may declare them to be ſeruantsservants, and vnderunder their maſtersmasters, and ſoso it will argue a reuerendreverend reſpectrespect of their maſtersmasters. One end of apparellapparel, is to ſhewshow a difference betwixt ſuperiourssuperiors and inferioursinferiors, perſonspersons in authoritieauthority and vnderunder ſubiectionsubjection. It pleaſedpleased the Holy GhoſtGhost to note this particular (and their 1. King. 10. 5. apparellapparel) as an obſeruableobservable point in Solomons ſeruantsservants.

div.head: §. 9. Of the faults of ſeruantsservants contrary to reuerencereverence in cariagecarriage.
div.p: The cariagecarriage of many ſeruantsservants towards their maſtermaster is cleaneclean contrary to the forenamed reuerencereverence. For

1. Some through rudeneſſerudeness, and want of good bringing vpup, 1. RudeneſſeRudeness. come to their maſtersmasters, and goego from them, as to and from their fellowesfellows: no teſtimonietestimony of reuerencereverence by any obeyſanceobeisance: they know not how to giuegive it: whereby they diſhonourdishonour their parents, and manner of education.

2. Others, if at firſtfirst commingcoming to their maſtermaster they giuegive ſomesome 2. Too much familiaritiefamiliarity. ſalutationsalutation, yet, through too much familiaritiefamiliarity with them, all the day after they will carry themſeluesthemselves fellow-like, ſcarcescarce vncoueringuncovering their heads in their maſtersmasters preſencepresence, not enduring to ſtandstand long before him, but either ſettingsetting themſeluesthemselves downedown, or ſlinkingslinking away when they ſhouldshould be in preſencepresence. DoubtleſſeDoubtless from this ouermuchovermuch familiaritiefamiliarity aroſearose this prouerbeproverb, Good morrow for all day. This vnmannerlyunmannerly familiaritiefamiliarity is commonly in ſuchsuch ſeruantsservants, as hauehave poorepoor and meanemean maſtersmasters: for rich and great mens ſeruantsservants can be ſoso full of curteſiecourtesy, as not a word ſhallshall be ſpokenspoken by their maſtersmasters to them, or by them to their maſtersmasters, but the knee ſhallshall be bowed withallwithal: they can ſtandstand hourehour after hourehour before their maſtersmasters, and not once put on their hat: if they be walking after their maſtersmasters, their maſtermaster ſhallshall not turneturn ſoonersooner then their hat will be off, and that ſoso oft as he turneth or ſpeakethspeaketh to them. Why ſhouldshould
rich maſtersmasters hauehave ſoso much reuerencereverence ſhewedshowed to them, and poorepoor maſtersmasters none at all? DoeDo not the poorepoor bearebear Gods image as well as the rich? Doth Gods word make any difference betwixt rich and poorepoor? Doth it ſaysay, SerueServe rich maſtersmasters with fearefear and trembling? Surely it is the corruption of mans heart, which maketh this difference. SeruantsServants naturally more regard their maſtersmasters outward abilitieability, then inward authoritieauthority: the honour which the world conferrethconferrethconfereth on men, more then the honour which God conferrethconferrethconfereth: for God hath giuengiven as much honour and authoritieauthority to a poorepoor maſtermaster as to a rich, in that he is a maſtermaster.

SeruantsServants commonly moſtmost failefail in this dutieduty of reuerencereverence towards their maſtersmasters there where they ſhouldshould moſtmost of all ſhewshow it, namely, in the courts of God, and aſſemblyassembly of Gods people, where the very Angels are preſentpresent to behold our ſeemlyseemly cariagecarriage: thus they cauſecause the miniſterieministry of the word to be euillevil ſpokenspoken of, and thereby make their ſinnesin ſoso much the more hainousheinous.

3. Exceeding great is the fault of ſeruantsservants in their exceſſeexcess in apparellapparel. 3. Pride. No diſtinctiondistinction ordinarily betwixt a mans children and ſeruantsservants: nay none betwixt maſtersmasters and their men, miſtreſſesmistresses and their maids. It may be while men and maids are at their maſtersmasters and miſtreſſesmistresses finding, difference may be made: though eueneven then alſoalso, if they can any way get wherewithallwherewithal, they will do what they can to be as brauebrave as they can. But if once they be at their owneown finding, all ſhallshall be laid out vponupon apparellapparel, but they will be as fine as maſtermaster or miſtreſſemistress: if not ſoso coſtlycostly, yet in ſhewshow as ſpeciousspecious and brauebrave. New faſhionsfashions are as ſoonesoon got vpup by ſeruantsservants as by maſtersmasters and miſtreſſesmistresses. What is the end of this, but to be thought as good as maſtermaster or miſtreſſemistress? If the QueeneQueen of Sheba were now liuingliving, ſheshe would as much wonder at the diſorderdisorder of ſeruantsservants in theſethese dayesdays, as then ſheshe wondredwondered at the comely order of Solomons ſeruantsservants. Let theſethese proud ſeruantsservants lookelook to it: for if God hauehave threatnedthreatened to viſitvisit Princes children that walkewalk in ſtrangestrange apparellapparel,
Zeph. 1. 8. can ſeruantsservants that ſoso walkewalk thinkethink to goego ſcotscot-free?

div.head: §. 10. Of ſeruantsservants obedience.
div.p:
No inferioursinferiors are more bound to obedience then ſeruantsservants: it
is their mainemain, and moſtmost peculiar function, to obey their maſtersmasters. It is therefore here in my text expreſlyexpressly mentioned (Seruantsservants obey your maſtersmasters) and all other duties are compriſedcomprised vnderunder it. Treat. 3. §. 17. The reaſonsreasons alleadgedalleged to mouemove wiueswives and children to obey, ought much more to mouemove ſeruantsservants. Treat. 5. §. 11.

They who are contrary minded, who are rebellious, and diſdainedisdain to be vnderunder the authority of another, and are ready to ſaysay of their Maſtermaster, We will not hauehave this man to reignereign ouerover vsus, are fitter Luke 19. 14. to liuelive among AnabaptiſtsAnabaptists, then orthodoxallorthodoxal ChriſtiansChristians. For to what end is the lawfulneſſelawfulness of authoritieauthority acknowledged, if ſubiectionsubjection be not yeeldedyielded vntounto it? ofOf the two a man were better be blinded with error, then not obey the truth which he knoweth.
In handling this point of obedience, I will follow the ſamesame order, which I did in laying forth the obedience of wiueswives and children, and conſiderconsider

list.item: 1. The parts of ſeruantsservants obedience wherein it conſiſtethconsisteth.
2. The extent thereof, how farrefar it reacheth.

div.p: The parts are two,

list.item: One negatiuenegative.
Another affirmatiueaffirmative.

div.p: The negatiuenegative is to abſtaineabstain from doing things of their owneown head, without or againſtagainst their maſtersmasters conſentconsent.
The affirmatiueaffirmative is readily to yeeldyield to doedo that which their maſtersmasters would they ſhouldshould doedo.

div.head: §. 11. Of ſeruantsservants forbearing to doedo things without their maſtersmasters conſentconsent.
div.p:
SeruantsServants ought to forbeareforbear doing of things on their owneown heads without or againſtagainst conſentconsent of their maſtersmasters, becauſebecause while the time of their ſeruiceservice laſtethlasteth, they are not their owneown, neither ought the things which they doedo, to be for themſeluesthemselves: both their perſonspersons and their actions are all their maſtersmasters: and the will of their maſtermaster muſtmust be their rule and guide (in things which are not againſtagainst Gods will.) The rite vſedused vnderunder the Law of boaringboring a ſeruantsservants eareear, implied as much. DauidDavid therefore alluding vntounto Exo. 21. 6. that rite, ſaithsaith to God (both of himſelfehimself, and alſoalso of ChriſtChrist, whom vnderunder a type he prefigured) mine earesears haſthast thou boaredbored; and from thence inferrethinferrethinfereth that he would do the will of God. We hauehave PſalPsal. 40. 6. a notable patternepattern hereof in AbrahamsAbraham's ſeruantservant, who in a buſineſſebusiness committed to his charge propounds ſuchsuch ſcruplesscruples as came Gen. 24. 5.
into his head to receiuereceive direction from his maſtermaster therein, leſtlest he ſhouldshould be forced to doedo ſomethingsomething of his owneown head without particular warrant from his maſtermaster.

This generallgeneral will the better be cleared, if it be exemplified in ſomesome particulars. Take therefore theſethese inſtancesinstances gathered out of the Scriptures of things which ſeruantsservants may not doedo without their maſtersmasters conſentconsent.

1. SeruantsServants may not goego whither they will. The phraſephrase which the Centurion vſethuseth (I ſaysay to one goego, and he goeth) implieth, that except his maſtermaster bid him goego, he ought not to goego. Mat. 8. 9.

2. They ought not to doedo their owneown buſineſſebusiness and affairesaffairs. It is noted of IaakobJacob being Labans ſeruantservant, that, though he Gen. 30. 35, 36. had flockesflocks of his owneown, yet he fed his maſtersmasters flockesflocks, and committed his owneown to his ſonnessons.

3. They ought not to doedo what buſineſſebusiness they liſtlist themſeluesthemselves. Ahimaaz had a great deſiredesire to carriecarry the newesnews of AbſolomsAbsoloms 2 Sam. 18. 19, &etcc. death to DauidDavid: yet without the leaueleave of IoabJoab his CaptaineCaptain and maſtermaster he would not doedo it. The good miſtreſſemistress giuethgiveth the portion to her maidesmaids, namely, the portion of workework: Pro. 31. 15. that therefore muſtmust they doedo which ſheshe giuethgiveth them to doedo. The ſeruantsservants of the Centurion did eueryevery one as by their maſtermaster Mat. 8. 9. Mat. 25. 16, 17. they were inioynedenjoined: and the ſeruantsservants that had talents committed to them looked each of them to their owneown talent.

4. They ought not to marymarry while the time of their couenantcovenant for ſeruiceservice laſtethlasteth, vnleſſeunless their maſtermaster giuegive conſentconsent thereto. The law of God thus ſettethsetteth forth the lawfulllawful mariagesmarriages of ſeruantsservants, If his maſtermaster hauehave giuengiven him a wife: whereby is implied; Exo. 21. 4. that if a ſeruantservant marymarry, it muſtmust be with his maſtersmasters conſentconsent.

div.head: §. 13. Of ſeruantsservants obedience to their maſtersmasters commandementscommandments.
div.p: The affirmatiueaffirmative and actiueactive part of ſeruantsservants obedience, conſiſtingconsisting in a ready yeeldingyielding to that which their maſtersmasters will hauehave done, hath reſpectrespect (as the like kindekind of childrens obedience) to the CommandementCommandment, InſtructionInstruction, ReproofeReproof, and Correction of their maſtermaster.

I. A maſtermaster hauinghaving power to command his ſeruantsservants, it is What maſtersmasters command, ſeruantsservants muſtmust doedo. a dutieduty of ſeruantsservants to obey their maſtermaster therein. The particular workework which appertaineth to a ſeruantservant by vertuevirtue of his place is to hauehave an eieeye to his maſtermaster, to ſeesee what he requireth at his hands. DauidDavid thus deſcribesdescribes the property of good ſeruantsservants, Their eieseyes lookelook to the hand of their maſtermaster. That looking, as it PſalPsal. 123. 2. implieth an expectation of releeferelief and ſuccoursuccour, ſoso alſoalso a readineſſereadiness to receiuereceive and execute any thing from them that they would hauehave done. The Centurion commendeth this duty Mat. 8. 9. in the example of his ſeruantsservants, who eueryevery one of them did what their maſtermaster commanded them to doedo. It is further commended in the examples of Gen. 24. 9. Abrams ſeruantservant, 1 King. 18. 43. Eliahs ſeruantservant, and many others. Note how farrefar the Lord ChriſtChrist exacteth this dutieduty of ſeruantsservants; Luk. 17. 7, 8. Though a ſeruantservant hath beenebeen all day plowing (a laborious and weariſomewearisome workework) yet when he commethcometh home, his maſtermaster commanding him to dreſſedress his ſuppersupper and wait, he muſtmust doedo it. By all theſethese proofesproofs it appeareth, that if a maſtermaster bid his ſeruantservant, come, goego, doedo this, or that, he muſtmust obey.

The contrary hereunto is the higheſthighest degree of diſobediencedisobedience, Contrary. RefuſingRefusing to be at command. 2 Sam. 19. 26. as when ſeruantsservants refuſerefuse to be at their maſtersmasters command, and to doedo what they charge them to doedo: as Ziba, who being commanded to ſaddlesaddle his maſtersmasters AſſeAss, went away and did it not: and IobsJobs ſeruantsservants, who being called would not anſweranswer. IobJob 19. 16. Of all other offences this doth moſtmost prouokeprovoke maſtersmasters: for it is a plaineplain contempt of their authoritieauthority.

div.head: §. 14. Of ſeruantsservants hearkninghearkening to their maſtersmasters inſtructionsinstructions in matters of their calling.
div.p: II. As a maſtermaster hath power to command, ſoso his dutieduty it is to See Treat. 8. §. 21, 38. inſtructinstruct his ſeruantsservants in the way of righteouſneſſerighteousness, and in that ciuillcivil courſecourse of life wherein he is to walkewalk. The dutieduty then of ſeruantsservants it is, in both to hearken and be obedient vntounto them.
1. Such ſeruantsservants as are vnderunder maſtersmasters to learnelearn their trade, are bound many waiesways to hearken to them.
1. That for the time they may doedo the better ſeruiceservice to their maſtersmasters.

2. That by learning a trade or skill in any good calling they may be the better able when the time of their ſeruiceservice is out to maintainemaintain themſeluesthemselves, to teach other ſeruantsservants which ſhallshall be vnderunder them, and to doedo the more good in the place where they ſhallshall liuelive.
3. That thus they may the better diſchargedischarge a good conſcienceconscience in that particular place wherein God hath ſetset them.

Contrary is the idle, ſluggiſhsluggish, dull diſpoſitiondisposition of many ſeruantsservants, who by reaſonreason of their careleſneſſecarelessness and vntowardneſſeuntowardness in doing that which they are taught, vex and grieuegrieve their maſtersmasters, yea and make them weary of inſtructinginstructing them. Many prentiſesprentices ſpendspend all the time of their prentiſhipapprenticeship without reaping any good at all: they neuernever proueprove their crafts maſtersmasters: ſoso many in the countreycountry liuelive vnderunder good husbands, many ClearksClerks vnderunder good Lawyers, many maids vnderunder good houſwiueshousewiveshouswives, and that many yearesyears together, yet through their negligence get no good at all, whereas if they would hauehave beenebeen attentiueattentive and carefullcareful, they might hauehave learned much. Enemies theſethese are to their maſtersmasters, to themſeluesthemselves, to the city and country where they liuelive, and to their friends and parents, eſpeciallyespecially if they hauehave any aliuealive.

div.head: §. 15. Of ſeruantsservants hearkninghearkening to their maſtersmasters inſtructionsinstructions in piety.
div.p: Such ſeruantsservants as hauehave religious maſtersmasters who are carefullcareful to Obedience of ſeruantsservants to pious inſtructionsinstructions. inſtructinstruct their houſholdhousehold in the way of righteouſneſſerighteousness, ought to be obedient to their inſtructionsinstructions: ſoso were IoſuahsJoshuasJosuahs ſeruantsservants, (or elſeelse could not IoſuahJoshua hauehave vndertakenundertaken for them IoſJos. 24. 15. as he did) and the ſeruantsservants of that Ruler of whom it was ſaidsaid that himſelfehimself beleeuedbelieved c IohnJohn 4. 53. and all his houſehouse: and the ſeruantsservants of LidiaLydia, and of the Iayl • erJailerJayler, concerning whom it is ſaidsaid, Acts 16. 15, She was baptiſedbaptised and her houſholdhousehold: 34. he beleeuedbelieved in God and all his houſehouse. VnderUnder theſethese words houſehouse and houſholdhousehold, none doubteth but that ſeruantsservants are compriſedcomprised.

Now then if the ſeruantsservants of theſethese had not hearkened and
yeeldedyielded to the inſtructionsinstructions of their maſtermaster and miſtreſſemistress, would they hauehave beleeuedbelieved in him in whom their maſtersmasters beleeuedbelieved, or beenebeen baptiſedbaptised when their miſtreſſemistress was? The like may be gathered out of this phraſephrase, Rom. 16. 5. Philem. v. 2. The Church in their houſehouse: for thereby is implied that all in the houſehouse were of the ſamesame faith that their maſtermaster and miſtreſſemistress were. It is expreſlyexpressly noted of the Act. 10. 7. SouldierSoldier that waited continually on Cornelius, that he was a deuoutdevout man, whereby it is preſuppoſedpresupposed that he hearknedhearkened to his maſtersmasters inſtructionsinstructions: for it is noted of the maſtermaster alſoalso, that VerſVers. 2. he was a deuoutdevout man and feared God.

The benefit which redoundeth to ſeruantsservants by obeying ſuchsuch inſtructionsinstructions, is vnſpeakableunspeakable: much more good may be got by following the ſpirituallspiritual directions of religious maſtersmasters, then the witty and commodious directions of the wiſeſtwisest ſtateſmenstatesmen, and the skilfulleſtskilfulest artiſtsartists, or tradeſmentradesmen that be: ſoso as there is a double bond to bindebind ſeruantsservants to obey this kindekind of inſtructionsinstructions:
1. The bond of duty.
2. The bond of profit and benefit to themſeluesthemselves.

div.head: §. 16. Of SeruantsServants faults contrary to obedience in matters of religion.
div.p: NotwithſtandingNotwithstanding the forenamed duty be ſoso behouefullbehoveful to ſeruantsservants, yet of all other duties is it by many leaſtleast thought to be a duty, and moſtmost neglected, the cleaneclean contrary for the moſtmost part being practiſedpractised, as may appeareappear by theſethese particulars.

1. Many ſeruantsservants are of ſoso impious a mindemind, as of all maſtersmasters Contrary, 1. Loth to ſerueserve religious maſtersmasters. they will not ſerueserve ſuchsuch as are religious, and make conſcienceconscience to inſtructinstruct their ſeruantsservants in the way to ſaluationsalvation: they had rather ſerueserve profane maſtersmasters, meeremere worldlings, and very PapiſtsPapists. For why? anyAny thing better agreeth to corrupt nature then to be kept within the bounds of religion: few like the ſtraitstrait gate and narrow way that leadeth to life: for the god of this world ſoso blindeth mens eieseyes, that they cannot ſeesee the bleſſingblessing of life at the end of this way, they only ſeesee the ſtraitneſſestraitness of it: or if they ſhouldshould ſeesee it a farrefar off, yet they ſoso ſauoursavour the things of the fleſhflesh, and of this preſentpresent euillevil world, as they would not regard that which is ſoso farrefar off. Now religious maſtersmasters will endeuourendeavour what they can to keepekeep all their ſeruantsservants in that narrow
way; but irreligious maſtersmasters will ſuffersuffer them to follow the ſwaysway of their owneown corruption, to ſweareswear, to profane the SabbothSabbath, and ſpendspend that whole day in ſleepingsleeping, ſportingsporting, eating and drinking: to goego to bed without prayer, or catechizing, or reading the word of God, and ſoso to riſerise againeagain and goego about their buſineſſebusiness: to which holy duties, ſuchsuch deuoutdevout maſtersmasters as Cornelius was, will hold their ſeruantsservants.

2. Others that are placed by their friends vnderunder ſuchsuch deuoutdevout 2. Mutter againſtagainst them being in ſeruiceservice. maſtersmasters, or not knowing before hand the diſpoſitiondisposition of their maſtersmasters, hauehave themſeluesthemselves couenantedcovenanted with them to be their ſeruantsservants, after they hauehave beenebeen a while in the houſehouse, thinkethink their maſtersmasters houſehouse a priſonprison to them, muttering and murmuring againſtagainst their ſtraitstrait keeping in, as they deemedeem it: and being called in to any religious exerciſeexercise, they will be ready to ſaysay, I was not hired for this, neither am I bound to you herein, ſetset me about your workework and I will doedo it.

3. Some againeagain are the more negligent and diſſolutedissolute in their 3. Negligent becauſebecause maſtersmasters religious. buſineſſebusiness, becauſebecause their maſtersmasters are religious. It is a common complaint, that profane, worldly maſtersmasters ſhalshall hauehave more ſeruiceservice then religious and godly maſtersmasters, yea though theſethese giuegive better wages, diet and lodging then thoſethose. Many thinkethink the fault hereof to be in the maſtermaster: but aſſuredlyassuredly for the moſtmost part the fault is the corrupt diſpoſitiondisposition of ſeruantsservants, that eſteemeesteem pleaſurepleasure in ſinnesin, and libertieliberty thereunto more then wages, diet, and lodging: whereby they ſhewshow themſeluesthemselves impious againſtagainst God, vngratefullungrateful to their maſtersmasters, iniuriousinjurious to themſeluesthemselves. Let this peruerſeperverse diſpoſitiondisposition be noted, that the rule of the ApoſtleApostle verievery pertinent to this point, may be the better obſeruedobserved, They 1 Tim. 6. 2. that hauehave beleeuingbelieving maſtersmasters let them not deſpiſedespise them, but rather doedo them ſeruiceservice, becauſebecause they are faithfullfaithful and belouedbeloved.

div.head: §. 17. Of ſeruantsservants obedience to reproofereproof and correction.
div.p: The ſamesame directions may ſerueserve for yeeldingyielding to reproofereproof and correction: for they may both be brought to one head: and in the generallgeneral they doedo both agree. For reproofereproof is a verballverbal correction, and correction is a reallreal reproofereproof.
The obedience which ſeruantsservants in regard of theſethese muſtmust ſhewshow to their maſtersmasters is twofold.
1. Patiently to bearebear all manner of reproofereproof and correction.
2. Readily to amend that for which they are iuſtlyjustly reprouedreproved or corrected.

For the firſtfirst of theſethese, ſeruantsservants hauehave an expreſſeexpress precept, enforced 1 Pet. 2. 18. &etcc. by many reaſonsreasons in theſethese words, Seruantsservants be ſubiectsubject to your maſtersmasters with all fearefear, not only to the good and gentle, but alſoalso to the froward. For this is thankethank worthy if a man for conſcienceconscience toward God endure griefegrief, ſufferingsuffering wrongfully. For what glory is it if when ye be buffeted for your faults ye take it patiently? butBut if wheywhen ye doedo well and ſuffersuffer for it, ye take it patiently, this is acceptable with God. Here we ſeesee,
1. That correction is patiently to be borne by ſeruantsservants: if correction, then much more reproofereproof.
2. That though correction be iniuſtlyunjustlyiniustly inflicted, yet it is patiently to be endured: therefore much more when it is deſerueddeserved.

3. That buffeting and that of a froward maſtermaster is to be borne: therefore much more lighter correction of a good and gentle maſtermaster. IoſephJoseph patiently endured PſalPsal. 105. 18. fetters, and yroniron chaineschains, and Gen. 39. 20. impriſonmentimprisonment inflicted vponupon him moſtmost vniuſtlyunjustly, eueneven for his faithfulneſſefaithfulness to his maſtermaster. Great was the recompencerecompense which God made vntounto him: & aſſuredlyassuredly God will recompencerecompense all the wrong, paine, and griefegrief, that in this caſecase ſhallshall be endured for conſcienceconscience ſakesake. For the ApoſtleApostle ſaithsaith, that this is thankworthy, that is, worthy of praiſepraise and commendation, and ſoso worthy of recompencerecompense and reward. AgaineAgain he ſaithsaith that it is acceptable to God, ſoso as God will recompencerecompense it, though men may account it but baſeneſſebaseness and blockiſhneſſeblockishness: yea though vniuſtunjust maſtersmasters may thereupon take occaſionoccasion the more to trample vponupon, and inſultinsult ouerover their ſeruantsservants.

To theſethese motiuesmotives I may addeadd the rule of our ChriſtianChristian profeſſionprofession (which is alſoalso intimated by the ApoſtleApostle in theſethese words, 1 Pet. 2. 21. EuenEven hereunto were ye called.) For our ChriſtianChristian calling requireth all men to Rom. 12. 19. giuegive place vntounto wrath:
Matt. 5. 39. To turneturn the other cheekecheek when one is ſmittensmitten:
Rom. 12. 21. To ouercomeovercome euillevil with goodneſſegoodness. 1 Pet. 2. 21. If all ChriſtiansChristians muſtmust ſhewshow ſuchsuch patience to all men, eueneven their equals: how much more ſeruantsservants to maſtersmasters? The ApoſtleApostle commendeth to ſeruantsservants the example of ChriſtChrist in this caſecase: he was reuiledreviled and much he ſufferedsuffered, and that moſtmost iniuriouſlyinjuriously, and
yet patiently did he bearebear all: if ſeruantsservants thus ſuffersuffer with him, they alſoalso ſhallshall reignereign with him.

div.head: §. 18. Of the extremes contrary to ſeruantsservants patient bearing of reproofereproof and correction.
div.p: Patient bearing of rebuke and blowesblows, ſeemethseemeth an hard ſayingsaying to moſtmost ſeruantsservants: they cannot endure to hearehear it: for their mindemind and carriage is cleaneclean contrary thereunto.

1. Some being but reprouedreproved, though iuſtlyjustly, are ready to anſweranswer againeagain, and to chop word for word: a ſinnesin Tit. 2. 9. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . expreſlyexpressly forbidden. div.p: AnſwAnsw. 1.
