word) is not otherwaiesotherways thankethank-worthy. If iuſtlyjustly thou beeſtbeest puniſhedpunished, thou haſthast but thy deſertdesert. If forcibly ſoso as thou canſtcanst not reſiſtresist, neceſſitynecessity maketh thee bearebear it. The ſturdieſtsturdiest theeuesthieves that be, being pinnied, ſuffersuffer themſeluesthemselves to be turned ouerover, becauſebecause they ſeesee a neceſſitynecessity. But ChriſtChrist (whoſewhose 1 Pet. 2. 21. example in this caſecase is ſetset before ſeruantsservants) Mat. 26. 53. could hauehave freed himſelfehimself but would not. If ſeruantsservants endure for conſcienceconscience ſakesake, they will not reſiſtresist, though they be able.

3. Others if they be ſmittensmitten by maſtermaster or miſtreſſemistress, will giuegive as much as they receiuereceive, they will ſmitesmite againeagain: a practiſepractise vnbeſeemingunbeseeming any ChriſtianChristian, but moſtmost vnſeemelyunseemly for ChriſtianChristian ſeruantsservants: who manifeſtmanifest thereby a deſpightdespitedespight of Gods image and power in their maſtersmasters.

4. Others are ſoso poſſeſſedpossessed with a deuilldevil, as they will ſeekeseek all the reuengerevenge they can, if they be corrected: whence it commethcometh to paſſepass that ſomesome hot, heady, hardy youth, ſtickestick not to challenge their maſtersmasters into the field: and others, more maliciouſlymaliciously minded, ſecretlysecretly endeuourendeavour to take away the life of their maſtersmasters. Many that hauehave not the opportunity to practiſepractise ſuchsuch villaniesvillainies, doedo notwithſtandingnotwithstanding in their hearts wiſhwish their maſtersmasters deſtructiondestruction, and make moſtmost fearefullfearful imprecations againſtagainst them; whereby they make themſeluesthemselves guilty of blood before God.

div.head: §. 19. Of ſeruantsservants amending that for which they are iuſtlyjustly reprouedreproved or corrected.
div.p:
More then patience is required of them that are deſeruedlydeservedly rebuked or corrected for their faults: namely See more of this point Treat. 5. §. 33. & 34. repentance, and amendment. Thus ſhallshall the ſmartsmart and paine which ſeruantsservants endure, be as good phyſickephysic vntounto them, and turneturn to their good. True amendment of former faults may make one a better ſeruantservant then he was before he committed thoſethose faults: witneſſewitness that which Saint Paul ſaithsaith of OneſimusOnesimus,
Philem. verſvers. 11. in time paſtpast he was to thee vnprofitableunprofitable, but now profitable to thee and me.

Contrary is their diſpoſitiondisposition, who notwithſtandingnotwithstanding all rebuke and correction goego on ſtillstill in their euillevil and lewd courſescourses: and continue to prouokeprovoke their maſtermaster more and more, and ſoso make them addeadd blow vntounto blow, and ſtrokestroke vntounto ſtrokestroke, till they hauehave no hope of them, but are forced to put them out
of dooresdoors. This commethcometh either from a ſcornfullscornful, diſdainfulldisdainful ſtomachstomach (for Pro. 13. 1. a ſcornerscorner heareth not rebuke) or from a baſebase, ſeruileservile, ſtupidstupid, blockiſhblockish, brutiſhbrutish nature, that is not mouedmoved with any ſmartsmart or paine, like a reſtieresty iadejade that will not ſtirrestir though he be whipt or beaten neuernever ſoso much. Pro. 26. 3. Solomon implieth thus much by putting into one leaſhleash an horſehorse, an aſſeass, and a foolefool: meaning by a foolefool a ſcornfullscornful, blockiſhblockish ſeruantservant: to whoſewhose backeback a rod is as a whip to an horſehorse: of ſuchsuch a foolefool he ſaithsaith, that Pro. 17. 10. an hundred ſtripesstripes enter not into him: and againeagain, Pro. 27. 22. Though thou ſhouldeſtshouldest bray a foolefool in a mortermortar among wheat with a peſtlepestle, yet will not his fooliſhneſſefoolishness depart from him.
But what ſhallshall we ſaysay of ſuchsuch as for rebuke and correction are the worſeworse? What, but that ſhameshame, beggerybeggary, and ſomesome ignominious death or other is like to befall them.
Hitherto of the kindeskinds of ſeruantsservants duties. The next point reſpectethrespecteth the manner of performing them.

div.head: §. 20. Of ſeruingserving with trembling.
div.p: The Manner how ſeruantsservants ought to performeperform their duties is noted in fourefour phraſesphrases:
The firſtfirst whereof is this, with fearefear and trembling. I.
FeareFear is both as a fountainefountain from whence all other duties flow: and alſoalso as a ſawcesauce to ſeaſonseason them all.

Commonly the ſeaſonseason and ſauoursavour of waters commethcometh from the fountainefountain: which Saint IamesJames implieth, where he ſaithsaith, no fountainefountain doth yeeldyield ſaltsalt water and freſhfresh: for if the fountainefountain be Iam. 3. 12. ſaltsalt, the ſtreamesstreams iſſuingissuing from thence will be ſaltsalt: and freſhfresh, if the fountainefountain be freſhfresh: ſoso if fearefear be ſeatedseated in the heart of ſeruantsservants, all their obedience and ſubmiſſionsubmission will be ſeaſonedseasoned therewith. Let therefore ſeruantsservants here learnelearn by their manner of performing all their duties, to declare that there is a true ſeruantservant-like fearefear ſeatedseated in their hearts. Hereof I ſhallshall need ſaysay no more then what hath beenebeen §. 4. before deliuereddelivered.

The other word See Treat. 1. §. 124. trembling added to fearefear, addeth emphaſisemphasis, ſhewingshowing that it is no ſmallsmall fearefear that is required of ſeruantsservants: and it giuethgiveth them to wit that their maſtersmasters hauinghaving a power to puniſhpunish them, they muſtmust ſoso carriecarry themſeluesthemselves as they prouokeprovoke not their maſtermaster to wrath, but be very carefullcareful and circumſpectcircumspect to auoidavoid his diſpleaſuredispleasure, that they giuegive him no iuſtjust occaſionoccasion
of offence. This care had that ſeruantservant of DauidDavid which firſtfirst eſpiedespied AbſolomAbsalom hanging in a tree, and told IoabJoab thereof: 2 Sam. 18. 12. he ſoso feared the diſpleaſuredispleasure of the king his maſtermaster, as to gainegain a thouſandthousand ſhekelsshekels of ſiluersilver he durſtdurst not kill AbſolomAbsalom. The like is noted of Obadiah, who was afraid to tell his maſtermaster Ahab where Eliah was, leftlest his maſtermaster might hauehave thought he had mocked him, if the Spirit had carried Eliah away. 1 King. 18. 9. &etcc.

This trembling fearefear is needfullneedful in regard of the ſmallsmall louelove that ſeruantsservants commonly bearebear to their maſtersmasters. There are not thoſethose motiuesmotives to ſtirrestir vpup louelove in ſeruantsservants to their maſtersmasters, as in children to their parents: except therefore through awe and dread they be kept in compaſſecompass, they will exceedingly tranſgreſſetransgress: and becauſebecause this is ſoso needfullneedful, ſeruantsservants muſtmust labour to nouriſhnourish it, as a meanesmeans to keepekeep them from ouerover-much boldneſſeboldness.

Contrary on the one ſideside is a proud deſpiſingdespising of a maſtersmasters authority (ſayingsaying, if not with their mouthesmouths, yet in their heart, as Gaal of Abimelech, who is he that we ſhouldshould ſerueserve him? or as thoſethose that deſpiſeddespised the gouernmentgovernment of ChriſtChrist their maſtermaster, IudgJudg. 9. 28.
Luk. 19. 14. we will not hauehave this man to reignereign ouerover vsus: and againeagain, PſalPsal. 2. 3. let vsus breakebreak his bonds aſunderasunder, and caſtcast away his cords from vsus.) And on the other ſideside a wretched careleſſeneſſecarelessness, not fearing any puniſhmentpunishment before they feelefeel it: like to many deſperatedesperate theeuesthieves that no whit fearefear the power of the IudgeJudge, but deſperatlydesperatelydesperatly ſaysay, we hauehave but one death to pay. The authority of God himſelfehimself is deſpiſeddespised, and his reuengingrevenging hand is lightly regarded by ſuchsuch proud and deſperatedesperate ſeruantsservants: ſoso as their ſinnesin is no ſmallsmall ſinnesin.

div.head: §. 21. Of ſeruingserving with ſinceritysincerity.
div.p:
The ſecondsecond branch concerning the manner of ſeruantsservants performing their dutieduty is in theſethese words, in ſingleneſſesingleness of heart, 11II. ſoso as all muſtmust be performed with an honeſthonest and vprightupright heart: whatſoeuerwhatsoever yeeye doedo, doedo it heartily, ſaithsaith the ApoſtleApostle to ſeruantsservants Col. 3. 23. in another place. Thus did IoſephJoseph in ſingleneſſesingleness of heart ſerueserve his maſtermaster: inſtanceinstance his refuſingrefusing to abuſeabuse his miſtreſſemistress in Gen. 39. 11, 12. a priuateprivate chamber when ſheshe deſireddesired it, and no other body was in the houſehouse. Happy were it for maſtersmasters to hauehave ſuchsuch ſeruantsservants: then might they take no more care then Potiphar did, but put Gen. 39. 6.
all that they hauehave into their ſeruantsservants hands. Neither would this rare vertuevirtue in ſeruantsservants be only profitable to their maſtersmasters, but alſoalso very comfortable to themſeluesthemselves, and bring them much peace of conſcienceconscience.

Contrary is hypocriticallhypocritical ſeruiceservice: when ſeruantsservants hauehave a heart, and a heart, making ſhewshow -of one heart outwardly, and hauehave another, eueneven a cleaneclean contrary heart within them. Such PſalPsal. 12. 2. an one was Gehazi, who came in and ſtoodstood before his maſtermaster, as if he had performed ſomesome good ſeruiceservice for his maſtermaster, when 22 King. King 5. 25. he had moſtmost highly diſhonoureddishonoured him: and ſuchsuch an one was IudasJudas who carried as fairefair a face to his maſtermaster as any of the diſciplesdisciples, and yet was an arrant traitor: for when he was thought to goego out to buy prouiſionprovision for his maſtermaster, he went to IohnJohn 13. 29. betray him.

All eye-ſeruiceservice is contrary to the forenamed ſingleneſſesingleness of heart: when ſeruantsservants are diligent ſoso long as their maſtersmasters eye is on them: Eye ſeruiceservice. like little children that will doedo any thing their mother will hauehave them doedo, while her eye is vponupon them; but nothing, when her backeback is turned. The world is full of ſuchsuch eye-ſeruingserving ſeruantsservants, who while their maſtersmasters are preſentpresent, will be as buſiebusy as Bees: but if he be away, then either idling at home, or gadding abroad, or nothing but wrangling, and eating, and drinking with the drunken; like that lewd ſeruantservant whom ChriſtChrist noteth in the parable Matth. 24. 49. Let the iudgementjudgment denounced againſtagainst him be noted of ſuchsuch ſeruantsservants.

div.head: §. 22. Of ſeruingserving for conſcienceconscience ſakesake.
div.p:
The third branch of the manner of ſeruantsservants performing III. Sit ſeruusseruus non vt ſeruusseruus ad oculum, ſedsed vt domini ſtudioſusstudiosus. ConſtitConstit. ApoſtApost. l. 4. c. 12. their dutieduty is in theſethese words, as vntounto ChriſtChrist, as the ſeruantsservants of ChriſtChrist, doing the will of God, as to the Lord: all which doedo ſetset forth a good conſcienceconscience, or ſuchsuch ſeruiceservice as is performed for conſcienceconscience ſakesake, or for the Lords ſakesake, which is all one: becauſebecause the conſcienceconscience hath an eye only to the Lord, to his will, and to his ordinance. Though there were no other motiuemotive in the world to mouemove them to obey their maſtersmasters, yet their conſcienceconscience to God would mouemove them. Such was IoſephsJosephs manner of ſeruingserving his maſtermaster, as the reaſonreason which he himſelfehimself rendrethrendereth to his miſtreſſemistress ſhewethshoweth, How can I doedo this great wickedneſſewickedness, and ſinnesin againſtagainst God? The Gen. 39. 9. prayer which AbrahamsAbraham's ſeruantservant made to God, and the thanks Gen. 24. 12, 27.
which he rendredrendered to him for bleſſingblessing his iourneyjourney, ſhewshow, that he ſeruedserved his maſtermaster for the Lords ſakesake. It is more cleareclear then needs be prouedproved, that ſuchsuch was IaakobsJacob's ſeruiceservice to his maſtermaster. This is the rather to be noted of ChriſtianChristian ſeruantsservants, becauſebecause herein lieth the greateſtgreatest difference betwixt beleeuingbelieving ſeruantsservants, and others: others may ſerueserve with fearefear and trembling, in ſingleneſſesingleness of heart, and with good will; but only Saints doedo ſeruiceservice as to ChriſtChrist for conſcienceconscience ſakesake: If this be not that which only they aimeaim at, yet aſſuredlyassuredly they doedo chiefly and principally aimeaim at it: which maketh them not to content themſeluesthemselves with doing the thing, but to endeuourendeavour to doedo it after the beſtbest manner that they can, ſoso as God may beſtbest accept thereof: whereby as they approueapprove themſeluesthemselves to God, ſoso they doedo much good to their maſtersmasters, and bring much comfort vntounto their owneown ſoulessouls.

Contrary is the mindemind of moſtmost, who doedo all the ſeruiceservice which SeruiceService on by-reſpectsrespects. they doedo on by-reſpectsrespects: they may performeperform much dutieduty, and it may be doedo much good to their maſtersmasters; and thereupon they may get good wages at their maſtersmasters hands, and extraordinarieextraordinary recompencerecompense alſoalso, and liuelive in much quiet vnderunder them: but no reward can they lookelook for at Gods hands: ſoso as I may ſaysay to ſuchsuch ſeruantsservants, as ChriſtChrist ſaidsaid to thoſethose who did all to hauehave glory of men, They hauehave their reward.
Matth. 6. 2.

div.head: §. 23. Of ſeruantsservants willingneſſewillingness to performeperform their dutieduty.
div.p: The fourth branch reſpectingrespecting the manner of ſeruantsservants performing IIII. their dutieduty, is noted in this phraſephrase, with good will. This good will of a ſeruantservant to his maſtermaster, hath reſpectrespect partly to the diſpoſitiondisposition of the ſeruantservant, and ſoso it implieth willingneſſewillingness and cheerefulneſſecheerfulness; SeruiceService to be done cheerefullycheerfully. and partly to the benefit of the maſtermaster, and ſoso it implieth faithfulneſſefaithfulness.

Of willingneſſewillingness to doedo that dutieduty which belongeth to a ſeruantservant, ChriſtChrist IeſusJesus (who Phil. 2. 7. tooketook vponupon him the formeform of a ſeruantservant) hath made himſelfehimself a worthy patternepattern. PſalPsal. 40. 8. I delight to doedo thy will, ſaithsaith he to him that ſentsent him: and againeagain, Joh. 4. 34. My meat is to doedo the will of him that ſentsent me, and to finiſhfinish his workework. Doth not a man eat his meat willingly, with delight and cheerefulneſſecheerfulness? euenEven ſoso did ChriſtChrist the workework of him that ſentsent him. So cheerefullycheerfully did IaakobJacob ſerueserve his VncleUncle Laban, that Gen. 29. 20. ſeuenseven yeeresyears ſeemedseemed to him but a few dayesdays.

div.head: ObiectObject. The reaſonreason thereof was the louelove he had to Rachel.
div.p: 1. AnſwAnsw. This was one reaſonreason, but not the only reaſonreason: had he not borne good will to his VncleUncle and Maſtermaster, as well as louelove to his wife, the time might hauehave ſeemedseemed tedious enough: but both meeting together, made the time paſſepass away the better.

2. AnſwAnsw. If the louelove he had to Rachel made him doedo his ſeruiceservice ſoso cheerefullycheerfully: then if ſeruantsservants louelove God, for whoſewhose ſakesake they ought to doedo their ſeruiceservice, it will cheerefullycheerfully be done.

1. That which the ApoſtleApostle applieth to giuinggiving of almesalms (2 Cor. 9. 7.) may be extended to all manner of duties which God requireth, God louethloveth cheerefulneſſecheerfulness: that workework therefore which is not ſeaſonedseasoned therewith God regardeth not.

2. As cheerefulneſſecheerfulness maketh God the better to like the workework, ſoso it maketh the workework much more eaſieeasy to him that doth it. Our common prouerbeproverb noteth as much, Nothing is hard to a willing mindemind.

3. ApoſtolusApostolus ſeruosseruos monet dominis ſuissuis ex animo cum bona voluntate ſeruireseruire, vt ſcilicetscilicet ſisi non poſſuntpossunt à dominis liberi fieri, ſuamsuam ſeruitutemseruitutem ipſiipsi quodammedo liberam faciant. Aug de Ciu. Dei, l. 19. c. 15. Direction. Let there be cheerefulneſſecheerfulness in a ſeruantsservants mindemind, and he is as free as his maſtermaster: for ſuchsuch a ſeruantservant is the Lords freeman (1 Cor. 7. 22.) and when he cannot be made free of his maſtermaster, he doth after a manner make his ſeruiceservice free.

HaueHave an eye to God, to his acceptation, and remuneration, and it will quicken thy ſpiritspirit. Mans reward maketh poorepoor men glad of workework, and cheerefullcheerful in doing their workework: it is as ſugarsugar to ſharpesharpsharpe wine. TradeſmenTradesmen, PhyſitiansPhysicians, Lawyers, all ſortssorts of men, are by gainegain drawnedrawn on with great willingneſſewillingness to take great painespains. Should not Gods recompencerecompense of our painespains make vsus much more willing? Surely it would, if we had ſuchsuch an eye of Heb. 11. 26. faith as MoſesMoses had, thereby to ſeesee the recompencerecompense of reward which he ſawsaw.

Contrary is heauineſſeheaviness of ſpiritspirit, and diſcontentedneſſediscontentedness of mindemind, Contrary, DiſcontentedneſſeDiscontentedness. when ſeruantsservants doedo their ſeruiceservice lowringly, grudgingly, by compulſioncompulsion (as BearesBears are brought to a ſtakestake) and of neceſſitienecessity, as ſlauesslaves in a galley. Such ſeruiceservice muſtmust needs be vntowardlyuntowardly done: but though outwardly it be well done, yet can the doer hauehave little comfort therein, becauſebecause God accepteth it not.

div.head: §. 24. Of ſeruantsservants quickneſſequickness and diligence in their ſeruiceservice.
div.p:
SeruantsServants, in teſtimonietestimony of their willingneſſewillingness and cheerefulneſſecheerfulness, muſtmust be both quickequick and diligent in their ſeruiceservice: for theſethese
are effects of willingneſſewillingness. QuickneſſeQuickness hath reſpectrespect to the time of doing a thing. Diligence to the painespains that is taken about it.

He that is quickequick in his ſeruiceservice taketh vpup no more time about QuickneſſeQuickness. one thing then muſtmust needs; but is ready to doedo one thing after another; and thus doth much more ſeruiceservice. It is expreſlyexpressly noted of Rebekah, that ſheshe Gen. 24. 18, 20. haſtedhasted, and let downedown her pitcher: and haſtedhasted and emptied her pitcher, and ran againeagain to the Well. And AbrahamsAbraham's ſeruantservant hauinghaving made what ſpeedspeed he could to the place whither he was ſentsent, Gen. 24. 33. would not eat till he had told his errand: after he had told it, if he had not ſpedsped, verſvers. 49. he would not hauehave delaieddelayed time, but hauehave gone againeagain forthwith: when he had well diſpatcheddispatched all, verſvers. 56. he would not ſtaystay vponupon any complements, but haſtedhasted away to his maſtermaster. 2 Sam. 18. 23. Ahimaaz ſtrouestrove with CuſhiCushi who ſhouldshould ſooneſtsoonest bring their meſſagemessage to their maſtermaster: and Ahimaaz outſtriptoutstript CuſhiCushi, for he had a very willing mindemind to doedo the buſineſſebusiness. The manner of charge which EliſhaElisha gauegave to his ſeruantservant, implieth all the ſpeedspeed he could make: it was this, 2 King. 4. 29. Gird vpup thy loynesloins, goego thy way: if thou meet any by the way, ſalutesalute him not: and if any ſalutesalute thee, anſweranswer him not againeagain.

He that is diligent in his ſeruiceservice, will not only be quickequick for the Diligence. time, but alſoalso hold on, and imployemploy all the labour and painespains that he can for the well effecting of that which he is to doedo. That generallgeneral charge laid vponupon all men, in particular appertaineth to a ſeruantservant ( Gen. 3. 19. In the ſweatsweat of thy face thou ſhaltshalt eat bread) and that which Solomon noteth ( Eccl. 9. 10. what ſoeuersoever thine hand findeth to doedo, doedo it with thy might.) Great was IaakobsJacob's diligence (for he ſaithsaith of himſelfehimself in doing his maſtersmasters buſineſſebusiness, Gen. 31. 40. In the day the drought conſumedconsumed me, and the frost by night, and my ſleepesleep departed from mine eyes.) Great alſoalso was the diligence of thoſethose ſhepherdsshepherds, that Luke 2. 8. kept watch ouerover their flockeflock by night: and of Mat. 25. 16, 17. thoſethose ſeruantsservants, that by their painespains doubled the talents which were committed to them. As diligence is by theſethese and many like examples commended vntounto vsus, ſoso is it further ſetset forth by the many promiſespromises which are made vntounto it, as, Pro. 10. 4. The hand of the diligent maketh rich:
& 12. 14. The recompencerecompense of a mans hands ſhallshall be rendredrendered vntounto him:
verſvers. 24. The hand of the diligent ſhallshall be arebear rule:
& 14. 23. In all labour there is profit.

The workework which ſeruantsservants are by their maſtermaster appointed to doedo, is to them the workework of God: whereupon the ApoſtleApostle ſaithsaith
to ſeruantsservants as well as to others, 1 Cor. 7. 17. as God hath called eueryevery one, ſoso let him walkewalk: but the workework of God is to be done with all diligence: for Jer. 48. 10. CurſedCursed is he that doth the workework of the Lord negligently.

Contrary is the idleneſſeidleness, lazineſſelaziness, ſlothfulneſſeslothfulness, and ſluggiſhneſſesluggishness IdleneſſeIdleness. of ſeruantsservants. TheſeThese are faults too too common. Solomon much inueighethinveigheth againſtagainst theſethese vices, ſettingsetting them forth in their kindekind, and ſettingsetting downedown the many miſchiefesmischiefs that follow thereupon.

Thus he deciphereth them; Pro. 26. 13, 14, 15. The ſlothfullslothful man ſaithsaith, there is a Lion in the way (that is, he pretendeth vnlikelyunlikely danger) As the dooredoor turneth vponupon the hinges, ſoso a ſlothfullslothful man vponupon his bed. The ſlothfullslothful hideth his hand in his boſomebosom, it grieuethgrieveth him to bring it againeagain to his mouth.
& 24. 33. Yet a little ſleepesleep, a little ſlumberslumber, a little folding of the hands to ſleepesleep.

TheſeThese are the miſchiefesmischiefs which he noteth to come from idleneſſeidleness and ſlothsloth, & 10. 4. PouertiePoverty,
& 12. 24. SeruitudeServitude,
& 13. 4. FruitleſſeFruitless wiſheswishes and deſiresdesires,
& 19. 15. Hunger,
& 20. 4. BeggerieBeggaryBeggery,
& 21. 25. Death. And to ſhewshow what ſmallsmall ioyjoy or comfort maſtersmasters may hauehave in ſlothfullslothful ſeruantsservants, he compareth them to vinegervinegar and ſmokesmoke, which are as irkeſomeirksomeirkesome to the teeth and eyes as can be: & 10. 26. As vinegervinegar (ſaithsaith he) is to the teeth, and ſmokesmoke to the eyes, ſoso is the ſluggardsluggard to them that ſendsend him. And becauſebecause many idle packs thinkethink and ſaysay they doedo no hurt, he further ſaithsaith, that & 18. 9. He that is ſlothfullslothful in his workework is brother to him that is a great waſterwaster: in which reſpectrespect ChriſtChrist ſtilethstyleth a ſlothfullslothful ſeruantservant, Mat. 25. 26, 30. a wicked and vnprofitableunprofitable ſeruantservant: and giuethgiveth him the portion of thoſethose who doedo much hurt.

How lightly ſoeuersoever many ſeruantsservants eſteemeesteem idleneſſeidleness and ſlothsloth, the truth is, that it is a plaineplain theft. For the beſtbest ſeruiceservice that ſeruantsservants can doedo, is due to their maſtermaster: and they ought to be as diligent in their maſtersmasters workework, as if it were their owneown. So as it is not enough to auoidavoid idleneſſeidleness in doing nothing at all, but they muſtmust take heed that they be not ſlothfullslothful in doing ſomethingsomething: for as good not at all, as neuernever a whit the better.

I hauehave the further preſſedpressed this point, becauſebecause it is noted as a blemiſhblemish in ſuchsuch ſeruantsservants as profeſſeprofess religion to be moſtmost lazielazy and negligent, leaſtleast ſeduloussedulous and diligent. Much of that time which they ſhouldshould ſpendspend about their maſtersmasters buſineſſebusiness (which is their
particular calling) they ſpendspend in prating about ſtatestate, and Church-buſineſſebusiness, (matters not belonging to them.) Thus they make their maſtersmasters weary of their ſeruiceservice; and by reaſonreason thereof they are oft ſhiftedshifted from houſehouse to houſehouse, and as rolling ſtonesstones, gather no moſſemoss: they neither learnelearn skill, whereby they may, when they are of themſeluesthemselves, maintainemaintain themſeluesthemselves, and doedo good to others: nor lay vpup any ſtockestock or portion, as others which are diligent doedo: yea they get ſuchsuch an habit of idleneſſeidleness, as they can neuernever ſhakeshake it off againeagain: for they who are ſlothfullslothful being vnderunder maſtersmasters, ſeldomeseldom proueprove diligent when they are for themſeluesthemselves. In theſethese is Solomons prouerbeproverb verified, The talketalk of the lips tendeth only to penury.
Pro. 14. 23.

div.head: §. 25. Of ſeruantsservants faithfulneſſefaithfulness.
div.p:
It was §. 23. before noted, that the good will here required of ſeruantsservants to their maſtersmasters had reſpectrespect to the profit and benefit which ſeruantsservants by their ſeruiceservice might bring to their maſtersmasters: and in that reſpectrespect it compriſethcompriseth faithfulneſſefaithfulness vnderunder it, FaithfulneſſeFaithfulness (I ſaysay) whereby ſeruantsservants doedo well diſchargedischarge that truſttrust which is committed to them. ExpreſlyExpressly it is commanded to ſeruantsservants, Tit. 2. 10. To ſhewshow all good faithfulneſſefaithfulness, and 1 Cor. 4. 2. it is required in ſtewardsstewards that a man be found faithfullfaithful. The phraſephrase which is vſedused of MoſesMoses,
Heb. 3. 5. He was faithfullfaithful as a ſeruantservant, ſhewethshoweth that faithfulneſſefaithfulness by a kindekind of proprietiepropriety appertaineth to a ſeruantservant: and Mat. 25. 21. where ChriſtChrist coupleth theſethese two, good and faithfullfaithful, he giuethgiveth vsus to vnderſtandunderstand that a ſeruantsservants goodneſſegoodness conſiſtethconsisteth in his faithfulneſſefaithfulness.
Great is the benefit that by ſeruantsservants faithfulneſſefaithfulness will redound both to maſtermaster and ſeruantservant.

The benefit which commethcometh to the maſtermaster, Solomon noteth in this prouerbeproverb, As the cold of ſnowsnow (is very acceptable, comfortable Pro. 25. 13. and profitable) in the time of harueſtharvest (when men are eueneven ſwelteredsweltered with heat) ſoso is a faithfullfaithful meſſengermessenger to them that ſendsend him: for he refreſhethrefresheth the ſoulesoul of his maſtersmasters: and againeagain in this, A faithfullfaithful ambaſſadourambassadour is health, that is, he bringeth ſafetiesafety to his maſtermaster. Pro. 13. 17.

The benefit which redoundeth to the ſeruantservant himſelfehimself by his faithfulneſſefaithfulness ChriſtChrist noteth in this his approbation, and remuneration thereof, Well done thou good and faithfullfaithful ſeruantservant,
Mat. 25. 21.
thou haſthast beenebeen faithfullfaithful ouerover a few things, I will make thee Ruler ouerover many things, enter thou into the ioyjoy of thy Lord. EueryEvery ſeruantservant ſhallshall be called to his account: if not by his maſtermaster on earth, yet by his maſtermaster in heauenheaven: he will ſaysay to eueryevery one, GiueGive an account of thy ſtewardſhipstewardship: now then if ſeruantsservants hauehave not beenebeen Luk. 16. 2. faithfullfaithful, what other diſchargedischarge can they lookelook for, then that which the wicked, ſlothfullslothful, and vnprofitableunprofitable ſeruantservant (who hid his talent in a napkin) receiuedreceived, namely this, CaſtCast ye the
Mat. 25. 30. vnprofitableunprofitable ſeruantservant into outer darkneſſedarkness, there ſhallshall be weeping and gnaſhinggnashing of teeth. Let all vnfaithfullunfaithful ſeruantsservants note this: for to faithfulneſſefaithfulness is contrary all vnfaithfulneſſeunfaithfulness, as negligence, deceit, theeuerythieverytheevery, treachery, and ſuchsuch like vices. Much dammagedamage, diſgracedisgrace, and vexation is brought by ſuchsuch ſeruantsservants to maſtersmasters: and better it had beenebeen that they neuernever had come into a mans houſehouse.

But that the point of faithfulneſſefaithfulness may be the better diſcerneddiscerned, and obſeruedobserved, I will exemplifieexemplify it in ſeuenseven particulars whereabout it ought eſpeciallyespecially to be exerciſedexercised, which are, 1. The Goods, 2. The BuſineſſesBusinesses and affairesaffairs, 3. The CounſelsCounsels and ſecretssecrets, 4. The other ſeruantsservants, 5. theThe Childrenchildren, 6. The Bedfellow, 7. The Perſonperson of their maſtermaster or miſtreſſemistress.

div.head: §. 26. Of ſeruantsservants faithfulneſſefaithfulness about their maſtersmasters goods.
div.p:
Two things are required of ſeruantsservants to teſtifietestify their faithfulneſſefaithfulness about their maſtersmasters goods. 1.
1. A ſafesafe keeping of them.
2. An increaſingincreasing of them.

1. WhatſoeuerWhatsoever is committed by maſtersmasters vntounto their ſeruantsservants, they muſtmust ſoso carefully preſeruepreserve, as it be not loſtlost, ſpoiledspoiled, or impaired SeruantsServants muſtmust well preſeruepreserve their maſtersmasters goods. vnderunder their hands, whether they be things within dooresdoors, or without. I may to this purpoſepurpose not vnfitlyunfitly apply that charge vntounto ſeruantsservants which in another caſecase the ApoſtleApostle gauegave to Timothy, 1 Tim. 6. 20. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . KeepeKeep that which is committed to thy truſttrust: the Metaphor is taken from ſeruantsservants, and ſoso ſhewethshoweth what is their dutieduty. Great was IoſephsJosephs faithfulneſſefaithfulness in this kindekind, which made his maſtermaster Gen. 39. 4. put all that he had into his hand. So great was IackobsJacobsJackobs faithfulneſſefaithfulness, that & 31. 38, 39. in twentietwenty yeeresyears his maſtersmasters ewes and ſheshe Goats, being vnderunder his hand, caſtcast not their young, nor the RammesRams were deuoureddevoured: if any thing were tornetorn of
beaſtsbeasts, he brought it not to his maſtermaster, but bare the loſſeloss of it himſelfehimself. If ſeruantsservants eſpieespy any dammagedamage or hurt done by others to their maſtersmasters goods, they muſtmust redreſſeredress it, if they can, or at leaſtleast make it knowneknown to their maſtersmasters, that he may giuegive order for the redreſſingredressing of it: as the ſeruantsservants of him that ſowedsowed good ſeedseed among which tares were ſowedsowed, mentioned Mat. 13. 27. in the parable.

MaſtersMasters that put ſeruantsservants in truſttrust, ſecurelysecurely goego about other affairesaffairs, and lookelook not themſeluesthemselves to thoſethose goods which are vnderunder their ſeruantsservants cuſtodiecustody, which is to be preſuppoſedpresupposed they would doedo, if they truſtedtrusted not their ſeruantsservants. Great reaſonreason therefore it is that ſeruantsservants be carefullcareful of thoſethose things which are ſoso committed to them.

2. They ought further to doedo what lieth in them to aduanceadvance SeruantsServants muſtmust endeuourendeavour to increaſeincrease their maſtersmasters eſtateestate. Gen. 30. 30. Mat. 25. 16, 17. their maſtersmasters eſtateestate, and to increaſeincrease his ſtockestock. The little which Laban had was by IaakobsJacob's faithfulneſſefaithfulness in this kindekind increaſedincreased vntounto a multitude. The talents which were committed to the two faithfullfaithful ſeruantsservants were by their induſtrieindustry increaſedincreased to as many more. So as it is not ſufficientsufficient for ſeruantsservants not to impaireimpair their maſtersmasters eſtateestate, but they muſtmust better it: for he that kept ſafesafe his maſtersmasters talent, and gauegave him his owneown againeagain, was counted an vnprofitableunprofitable ſeruantservant, and receiuedreceived the doomedoom of waſterswasters.

MoſtMost maſtersmasters take ſeruantsservants for their aduantageadvantage and benefit, for it is but little eaſeease for a maſtermaster to prouideprovide diet and lodging for many ſeruantsservants, and to giuegive them wages, if they reapereap no profit and benefit by them.

div.head: §. 27. Of ſeruantsservants careleſneſſecarelessness ouerover their maſtersmasters goods.
div.p:
Contrary to ſeruantsservants fidelitiefidelity in ſafesafe keeping their maſtersmasters goods committed to their charge is CareleſneſſeCarelessness and negligence in ſufferingsuffering loſſeloss and dammagedamage come to their maſtersmasters as in the fields, when they lookelook not to his ſencesfencessences and gatsgates: or neglect his cattellcattle ſoso as they be ſtolnestolenstolne, or ſuffersuffer diſeaſesdiseases to grow vponupon them, or giuegive them not fodder and water in due ſeaſonseason. Or in the houſehouse, when they leaueleave dooresdoors or windoweswindows open, and theeuesthieves come in and take away, or hookehook out their maſtersmasters goods: or careleſlycarelessly leaueleave the fire, or let candles burneburn
ſoso as the houſehouse may be ſeesetsee on fire: or ſuffersuffer houſholdhousehold-ſtuffestuff, and apparellapparel to lie till it be moth-eaten or otherwiſeotherwise ſpoiledspoiled: or ſuffersuffer any thing in the houſehouse to be broken: or victuallvictual to lie in corners moulding, or to be caſtcast vpup and downedown for dogs and cats. When ChriſtChrist ſoso increaſedincreased the bread and fiſhfish, wherewith many thouſandsthousands were fed, that many fragments were left, he bid his diſciplesdisciples gather vpup what remained, and rendredrendered this reaſonreason, that nothing be loſtlost. The dammagedamage which may come by IohnJohn 6. 12. ſeruantsservants careleſneſſecarelessness, may be more then euerever they can be able to make ſatisfactionsatisfaction for: and therefore they ought the more carefully to preuentprevent it.

div.head: §. 28. Of ſeruantsservants fraud.
div.p: Contrary to the other branch of ſeruantsservants faithfulneſſefaithfulness in increaſingincreasing their maſtersmasters eſtateestate, is all manner of theft and fraud, whether it be by retaining that which is due to their maſtersmasters, or by purloining from them that which they hauehave. Tit. 2. 10. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . The ApoſtleApostle expreſlyexpressly forbiddeth ſeruantsservants to purloinepurloin. The word tranſlatedtranslated purloinepurloin, is the ſamesame whereby the fraud of Ananias is ſetset forth, who Acts 5. 2. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . kept backeback part of the price of a poſſeſſionpossession which they ſoldsold: ſoso as thereby is forbidden not only open and manifeſtmanifest ſtealthstealth, as pilfering money out of their maſtersmasters purſepurse, cheſtchest, or counter; or conueyingconveying away their cornecorn, wares, or any other goods: but alſoalso putting more into the account of expencesexpenses then hath beenebeen expended, or into the account of debts leſſeless then is due (as the vniuſtunjust ſtewardsteward, who for a debt of an hundred meaſuresmeasures of oyleoil put in fiftiefifty, and for an hundred of Luke 16. 6, 7. wheat put in foureſcorefourescore) or ſpendingspending more then needs, or bringing in ill company into the houſehouse when their maſtersmasters are abſentabsent, and entertaining them on their maſtersmasters coſtcost, or concealing part of the price which hath beenebeen taken for any wares, or borowingborrowing money in their maſtersmasters names, or taking greater fees then their maſtersmasters wot of, or receiuingreceiving bribes or gifts which their maſtersmasters refuſerefuse (as Gehazi) or hiring others to doedo their workework vponupon their maſtersmasters coſtcost, or inueaglinginveigling away their maſtersmasters 2 King. 5. 22. cuſtomerscustomers, or purloining away other mens goods committed to their maſtersmasters truſttrust (as TaylorsTailors ſeruantsservants, who thereby both much diſcreditdiscredit their maſtersmasters, and alſoalso hinder their cuſtomecustom.)

div.head: ObiectObject. What if maſtersmasters detainedetain their ſeruantsservants wages? may they not by priuyprivy meanesmeans right themſeluesthemselves?
div.p: AnſwAnsw. A maſtersmasters ſinnesin is no warrant to make ſeruantsservants anſweranswer ſinnesin with ſinnesin. The law is as open for ſeruantsservants as for maſtersmasters: if not, Gods earesears are open for their complaints: he can and will redreſſeredress all, or here or hereafter. Gen. 31. 42. Note IaakobsJacob's example. Many make this a iuſtjust pretence: but whether it be iuſtjust or no, it is not ſafesafe to open this gap of deceit.

TheſeThese and ſuchsuch like kindeskinds of deceit are the more hainousheinous ſinnessins becauſebecause of that truſttrust which maſtersmasters repoſerepose in ſeruantsservants: for they violate both the bond of iuſticejustice, and of fidelity alſoalso. If a ſeruantservant imbezillembezzle or defraud his maſtermaster of any of his 21. Of Hen. 8. Stat. 7. And 5. of Eliz. Stat. 10. goods to the value of forty ſhillingsshillings, he is adiudgedadjudged a felon by our ſtatutestatute law.

div.head: §. 29. Of ſeruantsservants faithfulneſſefaithfulness in the buſineſſesbusinesses which they are to diſpatchdispatch for their maſtersmasters.
div.p:
In the buſineſſesbusinesses which maſtersmasters commit to the care of II. their ſeruantsservants to be diſpatcheddispatched by them, they muſtmust doedo their beſtbest endeuourendeavour that all may proſperprosper vnderunder their hands: as it is noted of IoſephJoseph,
Gen. 39. 2. he was a proſperousprosperous man: we hauehave not only a pregnant proofeproof, but alſoalso an excellent direction for this point, in the Gen. 24. example of AbrahamsAbraham's ſeruantservant, who was very faithfullfaithful in diſpatchingdispatching the buſineſſebusiness of fetching a wife for IſaakIsaac: therein let theſethese particulars be noted.

1. He feared God: the whole cariagecarriage of that buſineſſebusiness teſtifiethtestifieth as much. There is a double bond to tie ſeruantsservants hereunto: one in reſpectrespect of themſeluesthemselves, that in the thing which they doedo they may be accepted of God: another in reſpectrespect of their maſtersmasters, that their maſtersmasters buſineſſebusiness may proſperprosper vnderunder their hands: God proſperethprospereth ſuchsuch as fearefear him, in all things they take in hand: inſtanceinstance the examples of Gen. 30. 27. IaakobJacob,
& 39. 2. IoſephJoseph, and 1 Sam. 18. 14. DauidDavid.

2. He Gen. 24. 12. called vponupon God to proſperprosper his endeuoursendeavours: now prayer is the beſtbest meanesmeans that poſſiblypossibly can be vſedused to obtaineobtain any bleſſingblessing from the Lord. Without it all our endeuoursendeavours are vainevain ( PſalPsal. 127. 2. It is in vainevain to riſerise vpup early and ſitsit vpup late, and to eat the bread of carefulneſſecarefulness, except Gods bleſſingblessing accompany all.)

3. He Gen. 24. 27. gauegave thankesthanks when he ſawsaw the Lord begin to proſperprosper
that he tooketook in hand: thankſgiuingthanksgiving for the beginning of a bleſſingblessing, is an effectualleffectual meanesmeans for continuance of that bleſſingblessing: yea it is alſoalso an effectualleffectual meanesmeans to mouemove God to proſperprosper other things that we take in hand: ſoso as, if ſeruantsservants deſiredesire to proſperprosper in all the affairesaffairs which they vndertakeundertake for their maſtersmasters, they muſtmust render thanks for the firſtfirst ſucceſſesuccess which he hath giuengiven, and ſoso for the ſecondsecond, third, fourth, and for eueryevery ſucceſſesuccess.

4. He tooketook all the opportunities he could: Gen. 24. 17, 23. when he ſawsaw a maid to inquire of, he ran to her, and inquired what was behouefullbehoveful for his matter: when he had ground to thinkethink ſheshe was the maid, VerſVers. 22. he preſentedpresented gifts to her: VerſVers. 33. ſoso ſoonesoon as he was brought to the houſehouse, he falls vponupon the matter for which he came, eueneven before he did eat any thing: after matters to his liking were concluded, he maketh no tarrying, but with all ſpeedspeed cariethcarrieth the maid to IſaakIsaac. In a word, he omitted nothing that in the vttermoſtuttermost of his wiſdomewisdom he conceiuedconceived to be behouefullbehoveful for that matter: more he could not hauehave done, if the matter had wholly concerned himſelfehimself. I ſhallshall need no further to vrgeurge this point, then by ſettingsetting this patternepattern before ſeruantsservants.

Contrary is their diſpoſitiondisposition who care not whether the things which they doedo for their maſtermaster proſperprosper or no: if they hauehave taken any painespains therein, ſoso as their maſtermaster cannot ſaysay they hauehave altogether neglected it, there is all that they care for. If it ſucceedsucceed not well, they will ſaysay they are not in Gods place to make eueryevery thing which is done to proſperprosper. But though the whole bleſſingblessing reſtrest in God, yet hath he ſanctifiedsanctified meanesmeans for obtaining his bleſſingblessing (as faith, prayer, thankſgiuingthanksgiving, and the like) which becauſebecause they vſeuse not, they failefail in this point of faithfulneſſefaithfulness. Nay further, they vſeuse thoſethose things which doedo mainly hinder and keepekeep away Gods bleſſingblessing, and in ſteadstead thereof bring a curſecurse vponupon all they do, as profaneneſſeprofaneness, vncleanneſſeuncleanness, drunkenneſſedrunkenness, and all manner of riotouſneſſeriotousness, yea deſpiſingdespising Gods word and holy ordinances, reproaching his Saints, taking his name in vainevain by ſwearingswearing, forſwearingforswearing, and blaſphemingblaspheming, lying, alſoalso backbiting, pilfering, and other like vices. TheſeThese irreligious and wicked ſeruantsservants, as they ſinnesin
againſtagainst God and their owneown ſoulessouls, ſoso alſoalso againſtagainst their maſtermaster: it is not for maſtersmasters profit to keepekeep ſuchsuch ſeruantsservants.

div.head: §. 30. Of ſeruantsservants faithfulneſſefaithfulness in keeping their maſtersmasters ſecretssecrets, and concealing their infirmities.
div.p: By reaſonreason of that nearenear bond which is betwixt maſtermaster III. and ſeruantsservants, and their nearenear and continuallcontinual abiding together, and the many imploimentsemployments which maſtersmasters hauehave for their ſeruantsservants, ſeruantsservants come to know many of their maſtersmasters ſecretssecrets: faithfulneſſefaithfulness therefore requireth to keepekeep them cloſeclose. ProuidedProvided that they be not ſuchsuch ſecretssecrets as tend to the diſhonourdishonour of God, or to the danger of the Commonwealthcommonwealth and Church, no nor of a priuateprivate perſonperson: for 1 Sam. 20. 12. IonathanJonathan is commended for diſcoueringdiscovering the miſchiefemischief which Saul had ſecretlysecretly intended againſtagainst DauidDavid.

For proofeproof of the point, note what Solomon ſaithsaith, Pro. 11. 13. He that is of a faithfullfaithful ſpiritspirit concealeth a matter: namely, a ſecretsecret matter. Note alſoalso how faithfullfaithful IerJer. 38. 27. IeremiahJeremiah was in keeping Zedekiahs counſellcounsel: though the Princes enquired after it, yet would he not reuealereveal it to them.

To this head is to be referred a faithfullfaithful concealing of maſtersmasters infirmities: for the beſtbest that be are ſubiectsubject to many: and ſeruantsservants which are vnderunder their maſtersmasters rooferoof continually waiting on them, cannot chuſechoose but eſpieespy many: if herein ſeruantsservants be not faithfullfaithful, maſtersmasters were better be without ſeruantsservants in their houſeshouses.

Contrary to keeping cloſeclose the ſecretssecrets of maſtersmasters, is blabbing abroad all ſuchsuch things as ſeruantsservants know concerning their maſtersmasters: which is too common a fault: for when ſeruantsservants of diuersdivers houſeshouses men or maids meet together, all their talketalk for the moſtmost part is of their maſtersmasters and miſtreſſesmistresses, whereby it commethcometh to paſſepass that all the ſecretssecrets of an houſehouse are ſoonesoon knowneknown about the whole townetown or city. Solomon ſtilethstyleth ſuchsuch an one a tale-bearer: A tale-bearer, ſaithsaith he, reuealethrevealeth ſecretssecrets: or, he that
Pro. 11. 13. & 20. 19. reuealethrevealeth ſecretssecrets is a tale-bearer: for many of Solomons prouerbsproverbs are conuertibleconvertible, they may be turned either way. Now note how Solomon noteth out the miſchiefesmischiefs that tale-bearers workework: The words of a tale-bearer are as wounds, (they wound the pretiousprecious name and credit of a man) and they goego downedown into the innermoſtinnermost
Pro. 18. 8.
part of the belly, that is, they doedo, as it were, ſtrikestrike thorowthrough the very heart of a man. AgaineAgain he noteth them to be the cauſecause of all ſtriſestrifestrise, and to raiſeraise diſcorddiscord betwixt chiefechief friends: and in Pro. 16. 28. Pro. 26. 20. that reſpectrespect fitly reſemblethresembleth them to wood which is the very fuellfuel of fire. What enemies then are ſuchsuch ſeruantsservants to an houſehouse? They are eueneven as treacherous ſpiesspies, the moſtmost dangerous enemies that be. Thus we ſeesee that this is no light ſinnesin: yet is it ſoso much the more odious when maſtersmasters and miſtreſſesmistresses infirmities (the publiſhingpublishing whereof may much impaireimpair their credit) are made knowneknown.

div.head: §. 31. Of ſeruantsservants faithfulneſſefaithfulness in helping one another.
div.p:
Where many fellow ſeruantsservants are together, faithfulneſſefaithfulness requireth that one be helpfullhelpful to another in what they may; IV. as by good example, good counſellcounsel, incouragementencouragement in good courſescourses, diſſwaſiondissuasiondisswasion from lewd and wicked practiſespractises, peace and vnityunity, with the like. The Lord ChriſtChrist expreſlyexpressly calleth ſuchsuch an one a faithfullfaithful ſeruantservant, and pronounceth him bleſſedblessed.
Mat. 24. 45, 46.

Example and aduiceadvice of ones equallequal preuailethprevaileth much with another, ſoso as a fellow ſeruantservant may in this kindekind doedo more good then the maſtermaster himſelfehimself: and if by his meanesmeans he bring his fellow ſeruantsservants to be faithfullfaithful, his owneown faithfulneſſefaithfulness is doubled and trebled; and his maſtermaster receiuethreceiveth a double and treble benefit thereby: namely the benefit of this good ſeruantsservants faithfulneſſefaithfulness, and the benefit of all the other ſeruantsservants faithfulneſſefaithfulness whom he hath made faithfullfaithful.

Contrary is their practiſepractise who by their ill example corrupt Mat. 24. 49. their fellowesfellows (as that euillevil ſeruantservant, who, when his maſtermaster was away, did eat and drinkedrink with the drunken, that is, did cauſecause Gen. 37. 18, &etcc. others to be drunken with him) or by ill counſellcounsel draw one another on to euillevil (as the ſonnessons of IaakobJacob, who when they ſawsaw IoſephJoseph a farrefar off, ſaidsaid one to another, Behold this dreamer
Mat. 24. 49. commethcometh, come now and let us ſlayslay him, &etcc. and as they, who, when they ſawsaw their maſtersmasters ſonneson, ſaidsaid among themſeluesthemselves, This is the heireheir, come let us kill him, and let us ſeizeseize on his inheritance) or are euerever quarrelling with their fellowesfellows, and ſmitingsmiting them (as that forenamed euillevil ſeruantservant whom the Lord threatneththreateneth to cut off) or diſſwadedissuadedisswade one another from obedience and ſubiectionsubjection (as they who ſaidsaid, Let us breakebreak their bonds
PſalPsal.Psal 2. 3.
aſunderasunder, and caſtcast away their cords from vsus; and as Sheba, who ſaidsaid, we hauehave no part in DauidDavid: eueryevery man to his tents O IſraelIsrael.) 2 Sam. 20. 1. TheſeThese faults are very rife among ſeruantsservants: whence it commethcometh to paſſepass that there are ſoso few good, and ſoso many bad ſeruantsservants: too true is this prouerbeproverb, One skabbedscabbed ſheepesheep mars a whole flockeflock. Let there be in a great family one ſeruantservant that is profane, proud, riotous, ſtoutstout, rebellious, or otherwiſeotherwise vicious, and all will ſoonesoon be like him.

Among other parts of vnfaithfulneſſeunfaithfulness in this kindekind one of the moſtmost monſtrousmonstrous (which yet is too too frequent) is to allure one another to vncleanneſſeuncleanness, and men and maids to defile one another. We ſhewedshowed §. 11. before, that it was vnlawfullunlawful for ſeruantsservants during the time of their ſeruiceservice to mariemarry without their maſtersmasters conſentconsent: how abominable then is it to defile one another? The ſinnesin is doubled being betwixt ſeruantsservants: for as it is a beaſtlybeastly ſinsin in it ſelfeself, ſoso in the forenamed reſpectrespect it is greatly diſhonourabledishonourable to their maſtermaster and his houſehouse: beſidesbesides that the maid ſoso defiled is oft diſableddisabled to doedo her ſeruiceservice well: nay many times the charge of the childechild lieth vponupon the maſtermaster. Thus ſhameshame and diſhonourdishonour, griefegrief and vexation, loſſeloss and dammagedamage all meet together, the more to gall & pierce him to the very heart. Is not this then a great part of vnfaithfulneſſeunfaithfulness? DeſeruethDeservethDeserueth it not to be ſeuerelyseverely puniſhedpunished, and that openly, and publikelypublicly with ſhameshame and ſmartsmart too, thtthat others may take warning thereby? Many vſeuse meanesmeans to eſcapeescape the reuengingrevenging hand of man: but though they eſcapeescape mans hand, they ſhallshall be ſuresure to meet with Gods heauyheavy vengeance: whoremongers God will iudgejudge. Daily experience ſhewethshoweth what miſerymisery Heb. 13. 4. ſuchsuch wretches bring themſeluesthemselves vntounto, and how God meeteth with them, and that moſtmost fearefullyfearfully.

div.head: §. 32. Of ſeruantsservants faithfulneſſefaithfulness about their maſtersmasters children.
div.p:
Great faithfulneſſefaithfulness may ſeruantsservants manifeſtmanifest to their maſtersmasters V. in and about their children: as while they are young and not able to lookelook to themſeluesthemselves, to be tender ouerover them, and well to tend them: maids eſpeciallyespecially neatly to handle and lookelook to them, and cleanly to bring them vpup: and they that hauehave a particular charge of them, to ſeekeseek their good in eueryevery thing they can, and giuegive them their due portion: and (becauſebecause
children are much in ſeruantsservants company) to vſeuse in their hearing ſuchsuch ſpeechspeech as may miniſterminister grace to them, and to teach them good things, and (when they grow to ſomesome ripeneſſeripeness of yearesyears) to bearebear a reuerendreverend reſpectrespect to them, and eſteemeesteem them their betters becauſebecause they are their maſtersmasters children. It is noted of AbrahamsAbraham's ſeruantservant, that he called his maſtersmasters Gen. 24. 65. ſonneson, Maſtermaster.

Children are dearedear to parents: the honour and kindneſſekindness done to them they account as done to themſeluesthemselves: this kindekind of faithfulneſſefaithfulness therefore muſtmust needs be highly eſteemedesteemed by maſtersmasters in their ſeruantsservants: and aſſuredlyassuredly it is a great meanesmeans to workework a good reſpectrespect in maſtersmasters towards them.

Yet Contrarily doedo many ſeruantsservants carriecarry themſeluesthemselves towards Points of vnfaithfulneſſeunfaithfulness in ſeruantsservants about their maſtersmasters children. their maſtersmasters children, as is apparent by theſethese particulars.
1. Some in their cariagecarriage are very hoggiſhhoggish and churliſhchurlish to their maſtersmasters children when their parents are out of ſightsight.

2. Others are very careleſſecareless of them, and tend them very ſluttiſhlysluttishly, not caring how they goego: whereby they oft procure great diſpleaſuredispleasure from their maſtermaster and miſtreſſemistress.
3. Others get from their maſtersmasters children what they can: and depriuedeprive them of their allowance, turning it to their owneown gainegain.

4. Others exceedingly corrupt their maſtersmasters children with their filthy and corrupt communication: teaching them to ſweareswear, blaſphemeblaspheme, and vſeuse all manner of vncleaneunclean ſpeechesspeeches: thus is that prouerbeproverb verified, euillevil communications 1 Cor. 15. 33. corrupt good manners. ChildrenChildrenchildren oft times in their young yeeresyears learnelearn ſuchsuch ill language and behauiourbehaviour of lewd ſeruantsservants, as their parents can neuernever get them to leaueleave againeagain: ſoso as they may curſecurse the day that euerever ſuchsuch ſeruantsservants came into their houſehouse.

5. Others allure them to ſtagestage-plaiesplays, to dice-houſeshouses, and other like places, which are the very bane of youth: and draw them to ſpendspend in riot ſuchsuch allowance as their parents allow them, yea and beyond that allowance, ſoso as they runnerun in debt, and get ſuchsuch an habit of ſpendingspending, as at length they make away their whole eſtateestate.

6. Others inueagleinveigle their affections: and oft draw them to folly and vncleanneſſeuncleanness. This filthy kindekind of vnfaithfulneſſeunfaithfulness is ſoso much worſeworse then that which was §. 31. before noted betwixt fellow ſeruantsservants, by how much neerernearer and dearer children are to their parents then ſeruantsservants to their maſtersmasters.

7. Others that dare not commit this abominable wickedneſſewickedness, ſtickestick not to doedo that which is little better, namely to draw them on to be contracted, yea and mariedmarried to them often times, and that priuilyprivily without conſentconsent of their parents: whereby parents affections are oft ſoso alienated from their children, as they will not acknowledge them for children, but cleaneclean caſtcast them off. TheſeThese are the fruits of this lewd kindekind of vnfaithfulneſſeunfaithfulness in ſeruantsservants.

div.head: §. 33. Of ſeruantsservants faithfulneſſefaithfulness in regard of their maſtersmasters, or miſtreſſesmistresses bed-fellow.
div.p: So faithfullfaithful ought ſeruantsservants to be to their maſtersmasters and VI. miſtreſſesmistresses, that if one of them ſhouldshould labour to vſeuse a ſeruantservant in any manner of deceit to the other, the ſeruantservant ought not to yeeldyield. As if a maſtermaster ſhouldshould mouemove his maid priuilyprivily to take away iewelsjewels, plate, monymoney, linnenlinen, or any ſuchsuch thing as is in her miſtreſſemistress cuſtodycustody. It skilleth not that the maſtermaster hath the chiefeſtchiefest power ouerover all the goods: a ſecretsecret taking of them away without the priuityprivity of the miſtreſſemistress in whoſewhose cuſtodycustody they are, is in the ſeruantservant deceit, and a point of vnfaithfulneſſeunfaithfulness. Much leſſeless ought any ſeruantsservants be mouedmoved by their miſtreſſemistress priuilyprivily to take away their maſtersmasters cornecorn, wares, or any goods for her priuateprivate vſeuse. Of the two this is the greater part of vnfaithfulneſſeunfaithfulness.

If ſuchsuch deceit ought not to be vſedused about any goods, much leſſeless about the body of maſtermaster or miſtreſſemistress. As if a maſtermaster ſhouldshould allure his maid to commit folly with him, or a miſtreſſemistress her man, both their conſcienceconscience to God, and alſoalso their faithfulneſſefaithfulness to their maſtermaster or miſtreſſemistress ſhouldshould make them vtterlyutterly to refuſerefuse it, and to giuegive no place to any ſuchsuch temptation. Gen. 39. 7. &etcc.
IoſephJoseph is propounded as a patternepattern herein: and againſtagainst the ſuggeſtionsuggestion of his miſtreſſemistress he rendrethrendereth the two forenamed reaſonsreasons: his conſcienceconscience to God in theſethese words, how can I doedo this great wickedneſſewickedness and ſinnesin againſtagainst God? His faithfulneſſefaithfulness
to his maſtermaster in theſethese, He hath not kept backeback any thing from me but thee, how then &etcc.

To this head may be referred ſeruantsservants faithfulneſſefaithfulness in making knowneknown to their maſtermaster the ſinnesin of his wife, and to their miſtreſſemistress the ſinnesin of her husband, eſpeciallyespecially if it be ſuchsuch a ſinnesin as may tend to the ruineruin of the familiefamily, and that by the knowledge thereof, the party that is not blinded and beſottedbesotted with the ſinnesin, but rather free from it, may be a meanesmeans to redreſſeredress it. Thus 1 Sam. 25. 14. Nabals ſeruantsservants made knowneknown to Abigail the churliſhneſſechurlishness of Nabal towards DauidsDavid's ſeruantsservants: by which means the miſchiefemischief intended againſtagainst the houſehouse was preuentedprevented. Thus if ſeruantsservants know that their maſtermaster intendeth ſomesome mortallmortal reuengerevenge againſtagainst another, to tell his wife thereof in time, may be great faithfulneſſefaithfulness: or if they know their miſtreſſemistress hath appointed to goego away priuilyprivily from her husband, to tell him of it, is a part of faithfulneſſefaithfulness. This may be applied to many other like caſescases.

The contrary is yeeldingyielding to maſtersmasters or miſtreſſesmistresses in any point of deceit one againſtagainst another: whereunto ſeruantsservants are too prone, becauſebecause they thinkethink to be boulſtredbolsteredboulstred out by the authoritieauthority of the partieparty that ſettethsetteth them on workework to deceiuedeceive. But no authoritieauthority can be a warrant for any deceit, or wickedneſſewickedness.

div.head: §. 34. Of ſeruantsservants faithfulneſſefaithfulness about their maſtersmasters perſonspersons.
div.p: MaſtersMasters and Miſtreſſesmistresses are fleſhflesh and bloudblood as well as ſeruantsservants, VII. and ſoso ſubiectsubject to weakneſſeweakness, ſickneſſesickness, old age, and other diſtreſſesdistresses, wherein they may ſtandstand in great need of ſeruantsservants helpehelp: ſeruantsservants therefore muſtmust be faithfullfaithful in affording them the beſtbest helpehelp that they can. Sauls ſeruantsservants did a part of faithfulneſſefaithfulness to their maſtermaster, when, he being vexed with an euillevil ſpiritspirit, 1 Sam. 16. 16. they inquired after meanesmeans to eaſeease him. So did DauidsDavid's ſeruantsservants, when he being bedred, 1 King. 1. 2. they ſoughtsought out one to cheriſhcherish him. It was a point of faithfulneſſefaithfulness in Naamans 2 King. 5. 3. maid, to tell her miſtreſſemistress of a meanesmeans whereby her maſtermaster might be cured of his leproſieleprosy: and in his verſvers. 13. ſeruantsservants, to perſwadepersuade him to vſeuse the meanesmeans preſcribedprescribed by the Prophet.

Contrary is a ſeruantsservants vngratefullungrateful and inhumane leauingleaving of his maſtermaster in his time of need, as the ſeruantsservants of IobJob did: for when the hand of God lay heauyheavy vponupon him, and all his goods were taken from him, and his bodiebody full of ſoresore boilesboils, IobJob 19. 15, 16. they that dwelt
in his houſehouse, and his maids counted him for a ſtrangerstranger: and he was an aliant in their ſightsight: he called his ſeruantservant, and he gauegave him no anſweranswer. So did 2 Sam. 19. 26. Ziba leaueleave MephiboſhethMephibosheth in his greateſtgreatest need: and Mat. 26. 56. the DiſciplesDisciples fliefly from their maſtermaster IeſusJesus ChriſtChrist. But what ſhallshall we ſaysay of thoſethose that take occaſionoccasion from their maſtersmasters impotencieimpotency to murder him themſeluesthemselves, as 2 Sam. 4. 6. Rechab and Baanah; or to betray him to his enemies, as Mat. 26. 15. IndasJudas betrayed the Lord ChriſtChrist? whatWhat, but that ſuchsuch traiteroustraitorous ſeruantsservants may lookelook for ſuchsuch ends.

div.head: §. 35. Of the meanesmeans to make ſeruantsservants faithfullfaithful.
div.p:
Among many other meanesmeans to make ſeruantsservants faithfullfaithful to their maſtermaster, and carefullcareful to performeperform other duties ſincerelysincerely, willingly, cheerefullycheerfully, and diligently, as hath before beenebeen noted, this is one of the moſtmost generallgeneral, namely, that ſeruantsservants, in all things they doedo for their maſtermaster, make their maſtersmasters caſecase their owneown, and ſoso doedo for him as they would for themſeluesthemselves, or as they would hauehave their owneown ſeruantsservants doedo for them. The generallgeneral rule of the Law is, Leu. 19. 18. Louelove thy neighbour as thy ſelfeself; and Mat. 7. 12. whatſoeuerwhatsoever you would that men ſhouldshould doedo to you, doedo you even ſoso to them. If thus eueryevery man muſtmust reſpectrespect another, yea though he be a ſtrangerstranger, then much more muſtmust ſeruantsservants reſpectrespect their maſtermaster, becauſebecause all that they can doedo is after an eſpeciallespecial manner as a debt due to their maſtersmasters: in which reſpectrespect ChriſtChrist ſaithsaith, that when they hauehave done all that is
Luke 17. 10. commanded, they hauehave but done their dutieduty.

This I hauehave the rather noted, becauſebecause the practiſepractise of moſtmost ſeruantsservants is contrary thereunto. For while they workework for their maſtersmasters, they will cry out that they are ouerover-burdened, and tired with that workework which they will eaſilyeasily goego thorowthrough withallwithal when they workework for themſeluesthemselves. They that while they workework for their maſtermaster, muſtmust be called to it againeagain and againeagain, and forced to ſtandstand to it, and to hold out till it be done, what painespains will they take, how early will they riſerise, how late will they ſitsit vpup, how diligent will they be for themſeluesthemselves? When IourneymenJourneymen receiuereceive increaſeincrease of wages according to the workework which they doedo, they will diſpatchdispatch more then a prentiſeprentice that hath but cloth, food, and lodging. AgaineAgain, many that in their maſtersmasters goods are very lauiſhlavish, and waſtfullwastefulwastfull, when they come to beforbe for themſeluesthemselves are very ſparingsparing, ſauingsaving, and prouidentprovident. What doedo theſethese things argue but that ſeruantsservants doedo not bearebear to their maſtersmasters that mindemind which they
ſhouldshould: they doedo not for them as they would doedo for themſeluesthemselves. Very requiſiterequisite it is therefore that the forenamed generallgeneral rule be obſeruedobserved.
div.q: Hitherto of the ſeuerallseveral kindeskinds of ſeruantsservants duties, and of the manner of performing them. It remaineth to ſpeakespeak both of the extent of their duties, and alſoalso of the reſtraintrestraint of that extent.

div.head: §. 36. Of ſeruantsservants endeuourendeavour to make their iudgementjudgment agree with their maſtersmasters.
div.p:
The extent of ſeruantsservants duties is in my text only implied vnderunder this indefinite particle (Obey) (wchwchwhich being not reſtrainedrestrained to any particulars, muſtmust be extended to eueryevery thing) but in other places it is expreſlyexpressly laid downedown in theſethese generallgeneral termesterms, Col. 3. 22. Obey in all things,
Tit. 2. 9. PleaſePlease well in all things. It is not therefore ſufficientsufficient that ſeruantsservants performeperform their duties well in ſomesome things, they muſtmust doedo it in all things, yea in things that may be againſtagainst their owneown mindemind and liking, if their maſtermaster will hauehave it ſoso. For this end let ſeruantsservants note theſethese two rules. The ſamesame extent and reſtraintrestraint Extent of ſeruantsservants duties. that was Treat. 3. §. 63, &etcc. & Treat. 5. §. 35. before noted in laying forth the duties of other inferiors, is here alſoalso to be obſeruedobserved in the duties of ſeruantsservants: for therein they all agree. The ſamesame rules therforetherefore that were before ſetset downedown, may here againeagain be applied. I refer the reader to thoſethose places for a more large amplification of the generals: and here I will content my ſelfeself with adding ſuchsuch particular proofesproofs as are moſtmost proper and pertinent to ſeruantsservants.

1. That they labour to bring their iudgementjudgment to the bent of their maſtersmasters iudgementjudgment, and to thinkethink that meet and good which SeruantsServants muſtmust labour to bring their iudgementjudgment to agree with their maſtersmasters. he doth. Thus the IudgJudg. 19. 11, 12, &etcc. ſeruantservant of the LeuireLeviteLevire which thought it meeteſtmeetest to turneturn into one of the Cities of the IebuſitesJebusites to lodge there, becauſebecause the day was far ſpentspent, when he ſawsaw his maſtermaster to be of another mindemind, yeeldedyielded to him. So did Luk. 19. 25, &etcc. thoſethose ſeruantsservants yeeldyield to their maſtermaster, who at firſtfirst thought it vnmeetunmeet that he that had ten talents ſhouldshould hauehave one peecepiece more: and Mat. 13. 28, &etcc. thoſethose ſeruantsservants alſoalso, that at firſtfirst thought it meet that the tares ſhouldshould be plucked vpup from the wheat. This rule is to be obſeruedobserved in the particular points before deliuereddelivered, as the workework which ſeruantsservants doedo, and the manner
of doing it, their apparellapparel, their allowance, yea and in the correction which their maſtermaster giuethgiveth them, and the reſtrest.

Contrary is that great conceit which many ſeruantsservants hauehave of SeruantsServants conceit of their owneown wit. their owneown iudgementjudgment, wit, and wiſdomewisdom, thinking themſeluesthemselves wiſerwiser then their maſtersmasters; as Gehazi, who oppoſingopposing his owneown wit to his maſtersmasters wiſdomewisdom, ſaidsaid, 2 King. 5. 20. Behold my maſtermaster hath ſparedspared Naaman this Syrian, in not receiuingreceiving at his hands that which he brought: but as the Lord liuethliveth, I will runnerun after him, and take ſomewhatsomewhat of him. This was alſoalso a fault in 2 King. 2. 16. the children of the Prophets, that would not reſtrest on EliſhasElishas iudgementjudgment, but importuned him againſtagainst his mindemind to ſendsend ſomesome to ſeekeseek the bodiebody of Eliah. This ſelfeself-conceit is the cauſecause of many miſchiefesmischiefs: as of diſcontentedneſſediscontentedness at the workework their maſtermaster appointeth them, and at the allowance of meat and drinkedrink which they hauehave; of much libertieliberty they take to themſeluesthemselves, of pride in apparellapparel, and other vices before noted: if the forenamed rule were duelyduly obſeruedobserved, many of thoſethose miſchiefesmischiefs would be auoidedavoided, and much better obedience yeeldedyielded.

div.head: §. 37. Of ſeruantsservants yeeldingyielding to doedo ſuchsuch things at their maſtersmasters command, as they cannot thinkethink to be moſtmost meet.
div.p: The ſecondsecond rule which ſeruantsservants muſtmust obſerueobserve is this, that

Though they cannot in their iudgementjudgment thinkethink that fit to be done which their maſtermaster will hauehave done, yet vponupon his peremptorieperemptory command they muſtmust yeeldyield to the doing of it: It appeareth by Peters anſweranswer to ChriſtChrist that he did ſoso, for being commanded to let downedown his net for a draught, thus he anſwerethanswereth, Maſtermaster, we hauehave toyledtoiled all the night, and hauehave taken nothing (here he ſhewethshoweth that Luke 5. 5. his opinion was that it would be in vainevain to let downedown their nets) neuertheleſſenevertheless at thy word I will let downedown the net (here is his obedience againſtagainst his opinion.) More cleareclear is the example of IoabJoab for this purpoſepurpose: when the King commanded him to number the 2 Sam. 24. 2, &etcc. people, he declared that he thought it a very vnmeetunmeet thing to doedo, by this phraſephrase, Why doth my Lord the King delight in this thing? yet againſtagainst his iudgementjudgment he yeeldedyielded to the Kings peremptorieperemptory command, for it is ſaidsaid, that the Kings word preuailedprevailed against IoabJoab.

div.head: ObiectObject. This is no fit example, becauſebecause IoabJoab ſinnedsinned in obeying.
div.p:
AnſwAnsw. IoabJoab cannot iuſtlyjustly be charged with ſinnesin, becauſebecause it was
not ſimplysimply vnlawfullunlawful to number the people. DauidsDavid's ſinnesin was not in the act of numbringnumbering the people, but in his mindemind which mouedmoved him to doedo it: for there was no iuſtjust cauſecause to doedo it: only pride and curioſitiecuriosity mouedmoved him, as may be gathered out of his owneown reaſonreason in theſethese words, that I may know the number of the people. To doedo ſuchsuch a thing only to know it, was curioſitiecuriosity. Contrary is their peremptorineſſeperemptoriness, who by no meanesmeans will be drawnedrawn to doedo any thing at their maſtersmasters command, which they themſeluesthemselves thinkethink not moſtmost meet to be done.
