TheſeThese foolesfools bring much miſchiefemischief vponupon their owneown pates in diſobeyingdisobeying their maſtersmasters: for exceedingly they prouokeprovoke his wrath who hath power to take vengeance of them. Neither let them thinkethink to receiuereceive comfort in their ſufferingsuffering, becauſebecause they refuſerefuse an vnmeetunmeet thing, for meetneſſemeetness is not a ſufficientsufficient warrant againſtagainst vnlawfulneſſeunlawfulness. To diſobeydisobey in a thing which lawfully may be done, is vnlawfullunlawful: if therefore the pretext be only an vnmeetunmeet thing, meetneſſemeetness is preferred before lawfulneſſelawfulness, and vnlawfulneſſeunlawfulness leſſeless accounted of then vnmeetneſſeunmeetness.

div.head: §. 38. Of ſeruantsservants forbearing to obey their maſtermaster againſtagainst God.
div.p:
That the extent of ſeruantsservants obedience be not too farrefar ſtretchedstretched, ReſtraintRestraint of the extent of ſeruantsservants duties the ApoſtleApostle ſettethsetteth downedown an excellent limitation thereof: and that in theſethese fourefour phraſesphrases, As vntounto ChriſtChrist, As the ſeruantsservants of ChriſtChrist, Doing the will of God, As to the Lord; all which doedo ſhewshow that the Obedienceobedience which ſeruantsservants yeeldyield to their maſtermaster See the cautions, Treat. 3. §. 51, 52, &etcc. muſtmust be ſuchsuch as may ſtandstand with their obedience to ChriſtChrist. So that if maſtersmasters command their ſeruantsservants neuernever ſoso peremptorily to
doedo any vnlawfullunlawful thing, that is, any thing forbidden by Gods Nolite fieri ſeruiserui hominum, i. nolite eis parere cùm turpia praecipiunt. ChryſChrys. in 1 Cor. 7. hom. 19. Exo. 1. 17. word, they may not yeeldyield to it. The midwiuesmidwives of the Hebrew women did well in refuſingrefusing to doedo any thing to helpehelp forward the murderous practiſespractises of the King of Egypt in ſlayingslaying all the male-children of the HebrewesHebrews: it is expreſlyexpressly ſaidsaid, that they feared God and did not as the King commanded them: ſoso as their diſobediencedisobedience in this kindekind was a token of their fearefear of God. In this caſecase IoſephJoseph is commended for not hearkening to his miſtreſſemistress: and the ſeruantsservants of Saul for refuſingrefusing to ſlaieslay the Gen. 39. 9. 1 Sam. 22. 17. Lords PrieſtsPriests at their maſtersmasters command. Thus if a maſtermaster ſhouldshould command his ſeruantservant to kill, to ſtealesteal, to forſweareforswear himſelfehimself, to lie, to vſeuse falſefalse meaſuresmeasures and weights, to goego to maſſemass, or doedo any other vnlawfullunlawful thing, he ought not obey him.

AgaineAgain, if maſtersmasters forbid their ſeruantsservants to doedo that which Seruis competit vt obediant dominis in ijs quibus mandato Dei nihil derogatur. BaſilBasil. God hath commanded them to doedo, they muſtmust, notwithſtandingnotwithstanding their maſtersmasters prohibition, doedo it. The Rulers of IſraelIsrael forbid the ApoſtlesApostles to preach, yet becauſebecause ChriſtChrist had commanded them to preach, they would not forbeareforbear: nor would Daniel forbeareforbear to pray to God, though the King and Nobles Ethic. defin. 75. Act. 4. 19. Dan. 6. 10. by expreſſeexpress decree forbad him. So if a profane or popiſhpopish maſtermaster ſhallshall forbid his ſeruantservant to goego to Church, or to hearehear the word, or to take the Sacrament, or to dwell with his wife if he be mariedmarried, or to make reſtitutionrestitution of that which he hath fraudulently gotten, or any other bounden dutieduty, herein they muſtmust ſaysay, we ought to obey God rather then men. For when maſtersmasters Act. 5. 29. command and forbid any thing againſtagainst God, they goego beyond their commiſſioncommission, and therein their authoritieauthority ceaſethceaseth.

Contrary to this reſtraintrestraint is both a paraſiticallparasitical pleaſingpleasing of maſtersmasters: and alſoalso a baſebase fearefear of them. It is the property of a Ais? aio. Negas? nego. Terent. in Eun. paraſiteparasite to ſaysay what a maſtermaster will hauehave him ſaysay, and deniedeny what he will hauehave him deniedeny, and ſoso to doedo what he will hauehave him to doedo. Doeg that fawning dog at Sauls word ſlewslew all the Lords 1 Sam. 22. 18. PrieſtsPriests: and AbſolomsAbsoloms ſeruantsservants at his word killed Amnon: for 2 Sam. 13. 28, 29. all the reaſonreason which they had to commit that murder was this ſpeechspeech of their maſtermaster, hauehave not I commanded you? So prone are ſeruantsservants to ſoothsooth their maſtersmasters, as there is no ſinnesin ſoso horrible which at their maſtersmasters command they will not be ready to
doedo. Thus is that verified which the Prophet long ſincesince foretold, IſaIsa. 2424. 2. like maſtermaster like ſeruantservant, like mistreſſemistress like maid. It is alſoalso the propertieproperty of baſebase fearefullfearful ſeruantsservants to doedo nothing but what their maſtermaster will hauehave them doedo, and to forbeareforbear any dutieduty, though neuernever ſoso neceſſarynecessary, that he forbiddeth them to doedo. What dutieduty more neceſſarynecessary then praierprayer? We are commanded to pray continually: yet the ſeruantsservants of Darius were content to 1 TheſſThess. 5. 17. Dan. 6. 7, &etcc. forbeareforbear that dutieduty thirtiethirty daiesdays together, becauſebecause it was againſtagainst the decree of their Lord and King. The like is noted of the people in ChriſtsChrists time, they durſtdurst not make open profeſſionprofession of
IohJoh. 7. 13. & 9. 22. ChriſtChrist for fearefear of the IewesJews. So in our daiesdays many ſeruantsservants there be that dare not make profeſſionprofession of the GoſpellGospel, nor goego to Church, nor read the word, nor performeperform other holy religious duties, which they know to be bounden duties, for fearefear of their maſtersmasters. Had not then the ApoſtleApostle iuſtjust cauſecause to ſtrikestrike ſoso much vponupon this ſtringstring as here he hath done, expreſlyexpressly forbidding eieeye-ſeruiceservice, man-pleaſingpleasing, and doing ſeruiceservice to men, namely in oppoſitionopposition to God?

div.head: §. 39. Of ſeruantsservants chuſingchoosing good maſtersmasters.
div.p: As a iuſtjust conſequenceconsequence following from the forenamed extent and reſtraintrestraint of ſeruantsservants duties, I may further gather theſethese two leſſonslessons for ſeruantsservants.
1. It is very behouefullbehoveful that ſeruantsservants make choice of good maſtersmasters: at leaſtleast if it be in their power to chuſechoose.
2. It is behouefullbehoveful that they continue and abide vnderunder good maſtersmasters: at leaſtleast if they continue ſeruantsservants, and abide vnderunder any maſtersmasters.

That theſethese conſequencesconsequences iuſtlyjustly follow as aforeſaidaforesaid, is euidentevident: for ſeeingseeing ſeruantsservants are bound to obey in all things which are not againſtagainst God, and muſtmust obey in nothing but what is in the Lord, it is very requiſiterequisite that ſeruantsservants be vnderunder ſuchsuch maſtersmasters as bearebear the Image of God in the inward diſpoſitiondisposition, and grace of their heart, as well as in their outward function and place: and will goego along with God in vſingusing their authoritieauthority, commanding nothing but what a ſeruantservant may doedo with a good conſcienceconscience, and without tranſgreſſingtransgressing againſtagainst God: and forbidding nothing that God hath bound a ſeruantservant to doedo. There will be comfort in ſeruingserving ſuchsuch maſtersmasters: and our obedience
to them will be obedience to God. Such maſtersmasters therefore muſtmust be choſenchosen. Yea and with ſuchsuch muſtmust ſeruantsservants abide, (if not with the very ſamesame, yet with ſuchsuch as they are, of the ſamesame diſpoſitiondisposition) for if they goego to other, their former comfort will be taken away, and their ſeruitudeservitude will ſeemeseem ſoso much the more miſerablemiserable, by how much more knowledge and experience they hauehave had of the benefit of their former libertieliberty (for Qui fidelem habet dominum, ſaluosaluo eius dominio, diligat vt patrem. we may well call ſeruiceservice vnderunder vnconſcionableunconscionable maſtersmasters ſeruitudeservitude, and in oppoſitionopposition thereunto, ſeruiceservice vnderunder religious maſtersmasters, libertieliberty.) He therefore that hath a maſtermaster that is faithfullfaithful, due reſpectrespect had to his authoritieauthority, muſtmust louelove him as a father, and ConſtitConstit. ApoſtApost. l. 4. c. 12. ſoso abide with him.

For choice of good maſtersmasters, note what is Exo. 12. 38. recorded of many of the Egyptians and other people: they left their owneown countriecountry, and went out with the IſraelitesIsraelites: what ſhouldshould mouemove them but conſcienceconscience of the true God whom they knew that IſraelIsrael ſeruedserved? Now many of theſethese went out as ſeruantsservants, as may be gathered from thoſethose many Leu. 25. 45. Deut. 5. 14. & 12. 18. & 23. 15. & 23. 7. laweslaws which were made in the behalfebehalf of ſeruantsservants that were ſtrangersstrangers, and in ſpeciallspecial that were Egyptians. The knowledge which Ruth 1. 16. Ruth had that Naomi her mother in law ſeruedserved the true God, mouedmoved her to leaueleave her owneown countriecountry, and to goego as a ſeruantservant with Naomi.

For abiding with good maſtersmasters we hauehave a worthy patternepattern in the tweluetwelve DiſciplesDisciples. IohJoh. 6. 66. &etcc. When many of ChriſtsChrists DiſciplesDisciples at large, went backeback, and walked no more with him, ChriſtChrist asking the tweluetwelve whether they alſoalso would goego away, Peter in the name of all the reſtrest anſweredanswered, Lord to whom ſhallshall we goego? Thou haſthast the words of eternalleternal life.

Contrary is the mindemind and practiſepractise of many ſeruantsservants: they neuernever inquire after the religious diſpoſitiondisposition of their maſtermaster, nor care though he be popiſhpopish, or profane, ſoso they may hauehave good wages, diet and lodging: and yet by this meanesmeans, if at leaſtleast there be any ſparkespark of Gods fearefear in their heart, they caſtcast themſeluesthemselves vponupon many ſoresore temptations, and bring themſeluesthemselves into many hard ſtraitsstraits, and dangerous ſnaressnares. And, if God open their eieseyes to ſeesee that wretched condition whereinto they hauehave implunged themſeluesthemselves, they will be forced to criecry out and
complainecomplain as DauidDavid did, when he was in forraineforeign countries where he could not freely ſerueserve his God, PſalPsal. 120. 5. Woe is me that I ſoiournesojourn in MeſechMesech, that I dwell in the tents of Kedar.

Much more contrary is their mindemind and diſpoſitiondisposition who refuſerefuse to ſerueserve religious maſtersmasters, and ſhunshun them moſtmost of all: or being in their ſeruiceservice are neuernever quiet till they be out of it againeagain. Of theſethese we ſpakespake §. 16. before.
div.q: Hitherto hauehave we dealt about ſeruantsservants duties. The reaſonsreasons which the ApoſtleApostle rendrethrendereth to enforce thoſethose duties remaineremain to be declared.

div.head: §. 40. Of the firſtfirst motiuemotive, the place of maſtersmasters.
div.p:
The firſtfirst reaſonreason which the ApoſtleApostle vſethuseth to inforceenforce ſeruantsservants I. duties is implied vnderunder this phraſephrase, as to ChriſtChrist; it intimateth the place of a maſtermaster, which is to be in ChriſtsChrists ſteadstead. In this reſpectrespect the title Lord is giuengiven to a maſtermaster. The word which the ApoſtleApostle vſethuseth in GreekeGreek is that which in the new teſtamenttestament
〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . anſwerethanswereth to that proper Hebrew name of God IehouahJehovah, and it ſettethsetteth forth the abſoluteabsolute ſoueraigntysovereigntysoveraignty of God, and power ouerover all creatures: Matt. 28. 18. which power BecauſebecauseBecause the Fatherfather hath giuengiven to his ſonneson as Mediator, God-man, he is called the 1 Cor. 8. 6. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . one or only Lord: and becauſebecause maſtersmasters by vertuevirtue of their office and place bearebear ChriſtsChrists image, and ſtandstand in his ſteadstead, by communication of ChriſtsChrists authority to them, they are called Lords, yea alſoalso PſalPsal. 82. 6. Gods (for that which a MagiſtrateMagistrate is in the Commoncommon-wealth a maſtermaster is in the family)).

Hence it followeth that ſeruantsservants in performing duty to their maſtermaster performeperform duty to ChriſtChrist, and in rebelling againſtagainst their maſtermaster they rebellrebel againſtagainst ChriſtChrist; as the Lord ſaidsaid to Samuel of the peoples reiectingrejecting his gouernmentgovernment, they hauehave not reiectedrejected 1 Sam. 8. 7. thee, but they hauehave reiectedrejected me that I ſhouldshould not raignereign ouerover them. Is not this a ſtrongstrong motiuemotive to prouokeprovoke ſeruantsservants to all duty, and to reſtrainerestrain them from rebellion? ifIf it be well weighed what ChriſtChrist is, it cannot be but a weighty reaſonreason. For though maſtersmasters ſhouldshould neither reward their good ſeruiceservice, nor reuengerevenge their ill ſeruiceservice, yet will ChriſtChrist doedo both.

div.head: §. 41. Of the ſecondsecond motiuemotive, the place of ſeruantsservants.
div.p: The ſecondsecond reaſonreason is implied vnderunder this phraſephrase, as ſeruantsservants II. of ChriſtChrist: it noteth the place of a ſeruantservant: which though it may ſeemeseem to be a meanemean and baſebase place, yet is it indeed an honourable place. Men count it an honour to beebe ſeruantsservants to a King: but ChriſtChrist is higher then all Kings. On this ground the ApoſtleApostle ſaithsaith, Art thou called being a ſeruantservant? careCare not for it: 1 Cor. 7. 21, 22. and that vponupon this reaſonreason, He that is called in the Lord being a ſeruantservant, is the Lords freeman. This reaſonreason is to be noted againſtagainst the conceit that moſtmost hauehave of a ſeruantsservants place, that it is ſoso meanemean and baſebase as there can be no honour nor comfort in doing the duties thereof. But that is a fooliſhfoolish, and vniuſtunjust conceit: lookelook to ChriſtChrist the higheſthighest maſtermaster, and there is as much honour, and comfort in doing the duties of the loweſtlowest ſeruantsservants place, as of the higheſthighest maſtersmasters.

div.head: §. 42. Of the third motiuemotive, Gods will.
div.p: The third reaſonreason is implied vnderunder this phraſephrase, doing the III. will of God, which declareth the ground of ſeruantsservants ſubiectionsubjection. God in his word hath plainly made it knowneknown that it is his pleaſurepleasure that they who are vnderunder the authority of maſtersmasters ſhouldshould obey them, therefore as ſeruantsservants would pleaſeplease God, they muſtmust obey: if they refuſerefuse to obey, they thwart the will of God. This alſoalso is a motiuemotive of moment: for Gods will is that markemark which eueryevery one ought to aimeaim at, and it is much vrgedurged by the Holy GhoſtGhost, as a generallgeneral reaſonreason to all duty in theſethese and ſuchsuch like phraſesphrases, 1 TheſThes. 4. 3. This is the will of God, 1 Pet. 2. 15. So is the will of God: vponupon which ground we are exhorted to EphefEphes. 5. 17. vnderſtandunderstand, and to Rom. 12. 2. proueprove what is the will of God.
Good reaſonreason there is to preſſepress this reaſonreason: for
1. Gods will is the very ground of goodneſſegoodness: things are therefore good becauſebecause they are agreeable to Gods will: Gods will giuethgiveth the very being to goodneſſegoodness.
2. Gods will is a rule to ſquaresquare all our actions by, eueneven as the kings ſtatutesstatutes and proclamations are to his ſubiectssubjects.
3. It is a perfect rule (the law of the Lord is perfect) ſoso as we PſalPsal. 19. 7. may be ſuresure not to ſwerueswerve, if we hold cloſeclose thereunto.

4. It is a ſufficientsufficient rule, it will giuegive eueryevery one (and among other, ſeruantsservants) direction how to carry themſeluesthemselves in eueryevery thing they take in hand, yea in eueryevery thing that appertaineth to them. For, Gods word is giuengiven to make vsus perfect, thorowlythoroughly 2 Tim. 3. 17. furniſhedfurnished vntounto all good workesworks.

5. It is a good warrant to iuſtifiejustify vsus in all our actions: ſoso as, going along with it, we need not care what any man can ſaysay againſtagainst vsus. If a man be ſuresure that he hauehave ſtatutestatute law, or the kings proclamation on his ſideside, he is bold.
From this reaſonreason which is of ſuchsuch weight, I gather two propoſitionspropositions to addeadd force to this motiuemotive.

1. That ſeruantsservants obey their maſtersmasters, is no arbitrary matter, but a neceſſarynecessary duty: not left to his will whether he will doedo it or no, but a thing whereunto he is bound: and that not only by ciuillcivil conſtitutionsconstitutions of men, but alſoalso by a diuinedivine inſtitutioninstitution of God: ſoso as it is not only a matter of ciuillcivil policy, but alſoalso of conſcienceconscience, to be done for conſcienceconscience ſakesake.

2. That no creature can diſpencedispense with ſeruantsservants, ſoso as they ſhouldshould be exempted from doing their duty to their maſtermaster. If they could, they were greater then God, and their will aboueabove Gods will. Among creatures, maſtersmasters themſeluesthemselves are to be reckoned: now becauſebecause it is Gods will that ſeruantsservants ſhouldshould be in ſubiectionsubjection, their maſtersmasters cannot exempt them from it. MaſtersMasters may let them goego free: but retaining them as ſeruantsservants, they cannot exempt them from a ſeruantsservants ſubiectionsubjection. Wherefore though maſtersmasters be careleſſecareless in exacting dutieduty, yet let ſeruantsservants be conſcionableconscionable in yeeldingyielding duty, becauſebecause it is Gods will.

div.head: §. 43. Of the fourth reaſonreason, the reward of good ſeruiceservice.
div.p:
The fourth reaſonreason is plainly and largely expreſſedexpressed in theſethese IIII. words, Knowing that whatſoeuerwhatsoever good thing any man doth, the
Sciat ſeruusseruus Deum redditurum ſeruitutisseruitutis mercedem. ConſtitConstit. ApoſtApost. l. 4. c. 12. Col. 3. 24. ſamesame ſhallshall he receiuereceive of the Lord, whether he be bond or free. The generallgeneral ſummesum whereof is a Declaration of the reward of good ſeruiceservice. To which purpoſepurpose ſaithsaith the ApoſtleApostle to ſeruantsservants in another place, Of the LordyeLord ye ſhallshall receiuereceive a reward.

This firſtfirst is to be noted to addeadd force to the former reaſonsreasons.
For if any askeask, what if maſtersmasters ſtandstand in ChriſtsChrists ſteadstead, what maketh that to the purpose? ſurelySurely it maketh much to mouemove ſeruantsservants: becauſebecause maſtersmasters ſtandstand in his roomeroom who will reward that which is done for his ſakesake.
If againeagain they askeask, what benefit is it to be ChriſtsChrists ſeruantservant? itIt may be anſweredanswered, very great: for ChriſtChrist will reward all his ſeruantsservants.
If further it be asked, what is gotten by doing Gods will?
AnſwAnsw. EuenEven that which all aimeaim at, reward for ſeruiceservice.

As this addeth weight to alall the other reaſonsreasons, ſoso is it in it ſelfeself a weighty reaſonreason, as weighty as any can be to our corrupt nature. Hope of reward is it which maketh all ſortssorts of people to take the painespains which they doedo in their ſeuerallseveral places. But hauinghaving Treat. 1. §. 127. before handled this generallgeneral point of reward, I will here more diſtinctlydistinctly ſhewshow what kindekind of reward it is wherewith the Lord will recompencerecompense the good ſeruiceservice of faithfullfaithful ſeruantsservants.
Gods reward is both of temporalltemporal and eternalleternal bleſſingsblessings.

The temporalltemporal bleſſingsblessings which heretofore God hath beſtowedbestowed What reward God giuethgiveth to good ſeruantsservants. on faithfullfaithful ſeruantsservants, and which on that ground other like ſeruantsservants may expect, are theſethese eſpeciallyespecially.
1. He will mouemove maſtersmasters to reſpectrespect ſuchsuch ſeruantsservants, as he mouedmoved EſtEst. 6. 3. AhaſhAhash-veroſhverosh to recompencerecompense the fidelity of Mordecai.

2. If maſtersmasters failefail therein, he will mouemove ſtrangersstrangers to recompencerecompense them: as he mouedmoved Gen. 39. 21. the IaylorJailerJaylor to fauourfavour IoſephJoseph when his maſtermaster had caſtcast him in priſonprison: and & 41. 40. Pharaoh to aduanceadvance him to great dignity.

5. He will, when they come to keepekeep ſeruantsservants, prouideprovide ſuchsuch ſeruantsservants for them, as they were to their maſtersmasters. Gen. 43. 23. In Egypt God bleſſedblessed IoſephJoseph with a faithfullfaithful ſeruantservant. DauidDavid, who 1 Sam. 17. 34. ventured his life to ſauesave his fathers ſheepesheep, had 2 Sam. 21. 17. & 23. 15. many ſeruantsservants that ventured their liueslives for him.

To this purpoſepurpose may be applied that prouerbeproverb which
ChriſtChrist oft vſethuseth, Luk. 6. 38. with what meaſuremeasure yeeye mete ſhallshall it be meaſuredmeasured to you againeagain.

The eternalleternal reward is expreſſedexpressed in this phraſephrase, Col. 3. 24. the reward of the inheritance, for that inheritance is meant which ChriſtChrist mentioneth in this clauſeclause, Mat. 25. 34. Come ye bleſſedblessed of my Fatherfather, inherit the kingdomekingdom prepared for you from the beginning of the world, and Saint Peter in this, 1 Pet. 1. 4. an inheritance incorruptible, and vndeſiledundefiledundesiled, and that fadeth not away, reſeruedreserved in heauenheaven. What can be more ſaidsaid? What ſhallshall not be vndergoneundergone for this reward? How willingly doedo prentiſesprentices paſſepass ouerover their prentiſhipapprenticeship in hope of a temporarietemporary freedomefreedom of an earthly citiecity? Gen. 29. 20. Many yearesyears ſeruiceservice were but as a few daiesdays to IaakobJacob becauſebecause he liked his reward. But behold here a greater reward, which we muſtmust needs like much better. If this be not ſufficientsufficient to mouemove ſeruantsservants to all dutieduty, I know not what can be ſufficientsufficient.

div.head: The eighth TreatiſeTreatise. Duties of MaſtersMasters.
§. 1. Of the heads of MaſtersMasters duties.

epigraph.q: And yeeye Maſtersmasters doedo the ſamesame things vntounto them: forbearing threatningthreatening: Knowing that your Maſtermaster alſoalso is in heauenheaven: neither is there reſpectrespect of perſonspersons with him.

div.p:
INIn the laſtlast place the duties of maſtersmasters are declared by the ApoſtleApostle, and that in this verſeverse, where he noteth,
1. The kindeskinds of their duties.
2. A Reaſonreason to enforce the ſamesame.

The reaſonreason is taken from that ſubiectionsubjection wherein maſtersmasters are to an higher maſtermaster (knowing that your maſtermaster alſoalso.) And it is amplified,
1. By the equallequal ſubiectionsubjection of maſtersmasters and ſeruantsservants to that maſtermaster (your alſoalso.)
2. By the place where that maſtermaster is (in heauenheaven.)
3. By his property, in this phraſephrase (neither is there reſpectrespect of perſonspersons with him.)

BecauſeBecause the ſeuerallseveral duties of maſtersmasters are here but pointed at, and infolded vnderunder generallgeneral termesterms, I will (as in former
treatiſestreatises hath beenebeen done) propound a diſtinctdistinct order, whereby we may the better findefind out their duties, and handle them one after another.

All may be drawnedrawn vntounto theſethese two heads.
1. Care in chooſingchoosing good ſeruantsservants.
2. ConſcienceConscience in well vſingusing them.

For well vſingusing their ſeruantsservants, maſtersmasters muſtmust hauehave an eieeye to their place, and authority: and in reſpectrespect thereof,
1. WiſelyWisely maintainemaintain their authority.
2. Rightly manage the ſamesame.

The well managing of their authority is generally noted in this phraſephrase, doedo the ſamesame things: but more particularly in Col. 4. 1. another place referred to theſethese two branches
1. IuſticeJustice.
2. Equity.
Of theſethese in order.

div.head: §. 2. Of maſtersmasters chooſingchoosing good ſeruantsservants.
div.p: The firſtfirst thing that a man, who taketh vponupon him to be a maſtermaster, muſtmust take care of, is to entertaineentertain good ſeruantsservants into his ſeruiceservice. PſalPsal. 101. 6. Mine eieseyes (ſaithsaith DauidDavid) ſhallshall be vponupon the faithfullfaithful of the land, that they may dwell with me: he that walketh in a perfect way he ſhallshall ſerueserve me. What doth this phraſephrase (mine eieseyes ſhallshall be vponupon the faithfullfaithful) imply, but that he will diligently and carefully inquire after ſuchsuch: yea mine eieseyes (ſaithsaith he) not another mans eieseyes: he would not put all the truſttrust vponupon others: he would himſelfehimself make what proofeproof and trialltrial he could. Such an emphaſisemphasis hath this phraſephrase (mine eieseyes) where IobJob 19. 27. IobJob ſaithsaith; whom I ſhallshall ſeesee for my ſelfeself, and mine eieseyes ſhallshall behold, and not another for me.

1. SeruantsServants are of all other things (except wife and children) ReaſonsReasons. of beſtbest and greateſtgreatest vſeuse. If then men be carefullcareful in well chooſingchoosing other things, as houſeshouses, land, houſholdhousehold-ſtuffestuff, horſeshorses, and all manner of cattellcattle (as men are very circumſpectcircumspect therein) ſhouldshould they not be much more carefullcareful in well chooſingchoosing ſeruantsservants?

2. Thus will maſtersmasters ſhewshow that they ſeekeseek, and aimeaim at the good of their family: yea and in their family at the good of Church and common-wealth: for good members of a family are likelieſtlikeliest to proueprove profitable to Church & common-wealth.

3. When good ſeruantsservants are choſenchosen, there is hope of receiuingreceiving the more good from them, and doing more good vntounto them. They will be pliable to all good admonition, docible by all good inſtructioninstruction, ſeruiceableserviceable in all things they take in hand.

div.head: ObiectObject. A maſtermaster may make a bad ſeruantservant to become a good one.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. There is a great hazard and venture therein, eſpeciallyespecially if they be grownegrown to ripe yearesyears: no creature is eaſilyeasily tamed, or brought from the naturallnatural courſecourse it hath taken, after it is grownegrown vpup: a bough that hath grownegrown crooked many yearesyears together will hardly be made ſtraightstraight. It is not in mans power to make a bad ſeruantservant good: neither can man expect Gods bleſſingblessing therein, when he obſeruethobservethobserueth not a right courſecourse warranted by God.

div.head: QueſtQuest. What courſecourse is fitteſtfittest for choice of ſeruantsservants? Direction for chooſingchoosing of ſeruantsservants.
div.p: 1. If they be young, ſeesee how they hauehave beenebeen from their infancy educated. Great is the benefit of good education: and much good may be expected from thence: for it is the means which God hath ſanctifiedsanctified for good.
But if they be grownegrown to ripe yearesyears, chooſechoose ſuchsuch as fearefear God, ſuchsuch were they vponupon whom PſalPsal. 101. 6. DauidDavid caſtcast his eieseyes.
On this ground did Philem. verſvers.vers 10. Saint Paul aduiſeadvise Philemon to take OneſimusOnesimus againeagain, becauſebecause grace was then wrought in his heart.

1. Gods fearefear is the ground of all good obedience and Why ſuchsuch ſeruantsservants as fearefear God are to be choſenchosen. faithfulneſſefaithfulness: note the examples of ſuchsuch good and faithfullfaithful ſeruantsservants as are commended in Scripture, and you ſhallshall findefind them all to fearefear God.

2. Such will not only be diligent in their workework, but they will alſoalso faithfully call vponupon God to proſperprosper thoſethose things which they take in hand in their maſtersmasters behalfebehalf, inſtanceinstance the example of Gen. 24. 12. AbrahamsAbraham's ſeruantservant.

3. God will hauehave ſuchsuch reſpectrespect vntounto thoſethose ſeruantsservants which fearefear his name, as for their ſakessakes to bleſſebless their maſtersmasters houſehouse. Thus was Gen. 39. 5. Potiphars houſehouse bleſſedblessed for IoſephsJosephs ſakesake.

2. Make ſomesome trialltrial of their fitneſſefitness to that calling, workework
and ſeruiceservice whereunto thou ſhaltshalt put them. From ſuchsuch there may be hope of profit & benefit by their ſeruiceservice. Gen. 29. 14. Laban made trialltrial of IaakobJacob a monethmonth before he couenantedcovenanted for any long continuance.

3. Take ſuchsuch eſpeciallyespecially as are of meanemean and poorepoor eſtateestate, and know not how to maintainemaintain themſeluesthemselves but by ſeruiceservice. Thus will a double workework of charitiecharity be done therein: and thus maiſtmaist thou lookelook for better ſeruiceservice: for commonly ſuchsuch are moſtmost induſtriousindustrious, and moſtmost obedient to their maſtersmasters.

div.head: ObiectObject. When men hauehave taken all the care they can in their choice, they may be deceiueddeceived.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. 1. Then much more likely is it, that if they be careleſſecareless therein, they ſhallshall be deceiueddeceived.
2. Diligent, and wiſewise ſearchsearch, is a meanesmeans to findefind out the diſpoſitiondisposition and abilitieability of ſeruantsservants.

3. If hauinghaving vſedused the meanesmeans men be deceiueddeceived, they may hauehave the more comfort in bearing the croſſecross, becauſebecause they hauehave not wittingly or careleſlycarelessly pulled it vponupon themſeluesthemselves.

div.head: §. 3. Of maſtersmasters careleſneſſecarelessness in chuſingchoosing ſeruantsservants.
div.p:
Contrary is their careleſneſſecarelessness, who are ready to receiuereceive any into their houſehouse, eueneven AtheiſtsAtheists, PapiſtsPapists, ſwearersswearers, ſwaggerersswaggerers, profane wretches, vncleaneunclean perſonspersons, and ſuchsuch like, againſtagainst whom DauidDavid proteſtethprotesteth, he would not hauehave him that worketh deceit to dwell in
PſalPsal. 101. 7. his houſehouse; nor him that telleth lies to tarrietarry in his ſightsight. They who entertaineentertain ſuchsuch, make their houſeshouses to be cages of vncleaneunclean birds, ſeminariesseminaries of wicked perſonspersons, and vnprofitableunprofitable members: for one ſcabbedscabbed ſheepesheep is enough to infect a whole flockeflock. No maruellmarvell though many miſchiefesmischiefs fall vponupon ſuchsuch a familiefamily: for a man were as good bring ſoso many Snakes and Adders into his houſehouse, as ſuchsuch perſonspersons: yea with them is brought Gods curſecurse. Can any good then be looked for? Such fooliſhfoolish maſtersmasters regard neither themſeluesthemselves, nor their houſholdhousehold: no nor yet Church or Commoncommon-wealth. If none would entertaineentertain ſuchsuch, it might be a meanesmeans to make them alter their condition.

Many are not only careleſſecareless in chuſingchoosing good ſeruantsservants, but alſoalso except againſtagainst ſuchsuch as are religious; thinking it a matter of reproach to entertaineentertain them. By which conceit they oft put away Gods bleſſingblessing from their houſehouse.

Others ſoso ſtandstand vponupon a great portion of money with a prentiſeprentice,
or a clerkeclerk, or other ſeruantservant, as they will take none but rich mens children. Whence it commethcometh to paſſepass, that this point (which is a great point) of charitiecharity is neglected: perſonspersons moſtmost vnfitunfit for ſeruiceservice are entertained, and ſuchsuch many times as ſcornescorn to doedo ſeruiceservice. Thus their maſtersmasters grow weary of them: the ſeruantsservants loſelose their time: neuernever proueprove to be their crafts-maſtersmasters: and their parents repent the giuinggiving of ſuchsuch a portion with them.

div.head: §. 4. Of maſtersmasters maintaining their authoritieauthority.
div.p: After that maſtersmasters hauehave choſenchosen good ſeruantsservants, their dutieduty is well to vſeuse them: which by reaſonreason of the difference betwixt maſtersmasters and ſeruantsservants cannot be well done, except maſtersmasters wiſelywisely maintainemaintain their authoritieauthority. A maſtermaster therefore muſtmust be able 1 Tim. 3. 4. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . well to rule his owneown houſehouse: this is a dutieduty which the ApoſtleApostle in particular requireth of a BiſhopBishop, who is maſtermaster of an houſehouse, but it appertaineth in generallgeneral to all maſtersmasters of families. Women alſoalso who by vertuevirtue of their places are miſtreſſesmistresses, are commanded 1 Tim. 5. 14. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . to guide the houſehouse, or to rule, and performeperform the part of a miſtreſſemistress therein. It was the Mat. 8. 9. Centurions commendation, that hauinghaving ſeruantsservants vnderunder him, he had them at his command.
1. Gods image and authoritieauthority, which a maſtermaster carrieth, is thus preſeruedpreserved.

2. Thus ſhallshall a maſtermaster hauehave much better ſeruiceservice done. Not one ſeruantservant of a thouſandthousand, that is not kept vnderunder authoritieauthority, will doedo good ſeruiceservice. A like dutieduty to this was enioynedenjoined to an husband in relation to a wife, Treat. 4.

div.head: §. 4. Some of the reaſonsreasons, directions, & other points there handled, may be here applied. Read it therefore.
div.p: For this end three things are to be obſeruedobserved. Direction.

1. That maſtersmasters carriecarry themſeluesthemselves worthy of their place, and worthy of that honour which is due to them: which may beſtbest be done by making themſeluesthemselves a patternepattern of ſuchsuch good things as in their places appertaineappertain to them. JoſJos. 24. 15. I and my houſehouse will fearefear the Lord, ſaithsaith IoſuahJoshua: he would not only put them to it, but he alſoalso would doedo it, he would goego before them. I will behauebehave my ſelfeself wiſelywisely, I will walkewalk within my houſehouse with a perfect heart, ſaithsaith PſalPsal. 101. 2. DauidDavid.
2. That maſtersmasters keepekeep their ſeruantsservants in awe and fearefear. 1 Tim. 3. 4. Children muſtmust be kept in ſubiectionsubjection: much more ſeruantsservants.

3. That maſtersmasters doedo the things which they doedo in their cariagecarriage towards their ſeruantsservants with authoritieauthority: Command, forbid, rebuke (to vſeuse Tit. 2. 15. the ApoſtlesApostles phraſephrase) with all authoritieauthority. The manner of ſpeechspeech which the Centurion vſedused to his ſeruantsservants ( Mat. 8. 9. goego, come, doedo this) ſauoursavour of authoritieauthority. So the Church taking vponupon her the perſonperson of a miſtreſſemistress, vſethuseth a word of authoritieauthority, Cant. 3. 5. I charge you not to doedo this.

div.head: §. 5. Of maſtersmasters making their authoritieauthority to be deſpiſeddespised.
div.p: The aberrations in the defect contrary to the forenamed dutieduty How maſtersmasters loſelose their honour. and point of wiſdomewisdom, are many: as

1. When maſtersmasters carriecarry themſeluesthemselves baſelybasely and abiectlyabjectly before 1. By baſenesbaseness. their ſeruantsservants: being light in their behauiourbehaviour, fooliſhfoolish in their cariagecarriage, giuengiven to drunkenneſſedrunkenness, vncleanneſſeuncleanness, lewd companiecompany, and other vices. Nabal was ſuchsuch an one: for his ſeruantservant could ſaysay of him, 1 Sam. 25. 17. He is a ſonneson of Belial. DauidDavid, though he did not giuegive himſelfehimself ouerover to ſuchsuch foulefoul ſinnessins as theſethese are, yet he oft failed in an vnſeemlyunseemly cariagecarriage before his ſeruantsservants, as when 1 Sam. 21. 13. he changed his behauiourbehaviour, and fainedfeigned himſelfehimself mad, and ſcrabledscrabbledscrabled on dooresdoors, and let his ſpittlespittle fall downedown vponupon his beard: and againeagain, 2 Sam. 19. 3, 5. when he gauegave ſuchsuch reinesreins to his paſſionpassion, for the death of his traiteroustraitorous ſonneson AbſolomAbsalom, as his people being aſhamedashamed ſtolestole away from him, and IoabJoab his ſeruantservant was forced roundly to tell him of it, ſayingsaying, thou haſthast ſhamedshamed this day the faces of all thy ſeruantsservants, &etcc.

MiſtreſſesMistresses oft loſelose their authoritieauthority by conſpiringconspiring with their ſeruantsservants to goego abroad, take away goods, goſſipgossip, and doedo ſuchsuch other like things priuilyprivily without their husbands conſentconsent: they make themſeluesthemselves thereby ſlauesslaves to their ſeruantsservants, not daring to doedo any thing which may offend their ſeruantsservants, leſtlest they ſhouldshould diſcouerdiscover to their maſtersmasters ſuchsuch lewd pranks as their Miſtreſſesmistresses did.

2. When maſtersmasters are too remiſſeremiss and ſheepiſhsheepish: intreatingentreating and 2. By remiſnesremissnessremisnes. praying their ſeruantsservants to doedo ſuchsuch things as they ought to command and require at their hands: and if it be not done, all their remedieremedy is patience, or elſeelse to doedo it themſeluesthemselves. HowſoeuerHowsoever this might be counted meekneſſemeekness, and gentleneſſegentleness towards equals and ſtrangersstrangers, ouerover whom we hauehave no authoritieauthority, yet towards ſeruantsservants it is too baſebase remiſneſſeremissness: yea it is a relin quiſhingquishingrelinquishing of that power which God hath giuengiven, and whereof God will take an account.

3. When maſtersmasters ſuffersuffer their ſeruantsservants to be their companions, 3. By familiaritiefamiliarity.
playing, drinking, reuellingrevelling with them, and ſayingsaying (as it is in the prouerbeproverb) hailehail fellowesfellows met. Thus ſeruantsservants oft take libertieliberty to preſumepresume aboueabove their maſtermaster: for men are naturally prone to ambition; and, if an inch be giuengiven, they will take an ell. They who in this kindekind ſoso farrefar debaſedebase themſeluesthemselves, as to giuegive their ſeruantsservants power ouerover their owneown bodiebody, doedo make both themſeluesthemselves, and their true lawfulllawful bedfellow to be deſpiſeddespised: themſeluesthemselves, in that ſuchsuch ſeruantsservants as are ſoso made one fleſhflesh, will thinkethink to keepekeep in awe ſuchsuch a maſtermaster or miſtreſſemistress, as they hauehave knowneknown, through fearefear of reuealingrevealing that ſinnesin: their bedfellow, in that ſuchsuch ſeruantsservants will thinkethink to be maintained, and boulſteredbolsteredboulstered vpup by the maſtermaster or miſtreſſemistress, whom they hauehave ſoso knowneknown. On this ground was Gen. 16. 3, 4. Sarah deſpiſeddespised in the eyes of Hagar her maid.

4. When maſtersmasters are ouerover-ruled by their ſeruantsservants to doedo any 4. By letting goego the reinesreins. vniuſtunjust or vnlawfullunlawful thing: as 2 Chro. 14. 17. IoaſhJoash, who by his ſeruantsservants was drawnedrawn to idolatrieidolatry: and IerJer. 38. 5. Zedekiah, who gauegave the Prophet IeremiahJeremiah into his ſeruantsservants hands, vſingusing this baſebase and abiectabject ſpeechspeech, IerJer. 38. 5. The King is not he that can doedo any thing againſtagainst you. Thus will ſeruantsservants ſoonesoon proueprove maſtersmasters: and if they once come to this high pitch to rule, rather then to be ruled, they will quickly proueprove intolerable. For Pro. 30. 22. this is one of the fourefour things noted by the WiſemanWiseman, which the earth cannot bearebear, namely, a ſeruantservant when he reigneth: and Eccl. 10. 5, 7. this is one of thoſethose euilsevils which proceed from rulers, that ſeruantsservants ride vponupon horſeshorses, that is, are aduancedadvanced aboueabove their place and degree: whence it followeth, that Eccl. 10. 5, 7. GouernoursGovernors walkewalk as ſeruantsservants vponupon the earth, they are deiecteddejected below their place and degree. It falleth out in this caſecase betwixt ſeruantsservants and maſtersmasters, as betwixt ſcoalesscalesscoales, or ballancesbalances; if the weights that vſeuse to lie in one ballancebalance to keepekeep it downedown be taken away, it will ſuddenlysuddenly fliefly vpup, and ſoso the other ballancebalance will be kept downedown.

div.head: §. 6. Of maſtersmasters too great rigour.
div.p: The contrary in the exceſſeexcess is too great rigour and aufterityausterity manifeſtedmanifested in lookelook, ſpeechspeech, and actions.

1. In lookelook, when a maſtermaster cannot caſtcast a good eieeye on his ſeruantservant. Gen. 31. 2, 5. IaakobJacob was much diſcountenanceddiscountenanced by the countenance of his maſtermaster. Many maſtersmasters by their continuallcontinual frowning browesbrows, and fiery eieseyes, doedo much terrifieterrify their ſeruantsservants.

2. In ſpeechspeech, when maſtersmasters cannot giuegive a good word to their
ſeruantsservants, but if they be mouedmoved neuernever ſoso little, caſtcast vponupon them all the reproachfullreproachful names that they can call to mindemind: little thinking of this fearfullfearful doomedoom, Mat. 5. 22. WhoſoeuerWhosoever ſhallshall ſaysay, thou foolefool, ſhallshall be in danger of hell fire.

Thus did Saul manifeſtmanifest a malitiousmalicious and miſchieuousmischievous mindemind againſtagainst IonathanJonathan and DauidDavid by the foulefoul language he gauegave. Some hauehave ſuchsuch a froward and peruerſeperverse tongue, as they can neuernever ſpeakespeak directly to their ſeruantsservants: but if they command or forbid a thing, they will doedo it after ſuchsuch a manner as their ſeruantservant can ſcarcescarce tell what they meanemean: and this not only when their ſeruantservant hath offended them, but in their beſtbest mood. So ſhrewiſhshrewish are others, as their tongues ſeldomeseldom lie ſtillstill: but they are euerever chiding vponupon eueryevery ſmallsmall occaſionoccasion: whereby it commethcometh to paſſepass that their ſeruantsservants are no more mouedmoved with it, then the DouesDoves, and Stares that continually abide in BelfraiesBelfries, are mouedmoved with the ringing of belsbells. Such bitterneſſebitterness alſoalso is mixed with the childingschidings of many, as they belch out of their blackeblack mouthesmouths, moſtmost direfulldireful imprecations. What can be ſaidsaid of ſuchsuch tongues, but that they are Iam. 3. 6. ſetset on fire of hell? As other aberrations wherein maſtersmasters are reprouedreproved, are to be applied to miſtreſſesmistresses, ſoso this eſpeciallyespecially. For miſtreſſesmistresses doedo commonly moſtmost offend in ſhrewiſhneſſeshrewishness of ſpeechspeech.

3. In actions, when maſtersmasters are too frequent, and too furious Quamuis dominus ſeruoseruo praeſtetpraestet, tamen ſese aequalem iudicet quatenus homo exiſtitexistit. ConſtitConstit. ApoſtApost. l. 4. c. 12. ſtrikersstrikers: ſtrikingstriking their ſeruantsservants on eueryevery occaſionoccasion, not caring how they ſtrikestrike. In theſethese and other like euidencesevidences of too much auſteritieausterity and plaineplain arrogancy maſtersmasters forget that they are men. Though for outward order a maſtermaster be more excellent then a ſeruantservant, yet as a man he ought to iudgejudge himſelfehimself equallequal. This extreme can be no good meanesmeans to maintainemaintain authoritieauthority: but it is a plaineplain abuſeabuse thereof. MaſtersMasters ought ſoso Serui colant potius te quàm timeant. Senec. epiſtepist. 47. to carriecarry themſeluesthemselves as their ſeruantsservants may rather reuerencereverence, then dread them.

div.head: §. 7. Of maſtersmasters commanding power reſtrainedrestrained to things lawfulllawful. Extent of maſtersmasters power.
div.p: That a maſtermaster may the better know how to maintainemaintain his authoritieauthority, I will diſtinctlydistinctly declare the extent of his power, and that in theſethese fourefour particulars, 1. In Commanding. 2. In Correcting. 3. In ordering the mariagemarriage of their ſeruantsservants. 4. In diſpoſingdisposing their perſonperson.

Within the liſtslists of theſethese two vertuesvirtues IuſticeJustice and EquitieEquity (whereunto all the duties which maſtersmasters owe their ſeruantsservants ſhallshall §. 20, 21, &etcc. afterward be referred) muſtmust the commanding power of maſtersmasters be bounded.
1. IuſticeJustice requireth two things,
1. A reſtraintrestraint of maſtersmasters commandementscommandments.
2. An execution thereof.

The reſtraintrestraint is vntounto Gods law, that a maſtermaster command nothing againſtagainst it, but what is agreeable to it. AbiſhaiAbishai would Nothing vnlawfullunlawful to be commanded by maſtersmasters. 1 Sam. 26. 9. fainefain hauehave had DauidsDavid's warrant to hauehave killed Saul: but DauidDavid was ſoso farrefar from commanding him to doedo it, as he kept him from it.

MaſtersMasters are but ſubordinatesubordinate miniſtersministers vnderunder God: they muſtmust therefore command nothing againſtagainst his law. As a IudgeJudge, high-SheriffeSheriff, and all other officers vnderunder the King, muſtmust make the Kings law the ground of all thoſethose things which they require of the Kings ſubiectssubjects: ſoso maſtersmasters muſtmust make Gods law the ground of all thoſethose things which they require of their ſeruantsservants, who are alſoalso the ſeruantsservants of ChriſtChrist. BeſidesBesides, to what purpoſepurpose is it to command that which a ſeruantservant may and muſtmust refuſerefuse to doedo? But in no Treat. 7. §. 3838. vnlawfullunlawful thing may he obey.

div.head: §. 8. Of maſtersmasters preſumingpresuming aboueabove their authoritieauthority.
div.p: Contrary is the arroganciearrogancy and preſumptionpresumption of many maſtersmasters, who make their owneown will the rule of their ſeruantsservants obedience. This muſtmust needs be a leaden rule, which may be bowed this way, that way, and eueryevery way, becauſebecause of the flexible and variable humour of man. Hence is it that many moſtmost vile and horrible things are commanded, becauſebecause they are agreeable to the commanders humour. AbſolomAbsalom bid his ſeruantsservants commit a moſtmost deteſtabledetestable murder vponupon his owneown brother, and note how he preſſethpresseth it, HaueHave not I commanded you? 2 Sam. 13. 28.

More preſumptuouspresumptuous is he that taketh vponupon him to be the The Popes preſumptionpresumption. great commander of all ChriſtiansChristians, the Pope of Rome, and other maſtersmasters and gouernoursgovernors of IeſuitesJesuits, Friers, MonkesMonks, and other like orders, who command ſuchsuch as are vnderunder their authoritieauthority to commit treaſonstreasons, raiſeraise rebellions, kill Kings, and doedo other like execrable villaniesvillainies.

And to iuſtifiejustify the Pope from whom all inferiourinferior gouernoursgovernors

If he ſhallshall draw with him innumerable ſoulessouls of men into hell, yet none may ſaysay to him, what doeſtdoest thou? Doth not the ApoſtlesApostles 2 TheſſThess. 2. 4. Pontif. l. 4. c. 15. deſcriptiondescription of that man of ſinnesin, the ſonneson of perdition, agree to him of whom thoſethose things are ſpokenspoken? Is he not in PapiſtsPapists account, as God, ſhewingshowing himſelfehimself that he is God? Which is further confirmed by that power which they giuegive him of making laweslaws to bindebind the conſcienceconscience, and coining new articles of faith.

Not only popiſhpopish, but profane maſtersmasters alſoalso too much exceed in this preſumptuouspresumptuous vſeuse of their power aboueabove their power: as they who enioyneenjoin their ſeruantsservants to kill, to ſtealesteal, to ſweareswear, to forſweareforswear, to lie, to giuegive falſefalse meaſuresmeasures, and weights, to goego to maſſemass, to profane the Sabbath, with other like ſinnessins. In all theſethese, and all other things like to theſethese, being againſtagainst Gods law, maſtersmasters hauehave no power to command: they goego aboueabove their commiſſioncommission: and ſhallshall accordingly anſweranswer for it.

div.head: §. 9. Of maſtersmasters commanding ſeruantsservants to doedo their dutieduty.
div.p:
2. The execution of a maſtersmasters commanding power conſiſtethconsisteth in thoſethose things which God hath enioynedenjoined as bounden duties. TheſeThese a maſtermaster by vertuevirtue of his authoritieauthority muſtmust command his ſeruantsservants to doedo: as to worſhipworship God, to ſanctifiesanctify his Sabbath, to be diligent and conſcionableconscionable in his calling, with other like duties, which God compriſethcompriseth vnderunder theſethese words, the way of the Lord, righteouſneſſerighteousness and iudgementjudgment: and ſaithsaith that he knew that Abram would command his houſholdhousehold to doedo them.
Gen. 18. 19.

The charge giuengiven to maſtersmasters in the fourth commandementcommandment concerning ſeruantsservants, (thou nor thy man-ſeruantservant, nor thy maidſeruantmaidservant)
Exo. 20. 10. prouethproveth as much. IoſiahJosiah is commended for cauſingcausing his 2 Chr. 34. 32. people to ſtandstand to the couenantcovenant of God. On this ground if a maſtermaster hauehave ſeruantsservants that are papiſtspapists, ſeparatiſtsseparatists, or profane perſonspersons, he ought to command them, and cauſecause them to goego to the holy ordinances of God.

It is one of the principallprincipal ends why God hath giuengiven power and authoritieauthority to ſomesome ouerover others, that by their authoritieauthority they may cauſecause them which are vnderunder them to obſerueobserve the
commandementscommandments of God: eueneven as inferiourinferior officers hauehave authoritieauthority giuengiven them, to ſeesee the Kings laweslaws kept.

div.head: §. 10. Of the ſinnesin of maſtersmasters in ſufferingsuffering ſeruantsservants to neglect their dutieduty.
div.p: It is contrary to that commanding power which God hath giuengiven to maſtersmasters, to ſuffersuffer their ſeruantsservants to omit, and neglect thoſethose bounden duties which God hath commanded them: as if a ſeruantservant be ſoso popiſhpopish or profane as to refuſerefuse to goego to the word, or Sacrament, or to performeperform any dutieduty whereunto he is bound, to let him alone. Though they themſeluesthemselves doedo thoſethose duties, and though they doedo not hinder and keepekeep their ſeruantsservants from doing them, yet if they cauſecause not their ſeruantsservants alſoalso to doedo them, they make themſeluesthemselves acceſſarieaccessary to their ſeruantsservants ſinnesin.

ObiectObject. EueryEvery mans conſcienceconscience is free, and cannot be forced; therefore maſtersmasters may not compellcompel ſeruantsservants to ſuchsuch things as are againſtagainst their conſcienceconscience.

AnſwAnsw. Though the conſcienceconscience be free to a man, and out of anothers power, yet their outward actions are not free: and though faith, pietiepiety, righteouſneſſerighteousness, nor any grace can be forced into men, yet they may be forced to vſeuse the meanesmeans which God hath ſanctifiedsanctified for the breeding and increaſingincreasing of them. Though they cannot be forced to hauehave a religious and righteous heart, yet they may be forced to doedo religious and righteous duties: or if a maſtermaster cannot force theſethese, yet he may and ought to doedo his vttermoſtuttermost endeuourendeavour: by which means though he cannot free his ſeruantservant from death, yet he ſhallshall free his owneown ſoulesoul from the guilt of his death.

div.head: §. 11. Of a maſtersmasters wiſdomewisdom in ordering things indifferent.
div.p:
EquitieEquity hath reſpectrespect to thoſethose things which are in a maſtersmasters power to command or not command: ſuchsuch are all ciuillcivil actions as concerneconcern himſelfehimself, concerning the particulars whereof God hath giuengiven no direct charge for an abſoluteabsolute performance of them: as to goego of ſuchsuch an errand, to doedo ſuchsuch a meſſagemessage, to diſpatchdispatch ſuchsuch a buſineſſebusiness. Concerning theſethese things I may ſaysay of a maſtersmasters power, as the ApoſtleApostle doth of a parents power in 1 Cor. 7. 36, 37. another caſecase; If he ſeethseeth it meet to be done, and commandeth his ſeruantservant to doedo it, he doth well, he ſinnethsinneth not. If he ſeethseeth it
not meet to be done, and commandeth it not, he doth alſoalso well, he ſinnethsinneth not. Of this kindekind of things ſpeakethspeaketh the CenturianCenturion, Matt. 8. 9. where he ſaithsaith, I ſaysay to one, goego, to another, come, to a third, doedo this.

The markemark which maſtersmasters muſtmust aimeaim at in commanding or forbidding theſethese, muſtmust be expediency: for all things that are 1 Cor. 10. 23. lawfulllawful, are not expedient. Expediency dependeth much vponupon circumſtancescircumstances, and conſequencesconsequences which may follow vponupon the doing of any thing: in obſeruingobserving whereof the wiſdomewisdom of him who hath power to hauehave a thing done, or not done, eſpeciallyespecially appeareth. When DauidDavid ſufferedsuffered not HuſhaiHushai his good friend, 2 Sam. 15. 33, 34. and wiſewise counſellercounsellorcounseller, to goego with him when he fled from AbſolomAbsalom, but bid him returnereturn to the citiecity and there abide, he had an eieeye to the good conſequenceconsequence that might follow thereupon. And when IoabJoab commanded CuſhiCushi rather then Ahimaaz to 2 Sam. 18. 20, 21. carriecarry the newesnews of AbſolomsAbsoloms death, he had an eieeye to the meetneſſemeetness of the perſonspersons, and to the kindekind of meſſagemessage.

To apply this to our purpoſepurpose, Equity requireth that maſtersmasters (in commanding things indifferent, which they hauehave power to command or not to command) hauehave an eieeye to their ſeruantsservants ability, ſexsex, age, diſpoſitiondisposition, conſcienceconscience, and other like circumſtancescircumstances, that the thing which they command be ſomewhatsomewhat agreeable to them, not aboueabove their ability, not vnbeſeemingunbeseeming their ſexsex, not vnfittingunfitting their age, not thwarting their diſpoſitiondisposition, not againſtagainst their conſcienceconscience.

div.head: §. 12. Of maſtersmasters offence againſtagainst expediency.
div.p: It is contrary to equity for a maſtermaster to regard only himſelfehimself, and his own mind, eueneven in things that are lawfulllawful. Paul was not 1 Cor. 10. 33. of this mindemind, when he ſaidsaid, He ſoughtsought not his owneown profit: no nor his owneown will. Expediency and inexpediency were great motiuesmotives vntounto him, to forbeareforbear things which were otherwiſeotherwise lawfulllawful: yet little is this regarded by many: for

1. Many command things to the very vttermoſtuttermost of their ſeruantsservants ſtrengthstrength, if not aboueabove it, (as Pharaoh) or elſeelse things dangerous, Exod. 5. 7. which may bring much miſchiefemischief vponupon them. DauidDavid 2 Sam. 23. 17. was touched in heart for mouingmoving only by a wiſhwish his ſeruantsservants to fetch him water with the danger of their liueslives.
2. Others againſtagainst comelineſſecomeliness put men to doedo maids workesworks, and maids to doedo mens workework.
3. Others vponupon meeremere partiality keepekeep vnderunder old and good ſeruantsservants, and preferreprefer much younger before them.

4. Others will forcibly make ſeruantsservants doedo things againſtagainst their naturallnatural diſpoſitiondisposition, as to handle, yea and eat ſuchsuch things as they cannot endure to touch or ſeesee.
5. Others in doubtfulldoubtful matters will vrgeurge and preſſepress them againſtagainst their conſcienceconscience.

HowſoeuerHowsoever in theſethese and other ſuchsuch like things not vnlawfullunlawful, ſeruantsservants ought to doedo what they can to ſatisfiesatisfy their maſtersmasters command, if he be peremptory in vrgingurging them: yet ought not a maſtermaster to be too peremptory in preſſingpressing his authoritieauthority and power.

div.head: §. 13. Of the power of maſtersmasters to correct their ſeruantsservants.
div.p: The ſecondsecond point wherein a maſtersmasters power conſiſtethconsisteth is correction: which may be giuengiven by lookeslooks, words, or deeds.

By a mans lookelook his anger and wrath againſtagainst another is manifeſtedmanifested.

But words whether of rebuke, or threatningthreatening, doedo much more declare the ſamesame. This phraſephrase which Solomon vſethuseth Pro. 29. 19. (a ſeruantservant will not be corrected with words) ſhewethshoweth that there is a correction by words: and though it be negatiuelynegatively propounded, yet doth it not imply that correction by words is not to be vſedused to a ſeruantservant, but rather, if thereby he be not mouedmoved, that blowesblows muſtmust be added thereto: which is a correction by deeds, whereof ChriſtChrist maketh mention in the parable of thoſethose ſeruantsservants that according to the greatneſſegreatness of their fault are Luke 12. 47. to be beaten with many ſtripesstripes. It is therefore in a maſtersmasters power to correct his ſeruantservant with ſtripesstripes, or blowesblows. Which being ſoso, I will ſhewshow,
1. How farrefar his power herein extendeth.
2. How it is to be ordered.

div.head: §. 14. Of the reſtraintrestraint of maſtersmasters power: that it reacheth not to their ſeruantsservants life.
div.p: Concerning the extent of a maſtersmasters power in correcting his ſeruantservant, this queſtionquestion is to be reſoluedresolved, Whether a maſtermaster hauehave power for any fault to take away his ſeruantsservants life.
AnſwAnsw. His power reacheth not ſoso farrefar, as is euidentevident by theſethese reaſonsreasons.

1. There is no precept, nor approuedapproved example, nor any other warrant out of Gods word for it. The IewesJews had great power ouerover ſuchsuch ſeruantsservants as were ſtrangersstrangers: Of them they might
Leu. 25. 44, 45, 46. buy bond-men and bond-maids: they might hauehave them for a poſſeſſionpossession: and take them for an inheritance for their children after them, to be bond-men for euerever: they might be put to the moſtmost toylingtoiling, droylingdroiling, baſebase, and abiectabject workesworks that they had, as drawing water, hewing wood, and the like; but yet their maſtersmasters IoſJos. 9. 27. had not power ouerover their liueslives.

2. A maſtermaster might not diſmemberdismember his ſeruantservant: if vnawaresunawares he did ſmitesmite out an eieeye or tooth of his ſeruantservant, he muſtmust make a recompencerecompense: which was to let him goego free. Much leſſeless therefore Exod. 21. 26. might he take away his ſeruantsservants life.

3. If a ſeruantservant died vnderunder his maſtersmasters hand when he corrected him, though he intended not wilfully to murder him, that maſtermaster was to be puniſhedpunished. It was not therforetherefore lawfulllawful for Exod. 21. 20. a maſtermaster wittingly to kill a ſeruantservant.

4. The power of life is proper to the publikepublic magiſtratemagistrate, who doth all things in open publikepublic places, that ſoso there may be many witneſſeswitnesses of his iuſtjust proceeding. If maſtersmasters had this power, many might priuilyprivily be put to death, and no man know for what cauſecause, as it is in popiſhpopish inquiſitionsinquisitions.

5. Si Dominus ſeruumseruum ceciderit, vel lethalelethal vulnus inflixerit, reusrevs homicidij ſitsit. IuſtinJustin. Cod. l. 9. tit. 18. The approuedapproved laweslaws of men make it wilfullwilful murder for a maſtermaster to ſlayslay his ſeruantservant wittingly, though the ſeruantsservants fault be neuernever ſoso hainousheinous. Neither the authority of the maſtermaster, nor deſertdesert of the ſeruantservant, ſhallshall exempt the maſtermaster that ſlayethslayeth his ſeruantservant from the guilt and puniſhmentpunishment of felony.

div.p:
AnſwAnsw. They neuernever of right had it, though ſomesome might exerciſeexercise it. Among Gods people it was neuernever exerciſedexercised in any age of the world. That liberty which was taken, was among
the heathen: and yet among them as polities came to be more Apud Gentes animaduertere poſſumuspossumus Dominis in ſeruosseruos vitae, neciſ
que neciſquenecisque poteſtatempotestatem fuiſſefuisse. Sed hoc tempore nullis hominibus qui ſubsub imperio noſtronostro ſuntsunt, licet fine cauſacausa legibus cognita in ſeruosseruos ſuossuos ſuprasupra modum ſaeuiresaeuire Nam ex conſtitconstit. Domini mitiores eſſeesse debent. Cypr. TeſtimTestim. l. 3. c. 73. and more ciuillycivilly gouernedgoverned, that vſurpedusurped liberty by the laweslaws of MagiſtratesMagistrates was much reſtrainedrestrained: and when Emperors and Kings became ChriſtiansChristians, it was vtterlyutterly taken away.

div.head: ObiectObject. If a man take an enemieenemy by warrewar, he hath power to kill him.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. If in the time of the warrewar he ſlayslay him not, but then ſparespare him, and take him as a captiuecaptive, and make him his ſeruantservant, though but a bondſlauebondslave, he hath not power of his life.

div.head: §. 15. Of maſtersmasters exceſſeexcess in correcting ſeruantsservants.
div.p: Contrary to their iuſtjust and due power doedo they, who in their rage ſtabstab their ſeruantsservants, or otherwiſeotherwise make them away: yea they alſoalso who ſoso vnmercifullyunmercifully and vnmeaſurablyunmeasurably beat them with rod, cudgellcudgel, or any other thing, as death follow thereupon: for many there be who hauinghaving once begunnebegun to ſtrikestrike, know not when to ceaſecease, but lay on as if they were ſtrikingstriking ſtocksstocks and blocks, and not their owneown fleſhflesh. God foreſawforesaw that maſtersmasters were prone to ſuchsuch cruelty, and therefore Deut. 25. 3. ſetset a ſtintstint number of ſtripesstripes, which none that beat another might exceed.

Among theſethese may be reckoned ſuchsuch deſperatedesperate maſtersmasters as in their moodemood will ſtrikestrike their ſeruantservant with any thing that commethcometh next to hand, be it heauyheavy, cragged, hard, or ſharpesharpsharpe, they care not ( Pro. 26. 18. As a mad man who caſtethcasteth fire-brands, arrowesarrows, and death.) TheſeThese things may endanger a ſeruantsservants life, if not, they may breakebreak his head, or otherwiſeotherwise wound, bruiſebruise, and lame him.

It is beyond a maſtersmasters power by any correction to impaireimpair life, health, or ſtrengthstrength of his ſeruantservant, or any way in his body to diſabledisable him from doing that which otherwiſeotherwise he might hauehave beenebeen able to doedo.

If maſtersmasters, no not for puniſhmentpunishment of any ſinnesin, may not take away or endanger the life of his ſeruantservant, what may we thinkethink of ſuchsuch maſtersmasters, as without any fault of their ſeruantsservants, cauſecause them to be made away by putting them vponupon ſomesome deſperatedesperate attempt, either to maintainemaintain their owneown quarrellquarrel, or for ſomesome other vniuſtunjust end? 2 Sam. 11. 15. DauidDavid dealt thus with Uriah: but afterwards he PſalPsal. 51. 14. ſorelysorely repented this part of iniuſticeinjustice. At another
2 Sam. 23. 15, &etcc. time when three of his ſeruantsservants had fetched him water, which he longed for, with ieopardyjeopardy of their liueslives, though in ſafetysafety they returned, yet his heart ſmotesmote him for his longing, and he would not drinkedrink of that water becauſebecause they had ventured their liueslives to fetch it.

But what may we ſaysay of ſuchsuch maſtersmasters, as cauſecause their ſeruantsservants for their ſakessakes to commit felony, murthermurder, treaſontreason, rebellion, and ſuchsuch other things, as cauſecause the publikepublic magiſtratemagistrate to vnſheathunsheath his ſwordsword againſtagainst them, & cut them off? We noted this §. 8. before to be a grienousgrievous fault in regard of the vnlawfulneſſeunlawfulness of the thing: here further we may note it to be much more hainousheinous in regard of the miſchiefemischief that followeth thereupon, which is the loſſeloss of their ſeruantsservants life: ſoso as thus they make themſeluesthemselves acceſſaryaccessary to a deteſtabledetestable ſinnesin, and guilty of the bloudblood of their ſeruantservant.
