Smite a ſcornerscorner, ſaithsaith the wiſewise man: and againeagain, IudgementsJudgments are prepared for ſcornersscorners, and ſtripesstripes for the backeback of foolesfools.

Seeing ſeruantsservants in yearesyears are in this caſecase to be corrected, it is further requiſiterequisite to put a difference betwixt the kindekind or meaſuremeasure of correction which is giuengiven to them, and to the younger ſortsort: if they be corrected as children, they may either
make a toy of it, or the more diſdainedisdain at it. Pro. 20. 30. Heris in famulos ſaeuitiasaeuitia adhibenda eſtest, ſisi aliter teneri non poſſuntpossunt. Cic. Offic. l. 2. BlewneſſeBluenessBlewness, wound, and ſtripesstripes piercing into the inward parts of the belly, are a purging medicine againſtagainst euillevil, to ſtoutstout ſeruantsservants of ripe yearesyears.

2. If there be a maſtermaster and miſtreſſemistress ioyntjoint gouernoursgovernors ouerover an houſehouse, it is fitteſtfittest for the maſtermaster to correct men-ſeruantsservants, the miſtreſſemistress maids. Seruam verberare viro maximae ignominiae eſtest. ChryſChrys. hom. 26. in 1 Cor. 11. Abraham put his maid ouerover to Sarah in ſuchsuch a caſecase. Yet if a maid ſhouldshould wax ſtoutstout, and manniſhmannish, and turneturn againſtagainst her miſtreſſemistress, ſheshe being weakeweak, ſicklysickly, with child, or otherwiſeotherwise vnableunable to maſtermaster her maid, the maſtermaster may and muſtmust beat downedown her ſtoutneſſestoutness and rebellion: Exo. 21. 20. ſoso much did the law of God permit.

3. If ſeruantsservants be of an ingenious diſpoſitiondisposition, willing and forward to doedo that which belongeth vntounto them, ſorrysorry when they hauehave committed a fault, and carefullcareful to amend their faults, many things may be paſſedpassed ouerover in them, which muſtmust be corrected in others. To this may be applied the counſellcounsel of the wiſemanwiseman, Take no heed to all the words that are
Eccl. 7. 21. ſpokenspoken.

4. Correction muſtmust be meaſuredmeasured according to the greatneſſegreatness —AdſitAdsit Regula peccat is quae poenas irroget aequas: Nec ſcuticascutica dignum horribili ſecteresectere flagello. Horat. l. 1. Sat. 3. of the fault puniſhedpunished, and the circumſtancescircumstances whereby the fault may iuſtlyjustly be aggrauatedaggravated. The ſeruantservant that knew his maſtersmasters will and did it not ſhallshall be beaten with many ſtripesstripes: But he that knew not and did commit things worthy of ſtripesstripes, ſhallshall be beaten with few ſtripesstripes, Luk. 12. 47, 48.

Many aberrations are daily committed contrary to eueryevery branch of this direction, in that maſtersmasters and miſtreſſesmistresses in exerciſingexercising this part of their power are carried away with paſſionpassion, and doedo that which they doedo in this kindekind after their owneown pleaſurepleasure. Thus they turneturn a dutieduty into ſinnesin, and by vndueundue correcting of their ſeruantsservants prouokeprovoke God to correct them in his wrath, either here or in the world to come.

div.head: §. 17. Of maſtersmasters power ouerover their ſeruantsservants in and about their mariagemarriage.
div.p:
The third point to be noted concerning a maſtersmasters power ouerover his ſeruantservant, is about his ſeruantsservants mariagemarriage. Sundry queſtionsquestions
are mouedmoved about this point, which I will briefly reſolueresolve.

div.head: 1. QueſtQuest. HaueHave maſtersmasters power to order and diſpoſedispose their ſeruantsservants mariagemarriage as they pleaſeplease?
div.p: AnſwAnsw. No, not without the free conſentconsent of the ſeruantsservants themſeluesthemselves: for mariagesmarriages muſtmust be made with the free conſentconsent of the parties that are mariedmarried.

ObiectObject. The law implieth that a maſtermaster hath power to giuegive Exo. 21. 4. his ſeruantservant a wife, for it ſhewethshoweth whoſewhose thoſethose children ſhallshall be that are borne to that ſeruantservant, to whom a maſtermaster hath giuengiven a wife.

AnſwAnsw. 1. That law is to be vnderſtoodunderstood of ſuchsuch ſeruantsservants as being ſtrangersstrangers were bond-ſlauesslaves, ouerover whom maſtersmasters had a more abſoluteabsolute power then ouerover others.

2. The maſtersmasters power of giuinggiving did not ſimplysimply force the ſeruantservant to mariemarry the party ſoso giuengiven: but reſtrainedrestrained the ſeruantservant from maryingmarrying any other then whom the maſtermaster ſhouldshould giuegive.

div.head: 2. QueſtQuest. Is not a maſtersmasters power in the matter of mariagemarriage as great ouerover a ſeruantservant, as a parents ouerover a childechild?
div.p: AnſwAnsw. No. See the reaſonreason Treat. 5. §. 20.

div.head: 3. QueſtQuest. May a maſtermaster deniedeny his ſeruantservant liberty to mariemarry?
div.p: AnſwAnsw. Yea, for the time that the ſeruantservant hath couenantedcovenanted to be a ſeruantservant with his maſtermaster. For that time a ſeruantservant is part of his maſtersmasters goods, and poſſeſſionspossessions. As bond ſeruantsservants were a maſtersmasters poſſeſſionpossession for euerever: ſoso couenantedcovenanted ſeruantsservants are his poſſeſſionpossession for the time of their couenantcovenant. When God gauegave the deuilldevil leaueleave to ſeizeseize on all that IobJob had, by vertuevirtue of that IobJob 1. 15, 16. permiſſionpermission he ſeizedseized on all kindeskinds of IobsJobs ſeruantsservants bond and free, as well as on his goods: which he could not hauehave done, if IobsJobs ſeruantsservants had not beenebeen as his goods.

Yet notwithſtandingnotwithstanding if ſeruantsservants ſhallshall make it knowneknown to their maſtermaster, that neceſſitynecessity requireth they ſhouldshould mariemarry, ſuchsuch reſpectrespect ought to be had to the chaſtitychastity eueneven of ſeruantsservants, as in this caſecase I may vſeuse the phraſephrase with the ApoſtleApostle vſethuseth in reference to children, Let them be mariedmarried. 1 Cor. 7. 36.

div.head: 4. QueſtQuest. What if ſeruantsservants mariemarry without conſentconsent of maſtersmasters, is that mariagemarriage nullified thereby?
div.p:
AnſwAnsw. No. The mariagemarriage being otherwiſeotherwise rightly performed, Quod fieri non debet factum valet. remaineth a firmefirm mariagemarriage: though the ſeruantsservants in
ſoso doing hauehave ſinnedsinned: for which their maſtermaster may iuſtlyjustly puniſhpunish them.

div.head: 5. QueſtQuest. May a maſtermaster keepekeep his ſeruantsservants ſoso mariedmarried without his conſentconsent from their bed-fellowesfellows?
div.p: AnſwAnsw. He may exact the whole time of his couenantcovenant for ſeruiceservice: but that power which by the bond of mariagemarriage huſbandshusbands and wiueswives hauehave ouerover one anothers bodies, ſufferethsuffereth 1 Cor. 7. 3, 4. them not to be altogether ſeparatedseparated one from another. BeſidesBesides, our law freeth a maid-ſeruantservant when ſheshe is mariedmarried, from her maſtersmasters couenantcovenant.

div.head: §. 18. Of maſtersmasters rigour in forcing mariagesmarriages on ſeruantsservants: or in ſeparatingseparating man and wife.
div.p: Contrary to a maſtersmasters power doedo they, who force their ſeruantsservants to mariemarry whom they like not: as when a maſtermaster hath defloureddeflowered his maid, to couercover his ſhameshame he will make one of his ſeruantsservants mariemarry her.

They alſoalso doedo contrary to their power who ſeekeseek to ſeparatseparateseparat their ſeruantsservants that are mariedmarried from their bed-fellow: ſomesome will keepekeep the man at his houſehouse day and night from his wife, and ſoso the wife from her husband: others will ſendsend one of them into remote parts of the land, where the other ſhallshall not know: yea others will be ſuresure to keepekeep them one from another, for they will ſendsend one of them beyond ſeasea for many yearesyears together, if not for euerever. TheſeThese practiſespractises are againſtagainst the law of mariagemarriage, and too rigorous and vniuſtunjust.

div.head: §. 19. Of maſtersmasters power to diſpoſedispose their ſeruantsservants perſonspersons.
div.p: The fourth point to be noted of a maſtersmasters power ouerover his ſeruantsservants reſpectethrespecteth their perſonspersons, which ſoso properly belong to a maſtermaster for the time of their ſeruiceservice, as he may not only keepekeep them himſelfehimself for his owneown ſeruiceservice, but alſoalso paſſepass them ouerover, and giuegive, or ſellsell them to another. By Gods law not only Leu. 25. 39, 44. ſtrangersstrangers, but IewesJews alſoalso might be ſoldsold for ſeruantsservants.

The cuſtomescustoms and ſtatutesstatutes of our land doedo alſoalso permit maſtersmasters MaſtersMasters care in putting off ſeruantsservants. to make ouerover their ſeruantsservants from one to one: and on their death-beds to bequeath them to whom they will, eueneven as their goods and poſſeſſionspossessions.

That this power be not abuſedabused, in the executing thereof,
maſtersmasters muſtmust principally reſpectrespect the good of their ſeruantsservants: and for that end put them ouerover to fit maſtersmasters, ſuchsuch maſtersmasters as may doedo them good and not euillevil, all the time of their abode with them, and ſeruiceservice vnderunder them.

Contrary hereunto doedo they, who aimeaim meerelymerely at their owneown aduantageadvantage, not caring to whom they put ouerover their ſeruantsservants, ſoso they may make gainegain thereby. Some will ſellsell them, namely, when they hauehave them beyond ſeasea, to Turks and Infidels; ſomesome to PapiſtsPapists, and other Idolaters; ſomesome to profane perſonspersons; ſomesome to cruellcruel inhumane beaſtsbeasts; ſomesome to men of vnlawfullunlawful trades; ſomesome to men of no trades. Such maſtersmasters as make their ſeruantsservants ouerover to ſuchsuch as theſethese are, or like to theſethese, ſhallshall anſweranswer for all the wrong is done to them.

div.head: §. 20. Of maſtersmasters well managing their authoritieauthority.
div.p: This ApoſtleApostle in ColoſſColoss. 4. 1. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . another place giuethgiveth this charge to maſtersmasters, GiueGive vntounto your ſeruantsservants that which is iuſtjust and equallequal.
By doing theſethese two things maſtersmasters ſhallshall well manage their authoritieauthority.
IuſticeJustice reſpectethrespecteth the place, and ſeruiceservice of ſeruantsservants. Difference betwixt iuſtjust and equallequal dealing.
EquitieEquity reſpectethrespecteth their mindemind, and manner of doing ſeruiceservice.
All ſeruantsservants, in that they are ſeruantsservants, and doedo their maſtersmasters workework, muſtmust hauehave that which of right belongeth to ſeruantsservants. This is IuſticeJustice.

Such ſeruantsservants as bearebear an eſpeciallespecial louelove and liking to their maſtersmasters, doing ſeruiceservice not by conſtraintconstraint, or with eye-ſeruiceservice, as men-pleaſerspleasers, but in ſingleneſſesingleness of heart with good will, and all good faithfulneſſefaithfulness, ſeekingseeking to the vttermoſtuttermost of their power, their maſtersmasters good, muſtmust be accordingly reſpectedrespected and dealt withallwithal. This is EquitieEquity. As the ApoſtleApostle compriſethcompriseth IuſticeJustice vnderunder this phraſephrase (doedo the ſamesame things) for ſeruiceservice giuegive due recompencerecompense: ſoso more eſpeciallyespecially he compriſethcompriseth EquitieEquity vnderunder it: for ſeruantsservants good will and more then vſuallusual reſpectrespect of their maſtersmasters, let maſtersmasters returnereturn good will, and more then ordinarieordinary reſpectrespect to ſeruantsservants. S. Peter noteth theſethese two vertuesvirtues vnderunder two other words, good, 1 Pet. 2. 18. gentle: A maſtersmasters goodneſſegoodness hath relation to IuſticeJustice: his gentleneſſegentleness to EquitieEquity.

div.head: §. 21. Of maſtersmasters endeuouringendeavouring the ſaluationsalvation of their ſeruantsservants.
div.p: That IuſticeJustice which is required of maſtersmasters reſpectethrespecteth the ſoulesoul, bodiebody, and eſtateestate of their ſeruantsservants.

In reſpectrespect of their ſoulessouls good, maſtersmasters muſtmust ſeekeseek the ſpirituallspiritual I. IuſtiIusti patres ſecundumsecundum haec temporalia bona, filiorum ſortemsortem à ſeruorumseruorum conditione diſtinguebantdistinguebant: ad Deum autem colendum, in quo aeterna bona ſperandasperanda ſuntsunt, omnibus domus ſuaesuae membris pari dilectione conſulebantconsulebant. Aug. de Ciu. Dei l. 19. c. 15. edification of their ſeruantsservants. When Zacheus firſtfirst beleeuedbelieved, ChriſtChrist ſaidsaid, SaluationSalvation is come to this houſehouse (Luk. 19. 9.) why to this houſehouse, rather then to this perſonperson, but becauſebecause he knew that Zacheus would doedo the dutieduty of a good maſtermaster, and ſeekeseek the ſaluationsalvation of his houſholdhousehold? Herein muſtmust maſtersmasters bearebear an impartiallimpartial reſpectrespect to all in their houſehouse: as the holy Fathersfathers, who though about temporalltemporal goods they put difference betwixt the place of children, and condition of ſeruantsservants; yet in ſeruingserving God, wherein eternalleternal happineſſehappiness is looked for, they did with an equallequal reſpectrespect prouideprovide for all the members of their houſehouse. The proofesproofs alleadgedalleged for ſeruantsservants obedience to maſtersmasters care in this point, doedo ſhewshow that this dutieduty appertaineth to maſtersmasters. See Treat. 7. §. 15.
The reſpectrespect which maſtersmasters owe to God, themſeluesthemselves, their ſeruantsservants, the Church, and Commoncommon-wealth where they liuelive, requireth as much.

1. God hath commanded as much (Deut. 6. 7.) as this charge implieth, Thou ſhaltshalt talketalk of my LawesLaws when thou ſittestsittest in thine houſehouse: and God hath manifeſtedmanifested his approbation thereof, by commending Abraham for commanding his children and houſeholdhousehold to keepekeep the way of the Lord, Gen. 18. 19.

2. MaſtersMasters themſeluesthemselves reapereap great benefit by a faithfullfaithful diſchargedischarge De ſalutesalute eorum qui in domo tua ſuntsunt ſollicitussollicitus, ac peruigil exiſtasexistas, quia pro omnibus tibi ſubiectissubiectis rationērationen Domino reddes. Aug. de ſalutsalut. docum. cap. 29. of this dutieduty: and that both by diſchargingdischarging a good conſcienceconscience to God, (who requireth this at their hands, in that he hath made them prophets and prieſtspriests in their houſehouse, as well as kings; and will require an account of them for all that are vnderunder their gouernmentgovernment:) and alſoalso by bringing their ſeruantsservants to doedo more faithfullfaithful ſeruiceservice to them. For there is no ſuchsuch meanesmeans to ſtirrestir vpup ſeruantsservants to doedo all good dutieduty, as the fearefear of God planted in their hearts. That ſeruantservant that ſhallshall findefind true grace either firſtfirst wrought, or further increaſedincreased in him by his maſtersmeanesmasters meansmastersmeanes, will thinkethink him ſelfeself ſoso beholding to ſuchsuch a maſtermaster, as he ſhallshall neuernever be able to make any ſufficientsufficient recompencerecompense, & therefore will endeuourendeavour to do what good ſeruiceservice he can in way of thankfulnesthankfulness: he will not only be faithfullfaithful & diligent in his buſineſſebusiness, but he will call vponupon God
to proſperprosper his ſeruiceservice for his maſtersmasters good, and to recompencerecompense that kindneſſekindness which his maſtermaster hath done to him.

3. No earthly thing that a maſtermaster can doedo for his ſeruantservant (be it portion of money, preferment to any place of profit or credit, or skill in a good trade and calling) can be comparable to the edifying of a ſeruantservant in grace.

4. SeruantsServants well inſtructedinstructed in pietiepiety are likelieſtlikeliest to proueprove moſtmost profitable not only to the familiefamily, but alſoalso to the Church and Commoncommon-wealth where they liuelive.
That maſtersmasters may the better edifieedify their ſeruantsservants,

1. They muſtmust daily inſtructinstruct them in the principles of religion, Directions for edifying ſeruantsservants. and all duties of pietiepiety: admirable is the profit which will ariſearise from a daily and conſtantconstant vſeuse of religious exerciſesexercises: though but a little time be ſpentspent at once, yet will much knowledge be gained by a frequent vſeuse of them. This dutieduty is ſoso much the more neceſſarienecessary, becauſebecause publikepublic MiniſtersMinisters cannot take ſuchsuch particular notice of eueryevery ſeruantservant in their PariſhesParishes, as maſtersmasters may in their families.

2. MaſtersMasters muſtmust cauſecause their ſeruantsservants to goego to the publikepublic miniſterieministry of the word, and worſhipworship of God, to be further built vpup thereby, and confirmed in their faith. MaſtersMasters vnderunder the Law were Exo. 12. 44. commanded to let their ſeruantsservants eat of the PaſſeouerPassoverPasseover, which was a ſolemnesolemn ſacramentsacrament. The Law which enioynethenjoineth all males to appeareappear Deut. 16. 16. on the ſolemnesolemn feaſtfeast dayesdays before the Lord, implieth that ſeruantsservants alſoalso ſhouldshould goego. This dutieduty muſtmust eſpeciallyespecially be performed on the Lords day: for the charge giuengiven to maſtersmasters in the fourth commandementcommandment for ſanctifyingsanctifying that day, is extended to ſeruantsservants in theſethese words, Thou, nor thy man-ſeruantservant, nor thy maid-ſeruantservant.

3. MaſtersMasters, beſidebeside inſtructinginstructing ſeruantsservants at home, and cauſingcausing them to goego to Church, muſtmust take an account of their profiting, both by the publikepublic, and alſoalso by the priuateprivate meanesmeans of edification. OtherwiſeOtherwise they ſhallshall not know how to order their manner of inſtructinginstructing them: when to giuegive them milkemilk, & when ſtrongstrong meat.

4. To make the meanesmeans more effectualleffectual and profitable, they muſtmust to inſtructioninstruction addeadd prayer. MeanesMeans, without Gods bleſſingblessing vponupon the meanesmeans, are nothing. As they obſerueobserve any grace wrought in their ſeruantsservants, they muſtmust be thankfullthankful vntounto God for the ſamesame, and pray for the increaſeincrease of it.

div.head: §. 22. Of maſtersmasters neglecting to edifieedify their ſeruantsservants.
div.p: Contrary is the mindemind and practiſepractise of moſtmost maſtersmasters: they thinkethink if they allow their ſeruantsservants ſufficientsufficient diet, lodging, and clothing, or wages according to their couenantcovenant, they hauehave done all that they need to doedo: and anſwerablyanswerably they doedo no more: wherein they ſhewshow themſeluesthemselves no better then the heathen. For doedo not the heathen ſoso?

div.head: ObiectObject. At firſtfirst taking of a ſeruantservant no more was couenantedcovenanted.
div.p: AnſwAnsw. There are two couenantscovenants whereunto a maſtermaster ſtandethstandeth bound: one with God; the other with his ſeruantservant. Though his couenantcovenant with his ſeruantservant requireth no more then ſomesome temporalltemporal commodities, yet Gods couenantcovenant requireth ſpirituallspiritual edification. Many maſtersmasters are ſoso greediegreedy of their ſeruantsservants workework, as they are loth to afford any time, at morning or eueningevening, for religious exerciſesexercises: they thinkethink by their ſeruantsservants labour to thriuethrive, and thinkethink not of Gods bleſſingblessing which maketh rich. Some goego ſoso far therein, as they keepekeep their ſeruantsservants from the publikepublic worſhipworship of God, eueneven on the Lords day. Thus it commethcometh to paſſepass, that ſeruantsservants, who came ignorant and profane to a maſtermaster, after long abode with him, ſoso goego away as they came. Many that themſeluesthemselves make ſomesome conſcienceconscience of fearing God, much failefail herein: they regard not to teach their ſeruantsservants the fearefear of God, whereby they depriuedeprive themſeluesthemselves of much bleſſingblessing, and pull Gods curſecurse vponupon their perſonspersons and houſeshouses.

div.head: §. 23. Of allowing ſeruantsservants ſufficientsufficient food.
div.p: In regard that ſeruantsservants hauehave not bodies of braſſebrass, or ſteelesteelsteele, II. but of fleſhflesh and bloudblood as all others, maſtersmasters that hauehave the benefit of their ſtrengthstrength and abilitieability of their bodies, muſtmust be carefullcareful of nouriſhingnourishing, and cheriſhingcherishing them: and that both in health, and ſickneſſesickness.
For preſeruingpreserving ſeruantsservants health, reſpectrespect muſtmust be had to their Food, Clothing, Labour, ReſtRest.

A due prouiſionprovision of food for ſeruantsservants is commended in Solomons Sufficient food to be allowed to ſeruantsservants. Pro. 31. 15. & 27. 27. good houſehouse-wife, who giuethgiveth meat to her houſholdhousehold. And in the direction which he giuethgiveth to houſholdershouseholdershousholders, in theſethese words, Let the milkemilk of thy goats be ſufficientsufficient for thy food, and for the food of thy family.

The food which maſtersmasters prouideprovide for their ſeruantsservants muſtmust be
for qualitiequality, good and wholeſomewholesome; for quantitiequantity, ſufficientsufficient to preſeruepreserve health and increaſeincrease ſtrengthstrength; for time, giuengiven in due ſeaſonseason. It is noted that the hired ſeruantsservants of the father of the Luk. 15. 17. prodigallprodigal childechild had bread (by bread according to the Scripture phraſephrase is meant all kindekind of needfullneedful wholſomewholesome food: in which ſenſesense it muſtmust needs be there taken, becauſebecause it is oppoſedopposed to huskeshusks, which are not very wholſomewholesome, fitter for ſwineswine then men) yea they had bread enough. It is further noted of that good ſtewardsteward who was, as a maſtermaster, ruler ouerover the houſholdhousehold, that Luk. 12. 42. he gauegave the houſholdhousehold their portion of meat in due ſeaſonseason.

div.head: QueſtQuest. May not ſeruantsservants be ſtintedstinted of their food?
div.p: AnſwAnsw. In regard of ſuperfluitiesuperfluity they may and ought to be ſtintedstinted, but not in regard of ſufficienciesufficiency. It is not meet that all ſeruantsservants ſhouldshould hauehave as much as they can deuouredevour: for then many of them would doedo but little workework: but moſtmost meet it is that eueryevery one ſhouldshould hauehave as much as is needfullneedful for ſtrengthstrength, that ſoso he may be the better able to doedo and endure his workework: the GreekeGreek word tranſlatedtranslated in the Luk. 12. 42. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 . place before quoted portion, implieth as much.
There is a double bond to tie maſtersmasters to performeperform this dutieduty: one in regard of themſeluesthemselves: the other in regard of their ſeruantsservants.

MaſtersMasters themſeluesthemselves ſhallshall hauehave the profit and benefit of the health and ſtrengthstrength of their ſeruantsservants: for their owneown ſakessakes therefore it is requiſiterequisite to afford them ſufficientsufficient food. Men that deſiredesire to hauehave their workework well done by their beaſtsbeasts, or in their iourneyjourney to be well carried to the end thereof, will be carefullcareful that their beaſtsbeasts ſhallshall be well fed.

But beſidebeside this, conſideringconsidering the health and ſtrengthstrength of ſeruantsservants is ſpentspent in their maſtersmasters buſineſſebusiness, iuſticejustice requireth that their health and ſtrengthstrength ſhouldshould be repaired and preſeruedpreserved by them.

div.head: §. 24. Of defect and exceſſeexcess in allowing ſeruantsservants food.
div.p:
There are two extremes contrary to this dutieduty. One of thoſethose that are too niggardly, and (as we ſpeakespeak) miſerablemiserable in the allowance of food to their ſeruantsservants: and that ſometimessometimes in the quantitiequantity, when ſeruantsservants bellies are too much pinched: eueneven ſoso as their bodies are weaknedweakened for want of food. The ProdigallProdigal
childechild was thus ſeruedserved: theſethese are both vniuſtunjust and iniuriousinjurious Luk. 15. 16. maſtersmasters: vniuſtunjust to their ſeruantsservants: iniuriousinjurious to their ſeruantsservants, and themſeluesthemselves too. Sometimes againeagain ſuchsuch miſerablemiserable maſtersmasters offend in the qualitiequality of that food which they giuegive to their ſeruantsservants, as when it is kept too long, and grownegrown muſtymusty, mouldy, or otherwiſeotherwise vnſauouryunsavoury: or when the worſtworst kindekind of food, for cheapneſſecheapness ſakesake, is bought, eueneven ſuchsuch as is ſcarcescarce fit for mans meat: the more abundance that there is of ſuchsuch ſtuffestuff, the more loathſomeloathsome it is.

LaſtlyLastly, though I thinkethink it not meet to bindebind maſtersmasters vntounto ſetset houreshours for their ſeruantsservants mealesmeals (ChriſtChrist affordeth a greater Luk. 17. 7, &etcc. libertieliberty vntounto maſtersmasters, in the parable of a maſtersmasters vſageusage of his ſeruantservant after he came from his workework) yet there may be a fault, as there is, in many maſtersmasters, in keeping their ſeruantsservants too long from meat, not ſufferingsuffering them to interrupt their workework for meat ſakesake, but to tarry for their ſuppersupper till ten a clockeclock at night, when they giuegive ouerover workework: ſurelysurely this cannot be good for the bodies health and ſtrengthstrength.

Another extreme doedo ſuchsuch maſtersmasters fall into, as bring vpup their
Pro. 29. 21. ſeruantsservants too delicatlydelicately. Solomon hath expreſlyexpressly taxed ſuchsuch, and noteth that this miſchiefemischief is like to follow thereupon, he ſhallshall hauehave him become his ſonneson at the length: ſuchsuch a ſeruantservant will forget his place, ſcornescorn to be as a ſeruantservant, but aſpireaspire to be as his maſtersmasters childechild, which is next to a maſtersmasters mate.

div.head: §. 25. Of maſtersmasters care about their ſeruantsservants apparellapparel.
div.p:
A wiſewise care for ſeruantsservants cloathingclothing is alſoalso commended in the example of Solomons good houſewifehousewife, She is not afraid of the ſnowsnow for her houſholdhousehold, that is, for the coldeſtcoldest ſeaſonseason in winter, for all her houſholdhousehold are clothed with
Pro. 31. 21. 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉
double garments: that is, with ſuchsuch clothing as is fit for cold weather.

Fit and decent apparellapparel is both a meanesmeans of preſeruingpreserving health, and alſoalso a matter of good report, tending to the credit of a maſtermaster. Yet contrary is the humour of many: they care not how tagged and ragged their ſeruantsservants apparellapparel is: inſomuchinsomuch as many ſeruantsservants hauehave neither comely nor warmewarm apparellapparel.

The Hebrew word is oft vſedused for ſcarletscarlet. But according to the proper notation of it, it ſignifiethsignifieth things doubled: which I take to be moſtmost pertinent to this place, and therefore I hauehave ſoso tranſlatedtranslated it. The Kings tranſlatorstranslators hauehave noted as much in the margin.

This point concerneth thoſethose maſtersmasters eſpeciallyespecially that findefind their ſeruantsservants (as we ſpeakespeak) and prouideprovide all things for them: as in old time maſtersmasters did for moſtmost ſeruantsservants, and as now they doedo for prentiſesprentices whether male or female. If ſeruantsservants by couenantcovenant be at their owneown finding for apparellapparel, maſtersmasters are not ſoso ſtrictlystrictly bound therein: yet they muſtmust hauehave a care that their ſeruantsservants fall neither into the one extreme of too baſebase, ſlouensloven-like, or ſluttiſhsluttish apparellapparel, nor into the other of too gariſhgarish, or too coſtlycostly apparellapparel. MaſtersMasters hauinghaving authority ouerover their ſeruantsservants, muſtmust keepekeep them in order and good compaſſecompass, and hauehave reſpectrespect to decenciedecency in this as in other things. For apparellapparel is one of thoſethose outward ſignessigns whereby the wiſdomewisdom of maſtersmasters and miſtreſſesmistresses in well gouerninggoverning their ſeruantsservants is manifeſtedmanifested to the world. If therefore ſeruantsservants be attired vnſeemlyunseemly for their place and abilitieability, all that ſeesee them will thinkethink their maſtersmasters and miſtreſſesmistresses are of ſuchsuch a mindemind as the ſeruantsservants are, or at leaſtleast too remiſſeremiss and careleſſecareless of their gouernmentgovernment.

div.head: §. 26. Of moderating ſeruantsservants labour.
div.p: Though labour and painespains be proper to a ſeruantsservants place, yet he may be ſoso put vntounto it, as the health and ſtrengthstrength of his body may be impaired thereby. For the well ordering of this therefore a dutieduty lieth vponupon maſtersmasters: and that in two things eſpeciallyespecially.

1. That they well moderate the labour whereunto they put their ſeruantsservants, ſoso as they may be able for the time to vndergoeundergo it, and to endure ſoso long as their time of labour is appointed. It was a good reaſonreason which Saul rendredrendered to keepekeep DauidDavid from 1 Sam. 17. 33. entringentering combat with Goliah, becauſebecause (as he thought) DauidDavid was not able to fight againſtagainst the PhiliſtimPhilistim, DauidDavid being a youth, and Goliah a man of warrewar.
And indeed if DauidsDavid's faith had not exceeded the ſtrengthstrength of his body, it had beenebeen vnmeetunmeet to hauehave put DauidDavid to that tasketask.
They which are put to things aboueabove their abilitieability, are like to failefail, and ſinkesink vnderunder the burden of them.

It is contrary hereunto to put ſeruantsservants to ſuchsuch hard taskestasks
as impaireimpair their ſtrengthstrength, endanger their limslimbs, and venture their liueslives. Saul ſhallshall riſerise vpup in iudgementjudgment againſtagainst ſuchsuch: for he ſuppoſingsupposing that it was too hard a tasketask for DauidDavid to vndertakeundertake combat with Goliah, was loth to put him to it. DauidDavid exceedingly 1 Sam. 17. 33. failed herein, when he gauegave direction that VriahUriah ſhouldshould be ſetset in the forefront of the hotteſthottest battellbattle, and yet the Generallgeneral 2 Sam. 11. 15, with his ſtrengthstrength to retire from him. Many ſeruantsservants being put to ſeruicesservices aboueabove their ſtrengthstrength, either loſelose their liueslives thereby, or (as we ſpeakespeak) are neuernever their owneown men againeagain.

It is alſoalso a fault in this kindekind, to put ſeruantsservants to ſuchsuch toiling Memineris ſeruosseruos homines eſſeesse. Cato. Exo. 1. 13, 14. workesworks as are fitter for beaſtsbeasts then men: or to oppreſſeoppress them with too much workework, as the Egyptians oppreſſedoppressed the IſraelitesIsraelites. Let Gods hearing the cry of thoſethose ſeruantsservants ſoso oppreſſedoppressed, and reuengingrevenging their oppreſſorsoppressors for it, make all maſtersmasters take heed & 3. 7. of the like crueltiecruelty.

div.head: §. 27. Of affording ſeruantsservants fit meanesmeans for their workework.
div.p: 2. The other thing required of maſtersmasters for welwell ordering their ſeruantsservants workework is, that they afford their ſeruantsservants things needfullneedful, and behouefullbehoveful for that workework whereunto they are put: which mindemind was commendable in Saul, who aſſaiedassayedassaied if his 1 Sam. 17. 38. armour might be fit for DauidDavid when he was to goego againſtagainst Goliah. To reckon vpup all the particulars were an infinite tasketask: eueryevery ſeuerallseveral trade and workework hath proper meanesmeans of helpehelp appertaining to it: this generallgeneral direction may be ſufficientsufficient to mouemove maſtersmasters to applieapply it to the particular workesworks and ſeruicesservices whereunto they put their ſeruantsservants. Fit meanesmeans are ſuchsuch an helpehelp, as that which with them may eaſilyeasily be done, without them can hardly, if poſſiblypossibly at all be done.

It is contrary hereunto to dealedeal with ſeruantsservants as the Egyptians did with the IſraelitesIsraelites, exacting workework at their hands, and Exo. 5. 7. not affording them meanesmeans to doedo it: whereby many times they exact impoſſibilitiesimpossibilities. Some will hauehave much workework done in the night time, and not afford candle light: ſoso in other particulars.

div.head: §. 28. Of affording ſeaſonableseasonable reſtrest to ſeruantsservants.
div.p:
IntermiſſionIntermission, eaſeease, and reſtrest from labour at ſeaſonableseasonable times, is as needfullneedful and requiſiterequisite, as food and apparellapparel. The reaſonreason which God rendrethrendereth of the fourth commandementcommandment ſhewethshoweth
that maſtersmasters ought to afford reſtrest to their ſeruantsservants: it is this, that
Deut. 5. 14. thy ſeruantservant may reſtrest.

Without intermiſſionintermission and reſtrest the body cannot endure labour: it will wax weakeweak, faint, and vtterlyutterly vnableunable to continue: but, as labour decaiethdecayeth ſtrengthstrength, ſoso reſtrest repaireth it.

There are two eſpeciallespecial times of reſtrest, which ſeruantsservants may not be denied.
1. The reſtrest of the night.
2. The reſtrest of the Lords day.

The firſtfirst is ordinary for all liuingliving creatures: for it was one SeruantsServants muſtmust reſtrest in the night time. principallprincipal -reaſonreason why God cauſedcaused the light of the SunneSun to be withdrawenwithdrawn from the face of the earth, that the inhabitants thereof might reſtrest from their labour. VntillUntil the eueningevening man PſalPsal. 104. 23. goeth forth vntounto his labour and workework. Time of darkneſſedarkness is more fit for reſtrest then workework. Let not this be ſoso taken as if no workework were to be done, after the light of the day is taken away: (then would but little workework be done in the depth of winter, when the daiesdays are ſhortshort: and then would not God hauehave afforded artificiallartificial lights) but to ſhewshow that difference muſtmust be made betwixt the day and night: and that the night is afforded for that time wherein men are moſtmost to reſtrest.

The other time of reſtrest (being the Sabbath day) is by diuinedivine SeruantsServants muſtmust reſtrest on the Lords day. Gen. 2. 3. inſtitutioninstitution. It was ſanctifiedsanctified vntounto man in the time of AdamsAdam's innocency, when he ſtoodstood as a publikepublic head and ſtockestock of all mankindemankind. The very name Sabbath, (which in Hebrew ſignifiethsignifieth reſtrest) and the expreſſeexpress prohibition of doing any workework on that day, doedo ſhewshow that it is a day of reſtrest: and that one end thereof was for ſeruantsservants to reſtrest therein, is euidentevident by the reaſonreason thereof, that thy ſeruantservant may reſtrest. So as there is a double bond to tie maſtersmasters to afford reſtrest to their ſeruantsservants on the Lords day:
1. The bond of piety to God.
2. The bond of charity to ſeruantsservants: for in that God did thinkethink it meet for ſeruantsservants to reſtrest one day in ſeuenseven, we ought to MaſtersMasters who afford not time enough of ſleepesleep to ſeruantsservants offend. thinkethink that it is needfullneedful and behouefullbehoveful for them.

div.head: §. 29. Of denying ſeaſonableseasonable reſtrest to ſeruantsservants.
div.p:
Contrary to both the forenamed times of reſtrest doedo many maſtersmasters offend: as firſtfirst, they who make their ſeruantsservants watch
too long at night, and againeagain, riſerise too ſoonesoon in the morning, not affording ſoso much time of reſtrest and ſleepesleep as is needfullneedful for refreſhingrefreshing their bodies, and repairing their ſtrengthstrength: whereby it commethcometh to paſſepass that (beſidebeside the wrong done to their poorepoor ſeruantsservants) their workework cannot be done ſoso well.

div.head:
ObiectObject. It is ſaidsaid of the forenamed good houſwifehousewifehouswife, that her
Pro. 31. 18. candle is not put out by night.
div.p:
AnſwAnsw. That is a tropicalltropical ſpeechspeech: and ſomesome-what hyperbolicallhyperbolical. The word night is put for a part thereof. The phraſephrase only implieth vigilancy, ſhewingshowing that ſheshe is not, as many, in the eueningevening betimes in bed, and in the morning late vpup; but late downedown and early vpup. This phraſephrase (ſheshe riſethriseth while it is yet night)
VerſVers. 15. vſedused before, ſhewethshoweth that that which I hauehave noted, is the true ſenſesense. If not putting out her candle by night, ſhouldshould imply a ſittingsitting vpup all night long, how could it be ſaidsaid that ſheshe riſethriseth vpup?

div.head: QueſtQuest. What time may be thought ſufficientsufficient to afford ſleepesleep How long time for ſleepesleep to be allowed. vntounto ſeruantsservants?
div.p: AnſwAnsw. As the ſamesame quantity of food is not ouerover-ſtrictlystrictly to be proportioned to all alike, ſoso nor the ſamesame continuance of ſleepesleep. Yet by experience it hath beenebeen obſeruedobserved that for ſoundsound and healthy bodies, fiuefive houreshours is the leaſtleast time that may be allowed, and ſeuenseven houreshours is time ſufficientsufficient for any.

div.head: §. 30. Of maſtersmasters offence in keeping ſeruantsservants from the reſtrest of the Lords day.
div.p: 2. AgainſtAgainst the reſtrest of the Lords day, doedo too too many maſtersmasters offend: as
1. By keeping ſeruantsservants at their ordinary workework on that day.
2. By ſendingsending them vpup and downedown on that day on many errands, as to gather vpup debts, or to doedo ſuchsuch other ſeruicesservices as they are loth to afford time for on other daiesdays.

3. By making that the greateſtgreatest day of painespains and labour, namely to ſuchsuch as are in the kitchinkitchen, or hauehave any other buſineſſebusiness about feaſtsfeasts: for the Lords day is by many ordinarily made a day of feaſtingfeasting.

44. By keeping them vpup too late on Saturday nights: eueneven till one of the clockeclock. Many that make ſomesome conſcienceconscience of the Lords day vſeuse to offend herein: for that their ſeruantsservants might
not workework on that day, they keepekeep them vpup till the very moment that they thinkethink the Sabbath beginnethbeginnethbegineth: but herein they commit a double fault: one in not allowing their ſeruantsservants ſufficientsufficient time of reſtrest: another in making them vnfitunfit through want of ſleepesleep to doedo the holy ſeruicesservices of the Lords day.

div.head: §. 31. Of allowing time of recreation to ſeruantsservants.
div.p: Concerning times of recreation, I may ſaysay as the ApoſtleApostle doth in another caſecase, I hauehave no commandementcommandment of the Lord, 1 Cor. 7. 25. namely expreſſeexpress commandementcommandment to preſſepress vponupon the conſcienceconscience of maſtersmasters any ſetset time for recreation: yet queſtionleſſequestionless it is very meet that ſeruantsservants ſhouldshould hauehave ſomesome times to refreſhrefresh themſeluesthemselves this way: for recreation rightly vſedused is a great meanesmeans to put life, and addeadd ſpiritspirit, to youth eſpeciallyespecially. With workework and buſineſſebusiness not only mens bodies, but their mindesminds alſoalso are occupied and imployedemployed: herein the labour and trauelltravel of men differeth from the labour of beaſtsbeasts: for refreſhingrefreshing therefore both of body and mindemind is good and moderate recreation needfullneedful. But I referrerefer this point to the wiſewise conſiderationconsideration of maſtersmasters themſeluesthemselves, who may better by their owneown obſeruationobservation diſcernediscern what in this kindekind is fitteſtfittest, then we preſcribeprescribe.

div.head: §. 32. Of maſtersmasters care ouerover their ſeruantsservants in ſickneſſesickness, and after death.
div.p: MaſtersMasters prouidentprovident care for the good of their ſeruantsservants is not to be reſtrainedrestrained to the time of their health, but to the time of their ſickneſſesickness alſoalso, if it pleaſeplease God to viſitvisit them while they are in ſeruiceservice. Wherefore all things needfullneedful are in this caſecase to be prouidedprovided for them by their maſtermaster. FirſtFirst ſpirituallspiritual comfort for their ſoulesoul, that ſoso they may the better bearebear their infirmity: then ſuchsuch things as may for the preſentpresent giuegive them eaſeease and refreſhingrefreshing, and alſoalso, if it pleaſeplease God to addeadd his bleſſingblessing, workework a recoueryrecovery. The care of the Centurion for his ſickesick ſeruantservant is Matt. 8. 6. in Scripture commended: he did as much for his ſeruantservant as he could hauehave done for his ſonneson: The King of Arams care alſoalso 2 King. 5. 6. was in this kindekind commendable: he did not forbeareforbear to write to his enemieenemy, and to make himſelfehimself beholding to him, in the behalfebehalf of his ſeruantservant that was leprous.

If the ſeruantservant hauehave beenebeen formerly a faithfullfaithful, diligent, and ReaſonsReasons. 1. RecompenceRecompense. profitable ſeruantservant, recompencerecompense requireth as much. For it is
a moſtmost vnkindeunkind, and inhumane part to deniedeny that ſeruantservant ſuccoursuccour in ſickneſſesickness, who in health hath beenebeen profitable to his maſtermaster.

But if a maſtermaster be carefullcareful of his ſickesick ſeruantservant, affording vntounto 2. Future benefit. him the beſtbest meanesmeans he can for his eaſeease, and recoueryrecovery, and that ſeruantservant, through Gods bleſſingblessing vponupon the meanesmeans, recouerrecover, he will, if he hauehave any ſparkespark of goodneſſegoodness in him, hold himſelfehimself ſoso obliged to his maſtermaster, as he ſhallshall neuernever be able to make ſufficientsufficient recompencerecompense: and thereupon be mouedmoved to vſeuse all the diligence he can for his maſtersmasters good: ſoso that a maſtermaster may reapebenefitreap benefit to himſelfehimself by this kindekind of kindneſſekindness.

But though the ſeruantservant that is ſickesick hauehave in former time 3. Charity. beenebeen vnprofitableunprofitable, and there be little hope of future benefit by him, yet for charity ſakesake, and in ſubiectionsubjection to Gods diſpoſingdisposing prouidenceprovidence, whereby that ſeruantservant is fallen ſickesick in his maſtersmasters houſehouse, muſtmust he in that caſecase be well looked vntounto. If the Samaritan Luke 10. 33, 34. did well in taking care of a meeremere ſtrangerstranger out of his houſehouse, becauſebecause he ſawsaw him ſuccourleſſesuccourless, ſurelysurely that maſtermaster which neglecteth his ſeruantservant that is ſickesick in his houſehouse, doth very ill.

div.head: 1. QueſtQuest. What if he be not a couenantedcovenanted ſeruantservant for a ſetset time, but a IourneyJourney-man at will, or one that worketh by the day or weekeweek?
div.p: AnſwAnsw. Though a maſtermaster be not ſoso much bound to ſuchsuch an one, yet if he fall ſickesick in his houſehouse, he may not in that caſecase thruſtthrust him out of dooresdoors, vnleſſeunless he know where he may be welwell prouidedprovided for.

div.head: 2. QueſtQuest. What if a maſtermaster be poorepoor, and not able to prouideprovide that which is requiſiterequisite for a ſickesick perſonperson?
div.p: AnſwAnsw. If the ſickesick perſonperson hauehave friends and kindred that are better able, they muſtmust prouideprovide for him: if not, the Church muſtmust helpehelp: but it is the maſtersmasters duty, to make the ſickesick mans caſecase knowneknown to his friends, or to the Church.

If, after all good meanesmeans are vſedused for recoueryrecovery, the ſeruantservant SeruantsServants that die, to be decently buried. die, his maſtermaster muſtmust ſeesee the laſtlast duty in ſomesome ſeemelyseemly manner, performed for him, which is ChriſtianChristian buriallburial. Herein lieth a mainemain difference betwixt the vſageusage of mens bodies which after death ſhallshall be raiſedraised againeagain, and beaſtsbeasts that vtterlyutterly periſhperish.
IaakobsJacob's care of burying his mothers nurſenurse is expreſlyexpressly mentioned, Gen. 35. 8. in way of commendation.

div.head: §. 33. Of neglect of ſeruantsservants in ſickneſſesickness: and when they are dead.
div.p: Many maſtersmasters much offend in the contrary to the forenamed duties. For

1. Some, when they obſerueobserve their ſeruantsservants begin to be ſickesick, will put them out of their houſeshouses, and leaueleave them to ſhiftshift for themſeluesthemselves, as that cruellcruel Amalekite who left his ſickesick ſeruantservant 1 SamSam. 30. 13. abroad in the fields. But note the vengeance of God which followed thereupon: The leauingleaving of that ſickesick ſeruantservant in that caſecase was the occaſionoccasion of the deſtructiondestruction of that maſtermaster and all his company. By that meanesmeans they were diſcouereddiscovered to their enemies.

2. Others, when they cannot remoueremove their ſickesick ſeruantsservants out of their houſehouse, will ſuffersuffer them there to lie ſuccourleſſesuccourless, and to periſhperish for want of things needfullneedful. Many rich men that are able to prouideprovide well enough for them, will ſendsend them to ſomesome out, backeback roomeroom, and take no more care for them. In this kindekind many of them ſhewshow more kindneſſekindness to a doggedog, or other beaſtbeast that is not well, then to a ſeruantservant. An inhumane part.

3. Others, that ſeemeseem not ſoso inhumane, dealedeal too hardly with their ſeruantsservants in ſuchsuch a caſecase: they will afford them things needfullneedful, but all at the poorepoor ſeruantsservants coſtcost: and if thoſethose ſeruantsservants hauehave not preſentpresent money, they will cut it off their wages if they recouerrecover health to doedo them ſeruiceservice. Is this to vndoeundo the heauyheavy burdens? Or is it not to lay burden vponupon IſaIsa. 58. 6. burden?

4. Others, that are at ſomesome charges for their ſeruantsservants ſickneſſesickness, doedo ſoso mutter at their ſeruantsservants, and fling out ſuchsuch diſcontenteddiscontented ſpeechesspeeches (namely, that they tooketook them for their workework, and not to keepekeep them in their bed: to get ſomesome thing by them, not to be at ſuchsuch coſtcost with them: or that they make themſeluesthemselves more ſickesick then needs: they may riſerise, if they will, (with many other like diſcontenteddiscontented ſpeechesspeeches) that the poorepoor ſickesick ſeruantsservants are more grieuedgrieved and troubled with their maſtersmasters diſcontentdiscontent, then with their ſickneſſesickness: and oft mouedmoved to
ſtriuestrive aboueabove their ſtrengthstrength to riſerise, eueneven when death is ſeaſingseizingseasing vponupon them, and ſoso haſtenhasten the approach of death.

5. Many that may be carefullcareful enough of the bodily eſtateestate of their ſeruantsservants in ſickneſſesickness, See. §. 21, 22. hauehave no reſpectrespect at all to the ſpirituallspiritual comfort of their ſoulessouls, they neither giuegive them a word of comfort themſeluesthemselves, nor ſendsend for miniſterminister or any other to doedo it: but let them in this reſpectrespect lie, and die as beaſtsbeasts. Of all points of vnmercifulneſſeunmercifulness this is the greateſtgreatest: and moſtmost vnbeſeemingunbeseeming ChriſtiansChristians.
6. Others, if their ſeruantsservants die, will ſcarcescarce afford them a winding ſheetsheet, but ſaysay, let any one that will, buriebury them for their clothes.
Notice is to be taken of theſethese in humaneinhumane cariagescarriages, that the deteſtationdetestation of them may make other maſtersmasters more tender hearted towards their ſeruantsservants.

div.head: §. 34. Of maſtersmasters prouidingproviding for the future eſtateestate of ſeruantsservants.
div.p: Next to the SouleSoul, and Body of ſeruantsservants, maſtersmasters muſtmust hauehave ſomesome care of their eſtateestate: and that not only to keepekeep them while they are in their ſeruiceservice, but alſoalso to endeuourendeavour and prouideprovide that they may liuelive of themſeluesthemselves, and doedo good to others. When ſhallshall I prouideprovide for mine owneown houſehouse? ſaithsaith IaakobJacob to his Gen. 30. 30. maſtermaster. Which expoſtulationexpostulation ſhewethshoweth that this is a maſtersmasters dutieduty.

Contrary is the mind of moſtmost maſtersmasters: for in entertaining ſeruantsservants they thinkethink of nothing but ſeruingserving their owneown turneturn. Whence it commethcometh to paſſepass that when maſtersmasters die many ſeruantsservants are put to very hard ſhiftsshifts. Some forced to beg, others mouedmoved to filch and ſtealesteal. Thus caterpillars are nouriſhednourished to annoy the common-wealth.

That I may not be thought to lay the care of parents on maſtersmasters, and to equallequal ſeruantsservants with children, I will note out fourefour particulars which will ſhewshow what manner of care and prouidenceprovidence it is that is here required of maſtersmasters in regard of their ſeruantsservants eſtateestate.
One is, that maſtersmasters accuſtomeaccustom their ſeruantsservants to painespains.
Another is, that they exerciſeexercise them in ſomesome vſefulluseful calling.
A third is, that they giuegive them ſufficientsufficient wages.
A fouthfourth is, that after ſufficientsufficient ſeruiceservice they ſuffersuffer them to prouideprovide for themſeluesthemselves.

div.head: §. 35. Of well imployingemploying ſeruantsservants.
div.p:
That charge which the maſtermaster gauegave to his ſeruantsservants when he was going abroad (occupieoccupy till I come) ſhewethshoweth that maſtersmasters Luk. 19. 13. muſtmust keepekeep their ſeruantsservants exerciſedexercised and imployedemployed about ſomesome buſineſſebusiness or other: which is alſoalso implied vnderunder this part of a good miſtreſſesmistresses commendation, ſheshe giuethgiveth a portion to her maidens,
Pro. 31. 15. meaning a portion of workework. As there is neuernever an idle member in a naturallnatural body, but eueryevery one is imploiedemployed, ſoso ſhouldshould it be in a family.

1. Thus ſeruantsservants being, while they are in ſubiectionsubjection, inured to painespains, they will be more induſtriousindustrious when they are of themſeluesthemselves: yea they will both more willingly vndergoeundergo, and more eaſilyeasily goego thorowthrough matters which require painespains and diligence. UſeUse maketh perfect.
2. Thus will maſtersmasters themſeluesthemselves, and others afterward receiuereceive the more profit, and greater benefit by them.

3. Thus will many temptations be auoidedavoided, and euilsevils preuentedprevented: continuallcontinual imploymentemployment to the corrupt nature of man is as a running ſtreamestream which carrieth away all the mud and filth in a brookebrook, ſoso as none ſetlethsettlethsetleth there.

It is contrary hereunto to harbour idle-packespacks in a mans Contrary. houſehouse: to giuegive meat, and drinkedrink, and lodging to ſuchsuch as doedo no workework at all. The ApoſtleApostle expreſlyexpressly commanded, That if 2 TheſThes. 3. 10. any man would not workework, neither ſhouldshould he eat.

TheſeThese are not only a prey to the deuilldevil, but alſoalso inſtrumentsinstruments of the deuilldevil, by which he worketh much miſchiefemischief: for theſethese are they that are moſtmost ready to diſcouerdiscover the ſecretssecrets of an houſehouse, to be tatlingtattling of eueryevery thing that is done, to ſortsort themſeluesthemselves with all companies, and not content to doedo no good themſeluesthemselves, diſturbedisturb, interrupt, and draw away ſuchsuch as are buſiebusy at their workework.

div.head: §. 36. Of exerciſingexercising ſeruantsservants to a calling.
div.p:
Though it be a good thing to keepekeep a ſeruantservant alwaiesalways occupied and imploiedemployed, yet for the benefit of the ſeruantservant it is further requiſiterequisite, that his imploymentemployment be about ſomesome ſetledsettled matter, whereabout he may alſoalso exerciſeexercise himſelfehimself when he is out
of ſeruiceservice. This eſpeciallyespecially concerneth ſuchsuch as hauehave taken MaſtersMasters muſtmust teach their prentiſesprentices their trade. prentiſesprentices. They muſtmust teach them their trade.
1. For that end are prentiſesprentices bound to maſtersmasters.
2. The couenantscovenants on the maſtersmasters part require as much.
3. The good which thence is like to come to the maſtermaster himſelfehimself, his prentiſeprentice, and others, will recompencerecompense the painespains.

Other ſeruantsservants alſoalso muſtmust be tied to a workework which may be a meanesmeans of maintenance: as in a great houſehouse, to offices about that houſehouse: in the country, to husbandry: in offices about the law, to ſomesome imploymentemployment therein; and ſoso in other callings.

It is contrary hereunto for maſtersmasters to enuyenvy their prentiſesprentices the myſteriemystery of their trade: to imployemploy them from time to time about meſſagesmessages, and errands, and ſuchsuch things as tend only to the maſtersmasters preſentpresent need, but cannot be profitable for the ſeruantsservants in time to come. TheſeThese are like old, grownegrown, broad trees, which keepekeep all the ſunſhinesunshine from the ſhrubsshrubs that grow vnderunder them, and ſoso keepekeep them downedown from growing.

ObiectObject. PrentiſesPrentices will be as iuyivy to the trees about which they cling, ſoonesoon ouerover-topping them, and foking all the life out of them: they will hinder their maſtersmasters trading, and get away all his cuſtomecustom, if they be too expert in his trade.

AnſwAnsw. 1. This is but a meeremere ſurmiſesurmise. It implieth that ſuchsuch maſtersmasters as fearefear that which is pretended, dealedeal not ſoso currently, and faithfully with their cuſtomerscustomers as they ſhouldshould; or elſeelse how could they ſurmiſesurmise that wiſewise chapmen would leaueleave one of whom they hauehave had long and good experience, to goego to a new beginner?

2. Daily experience ſhewethshoweth that God by his prouidenceprovidence ſoso ordereth mens affairesaffairs, that maſtersmasters who from time to time trainetrain vpup and ſendsend forth many prentiſesprentices well exerciſedexercised and skilfullskilful in their trade, doedo hold on, yea and increaſeincrease in their owneown dealings and gainegain which they get thereby; and yet withallwithal their prentiſesprentices alſoalso come well forward. Why ſhouldshould any maſtersmasters ſoso diſtruſtdistrust Gods prouidenceprovidence, as to be afraid to make their prentiſesprentices skilfullskilful in their trade?

3. When maſtersmasters by death or otherwiſeotherwise giuegive ouerover trading, how ſhallshall trades be continued, if maſtersmasters be ſoso enuiousenvious, and diſtruſtfulldistrustful? What if their maſtersmasters had ſoso dealt with them?
And what if all maſtersmasters ſhouldshould ſoso dealedeal? For what one doth in ſuchsuch a caſecase, he muſtmust preſuppoſepresuppose that all may doedo.

In this kindekind alſoalso doedo ſuchsuch miſtreſſesmistresses offend as keepekeep their maids many yearesyears together to drudgery workework, and neuernever teach them, nor afford them meanesmeans or leiſureleisure to learnelearn points of huſwiferyhousewiferyhuswifery, things whereby they may get better maintenance for themſeluesthemselves.

Such maſtersmasters and miſtreſſesmistresses vſeuse their ſeruantsservants as beaſtsbeasts, only for their owneown turneturn, without any reſpectrespect to the ſeruantsservants good: whereby they peruertpervert the mainemain end of that relation betwixt maſtermaster and ſeruantservant, which is a mutuallmutual and reciprocallreciprocal good to paſſepass from the one to the other.

div.head: §. 37. Of appointing to eueryevery ſeruantservant his particular function.
div.p: For the better exerciſingexercising of ſeruantsservants vntounto ſomesome calling, let theſethese Directions for fitting ſeruantsservants to ſomesome function. directions be noted.

1. That maſtersmasters appoint to their ſeruantsservants their proper and peculiar workework, that they may know what to doedo, and wherein to exerciſeexercise themſeluesthemselves. And if there be many ſeruantsservants in one houſehouse, to ſetset vntounto eueryevery one their diſtinctdistinct function. The phraſephrase before noted of the good miſtreſſemistress (ſheshe giuethgiveth a portion to her maidens)
Pro. 31. 15. prouethproveth thus much. This was one thing which the QueeneQueen of Sheba obſeruedobserved and admired in Solomons houſehouse, the ſtandingstanding of 1 King. 10. 5. his ſeruantsservants, namely, eueryevery one in his owneown place, at his owneown tasketask. To this purpoſepurpose it is noted, that the great maſtermaster gauegave to Matt. 25. 15. each of his ſeruantsservants their diſtinctdistinct talents. It is thus in the bodiebody naturallnatural: eueryevery member is not only imployedemployed, but alſoalso imployedemployed 1 Cor. 12. 8. &etcc. Quod plurimorum commune eſtest, in eo procurando minima diligentia adhibetur. Rerum enim propriarum maximam curam habent, communium autem minorem. AriſtArist. de Repub. l. 2. c. 3. in his owneown function: the eye in ſeeingseeing, the eareear in hearing, the foot in ſtandingstanding or going, and ſoso the reſtrest. It is thus alſoalso in ChriſtsChrists myſticallmystical bodiebody: one hath the ſpiritspirit of wiſdomewisdom, another of knowledge, another of faith, and ſoso in other gifts. Thus alſoalso ought it to be in a familiefamily where are many ſeruantsservants.

This is an eſpeciallespecial meanesmeans to make eueryevery one the more diligent and faithfullfaithful. For when eueryevery one hath his particular workework, they know, that they in particular are to giuegive an account thereof: ſoso as if it be not done, or ill done, they ſhallshall bearebear all the blame: if done, and well done, they ſhallshall hauehave all the praiſepraise.

2. Thus ſhallshall eueryevery one be made skilfullskilful and expert in ſomesome
thing, by continuallcontinual attending vponupon it, and exerciſingexercising themſeluesthemselves therein.

div.head: §. 38. Of diſorderdisorder in families through maſtersmasters negligence.
div.p: The great diſorderdisorder which is in many families is contrary hereunto: for there are many maſtersmasters that hauinghaving ſundrysundry ſeruantsservants doedo lookelook that all things ſhouldshould be well done, and yet appoint no particular place or workework to any one; but thinkethink and ſaysay, that eueryevery one ſhouldshould be forward to doedo eueryevery thing; and when they findefind Praeter alias cauſascausas eoſunteosunt in rebus communibus negligentiores, quod eus alijs curae eſſeesse exiſtimentexistiment: quemadmodum euenire ſoletsolet in miniſterijsministerijs ſervilibusservilibus. AriſtArist. loc. citat. not things done to their mindemind, they fret and fume, and complainecomplain that they keepekeep ſoso many ſeruantsservants, and yet nothing well done. Such ſeruantsservants are not free from all blame: but ſurelysurely the maſtersmasters hauehave greateſtgreatest cauſecause to complainecomplain of themſeluesthemselves, and of their owneown diſorderdisorder in gouerninggoverning. For their negligence in appointing no ſetset workework to their ſeruantsservants, is the cauſecause that all is neglected. For where many things to be done are left to many ſeruantsservants, one will put off this, and another that, and ſaysay it belongeth not to them. Thus is it verified, that what is ſpokenspoken to all is ſpokenspoken to none: and that generallgeneral charges, are no charges.

div.head: §. 39. Of maſtersmasters ouerſeeingoverseeing the wayesways of their ſeruantsservants.
div.p: The ſecondsecond direction is, that maſtersmasters vſeuse inſpectioninspection ouerover their ſeruantsservants, and hauehave an eye vponupon their ſeruantsservants, to ſeesee how they ſpendspend their time, and diſpatchdispatch the buſineſſebusiness committed to them. The good miſtreſſemistress looketh well to the wayesways of her houſholdhousehold. This Pro. 31. 27. Ruth 2. 4. is noted of BoozBoaz, that he went to his field to ſeesee what his reapers did.

The eye of a maſtermaster is a great motiuemotive to make a ſeruantservant diligent and faithfullfaithful: for thus he knoweth that both his diligence, and alſoalso his negligence ſhallshall be ſeeneseen, and accordingly dealt withallwithal. Hence aroſearose that prouerbeproverb, The eye of the maſtermaster maketh the horſehorse
Oculus Domini paſcitpascit equum. Matt. 24. 48. fat. The conceit which the euillevil ſeruantservant had that his maſtermaster delayed his commingcoming, and ſoso could not ſeesee what he did, made him ſoso vnfaithfullunfaithful as he was.

If a maſtersmasters place will bearebear it, it is behouefullbehoveful that he be preſentpresent with his ſeruantsservants, and as a good preſidentpresident goego before them. It is recorded of the good miſtreſſemistress, that ſheeshe riſethriseth and giuethgiveth a
Pro. 31. 13, 15. portion to her maids: ſheeshe is with them her ſelfeself; ſheeshe worketh willingly with her hands. This note of difference is put betwixt a prouidentprovident thriuingthriving maſtermaster, and a diſſolutedissolute careleſſecareless maſtermaster: This
man ſaithsaith to his ſeruantsservants, goego yeeye: but that man ſaithsaith, goego we; or thus, goego ſirssirs, and ga'w ſirssirs.

It is contrary hereunto to let all goego (as we ſpeakespeak) at ſixsix and Contrary, careleſneſſecarelessness. ſeuenssevens; and neuernever to ſeesee what ſeruantsservants doedo. How can ſuchsuch expect that their ſeruantsservants ſhouldshould be diligent in doing that which tendeth to their maſtersmasters good, when they themſeluesthemselves are negligent in ouerſeeingoverseeing that which tendeth to their owneown good? Such maſtersmasters as giuegive themſeluesthemselves to gaming, and following their paſtimespastimes all day long, doedo much offend herein. So alſoalso ſuchsuch miſtreſſesmistresses as ſpendspend all the morning in lying a bed and dreſſingdressing themſeluesthemselves (a cuſtomecustom cleaneclean contrary to that which is noted of the good miſtreſſemistress) ProuProv. 31. 15. and at noonenoon when they come out of their chamber, chide and brawlebrawl, becauſebecause things are not more forward.

div.head: §. 40. Of prouokingprovoking ſeruantsservants to their dutieduty both by fairefair and foulefoul meanesmeans.
div.p: The third direction is, that maſtersmasters vſeuse what meanesmeans they can to prouokeprovoke and ſtirrestir vpup their ſeruantsservants to be diligent and faithfullfaithful: as in the firſtfirst place, exhortation, admonition, perſwaſionpersuasion, promiſespromises of reward, with other like fairefair meanesmeans. Such were the meanesmeans which Saul vſedused to make his ſeruantsservants faithfullfaithful vntounto him, when he ſaidsaid, Will the ſonneson of IeſſeJesseJess giuegive eueryevery one of you fields, and vineyards, 1 Sam. 22. 7. &etcc. hadHad the thing which he expected from them beenebeen good, this manner of dealing with them had beenebeen commendable. But if fairefair meanesmeans preuaileprevail not, then they may and ought to See §. 13. rebuke, threaten, and correct their ſeruantsservants.

And if ſeruantsservants be impudent in ſinningsinning, and neither fairefair nor foulefoul meanesmeans will reclaimereclaim them, they muſtmust then be thruſtthrust out of dooresdoors. Note what the maſtermaster in the parable ſaidsaid to his ſeruantservant, Thou maiſtmaist be no longer ſtewardsteward: to which purpoſepurpose DauidDavid alſoalso Luke 16. 2. PſalPsal. 101. 7. ſaidsaid, He that worketh deceit ſhallshall not dwell within mine houſehouse: he that telleth lies ſhallshall not tarry in my ſightsight.

When IſmaelIsmael grew a ſcofferscoffer at Gods word, Abraham thruſtthrust Gen. 21. 9. &etcc. him and his mother out of dooresdoors, and that by Gods appointment. The parable of cutting downedown the fruitleſſefruitless figtree may fitly be applied to this point: and the reaſonreason alſoalso there rendredrendered (why comberethcumbereth it the ground?) Why ſhouldshould incorrigible ſeruantsservants Luke 13. 7. &etcc. take vpup the roomeroom of good ſeruantsservants? yeaYea why ſhouldshould they remaineremain to inſectinfectinsect and peruertpervert other ſeruantsservants?

div.head: ObiectObject.
div.p: This is ſoso farrefar from helping ſeruantsservants in their eſtateestate, as it may proueprove their vtterutter vndoingundoing.

AnſwAnsw. 1. They hauehave then none iuſtlyjustly to blame but themſeluesthemselves,. IuſticeJustice (in caſecase of neceſſitienecessity) muſtmust hauehave her courſecourse, though through the iniquitieiniquity of man ſomesome miſchiefemischief follow thereupon.
2. The execution of this on ſomesome, may make others better lookelook to themſeluesthemselves.
3. It may make them that are thruſtthrust out to be the more dutifulldutiful vnderunder another maſtermaster, or more diligent in another courſecourse of life.

Contrary is their courſecourse who obſerueobserve no courſecourse, or order A ſeruantservant is not for eueryevery offence to be thruſtthrust out of dooresdoors. in drawing on their ſeruantsservants to doedo their dutieduty, but begin with that which ſhouldshould be laſtlast: nay only vſeuse that remedy which ſhouldshould not be vſedused, vnleſſeunless no remedy will ſerueserve the turneturn, which is to turneturn their ſeruantsservants out of dooresdoors for eueryevery ſmallsmall occaſionoccasion. No inſtructioninstruction, perſwaſionpersuasion, admonition, rebuke, threatningthreatening is vſedused by many when their ſeruantsservants hauehave offended, but this thunderbolt caſtcast at them, be gone, get you out of dooresdoors. If this were taken notice of as a fault, longer might ſeruantsservants tarry in an houſehouse then ordinarily they doedo: and more good might maſtermaster and ſeruantservant reapereap one from another: yea and the ſecretssecrets of an houſehouse be better kept; for the oft chopping and changing of ſeruantsservants is it that maketh all things done priuatlyprivatelyprivatly in houſeshouses to be blazed vpup and downedown.

div.head: §. 41. Of paying ſeruantsservants their wages.
div.p: A third thing required of maſtersmasters in reſpectrespect of the eſtateestate of their ſeruantsservants, is to giuegive them their iuſtjust wages: eueneven this is included vnderunder that generallgeneral precept, Rom. 13. 7. render to all their dues: and more particularly expreſſedexpressed in the example of Matt. 20. 8. that maſtermaster who hired labourers into his vineyard and at the end of their workework gauegave them eueryevery one their wages: yea there is an expreſſeexpress Deut. 24. 15. law to this purpoſepurpose.

div.head: ObiectObject.
div.p: TheſeThese places concerneconcern labourers hired by the day.

AnſwAnsw. SeruantsServantsservants are in the ſamesame rankerank: and the ground for both is the ſamesame: for both workework for wages. Yea the argument will more ſtronglystrongly follow from the leſſeless to the greater thus, If a labourer and ſeruantservant for a day muſtmust hauehave his wages
iuſtlyjustly paid, much rather a ſeruantservant, and labourer for a yeereyear and yeeresyears.

1. A maſtersmasters couenantcovenant requireth as much: if there were no other bond, yet that bond whereby he voluntarily bindeth himſelfehimself, tyethtieth him in conſciencconscienceconscienc thereto. Among the fruits of the Spirit Gal. 5. 22. S. Paul reckoneth Faith, meaning thereby fidelitiefidelity in keeping promiſepromise and couenantcovenant.

2. Common equitieequity and iuſticejustice requireth as much: for wages is as due for labour, as money for wares. ChriſtChrist taketh it for an vndeniableundeniable principle, that Luke 10. 7. the labourer is worthy of his hire: ſoso alſoalso doth 1 Tim. 5. 18. the ApoſtleApostle.
This dutieduty is to be performed to ſuchsuch as are hired for wages: of them that are found all things by their maſtermaster, I ſpakespake §. 23, 25. before.
In giuinggiving ſeruantsservants their wages theſethese three things are to be Direction for giuinggiving wages. obſeruedobserved.

1. That there be a ſufficientsufficient competency of wages allowed: eueneven ſoso much at leaſtleast as may ſerueserve to prouideprovide ſuchsuch neceſſariesnecessaries as are fit for a ſeruantservant: for there is great reaſonreason, that he that worketh ſhouldshould liuelive of his workework.

2. That it be giuengiven in due ſeaſonseason. Leu. 19. 13. Deut. 24. 15. God would not hauehave the labourers hire be vnpaidunpaid one night after it was due. The time couenantedcovenanted by a ſeruantservant for his wages, is the ſeaſonableseasonable time: then he expecteth it: to that time he putteth his occaſionsoccasions of vſingusing it: at that time therefore it ought to be giuengiven him.
3. That it be paid to the full, according to the couenantcovenant: the maſtersmasters promiſepromise, and the ſeruantsservants need require as much.

div.head: §. 42. Of maſtersmasters iniuſticeinjustice about their ſeruantsservants wages.
div.p: IniuſticeInjustice contrary to the forenamed dutieduty of due paying their ſeruantsservants wages is many waiesways committed.
1. When maſtersmasters doedo altogether detainedetain their ſeruantsservants wages: Deut. 24. 15. Jam. 5. 4. this is a crying ſinnesin, which entrethentereth into the earesears of God.

2. When they make their ſeruantsservants askeask for their wages againeagain and againeagain, eueneven till they be aſhamedashamed: yea to ſtaystay and wait for it till they be forced to ſighsigh vntounto God: or elſeelse to filch and ſtealesteal to ſupplysupply their neceſſitiesnecessities: though theſethese maſtersmasters
